en: Salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Salutations to Sarasvatī.
Now begins the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Therein, first, the preceding section known as the Karmakāṇḍa is commenced:
Om! Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then proclaim the Jaya. (GarP Mangala 1)

Oṃ! I bow to that one Hari, who is unborn, undecaying, infinite, whose nature is knowledge, the Great One, auspicious, stainless, and beginningless; who is devoid of a body composed of elements and the like, free from all sense organs, abiding within all beings, pure, free from illusion, and all-pervading. GarP_1,1.1 //
I perpetually pay homage with my mind, speech, and actions to Hari, Rudra, Brahmā, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and the Goddess Sarasvatī.
To the charioteer Sūta, a knower of the Purāṇas, peaceful, proficient in all the scriptures,
a devotee of Viṣṇu, and a great-souled one who had arrived at the Naimiṣa forest.
While the sinless sage was seated upon an auspicious seat in the course of his pilgrimage, they worshipped and praised that poet as he meditated upon Viṣṇu.
The highly fortunate Śaunaka and others, the ascetics of Naimiṣa whose wealth is their penance,
were sages radiant as the sun, tranquil, and devoted to sacrifice.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, you know everything; therefore we ask you this:
among the deities, who indeed is the god who is the Lord, and who is truly worthy of worship?"
Who is to be meditated upon? Who is the creator of the world, and who protects and destroys it?
From what does dharma proceed, and who is remembered as the slayer of the wicked?
What is the form of that god? How is the creation of the world considered by him?
By what vows is he pleased, or by what yoga is he attained?
Who are his incarnations, and how did the origin of his lineage and so forth come about? Who is the protector of the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life, and who is their instigator?
O Sūta of great intelligence, tell us all of this and whatever else there is;
relate to us all the supreme accounts concerning Nārāyaṇa.
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, the essence which rests upon the narrations of Viṣṇu;
it was spoken by Garuḍa to Kaśyapa in ancient times, and heard by me from Vyāsa.
The one god Nārāyaṇa is the Lord of the lords of gods;
he is the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, from whom the birth and so forth of this universe proceed.
For the sake of protecting the world, Vāsudeva— the unborn, undecaying, and immortal—
manifests incarnations in the form of Kumāra and others.
O Brahmin, that Lord Hari, having first established the Kaumāra creation, practiced the difficult vow of unbroken celibacy.
But for the second time, the Lord of Sacrifice assumes the form of a boar, intending to uplift the earth that has sunk into the netherworld for the sake of this world's continued existence.
In the third creation, that of the sages, having attained the status of a divine sage (devarṣi),
he expounded the Sātvata system, since therein the cessation of ritual actions is achieved through action itself.
Having become Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Hari performed austerities in the fourth [age] for the sake of protecting Dharma; he was worshipped by both gods and demons.
The fifth, the lord of perfected beings named Kapila, proclaimed to Sūri the Sāṅkhya, which determines the collection of principles and is not corrupted by time.
Datta, the sixth son of Atri, was obtained by Anasūyā;
he taught the science of logic (ānvīkṣikī) to Alarka, Prahlāda, and others.
Then, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, after Yajña had performed sacrifices with the hosts of gods beginning with Sutrāman, seven [sons] were born to Ruci through Ākūti.
In the eighth [incarnation], Urukrama was born to Nābhi from Merudevī,
demonstrating the path for women that is honored by all stages of life.
Entreated by the sages, he assumed a ninth earthly form;
by means of the great medicinal herbs milked from him, O brahmins, the subjects were restored to life.
During the dissolution at the end of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, he assumed the form of a fish and,
having placed Vaivasvata Manu upon a boat made of earth, rescued him.
In his eleventh incarnation, the Lord, assuming the form of a tortoise, supported on his back Mount Mandara as the gods and demons churned the ocean.
The twelfth was Dhānvantara, and the thirteenth was indeed Āpyāyan;
he deluded the other gods with the enchanting woman Mohinī.
In the fourteenth [incarnation], as the Nārasiṃha Caitya,
he tore apart the powerful lord of the Daityas with his fierce claws, just as one might crush a reed with the edge of a sword.
On the fifteenth day, having become a dwarf, he went to the sacrifice of Bali,
requesting three paces of land while intending to reclaim the triple heaven.
In his sixteenth incarnation, seeing kings who were enemies of Brahman,
he became enraged and thrice seven times rid the earth of the Kṣatriya caste.
Then, in the seventeenth [generation], he was born to Satyavatī from Parāśara;
seeing that men were of diminished intellect, he fashioned the branches of the tree of the Veda.
Having attained the status of a god among men with the desire to accomplish the work of the gods,
he thereafter performed deeds such as the subduing of the ocean.
Having taken birth among the Vṛṣṇis in the nineteenth and twentieth [incarnations],
the Blessed One, as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, removed the burden of the earth.
Then, at the end of the twilight of the Kali age, for the sake of deluding the enemies of the gods,
a son of the Jina named Buddha will appear among the Kīkaṭas.
Then, at the eighth twilight, when the kings have almost perished,
Viṣṇuyaśas shall become the Lord of the World by the name of Kalki.
O twice-born ones, the incarnations of Hari, the treasury of beings, are indeed innumerable;
for all the ancient knowers of the Manu-veda are remembered as portions (kalā) of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, the creation and other [cosmic phases] have arisen and are to be honored through vows and other rites;
Vyāsa previously told this Purāṇa, the Gāruḍa, to me.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Cause for the Manifestation of this Purāṇa," in the Karmakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The Sages said:
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—2.
The Sages said:
How was the Gāruḍa Purāṇa told to you by Vyāsa in the past?
Tell me all of this in its entirety, for it is supremely based upon the narrative of Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:
"Indeed, I went to Badarikāśrama together with the sages;
there I saw Vyāsa meditating upon the Supreme Lord."
Having bowed to him, I sat down and questioned the Lord of Sages.
Sūta said:
"O Vyāsa, tell me now of the form of Hari and the creation of the universe and so forth."
"I think you meditate upon him, and therefore you know that all-pervading Lord.
O brahmins, listen to how he spoke when thus questioned.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O Sūta; I shall proclaim to you the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, just as Brahmā spoke it to me in the presence of Nārada, Dakṣa, and others.
Sūta said: How did Brahmā speak to you— joined by Dakṣa, Nārada, and other leaders— regarding the meritorious Śrī-Gāruḍa Purāṇa, which expresses the essential truth?
Vyāsa said:
Having prostrated before Brahmā, who had gone to the world of Brahmā, I, Nārada, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, and others asked him, "Tell us the essence. 1.2.7.
Brahmā said: O Vyāsa, just as Viṣṇu spoke to me, along with the gods, regarding the essence of the Purāṇas— the Gāruḍa and the Rudra— I shall speak it to you.
Vyāsa said:
O Brahmin, tell me how Hari formerly spoke with the gods regarding Rudra; speak of that ancient essence of the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, which is of great significance.
Brahmā said:
I went to Mount Kailāsa together with Indra and the other deities;
there I beheld Rudra meditating upon the supreme state.
"Having been questioned and saluted, [he said: 'O Śaṅkara, whom do you meditate upon as the god?
I know no supreme god other than you; therefore, tell me.'"
Desiring to hear the reality that is the most essential of all essentials, Rudra, together with the gods, said:
"I meditate upon that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, the Lord."
He is the giver of all, the all-pervading, the All, residing in the hearts of all living beings;
his body is smeared with ashes and adorned with a mass of matted locks.
"O Grandfather, for the sake of propitiating Viṣṇu, I am engaged in the practice of vows;
let us go to him and ask about that very essence which I am contemplating. (GarP 1.2.14)
Viṣṇu, the Victorious, the Lotus-navelled, Hari, who is devoid of body;
the Pure One, seated in purity, the Swan, that supreme state, the Supreme Lord.
With my whole being, I meditate upon that God as the Self, in whom all beings abide and into whom they enter. (GarP 1.2.16)
In the Lord of Beings, all qualities reside like clusters of gems upon a thread;
he who has a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, a thousand thighs, and a beautiful face.
The most minute among the minute, the largest among the large,
the heaviest among the heavy, and the best even among the excellent.
Him who performs true actions, the Truth itself among truths, whom they praise in the *vākyas*, the *anuvākyas*, the *niṣads*, and the *upaniṣads*, and in the *sāmans*.
He is declared the Ancient Puruṣa; he is declared Brahmā among the twice-born;
at the time of dissolution, he is declared Saṅkarṣaṇa—we worship him who is worthy of worship.
In which these worlds quiver like birds upon the water—
that single-syllabled Brahman, the Truth (Ṛta), which is beyond both being and non-being.
The gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas worship him,
whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is space, and whose feet are the earth.
I meditate upon that God whose eyes are the moon and the sun,
within whose belly are the three worlds, and whose arms are the cardinal directions.
I meditate upon that God whose breath is the wind,
in whose hair are the clouds, and in the joints of whose limbs are all the rivers.
Within his belly are the four oceans; I meditate upon that God who is beyond time, beyond sacrifice, and beyond both being and non-being.
I meditate upon that God who is the beginningless origin of the universe,
for whom the moon is the mind and the sun is the eye.
Fire was born from his mouth; I meditate upon that god, from whose feet the earth arose and from whose two ears the directions likewise emerged.
I meditate upon that God whose summit reaches to heaven;
[I contemplate] the primary creation, the secondary creation, the genealogies, and the periods of the Manus.
Since I am contemplating that god who is the history of the lineage,
I shall go forth from this [place] to perceive the essential core of what I meditate upon.
Brahmā said:
Having been addressed thus in the past, I, along with the gods, praised and bowed down to that Viṣṇu who dwells in Śvetadvīpa, and stood there desiring to hear [his words], O Rudra.
From among us, Rudra, having bowed down to that Supreme Lord Viṣṇu—the essence of all essences—indeed questioned him. (GarP 1.2.31)
Brahmā said:
O Vyāsa, just as he questioned me,
so did that blessed Lord Bhava question Viṣṇu while the gods and other immortals listened together.
Rudra said: O Hari, tell me, O Lord of Gods—
who is the God of gods, the Sovereign?
Who is to be meditated upon, and who indeed is to be worshipped? By what vows is the Supreme One pleased?
By what qualities, by what observances, or by what worship of the Dharma, and by what conduct would he be pleased? And what indeed is his form? 2.34.
From which god was the world born, and who protects the world?
By what kinds of incarnations does he do so, and into whom does the world go for dissolution?
From which deity do creation, secondary creation, the genealogies, and the periods of the Manvantaras proceed? Upon what is all this established?
O Hari, tell me all of this, as well as anything else whatsoever,
such as the majesty of the Supreme Lord and the practice of yoga through reasoning.
Likewise, [he taught] the eighteen branches of knowledge to Hari and Rudra; then Hari spoke to Rudra:
"Listen, O Rudra, I shall proclaim [this] together with Brahmā and the gods."
For I am indeed the god of gods, the Lord of the lords of all worlds;
I am to be meditated upon and worshipped, and I am to be praised by the gods with hymns of praise.
For when I am worshipped, O Rudra, I grant the supreme goal;
I am pleased by the restraints, the vows, and the conduct of men.
O Śiva, I am the seed of the world's existence and I am the creator of the world;
O Hara, I am indeed the punisher of the wicked and the protector of dharma.
Through my incarnations as the Fish and others, I protect the entire world;
I am the mantras, the meaning of the mantras, and indeed I am devoted to worship and meditation.
I am the creator of heaven and the like, and I alone am heaven and the like;
I am the primordial yoga, and I alone am the ancient scriptures.
The knower, the hearer, as well as the thinker, the speaker, and that which is to be spoken—
all this is the God who is the soul of all, the supreme bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
I am meditation and the offering of worship; I alone am the mandalas.
O Rudra, I am the Itihāsas;
indeed, O Śiva, I am all the Vedas.
O Śambhu, I am all knowledges;
I am the Self that is Brahman, I am Śiva.
I am Brahmā, the entire world, for I am indeed the Self of all the gods.
I am the personified practice of right conduct, I am indeed Dharma, and I am the Vaiṣṇava;
likewise, I am the castes and stages of life, as well as their ancient dharma.
I am Yama, I am Niyama, and O Rudra, I am the various vows;
I am likewise the sun, the moon, and Maṅgala and the other planets.
In ancient times, the bird Garuḍa propitiated me on earth through ascetic penance;
being pleased, I said, "Choose a boon from me," and he chose a boon from me.
Garuḍa said:
"O Hari, my mother Vinatā has been made a slave by the Nāgas;
O Lord, just as I have vowed, I shall conquer them and bring back that nectar."
I shall liberate you from slavery, just as my mount is yours—
possessing great strength and great heroism, omniscient, and the subduer of the nagas.
"Act in such a way that I may become the author of a Purāṇa-saṃhitā.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Garuḍa, everything shall happen exactly as you have spoken."
Through the gift of the Naga, you shall liberate your mother Vinatā;
and having conquered all the gods and others, you shall indeed bring back the nectar of immortality.
"By my grace, you shall become a mighty vehicle, a destroyer of poison;
and through my favor, you shall proclaim my greatness as an ancient text."
As for that which was said— that my own form shall manifest to you—
that Gāruḍa [tantra] shall become famous in the world under your name.
"Just as I am known as the glory of the gods of gods, O son of Vinatā,
so shall the Gāruḍa Purāṇa attain renown among the Purāṇas."
Just as I am to be glorified, so too are you in your form as Garuḍa;
O chief of birds, meditating upon me, proclaim this Gārūḍa Purāṇa.
Thus addressed by Rudra, O Garuḍa,
he spoke to the inquiring Kaśyapa;
having heard the Gāruḍa [teachings], Kaśyapa restored a burnt tree to life.
Having yourself become single-minded, you shall revive others by means of this knowledge.
O Yakṣiṇī, reciting "Oṃ Uṃ Svāhā," this is the supreme Gāruḍī vidyā.
Indeed, O Rudra, listen to the Gāruḍa [tantra] spoken by Garuḍa.
Consisting of me.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 3 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
Thus the sage Vyāsa heard from Brahmā, who was born from the lotus of Rudra;
and I shall speak it to you, O Śaunaka, at Naimiṣa, having heard it from Vyāsa.

In the midst of the sages who were listening, [the following] was spoken here: the worship of the gods at the beginning of creation, the sacred fords, the structure of the universe, and the periods of the Manvantaras.
The duties of the castes and stages of life, as well as the duties such as giving and kingship;
legal procedure, vows, genealogies, and medicine along with its diagnostic causes.
The limbs, dissolution, and the supreme knowledge of dharma, desire, and wealth—
whether with conceptual elaboration or free from conceptual elaboration— are declared to be the deeds of Viṣṇu.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa, it is said that the Lord Garuḍa was endowed with all [powers] and an excellence of capability through the grace of Vāsudeva.
Having become the vehicle of Hari and the cause of creation and the other cosmic processes,
Garuḍa likewise conquered the gods and brought back the nectar of immortality.
Within the belly of Hari, the universe was devoured by hunger;
upon seeing him, and merely by remembering him, there is the destruction of the serpents and the Dīnas.
Since Kaśyapa restored to life the tree that had been burnt by Garuḍa, he is called Garuḍa; and because of that, Hari spoke thus to Śrī-Kaśyapa.
Having bowed to Vyāsa, I shall speak of that glorious, meritorious *Rāma-gītā*, which bestows all things upon you who recite it; listen, O Śaunaka, to how it is so.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of Subjects," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 4] Rudra said:
Primary creation, secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— please tell us this, O Janārdana.
Hari said: "Listen, O Rudra, I shall proclaim that ancient sport of Viṣṇu, which destroys sins and consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution."
The god Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, the stainless one,
the supreme self, the supreme Brahman, is the cause of the origin and dissolution of the world.
All this, indeed, exists in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest;
likewise, it exists in the form of the Puruṣa and in the form of Time.
The manifest, as well as the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and Time itself—behold his activity, which is like that of a playing child. (GarP 1.4.5)
The Sustainer is without beginning or end, infinite, and the Supreme Person;
from him arises the Unmanifest, and from that, the Self is also born.
From that [the Self] arose intellect, from that the mind, from that the ether, from that the wind;
from that arose fire, from that the waters, and from that the earth came into being.
O Rudra, that golden egg indeed exists by itself within it;
the Lord himself first assumes a body for the sake of creation.
Brahmā, having become four-faced and always possessing a preponderance of the quality of rajas,
assumed a body and created this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Within the egg is the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans;
Viṣṇu, the creator, creates himself, and he protects that which is to be protected.
At the end, he is withdrawn and he himself is the destroyer, O Hara;
having become Brahmā, he created, and Hari himself, as Viṣṇu, protects the world.
In the form of Rudra, he destroys the entire world at the end of the kalpa;
but Brahmā, at the time of creation, [supports] the earth situated within the waters.
Having assumed the body of a boar, he lifted [the earth] up with his tusk; knowing this, O Śaṅkara, listen as I describe the creation of the gods and others in brief. // GarP_1.4.13 //

(1) The first creation was that of Mahat, which is indeed the formless [creation] of Brahmā; (2) the second, however, is known as the creation of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which is the creation of the gross elements (*bhūta*).
The third creation is that of the vaikārika, which is known as the creation of the senses.
Thus, this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) has arisen preceded by intelligence.

The fourth is the primary creation (*mukhyasarga*); indeed, the immobile beings (*sthāvara*) are known as the primary ones. That which is called the "sideways-stream" (*tiryaksrotas*) is said to be the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*). (GarP 1.4.16)

(6) That which follows with the upward-streaming [beings] is remembered as the sixth creation, that of the gods; (7) thereafter, the seventh creation is that of those with downward-streaming [beings], which is the human creation.
The eighth is the creation of grace; that [creation] is both characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*) and characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*).
These five are known as the secondary creations (*vaikṛta*), while three are remembered as the primary creations (*prākṛta*).
The natural and the modified, as well as the ninth known as the youthful—
these, O Rudra, are the creatures beginning with the gods and ending with the stationary beings.
They are of four kinds. // GarP_1,4.19 //
As Brahmā was performing the act of creation, mind-born sons were born to him;
from them arose the fourfold group consisting of gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans.
Desiring to emit these waters, the Lord of Creatures joined his own self;
from that Prajāpati, whose nature was manifest, the qualities of darkness (tamas) were intensified.
From the loins of Him who desired to create, the Asuras were first born;
thereafter, He cast off that body which was composed of the quality of darkness (tamas).
The subtle body consisting of pure darkness was cast off and became Śaṅkarā, the Night;
then the Yakṣas, Upakṣas, and the gods found delight in her form.
O Hara, those who were born from the mouth of Brahmā were predominant in *sattva*;
that body of his, consisting mostly of *sattva*, was cast off by him, and it became the day.
For from that [state], the Asuras were powerful by night and the deities by day;
and from that, the Pitṛs came into being, having assumed bodies consisting of pure sattva.
And that twilight, which exists as the interval between day and night,
having assumed a body consisting of the quality of passion (rajas), from it humans came into being.
That moonlight which was previously called the morning twilight became abandoned;
indeed, moonlight, night, day, and twilight were his very bodies.
Taking up a minute particle of dust, hunger and anger arose;
those who were protectors became Rākṣasas, emaciated by hunger and thirst, and devourers of raw flesh. (GarP 1.4.28)
They are to be known as Yakṣas because of their devouring (jakṣaṇa); the serpents (sarpa) indeed [arose] from the gliding of hair;
those beings were born from anger, and from that, the Gandharvas were produced.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases were born singing the Veda;
Dyaus made heaven his breast, and the Unborn One (Aja) was well-pleased by that sacrifice.
From his belly and from his two sides Prajāpati created [the intermediate creatures],
and from his feet he likewise created the elephants, buffaloes, camels, and sheep.
From his body hairs were born medicinal herbs bearing fruits and roots;
likewise, the cow, the goat, the man, the sacrificial animal, as well as the horse, the mule, and the donkey.
These are said to be the domestic animals; now learn from me the wild ones:
beasts of prey, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth.
Aquatic animals were the sixth, and reptiles the seventh;
from the eastern and other faces, the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas were born.
From his mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born; from his two arms the Kṣatriyas are recorded [to have been born];
from his thighs the Vaiśyas were created; and from his feet the Śūdra was born.
The world of Brahmā belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, that of Śakra to those born as Kṣatriyas,
the station of the Maruts to the Vaiśyas, and that of the Gandharvas to those born as Śūdras.
For those established in the vow of celibacy, the world of Brahmā arises;
for householders who act according to the prescribed rules, the world of Prajāpati arises.
There is the abode of the seven sages and likewise of those who dwell in the forest;
it is the imperishable station for ascetics who always go wherever they please.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 5.
Viṣṇu said:
Having established his residence in this world and the next, and having performed the mental creation of progeny,
the Lord then produced the mind-born sons who were the creators of further beings.
Dharma, Rudra, Manu, Sanaka, Sanātana, Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, as well as Ruci and Śraddhā; // GarP_1,5.2 //
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha,
Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, and Nārada, as well as the Barhiṣad Pitṛs.
The Agniṣvātta, the Kavyāda, the Ājyapa, and the Sukālins;
likewise the Upahūta, the Dīpya,
and the three who are devoid of physical form.
The Lotus-born [Brahmā] created the four [sages] endowed with forms; from his right thumb he created the Lord Īśvara, and from his left thumb he created his wife.
Upon her, Dakṣa begot auspicious daughters;
he gave them to the sons of Brahmā, but he gave Satī to Rudra.
Indeed, Rudra had countless sons of great strength;
and he gave Khyāti, who was auspicious and peerless in beauty, to Bhṛgu.
That auspicious woman gave birth to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ for Bhṛgu,
and she also gave birth to Śrī, who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa.
Upon her, Hari himself begot Balonmada and Āyati and Niyati,
the two daughters of the high-souled Manu.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ had two wives, and from them were born two sons:
Prāṇa and Mṛkaṇḍu; and from Mṛkaṇḍu was born Mārkaṇḍeya.
Marīci’s wife, Sambhūti, gave birth to Paurṇamāsa;
Virajas and Sarvaga were the two sons of that high-souled one.
And from Smṛti were born the sons of Aṅgiras, as well as daughters:
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati. (GarP 1.5.12)
In the same manner, Anasūyā bore to Atri three stainless sons:
Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogi Dattātreya.
To Prīti, the wife of Pulastya, was born a son named Dattoli;
he had three sons: Karṇaśa, Arthavīra, and Sahiṣṇu.
Kṣamā, the wife of the progenitor Pulaha, gave birth [to the Kṣamācyutas]; and Sumati, the wife of Kratu, gave birth to the Bālakhilyas. (GarP 1.5.15)
There were sixty thousand sages of perpetual celibacy,
the size of a thumb’s joint, and possessing a radiance like that of the blazing sun.
In Ūrjā, seven sons were indeed born to Vasiṣṭha:
Rajas, Gātra, Urdhvabāhu, Śaraṇa, and likewise Anagha.
Sutapāḥ and Śukra—these were all the stainless Seven Sages (Saptarṣis). Dakṣa also gave Svāhā to Agni, who was without a body.
Therefore, O Hara, Svāhā obtained three sons of noble vigor—
Phāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci— who subsist on water.
From the Pitṛs, Svadhā gave birth to Menā and likewise Vaitaraṇī;
both of them were exponents of the Veda. Himācala [took] Menā as his wife.
The Lord first begot Maināka and Gaurī, who was formerly Satī;
thereafter, the Self-born Lord [beget] Svāyambhuva Manu, who was born from his own self.
O Hara, you made Manu himself the protector of creatures,
and Śatarūpā that woman whose impurities were destroyed by ascetic penance.
The divine and omnipresent Manu Svāyambhuva took her as his wife;
and from that Puruṣa, the goddess Śatarūpā was born.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were born [to Manu] from those named Prasūti and Ākūti;
among them, Manu gave Devahūti to Ruci and Ākūti to Dakṣa.
He gave Prasūti to Dakṣa and Duhitṛ to Kardama;
from Ruci, Yajña was born, and from Dakṣiṇā, he was born of Yajña.
There were twelve sons named Yāmas of great strength,
and Dakṣa created twenty-four excellent daughters.
Faith, movement, fortitude, contentment, nourishment, intelligence, action, as well as wisdom, modesty, form, tranquility, supernatural power, and fame as the thirteenth. (GarP 1.5.27)
The lord Dharma accepted Khyāti, Satī, Sambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and Kṣamā as wives from the daughters of Dakṣa.
Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā; Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, and the sage Aṅgiras as well. GarP_1,5.29 //
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise Atri, the best of sages; Vasiṣṭha, Vahni, and the Pitṛs, in due order.
The sages, the best of munis, took these daughters: Khyāti and the others took Kāma; Śraddhā took Darpa; and Calā took Niyama as her son. Dhṛti took Ātmaja as her son. GarP_1,5.31.
Contentment gave birth to satisfaction, and Puṣṭi gave birth to greed; Medhā gave birth to sacred learning, Kriyā to punishment, Layā to dissolution, and Vinaya likewise.
Buddhi gave birth to Bodha, as well as Lajjā, Vinaya, Vapu, and Ātmaja;
Vyavasāya was indeed born from her, and Śānti gave birth to Kṣema.
Happiness, supernatural power, fame, and renown—these are the sons of Dharma;
and Rati is the wife of Kāma, and their son is said to be Harṣa (Joy).
Once Dakṣa performed a horse sacrifice (hayamedha);
all his sons-in-law, having been invited, went to that sacrifice.
All were accompanied by their wives, with the exception of the goddess Satī and Rudra; Satī had arrived uninvited and was insulted by Dakṣa himself.
Having abandoned her body, she was born again from Himālaya as Menā;
she became the wife of Śambhu as Raurī, and from her Vināyaka was born.
And the powerful Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, being the enraged Bhṛṅgīśa Kumāra, having destroyed the sacrifice, cursed Dakṣa:
"You shall become a human born of the lineage of Dhruva. (GarP 1.5.38)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Creation of the Procreators and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 6, Hari said:
From Uttānapāda and Suruci was born a son named Uttama;
and from Sunīti was born a son named Dhruva, who attained the highest station.
Through the grace of the Sage, having propitiated Janārdana, the god of gods,
Śliṣṭi, the son of Dhruva, possessed great strength and prowess.
His son was Prācīnavarhis; his son was Udāradhī; his son was Divañjaya; and his son is recorded as Ripu.
Likewise, the illustrious Cākṣuṣa is celebrated as the son of Ripu;
his son was the glorious Ruru, and Aṅga was his offspring as well.
The son of Aṅga was Veṇa, who was an atheist, devoid of dharma,
and a doer of unrighteousness; he was slain by the sages with blades of kusha grass.
They churned his thigh for the sake of a son; from that, a son was born to him who was exceedingly short and dark-limbed. Thereupon they said, "Let him sit down (niṣīda). Thus he became Niṣāda.
From him was born Niṣādastena, who dwelt upon the Vindhya mountains;
then the twice-born ones suddenly churned his right hand.
Therefore, a son was born to him who bore a form like that of Viṣṇu’s mind;
he, the son of Veṇa named Pṛthu, ascended to heaven.
Indeed, King Antardhāna milked the earth for the livelihood of his subjects;
his son was Pṛthu, and Havidhāna was his offspring.
His son, Prācīnabarhis, shone as the sole sovereign of the earth;
he indeed married the daughter of the salt ocean.
Therefore, Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis;
all were known by the name Prācetasas, and they were masters of the science of archery.
Practicing the dharma without deviation, they performed great austerities for ten thousand years, dwelling within the waters of the ocean.
O noble one, having attained the status of Prajāpati, Dakṣa became their husband through the curse of Bhava; from her, he was born thereafter.
In the beginning, Dakṣa created beings of four classes by means of his mind;
however, they did not multiply because they were cursed by Hara.
Then Prajāpati desired to effect creation through sexual union;
he took Asiknī, the daughter of the Prajāpati Vīraṇa, as his wife.
He had a thousand sons born of Vairaṇī;
they went to the ends of the earth as instructed by Nārada, but they did not return.
And when those thousand sons of Dakṣa had perished, he created the Śabalāśvas;
O Hara, they too followed the path of their brothers.
Then Dakṣa, enraged, cursed Nārada, saying, "You shall undergo birth again.
Thus Nārada became once more the son of the sage Kaśyapa.
Then, when the sacrifice had been destroyed, Dakṣa also cursed Maheśvara fiercely;
but having praised you with ritual offerings, O Śaṅkara, they shall worship you.
"O Śaṅkara, even in another birth they will perish through enmity;
therefore, one should never harbor enmity toward anyone,
even [toward] Asiknī (the queen)."
Then Dakṣa indeed begot daughters.
He gave sixty beautiful maidens to Aṅgiras,
two to Kṛśāśva, and ten to Dharma.
He gave fourteen [daughters] to Kaśyapa, twenty-eight to Indu, and likewise the beautiful Suprabhā to Bahuputra.
O Mahādeva, Dakṣa gave four daughters— Manoramā, Bhānumatī, Viśālā, and Bahudāmā— to Ariṣṭanemi.
He gave Suprajā and likewise Jayā to Kṛśāśva;
[and he gave] Arundhatī, Vasu,
Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, and Marudvatī.
Saṅkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā—these ten are declared to be the wives of Kaśyapa; I shall now describe them.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyuḥ, Siṃhikā, Muni, Kadrū, Sādhyā, Harā, Krodhā, Vinatā, Surabhi, and Khagā. (GarP 1.6.26)
The Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas; from Marutvatī the Marutvats were born, and likewise the Vasus from Vasu.
O Rudra, from Bhānu come the Bhānus,
and from Muhūrta come the Muhūrtajas;
from Lambā comes Ghoṣa, and from Yamitā comes Nāgavīthi.
The entire realm of the earth was born from Marutvatī;
and from Saṅkalpā, the Soul of All was indeed born as Saṅkalpa himself.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are remembered as the Vasus by their names.
Āpasya’s sons were Vetuṇḍi (or Veṇḍa), Śrama, Śrānta, and Dhvani;
and the son of Dhruva was the Lord Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds.
The venerable Varcas was born from Soma; by him a radiant one is produced.
Druhiṇa, the son of Dhara, is likewise the bearer of the oblations.
From Manoharā were born Śiśira, Prāṇa, and likewise Ramaṇa.
Anila’s wife was Śivā, and her son was Pulomaja.
Furthermore, Avijñātagati was one of the two sons of Anila;
Agniputra, however, Kumāra, was born within a clump of reeds.
His offspring were Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya, born from his back; and because he was the child of the Kṛttikās, he is known as Kārttikeya.
They know Pratyūṣa’s son to be the ṛṣi named Devala;
Viśvakarman is the renowned celestial architect (devavardhaki) of Prabhāsa.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the heroic Rudra;
and also the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, his own offspring Viśvarūpa, who is possessed of great ascetic power.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Aparājita,
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and likewise Raivata.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Kapālī, O great sage—
these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
From Kaśyapa and Aditi, twelve sons were born to Sūryā:
Viṣṇu, Śakra, Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Pūṣan.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aṃśumat, and Bhaga— these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
There were twenty-seven wives of Soma known as the lunar mansions (nakṣatra).
At that time, Hiraṇyākṣa was born to Diti, who possessed a golden sacrificial seat (hiraṇyakaśipu).
And Siṃhikā became the daughter who was wedded to Vipracitti;
and Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of immense vigor.
Anuhrāda, Hrāda, the heroic Prahrāda, and Saṃhrāda were their younger brothers;
among them, Prahrāda was devoted to Viṣṇu.
The venerable Śibi Vāṣkala was the son of Saṃhrāda, and Virocana was the son of Prahrāda;
from Virocana, Bali was born.
O Bull-bannered One, Bali had a hundred sons with Bāṇa as the eldest;
and all the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were likewise possessed of great strength.
Utkura and Śakuni, as well as Bhūtasantāpana;
Mahānāga, Mahābāhu, and another, Kālanābha.
And there were the sons of Anubhava: Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkara, Ayomukha, Śaṅkuśiras, Kapila, and Śambara.
Ekacakra, Mahābāhu, Tāraka of great strength,
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the great Asura Puloman.
These are known as the sons of Danu, along with the powerful Vipracitti;
Svarbhānu’s daughter was Suprabhā, and Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Upadānavī and Hayaśirā were two renowned and excellent daughters;
both Pulomā and Kālakā were likewise the daughters of Vaiśvānara.
Both of those illustrious women were the wives of Mārīca;
from them were born sixty thousand sons, the most excellent of the Dānavas.
The Paulomas and Kālakañjas are known as the sons of Mārīca;
likewise, the sons of Vipracitti were born from Siṃhikā.
Vyaṃśa, Śalya, the powerful Nabhas, the very mighty Mahābala,
Vātāpi, Namuci, Ilvala, and likewise Khasṛmān.
Añjaka, Naraka, Kālanābha, and likewise the Nivātakavacas—
these Daityas were born in the lineage of Prahlāda.
And six sons, who were great beings, are proclaimed as the offspring of Tāmrā:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Śuci, and Gṛdhrikā.
Śukī gave birth to parrots, Ulūkī to owls,
Śyenī to hawks, Bhāsī to bhāsa birds, and Gṛdhryā to vultures.
Sugrīvī gave birth to flocks of parrots and water-birds;
the lineage of Tāmrā is proclaimed to consist of horses, mules, and donkeys.
Vinatā, moreover, had two famous sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa.
And there were a thousand Surasās, serpents of immeasurable power.
And there were a thousand hooded serpents of Kadrū’s lineage, possessed of immeasurable power;
among them, O Lord of Beings, Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka were the foremost.
Śaṅkha, Śveta, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, Kambala and Aśvatara, as well as the nāga Elāpattra, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya.
Know that the Gaṇas are under the control of Krodha, and they are all fanged;
moreover, Krodhā gave birth to the Piśācas of great strength.
Surabhi gave birth to cows as well as buffaloes;
Irā produced trees, creepers, shrubs, and all varieties of grasses in every way.
Khagā gave birth to the yakṣas and rākṣasas, while Muni gave birth to the apsarases;
Ariṣṭā, however, gave birth to the great beings, the gandharvas.
The gods were indeed the forty-nine Maruts;
likewise, there were those of one light, two lights, and four lights.
Ekaśukra, Dviśukra, and the mighty Triśukra;
likewise Īdṛk, Sadṛk, Anyādṛk, and Pratisadṛk.
Mita, Samita, and the mighty Sumita;
likewise Ṛtajit, Satyajit, Suṣeṇa, and Senajit.
Atimitra, Amitra, Dūramitra, Ajita, as well as Ṛta, Ṛtadharmā, Vihartā, Varuṇa, Camasa, and Dhruva.
Vidhāraṇa, Durmedhas—this is remembered as one group;
likewise Īdṛśa, Sadṛkṣa, Etādṛkṣa, and Mitāśana.
By this [lineage] were born Prasadṛkṣa, Surata, and Mahātapas; likewise Hetumān, Prasava, Surabha, and Mahāyaśas.
Nādi, Rugra, Dhvani, Bhāsa, Vimukta, Vikṣipa, Saha, Dyuti, Vasu, Anādhṛṣya, Lābha, Kāma, Jayin, and Virāj. (GarP 1.6.71)
The group known as Udveṣaṇa is indeed in the seventh layer of wind;
all this is the form of Hari—the kings, the Dānavas, and the gods.
Together with their retinues, beginning with Sūrya, Manu and the others worshipped Hari.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Lineage of Uttānapāda and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 7.
Rudra said:
O Vyāsa, tell me in brief the supreme essence of the worship of the Sun and other deities, as performed by Svāyambhuva and others, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Hari said:
I shall describe the worship of the Sun and other deities, which brings about merit, the fulfillment of desires, and so forth.
Oṃ, homage to the seat of the Sun.
Oṃ, homage to the form of the Sun.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, homage to the Sun.
Oṃ, homage to Soma.
Oṃ, homage to Maṅgala.
Oṃ, homage to Budha.
Oṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati.
Oṃ, homage to Śukra.
Oṃ, homage to Śanaiścara.
Oṃ, homage to Rāhu!
Oṃ, homage to Ketu!
Oṃ, homage to Tejaścaṇḍa! // GarP_1,7.3 //
The seat, the invitation, water for the feet, the arghya offering, and likewise water for sipping;
as well as the bath, clothing, the sacred thread, perfume, flowers, and incense.
O Bull-bannered One, one should always perform the offering of lamps, prostrations, circumambulations, and the ritual dismissal for the Sun and other deities with these mantras.
Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Śiva.
Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the embodiment of auspiciousness. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ hrai, huṃ to the armor.
Oṃ hrauṃ, vaṣaṭ to the three eyes. Oṃ hraḥ, namaḥ to the weapon.
Oṃ hrāṃ, namaḥ to Sadyojāta.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hrūṃ, salutation to Aghora.
Oṃ hraiṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa.
Oṃ hrauṃ, homage to Īśāna.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Gaurī. Oṃ hrauṃ, homage to the Gurus.
Oṃ hrauṃ, homage to Indra.
Oṃ hrauṃ, homage to Caṇḍa.
Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to Aghora.
Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāsudeva. Oṃ, obeisance to the form of Vāsudeva.
Oṃ Aṃ Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva. Oṃ, obeisance!
Oṃ āṃ oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Saṅkarṣaṇa; homage! Oṃ aṃ oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Pradyumna; homage! Oṃ aḥ oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Aniruddha; homage!
Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa. Oṃ, homage to the Brahman whose essence is that [syllable]. Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu.
Oṃ kṣauṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, to Narasiṃha; salutation!
Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, to Varāha; salutation!
Oṃ kaṃ ṭaṃ paṃ śaṃ, salutation to Vainateya; salutation!
Oṃ jaṃ khaṃ raṃ, homage to Sudarśana.
Oṃ khaṃ ṭhaṃ phaṃ ṣaṃ, homage to Gadā.
Oṃ vaṃ laṃ maṃ kṣaṃ, homage to Pāñcajanya.
Oṃ ghaṃ ḍhaṃ bhaṃ haṃ, obeisance to Śrī. Oṃ gaṃ ḍaṃ vaṃ saṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi. Oṃ dhaṃ ṣaṃ vaṃ saṃ, obeisance to Vanamālā.
Oṃ saṃ daṃ laṃ, homage to Śrīvatsa. Oṃ ṭhaṃ caṃ bhaṃ yaṃ, homage to the Kaustubha gem.
Oṃ, homage to the gurus.
Oṃ, homage to Indra and the other guardians of the directions.
Oṃ, homage to Viṣvaksena. GarP_1,7.6.
O Bull-bannered One, one should offer the seat and other articles to Hari with these mantras.
Now hear the auspicious worship of Viṣṇu’s Śakti, Sarasvatī. GarP_1,7.7 //
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī.
Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the head.
Oṃ hrūṃ, homage to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ hraiṃ, homage to the armor (kavaca).
Oṃ hrauṃ, homage to the three eyes (netratraya).
Oṃ hraḥ, homage to the weapon. GarP_1,7.8.
Śraddhā, Ṛddhi, Kalā, Medhā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, Mati, Oṃ, Hrīṅkāra, and so forth, ending with "namas"—these are the powers (śaktis) of Sarasvatī. (GarP 1.7.9)
Homage to the protector of the field.
Oṃ, homage to the gurus. Oṃ, homage to the supreme gurus. (GarP 1.7.10)
One should arrange the seat and other offerings for Sarasvatī seated upon a lotus;
likewise, one should perform the rite of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa) for the Sun and the others with their respective mantras.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Worship of the Sun and Other Deities as well as Sarasvatī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 8,
Hari said:
Having bathed in a pavilion situated on the ground, one should worship Viṣṇu in the mandala;
the mandala should be a "thunderbolt-navelled" one made with powder of five colors.
O Rudra, one should have it measured there by sixteen squares;
one should then cause the laying of the lines upon the fourth and fifth corners.
From each of the two corner-lines, the wise one should cast the measuring lines toward those corners situated there.
In the corners immediately following those, one should likewise cause [the lines] to be made;
the first navel is thus designated at the intersection of the central lines.
And in all the intermediate spaces, there are eight navel-lines;
one should then rotate the cord from the eastern and middle navels.
O Hara, O Śiva, that best of the twice-born should rotate [the compass] three-quarters of the way between those two;
by this means, he should rotate the pericarp of the navel-line.
The wise one should draw the filaments with a portion equal to two parts of the pericarp;
at their tips, the learned one should always paint the petals.
O observer of noble vows, the instructor who knows the ultimate truth should fashion those lotuses in all the navel-fields according to this measurement.
One should arrange the doors according to the division of the initial sūtra;
likewise, one should fashion the beauty of the doors there with half of that measure.
The pericarp is yellow in color, with filaments that are white, red, and so forth;
the interior is blue in color, and the petals are black.
One should fill the square with black-colored powder;
the doors and the five lines in the mandala should be white-colored.
White, red, yellow, and black, respectively;
having first prepared the mandala and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship Hari.
One should place Viṣṇu in the center of the heart, and likewise Saṅkarṣaṇa in the throat;
having placed Pradyumna on the head, one should place Aniruddha on the crest-lock.
Having meditated on Brahmā in all the limbs and likewise Śrīdhara in the two hands,
one should place Hari in the pericarp, thinking, "I am Viṣṇu."
One should place Saṅkarṣaṇa in the east, Pradyumna in the south,
Aniruddha in the west, and Brahmā in the north.
One should place Śrīdhara in the corners of Rudra and Indra and the others in the cardinal directions;
then, having worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings, one shall attain the supreme state.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Vajranābha Maṇḍala Useful for the Worship of Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 9. Hari said:
At that time, the initiated disciple, with his eyes bound by a cloth, should have one hundred and eight oblations offered for him with the root mantra. (GarP 1.9.1)
O Rudra, for a *putraka* initiate, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is considered to be twofold; for a *sādhaka*, it is held to be threefold; and for a *nirvāṇadeśika*, it is declared to be fourfold.
One who kills a guru, Viṣṇu, a brahmin, or a woman is to be bound by those who have not been initiated.
Now, I shall explain initiation, which brings about the destruction of both merit and demerit.
Having seated the disciples outside, he should cause them to perform dhāraṇā;
O Rudra, he should contemplate them as being dried up by the Vāyavyā kalā.

Having unified that living being with the fires and the fires by means of the fire-mantra (āgneyī), he should cast it away, [visualizing it] as being both consumed by fire and drenched again by water.
One should contemplate the *prāṇava* in the void within the body; however, there is another cause.
Therein, one should conquer each [element] individually, [and finally] the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) from its causal basis, the body.
O Bull-bannered One, one should first generate each [deity] individually and subsequently join them;
however, one who is incapable in the construction of mandalas and the like should worship Hari by means of mental visualization.
It should have four gates following the sequence starting from the Brahma-tīrtha;
it is declared that the hand is a lotus, and its fingers are known as the petals.
The palm of the hand is the pericarp, and its nails are the filaments;
having meditated upon Hari there, one should worship Him as being within the sun, moon, and fire.
With a concentrated mind, one should place that hand upon the head of the disciple;
because Viṣṇu resides in the hand, it is therefore called the "Hand of Viṣṇu. By the touch of it, all sins whatsoever are destroyed.
The Guru, having honored the disciple and bound his eyes with a cloth,
should then have him place a flower before the Lord;
wherever that flower falls upon the head of the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow, [that is his deity].
The wise man himself should cause a name to be given to him marked with the names of women; for Śūdras, however, he should cause a name joined with the word "dāsa" (servant) to be made.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu-initiation," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—10. Hari spoke:
I shall perform the worship of Rāśi and the others upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and other sites for the sake of accomplishment.
*Śrīṃ hrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*.
*Śrāṃ śrīṃ śrūṃ śraiṃ śrauṃ śraḥ*—these are, in order, for the heart, the head, and the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
One should worship the armor, the eye, the weapon, the seat, and the form.
In the mandala, within the center of a lotus and provided with four gates marked by colored powders,
there is a mandala consisting of sixty-four, eight, and so forth, up to fifty-six, and fifty-six and so forth.
All [the deities] are located at the sky (0), eye (2), moon (1), and sun (12) [counting from the southeast], by proceeding through the sky (0), Vedas (4), and moon (1);
Lakṣmī and the limbs are in one corner, as are Durgā, Gaṇeśa, and the Guru.
Then, desiring his desires, he offered oblations into the fire and other elements for the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla):
*Oṃ ghaṃ ṭaṃ ḍaṃ haṃ, obeisance to Śrī Mahālakṣmī*. (GarP 1.10.4)
With this, one should worship Lakṣmī along with the previously mentioned retinue:
Oṃ saiṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hrīṃ saiṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. (GarP 1.10.5)
Oṃ hrīṃ vadavada vāgvādini svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ to Sarasvatī, obeisance! // GarP_1,10.6 //
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Lakṣmī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 11,
Hari said:
I shall now describe the worship of the nine arrays as it was indeed told to Kaśyapa:
having extracted the living soul from the head, one should establish it in the void at the navel.
Then, one should burn the body composed of the elements with the seed-syllable *raṃ*;
and by means of the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, one should cause all of that to perish.
With this seed-syllable *laṃ*, one should flood the entire world of moving and non-moving beings;
then, with this seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should contemplate nectar.
Then, in the center of that bubble, one should contemplate oneself through meditation as being me, four-armed and clad in yellow garments. (GarP 1.11.4)
Then one should perform the threefold mantra-installation (nyāsa) on the hands and the body,
using the twelve-syllable seed-mantra and subsequently with the aforementioned seed-mantras.
Then, one should perform the six-limbed rite by which Hari becomes manifest;
beginning from the right thumb, one should place [the mantras] upon the middle finger and the thumb-petal.
Having placed the two seed-syllables in the center, one should then place them on the limbs:
at the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the face, the eyes, the water-element, and the back.
One should place [the hands] upon the arms, the two hands, the knees, and also the feet;
having formed the hands into the shape of a lotus, one should place the thumbs in the middle.
Therein, one should contemplate the supreme, stainless reality, the Lord of All;
then, one should gradually place these seed-syllables upon the index finger and the other fingers.
Then one should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the head, eyes, mouth, throat, heart, navel, secret place, knees, and feet.
Having assigned the six seed-syllables of the limbs to the two hands, one should then assign them to the body;
one should assign the five seed-syllables from the thumb to the little finger.
The seed-syllable of the eye is in the middle of the hand; this is also the sequence for the assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa):
having assigned the heart to the heart, one should assign the head to the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] upon the crest, one should place the *kavaca* [mantra] everywhere on the body;
the *netra* [mantra] should be applied to the eyes, and the *astra* [mantra] to both hands.
Having bound the directions with that very [mantra], one should then perform the ritual of worship;
first, being composed, one should contemplate the yoga-throne within the heart.
One should place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in order in the southeast and the other directions starting from the east; and one should likewise assign Adharma and the others.

Then, one should visualize the infinite [deity] whose body is enveloped by these [elements], who has become the pedestal and consists of that very nature, standing with the previous [element] elevated at the front.
Then one should know that from the lake arises a lotus with eight petals corresponding to the directions,
a white lotus rich with a hundred petals, its pericarp spread upward.

Having meditated [on this] with the *vedādi* mantra and so forth, one should subsequently contemplate the mandalas of the sun, moon, and fire in this manner, one above the other, in their proper sequence.
Then, one should assign the eight Śaktis beginning with Vimalā, who reside in the directions starting from the east and are within the sphere of Keśava, and the ninth, located in the pericarp.
Having meditated thus and worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha immediately thereafter,
one should mentally invoke the Lord Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and install him there once more.
One should then place the heart-mantra and the others in the petals of the four directions starting from the east, the eye-mantra in the center, and the weapon-mantra in the corners.
One should place the seed-syllables of Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others in order starting from the east,
and one should install Vainateya at both the eastern and western gates.
One should place the Sudarśana disc with its thousand spokes at the southern gate;
having placed Śrī to the south, one should likewise place Lakṣmī to the north.
Having placed the mace at the inner door, one should place the conch in the corners;
the wise one should place the Śārṅga bow to the right of the deity and likewise on the left.
In the same manner, one should place a sword and a discus, two on each of the two sides;
then, one should install the inner world-protectors according to their respective directions.
One should likewise position the weapons, such as the vajra and others;
one should contemplate Brahmā above and Ananta below.
Having meditated upon everything in this way and performed worship, one should then display the mudrās.
The first mudrā is the añjali; it swiftly brings about the propitiation of the deity.
The *vandanī* [mudrā] is formed by placing the right hand raised over the heart,
with the left fist positioned above, binding the right thumb.
The thumb of that left hand is proclaimed as Uddhva;
these three are indeed common [to all], though conceived through the differentiation of forms.
By releasing [the fingers] starting from the little finger, one should understand the eight mudrās in their proper order,
corresponding respectively to the eight preceding seed-syllables.
Having bent the three fingers from the thumb to the little finger,
and having turned both hands face down, this is the mudrā of Narasiṃha.
Having likewise turned the left hand upward, one should slowly rotate it upward;
this is remembered as the ninth mudrā, always favored by Varāha.
Then, with both hands turned upward, one should release them one by one straight;
having released them all, one should contract [the fingers]—this is called the limb-mudrā.
Then, having likewise bound the two fists in this very same sequence,
one should perform the mudrās of the ten world-protectors according to their respective order.
Suramādyam is the second, Upāntya the penultimate, and Antya the last;
these correspond respectively to Vāsudeva, Bala, Kāma, and Aniruddha.
The Praṇava, "Tat-sat," "Huṃ," "Kṣaiṃ," and "Bhūḥ" are the mantras;
likewise [the deities] are Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Siṃha, and the sovereign Varāha.
White, reddish, yellow, blue, dark, red, cloud-colored, fire-colored, and tawny—these are the nine names according to their colors. (GarP 1.11.37)
Kaṃ, ṭaṃ, paṃ, and śaṃ are Garuḍa; jaṃ, khaṃ, and vaṃ are Sudarśana; ṣaṃ, caṃ, phaṃ, and ṣaṃ are the goddess Gadā; and vaṃ, laṃ, maṃ, and kṣaṃ are the conch (Śaṅkha).
Ghaṃ, ḍhaṃ, bhaṃ, and haṃ constitute Śrī; gaṃ, jaṃ, vaṃ, and śaṃ constitute Puṣṭikā; ghaṃ and vaṃ constitute Vanamālā; and daṃ and saṃ constitute Śrīvatsa.
"Chaṃ, ḍaṃ, paṃ, yaṃ; Kaustubha is proclaimed, and I myself am indeed Ananta—these are the ten limbs of the God of gods, according to their respective application."
Garuḍa resembles a lotus, and the mace has a dark appearance;
Puṣṭi has the luster of a śirīṣa flower, and Lakṣmī is like gold.
The conch resembles the full moon; the Kaustubha gem possesses a reddish luster;
the discus has the brilliance of a thousand suns; and the Śrīvatsa mark is like a kunda flower.
The garland indeed has the appearance of five colors, while Ananta resembles a cloud;
and as for those weapons which have the form of lightning, they have not been described by color.
One should indeed offer the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa mantra.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Worship of the Nine Vyūhas," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 12, Hari said:
For the sake of accomplishing the sequence of worship, the sequence of worship is now declared:
first, there is the recollection of the Supreme Self with "Oṃ Namaḥ" and so forth.
Yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ constitutes the purification of the body;
oṃ namaḥ constitutes the self-manifestation as the four-armed deity.
Then follows the threefold placement of the hand-gestures (*karakāyanyāsa*).
Then comes the worship of the yoga-throne situated within the heart:
*Oṃ, homage to Ananta*.
Oṃ, homage to Dharma.
Oṃ, homage to Jñāna.
Oṃ, homage to Vairāgya.
Oṃ, homage to Sovereignty. Oṃ, homage to Non-virtue. Oṃ, homage to Ignorance.
Oṃ, homage to non-detachment. Oṃ, homage to lack of sovereignty.
Oṃ, homage to the lotus.
Oṃ, homage to the solar disc.
Oṃ, homage to the lunar disc. Oṃ, homage to the fiery disc.
Oṃ, homage to Vimalā. Oṃ, homage to Utkarṣiṇī.
Oṃ, homage to Jñānā.
Oṃ, homage to Kriyā.
Oṃ, homage to Yogā. Oṃ, homage to Prahvī.
Oṃ, homage to Satyā.
Oṃ, homage to Īśānā.
Oṃ, homage to Sarvatomukhī.
Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Hari, together with its limbs and ancillaries.
Then, upon the pericarp: aṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva;
āṃ, salutation to the heart.
Īṃ, salutation to the head;
Ūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock;
Aiṃ, salutation to the armor.
Oṃ, salutation to the three eyes.
Aḥ phaṭ, salutation to the weapon. Āṃ, salutation to Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Aṃ, obeisance to Pradyumna. Aḥ, obeisance to Aniruddha.
Oṃ Aḥ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa.
Oṃ, salutation to Brahman, the Word (Tatsadbrahmaṇe).
Oṃ huṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Kṣaiṃ, to Narasiṃha; bhūr, to Varāha; kaṃ, to Vainateya; jaṃ khaṃ vaṃ, to Sudarśana; khaṃ caṃ phaṃ.

*Ṣaṃ* to the mace; *vaṃ*, *laṃ*, *maṃ*, *kṣaṃ* to the Pāñcajanya conch; *ghaṃ*, *ḍhaṃ*, *bhaṃ*, *haṃ* to Śrī; *gaṃ*, *ḍaṃ*, *vaṃ*, *śaṃ* to Puṣṭi; *dhaṃ*, *vaṃ* to the forest garland (*vanamālā*); *daṃ*, *śaṃ* to the Śrīvatsa mark; *chaṃ*, *ḍaṃ*, *yaṃ* to the Kaustubha gem; *śaṃ* to the Śārṅga bow; *iṃ* to the two quivers; *caṃ* to the shield;
*khaṃ* to the sword. To Indra, lord of the gods and protector; to Agni, lord of splendor; to Yama, lord of Dharma; to Nairṛta, lord of the Rākṣasas.

Yam for Varuṇa, lord of the waters; Vām for Vāyu, lord of the vital breaths; Dhām for Dhanada, lord of wealth; Hām for Īśāna, lord of knowledge; Oṃ for the Vajra, for the Śakti; Oṃ for the Daṇḍa, for the Khaḍga; Oṃ for the Pāśa, for the Dhvaja, for the Gadā, and for the Triśūla; Lam for Ananta, lord of the netherworld; Khaṃ for Brahmā, lord of all worlds; Oṃ.
Homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva! Homage! Oṃ oṃ, homage! Oṃ naṃ, homage!
Oṃ moṃ namaḥ / Oṃ oṃ bhaṃ namaḥ / Oṃ gaṃ namaḥ /
Oṃ vaṃ namaḥ / Oṃ teṃ namaḥ / Oṃ vāṃ namaḥ /
Oṃ suṃ namaḥ / Oṃ deṃ namaḥ / Oṃ vāṃ namaḥ /
Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ / Oṃ oṃ namaḥ / Oṃ naṃ namaḥ /
Oṃ moṃ namaḥ / Oṃ nāṃ namaḥ / Oṃ rāṃ namaḥ /
Oṃ ṇāṃ namaḥ / Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ / Oṃ naṃnoṃ to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva; Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance.
Oṃ, homage to the Supreme Person. GarP_1,12.3.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe.
Salutations be to you, O Subrahmaṇya, O Great Being, O Primordial One.
And for these, one should prepare the oblation with the word "svāhā" at the end;
having thus recited [the mantra] according to the rule one hundred and eight times.
Having offered the *argha* and prostrated again and again, saying "Victory to him!",
one should then worship and sacrifice to him in the fire according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having first inscribed the God of gods, Acyuta, with his own seed-syllable and with the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth, the knower of mantras should sprinkle him with the *praṇava*.
Having circumambulated the fire in the pit, one should worship it with auspicious fruits;
having first meditated upon all that [in its entirety], one should mentally place it within the mandala.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the principle known as Vāsudeva,
one should likewise worship the group of six with the seed-syllables of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others.
Likewise, he should offer three sets of three oblations for each of the limbs, as well as for each of the lords of the directions;
and at the end, having properly approached, he should likewise offer the final full oblation.
One should lead the self into dissolution within the supreme reality that transcends speech;
having sat down again, one should display the mudrā and bow once more.
Such a fire-oblation should be performed constantly; on special occasions, it should be doubled.
Go, go to the supreme abode where the stainless God resides.
May all the deities depart for the sake of remaining in their own abodes:
Sudarśana, Śrī Hari, Acyuta, and Trivikrama.
The four-armed Vāsudeva, and Pradyumna as the sixth, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the Puruṣa; thus [he is] the ninefold manifestation and the tenfold self.
Aniruddha consists of twelve aspects, and then there is Anantaka above;
these deities are to be recognized and characterized by means of wheels numbering one and so forth.
One shall be honored by those marked with the wheel-signs and always protected by men within the household.
*Oṃ cakrāya svāhā*,
*oṃ vicakrāya svāhā*.
Oṃ, svāhā to the Excellent Wheel; Oṃ, svāhā to the Great Wheel;
Oṃ, to the Great Wheel, the Destroyer of Asuras, hūṃ phaṭ; Oṃ hūṃ, thousand-spoked one, hūṃ phaṭ.
This worship of the Dvārakā-cakra is auspicious and provides protection for the home.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Sequence of Worship," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 13—
Hari said:
Now I shall proclaim this auspicious Vaiṣṇava Pañjara: "Obeisance, obeisance to you! O Knower of All, take up the Sudarśana discus! (GarP 1.13.1)
Protect me in the eastern direction, O Viṣṇu;
I have come to you for refuge.
Take up the mace Kaumodakī, O Padmanābha; salutations be unto you!
O Viṣṇu, protect me from the south!
I have come to you for refuge.
O Puruṣottama, salutations to you who hold the Saunanda plow! GarP_1,13.3 //
Protect me in the western direction, O Viṣṇu!
I have come to you for refuge.
Grasping your churning-pestle, O lotus-eyed one, protect me!
O Lord of the World, having taken refuge in you from the north,
I have come with sword, shield, and various weapons and sciences, O Hare.
Salutations to you, O destroyer of demons, protect me! Having sought refuge in the northeast,
[I praise] the great conch Pāñcajanya and the resounding lotus.
"Seizing [it], protect me, O Viṣṇu; protect me in the south-eastern quarter, O Sūkara!
Likewise, having grasped the moon and sun, as well as the sword of the moon," GarP_1,13.7 //
O divine-formed one, O man-lion, protect me in the southwest;
hold fast to the Vaijayantī garland and the Śrīvatsa, the ornament of your throat.
O Lord Hayagrīva, protect me from the northwest; salutations be unto you!
O Janārdana, having mounted Vainateya, [protect me] in the intermediate space.
Protect me always, O Unconquered One; homage be to you, the Unvanquished!
Having mounted Viśālākṣa, protect me in the subterranean realm (rasātala).
O Akūpāra, homage to you; O Mahāmīna, homage be to you!
You are truth in the hands, the head, and the fingers; you are the cage of the arms.
"Having fashioned it, protect me, O Viṣṇu; salutations to you, O Supreme Person.
Thus was this great Vaiṣṇava armor spoken to Śaṅkara.
O Bull-bannered Lord, in former times, for the sake of protecting Īśānī,
Kātyāyanī brought about the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura and his immortals.
A person who recites this with devotion always conquers the Dānavas, Raktabīja, and other thorns of the gods, as well as their enemies.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Viṣṇupañjara Hymn," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the glorious Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Hari said: Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa—14.
Hari said:
Now I shall proclaim the supreme Yoga, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
by means of meditation, Hari, the Lord, who is to be meditated upon, is proclaimed by those who practice meditation.
Listen to that, O Maheśāna, which destroys all sins:
Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, the Infinite, who is devoid of the six states of worldly existence.
I am indeed Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, the Self that is Brahman;
I am eternally situated within the bodies of embodied beings, yet forever free from all bodies.
Devoid of bodily attributes and free from the perishable and the imperishable,
he is the seer, the hearer, and the smeller, abiding within the sixfold [objects] yet transcending the senses.
Devoid of those qualities, the Creator is free from name and lineage;
He is the thinker who abides in the mind, yet is Himself devoid of the mind.
Devoid of mind and mental objects, consciousness and gnosis alike,
he is the knower, established in awakening, the witness, the omniscient one, yet free from the intellect.
Devoid of the qualities of the intellect, all-pervading,
the mind is entirely free from all living beings and divested of the qualities of vital breath.
The life of life, the greatly peaceful, entirely free from fear,
devoid of egoism and the like, and likewise free from that [notion of] dharma.
The witness of that, its controller, whose nature is supreme bliss, abides in waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; it is the witness of those states, yet remains free from them.
I am Śiva, the Self—truthful, pervasive, ageless, awakened, and liberated; the fourth state, the supreme sustainer, whose form is pure consciousness and who is devoid of qualities.
In this way, those wise men who meditate upon the Lord, the supreme state, shall attain His very form; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus has meditation been fully explained to you, O Śaṅkara of noble vows;
he who constantly recites this goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Meditation," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 15.
Rudra said:
"O Lord, what should a man recite to be liberated from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra? O Janārdana, please teach me that supreme mantra to be recited."
Hari said:
By praising Viṣṇu— the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable Supreme Self— with a thousand names, a person shall be liberated.
O Bull-bannered One, listen attentively as I declare that supreme *brahman* which is to be recited, which destroys all sins. (GarP 1.15.3)

the child resembling the young moon, Bāla, Balabhadra, and the Lord of Strength.
The creator who bound Bali,
the most excellent one, the knower of the Vedas, the source of all,
the author of the Vedas, whose form is the Veda, the one to be known, and he who is immersed in the Vedas.

he is changeless, the Lord of boons, Varuṇa, and the sovereign of Varuṇa.
The slayer of heroes, the great hero, the praised supreme lord;
the self, the supreme self, the inner self, and that which is beyond the ether. (30) 7. Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.7.

Pure (60), consisting of light, holy, and a protector;
free from thirst, worthy of worship, the Supreme Person, and likewise primordial nature.
The Primal Matter, the Earth-Lotus, the One with a Lotus Navel (70), the Bestower of what is dear,
the Lord of All, the All-pervading, the All, the All-knowing, the Giver of All, the Divine.

the God who bestows grace upon all, dwelling in the heart of every living being. (80)

The protector of all, the ultimate refuge of all, the cause of all causes;
the object of meditation for all, the friend of all, who assumes the form of the lords of all lands.

The protector of truth, Sannābha, Lord of the Siddhas, praised by the Siddhas;
he who accomplishes the Siddhas, the perfected Siddha, the one by whom the Sādhyas are perfected, the Lord of the Heart.

he is the doer of good, the beautiful, the gentle, the truthful, and one whose prowess is truth.

likewise the lord of Kapila;

The Great-Souled One, the Auspicious, the Measurable, Mandara, the Lord of Mandara, Meru, the Mother, the Standard of Measure, Mādhava, and the One Free from Impurity.
Mālādhara, Mahādeva—who is worshipped by Mahādeva—Mahāśānta, Mahābhāga, and Madhusūdana as well. (GarP 1.15.33)
Possessing great heroism and great vital power, he is saluted by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya;
his nature is illusion, yet he is bound by illusion and also liberated from illusion.
The sage praised by sages, the friendly one, the great hero, and the one with great jaws.
Possessing great arms and being greatly self-controlled, he is exempt from death.
He has great arms, a great soul, a great body, and a great belly;
he has great feet, a great neck, great pride, and a great mind.
He of the great course, the one of great fame, the one of great form, and the great Asura;
he who is Madhu and Mādhava, the Great God, the Supreme Lord.
He is the sacrifice,
the one in the form of the sacrifice,
and the venerable lord of sacrifice; he is the great wind, the highly fortunate one, the great lord who transcends humanity.
Mānava and Manu, the bringer of joy to human beings;
Mṛga and Mṛgapūjya, as well as the lord of the deer. (240) GarP_1,15.39 //
He is the lord of Mercury, the lord of Jupiter,
the lord of Saturn, and likewise the lord of Rāhu and Ketu.
Lakṣmaṇa, Lakṣaṇa, Lambauṣṭha, and likewise Lalita—adorned with various ornaments and anointed with various kinds of sandalwood paste. (250) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.41.
With faces radiant with various expressions and adorned with diverse flowers,
Rāma, the Lord of Ramā, the Supreme Sovereign, was accompanied by his wife.
The jewel among jewels and the stealer of jewels, possessed of form yet devoid of form;
he who is of great form and fierce form, and likewise of gentle form.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, pure, and likewise resembling a pale cloud;
smoke-colored, the color of a leaf, having various forms, and indeed colorless.
He is the deformed and the beautiful, as well as the white-colored; he is all colors, the great yogin, the sacrifice, the one to be sacrificed for,
and the performer of the sacrifice.
Suvarṇavarṇavān, Suvarṇākhya, Suvarṇāvayava, Suvarṇa, and Svarṇamekhala. (280) 46.
He is the giver of gold, the lord of gold,
the beloved of gold,
and likewise one who is rich in gold. (290) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.47.
Suparṇa, Mahāparṇa, and the cause of Suparṇa; likewise Vainateya, Āditya, the primordial source, and Śiva. GarP_1,15.48 //
He is the cause of the Great One (mahat) and the cause of primordial matter (pradhāna);
he is the cause of the intellects (buddhi) and likewise the cause of the mind (manas).
He is the cause of the mind and the cause of the ego;
likewise, he is the cause of the elements and the cause of fire.
In the same way, he is the cause of space, the supreme cause of the earth,
the cause of the cosmic egg, and likewise the cause of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The cause of the body, as well as the cause of the eye,
likewise the cause of the ear, and similarly the cause of the skin; (310) GarP_1,15.52.
The cause of the tongue and the cause of the vital breath,
as well as the cause of the two hands and likewise the cause of the two feet.
In the same way, it is the cause of speech and the cause of the anus;
it is the cause of Indra and the cause of Kubera.
The cause of Yama, the cause of Īśāna, the cause of the Yakṣas, and the supreme cause of the Rākṣasas. (320) GarP_1,15.55 //
It is the supreme cause of kings, the very cause of dharma,
the cause of all living beings, and the highest cause of riches.
He is the cause of the Manus, the supreme cause of the birds, the most excellent cause of the sages, and the supreme cause of the yogins. (330) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.57.
It is the cause of the Siddhas and the supreme cause of the Yakṣas;
it is the cause of the Kinnaras and the cause of the Gandharvas. (340) GarP_1,15.58 //
The cause of the male rivers and the supreme cause of the female rivers,
the cause of the oceans as well as the cause of the trees.
He is the cause of the plants and likewise the cause of the worlds;
he is the cause of the netherworld (pātāla) and likewise the cause of the gods.
It is the cause of serpents, as well as the cause of blessings;
it is the cause of cities, and likewise the cause of all things.
The self of the body, the self of the senses, and likewise the self of the intellect;
and similarly the self of the mind, and the self of the ego-consciousness and the consciousness.
The Self of the waking and the sleeping,
the Great Self,
the Supreme Self, the Self beyond primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the Self of space, and likewise the Self of the waters; (GarP 1.15.63).
He is the supreme self of the earth, and likewise the self of taste;

The person is likewise the essence of sound, the essence of speech, the essence of touch,
the essence of hearing, the essence of skin, and the supreme essence of the tongue.

The self of Indra, the self of Brahmā, the self of Rudra, as well as that of Manu,

The Self is likewise supreme.
Īśātmā, Paramātmā, Raudrātmā, Mokṣavidyati, Yatnavān, as well as Yatna, Carma, Khaḍgin, and Murāntaka. (GarP 1.15.68)
Hari is the one whose nature is to promote modesty, who is devoted to the welfare of ascetics,
who takes the form of an ascetic, who is a yogi, who is the object of meditation for yogis, and who is dark-hued.
Consciousness, intelligence, time, heat, the rainy season, and likewise the mind;
the year, the bringer of liberation, and likewise the destroyer of delusion. (410)
The creator of delusion for the wicked is Māṇḍavya, as well as Vaḍavāmukha;

Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Pulastya, and Kutsa;
Yājñavalkya, Devala, Vyāsa, and Parāśara.
Gāṅgeya, Hṛṣīkeśa, Bṛhacchravas;
Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, Sukarṇa, and Karṇavarjita.
The highly fortunate Nārāyaṇa is indeed the lord of Prāṇa, as well as the lord of Apāna and the lord of Vyāna. (440) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.74.
He is the supreme lord of the udāna breath, and likewise the lord of the samāna breath;
he is the supreme lord of sound and indeed the lord of touch.
He is the primordial lord of all forms, holding a sword in his hand,
armed with a plow, bearing a discus in his hand, wearing earrings, and likewise marked with the Śrīvatsa upon his chest.
Prakṛti, Kaustubhagrīva, and likewise Pītāmbaradhara; Sumukha and Durmukha, who is indeed devoid of a mouth.
Ananta, Anantarūpa, Sunakha, Suramandara,
Sukapola, Vibhu, Jiṣṇu, Bhrājiṣṇu, and likewise Eṣudhi.
The slayer of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the crusher of Hiraṇyākṣa, the destroyer of Pūtanā, and the annihilator of the Sun at the end of time. (470) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.79.
The crusher of Keśin, the subduer of Muṣṭika,
the destroyer of the Dānava Kaṃsa, and the annihilator of Cāṇūra.
The destroyer of misfortune and the beloved of Akrūra;
he who is Akrūra yet possesses a fierce form, and is praised by those dear to Akrūra. (480) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.81.

The Blessed One is the destroyer of fortune, the Sun, and likewise the Lord of the Bhāgavatas; he is himself possessed of his own cows, and Uddhava is his servant, for the Lord of Uddhava is meditated upon through sport.
The bearer of the wheel, the restless one, and indeed that which is free from moving and unmoving;
the mind, the sky, the earth, and water are like the notion of "I. (GarP 1.15.83)
Wind, the eye, as well as the ear, the tongue, and the nose; speech, the hands, the feet, the organ of generation, and likewise the anus and the organ of excretion. (500) GarP_1,15.84 //
Śaṅkara, Sarva, the giver of patience, the man who practices patience, the lover of devotion, the sustainer, the devoted one, and the increaser of devotion. (511) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.85.
Praised by devotees, devoted to devotees, bestower of fame, increaser of fame, fame itself, splendor,
forgiveness, beauty, and indeed the devotee himself.
Compassion is supreme.

He is the gift, the giver, and the agent; he is dear to the God of gods, pure, and possessed of purity. He is the bestower of happiness, liberation, desire, and wealth; he is the thousand-footed one. (531) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.87.
Sahasraśīrṣā, Vaidya, and likewise Mokṣadvāra; Prajādvāra, Sahasrākṣa, and Sahasrakara as well. (540)
Śukra, Sukirīṭin, Sugrīva, and likewise Kaustubha;
Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Hayagrīva, and Sūkara.
Matsya, Paraśurāma, Prahlāda, and Bali; Śaraṇya, Nitya, Buddha, and Mukta, who bears a body. (550) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.90.
The slayer of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, the crusher of Rāvaṇa,

The slayer of Kumbha and Indrajit, the crusher of Kumbhakarṇa,

He is the slayer of the wicked asuras and likewise the enemy of Śambara;

The destroyer of Yama and Arjuna, the one who bestows the benefit of austerity,
the musical instrument, the music itself, the Buddha, and the granter of boons.
The essence, the lover of the essence, the solar one, the destroyer of the slayer of time (Kāla), Agastya, Devala, Nārada, and the beloved of Nārada. (580) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.95.
Prāṇa, apāna, and likewise vyāna; rajas, sattva, and tamas; śarad; udāna and samāna; and likewise the medicine and the physician. (590) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.96.
He is immutable, of pure nature, and devoid of all bodies;

Deprived of the faculty of the hands and lacking feet, he was also devoid of the anus and genitals, and was bereft of vital breath.
Devoid of awakening and utterly lacking intellect,

Devoid of apāna and abandoned by vyāna, devoid of udāna and abandoned by samāna. (610) // GarP_1,15.100 //
Devoid of space and entirely lacking wind,
devoid of fire and bereft of water.
Devoid of earth and devoid of sound, devoid of touch and devoid of all forms. (620)
He is indeed free from passion and abandoned by sin;
he is devoid of sorrow and released from speech.
He is indeed free from passion and the sixfold transformations;
he is devoid of desire and completely abandoned by anger.
Free from greed and likewise devoid of hypocrisy,
he is subtle and exceedingly subtle,
yet also grosser than the gross.
He is the fearless one, the commander of the powers, the agitator of all,

Hari is indeed unapproachable by the two hands, and likewise unapproachable by the feet;

I am to be grasped by the intellect and likewise to be grasped by the mind; I am Śaṅkhapāṇi, the Imperishable, and likewise Gadāpāṇi. (660)
The wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇa, is the embodiment of knowledge, the scorcher of foes;

He is the object of knowledge and devoid of objects of knowledge; he is cognition whose nature is consciousness.
He is existence, that which is to be meditated upon, the creator of existence, the meditator, and the destroyer of existence.
He who has come as the protector of the cows (*gopati*), the cowherd (*gopa*) who bestows happiness upon all the cowherdesses (*gopī*);
