Upendra, Nṛsiṃha, Śauri, and Janārdana;
Āraṇeya, Bṛhadbhānu, and likewise Bṛhaddīpti.
Dāmodara, the three times, the knower of time, and the one beyond time;
the three junctions, the Dvāpara age, the Tretā age, the gateway for progeny, and Trivikrama. (700)
He is valor, he has the staff of punishment in his hand, he is the single-staffed ascetic, and the bearer of the triple-staff;
he is conciliation, the means of dissension, and likewise the means of success; he is the embodiment of peace and the singer of the Sāman hymns.
The Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, well-performed rites, and beautiful forms;

He is the form of the *Ṛk* and the *Ṛgveda*, established within the *Ṛgvedas*; he is the many-footed, the well-footed, and likewise the thousand-footed; he is the four-footed and the two-footed, as well as memory, logic, Yama, and the powerful one. (730) GarP_1,15.120.
Sannyāsin, and likewise sannyāsa, as well as the four stages of life (āśramas):

A Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and likewise a Śūdra caste;
one who possesses good conduct, endowed with virtue, and who has abandoned evil conduct. // GarP_1,15.122 //
Liberation is entered within the self; the praise, the praiser, and the worshiper;

He is the ford, the one who leads to the ford, and the knower of the ford.

He is the Praṇava, the Lord of the Praṇava, and is praised by means of the Praṇava. (770)

He who reclines upon the waters, who reclines in yoga, who reclines upon Śeṣa, and who reclines on the lotus;

Prajāpati, the eternal, the desirable, the desirer, the Virāj,

He is wealthy, a bestower of wealth, blessed, and devoted to the welfare of the Yādavas;

He is the giver of nectar, the ocean of milk, and the milk itself;
he is the son of Indra, its protector, and likewise the upholder of Mount Govardhana. (820)
Likewise, he is the destroyer of Kaṃsa, the elephant-driver who destroyed the elephant,
Śipiviṣṭa, the gracious one, and the destroyer of the suffering of all worlds.
He is the seal (mudra) and the hand, yet he is devoid of all seals;
he is the embodied one, residing within the body, and the controller of the body.
The ear, the controller of the ear, that which is to be heard, and likewise the act of hearing;
having touched the object of touch, as well as the sense of touch itself.
The seer of forms resides in the eye, as does the controller of the eye;
likewise, the knower of tastes and the regulator resides in the tongue regarding that which is seen [and tasted]. (850)
Abiding in the nose, he is the maker of the nose, the smeller, and the controller of the olfactory faculty;
abiding in speech, he is the speaker, that which is spoken, the speech itself, and the controller of speech.
Abiding in living beings, he is the artisan who fashions artistry, and he is the controller of the two hands;
he is the path and the traveler, as well as the destination and the act of going.
The controller of the two feet is the recipient of the foot-water (pādya) and the agent of emission;
likewise, that which resides in the generative organ is the controller of emission as well as pleasure. (870) GarP 1.15.138.
And likewise Upastha’s restrainer, who brought him joy;
Śatrughna, Kārtavīrya, and Dattātreya as well.
He who is beneficial to Alarka, the slayer of Kārtavīrya, Kālanemi, Mahānemi, Megha, and likewise Meghapati. (880) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.140.
The giver of food, the one whose form is food, the eater of food, and the promoter of food—
the supreme son of Devakī.
He is the delight of Devakī, the joy of Rohiṇī,
the beloved of Vasudeva, and likewise the son of Vasudeva.
Dundubhi, Hāsarūpa, and likewise Puṣpahāsa;
Aṭṭahāsapriya, Sarvādhyakṣa, Kṣara, and Akṣara. (900)
He is the infallible one, the Lord of Truth, the beloved and excellent husband of Satyā,
the husband of Rukmiṇī, and likewise the one most dear to Rukmiṇī.
He is the beloved of the gopīs (910), the one of holy fame, and the renowned;
he is Vṛṣākapi, Yama, Guhya, Makula, and likewise Budha.
Rāhu, Ketu, the planet, the seizer, the one with the face of a lordly elephant,
the destroyer of the crocodile, as well as the village-dweller and the protector.
Kinnara, Siddha, Chanda, Svacchanda,
Viśvarūpa, Viśālākṣa,
and Daityasūdana. (930) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.147.
He is of infinite form, abiding in the elements, established as gods and dānavas;
he is situated in deep sleep and is deep sleep itself, as well as the state and the very end of all states.
Abiding in the waking state, he is awake; likewise, the waking state is his locus.
Abiding in the dream state, he knows the dream; the dream is his locus, and the dream is likewise [his nature]. (940) Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.15.149.
Devoid of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, he is indeed the fourth state;
he is consciousness and the form of the object of knowledge, as well as the individual soul and the animator. (950) GarP_1,15.150 //
He is the lord of the worlds and the regulator of the worlds;
he dwells in Pātāla and is the destroyer of all fevers in Pātāla.
He is the embodiment of supreme bliss and the promoter of all phenomena;
he is both easily attained and difficult to attain, and likewise devoted to the practice of breath control. (960)
Pratyāhāra, Dhāraka, and likewise Pratyāhārakara; Prabhā, Kānti, and Arcis, which resembles pure crystal.
Agrāha, Gaura, Sarva, Śuci, Abhiṣṭuta,
Vaṣaṭkāra, Vaṣat, Vauṣaṭ, Svadhā, Svāhā, and likewise Rati.
The cooker, the one who causes joy,
the enjoyer, the knower, and likewise the one who cultivates;
the self of knowledge and the self of the body— thus [is he].
Do not [speak of] the Lord of all lords.
Nadī, Nandī, Nandīśa, Bhārata, Taruṇāśana,
Cakrapa, and Śrīpati are the lords of the universal monarchs (cakravartin).
And Īśa, the lord of all the gods, likewise resides in Dvārakā;
Puṣkara, the presiding deity of Puṣkara, and Puṣkaradvīpa itself. (1000)
Bharata, Janaka, and Janya are devoid of all forms;
they are formless, signless, free from affliction, and without support. (1008)
Thus, O Lord whose banner is the bull, this thousand names of the divine Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, has been proclaimed; it is the destroyer of all sins.
By reciting this, a twice-born man attains the state of Viṣṇu; a Kṣatriya obtains victory;
a Vaiśya gains wealth and happiness; and a Śūdra, endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, likewise attains these.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrī Viṣṇu Sahasranāma Stotra," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—16.
Rudra said:
O bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, please explain again the meditation upon Viṣṇu,
the Lord, the God, the pure Supreme Self.
Hari said:
Listen, O Rudra, to the meditation upon Hari, which destroys the tree of saṃsāra;
he is the form of pure vision, infinite, all-pervading, unborn, and immutable.
The imperishable, all-pervading, eternal, and absolute Great Brahman exists;
it is the root of the entire world, all-pervading, and the supreme Lord.
He who dwells in the hearts of all beings, the great lord of all beings,
the support of all yet himself without support, the cause of all causes.
Likewise, it is unanointed, liberated, contemplated by liberated yogis,
devoid of the gross body, and bereft of the eyes.
Devoid of the faculty of speech and lacking the qualities of a living being;
devoid of the faculty of feet and deprived of the quality of speech;
devoid of the anus and genitals, and lacking all the sense faculties.
Likewise, he is devoid of mind and free from mental phenomena;
the Lord of Gods is bereft of intellect and entirely abandoned by consciousness.
Indeed, it is devoid of egoism, free from the qualities of the intellect,
and likewise bereft of both the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
[The body] is indeed devoid of the wind called vyāna and destitute of the function of prāṇa.
Hari said:
"I shall again describe the worship of the Sun, which was formerly told to Bhṛgu. (GarP 1.16.9)
Oṃ, homage to Khakholka!
This is the root mantra of the Sun, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (GarP 1.16.10)
Oṃ, homage to Khakholka, the thirty-third deity.
Oṃ vici ṭhaṭha, homage to the head. Oṃ jñānine ṭhaṭha, homage to the crest-lock.
Oṃ, to the one with a thousand rays, ṭhaṭha; homage to the armor. GarP_1,16.11.
Oṃ, to the Lord of All Splendor, ṭhaṭha, homage to the weapon! Oṃ, blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up! ṭhaṭha, homage! // GarP_1,16.12 //
This is the mantra for the fire-enclosure, which destroys the sins of the sun:
Oṃ, let us know the Āditya; let us meditate upon the Illuminator of the Universe.
May that Sūrya inspire us.
One should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa for Rātri and Bhāskara;
[one should place] "to Dharman" in the east and "yamāya" in the south.
Then, one should worship Daṇḍanāyaka and Daivatāya in the north;
and one should worship Śyāma and Piṅgala in the northeast and the southeast, as well as Dīkṣita.
And Vajrapāṇi in the southwest, and Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ in the northwest.
Oṃ, homage to Candra, the lord of the constellations. Oṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka, the son of the Earth.
Oṃ, homage to Budha, the son of Soma.
Oṃ, homage to Vāgīśvara, the lord of all sciences.
Oṃ, homage to Śukra, the great ṛṣi, the son of Bhṛgu.
Oṃ, homage to Śanaiścara, the son of Sūrya.
Oṃ, homage to Rāhu.
Oṃ, homage to Ketu. (GarP 1.16.16)
O Bull-bannered One, these [deities] from the east to the northeast are to be worshipped:
Oṃ, homage to Anūka;
Oṃ, homage to Prathamanaṭha.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha! GarP_1,16.17
Oṃ, Blessed One, garlanded with immeasurable rays of light,
Lord of the entire world,
whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses!
Four-armed one,
bestower of supreme accomplishment,
tawny with sparks of fire!
Then: "Come, come! O you who are not naked, take, take this *arghya* which has reached my head, you of fierce radiant form!
Blaze, blaze! *ṭhaṭha namaḥ*! (GarP 1.16.18)
Having invoked [the deity] with this mantra, one should then dismiss the Sun with:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Āditya, the possessor of a thousand rays; go in happiness, for the sake of returning again. (GarP 1.16.19)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Meditation on Hari and Worship of the Sun," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 17. Hari said:
Furthermore, I shall describe the worship of the Sun as it was indeed taught to Dhanada:
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in a clean place.
Then, having formed the invocation mudrā, one should invoke the Sun;
having established the Khakholka mudrā, one should establish the mantra-form.
O Śiva, one should place the heart of the deity in the south-eastern direction;
the head should be placed in the north-eastern direction, and one should install the crest-lock (śikhā) in the south-western direction.
With a mind fixed in one-pointed concentration, he should place Dharma in the eastern direction (paurandaryā),
Netra in the northwestern direction (vāyavyā), and Astra in the western direction (vāruṇyā).
One should place Soma in the northeast, Lohita in the east,
the son of Soma (Budha) in the southeast, and Bṛhaspati in the south.
In the southwest, the preceptor of the Dānavas; in the west, Śanaiścara;
likewise in the northwest, Ketu; and in the north, Rāhu.

In the second enclosure, however, one should worship twelve Suns: Bhaga, Sūrya, Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa; ||| GarP_1,17.7 ||| tathā pūṣā tvaṣṭā caiva viṣṇurviṣṇustathaiva ca / indraścendrajayaścaiva vivasvānsavitā tathā // GarP_1,17.8 // Likewise Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, and indeed Viṣṇu again; Indra, Indrajaya, Vivasvat, and Savitṛ. ||| GarP_1,17.8 ||| tṛtīyāyāṃ tu kakṣāyāṃ vasavo 'ṣṭau prapūjayet / dhruvo 'tha mārutaścaiva somo 'tha varuṇastathā // GarP_1,17.9 // In the third enclosure, however, one should worship the eight Vasus: Dhruva, Māruta, Soma, and Varuṇa; ||| GarP_1,17.9 ||| āpaścaivānalaścaiva pratyūṣaśca prabhāsakaḥ / ete vasava ityuktā nāmabhiḥ parikīrtitāḥ // GarP_1,17.10 // Āpa, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsaka; these are declared to be the Vasus, thus proclaimed by their names. ||| GarP_1,17.10 ||| caturthyāṃ tu punaḥ kakṣāyāṃ pūjayeddvādaśartavaḥ / hemantaśiśirau caiva vasantagrīṣmavarṣāśca // GarP_1,17.11 // Furthermore, in the fourth enclosure, one should worship the twelve seasons: Hemanta, Śiśira, Vasanta, Grīṣma, and Varṣā; ||| GarP_1,17.11 ||| śaraditi caiva khyātā ṛtavaḥ parikīrtitāḥ / pañcamyāṃ tu punaḥ kakṣāyāṃ pūjayeddvādaśādityān // GarP_1,17.12 // and Śarad—thus the seasons are proclaimed. Furthermore, in the fifth enclosure, one should worship the twelve Ādityas: ||| GarP_1,17.12 ||| dhātāryamā ca mitraśca varuṇo 'ṃśo bhagastathā / indro vivasvānpūṣā ca parjanyo daśamaḥ smṛtaḥ // GarP_1,17.13 // Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga; Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth; ||| GarP_1,17.13 ||| tatas tvaṣṭā tato viṣṇurajaghanyo jaghanyajaḥ / ete dvādaśa sūryāstu nāmabhiḥ parikīrtitāḥ // GarP_1,17.14 // Then Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, who is neither the least nor born of the least; these are the twelve Sūryas, thus proclaimed by their names. ||| GarP_1,17.14 ||| ṣaṣṭhyāṃ tu punaḥ kakṣāyāṃ pūjayeddvādaśa grahān / ādityaś candramāścaiva aṅgārakaśca ketavaḥ
Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and Vivasvat of great strength;
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and likewise Indra—the twelfth is said to be Viṣṇu.
A person should worship with faith the gods beginning with Indra in the east; likewise,
one should worship Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and the other Nāgas, and so forth.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Sun," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said:
[Chapter 18 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
I shall proclaim to Kaśyapa the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya as spoken by Garuḍa;
it is meritorious, preceded by its extraction, and is considered to embody all the gods.
Having first extracted the syllable Oṃ, and immediately thereafter the syllable Huṃ, the third should be with the Visarga; this is the crusher of death and poverty. (GarP 1.18.2)
The armor-mantras (kavaca) of Īśa, Viṣṇu, Arka, Devī, and others accomplish all goals;
the great mantra Amṛteśa consists of three syllables, and its worship is equal [in power]. By reciting it, one becomes free from death and liberated from all sins.
By reciting it one hundred times, one obtains the fruit of the Vedas and the fruit of sacrifices and sacred fords;
by reciting it one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day, one conquers death and the enemy.
And one should meditate upon Amṛteśvara as seated upon a white lotus, with his two [upper] hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
while the other two hands hold a jar of nectar.
One should visualize the goddess Amṛtāmṛtabhāṣiṇī as being situated upon his very body,
holding a flask in her right hand and a lotus in her left hand.
One should indeed recite it eight thousand times during the three junctions of the day for one month;
this bestows auspicious peace against old age, death, great diseases, and enemies.
Invocation, installation, confinement, bringing into proximity, and seating;
water for the feet, water for sipping, bathing, the respectful offering (arghya), a garland, and unguent.
The lamp, the garment, the ornament, the food offering, the drink, the fan, the measure, the mudrā, the recitation, the meditation, the sacrificial fee, the oblation, and the praise.
Instrumental music, circumambulation, dance, the application of ritual placement, the rightward circuit, prostration, the mantra, the bed, salutation, and dismissal. // GarP_1,18.10 //
He who knows the worship as proclaimed from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, according to the sequence taught through the six-limbed [rite] and other methods, is a true worshipper. (GarP 1.18.11)

First, one should perform the worship of the *arghyapātra* vessel; then, the striking with the *astra-mantra*, the purification with the *kavaca-mantra*, and thereafter the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).

One should perform the worship of the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti) and so forth, as well as breath control (prāṇāyāma) on the seat; then one should perform the purification of the throne through drying and other means, and thereafter one should meditate.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs upon oneself as having the form of the deity;
thereafter, one should worship oneself in the form of light arising from the lotus of the heart.

One should cast a radiant flower either upon an image or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for the purpose of the invocation and the worship of the gateway; and the worship begins from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti).
The wise should perform the invocation of the deity, the worship of the retinue, and indeed the worship of the six limbs.
Dharma and the others, Śakra and the rest, along with their weapons and retinues,
as well as the Yugas, Vedas, and Muhūrtas— this worship brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
First, one should worship the Mātṛkās and the Gaṇas, as well as Nandin and Gaṅgā;
and previously, one should worship Mahākāla and Yamunā at the threshold.
Oṃ amṛteśvara oṃ bhairavāya namaḥ.
Likewise, oṃ juṃ haṃsaḥ sūryāya namaḥ. (GarP 1.18.19)
In this manner, one should worship Śiva, Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, and Gaṇa, as well as Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and the others.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Worship of Amṛteśa and Mṛtyuñjaya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 19.
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the Prāṇeśvara and Gāruḍa [tantras] spoken by Śiva;
first, I will describe the locations where one bitten by a snake does not survive.
If three lines are found hidden on a person's body at a funeral pyre, an anthill, a mountain, and so forth; or on the head, a monkey, a hole, or a tree; or on a bite mark—such a person does not live.
On the sixth lunar day, during the zodiac signs of Cancer and Aries, and under the asterisms of Mūla, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and others,
[afflictions occur] in the armpits, hips, throat, joints, temples, ears, abdomen, and so forth.

A mendicant carrying a staff and bearing weapons, or one who is not a true monk but a messenger of Death (kāladūtaka), causes death when bitten on the arm, the face, or the neck; indeed, such a person does not survive.
First, the Lord of Day (the Sun) enjoys [the first] half-yāma;
thereafter, the remaining six planets take their turn every day in succession.
The coils of the Nāgas are to be known in sequence during the night by the revolutions of the arrows (five):
Śeṣa is the Sun, Phaṇīpa is the Moon, and Takṣaka is said to be Mars.
Karkoṭaka is Mercury, Padma is Jupiter, Mahāpadma is Venus, Śaṅkha is Saturn, Rāhu is Kulika, and Āhi is the Sun; these are the planets.
During the day, Amarāntaka is in the portion of the Preceptor of the Gods (Jupiter);
at night, Rāhu is situated with Kulika during the time of Paṅgu.
One should observe the time-period known as Kālavatī, which is situated at the junction of two half-yāmas;
it consists of one part each of five, six, three, seven, two, four, one, and one [units].
During the day, by means of the divisions of six, six, two, one, seven, five, three, and one human [units],
[the breath] resides in the big toe, the back of the foot, the ankle, the knee, and the genitals.
At the navel, the heart, the slope of the breasts, the throat, the nostrils, the eyes,
the ears, the eyebrows, the temples, and the head— in this sequence, one by one.
The moon remains and the life-force (jīva) resides in the right side of a man's body,
while in a woman, it resides in the left side of the body, from the hand that carries the wind.
The delusion produced by that [ignorance] ceases through its destruction;
it is the supreme seed of the Self, known as Haṃsa, pure as crystal. (GarP 1.19.13)
The fourfold seed-syllable that destroys poison and sin should be given:
the first is said to be joined with the vowel *u* and a *bindu*;
the second is mounted on the sixth [vowel]; the third is likewise; and the fourth is accompanied by the *visarga*.
Oṃ kuru kule svāhā.
In ancient times, this Vidyā was held by Garuḍa for the sake of protecting the three worlds;
desiring the destruction of the serpent-demons, one should then place the Praṇava in his mouth.
The wise one should place *gale* on the throat; *kule* is prescribed for the two ankles.
*Svāhā* is for the pair of feet, and this is declared to be the *yugahā* placement.
Wherever [the mantra] is inscribed in the house, the nāgas abandon that place;
likewise, by reciting the thousandfold mantra, a thread is worn upon the ear.
If sand consecrated by this mantra is thrown into a house, the *nāgas* will abandon it;
indeed, by reciting it seven hundred thousand times, even the gods and asuras have attained accomplishment.
Oṃ suvarṇarekhe kukkuṭavigraharūpiṇi svāhā!
Thus, one should write two syllables on each petal of the eight-petaled lotus. GarP_1,19.19 //
One who has bathed with these streams of water, even if bitten, shall cast off the poison:
Oṃ pakṣi svāhā! (GarP 1.19.20)

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hand from the thumb to the little finger, one should then perform it upon the body of Garuḍa: at the head (*ke*), the mouth (*vakkre*), the heart (*hṛdi*), the genital organ (*liṅge*), and the feet (*pādayoḥ*).
Even poisonous serpents do not step upon its shadow even in a dream; moreover,
whoever should recite its hundred-thousand-fold mantra will destroy poison by merely looking at it.
Oṃ hrī hrau hrīṃ bhīruṇḍāyai svāhā. This vidyā, when recited into the ear, shall remove the poison of one who has been bitten. GarP_1,19.23 //

One should place *a* on the tips of the feet; *i* and *ī* on the ankles and the knees; *u* and *ū* on the surface of the hips; *e* and *ai* on the navel; and one should place *o* at the heart and *au*. 19.24.
One should indeed place the syllable *aḥ* on the crooked and unliberated limbs, conjoined with the *haṃsa*.
When chanted, meditated upon, and worshipped, the *haṃsa* removes poison and other afflictions. (GarP 1.19.25)
Having meditated, "I am Garuḍa," one should perform the rite that removes poison;
the *haṃ* mantra, when applied to the limbs, is said to remove poison and other afflictions.

Having placed the *haṃsa* mantra on the left hand and blocking the nostrils and mouth, the mantra shall remove the poison located in the skin, flesh, and other parts of the bitten person. (GarP 1.19.27)
Drawing it out with the breath, one should remove the venom of those who have been bitten; one should place [the mantra] upon the body of the victim and meditate upon Nīlakaṇṭha and the others.
The root of *pratyaṅgirā* drunk with rice-water removes poison;
likewise, the root of *punarnavā* and *phalinī* produced from the mouth [of the deity] has such power.
The root of white bṛhatī, karkoṭī, and gairikarṇika,
rubbed with water and applied as an ointment mixed with ghee, destroys poison.
He who drinks hot clarified butter along with the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree, as well as that produced from the *gṛñjana*, shall not suffer the increase of poison.
By smearing it on all the limbs or by drinking it, one becomes a destroyer of poison:
*hrīṃ*, the remover of poisons such as those from the *gonasā* snake. (GarP 1.19.32)
When meditated upon at the heart, the forehead, and ending with the *visarga*, it brings about subjugation and other effects;
when placed upon the vulva, it subdues a maiden and makes her flow with the water of passion.
Having recited it seven or eight thousand times, one becomes all-pervading like Garuḍa;
one becomes a poet and a possessor of a retentive memory, women become submissive, and one attains long life.
It destroys poison just as the *kathā* does; O Vyāsa, this mantra is certainly remembered as a jewel.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Means for Removing Snake Poison (the Prāṇeśvara-vidyā)," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 20.
Sūta said:
I shall declare that supreme secret, the collection of mantras spoken by Śiva:
the noose, the bow, the discus, the mallet, the trident, and the sharp-edged spear.
With these very weapons and mantras, the king shall conquer his enemies in battle. The extraction of the mantras is as follows: one should write them starting from the east upon a lotus-leaf.
The eightfold group and the eighth are renowned on the leaf of Īśāna;
the syllable *oṃ* is the seed-syllable of Brahmā, and the syllable *hrīṃ* is indeed Viṣṇu.
One should place the syllable *hrīṃ* and Śiva upon the three-pronged trident in sequence:
*oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*. (GarP 1.20.4)
Taking a trident in his hand and brandishing it toward the sky,
the gods and nāgas, upon seeing it or even merely perceiving it, shall meet their destruction.
Having meditated on a hand, smoke-colored and red, in the center of the sky, a person should contemplate it;
then evil nāgas, planets, clouds, and rākṣasas are destroyed.
This mantra protects the three worlds; what need is there to mention the world of mortals?
Oṃ jūṃ sūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. (GarP 1.20.7)
Having consecrated eight stakes made of khadira wood with mantras, one should plant them in the field;
there, no calamity such as the fall of lightning or thunder will occur.
One should consecrate eight stakes twenty-one times with the great mantras spoken by Garuḍa, and bury them in the field at night.
There is indeed affliction from lightning, mice, thunderbolts, and so forth;
Sadāśiva is *hara-kṣama-la-va-ra-yū* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva;
one should place the *piṇḍa*, which has the luster of a pomegranate flower, upon the index finger. (GarP 1.20.11)
By the mere sight of him, evil clouds, lightning, and the like,
as well as rākṣasas, bhūtas, and ḍākinīs, flee in the ten directions.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa. (Oṃ hrīṃ), obeisance to the wheel of immobilization and so forth. Oṃ aiṃ, obeisance to the Brahma-yāmalatantra, the Ḍāmara of the three worlds.
The *piṇḍa* of Bhairava has been declared to remove poison, sin, and malevolent planets;
it is the protection of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) and the crushing of spirits, *rākṣasas*, and the like.
Oṃ, homage!
Having visualized Indra’s thunderbolt in one’s hand as a protection against wicked clouds and the like, poison, hosts of enemies, and spirits are destroyed by the thunderbolt mudrā. GarP_1,20.15 //
Oṃ kṣuṃ (kṣa) namaḥ. One should visualize a noose in the left hand; by this, poisons, malevolent spirits, and the like are destroyed. Oṃ hrāṃ (hro) namaḥ.
Through its recitation, the mantra removes poisons, clouds, malevolent planets, and other such afflictions.
Having meditated upon Kṛtānta, one should indeed burn the world with the weapon of cutting:
*oṃ kṣṇaṃ (kṣma) namaḥ*. Having meditated upon Bhairava, one should perform [the rite] that removes the poison of spirits and elemental beings.
Oṃ lasaddvijihvākṣa svāhā!
This [mantra] wards off seizing spirits, elemental beings, and the like, as well as poisons and predatory birds, in fields and other such places. (GarP 1.20.18)
Oṃ kṣva (kṣṇaṃ) namaḥ. By writing [this] with blood upon a drum, the Grahas and other spirits will be made to cry out. Oṃ mara mara māraya māraya svāhā.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.20.19.
Having consecrated the trident with one hundred and eight recitations, it draws away the host of enemies by its whirling;
through the descent of the upper power, one should contract the lower power.
Mantras filled during *pūraka* (inhalation), well-consecrated during *kumbhaka* (retention),
and nourished by the *praṇava* (oṃ) when uttered—
mantras thus nourished bestow fruits like servants.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Collection of Mantras for Removing Poisons and Other Harmful Substances," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 21 of the Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
I shall describe the worship of the five-faced [Lord], which separately bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Oṃ bhūḥ! To Viṣṇu, the primordial being, the support of all, the embodied one—svāhā! (GarP 1.21.1)
First, one should perform the invocation of Sadyojāta with this [mantra]:
"Oṃ hāṃ, to Sadyojāta indeed; for eight kalās are proclaimed. (GarP 1.21.2)
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthiti (8);
Oṃ Hīṃ, to Vāmadeva—these are his thirteen digits. GarP_1,21.3 //
Rajā, Rakṣā, Rati, Pālyā, Kānti, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā, Kāmā, Buddhi, Rātri, Trāsanī, and likewise Mohinī. (13) // GarP_1,21.4 //
Manonmanī, Aghorā, as well as Mohā, Kṣudhā, Nidrā, Mṛtyu, and Māyā— these eight kalās are terrifying. (8) GarP_1,21.5 //
Oṃ haiṃ! To Tatpuruṣa belong Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti, not alone.
Oṃ hauṃ! Homage to Īśāna; [the goddesses] Niścalā, Nirañjanā, Śaśinī, Aṅganā, Marīci, and likewise Jvālinī.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Worship of the Five-Faced One," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
**The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 22** Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the supreme worship of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is peaceful, omnipresent, void, and established within the twelve measures (mātrās).
The five crooked [syllables] are short, and the limbs are long with the *bindu*;
one should utter the weapon-mantra (*astra*) together with the *visarga*, and likewise Śiva above.
With the sixth [syllable], the great mantra *haum*, which grants all objectives, one should touch the feet with both hands, and from the feet upward to the crown of the head. (GarP 1.22.3)
One should indeed perform the ritual placement of hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) for all [deities] through the Mahāmudrā;
one should purify the back with the *tālahasta* gesture and the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). (GarP 1.22.4)
Beginning with the little finger, one should assign the fingers as the limbs;
I shall now fully explain the worship within the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, and the others with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should offer the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the water for the feet (pādya), and the respectful offering (arghya) with the heart-mantra.

I shall describe the procedure for the fire ritual (agnikārya), which is equal to the single-vessel offering consisting of rinsing, bathing, and worship; one should perform the tracing of the site with the weapon-mantra (astra).
One should perform the sprinkling with the armor-mantra (varman) and carry out the placement of the power (śakti-nyāsa) with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Alternatively, one should cast the fire (jātavedas) into the heart or into the cavity of the śakti.
Having performed the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and the final expiation (niṣkṛti),
and having performed all the ritual actions with the Heart-mantra, one should offer the oblation (homa) to Śiva together with his limbs (sāṅga).
One should worship Śambhu in the maṇḍala within the interior of a lotus, marked by the syllable *ga*;
[the maṇḍala] consists of sixty-four, eight, and so forth, beginning with the sky-eyes (two) and the sky-eaters (ten).
One should cause an auspicious, semi-circular pit to be made in the southeast, measuring thirty-six [units] by forty-four [units]. GarP_1,22.11 //
The fire-mantra (agni-śāstra) is situated at the end of the life-force (parāyuḥ), and the group beginning with the heart (hṛdayādi-gaṇa) is proclaimed.
The weapon-mantra (astra) belongs to the directions, while Sadāśiva resides in the pericarp of the excellent lotus.
I shall describe initiation (*dīkṣā*), which resides within the five principles (*pañcatattva*) beginning with earth and ending with the Supreme.
Nivṛtti is [associated] with earth, Pratiṣṭhā and the others with water, Vidyā with fire, and Śānti with one's own [self]. 13.13.
Beyond Peace (śāntyatīta) is space; it is supreme, peaceful, and imperishable.
One should thus perform five hundred oblations for each [of the preceding stages].
Afterward, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should remember Śiva with joy;
for the sake of purification through expiation, one should offer eight oblations each in sequence.
One should perform the oblation with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja) and thus complete the initiation;
apart from the sacrifice, this supreme consecration is to be kept secret.
Thus, for one whose formative impressions are purified, the state of Śiva arises with certainty.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Method of Worshipping Śiva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 23] Sūta said:
I shall now describe the worship of Śiva, which is the means for attaining dharma, desire, and the other goals of life.
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with three mantras that begin with the syllable Om and end with Svāhā.
Oṃ hāṃ, to the principle of the self (ātmatattva); hīṃ, likewise to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva);
oṃ hūṃ, to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) svāhā—with these words from the heart-mantra, there should be the salutation to the ears.

The ash-bath and the libation are performed with "Oṃ hāṃ svāhā," which serves as the mantra for all [rites]. All deities and all sages [are invoked] with mantras ending in "namaḥ" or ending in "vauṣaṭ. (GarP 1.23.3)
All the ancestors end with *svadhā*, and the grandfathers also end with *svadhā*;
likewise, *oṃ hāṃ* is for the great-grandfathers, as well as for the maternal grandfathers and others.

"Hāṃ! Salutation to all the Mothers"; thereafter, one should perform the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma), then the sipping of water (ācamana) and the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and then recite the Gāyatrī mantra.
Oṃ hāṃ! Let us know that Great Lord; let us meditate upon Him whose speech is pure; may that Rudra inspire us. (GarP 1.23.6)
Having performed the ritual attendance upon the Sun, one should worship with the solar mantras:
*oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ śivasūryāya namaḥ* / *oṃ haṃ khakholkāya sūryamūrtaye namaḥ* /
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, homage to Sūrya. GarP_1,23.7.
Then one should remember Daṇḍin, Piṅgala, and the spirits (bhūtas);
having worshipped Vimaleśāna starting from the southeast, one attains supreme bliss.
One should worship Padmā with *rāṃ*, Dīptā with *rīṃ*, Sūkṣmā with *rūṃ*, Jayā with *reṃ*,
Bhadrā with *raiṃ*, Vibhūti with *roṃ*, Vimalā with *rauṃ*, and Amoghā with *raḥ*.
Raṃ for the lightning goddesses in the east and other directions, and raṃ in the center for the All-facing One;
the sun-seat for the Sun-form, hrāṃ hrūṃ (hrīṃ).
He should worship the Sun.
Oṃ Āṃ, for the heart and the crest; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Oṃ, for the topknot; Jvālinī Hraṃ, for the armor; and the weapon-mantra for the consecrated kings. (GarP 1.23.11)

One should worship all [the planets] with the heart-mantra of the Sun: *Soṃ* for Soma, *Maṃ* for Maṅgala, *Baṃ* for Budha, *Bṛṃ* for Bṛhaspati, *Bhaṃ* for Bhārgava, and *Śaṃ* for Śanaiścara. (GarP 1.23.12)
One should worship Rāhu with "Raṃ" and Ketu with "Kaṃ"; one should worship Tejaścaṇḍa with "Oṃ.
Having worshipped the Sun and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should assign the limbs [of the deity] beginning from the little finger.
HĀṂ for the heart, HŪṂ for the head, HEṂ for the crest-lock, VARṂ for the armor, and HAUṂ for the eyes;
HO for the weapon—having established the abiding power [of these mantras], one should again perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then, having prepared the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should sprinkle it with those waters and perform the worship.
One should visualize oneself seated upon a lotus with the syllable *hauṃ* for Śiva;
then, outside of that, at the door, [one should place] Nandin and Mahākāla, as well as Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the Earth.
One should worship Śrī, Astra, Vāstvadhipati, Brahmā, Gaṇa, and Guru;
then, in the center, Śakti and Ananta, and in the east and other directions, Dharma and the others.
Adharma and the others are in the fire and other directions; Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā are in the pericarp of the lotus in the center; and Raudrī and Kālī are in the eastern and other directions.
Oṃ hauṃ, [homage] to Kalavikariṇī; then to Balavikariṇī;
then to Balapramathinī, the subduer of all beings.
One should worship these [energies] beginning with Manonmanī in the middle of the row in front of Śiva;
likewise, one should worship the Seat of Śiva (Śivāsana), the Great Form (Mahāmūrti), and Śiva himself within the midst of the forms.
Invocation, installation, presence, confinement,
the rite of making complete (sakalīkaraṇa), the display of mudrās, and the offering of water for honor (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya).

One should provide water for rinsing the mouth, oil for anointing, fragrant unguents for rubbing the body, a bath, and massage; one should offer clothing, ointment, flowers, incense, a lamp, and sacrificial food (caru).

One should perform the rite of supreme consecration (paramīkaraṇa) using rinsing water (ācāma), mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa), betel (tāmbūla), hand-cleanser (hastaśodhana), the sacred umbrella and fly-whisk (chatracāmara-pāvitra).

The offering of the recitation should be performed by means of a mental image, consisting of a single-day recitation, praise, prostration, and worship with the heart-mantra and so forth; this is to be known as the limb of worship through names.
In the southeast, southwest, northwest, and center, one should worship the deities of the Tantras starting from the east;
one should also worship Indra and the others, as well as Caṇḍa, and offer the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) to him.
O protector of the most secret within the cave [of the heart], accept this recitation performed by us;
O God, may success be mine through your grace, for my stability rests in you.
Whatever action is performed, whether good or evil,
O Rudra, O Śaṅkara, destroy that for me who am established in the state of Śiva.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world;
Śiva is victorious everywhere, and he who is Śiva is indeed I myself.
Whatever has been done and whatever I shall do—all that is your well-done deed.
You are my protector and the leader of the universe; O Śiva, I have no other lord.
Now, I shall describe the worship of Śiva in another manner:
Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, Nandin, Mahākāla, and then Gaṅgā.

The Wind-weapon (pavanāstra) and Vāstvadhipa [are placed] at the door; furthermore, these [deities] beginning with Indra are to be worshipped from the east onwards, as well as the principles (tattvas): earth and water.
Fire, wind, space, smell, taste, form, and sound;
touch, speech, hands, feet, the anus, the generative organ, hearing, and the skin. GarP_1,23.32 //

I am the eye, the tongue, the nose, the mind, and the intellect, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti); I am the person (puruṣa), the serpent (nāga), the intellect (buddhi), knowledge (vidyā), the constituent parts (kalā), time (kāla), and necessity (niyati).
Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva—one who knows them becomes a liberated knower and shall become Śiva himself. (GarP 1.23.34)
He who is Śiva is Hari, he is Brahmā; I am that Brahmā, O Śaṅkara.
I shall now proclaim the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), by which one who is purified becomes Śiva.
In the heart-lotus resides the Sadyojāta mantra, the Nivṛtti-kalā, and the iḍā-nāḍī.
The two channels are Piṅgalā and [Iḍā], while the vital winds are Prāṇa and Apāna;
the body is Indra, the cause of Brahman, and the mandala is square.
The arrows, possessing the quality of a single upward thrust, bore the wind marked by the mouth; their sound resembled the resonance of the *ṛt* position and extended for a hundred *koṭis*.
Oṃ hrīṃ pratiṣṭhāyai hrūṃ hraḥ phaṭ / Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ vidyāyai hraṃ hraḥ phaṭ / The extent of the ground-tantra is eighty-four million [verses].
In the center of that, one should contemplate the tree of existence and oneself;
then, by [visualizing] the earth as facing downwards, that very thing will certainly become purified.
Vāmā is the goddess Pratiṣṭhā, and Suṣumnā is likewise the sustainer;
Samāna, Udāna, and Varuṇa are the deities, and Viṣṇu is the cause.
The Vedas are its four quarters and its qualities; likewise, white meditation is its form.
In this manner, one should fashion the throat-lotus as the maṇḍala known as the half-moon.
One should meditate upon oneself as being marked with a lotus, twenty-two koṭis in extent,
ninety-four [yojanas] in height, and facing downwards.

The palate is the location, the lotus is the seat, and Aghora is endowed with the Vidyā; the deity is the serpent Agni, whose meditation is upon the elephant-tongue at the junction of the navel and the lips.
The cause of Rudra is the threefold obstructor, possessing the three qualities and red in color;
it is a triangle in the form of a flame, measuring four hundred million [yojanas].
One should contemplate the Rudra-tattva as vast and elevated;
on the forehead is Tatpuruṣa, and that which is the peaceful Śādvala is known by the wise as Vṛṣa.
The tortoise, the lizard, the wind, and the god Īśvara as the cause;
the two opposing elements, the two qualities, and the smoky hexagonal mandala.
One should contemplate the wind-element as marked by the *bindu*, extending for eighty million [yojanas] and likewise rising for one hundred and fourteen million [yojanas].
In the twelve lotuses are the Śāntis, the Atītās, and likewise the Īśvaras;
also the channels Kuhū and Śaṅkhinī, and [the winds] Devadatta and Dhanañjaya.
The cause of the Śikhā and Īśāna is known as Sadāśiva;
one should meditate upon this single attribute as the Uddhāta, like pure crystal.
One should contemplate the sky as being sixteen crores in extent and twenty-five krores in height, and circular; this is declared to be the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
On the petals starting from the east, there are Guṇa-guru, Bīja-guru, Śakti-ananta, and Dharma, endowed with knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.

One should always meditate upon that which is called Śiva, consisting of two faces— one downward and one upward— the pericarp and filaments of a lotus, and the [energies] beginning with Vāmā, namely Ātma and Vidyā.
The reality is the Śivāsana; the form is "He Hauṃ," and obeisance to the body of knowledge.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, white in complexion, he is sixteen years of age.
The Lord has five faces and, with his ten hands, holds the gestures of fearlessness and grace, as well as a spear, a trident, and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
With his right and left hands, he holds a serpent, a rosary,
a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a blue lotus, and an excellent citron fruit.
Indeed, Sadāśiva possesses the three powers of will, knowledge, and action, and has three eyes;
likewise, one who meditates upon the worship of Śiva is forever free from time.
In this world, by the movement for one day and night, a person lives for three years;
by the movement for two days, a man lives for two years.
By moving through three days [of the breath], he lives for one year;
death does not occur prematurely, whether the cause be cold or indeed hot.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Śiva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
(Thus the worship of Śiva and others is completed.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 24.
Sūta said:
I shall describe the supreme worship of Gaṇeśa and others, which always bestows heaven;
one should worship the seat of Gaṇa, the form of Gaṇa, and the Lord of Gaṇas.
The limbs such as the heart-mantra beginning with *gām* for Durgā, the sandals of the Guru,
the seat of Durgā, her form, and the mantra *hrīṃ durge rakṣaṇī*.
The nine powers beginning with Tṛṭ are Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā,
Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, and Caṇḍavatī, in sequence.
Caṇārūpā, she known as Caṇḍikā, Durgā, and Durgā-rakṣiṇī;
the mudrās such as the vajra and sword, and Śivā and the others, starting from the southeast.
Or likewise, [one may worship] Sadāśiva as the Great Preta upon a lotus seat:
Aiṃ Klīṃ (Hrīṃ) Sauḥ, obeisance to Tripurā.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ kṣeṃ kṣaiṃ strīṃ skīṃ roṃ spheṃ sphīṃ śāṃ; [one should worship] the lotus seat, the form, and the heart-mantra of Tripurā, and so forth.
On the lotus of the seat, however, Brāhmī and the others are to be worshipped: Brāhmāṇī, Maheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Indradevatā.
Cāmuṇḍā and Caṇḍikā are to be worshipped; thereafter, one should sacrifice to those known as the Bhairavas:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra are the eight Bhairavas;
Rati, Prīti, Kāmadeva, the five arrows, and Yoginī [are the attendants].
One should contemplate Vaṭuka, Durgā, Vighnarāja, the Guru, and Kṣetrapa within the heart, in the lotus-womb mandala and the triangle.

White in color, endowed with the gestures of granting boons, holding a rosary and a book, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness— by reciting her mantra one hundred thousand times and by performing fire oblations, Tripurā becomes the bestower of spiritual accomplishments.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Tripura and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 25.
Sūta said:
Aiṃ Krīṃ Śrīṃ Spheṃ Kṣaiṃ, I worship the sandals of Anantaśakti; obeisance! GarP_1,25.1
Aiṃ Śrīṃ Phraiṃ Kṣaiṃ, I worship the sandals of Ādhāraśakti; obeisance! Oṃ Hraṃ, I worship the sandals of Kālāgnirudra; obeisance! (GarP 1.25.2)
Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ, I worship the sandals of the deity Hāṭakeśvara; homage!
Oṃ hrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the venerable Śeṣa; homage! (GarP 1.25.3)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship and pay homage to the seat named Ananta—the earth, its corresponding worlds, continents, oceans, and directions—and to the lotus seat. GarP_1,25.4 //
*Hrīṃ śrīṃ*— the *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti, the *tattvas* beginning with Earth, the worlds (*bhuvanas*) beginning with Ananta, the phonemes (*varṇas*) beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*,
the nine-fold words (*padāni*) beginning with the letter *Ha*, the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, and the limbs (*aṅgas*) beginning with *Hrāṃ* for the heart;
thus is the Great Lord of Mantras (*Mantramaheśvara*), whose nature is the perfected Vidyā, the ocean of supreme nectar, who is all beings, the directions, and the entirety of the six limbs.

I worship and pay homage to the sandals upon the lotus-seat arisen from the three root-mandalas, consisting of the earth, formed by the nine powers beginning with Śiva, and having as its pericarp the Rudra-power of the Jyeṣṭhā-cakra, characterized by the full knowledge and agency of Vidyā and Umā, which is the glorious abode of the winged ocean filled with the waters of the sea of Sadāśiva. GarP_1,25.5.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of the Seat," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 26.
Sūta said:
Immediately thereafter, the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) is performed;
the purification that brings about the Vidyā should be carried out.
Having formed the lotus mudrā, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa).
Kaiṃ, salutation to the little finger; Naiṃ, salutation to the ring finger; Maiṃ, salutation to the middle finger.
TAIM, salutation to the index finger; AṂ, salutation to the thumb;
LĀṂ, salutation to the palm.
Salutation to Vām Karapṛṣṭhā.
Now, the placement upon the body (*dehanyāsa*):
*Smaṃsmaṃ*, salutation to the wrists;
*Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, salutation to the clapping of the hands.
One should perform the clapping of hands with the sound "huṃ huṃ," which is the form of great splendor.

Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ sphaiṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, salutation to Kubjikā, sphaiṃ! Hraṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ ṅa ña ṇa na ma, O Aghorāmukhī! Hrāṃ hrīṃ kilikili vicce, O Sthaulyakrośī! Hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, salutation to the Upper Face!
Sphaiṃ, salutation to Kubjikā, the Eastern Face!
Hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ ṅa ā ña ṇa na me, salutation to the southern face.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kili kili, salutation to the western face.
Oṃ akhoramukhi, salutation to the northern face.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One; homage to the Heart! Kṣaiṃ (Kṣeṃ Aiṃ), to Kubjikā, Svāhā to the Head! Hrīṃ Krīṃ Hrīṃ Āṃ Ṅa Ña Ṇa Name, Vaṣaṭ to the Crest-lock!
Aghorāmukhi, *huṃ* for the armor;
*haiṃ haiṃ īṃ*, *vauṣaṭ* for the three eyes;
*kilikili vicce*, *phaṭ* for the weapon. (GarP 1.26.3)
(1) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the great trident-maṇḍala whose form is an unbroken circle.
(2) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the wind-maṇḍala. (3) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the moon-maṇḍala.
(4) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the maṇḍala of the great lineage of the series of awakenings.
(5) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the maṇḍala of the great Kaula.
(6) Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the maṇḍala of the gurus. (7)
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the Sāma-maṇḍala (8);
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [to] Samagra (9), [and] Siddha (10).
Salutation to the great lineage-maṇḍala of the Yoginī-pīṭhas, upapīṭhas, kṣetras, upakṣetras, and [others].
In this manner, the twelve maṇḍalas are to be worshipped in sequence. GarP_1,26.4 //
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of Karanyāsa and Other Rituals," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 27 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:

Oṃ kaṇicikīṇikakrāṇī carvāṇī, O you who seize beings, O you who possess the poison of serpents, O you who are the Narayana of the chariotless, O Uma! Burn, burn! O fierce one, O terrible one, O Maheshvari, O great-faced one, O flame-faced one, O spike-eared one, O parrot-headed one! Slay, slay the enemy! O destroyer of all! Sweat [him]! O Goddess, look upon the blood of his entire body with your mind; utterly delude, utterly delude him for the sake of Rudra!
Born in the heart of Rudra, you abide in his heart;
O Goddess, in your fierce form, protect me, protect me! Hrūṃ māṃ hrūṃ pha-pha-pha ṭha-ṭhaḥ! You who remove Skanda, the girdle-demons, infant-seizers, enemies, and poisons!
Oṃ śāle māle hara-hara! O you who possess the speed of the syllable *oṃ* and the force of poison! Hāṃ hāṃ Śavari! Huṃ Śavari! O Mistress of the *ākaula* speed!
O Viñcameghamāla, [this is] the remover of all poisons, including those of the nāgas and other beings.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of Mantras for Removing Various Poisons such as Those of Serpents," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sūta said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 28.
The Sūta said:
I shall describe the worship of Gopāla, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
At the door are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ together with Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
and likewise Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi, along with Sāraṅga, Śarabha, and Śrī.
In the east are Bhadra and Subhadra; in the south are Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka.
In the west, one should worship Bala, Prabala, Jaya, and Vijaya;
in the north, Śrī; and at the four gates, Gaṇa, Durgā, and Sarasvatī.

In the corners of the field, beginning with the southeast, and in the cardinal directions, beginning with the east, one should worship the Siddha Nārada and the others, as well as the Guru, Nalakūbara, and the Blessed One in the corner.
First, one should worship Viṣṇu, the austerity of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇutapas), and the power of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇuśakti);
then the retinue of Viṣṇu, and in the center, Śakti and Kūrma.
Ananta, Pṛthivī, Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya from Agni,
Aiśvarya preceded by Vāyu, and Prakāśātman in the north.

One should worship Ka, the principle of the crow (kākatattva), for the sake of *sattva* which is of the nature of the primordial essence (*prakṛti*), for *rajas* which has the form of delusion, and for *tamas*, the bulbous root of the lotus. GarP_1,28.7 //
One should worship the supreme principle of Vidyā, the mandalas of the Sun,
Moon, and Fire, and the seats beginning with Vimalā in the east, [uttering] "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ."
The mantra is said to end with "svāhā" for Gopījanavallabha;
its limbs (aṅgas) are, in order: Āca, Cakra, Sucakra, and likewise Vicakra.
The Sudarśana discus, the enemy of the asuras and protector of the three worlds, [is placed] in the first corners starting from the heart; the weapon (astra) and the spear (śakti) are in the east.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Sunandā, Nāgnajitī,
Lakṣmaṇā, Mitravindā, Jāmbavatī, and Śuśīlā.
One should worship the conch, discus, mace, lotus, club, and Śārṅga bow;
one should worship the sword, noose, and goad in the east, as well as the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem.
One should worship the crown, the garland of *vala*, the chief banners of Indra and the others, Kumuda and the other attendants, Viṣvaksena, and Kṛṣṇa together with Śrī.
Through recitation, meditation, and worship, one shall attain all desires.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Śrī Gopāla," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 29—
Hari said:
I shall now describe Trailokyamohinī, who is foremost among the forms of Puruṣottama,
as well as the worship mantras beginning with Śrīdhara, which bestow dharma, desire, and the other goals of life.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrūṃ oṃ namaḥ! O Puruṣottama, O Peerless One, O Abode of Lakṣmī, O Agitator of the World, O Piercer of the Hearts of All Women, O You who Cause Intoxication and Madness in the Three Worlds, [you who] burn, burn the minds of the beautiful women among gods, asuras, and humans; dry up, dry them up; kill, kill them; paralyze, paralyze them!
Cause to run, cause to run! Draw forth, draw forth!

O most fortunate one, maker of all good fortune, granter of all desires! Slay, slay so-and-so with the discus, with the mace, with the sword, and with all arrows; pierce, pierce! Crush, crush with the noose! Strike, strike with the goad! Hurry, hurry! Why do you stand still?
Deliver, deliver me until my desire is accomplished! Hrīṃ (Hrūṃ) Phaṭ! Namaḥ! // GarP_1,29.2 //
Oṃ śrīṃ (śrīḥ), obeisance to Śrīdhara, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds. Klīṃ, obeisance to Puruṣottama, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds. GarP_1,29.3 //
Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds. Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds. (GarP 1.29.4)
All mantras that enchant the three worlds accomplish every purpose;
they may all be contemplated either individually or collectively, whether in detail or in brief.
The seat, the form-mantra, and the six ancillaries beginning with the fire-oblation;
the discus, the mace, the sword, the pestle, the conch, and the horn-bow.
By worshipping Viṣvaksena— who is joined by Lakṣmī and Garuḍa, and who holds an arrow, a noose, and a goad—
the monkey shall obtain everything in full detail.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Trailokyamohinī (Śrīdhara)," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 30 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa]
Sūta said:
I shall describe in detail the auspicious worship of Śrīdhara;
indeed, the retinue of all [the deities] should be understood as identical by the wise.
Oṃ śrāṃ, homage to the heart.
Oṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to the head.
Oṃ śrū, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ śraiṃ kavacāya huṃ / Oṃ śrauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ / Oṃ śraḥ astrāya phaṭ. // GarP_1,30.2 //
One should display one's own mudrās, such as those of the conch, discus, and mace;

Homage to the one with the excellent wheel, to the one with the diverse wheels, to the differentiator of all mantras, to the progenitor, to the sustainer of the world, and to the destroyer of the world.
Salutations again and again to the one who exists for the protection of the worlds, to the destroyer of wicked Asuras, to the fierce and the gentle, and to the wrathful.
Salutations to the Eye, whose form is the sky; salutations again and again to Śiva, the shatterer of the fear of saṃsāra and the breaker of the cage of māyā.
Salutations to the Lord of the planets, who takes the form of both the planets and their over-controllers;
salutations again and again to Time, to Death, and to the Terrible One.
Salutations again and again to the bestower of grace upon devotees, to the protector of devotees,
to the one whose form is Viṣṇu, to the peaceful one, and to the wielder of weapons.
"Obeisance to the discus, the weapon of Viṣṇu; obeisance again and again.
Thus has this highly meritorious hymn to your discus been proclaimed.
He who recites this with supreme devotion goes to the world of Viṣṇu. O Rudra, he who, having conquered his senses, recites the ritual procedure for the worship of the Discus,
reduces his sin to ashes and becomes fit for the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Sudarśana," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—34.
Rudra said:
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Gadādhara, speak again of the worship of the gods;
there is no satiety for me as I listen to your discourse on their adoration."
Hari said: I shall describe to you the worship of the god Hayagrīva;
listen to that, by which Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, is well-pleased.
O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, I shall first proclaim the root mantra of Hayagrīva, which expresses his nature and is supremely meritorious; listen to it. GarP_1,34.3.
"Oṃ saiṃ kṣaiṃ, salutation to the head"—this nine-syllable mantra, joined with the Praṇava, bestows all branches of knowledge. (GarP 1.34.4)
O Mahādeva, O Bull-bannered One, hear now its limbs:
"Oṃ kṣāṃ, salutation to the heart;
oṃ kṣīṃ, svāhā to the head—the head is thus declared; likewise, kṣūṃ vaṣaṭ. (GarP 1.34.5)
O Bull-bannered One, the crest-lock (śikhā) of the God is to be known as joined with *oṃ kāra*;
*oṃ kṣaiṃ kavacāya huṃ* is indeed proclaimed as the armor (kavaca). GarP_1,34.6 //
Oṃ kṣaiṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; this is proclaimed as the eye of the God. Oṃ haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon; this is proclaimed as the weapon of the God. (GarP 1.34.7)

I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for worship; listen as I speak it to you. Having first bathed and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then proceed to the sacrificial hall.
Then, having entered, one should perform the rites of drying and so forth according to the rules;
having solidified [the ground] with the seed-syllables *yaṃ*, *kṣaiṃ*, and *raṃ*, and with *laṃ*.
Having produced the egg, one should then split it with the syllable Oṃ alone;
within the center of the egg, one should contemplate oneself as Hayagrīva.
White as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, with the luster of a lotus stalk or silver,
resembling cow’s milk and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns;
he has four arms, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
The Lord wore a crown and earrings, was adorned with a forest garland,
possessed beautiful wheels and lovely cheeks, and was clothed in blue garments.
Having meditated upon the Great-Souled One accompanied by all the gods,
one should then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the limb-mantras and likewise with the root-mantra.
Then, O Śaṅkara, one should display auspicious mudrās such as the conch and the lotus; having meditated upon Viṣṇu, one should worship him with the root mantra.
Then one should invoke the deities of the seat of Rudra:
"Oṃ, O deities of the seat of Hayagrīva, please come! (GarP 1.34.15)
Having invoked them into the mandala, one should worship them in a svastika and other such designs;
O Bull-bannered One, the worship of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ should be performed at the door.
"Salutation to the one with his entire retinue, the infallible one"—
with this [mantra], worship should be performed in the center, and one should also honor Gaṅgā at the door.
One should worship the great goddess Yamunā, as well as the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma, and Garuḍa in front; one should worship Śakti in the center.
O Mahādeva, one should then worship the one called Ādhāra, followed by Kūrma; thereafter, one should worship Ananta and Pṛthivī, and then Dharma and Jñāna.
One should worship detachment and sovereignty in the [deities] beginning with Āgneya;
however, one should worship unrighteousness, ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of sovereignty in the east and other directions.
One should then worship Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas in the middle region;
one should also worship the bulb, the stalk, and the lotus in the center.
"O Rudra, it is proclaimed that the worship of the mandalas known as Arka, Soma, and Agni must be performed in the central region."
O Bull-bannered One, Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Yogeśvarī, Prahvī, Satyā, and Īśānā—these are indeed the powers (śaktis) in the yoga of action. GarP_1,34.23.
And on the petals in the east and other directions, Vimala and the others are to be worshipped;
by men seeking the highest good, Anugrahā should be worshipped in the pericarp.
O Mahādeva, one should worship the seat with these mantras consisting of the names preceded by the syllable *praṇava*, ending in *namaḥ*, and in the dative case.
Through the offering of bathing water and perfumes, the offering of flowers and incense,
and the giving of lamps and food offerings, the worship of the seat is auspicious.
"O Hara, it has been proclaimed to you that this must be performed according to this rite;
thereafter, one should invoke the god Hayagrīva, the lord of the gods."
One should visualize him as coming through the left nostril;
O Śaṅkara, he comes by means of this practice using the root mantra.
The invocation of the God of gods, the bearer of the conch, should be performed;
having invoked him into the mandala, one should unweariedly perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon it.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate the Supreme Lord Hayagrīva, the Great God who is saluted by gods and asuras, residing therein.
Having visualized the imperishable Viṣṇu joined by Indra and the other world-protectors,
one should display the auspicious mudrās, such as those of the conch and the discus.
Then one should offer water for the feet, the respectful oblation, and water for sipping to Viṣṇu;
thereafter, one should bathe the healthy Lord Padmanābha.
Having installed the deity according to the prescribed rite, O bull-bannered one, one should offer a garment;
then indeed one should offer water for sipping (ācamana), and thereafter a beautiful sacred thread (upavīta).
Then, O Rudra, one should meditate upon the Lord, the Supreme Ruler, within the mandala;
having meditated, O Śaṅkara, one should again offer water for the feet and other honors to the God.
O Śaṅkara, one should offer [oblations] to the god Bhairava with the root mantra;
with "Oṃ Kṣāṃ, obeisance to the heart," one should worship the heart.
Oṃ kṣīṃ, salutation to the head; thus there shall be the worship of the head. Oṃ kṣūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock; with this one should worship the crest-lock. (GarP 1.34.36)
Oṃ kṣaiṃ, obeisance to the armor; one should worship the armor. Oṃ kṣaiṃ, obeisance to the eyes; with this [mantra], one should worship the eyes. (GarP 1.34.37)
With "Oṃ kṣaḥ, obeisance to the weapon," one should worship the weapon;
likewise, the heart, the head, the crest-lock, and the armor.
One should indeed worship these in the directions starting from the east;
O Rudra, one should worship the Weapon-mantra in the corners and worship the Eye-mantra in the center.
One should worship the supreme goddess Lakṣmī, the auspicious bestower of fortune;
one should worship the conch, the lotus, the discus, and the mace, starting from the east.
O Rudra, one should worship the sword, the mace, the noose, the goad, and the bow with arrow in the east, using these mantras consisting of their respective names.
O Rudra, one should worship from the east the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, the garland, and the auspicious yellow garment, as well as the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace.
Likewise, [he should worship] Brahmā, Nārada, the Siddha, the Guru, and the Paraguru,
as well as the sandals of the Guru and those of the Supreme Guru.
Then Indra with his mount and likewise surrounded by his retinue,
as well as Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Vāyu.
O Bull-bannered One, one should thus worship Soma, Īśāna, and Brahmā; one should worship them starting from the east and extending upward to the zenith.
Then one should worship the weapons: the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner, the mace, the trident, and the wheel and lotus.
Then, O Bull-bannered One, one should worship the god Viṣvaksena in the northeastern direction with these mantras, preceded by the syllable Om and ending in "namaḥ."
O Mahādeva, O bull-bannered one, worship must be performed for Ananta;
O bull-bannered one, the worship of the deity must be performed with the root mantra.
One should offer him fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings, as well as circumambulation, prostration, and the recitation of mantras.
O Bull-bannered One, one should also praise with other hymns beginning with the *praṇava*:
"Oṃ, salutation to Hayaśiras; salutation indeed to the Overseer of Knowledge."
Homage to the one whose nature is knowledge, homage again and again to the giver of knowledge;
homage to the peaceful deity, homage to the Self consisting of the three qualities.
Salutations indeed to the slayer of gods and asuras, the destroyer of all the wicked,
the sovereign of all worlds, who possesses the form of Brahmā.
Homage to the one worthy of worship by the lords, who bears the conch and the discus;
homage to the primordial one, the self-controlled, and the benefactor of all beings.

Salutations again and again to the one who consists of the three qualities yet is himself without qualities, whose nature is that of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the creator and the destroyer, the Lord of gods, who is omnipresent.
Having thus performed this praise, O Rudra, one should meditate upon the God of gods within the stainless lotus of the heart, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Resembling ten million suns, beautiful in every limb,
Hayagrīva, the Lord of the lords of the earth, the imperishable Supreme Self.
Thus, O Śaṅkara, the worship of Hayagrīva has been described to you;
he who recites this with supreme devotion shall go to the highest state.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of Hayagrīva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 35. Hari said:
I shall now proclaim the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites of the *Gāyatrī*; listen, O Śaṅkara!
Viśvāmitra is its seer (*ṛṣi*), and Savitṛ is its deity.
She has the head of Brahmā, the crest-lock of Rudra, and resides in the heart of Viṣṇu;
she has the ritual application as her sole eye and is born of the lineage of Kātyāyana.
She who moves through the three worlds should be known as residing within the womb of the Earth;
having understood Gāyatrī thus, one should recite her mantra twelve hundred thousand times.
It should be known that [the mantra] consists of three quarters with eight syllables each, or four quarters with six syllables each;
it is prescribed as being in three quarters for recitation (japa) and in four quarters for ritual worship (arcana).
In the ritual placement (nyāsa), in recitation (japa), as well as in meditation (dhyāna), in the fire-ritual (agnikārya), and likewise in worship (arcana),
one should constantly apply the Gāyatrī, which destroys all sins.
Know [the sequence] at the toes of the feet, in the middle of the ankles, in the two shanks, in the two knees, in the two thighs,
in the private parts, in the scrotum, in the channel, in the navel, and in the slender belly.
On the two breasts, the heart, the throat, the lips, the mouth, the palate,
the two shoulders, the eyes, the eyebrows, and the forehead— [these are the locations] in the east, south, and north.
One should place the letter *Ā* on the fifth [finger], at the head; I shall now describe the colors:
sapphire-blue, fire-colored (red), yellow, dark-green, and tawny like a Kapila bull.
White, with the luster of lightning, star-like, black, red—in that sequence;
then dark-blue, white, yellow, and white like a ruby.
The color of a conch, pale white, red like wine,
resembling the color of the sun, gentle, like a conch, and even pure white.
Whatever one touches with the hand and whatever one sees with the eye, all that becomes purified; they know nothing superior to the Gāyatrī.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gāyatrī Nyāsa," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 36.
Hari said:
I shall proclaim the ritual of the twilight (sandhyā-vidhi), which destroys the sins of Rudra; listen!
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should commence the twilight bath.
One should recite the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Praṇava, the Vyahṛtis, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
A twice-born man should burn away the defects born of mind, speech, and body through breath-control (prāṇāyāma);
therefore, at all times, he should be devoted to breath-control.
Having recited "Agniś ca mā" in the evening, one should drink water in the morning with the mantra "Sūryaś ca mā";
at midday, having touched water according to the prescribed rule, one should drink it with the mantra "Āpaḥ punantu. (GarP 1.36.4)
One should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with water from *kuśa* grass using the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā";
however, at every step, one should pour water while joined with the syllable *praṇava*.

One should burn away these nine defects—those arising from passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and one's own delusion (moha); those born of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; and those produced by speech, mind, and action—by means of the nine [breaths].
Having drawn up water into his hand and recited the *Drupadā* mantra, he should pour it out;
he should perform the *Aghamarṣaṇa* rite three, six, eight, or twelve times.
One should worship the Sun with the two verses beginning with "ud u tyam" and "citram";
whatever sin has been committed by day or by night, all of it perishes instantly.
One should stand during the morning twilight reciting [the Gāyatrī], and sit during the evening twilight,
reciting the Gāyatrī joined with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and accompanied by the Praṇava.

The Gāyatrī destroys the evil committed in ten lifetimes by means of a hundred recitations, that committed in the past by means of a thousand, and that committed over three ages (yugas) by means of ten thousand.
Gāyatrī is red, Sāvitrī is white in color, and Sarasvatī is to be known as black; thus the three junctions (saṃdhyā) are described.
Having assigned *oṃ bhūḥ* to the heart, one should assign *oṃ bhuvaḥ* to the head;
and *oṃ svar*, the first foot of the Gāyatrī, to the crest-lock.
The wise one should perform the placement for the armor; he should place the second [syllable] upon the eyes, the third as the placement of the limbs, and the fourth he should place everywhere.

At the time of twilight, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas; may there be auspiciousness for him throughout the entire day. One intent on breath control (prāṇāyāma) should perform the placement during the morning.
The three-footed Gāyatrī is indeed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; having understood its application, seer, and meter, one should begin the recitation.
Freed from all evil, one shall attain the world of Brahmā;
that which is beyond the dust [of passion], accompanied by the syllable *sāvada* and *oṃ*, is declared to be the fourth state (*turīyapada*).
The Sun destroys that [merit] of one who does not perform the twilight worship;
however, the seer of even the fourth state remains truly stainless.
The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Sandhyā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 37—
Hari said:
The Gāyatrī is the supreme goddess, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for whoever recites her, even his greatest sins are destroyed. (GarP 1.37.1)
I shall now proclaim the Gāyatrī-kalpa, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one should recite it one thousand and eight times, or otherwise, one hundred and eight times.
Having recited it one hundred times at the three junctions of the day, one shall attain the world of Brahmā;
at the time of twilight, one should invoke and worship the Goddess, the destroyer of all sins.
Accompanied by the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and the twelve names, [one should offer salutations] with: "Obeisance to Gāyatrī;
repeated obeisance to Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī."
To Vedamātrā, Sāṃkṛtyā, Brahmāṇī, and Kauśikī in sequence;
to Sādhyā, Sarvārthasādhinī, Sahasrākṣī, and Bhūrbhuvaḥ.
One should thus offer oblations into the fire— fuel sticks, clarified butter,
and sacrificial grain— either one thousand and eight times, or else eight hundred times with clarified butter.
For the sake of accomplishing desires for the Dharma and other goals, one should perform oblations in all rites after having worshipped an image fashioned from sandalwood or gold.
Just as one hundred thousand recitations should be performed while subsisting on milk, roots, and fruits,
so by performing twenty thousand fire-offerings, one shall obtain all desires.
Born on the northern peak, dwelling upon the mountain on earth, you have been granted permission by Brahmā; go, O Goddess, as you please.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Gāyatrī-kalpa," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—38.
Hari said:
On the ninth day and so forth, one should worship Durgā with the mantra: "Hrīṃ! O Durgā, the Protectress!
O Mother, O Mother, O Excellent Durgā, the accomplisher of all desires and goals! (GarP 1.38.1)
By this offering of oblation, grant me all my desires:
Gaurī, Kālī, Umā, Durgā, Bhadrā, Kānti, and Sarasvatī.
Maṅgalā, Vijayā, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Nārāyaṇī, in this order—
one who worships them starting from the third day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa shall never suffer separation.
She has eighteen arms, holding a shield, a bell, a mirror, and a threatening gesture;
a bow, a banner, a hand-drum, an axe, and a noose.
One should visualize her with eighteen arms, holding a spear, a mace, a trident, a skull-cup, an arrow, a goad, a vajra, a wheel, and a probe.
I shall now proclaim the mantra of the Blessed Lady, as well as the rules for its recitation and other rites.

Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Cāmuṇḍā, dweller in the cremation ground, holding a skull in hand, mounted upon a great *preta*, surrounded by a multitude of great celestial palaces, O Night of Doom, encircled by many hosts, with a great mouth and many arms, adorned with fine bells, *ḍamaru* drums, and small bells, laughing with loud,
boisterous laughter, uttering *kili-kili* and *huṃ*, abounding in all sounds and noises, her body clothed in elephant hide, smeared with blood and flesh, with a lolling tongue.
O Great Rākṣasī, fierce with terrible fangs, possessing a terrifying and loud *aṭṭāṭṭa* laugh, with a radiance like flashing lightning; move, move!

O you with wide, gaping eyes, *hili hili*, O you with a quivering tongue, *hrauṃ hrīṃ*, O you whose face is knit in a frown, O you seated upon the auspicious seat of the syllable *oṃ*, encircled by a garland of skulls, wearing a crown of matted hair and the moon; O you with the *aṭṭāṭṭa* laugh, *kilikili*, *huṃ huṃ*, O you who create a terrible darkness with your fangs, O destroyer of all obstacles!
Accomplish this rite, accomplish it quickly! Perform, perform! Ka-ha-ka-ha! Cause [them] to enter the goad! Group by group, cause to tremble, cause to tremble!
Move, move! Cause to shake, cause to shake! O you who delight in blood, flesh, and wine! Strike, strike! Pound, pound! Cut, cut!
Kill, kill! Anubūma, anubūma! Accomplish, accomplish the adamantine body—even one that has gone to the three worlds, whether wicked or not wicked!
Whether seized or unseized, enter, enter! Step forward, step forward! Dance, dance! Bind, bind! Leap, leap!
O you with hollow eyes, O you with upraised hair, O you with the face of an owl, O you who wear hand-bells and a garland of skulls! Burn, burn! Cook, cook!
Seize, seize! Cause [him] to enter into the center of the mandala! Why do you delay? By the truth of Brahmā, by the truth of Viṣṇu!
By the truth of the Ṛṣis, by the truth of Rudra, cause [them] to enter, cause [them] to enter! Kilikili! Khilikhili! Milimili! Cilicili! O you who assume a deformed shape!
O you whose body is entwined by black serpents! O you who cause all seizing spirits to enter! O you with hanging lips! O you whose nose is buried between your brows! O you with a hideous face!
O you with tawny matted hair! O Brāhmī! Break, break! Blaze, blaze! O you with a dark face! Khalakhala! Kharakharaḥ! Cause them to fall, cause them to fall!

O Red-Eyed One! Shake, shake! Cause the earth to tremble! Strike down, strike down! Seize the head, seize it! Close the eyes, close them! Break, break the feet! Seize them, seize them! Shatter, shatter the seal! *Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*! Tear asunder, tear asunder!
Pierce, pierce with the trident! Strike, strike with the vajra! Beat, beat with the staff! Cut, cut with the discus!
Pierce, pierce with the spear;

bite, bite with the fang; nail, nail with the stake; split, split with the knife; seize, seize with the goad! O Brahmāṇī, come, come! O Māheśvarī, come, come! O Kaumārī, come, come! O Vārāhī, come, come!
Aindri, come, come! Cāmuṇḍā, come, come! Vaiṣṇavī, come, come! O wanderer of the Himalayas, come, come! O dweller of Kailāsa, come, come!

Cut, cut the spells of others! Kilikili! Bimbe! Aghore! You of terrible form! Cāmuṇḍā, you who have issued forth from the darkness of Ruru’s wrath! Destroyer of the Asuras! O sky-goer, bind, bind with the noose! Stay, stay at the moment of the commitment! [Enter] the maṇḍala!

Enter, enter! Fall, fall! Seize, seize! Bind the mouth, bind, bind! Bind the eyes, bind, bind! Bind the heart, bind, bind! Bind the hands and feet, bind, bind! Bind all evil grahas, bind, bind! Bind the cardinal directions, bind, bind! Bind the intermediate directions, bind, bind! Bind above, bind, bind! Bind below with ashes, bind, bind!
With water, clay, or mustard seeds, cause [them] to enter, cause [them] to enter! Strike them down, strike them down! O Cāmuṇḍā, kilikili vicche hrīṃ (huṃ) phaṭ svāhā!
