Indeed, the recitation of the garland-mantra consisting of one hundred and eight phrases is performed with eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets, offered for each individual phrase eight thousand times.
One should worship each individual word one thousand and eight times with human flesh smeared with the three sweets;
and one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets. (GarP 1.38.9)
Alternatively, human flesh mixed with the three sweets accomplishes all rites;
by casting water, mustard seeds, ashes, and so forth, one gains victory in battle and similar contests.
She should be meditated upon as having twenty-eight arms, or eighteen arms;
or she may be meditated upon as having twelve, eight, or even four arms.
Two hands are equipped with sword and shield, two others are joined with mace and staff,
two more are provided with arrow and bow, and two are endowed with sword and mudrā.
Two others are equipped with a sword and a bell; two others are joined with a banner-staff;
two others are enriched with an axe and a discus; and two others are provided with a hand-drum and a mirror.
And two others rest upon their hands holding spears, while others are equipped with clubs;
some are joined with nooses and javelins, and others with ḍhakās and paṇavas.
Threatening others with her very hand, she makes a tumultuous sound;
she holds the gestures of fearlessness and the svastika, and as Mahiṣaghnī, she rides upon a lion.
Victory to you, O Mistress of Beings, surrounded by all beings!
Protect me from your own creatures; accept this offering; homage be to you!

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Mantras for the Recitation, Worship, and Offering to Durgā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—39.
Rudra said:
O Janārdana, please speak again briefly of the worship of the Sun,
who is a form of Viṣṇu, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Vāsudeva said:
Listen, O Rudra, I shall speak again of the worship of the Sun:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Uccaiḥśravas; Oṃ, obeisance to Aruṇa."
Oṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin;
Oṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala.
These two should indeed be worshipped at the gateway with these mantras, O Bull-bannered One.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Prabhūtā! One should worship this one named Prabhūtāmaḷa in the center.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Vimalā!
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Sāra.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Ādhāra.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Paramamukha.
Thus, Vimalā and the others are indeed to be worshipped in the corners beginning with the southeast.
Oṃ, obeisance to the lotus; oṃ, obeisance to the pericarp.
O Rudra, one should worship in the center, and likewise in the directions beginning with the east.
One should worship Dīptā and the others in the center, and worship those who face in all directions.
Oṃ vāṃ (rāṃ), obeisance to Dīptā. Oṃ vīṃ (rīṃ), obeisance to Sūkṣmā.
Oṃ vūṃ (rūṃ), obeisance to Bhadrā.
Oṃ vaiṃ (raiṃ), obeisance to Jayā.
Oṃ vauṃ (rauṃ), obeisance to Vibhūti.
Oṃ vaṃ (raṃ), obeisance to Adhorā.
Oṃ vaṃ (raṃ), homage to Vaidyutā.
Oṃ vaḥ (raḥ), homage to Vijayā.
Oṃ raḥ, homage to Sarvatomukhī. // GarP_1,39.4 //
Oṃ, homage to the seat of the Sun. Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to the form of Sūrya.
One should worship these in the center; now hear the hṛn-mantras, O Śaṅkara.

Oṃ haṃ saṃ khaṃ, to Khakholka, krāṃ krīṃ saḥ svāhā; homage to the form of the Sun. With this [mantra], one should perform the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the bringing into proximity (sannidhāpana), and likewise the ritual integration of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa) using the mantra for the complete immersion (sanniropana).
O Rudra, O Hara, show the mudrā, or [show it] with the root mantra;
[it is] of the nature of brilliance, red in color, standing upon a white lotus,
mounted on a chariot with a single wheel, two-armed, and holding a lotus.
One should thus always meditate upon the Sun; now hear the root mantra:
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryāya namaḥ.
Three times one should display the lotus mudrā and the image (bimba) mudrā.
Oṃ āṃ, homage to the heart;
oṃ arkāya, svāhā to the head.
Oṃ aḥ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, vaṣaṭ to the flaming crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ huṃ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca).
Oṃ bhāṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two eyes (netra).
Oṃ vaḥ astrāya phaṭ. (GarP 1.39.8)
One should worship Hara in the southeast, the northeast, or the southwest;
one should worship the heart and so forth in the northwest, and worship the eye within.
O Rudra, one should worship Soma, who is clothed in rags and white in color;
O Rudra, on the eastern petal, one should worship Budha, who has the luster of gold.
One should worship Rudra in the south and worship the Guru of the same color;
likewise, Bhūteśa in the west and the white Bhārgava in the north.
O Hara, one should worship the red Aṅgāraka in the southeast;
one should worship Śanaiścara, who is black in color, in the southwestern direction.
O Hara, one should worship Rāhu in the northwest, resembling a *nandyāvarta* flower,
and Ketu in the northeast, of smoky color.
O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, listen to these mantras as well.
Oṃ soṃ, homage to Soma.
Oṃ buṃ, homage to Budha.
Oṃ bṛṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati.
Oṃ bhaṃ, homage to Bhārgava. Oṃ aṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka.
Oṃ śaṃ, homage to Śanaiścara.
Oṃ raṃ, homage to Rāhu.
Oṃ kaṃ, homage to Ketu. Thus [it is said].
O Śaṅkara, having offered the water for the feet and the other items with the root mantra to Sūrya,
the best of practitioners should display the cow-mudrā at the conclusion of the food offering.
Having recited it eight thousand times, one should offer it to him;
then, in the northeastern direction, one should worship Tejaścaṇḍa, the Lord of Beings.
Oṃ tejaścaṇḍāya huṃ phaṭ svadhā svāhā pauṣaṭ.
O Hara, one should offer him the remains of the flowers (nirmālya) and then present the water for honor (arghya).
Combined with sesame seeds and rice, anointed with red sandalwood,
mixed with scented water, and provided with flowers and incense.
Placing that vessel upon his head and kneeling upon the ground,
O bull-bannered one, he should offer the arghya to the Sun with the heart-mantra.
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa and all the gurus, one should then worship all the gods:
Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to the gurus. (GarP 1.39.21)
The worship of the Sun has been described; by performing this, one becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Method of Worshipping the Sun," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 40.
Śaṅkara said:
O wielder of the conch and mace, tell me the worship of Māheśvarī,
knowing which, O Supreme Lord, human beings attain perfection.
Hari said:
Listen, O bull-bannered one, as I describe the worship of Maheśvara;
having first bathed, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and sat down upon a seat.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the mandala, one should indeed worship Maheśvara,
O Great Lord, with these mantras, together with his retinue, Hara.
"Oṃ hāṃ! O deities of Śiva’s throne, come!
With this, one should invoke the Rudra deities who belong to the throne.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṇapati.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sarasvatī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nandin.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahākāla. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṅgā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Lakṣmī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahākalā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Weapon-mantra (astra). Thus [it is said]. GarP_1,40.5.
O Hara, these indeed should be worshipped at the gateway with baths, perfumes, and other offerings:
*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the gurus.*
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to knowledge! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to dispassion!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to sovereignty!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to non-virtue (adharma). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to ignorance (ajñāna).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to lack of detachment (avairāgya).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Anaiśvarya.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Urdhvacchanda.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Adhaśchanda.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lotus. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the pericarp.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāmā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Raudrī.
Oṃ, homage to Kālī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kalavikaraṇī. Oṃ, homage to Balapramathinī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sarvabhūtadamanī.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Manonmanī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the three mandalas.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ haṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipati). Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hauṃ, homage to Śiva.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Heart.
Oṃ, homage to the head.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the crest-lock. Oṃ haiṃ, homage to the armor.
Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the three eyes.
Oṃ haḥ, salutation to the weapon.
Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta. (GarP 1.40.6)
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Siddhi! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ṛddhi!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vidyutā!
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bodhā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Svadhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Prabhā! (GarP 1.40.7)
The eight digits of Truth (satya) are to be known; they are to be worshipped, situated in the directions starting from the east.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rajas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rakṣā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rati. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kanyā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kāmā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jananī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kriyā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vṛddhi.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kāryā. Oṃ rā(dhā), homage to Rādhā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhrāmaṇī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mohinī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kṣavarā.
O Bull-bannered One, the Vāmadeva-kalā is to be known as the thirteenth.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Tatpuruṣa.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nivṛtti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pratiṣṭhā.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vidyā;
oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śānti.
O Bull-bannered One, these four are to be known as belonging to Tatpuruṣa alone.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Tṛṣṇā. O Hara, the six parts (kalās) of Akhora should be known as Bhairava. GarP_1,40.11.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Samiti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aṅgadā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kṛṣṇā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Marīcī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jvālā.
O bull-bannered one, know that there are five kalās of Īśāna.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the retinue of Śiva!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Indra, the lord of the gods!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Agni, the lord of brilliance!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama, the lord of the pretas.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nirṛti, the lord of the rākṣasas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa, the lord of the waters.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Soma, the lord of the eyes.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna, the lord of all vidyās.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ananta, the lord of the nāgas.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of all worlds.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dhūlicaṇḍeśvara. (GarP 1.40.13)
O Śaṅkara, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the bringing near (sannidhāna),
as well as the confinement (sannirodha) and the ritual of making [the deity] complete (sakalīkaraṇa).
The placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), the display of the mudrās, and meditation itself;
the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), flowers, and the application of unguents (abhyaṅga).
Then [he should offer] fragrant unguents for rubbing the body, bathing, scented ointments,
garments, ornaments, enjoyments, the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), and incense.
The offering of a lamp, the gift of food offerings, the rubbing of the hands,
as well as water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, fragrance, betel, song, and instrumental music.
Dancing, the making of parasols and other implements, the display of mudrās,
as well as form, meditation, recitation, and the state of oneness.
One should indeed perform the recitation, worship, and offering with the root mantra;
O Rudra, this worship of Māheśī has been described as the destroyer of sins.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of Maheśvara," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 41 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Vāsudeva said:
Oṃ! The Gandharva named Viśvāvasu is the lord of maidens; I obtain for you a maiden, having produced her for that Viśvāvasu—svāhā!
Through the recitation of this mantra, there is the attainment of a woman; now I shall speak of Kālarātri.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, O Ṛkṣakarṇī, four-armed one, with hair standing erect, three-eyed, O Kālarātri, consumer of the fat and blood of humans! Bestower of death upon [the name] who has reached his time, hūṃ phaṭ! Slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook the flesh and blood! O wife of the bear, svāhā!
No lunar day, no asterism, and no fasting is prescribed. (GarP 1.41.2)
Enraged, having wiped his hands with blood and grasping them with both hands, he should recite the mantra over the *liṅga* at dusk; by means of an unbaked earthen vessel, he shall cause death.
*Oṃ namaḥ sarvatoyantrāṇi etad yathā jambhani mohani sarvaśatruvidāriṇi rakṣa rakṣa mām amukaṃ sarvabhayopadravebhyaḥ svāhā.*
O Mahādeva, when Śukra has perished, I shall here describe the protection of the twice-born.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of Mantras for Accomplishing Subjugation and Other Aims," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 42—
Hari said:
O Hara, I shall describe the Pavitrāropaṇa rite, which destroys the inauspiciousness of Śiva; the Ācārya, the Sādhaka, the Putraka, and the Samayin should perform it.
Otherwise, Vighneśa seizes the worship performed throughout the year;
one should perform it in the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Māgha, or Bhādrapada.
The threads for the knots should be known, in order, as being made of gold, silver, copper, and cotton; they should be collected starting from Mars and so forth, and must be spun by a virgin.
Having tripled the thread three times, one should then fashion the purifier (pavitraka).
O Śiva, one should tie the knots with the Vāmadeva mantra and wash it with the Satya mantra.
Having purified it with the Aghora mantra, it should be bound with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
one should fumigate it with the Īśāna mantra—these are remembered as the deities of the threads.
Oṃkāra, Candramas, Vahni, Brahmā, Nāga, Śikhidhvaja, Ravi, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are declared to be the deities in the threads in successive order. (GarP 1.42.6)
One should perform one hundred and eight, fifty, or twenty-five [recitations];
Rudra is to be known as the best and so forth, and there should be ten knots as the measure.
The intervals between the knots should be four finger-breadths wide, and their names, in order,
are Prakṛti, Pauruṣī, Vīrā, and the fourth is Aparājitā.
Jayā, Vijayā, Rudrā, Ajitā, Sadāśivā, Manonmanī, and Sarvamukhī; [the distance between them] may be two finger-breadths or even one finger-breadth.
One should dye it with saffron and other substances and fashion the *pavitraka* from threads;
this should be done on the seventh or the thirteenth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight.
Having bathed the Liṅga with milk and other substances, one should worship it with perfumes and so forth;
O Hara, one should then offer a fragrant purifier to oneself and to Brahmā.
One should offer a flower endowed with fragrance in the northeast direction with the root mantra;
likewise, a staff of wood in the east and the fruit of the *āmalakī* tree in the north.
The knower of mantras should offer earth in the west, ashes for prosperity in the south,
and aloe-wood in the southwest, using the *śikhā* mantra.
O Bull-bannered One, one should offer mustard seeds in the northwestern direction with the *kavaca* mantra;
having encircled the house with a thread, one should offer a fragrant purifying wick.
Having performed the fire sacrifice and offered the oblation to Agni, one should likewise present the bali-offering to the spirits:
"O Maheśvara, Lord of Gods, you are invited together with your attendants."
"I shall worship you tomorrow morning; remain present here.
Having invited him with this, he should stay through the night, performing songs and other such acts.
One should place the consecrated purifiers beside the deity;
having bathed on the fourteenth day, one should first worship the Sun and then Rudra.
Having meditated upon the Self as the universal form situated on the forehead, one should worship it;
thus, having sprinkled [the offerings] with the Astra-mantra, they are then honored with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should offer those very items consecrated with mantras and perfumed with incense;
first that which consists of the Śiva-tattva, and then that which consists of the Vidyā-tattva.
Thereafter, one should worship that which consists of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), known as Devakā;
then [one should worship] with: "Oṃ hauṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-principle (śivatattva).
Oṃ hīṃ (hīḥ), obeisance to the Knowledge-principle (vidyātattva). (GarP 1.42.20)
Oṃ hāṃ (hauḥ) homage to the principle of the self (ātmatattva).
Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ kṣaiṃ homage to the universal principle (sarvatattva).
O Lord, whatever has been seen by you, whose nature is Time, in my ritual procedure— [GarP_1,42.21]

O Śambhu, whatever has been done— whether afflicted, abandoned, offered as an oblation, or kept secret— I have performed it with my whole being, through myself, by means of the purifier that is Your will.
Fulfill, fulfill that vow of sacrifice for the Lord of Restraints, who is the essence of all principles and the protector of all causes: Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva! GarP_1,42.23.
Whoever offers four purifiers with this [mantra] as prescribed by the ancients,
having offered a purifier to the fire, he should bestow a sacrificial fee upon the preceptor.
Having offered the bali-oblation and fed the twice-born, one should dismiss Caṇḍa toward the east.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Investiture of the Sacred Thread for Śiva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: [Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—43] Hari said:
I shall describe the Pavitrāropaṇa rite of Hari, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Long ago, during the war between the gods and the asuras, Brahmā and the other deities went for refuge.
And Viṣṇu gave those gods a banner and a neck-ornament;
seeing these two, the Dānavas shall perish—so Hari spoke.
When Viṣṇu had spoken thus, the Nāga who was the younger brother of Vāsuki then said:
"O Bull-bannered One, let him choose this boon known as 'the sacrificer' (vapitrākhya). (GarP 1.43.3)
"The neck-ornament given by Hari shall attain fame under my name.
When he had spoken thus, those gods knew that boon by his name.
But those mortals who do not worship with purificatory blades during the rainy season,
their annual worship shall become fruitless.

Therefore, the offering of the *pavitra* (sacred thread) for all the deities should be performed in sequence; whichever lunar day (*tithi*) is prescribed for each, beginning from the first day (*pratipad*) and ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

O Hara, O Śiva, on the twelfth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight, or during a Vyatīpāta yoga, at the solstices, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, an offering should be made to Viṣṇu.
For Viṣṇu, for rites of prosperity, and likewise upon the arrival of a guru, this is prescribed as a constant purifier; however, it is mandatory during the rainy season.
Silk thread, or cotton thread, or linen, or even kuśa grass thread may be used for the twice-born; for kings, however, silk and woven cloth are appropriate.
For Vaiśyas, bark cloth or linen is prescribed; for Śūdras, that made from hemp or bark;
and for all, O Lord, cotton or lotus-fiber is also commended.
The thread spun by the Brahmin woman is tripled and then tripled again;
it is indeed Oṃkāra, Śiva, Soma, Agni, Brahmā, the Serpent, and the Sun.
Vighneśa and Viṣṇu—these deities reside in the threads;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are remembered as the deities in the triple-thread.
One should place [the vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, bamboo, or clay;
the best [vessel] measures sixty-four finger-breadths by the thumb, and the middling one half of that.
Half of that shall be the smallest; the thread should be one hundred and eight [fingers] long, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior, as before.
The knots are prescribed as being the size of the thumb for the best [type of thread], the middle finger for the middling,
and the little finger for the inferior.
Whether in a celestial chariot or on a sacrificial mound, this is the general characteristic;
one should likewise have the purifying rite extracted by Śiva performed for an image.
Reaching from the heart and the navel down to the thighs and hanging down to the knees,
four knots are recorded as being [formed] by one thousand and eight [loops].

Alternatively, the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) for the superior and other [levels] should be known to have thirty-six, twenty-four, or twelve knots, or else it may be made with [specific] sections (*parvan*). 18. GarP_1,43.18.
Having smeared the sacred thread with saffron or with turmeric and sandalwood paste,
one who observes a fast should consecrate it while it remains within its vessel.
A staff made of wood and the tip of a *kuśa* blade are placed within a vessel made of *aśvattha* leaves in the eight directions; in the east, it is established by Saṅkarṣaṇa.
With Rocanā and saffron, one should worship Pradyumna in the south;
for the purpose of battle and the attainment of results, one should worship Aniruddha in the west.
One should place sandalwood mixed with blue [pigment], sesame ashes, and unbroken rice grains in the corners starting from the southeast, in the sequence for Śyāma and the others.
Having consecrated the purifier with the Vāsudeva mantra one by one,
and having looked upon it again and worshipped it, he should then carefully cover it with a cloth.
It should be placed before the deity, or before the maṇḍala of the images;
likewise in the west, the south, and the north, following the sequence as previously described.
Having also established the Brahma and other [deities], one should worship the water-pot;
having delineated the mandala with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should offer the food oblation (naivedya).
Having consecrated the purifier with three strands or with a new one, and having encircled the altar, as well as oneself, the jar, and the ghee; GarP_1,43.26.
Having taken a single thread, one should place it upon the head of the deity for the fire-pit, the celestial chariot, the pavilion, and the house itself.
Having made offerings and worshipped Maheśvara, one should recite this mantra:
"O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Lord, you have been invoked for the sake of worship. (GarP 1.43.28)
"I shall worship that at dawn; be present in the vicinity of the ritual materials.
Having consecrated the *pavitraka* for one night or three nights," (GarP 1.43.29).
Having kept a vigil at night and having worshipped Keśava in the morning,
one should install [the images] in order— namely, the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Having fumigated the purifier, one should consecrate it with the mantra itself;
having tied a knot while reciting the mantra, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings.
Having worshipped the deity honored with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should cause [the recipient] to give;
together with sons, wife, and others, one should wear the cord and the tail.
O God, I wear before you this beautiful rosary with pure knots, which destroys great sins and brings about the exhaustion of all evil deeds.
Having thus worshipped with incense and other offerings, one should present the middle [thread] and the others—
the Vaiṣṇava purifier, a splendor that destroys all sins.
For the sake of accomplishing the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, I wear this upon my own neck;
having worshipped it, one should cause it to be given with its own mantra.
Having offered various kinds of food offerings, one should present the bali-offering with flowers and other items;
there too, one should satisfy the fire with a [mound] measuring twelve finger-breadths.
One should offer one hundred and eight single-strand sacred threads;
having first offered the *arghya* to the Sun, one should place a single sacred thread there as well.
Then, having worshipped Viṣvaksena with water for the feet, arghya, and other offerings,
O Hara, one should stand before the deity with palms joined in reverence and recite the mantra.
Whether performed with knowledge or without knowledge, whatever worship and other rites have been performed by me— may all that become complete through your grace, O Lord of the Gods.
With garlands of gems and coral, and with mandāraka flowers and the like—
may this be your annual worship, O you whose banner is Garuḍa!
O Lord, just as you always bear the Kaustubha gem upon your heart,
so too should you wear this sacred garland of threads upon your heart.
Having thus petitioned the twice-born, fed them, and given them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
he should dismiss them on that very same evening or on the following day.
"Having duly performed this annual worship by me,
O Pavitra, you shall now depart for the world of Viṣṇu, having been dismissed."
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Offering of the Sacred Thread to Viṣṇu," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: [Chapter Forty-four of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Hari said:
Having worshipped with the sacred thread (*pavitra*) and other offerings, and having meditated upon Brahman, one becomes Hari.
I shall now describe the meditation on Brahman, which crushes the machine of *māyā*.
The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should offer that [restrained mind] into knowledge within the self.
He who desires knowledge within the self should restrain knowledge within the Great One (mahat).
It is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego;
it is free from the gross elements and subtle potentials, as well as from the qualities (guṇas), birth, eating, and so forth.
Self-luminous, formless, eternally blissful, and free from the afflictions such as desire; it is eternal, pure, awakened, sovereign, true, blissful, and non-dual.
I am the fourth syllable, Brahman, the supreme state;
the abiding in the realization "I am Brahman" is likewise proclaimed as samādhi.
Know the self as the rider, and the body as the chariot itself;
know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins.
They say the senses are the horses, and their objects are the range of motion for them.
"Those who are wise in the self-sciences (ātmavidyā) declare that the enjoyer is the self joined with the senses and the mind;
but he who is always joined with the external consciousness through the mind," GarP_1,44.7.
But he attains that state, for he is not born again—
the man who has discernment as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind.
One reaches the far shore of the celestial river; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Non-violence and the like are declared to be *yama*, while purity and the like are remembered as *niyama*.
The postures such as the lotus and others have been taught; breath control is the mastery over the vital winds;
withdrawal of the senses is declared to be mastery [over the objects]; and meditation is the contemplation of the Lord.
Mental steadfastness is retention (*dhāraṇā*), and concentration (*samādhi*) is abiding in Brahman.
First, the mind must not be steady; thereafter, one should contemplate the form.
In the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, he holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he is endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and is graced by the beauty of a forest garland.
I am the Self, eternal, pure, endowed with prosperity, called truth and bliss, supreme, the highest Brahman, and indeed the supreme light. (GarP 1.44.13)
He who exists as the twenty-four forms residing in the Śālagrāma stone,
and who resides in the stones of Dvārakā and other places— he is I, and he is to be meditated upon and worshipped.
Having obtained whatever the mind desires, one becomes a god dwelling in a celestial chariot;
but being free from desire, while meditating upon, praising, and reciting [the mantra], one attains liberation.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Meditation on the Form of Brahmā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 45—
Hari said:
In this context, I shall describe the characteristics of the Śālagrāma;
by the mere touch of a Śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million births are destroyed.
The one known as Keśava has hands bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he is the wielder of the mace.
The all-pervading Nārāyaṇa holds the lotus, the mace, the discus, and the conch.
(Mādhava) holds the discus, conch, lotus, and mace; Śrī Gadādhara likewise holds the mace, lotus, conch, and discus; or Govinda holds the mace, lotus, conch, and discus.
The wielder of the mace is the one to be praised.
Salutations to you who hold the lotus, conch, sword, and mace (in the form of Viṣṇu); salutations to the form of Madhusūdana who holds the conch, lotus, mace, and discus.
Homage to the one who possesses the mace, discus, conch, and lotus (the Traivikrama form),
and to the Vāmana form who holds the śārṅga bow, the kaumodakī mace, the lotus, and the conch.
Salutation to the one who holds the discus, lotus, conch, and mace (the form of Śrīdhara); salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa, who holds the lotus, mace, conch, and discus.
Salutation to the lotus-navelled one (Padmanābha), who possesses the lotus, discus, mace, and conch;
salutation to Dāmodara, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. GarP_1,45.7 //
Salutation indeed to Vāsudeva, who holds the sword, conch, mace, and lotus; and salutation to Saṅkarṣaṇa, who wields the conch, lotus, discus, and mace.
Salutation to the form of Pradyumna, who holds a beautiful conch, a beautiful mace, a lotus, and an enemy; salutation to Aniruddha, who wields a mace, a conch, a lotus, and an enemy.
Salutations to the form of Puruṣottama, who holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus;
salutations to the form of Adhokṣaja,
who bears the mace, conch, discus, and lotus.
Salutation to the form of Nṛsiṃha; salutation to the form of Acyuta, who bears the lotus, mace, conch, and discus, and who holds the lotus, discus, conch, and mace.
I invoke Janārdana here, who holds the conch, discus, lotus, and mace; salutations to Upendra, who possesses the mace, the arrow, the lotus, and the conch.
Salutation to the form of Hari, who possesses a beautiful wheel, lotus, mace, and conch; salutation to the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who holds a mace, lotus, discus, and conch. // GarP_1,45.13 //
May he who bears two wheels fixed upon the surface of the entrance of a Śālagrāma stone,
who is white-hued (known as Vāsudeva),
and who holds the glorious mace, protect you.
Saṃkarṣaṇa has two joined wheels, is red in appearance, and his eastern portion is abundant; Pradyumna,
however, has a subtle wheel and is yellow.
That which is long with a hole at the head is the Unobstructed; that which is circular, blue, marked with three lines at the opening, and dark is Nārāyaṇa.
In the middle, the lines are well-formed; the navel-wheel is very prominent;
his chest is broad—[Nṛsiṃha].
May Kapila Tribinduka protect you.
Alternatively, for a celibate student, there is the worship of the five points;
may the Śakti-liṅga, which possesses two unequal wheels, protect you. (Varāha) 1.45.18.
May he who has three blue lines, who is thick, who possesses the form of a tortoise and a dot, who is black, who has circular whirlpools, and whose back is bowed—may he protect you! (GarP 1.45.19)
(Śrīdhara) has five lines; (Dvanamālī) is marked with a mace;
(Vāmana) is circular or short; (Rā) [is so].
The Lord of the Gods possesses the great discus.
Nānāvarṇa, Anekamūrti, and Nāgabhogin (Anantaka); Sthūla (Dāmodara), Nīla, Madhyevakra, and Sunīlaka.
May that Brahmā, whose gateway is crowded, who is deep red,
who possesses long lines, who is hollow, whose lotus has a single wheel, and who is broad, protect us.
One with broad openings and thick rims is Viṣṇu; it is like a wood-apple fruit.
Hayagrīva is shaped like a goad and possesses five lines along with the Kaustubha gem.

May Vaikuṇṭha—the dark-colored Matsya, possessing the luster of a precious jewel, with a single wheel and a lotus, long and shaped like a lotus, marked with lines at the gates—protect you all. (GarP_1,45.24)
May the dark-complexioned Trivikrama, who possesses the discus of Rāma and the line of the right hand, protect me;
salutations to the wielder of the mace who resides in Śālagrāma and Dvārakā.
Having one door and four wheels, adorned with a garland of forest flowers,
endowed with golden lines, and graced by the mark of a cow’s hoofprint.
May Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, who has the form of a Kadamba flower, protect us;
may Sudarśana, who bears teeth and is marked by the single [disc], extend his protection.
With two [forms] he is Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa; with three, Trivikrama;
and with four, Caturvyūha.
And Vāsudeva with five [arrows]. GarP_1,45.28.
Pradyumna would be with six [faces], while Saṃkarṣaṇa would be here and there;
[and] Puruṣottama.
With eight [syllables] there would be a ninefold array, marked with the number nine.
May Aniruddha protect us with his ten incarnations; then may the twelve-fold one [protect us].
Beyond twelve [yojanas], it is infinite.
Whoever recites this hymn consisting of the forms of Viṣṇu shall go to heaven;
[he becomes] the four-faced Brahmā, staff-bearing and endowed with a water-pot.
(He is) Maheśvara,
five-faced, ten-armed, with the bull as his emblem;
Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, and Sarasvatī likewise possess the same weapons.
Mahālakṣmī and the Mothers, the lotus-handed [Divākara],
the elephant-faced Gaṇa, Skanda, and the six-faced one possess manifold qualities.
When these [images] are honored and installed in a temple where the site has been worshipped,
a person attains dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa, and other goals.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Śālagrāma Image," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 46— Hari said:
I shall briefly describe the ritual for the site (vāstu), which destroys obstacles in houses and other structures;
one should perform the worship on a grid of eighty-one squares, beginning from the northeast corner.

The head [should be placed] in the northeast and the feet in the southwest; the hands in the southeast and northwest; [and the body] in the dwelling, the house of Indra, and so forth, whether in a city, a village, or on a merchant's path.
In palaces, gardens, forts, temples, and monasteries,
one should worship twenty-two deities on the exterior and thirteen within.
Īśa, Parjanya, Jayanta, the one whose weapon is the thunderbolt (Kuliśāyudha),
Sūrya, Satya, Bhṛgu, Ākāśa, and Vāyu.
Pūṣan and Vitatha, both of whom are lords of planets and asterisms;
Gandharva, Bhṛgurāja, Mṛga, and likewise the Pitṛgaṇa.
Then there are the gatekeepers Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta, the lord of the Gaṇas;
the Asuras Śeṣa and Pāpa, as well as Roga and the one known as Ḍahimukha.
Bhallāṭa, Soma, Sarpa, Aditi, and likewise Diti—these thirty-two are on the outside; now hear of the four within them.
The wise one should worship those situated in the four corners beginning with Īśāna:
Āpa, Sāvitrī, Jaya, and likewise Rudra.
In the center of the nine squares is Brahmā; now hear by name these eight deities situated near him, starting from the east and proceeding in order.
Aryaman, Savitṛ, Vivasvat the lord of the gods,
Mitra, Rājayakṣman, and likewise Pṛthvīdhara, in due order.
The eighth is Apavatsa; these are remembered as being around Brahmā.
Starting from the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa), that which is known as the lineage (vaṃśa) is said to be located in the Durga [region].
Starting from the southeast corner, there is the lineage of Durdhara;
these three are Aditi, Himavat, and Jayanta.
Furthermore, having worshipped the Vāstu deities beginning with Śakra, Kālikā by name, and the Gandharvas, one may become a builder of houses and palaces.
The preceptor should be placed in front, the kitchen in the southeast,
and the sacrificial pavilion to the east, by which the monkeys may exit.
A house for perfumes and flowers, provided with silk hangings, should be constructed in the northeast;
a storehouse in the north, and a stable for cattle in the northwest.
In the southwest (Vāruṇī) should be the elevated dwelling provided with windows;
in the southwest (Nairṛta) should be the place for fuel of wood and kuśa grass, as well as for weapons.
The guest-chamber, provided with delightful beds, seats, and footstools,
and equipped with water, fire, lamps, and excellent servants, should be situated to the south.
One should arrange all the interior rooms so that they are beautified by water-filled plantain groves and flowers of five colors.
One should provide a wall outside of that measuring five cubits;
thus one should construct the hermitage of Viṣṇu, endowed with groves and gardens.
The site-plan (vāstu) consisting of sixty-four squares is worshipped in temples and other such structures;
in its center is the four-square Brahmā, while Aryaman and the others occupy two squares each.
And Karṇa, as well as Śikhin and the other gods, have been proclaimed;
for from them, on both sides, there arose other bipedal deities.
The gods are thus proclaimed to be sixty-four in number:
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī; 46.22.
Then, on the exterior starting from Īśāna, are Deva and the others, Hetuka and the rest;
[these are] Hetuka ending with Tripura, Agni, Vetālaka, and Yama.
Agnijihva, Kālaka, Karāla, and Akapādaka—these are of fearsome form in the northeast; while the leader of the pretas resides in the netherworld (pātāla).
In the space [above], there should be Gandhamālin; then one should worship the Kṣetrapālas.
One should calculate the total of the Vāstu by multiplying its length by its breadth.
Having made a division by eight, one should bind the remainder and indicate the *yama*;
then, having multiplied again by eight, one should divide it by seven.
Whatever remains shall be the asterism; having divided it by the [stellar] portions, the remainder becomes the *avyaya*.
Having multiplied the asterism by four and divided it by nine, [the result is determined].
One should understand the remaining portion according to the opinion of Devala:
the *piṇḍa* multiplied by eight, divided by sixty.
Whatever remains shall be the living space; death is that which has been taken by the master. A man should always build his house within the belly of the site, never at its back.
One should sleep on one's left side; no deliberation is required here.
Furthermore, during the months of Leo, Virgo, and Libra, the northern door shall be purified.
And thus, in the case of the scorpion and other [mandalas], there should be doors in the east, south, and west;
the width [of each door] is half the length, and eight doors are prescribed.

Through Raudra [the Moon], there is low status as a servant in one's lineage and gold ornaments for one's own vehicle; however, through Dakṣiṇa, one is bereft of sons and likewise has one's virility destroyed.
In the southeast (Agni), there is destruction; in the north (Vasu), it grants increase of life, the acquisition of sons, and great satisfaction;
in the northeast (Dhanada), it causes affliction from kings; in the west (Varuṇa), it destroys calamities; and in the north (Jala), it bestows disease.

A son born under Nṛpabhīti causes the death of children; one born under Anapatya is childless; one born under Vairada brings loss of wealth; one born under Arthada leads to the destruction of wealth; and one born under Doṣada brings about the death of a son.
I shall now describe the eastern doors, which are known as the "northern" ones:
there is fear of fire, many daughters, wealth, honor, and the grounds for anger.

The eastern gate is said to result in the destruction of kings and the provocation of anger; the southern gate should be in the northeast and so forth, while the western gate should be in the southeast and so forth.
In the southwest and other directions, the western [gate] should be placed; in the northwest and other directions, however, the northern [gate].
When the area is divided into eight parts, this determines the fruit or lack of fruit regarding the gates.
The Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha trees should be planted in the east and other directions, while the Udumbara is said to be auspicious for the house; furthermore, the Sālmali tree,
when worshipped in the northeast, removes obstacles for both the temple and the house.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Measurement of the Vāstu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 47 of the Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
O Śaunaka, I shall now describe the characteristics of palaces; listen to that.
Having divided the ground into sixty-four squares, marked by the cardinal and intermediate directions— // GarP_1,47.1 //
It should be quadrangular with four doors numbering twelve (twelve being the number of the sun),
and the arrangement of the walls should consist of forty-eight [parts].
The shank should be equal in height to the upper portion;
the width of the *śukāṅghri* (the base of the pillar) should be twice half the height of the shank, and it is prescribed to be as wide as the interior width of the sanctum.
That [projection] should be made as one-third or again as one-fifth [of the width];
the projection of the parrot-foot [pedestal] has a height reaching half that of the spire.
Having divided the pinnacle into four parts, the construction of the altar-base (*vedī*) is in the third part;
furthermore, in the fourth part of this very [pinnacle], the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is established from the base upward.
Alternatively, having made the site level and divided it into sixteen parts,
one should first construct the womb-chamber (garbha) in its center, occupying four parts.
The height of the walls should be one-fourth of their [the structure's] measurement according to the prescribed proportions.
The height of the spire should be double the height of the wall in measurement;
the circumambulatory paths (pradakṣiṇā) should be made with a width equal to half the height of the spire.
The wise should likewise understand the exit in the four directions;
having divided the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha) into five parts, the discerning one [should proceed].
Having taken one part, one should again fashion the exit;
the front portico (mukhamaṇḍapa) shall be equal in measure to the central axis (garbhasūtra) extending forward from that part.
This indeed has been declared as the general characteristic of the temple;
now I shall describe the measurement of the *liṅga*, wherein the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be equal in size to the *liṅga*.
O Śaunaka, the womb-cavity (garbha) is certainly twice as large on all sides;
fear is twice that size, and the shank is half the width of that.
O Śaunaka, the pinnacle (śikhara) is said to be twice the height of the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā);
the work of the pedestal and the inner sanctum (garbhāvara) is likewise, and the "parrot-foot" (śukāṅghrika) is measured according to that same proportion.
The exit is declared to be the same, while the remainder is exactly as before;
this is remembered as the measurement of the linga, and now the measurement of the door is described.
Having made the tip of the hand like a Veda, the door shall be one-eighth of that;
its width has been fully described, and it may be double that size according to one's own desire.
In the center of the Dvāravat-pīṭha, there should be a hollow space for Śeṣa;
the remaining portion, measuring one-fourth, constitutes the wall, which is encompassed by half the height of the door.
The shank should be equal in width to that [pedestal], and the pinnacle (śikhara) should be twice as high.
The parrot-foot (śukāṅghri) is to be understood as before; its projection and height should be the same.
This is the measurement for the pavilion; now I shall describe its other essential form:
one should cause the sacred field (kṣetra) to be made threefold, wherein the deities reside.
By means of the measurement thus performed,
the rim of the palace was extended outward on all sides by one foot.

The inner sanctum (garbha) should be made double [the size of the door], and the measurement of the rim (nemi) should be the same here; that very measure is the height of the wall, and the pinnacle (śikhara) is considered to be double that.
And I shall describe the measurement and the origin of the palaces according to their dimensions:
the Vairāja, the one named Puṣpaka, Kailāsa, and the one called Mālikā.
And these five palaces of Triviṣṭapa are the source of all [architectural] forms:
the first is indeed square, while the second is rectangular.
Circular, oblong, another octagonal, and here a fifth [type];
from these very [forms] have arisen the most beautiful palaces.
Likewise, from all those who have become the primordial nature, there are forty;
and Meru, Mandara, and another celestial palace (vimāna).
Bhadraka, Sarvabhadra, Rucaka, Nandana,
the one named Nandivardhana, and Śrīvatsa— these are the nine.
It should be understood that these square structures arose from the Vairāja [village];
namely, the *valabhī*, the *gṛharāja*, the *śālāgṛha*, and the *mandira*.
The celestial chariot, the Brahma-palace, the mansion,
the pillar, the palanquin, and the house— these nine are born from the Puṣpaka.
Valaya, Dundubhi, Padma, and another, Mahāpadma; Mukuli, Uṣṇīṣin, Śaṅkha, and likewise Kalaśa.
The Guvā tree and others, as well as round fruits originating from Kailāsa;
then the elephant, the bull, the swan, Garuḍa, and that which is named the lion.
Bhūmukha, Bhūdhara, Śrījaya, and Pṛthivīdhara—
these nine, who were round and tall, emerged from the one named Maṇika.
The vajra, the wheel, and likewise another called the fist, the vabhru,
the crooked one, the svastika, the sword, the mace, and the śrīvṛkṣa.
Vijaya by name is white and originates from Triviṣṭapa;
[the shapes are] the triangle, the lotus, the crescent moon, the quadrangle, and the two octagons.
The structure of the pavilion should be arranged here and there for the sake of sovereignty, prosperity, and indeed the increase of longevity.
The acquisition of a son, prosperity for women, and so forth shall occur according to the sequence starting from the trine;
one should construct the main hall and likewise the inner sanctum at the well-known entrance.
The jeweled pavilion (maṇāḍapa) and the thread-marking (sūtraka) are multiplied by the same number;
the wise practitioner should construct the auspicious hall (bhadra) from one-fourth of the pavilion's dimensions.
It may be provided with windows for competition [in beauty], or it may be without windows;
furthermore, it should be constructed according to the measurement of half a wall or the full measurement of a wall.
Alternatively, pavilions may sometimes be constructed with twice the height of the wall;
on the palace, a multi-colored gallery with uneven floors should be made.
Adorned with irregular lines due to contradictions in measurement,
the base, however, has four spouts and is beautified by four pavilions.
Meru is the supreme temple, endowed with a hundred peaks;
its pavilions should be constructed, adorned with three auspicious [features].
Those who possess the measure of speech are both distinct and non-distinct;
how many are there among them, some of whom have a support and some of whom are without support?
Through the differentiation of the individual plots, those palaces come into being;
they do not intermingle with one another because there is no distinction between their respective structures.
Many temples are prescribed for the sake of specific deities;
however, there is no restrictive rule regarding the temples of self-manifested (svayambhu) deities.
One should first have those very [structures] made for the deities according to the previous measurement;
they should be rectangular and provided with four corners.
It should be provided with a moon-chamber (candraśālā) and joined with a pinnacle (bherīśikhara);
and in front of the mounts, pavilions for the auspicious moment (lagnamaṇḍapa) should be constructed.
A dance hall should be constructed adjacent to the gateway;
and in the palaces of the deities, [shrines] should be made in all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The chief gatekeepers should be appointed separately at each entrance,
and monasteries for those who depend upon them should be constructed nearby.
The courtyard should be covered and provided with fruits, flowers, and water;
having established the gods in the pavilions, a person should worship them with offerings.
Vāsudeva is the god of all gods, the partaker of all, and the creator of their dwellings and so forth.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Temples, Lingas, Pavilions, and Other Structures," in the Ācārakāṇḍa, the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sūta said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 48.
The Sūta said:
I shall briefly describe the consecration of all the deities;
on an auspicious lunar day and other such occasions, the Guru should perform the delightful consecration.

Together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij), he should choose an Ācārya from the Middle Country according to the procedure prescribed in his own Vedic branch, or else by means of the syllable Om (praṇava).
One should offer water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya) with five or many [substances],
as well as with rings, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), the Guru should then commence the rite;
he should construct a pavilion ten cubits in size in front of the temple.
One should construct a pavilion twelve cubits in size, provided with sixteen pillars;
and in its center, one should have an altar made four cubits in measure, adorned with eight banners.
One should have sand brought from the confluence of rivers and placed there,
in a shape that is either square, bow-shaped, circular, or lotus-like.
Beginning from the east, one should construct five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas);
or alternatively, one may have all of these made square.
For the sake of accomplishing all desired aims through the performance of pacifying rites (*śāntikarma*),
the preceptor (*ācārya*) should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) at the head of the deity.
Some desire [the mandala] in the northeast; having smeared the auspicious ground and having made four doors near the archways.
The archways, made of nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, bailva, pālāśa, and khadira wood,
shall be five cubits in height and adorned with cloth, flowers, and other ornaments.
One should bury them one by one at the eighth [position], four in each of the four directions;
at the eastern gate, however, [one should place] the lion-king, and at the southern [gate], the king of horses.
In the west is the one named Gopati, and in the north is Suraśārdūla;
first, one should place [the deity] in the east with the mantra "Agnim īle."
With the mantra "īṣetvā," he places the second [brick] in the south;
with the mantra "agnāyi," he places the third in the west.
With the mantra "śanno devī," one should perform the fourth [offering] in the north;
in the east, she should be made like a cloud, and in the southeast, she has the form of smoke.
In the southern direction she is indeed black in form, while in the southwestern direction she should be dark gray;
she is to be known as pale white in the western direction and yellow in color in the northwestern direction.
In the north, however, there is a banner of red color with a white crest;
likewise, Bahurūpā is in the center, while Indravidyā is in the east.
One should worship Agni with the *saṃsupti* mantra, Yama in the south with the *nāga* mantra, and likewise in the west and the north with the *rakṣohaṇa* mantra.
Then, having consecrated him with the mantra "vāta" [in the eastern direction], and with "āpyāyasva" in the north;
likewise with "tam īśānam" in the northeast, and with "viṣṇornuka" in the center.
Then, two water-pots each should be placed near the archways,
provided with pairs of cloths and well-adorned with sandalwood paste and other offerings.

Then the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), consecrated with the primary syllables and [offered] many flowers and canopies, should be worshipped according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
With the mantra "trātāram indra," and with "agnir mūrdhā" as another;
"asmin vṛkṣe" and "itaḥ" are likewise [recited], while "pracārī" is remembered as the subsequent one.
Having worshipped the deities of the directions with "kiṃcedadhātu," "ācatvābhitvādeti," and "imā rudra," the wise one [proceeds].
The preceptor should place the materials for the fire-oblation, along with their accessories, in the northwest;
he should then place white conchs, as prescribed by the scriptures, upon his two eyes.
Objects attain purity through inspection, of this there is no doubt;
likewise, the heart and other limbs [of the ritual] are purified by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*.
This is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of all the weapons (astra), which fulfills all desires;
one should also offer unbroken grains (akṣata) and a seat (viṣṭara), consecrated by the weapon-mantra itself.
One should touch the articles prepared for the sacrificial pavilion with the *viṣṭara*;
thereafter, one should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), purified by the *astra* mantra, all around.
Then, starting from the direction of Śakra and extending as far as the domain of Īśāna,
having strewn unbroken grains of rice, he should thereafter smear the pavilion.
The Guru should place the collection of mantras upon the arghya vessel using perfumes and other substances;
with that water from the arghya vessel, he should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion.
One should place the pitcher named after the deity whose consecration it is;
one should worship it in the northeast, and the *vardhanī* vessel in the south with the *astra-mantra*.

The preceptor should recite the mantra known as the Praṇava over the water-pot (kalaśa), the secondary vessel (vardhanī), the planetary deities (grahas), and likewise Vāstoṣpati, placing them all upon their seats.
The preceptor should worship the flask, which has a neck adorned with thread, contains a jewel within, is wrapped in a pair of cloths, and is smeared with all medicinal herbs and fragrances.
The deity should be worshipped in the water-pot (kalaśa), and the excellent cloth upon the *vardhanī*;
one should then cause the water-pot, joined with the *vardhanī*, to be circumambulated.
Then, sprinkling with a stream from the *vardhanī* vessel, he should hold it before him;
having worshipped the *vardhanī* jar, he should worship the deity upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having invoked the jar in the northwest with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," and having [invoked] the Sadgaṇa,
the wise one should recite the Vāstoṣpati hymn for the deity in the northeast corner.
With the mantra "vāstoṣpate," for the pacification of defects in the site,
one should offer an oblation to the deity Gaṇa, who is present to the east of the water-pot.
The wise man should recite the vidyās and perform the touching;
with the mantra "yoge yoge," he should spread out a bed of green grass and kuśa blades.

Then the preceptor, acting as the guru, together with the officiating priests on the bathing throne, [performed the rite] with various Vedic chants and auspicious proclamations of "Hail! and "Victory! (puṇyāha-jaya-maṅgala).
Having placed the deity upon the Brahma-chariot, the twice-born should then depart;
the Guru should bring the pedestal to the northeast and install it within the pavilion.
Then, having bathed with water made from thread and bark,
one should perform the extraction of the marks after bathing [the image] while sounding musical instruments and the like.
One should apply honey and clarified butter, mixed together, into his eyes using a golden probe, either in a bronze or copper vessel.
One should perform the opening of the eyes with the mantra "Agni is light";
while the ritual characteristics are being performed, the officiant (sthāpaka) should utter a single name.
One should perform a cooling treatment on the eyes with this mantra of mine;
one should apply earth from an anthill with the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā."
One should offer the five decoctions of bilva, udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, and pālāśa with the mantra "yajñā yajñā."
Then one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with [herbs] such as sahadevī;
namely, sahadevī, balā, śatamūlī, and śatāvarī.
With the mantra "yā oṣadhī," one should perform a bath with water mixed with the medicinal herbs kumārī, guḍūcī, siṃhī, and likewise vyāghrī.
The ritual bath with fruits is prescribed by means of the mantra "yāḥ phalinī," and the wise should perform the application of unguents by means of the mantra "drupadādiva."
And having placed [the substances] in the jars in sequence, beginning with the north:
gems, grains, and the herb śatapuṣpikā.
One should consecrate the water-pot with the mantras "Āpyāyasva," "Dadhikrāvṇaḥ," "Yā oṣadhīḥ," and "Tejo 'si. (GarP 1.48.49)
Furthermore, one should bathe [the image] again with four jars known as the "oceans";
once bathed and well-attired, incense of *guggulu* should be offered.
For the consecration, one should place the various sacred fords (tīrthas) within the jars—
whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, as well as the rivers and the oceans.
One should consecrate the water-jar with the mantra beginning "yā oṣadhī";
whoever bathes with that water shall be liberated from all sins.
Having consecrated [the image] with the oceans, one should then again offer the arghya;
and with the mantra "gandhadvārām," one should apply fragrance and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) using Vedic mantras.
Having obtained the garments prescribed by his own scriptures according to the *yuvam-vastre* [mantra],
he should lead [the initiate] to the auspicious pavilion with the mantra *kavihāva*.
One should place [the deity] upon the bed with the mantra *śambhavāya*,
and one should perform the rite of the manifest and the unmanifest with the mantra *viśvataścakṣuḥ*.
And having established oneself in the supreme reality, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa);
the mantra-placement prescribed by one's own scripture is declared to be performed in that manner.

Having covered it with a cloth, he should worship it according to its own nature; then, having prepared the offerings according to the scriptures, he should cause them to be placed at the base of the feet.
Then, one should place the water-pot, joined with the Praṇava, wrapped in a pair of cloths, and containing gold, upon the head.
Then, having stood near the sacrificial pit, the Guru should perform the installation of the fire with mantras prescribed in his own scriptures or those declared in the Vedas.
One who is well-versed in the Rigveda should recite the Śrīsūkta, the Pāvamānya hymns, the Vāsadāmya, the Savājina,
the Vṛṣākapi, and the Mitra hymn in the east.
The Adhvaryu priest shall mutter, on the south side, the Rudra-hymn, the Puruṣasūkta, the Ślokādhyāya, the Śukriya, the Brahmaṇa, and the Pitṛmaitra.
A Chāndogya should mutter the Veda-vrata, the Vāmadevya, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Rathantara,
and the Bheruṇḍa Sāmans in the west.
One should recite the Atharvaśiras, the Kumbhasūkta of the Atharvans,
the Nīlarudras, the Maitra, and the Uttarātharvaṇa.
The preceptor, having especially consecrated the sacrificial pit with the Astra-mantra,
[should place the offering] in a copper vessel, a clay bowl, or even according to his means.
Having brought Jātavedas, one should seat him in front;
one should ignite the fire with the Astra-mantra and encircle it with the Kavaca-mantra.
After having rendered it immortal with all the mantras,
the preceptor should then take the vessel with both hands, circle it over the sacrificial pit, and then [proceed] again.
One should project the supreme splendor by means of the Vaiṣṇava yoga;
one should place the Brahman vessel to the south and the Praṇītā vessel to the north.
Then, with a common mantra or one prescribed in his own sūtra,
he should place a boundary fence (paridhi) in each of the directions together with sacrificial grass seats (viṣṭara).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśāna are to be worshipped with common offerings;
one should place the fire upon darbha grass and surround it with darbha grass.
Touched with water from *darbha* grass, one becomes pure even if devoid of mantras;
[using] blades that are unbroken, with their tips pointing east, north, or west.
Fire that is surrounded by extended [threads] will come of its own accord into its presence;
this is the ritual act prescribed for the protection of the fire by one who knows the mantras.
Some teachers maintain that immediately after the birth-rite (jātakarman) and other ceremonies,
one should prepare the purifier (pavitra) and then perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya).
Then the preceptor, having also gazed upon the consecrated clarified butter used for the lustration rite,
should observe the procedure up to the portioning and sprinkling of the butter for the sake of its perfection.
Immediately thereafter, having offered five sets of five oblations of clarified butter,
[he should perform the rites] beginning with *garbhādhāna* up until the *godāna*.
One should perform the oblation with the mantras prescribed in one's own scripture and with the syllable Om;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should attain the fullness that arises from the full.
Thus kindled, the fire grants success in all rites;
having worshipped the fire, one should then proceed likewise with it within the sacrificial pits.
With the respective mantras of Indra and the other deities, one should likewise offer a hundred oblations for each;
at the end of the hundred [oblations], one should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for all of them.
Then the Hotṛ priest should place his own oblation into the clarified butter within that pitcher,
as well as the deities, the mantras, and likewise Jātavedas.
Having placed oneself on one side, one should then cause the full [offering] to be given;
having drawn it out, the preceptor should offer the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions.
Through the application of the elements, the gods, and the nāgas,
sesame seeds and sacrificial fuel are recorded as the two-fold materials for the oblation.
Clarified butter is the auxiliary for those two;
that which is primary for the two eyes is the *paruṣasūkta* with the former [mantra], while for the Rudra [rite] it is indeed with the one on the right.
The Jyeṣṭhasāman and the Bhāruṇḍa [are used] in the west with the mantra "I lead him";
[then there is] the great mantra of Nīlarudra and the Kumbhasūkta of the Atharvaveda.
Having offered one thousand oblations for each, one should assign a deity to the head;
likewise in the middle and in the feet, and again with the final full oblation.
One should offer oblations at the locations of the head and enter [the body] in due order,
either with the opening mantras of the Vedas, or with mantras consisting of the names of the deities.
Or those twice-born ones may perform it with the mantras prescribed in their own scriptures, or with the Gāyatrī;
or the preceptor may do so with the Gāyatrī, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Praṇava.
Having thus performed the rite of the fire-oblation (homa), the preceptor should place the mantras:
"agnim īḷe" at the two feet, and "iṣe tvā" situated at the two ankles.
One should place "O Agni, come hither" on the two shanks; "May the goddesses be auspicious to us" on the two knees;
the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] on the two thighs; and the Svātinī [verse] on the bellies.
One should place "For long life" (dīrghāyuṣṭvāya) on the heart, "Obeisance to Śrī" (śrīśca te) on the throat,
"The protector Indra" (trātāram indram) on the chest, and "Tryambaka" on the two eyes.
Likewise, when [the mark] has reached the crown of the head, one should perform the oblation;
then one should cause the deity to rise with the mantra: "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati! (GarP 1.48.89).

Accompanied by the sound of Vedic recitations and auspicious proclamations, the knower of mantras, having performed the circumambulation of the temples and the touching of the pedestal with the mantra "devasya tvā," [should proceed].
Together with the guardians of the directions, the jewels, the minerals, and likewise the medicinal herbs, the perfected metals and seeds; thereafter, one should install the deity.
One should not place the deity within the womb, nor should one abandon the womb;
rather, having left a small space in the middle, that [image] will remove all defects.
One should bring a little more than a mere husk of sesame; [reciting]:
"Oṃ, be firm, be auspicious, and salutations again and again to the progeny. (GarP 1.48.93)

"By the grace of the god Savitṛ," the Guru should indeed place [the mantras] upon the six [parts]; O daughter of Prajāpati, [he should do so] according to the measure of the principles, syllables, and kalās. GarP_1,48.94.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the six [limbs], one should consecrate the Siddhārtha [grains] with the *dhruva* mantras;
then, one should bathe the well-established [deity] with the *sampāta* water from the jar.
One should worship with lamps, incense, fragrant scents, and food offerings;
having offered the *arghya* and paid obeisance, one should then ask the deity for forgiveness.
A bowl, a pair of garments, an umbrella, as well as a divine ring,
and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability should be given to the officiating priests.
Thereafter, the sacrificer, with a concentrated mind, should offer the fourth oblation;
having offered one hundred oblations, he should then cause the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be presented.
Having gone outside, the preceptor should offer an oblation to the guardians of the directions;
with flowers in hand, the preceptor should dismiss them, saying, "Forgive me."
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should give a tawny cow to the preceptor,
as well as a fly-whisk, a crown, earrings, a parasol, armlets, and a waist-belt.
One should provide a fan, village garments, and so forth, along with furnishings and a well-adorned pavilion,
as well as a grand feast; thus the patron becomes one who has fulfilled his duty and shall be liberated through the grace of the consecrator.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Installation of Deities and Other Rites," in the Ācārakāṇḍa (Section on Conduct) of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The section on installation (Pratiṣṭhāprakaraṇa) is hereby completed.
Brahmā said:

Hari, the creator of the beginning of creation, is indeed to be worshipped by Svāyambhuva Manu and others, as well as by the Brahmins and other castes, each through their own specific duty. O Vyāsa, listen now to that dharma.
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts, teaching, and studying— these are the six duties of the best of the twice-born.
Giving, study, and sacrifice are the duties of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya;
for the Vaiśya, agriculture and the tending of cattle are likewise commended as his duty.
For Śūdras, the means of accomplishing dharma is solely the service of the twice-born;
likewise, their livelihood consists of manual crafts, and according to dharma, they may also perform the *pākayajña* sacrifice.
Begging for alms, service to the teacher, as well as private Vedic study,
the performance of twilight rituals, and the tending of the sacred fire— this is the duty of the religious student.
Furthermore, for all the stages of life (āśramas), there is a twofold division which is fourfold:
the student (brahmacārin) who is a temporary student (upakurvāṇa), and the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) who is solely intent upon Brahman.
He who, having studied the Vedas according to the rules, enters the stage of the householder is to be known as an *upakurvāṇaka*; he who remains until death is a *naiṣṭhika*.
The maintenance of the sacred fires, service to guests, sacrifice, charity, and the worship of the gods—
this, O best of the twice-born, is the duty of the householder in brief.
The householder may be of two kinds: the indifferent and the practitioner.
That householder who is devoted to the maintenance of his family is the practitioner.
Having discharged the three debts and abandoned wife, wealth, and so forth,
he who wanders alone and indifferent is one intent on liberation.
Subsisting on roots and fruits on the ground, the study of sacred texts, austerity,
and the equitable distribution [of resources] according to rule— this is the dharma of one dwelling in the forest.
He who performs austerities in the forest, sacrifices to the gods, offers oblations,
and is devoted to the private study of the Vedas is a forest-dweller, the best among ascetics.
He who, excessively emaciated by austerity, becomes intent upon meditation,
should indeed be known as a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) established in the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
One who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, desiring to ascend [to liberation], having conquered the senses,
and who lives as a mendicant for the sake of knowledge, is called a *pārameṣṭhika*.
But he who delights only in the Self, who is eternally contented, a great sage,
and perfectly endowed with self-restraint— he is called a yogi, a mendicant.
Alms-gathering, sacred learning, silence, austerity, and especially meditation,
along with perfect knowledge and dispassion— this is considered the dharma for a mendicant.
Some are renunciants of knowledge, others are renunciants of the Vedas, and some are renunciants of action; such is the threefold renunciation pertaining to the supreme state.

The yogin should be known as threefold: the elemental, the kṣattriya, and the third is declared to be the one in the final stage of life (antyāśramī), who has fully established himself in the form of yoga.
The first cultivation was previously taught for liberation; the second is the cultivation of non-difficulty; and the third is declared to be the final cultivation, that of the Supreme Lord.
From dharma liberation is born; from artha desire is produced. Vedic action is twofold: engagement and renunciation.
Knowledge would have ceased previously, and [the fire] produced by the god Agni has now proceeded; likewise,
forbearance, self-restraint, compassion, generosity, freedom from greed,
and spiritual practice [have also ceased].
Straightforwardness, freedom from envy, as well as visiting sacred fords; truthfulness, contentment, faith, and likewise restraint of the senses.
Worship of the deities, especially the honoring of Brahmins;
non-violence, speaking kindly, refraining from slander, and absence of harshness.
I shall now describe these duties pertaining to the stages of life for the four castes:
the station of those Brahmins who perform their ritual duties is traditionally held to be that of Prajāpati.
The station of Indra belongs to Kṣatriyas who do not flee in battles;
the station of the Maruts belongs to Vaiśyas who follow their own dharma.
The Gāndharva [veda] was for those of the Śūdra caste who were engaged in service,
as well as for the eighty-eight thousand sages of perpetual celibacy.
The very abode that is remembered for them is indeed the abode for those dwelling in the forest;
the abode of the Seven Sages is indeed the abode for the forest-dwellers.

That state is Brahman-bliss, belonging to the ascetics who have controlled their minds, who have renounced all attachments, and whose vital energy is drawn upward; from that place, the sage does not return.
The abode of immortality for yogins is called the void, the supreme syllable;
it is the bliss of the Lord, from which a liberated man does not return.
Liberation comes from the knowledge of the eight limbs; hear that briefly as it is. The five restraints (yamās) begin with non-violence; non-violence is the non-injury of living beings.

Truthful speech that is beneficial to living beings, non-stealing which is supreme in its lack of grasping, celibacy which is freedom from sexual intercourse, and non-possessiveness which is the renunciation of everything.
The five observances (niyamas), beginning with truthfulness, are twofold: external and internal;
they are purity, contentment, austerity, and restraint of the senses. (GarP 1.49.32)
Self-study consists of the recitation of mantras; dedication is the worship of Hari.
The prescribed postures are the lotus and others; breath control is the mastery over the vital air.
Meditation on the mantra is the *sagarbha* [type], while the reverse is the *agarbhaka*.
Thus it is described as being twofold or even threefold; and that which completes [the process] is the *pūraka*.
Kumbhaka is so called because of its immobility, and recaka is so called because of exhalation; thus, breath control is threefold.
The light [breath] consists of twelve mātrās, while the next consists of twenty-four.
The best withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) consists of thirty-six measures (*mātrā*), as does the restraint (*rodhana*);
meditation (*dhyāna*) is the contemplation of the Self as Brahman, while concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the steadying of the mind.
The state of abiding in the thought "I am Brahman" is samādhi; it is the dwelling in Brahman.
I am the Self, the Supreme Brahman, which is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
Brahman is consciousness and bliss; that alone is your true self.
"I am Brahman," "I am Brahman"—bodiless, beyond the senses. (Garuda Purāṇa 1.49.38)
It is devoid of the "I-notion," mind, intellect, the great principle (mahat), ego, and so forth;
it is that very light which is associated with the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the rest.
"Constantly pure, awakened, liberated, true, blissful, and non-dual—
He who is that Person in the Sun, He am I, indivisible.
Meditating thus, a Brahmin is released from the bondage of worldly existence.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Castes and Stages of Life," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 50.
Brahmā said:
He who performs his duties day after day shall attain knowledge;
having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, he should contemplate both dharma and artha.
When the time of dawn has arrived, the wise man, having performed his necessary duties, should meditate in his heart upon Hari, the imperishable bliss, seated upon a lotus.
One should bathe in pure rivers after performing purification according to the prescribed rule;
by bathing in the morning, even those people who are doers of evil are purified.
Therefore, one should perform the morning bath with every effort;
for they praise the morning bath as that which brings about both visible and invisible results.
For saliva and other secretions constantly flow from one who has slept in comfort;
therefore, one should not perform ritual acts without first bathing.
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—all these sins are shaken off by bathing at dawn; of this there is no doubt.
No ritual act is remembered as being commendable for men without bathing, especially in the case of burnt offerings and the recitation of mantras; therefore, one should perform the bath.
In case of inability, however, a headless bath (aśiraska-snāna) is prescribed for him;
or else, the cleansing of the body by means of a wet garment is recorded as the traditional rule.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual bath (ṣaḍaṅga-snāna), which is declared to consist of the Brāhma, Āgneya, Vāyavya, Divya, Vāruṇa, and likewise the Yaugika baths.
The *brāhma* purification consists of sprinkling water drops with *kuśa* grass while reciting mantras;
the *āgneya* purification consists of shaking the body from head to foot while using ashes.
For the sprinkling with the dust of cows is declared to be the supreme Vāyavya bath;
that which is performed during rain while the sun is shining is called the Divya bath.

The bath in the waters of Varuṇa, the bath of immersion, the bath of pride, the bath of self-knowledge, and the medicinal bath—these are declared; the bath by means of yoga is the contemplation of Hari through yoga.
Known as the "Self-tirtha," it is frequented by those who discourse on Brahman;
it is auspicious, produced from milk-trees and originating from *mālatī* flowers.
For the cleansing of the teeth, one should use apāmārga, bilva, or karavīra; facing either north or east, one should consume the tooth-stick.
Having washed and eaten, he should discard that [leavings] in a clean place with a concentrated mind;
then, having bathed, he should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and likewise to the hosts of ancestors.
Having sipped water according to the rule, and having sipped water again while remaining silent,
he should purify himself with *kuśa* grass blades moistened with drops of water, using the sacred mantras.
With the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and auspicious hymns to Varuṇa,
as well as the *gāyatrī*— the mother of the Vedas— joined with the *oṃkāra* and the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having recited [the mantra], one should offer a handful of water toward the sun with the mind fixed on that;
then, remaining well-composed, one should stand upon *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the east.
"Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should then meditate upon Sandhyā; such is the Vedic revelation.
That which is Sandhyā is the progenitor of the universe, indeed beyond Māyā and partless."
The wise man, having meditated upon the sovereign, absolute Śakti who arises from the three principles— red, white, and black— should indeed recite the Gāyatrī.
A Brahmin should always perform the twilight worship facing the east;
one who neglects the twilight worship is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts.
Whatever else one may do, one shall not partake of its fruit;
such is the view of the virtuous Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and possess undistracted minds.
Having duly performed the twilight devotions (sandhyā) and attained the supreme goal,
that best of the twice-born who exerts effort elsewhere in matters of religious duty [is as follows].
Having abandoned the salutation at the twilight, he goes to ten thousand hells;
therefore, one should perform the twilight worship with every effort.
By him, the supreme deity whose body is yoga should be worshipped constantly—
[reciting] at most a thousand times, a hundred times in the middle, and at least ten times.
A wise man, self-restrained and pure, facing the east, should indeed recite the Gāyatrī;
then, with a concentrated mind, he should worship the sun as it stands at its rising.
