Having performed worship with various solar mantras known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
he approached the Great Yoga, the Sun, the God of gods.
Having been consecrated with the mantra, "Oṃ, to Khakholka, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes," he should prostrate himself upon the ground with his head.
I offer myself unto you; salutations to you whose form is knowledge!
You alone are the supreme Brahman, water, light, essence, and the immortal.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, you are the syllable Om, the all-pervading, eternal Rudra.
Having recited this supreme hymn, which is indeed the Heart of the Sun (Sūryahṛdaya), [one attains fulfillment].
At dawn and at midday, one should pay homage to the Sun;
then, having returned home, the Brahmin should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.
Having kindled the fire according to the rules, one should offer oblations into the Jātavedas;
the officiating priest, the son, the wife, the disciple, or even a uterine brother may do so.
Having obtained specific permission, one should perform the oblation according to the ritual rules;
for any rite performed without the mantra yields no fruit, neither in this world nor in the next.
One should pay homage to the deities and present offerings;
one should also attend upon the guru and practice what is beneficial for him.
Thereafter, the twice-born should diligently practice the study of the Vedas according to his ability;
he should recite them, teach them to disciples, retain them in memory, and indeed investigate their meaning.
And the best of the twice-born should study the treatises on dharma and other subjects,
as well as the Vedic scriptures and all the Vedāṅgas in their entirety.
Then, for the sake of securing his livelihood and well-being, the twice-born man should employ the Lord to accomplish various purposes for the sake of his family.
Then, at the time of midday, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing,
as well as flowers, unbroken grains of rice, sesame seeds, kusha grass, and pure cow dung.
One should perform one's bath in rivers, natural pools, tanks, and lakes, but never at all in those belonging to others.
If one does not extract five lumps [of earth], one always defiles the bath;
the head should be washed with one lump of earth, and likewise the area above the navel with two.
The lower part should be washed with three [applications of clay], and the feet likewise with six;
the amount of earth prescribed is equal to a large myrobalan fruit.
Having applied cow dung to his limbs according to the prescribed measure,
he should then wash them, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule, and bathe with a concentrated mind.
Having smeared [the ground] while standing on the bank, he should consecrate the water with mantras, using those very same signs and auspicious Varuṇa mantras.
At the time of bathing, one should remember Viṣṇu, for water is Nārāyaṇa;
having gazed at the sun and the syllable Om, one should immerse oneself three times in the body of water.
Having sipped water once, the knower of mantras should sip again with this mantra:
"You move within all beings, in the secret cave of the heart, facing every direction."
"You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the waters, light, essence, and immortality.
Or, one may repeat the *drupadā* verse three times, accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*.
A wise man should recite the Sāvitrī or likewise the Aghamarṣaṇa;
thereafter, he should perform the sprinkling with the verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ."
Then, with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should likewise pour out this water;
thereafter, he should consecrate the water with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Submerged underwater and facing downwards, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times,
or the Drupadā verse, or the Sāvitrī, or the "tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam" mantra.
Or one should revolve the *praṇava* and delight in Hari, the God of gods;
having taken water in the hand and performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) after reciting [the mantra].
Having placed that water upon his head, he is liberated from all sins;
having performed the twilight devotions and sipped water for purification, he should constantly remember the Lord.
Then, one should worship the sun with hands joined in *añjali* holding flowers above;
having cast them [into the water], one should gaze at the god as he rises, for it is not possible [to look directly].
With the mantras "ud u tyam," "citram," and "tat cakṣuḥ," as well as with the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" and especially with the Sāvitrī, [he should perform the rite].
Then, one should recite the Gāyatrī with other solar and Vedic mantras,
and subsequently various other mantras while seated on a grass mat with the tips pointing eastward.
Standing and gazing at the sun, one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind,
using beads made of crystal, lotus seeds, rudrākṣa, or those produced from the putrajīva tree.
In that case, it is traditionally taught that there should be an interval of skin-thickness [between the water and the body];
however, if one is indeed wearing wet clothes, one may perform the rite while standing in the midst of the water.
Otherwise, being composed, on pure ground and upon *darbha* grass, having circumambulated clockwise and then prostrated on the earth; ||| GarP_1,50.57 |||
Having sipped water according to the scriptures, one should perform the private recitation (svādhyāya) according to one's ability;
thereafter, one should likewise satiate the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ* and [the word] "namas" at the end, as well as "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*),
one should satisfy the gods and the brahminical seers with water containing unbroken grains.
One should worship the ancestors, the gods, and the sages with devotion, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra.
The wise man should satisfy the celestial sages and the ancestors with handfuls of water;
he should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī) for the gods, and around the neck (nivītī) during the libation to the sages.
But for the ancestral rites, O Bhārata, he should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and use that same [southern] part of the hand;
having wrung out his bathing garment and sipped water, he should remain silent.
One should worship the gods with their own respective mantras using flowers, leaves, and likewise water—
namely Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Sūrya, and likewise Madhusūdana.
O Hara, being free from anger, one should also offer other desired deities with devotion,
presenting flowers and other offerings while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
By this, all the deities, who are indeed the waters, have been perfectly worshipped;
for, being concentrated on the water, he has meditated upon the Lord preceded by the syllable Om.
One should indeed place the sacrificial offerings separately with each salutation;
for no Vedic rite exists that yields merit without worship.
Therefore, one should hold Hari in the mind at the beginning, middle, and end of that [rite],
using the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and the Puruṣa Sūkta.
And with his mind fixed on the supreme self, being tranquil, he should offer himself to Viṣṇu of stainless splendor by means of the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ."
Having bathed with his head uncovered and having worshipped Hari in the Puṣpaka [chariot], he should perform the five sacrifices:
the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, as well as the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to Brahman. GarP_1,50.69 //

If it were possible [to perform the sacrifice] before the libation (tarpaṇa), how could there be a human sacrifice (manuṣyayajña)? Having indeed performed the human sacrifice, one should then practice the private recitation of the Vedas (svādhyāya).

The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed; that is traditionally known as the Devayajña (sacrifice to the gods). That which is this offering (bali) to all beings is to be understood as the Bhūtayajña (sacrifice to the spirits).
The best of the twice-born should give food upon the ground outside for dogs, for those who cook dogs, for outcasts and others, and likewise for birds.
O best of men, one should feed even a single Brahmin with the ancestors in mind;
that daily śrāddha, intended for the ancestors, is a sacrifice to the manes that bestows a favorable rebirth.
Or, having set aside some food according to his ability, being composed in mind,
he should offer it to a twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
One should always honor the guest, bow to and worship the twice-born who is tranquil,
welcoming them into one's own home with thoughts, words, and deeds.
They say that alms (bhikṣā) consist of a single mouthful of food; four times that amount is a puṣkala, and four times a puṣkala is said to be an hantakāra.
A guest should indeed wait for as long as it takes to milk a cow;
one should honor a guest who has arrived according to one's ability. // GarP_1,50.77 //
One should indeed give alms according to the rule to a mendicant who observes the vow of celibacy;
free from greed, one should give food to those in need according to one's ability.
Restrained in speech and without disparaging the food, he eats together with his kinsmen;
yet, O best of the twice-born, if that brahmin has not performed the five great sacrifices, [he incurs sin].
If that deluded soul eats [forbidden food], he goes to the womb of an animal;
therefore, one should daily practice the study of the Vedas according to one's ability and be capable of performing the great sacrifices.
Likewise, the worship of the gods swiftly destroys sins;
yet he who, out of delusion or laziness, fails to perform the worship of the deities...
He who eats this goes to the hells and is born among swine;
I shall now fully declare impurity—he is always impure and a sinner.
Impurity arises from association, and purification comes from avoiding such association;
all wise Brahmins declare that impurity lasts for ten days.
O best of the twice-born, among Brahmins, in the event of deaths or births, purification is immediate until the eruption of teeth; until the *cūḍā* ceremony, it lasts for one night.
For three nights following the initiation ceremony, and ten nights thereafter;
for a Kṣatriya, twelve days; and for a Vaiśya, fifteen days.
A Śūdra is indeed purified in one month; for ascetics there is no sin.
In cases of miscarriage, purification is achieved through nights equal in number to the months [of pregnancy].
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of Daily Duties and Impurity," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 51,
Brahmā said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the unsurpassed dharma of giving:
the offering of wealth with faith to a worthy recipient.
The knowers of that have declared that giving bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one should acquire wealth through righteous means, for that results in both the fruits of giving and enjoyment.
They say that teaching and officiating at sacrifices are the means of livelihood, as is the acceptance of gifts;
however, one following the conduct of a Kṣatriya should avoid usury, agriculture, and trade.
That which is given to worthy recipients is proclaimed as "giving" (dāna). Giving is said to be of four kinds: constant, occasional, for a specific desire, and pure.
Day after day, whatever is given to one who does not return the favor,
specifically to a Brāhmaṇa, should always be done without aiming for any reward.
That which is given into the hands of the learned for the pacification of evil is designated as occasional (naimittika) giving, as practiced by the virtuous.
That gift which is bestowed for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty,
or heaven is declared as "kāmya" (desire-based) by the sages who contemplate dharma.
When that which is known as Brahman is bestowed upon those who know it for the sake of pleasing the Lord,
with a mind endowed with goodness— that gift is stainless and auspicious.
He who gives land covered with sugarcane, barley, wheat,
and rice to one learned in the Vedas is not born again.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of land;
by giving knowledge to a Brahmin, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One who gives alms daily with faith to a celibate student shall be liberated from all sins and attain the abode of Brahman.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, a wise man, having fasted, should honor seven or five Brahmins with honey, sesame seeds, and clarified butter.
Having honored [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings, one should have [another] recite or speak for oneself:
"May the King of Dharma be pleased," according to what is in one's mind.
Whatever sin has been committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment by placing sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, along with gold, honey, and clarified butter.
He who gives ghee, food, and water to a Brahmin, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, overcomes all evil deeds.
Having instructed the King of Dharma, he is liberated from fear;
by fasting on the twelfth day and worshipping Viṣṇu, one destroys all evil.
A man who desires to propitiate whichever deity he wishes to worship certainly becomes liberated from all sins. (GarP 1.51.17)
One desiring progeny should constantly worship the Brahmins with gifts, feed women and the gods,
and indeed worship Purandara.
One desiring spiritual luster should worship the Brahmins with a firm resolve in the Veda;
one desiring health should worship the Sun; and one desiring wealth should worship the Fire-god.
One who desires the success of one's actions should indeed worship Vināyaka;
one who desires enjoyments should worship the Moon, and one who desires strength should worship the Wind.
One who desires liberation from the entire cycle of worldly existence should worship Hari with diligent effort;
whether free from desire or possessing all desires, one should indeed honor Gadādhara.
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision. (GarP 1.51.22)
The giver of land obtains everything; the giver of gold obtains long life;
the giver of a house obtains the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver obtains supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses, the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull, abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow, the realm of the Sun.
The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda obtains the eternal Brahman.
One who bestows knowledge upon those learned in the Vedas is glorified in the heavenly world;
by providing fodder for cows, one is liberated from all sins.
By the provision of fuel, a man’s fire becomes kindled;
likewise, medicine, oil, and food are provided for the pacification of a patient's disease. (GarP 1.51.27)
One who gives [gifts] becomes free from disease, happy, and long-lived;
[he avoids] the path of the Forest of Sword-leaves, which is lined with razor edges.
A man who gives an umbrella and sandals crosses over both the heat and the sharp [suffering];
whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to him in his home—[that he attains].
One who desires that very gift to be inexhaustible should give it to one possessed of those respective qualities on the Ayana,
at the equinox, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
What is given at times such as the solstices and others becomes inexhaustible,
especially at sacred fords such as Prayāga and Gayā.
No dharma superior to the dharma of giving exists for living beings;
therefore, one who desires heaven, long life, and prosperity, and seeks the pacification of evil, should practice giving.
But that sinful man who, out of delusion, prevents gifts from being given to cows, Brahmins, fire, or deities,
shall go to the womb of an animal.
But he who does not provide food during a time of famine,
while Brahmins are dying, is a slayer of a Brahmin and is censured.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Giving," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śrī Brahmā said: The *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 52.
Brahmā said:
Henceforth, O twice-born ones, I shall proclaim the rules for expiation:
the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed.
"These five are the great sinners (pātakin), and the fifth is one who associates with them;
the gods have declared that minor offenses (upapāpa) include the killing of cows and so forth."
A slayer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years having constructed a hut,
or else he may practice fasting, or even throw himself from a precipice.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should either enter a blazing fire or enter the water oneself, even at the cost of completely relinquishing one's life.
By giving food to a learned man, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
or, by bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice, a twice-born man is liberated.
Or one should cause all one's possessions to be given to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas at the world-renowned confluence of the river Sarasvatī.
A twice-born man who is pure, having bathed at the three daily junctures and fasted for three nights,
is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin by bathing at Setubandha.
Having bathed at Kapālamocana and likewise in Vārāṇasī,
the best of the twice-born who has drunk liquor— having consumed liquor that is fire-colored— [is purified].
By drinking milk, ghee, or cow urine, one is liberated from that sin;
even a thief of gold shall be freed if struck with a mace by kings.
Clad in bark garments, the twice-born man shall perform the vow for killing a Brahmin in the forest;
likewise, a Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by lust, has sexual intercourse with his teacher’s wife [must do so].
One who has approached the wife of his teacher shall embrace a red-hot, glowing image made of black iron;
and those who have approached the wives of their gurus shall perform the vow of a Brahmahatyā.
Or he who is a twice-born man and associates with one who has fallen from his caste should perform five or four *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
To remove that sin, he should perform the very same vow for that [offense],
or else he should diligently perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for one year.
The gift of all one's possessions according to the prescribed rule purifies all sins,
as does the Cāndrāyaṇa penance performed according to the rule, and likewise the Atikṛcchra.
Traveling to sacred fields such as Gayā and other sites is destructive of sin;
moreover, he who, having reached the lunar day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), propitiates Bhava [Śiva], [attains great merit].
Having fed the Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, one who has fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight with a concentrated mind [attains the same].
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.
Having bathed in a river in the forenoon, one should offer seven handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds for each [deity]; thus one is liberated from all sins. (GarP 1.52.18)
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, observe fasts, and worship the twice-born;
while engaged in these vows, one should remain peaceful with a restrained mind.
Having fasted on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one who is composed should worship the Sun-god on the seventh; he is liberated from all sins.
By fasting on the eleventh day and worshipping Janārdana,
one is liberated from great sins on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Austerity, recitation, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of gods and Brahmins during times such as eclipses destroy even the most heinous sins.
Even a man burdened with every kind of sin, if he should give up his life at sacred pilgrimage sites according to the prescribed rules, is liberated from all transgressions.
Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or defiled by a mortal sin,
a woman may rescue him by entering the fire along with him.
But for that woman who is devoted to her husband and eager to serve him,
no sin exists either in this world or in the next.
Likewise, Rāma’s auspicious wife Sītā, the goddess renowned throughout the three worlds and daughter of Daśaratha, conquered the lord of the rākṣasas.
"Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and other such sites, one obtains the fruit of all proper conduct," so said the Blessed Viṣṇu to me in the past, O you of firm vows.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Expiatory Rites," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
*Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—53* Sūta said:
Having thus heard about the eight treasures of Hari, Brahmā spoke as follows:
"Among them are Padma and Mahāpadma, as well as Makara and Kacchapa."
Mukunda, Kunda, Nīla, and Śaṅkha are the other treasures;
these appear when prosperity is true. I shall now describe their essential nature.
A man marked with a lotus is born as one of the *sāttvika* type;
such a person, whose essence is courtesy, engages in the accumulation of gold and other precious things.
One should fashion objects of silver and so forth and give them to ascetics, those who sacrifice to the gods, and others;
one marked with the great lotus should give wealth and other gifts to the righteous.
The two treasures, Padma and Mahāpadma, are recorded as being of the nature of sattva;
they are marked with a crocodile and are the possessors of swords, arrows, spears, and other weapons.
He should bestow [wealth] upon one who has heard [the Dharma], he attains constant friendship with kings,
and for the sake of wealth, he may even meet his destruction at the hands of an enemy in battle.
The Makara and the Kacchapa are indeed remembered as the two treasures of Tamas;
the Kacchapī trusts no one, she neither enjoys nor gives.
That treasure also makes a hoard upon the earth, yet it belongs to a single man;
Rājasena and Mukunda were recognized as the possessors of the kingdom.
Having enjoyed his pleasures, he should give [wealth] to singers and to courtesans and the like; Nandin, who is composed of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), shall be the support of the family.
When praised, he indeed becomes pleased; he comes to have many wives, shows laxity toward former friends, and forms attachments with others.
Marked by the color blue and endowed with the splendor of *sattva*, he becomes a collector of clothing, grain, and other goods, and constructs tanks and similar works. (GarP 1.53.11)
One should cause a triple-storehouse and mango groves and the like to be established;
for one person there shall be a conch-storehouse, which he himself enjoys until the end of his wealth.
One who eats poor food, whose attendants do not wear fine garments,
and who is intent only on nourishing himself— even if he holds a conch shell— bestows his gifts upon other men in vain.
Because they yield mixed fruits through their mixed observation,
the nature of the treasures has been described by Hari as well as by Hara and others;
just as Hari spoke regarding the *Bhuvanakosa* and so forth, so shall I speak.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Nine Treasures," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 54—
Hari said:
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vapuṣmat, Dyutimat,
as well as Medhā, Medhātithi, Bhavya, Śabala, and Putra.
Jyotiṣmat was born as the tenth; these indeed were the sons of Priyavrata.
Medhā, Agnibāhu, and Putra—these three were devoted to yoga.
Those highly fortunate ones, who remembered their past lives, desired to be rid of kingship;
the king, having divided the seven continents, bestowed them upon the seven [brothers].
To the extent of fifty koṭis of yojanas,
the earth has risen above the waters and remains there like a boat upon the water of a river.
O Hara, the islands named Jambū and Plakṣa, and another, Śālmala;
then Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara is the seventh.
These continents are surrounded by seven oceans,
equal [in number], consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.
O Bull-bannered One, each continent and each ocean is twice the size of the preceding one;
Mount Meru stands in Jambūdvīpa, extending for one hundred thousand yojanas.
Its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas;
it enters sixteen thousand yojanas below [the surface] and is thirty-two thousand yojanas wide at its summit.
Below, extending for sixteen thousand [yojanas] and shaped like a pericarp,
are the Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha mountains on its southern side.
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are the mountain ranges in the north;
O Rudra, those eternal men who dwell in the regions beginning with Plakṣa [reside there].
Furthermore, for them there was no division of the ages (yugas) in any way;
for from Agrīdhna, the lord of Jambūdvīpa, nine sons were born.
Nābhi, Kimpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta,
Ramya, the one called Hiraṇmaya, Kuru, and Bhadrāśva.
King Ketumāla gave those regions, bearing their respective names, to them;
and from Nābhi and Merudevī, O Hara, a son named Ṛṣabha was born.
His son was named Bharata, who remained at Śālagrāma as one observing a vow;
Sumati was the son of Bharata, and his son was Taijasa.
Indradyumna was his son, and from him Parameṣṭhin is remembered;
Pratīhāra was his son, and Pratihartṛ was his offspring.
Suta was born from him; then Prastāra was his son, and Vibhu was his son.
Pṛthu was his son, and Nakta was his son; Gaya is recorded as the son of Nakta.
Nara was the son of Gaya; his son was Virāj Agata. From him was born the wise and highly effulgent Bhauvana, who was his son.
Tvaṣṭṛ was born from Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viraja was his son; Rajas was also his son, and Śatajit was the son of Rajas; Viṣvagjyotis is recorded as the son of that [Śatajit].

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Priyavrata for the Purpose of Describing the Cosmic Egg," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Hari said:
In the center, O bull-bannered one, is the region of Ilāvṛta; to the east is the wonderful Bhadrāśva;
and to the southeast is the region of Hiraṇvān.
Beyond that, the region of Kimpuruṣa is said to lie to the south of Meru;
Bhārata is declared to be to the south, and Hari is to the southwest.
In the west is Ketumāla, and Ramyaka is in the north-west;
and in the north is the region of Kuru, which is covered with wish-fulfilling trees.
O Rudra, spiritual accomplishment is natural everywhere except in Bhārata;
[this applies to] Indradvīpa, Kaśerumān, Tāmravarṇa, and Gabhastimān.
Nāgadvīpa, Kaṭāha, Siṃhala, and likewise Vāruṇa— this, however, is the ninth among them, an island surrounded by the ocean.
O Rudra, the Kirātas dwell to its east, the Yavanas are situated to its west, the Andhras are to the south,
and the Turuṣkas are also to the north.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras dwell within it;
so too do Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and the Ṛkṣa mountain.
The Vindhya, the Pāriyātra, and seven other principal mountain ranges are here;
as well as the Vedasmṛti, the Narmadā, the Varadā, the Surasā, and the Śivā.
The Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Sarayū, Kāverī, and likewise the Gomatī;
the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and the Mahānadī.
The Ketumāla, Tāmraparṇī, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī,
Ṛṣikulyā, Kāverī, Mattagaṅgā, and Payasvinī.
The Vidarbhā and the Śatadrū are auspicious rivers that remove sin;
people from the Middle Country and other regions drink their waters.
The Pañcālas, Kurus, Matsyas, Yaudheyas along with the Paṭaccaras,
the Kuntis, and the Śūrasenas are known as the people of Madhyadeśa.
O Bull-bannered One!
The people of Padma, the Sūtas, Māgadhas, Cedis, and Kāśis.
And the Videhas, as well as the Kosalas in the east.
The Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras, Aṅgas, Vaidarbhas, and Mūlakas,
as well as the regions situated within the Vindhyas, are recorded as being in the southeast.
The inhabitants of Pulinda, Aśmaka, Kīmūta, Naya, and Rāṣṭra; the Karṇas, Ānartas, Kambojas, and Ghaṇas; and those dwelling in the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha).
The Ambaṣṭhas, Draviḍas, Lāṭas, Kāmbojas, Śakas with women’s faces,
and those dwelling in Ānarta are to be known as being in the southwest of Yakṣiṇī.
The Strīrājyas, the Saindhavas, the Mlecchas, the Kāyasthas, and the Yavanas are to be known as being in the west, along with the Mathuras and the Naiṣadhas.
The Māṇḍavyas, the Tuṣāras, the Mūlikas, the Aśvamukhas, the Khaśas,
the Mahākeśas, and the Mahānāsas are the regions in the north-west.
The Lambas, Mūṣakas, Stanapās, as well as the Madras, Gāndhāras, and Bāhlikas—
the Mlecchas whose abode is the Himālaya— dwell in the northern direction.
The Trigartas, Nīlakolas, Ātas, Brahmaputras, along with the Ṭaṅkaṇas,
the Abhīṣāhas, and the Kāśmīras, are proclaimed as being situated to the north.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 56— Hari said:
Medhātithi, the lord of Plakṣadvīpa, had seven sons:
the eldest was named Śāntabhava, and Śiśira was the one after him.
Sukhodaya, Nanda, Śiva, Kṣemaka,
and Dhruva as the seventh— these indeed were the lords of Plakṣadvīpa.
Gomeda, Candra, Nārada, Dundubhi,
Somaka, Sumanas, and the mountain Baibhrāja is the seventh here.
Anutaptā, Śikhī, Vipāśā, Tridivā, Kramu,
Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā— these seven are the rivers there.
The lord of Śālmaladvīpa is Vapuṣmān; his sons, who give their names to the regions, are Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, and Rohita.
Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Saprabha as the seventh;
then Kumuda, Unnata, Droṇa, Mahiṣa, and Balāhaka.
Krauñca, Kakudmat—these indeed are the mountains; and these are the rivers:
Yonitoyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, and Vimocanī.
Vidhṛti is remembered as the seventh among them; they are known to grant the pacification of sins.
Hear now of the seven sons of Jyotiṣmat in Kuśadvīpa.
Udbhida, Veṇumān, Dvairatha, Lambana, Dhṛti,
Prabhākara, and Kapila— these are the sequence of regions named after them.
Vidruma, Hemaśaila, Dyutimān, Puṣpavān,
Kuśeśaya, Hari, and Mandarācala as the seventh.
Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, Sanmati, Vidyudabhrā, Mahī, and another; these are the destroyers of all sins.
In Krauñcadvīpa, the sons of the high-souled Dyutimat were seven:
Kuśala, Mandaga, Uṣṇa, Pīvara, and then Andhakāraka.
O Hara, Muni and Dundubhi—these seven were his sons;
as well as Krauñca, Vāmana, and the third, Andhakāraka.
Divāvṛt is the fifth, and there is another, Dundubhi Puṇḍarīkavat;
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, and Manojava.
Khyāti, Puṇḍarīkā, and the others—these seven are the rivers of the [seven] regions.
From Bhavya, the lord of Śākadvīpa, seven sons were born.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Aruṇī, Baka,
Kusumoda, Samodārki, and the seventh, Mahādruma.
Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī, and Dhenukā; Ikṣu, Veṇukā, and likewise Gabhastī as the seventh.
From Śabala and Puṣkareśa were born Mahāvīra and Dhātaki;
and likewise, there was the Mānasottara mountain, spanning two varṣas.
It rises fifty thousand yojanas upward,
and it is likewise as many [yojanas] in extent, being perfectly circular on all sides.
Puṣkara is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water;
beyond the ocean of sweet water, the configuration of the world is seen.
Twice as large is the golden earth, devoid of all living beings;
beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas in extent;
the mountain is enveloped by darkness, and the darkness is enclosed by the shell of the cosmic egg.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 57—
Hari said:
The height of the earth is said to be seventy thousand [yojanas];
each of the netherworlds (pātāla), O Bull-bannered One, is ten thousand [yojanas] deep.
Aṭala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat,
the one called Mahātala, Sutala, and Pātāla as the seventh.
It is black, white, reddish, yellow, sandy, rocky, and golden;
moreover, Daityas and serpents dwell there.
In the Raudra region of Puṣkaradvīpa, however, there are hells; hear of them:
Raurava, Sūkara, Rodha, Tāla, and likewise Vinaśana.
Mahājvāla, Taptakumbha, Lavaṇa, Vimohita,
the one called Rudhira, Vaitaraṇī, Kṛmiśa, Kṛmibhojana, and Jana.
The Asipatravana, Kṛṣṇa, and the dreadful Nānābhakṣa; likewise the sinful Pūyavaha, Vahnijvāla, and Adhaḥśiras.
Saṃdaṃśa, Kṛṣṇasūtra, Tamaḥ,
Avīci, Śvabhojana, Apratiṣṭha, and Uṣṇavīci are known as the hells.
O Rudra, those sinners who administer poison, weapons, or fire are cooked within them; indeed, the worlds of the Bhūtas and others are situated one above the other.
O Rudra, that egg was enveloped by water, fire, air, and ether, as well as by the *bhūtādi*; it was further encased by the Great Principle (*mahat*) and by primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
Nārāyaṇa abides pervading the egg, which is tenfold [in extent].

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Netherworlds, Hells, and Other Regions within the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Hari said:
I shall describe the dimensions and configuration of the chariots of the Sun and the other planets; listen to me. The chariot of the Sun is nine thousand *yojanas* in length.
Likewise, O Bull-bannered One, its pole is twice that length;
it measures one and a half koṭis and seven additional niyutas.
Its axle measures a yojana, and upon it is established a wheel with three hubs, five spokes, and six rims, which is imperishable by nature.
The entire wheel of time, consisting of a full year, is established upon it;
the second axle of Vivasvat is forty thousand [yojanas] long.
But for the chariot of the bull-bannered god, O Lord, the measurement of both axles is five and a half [cubits],
while the measurement of the two halves of the yoke is the same.
The shorter axle of the chariot, which rests upon the support of the Pole Star (Dhruva), is equal to half that [longer] yoke;
the second wheel, however, is situated upon the Mānasa mountain.
Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, Jagatī, Triṣṭubh,
Anuṣṭubh, and Paṅkti— these are said to be the meters that serve as the bay horses of the Sun.
Dhātṛ, Kratusthalā, Pulastya, Vāsuki,
Rathakṛt the grāmaṇī, Heti, and Tumburu [preside] during the month of Caitra.
Aryaman, Pulaha, Rathojas, Puñjikasthalā,
Praheti, Kacchanīra, and Nārada [are the deities] in the month of Mādhava.
Mitra, Atri, Takṣaka, Rakṣas, Pauruṣeya,
Menakā, Hāhā, and Rathasvana— these are stationed on the chariot of Bhānu in the Jyeṣṭhā constellation.
Varuṇa, Vasiṣṭha, Rambhā, Sahajanyā, Kuhū, Budha,
Rathacitra, and Śukra dwell in the month known as Āṣāḍha.
Indra, Viśvāvasu, Srotra, Elāpatra, as well as Aṅgiras,
Pramlocā, and Nabhas— these indeed reside in the month of Āṣāḍha; and in the month of Śrāvaṇa, there are the serpents.
Vivasvān, Ugrasena, Bhṛgu, Āpūraṇa,
Anumlocā, Śaṅkhapāla, and Vyāghra— these were the [deities] in Bhādrapada.
When the sun is in Āśvinī, Pūṣan, Suruci, Dhātṛ, Gautama, Dhananjaya, Suṣeṇa, and another, as well as Dhṛtācī, dwell there.
Viśvāvasu, Bharadvāja, Parjanya, Airāvata,
Viśvācī, Senajit,
and Āpa are the presiding deities in the month of Kārttika.
Aṃśu, Kāśyapa, Tārkṣya, Mahāpadma, Urvaśī,
Citrasena, and likewise Vidyunmārga are the presiding deities of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Kratu, Bharga, Urṇāyu, Sphūrja, Karkoṭaka,
Ariṣṭanemi, and another, Pūrvacitti—
the best of sages— these seven dwell in the solar disc during the month of Pauṣa.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Jamadagni, Kambala, Tilottamā,
Brahmāpeta, Ṛtajit, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra as the seventh—
these seven dwell within the solar orb during the month of Māgha.
Viṣṇu, Aśvatara, Rambhā, Sūryavarcas, Satyajit,
Viśvāmitra, as well as Rakṣas and Yajñāpetas were indeed born in the month of Phālguna.
O Brahmin, in the orb of the Sun, sages empowered by the energy of Viṣṇu praise the Sun, while Gandharvas sing before him.
The Apsarases dance as they go, followed by the night-stalkers;
the Pannagas carry [the chariot], while the Yakṣas hold the reins.
Likewise, the Bālakhilyas sit surrounding him;
Soma’s chariot has three wheels, and his horses have the luster of jasmine.
Yoked on the left and right by those ten, he moves about;
the chariot of the son of the Moon is produced from the substance of *vārya* (or *yva*) and *granidravya*.
Yoked to eight tawny horses with the speed of the wind, he was equipped with a protective fender and a chassis,
drawn by steeds born of the earth.
The great chariot of Śukra is equipped with quivers and banners;
the chariot of the son of the Earth (Mangala) is likewise like molten gold.
The great chariot of Bhauma was also golden, magnificent, and drawn by eight horses.
He is joined with eight white horses born of fire, yoked to a golden chariot, and [drawn by] steeds as crimson as rubies.
Bṛhaspati indeed remains for a year in each zodiac sign;
his chariot is yoked with dappled horses born of the sky.
Having ascended, Śanaiścara, the slow-moving one, proceeds slowly;
for Svarbhānu’s horses are eight in number, bee-black in hue, and they draw his grey chariot.
O Lord of Beings, O Śiva, those horses of the chariot of Ketu, once yoked, carry it incessantly; they are eight in number and possess the speed of the wind.
Having the hue of smoke from burning straw, reddish like lac-dye, the islands,
rivers, mountains, and oceans are the body of Hari.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Now begins] the Jyotiḥśāstra.
Sūta said:
Having explained the measurement of the earth and the stellar sphere, Keśava, the giver of all, spoke to Rudra the essence of Jyotiṣa, consisting of four hundred thousand verses.
Hari said:
"The Kṛttikās have Agni as their deity; the Rohiṇīs are remembered as belonging to Brahmā;
the Ilvalās have Soma as their deity; and Ārdrā is declared to belong to Rudra."
Likewise, Punarvasu has the Sun as its deity, and Tiṣya has Jupiter as its deity;
Aśleṣā has the serpents as its deity, and Maghā has the ancestors as its deity.
Bhaga and Pūrvaphalgunī, as well as Aryaman and Uttarā;
Sāvitra and Hastā, and Citrā is proclaimed to be Tvaṣṭṛ.
The constellation Svātī is proclaimed to have Vāyu as its deity;
O Bull-bannered One, Viśākhā is said to have Indra and Agni as its deities.
Mṛgaśiras, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and Anurādhā are proclaimed as belonging to Mitra; Jyeṣṭhā is declared to belong to Śakra;
likewise, Mūla is stated by the knowers of truth to have Nirṛti as its deity.
Āṣāḍhā is said to belong to the Āpyas; the two Uttarās are dedicated to the Viśvedevas;
Abhijit is declared to be Brāhma; and Śravaṇā is remembered as Vaiṣṇava.
Vāsava, likewise Ṛkṣa, and Dhaniṣṭhā are declared by the wise;
likewise, O auspicious one, the constellation Śatabhiṣā is called Vāruṇa.
The asterism Āja is Pūrvabhādrapadā; likewise, Ahirbudhnya is Uttarabhādrapadā;
Pauṣṇa is the asterism Revatī; and Aśvayuj is the asterism whose deity is the horse (Aśvin).
Bharaṇī, the asterism, and likewise Yāmya—these have been declared to be the deities of the asterisms;
Brahmāṇī is established in the east on the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight.
Māheśvarī is in the north on the second lunar day of the tenth fortnight,
and Vārāhī is situated in the south on the fifth and the thirteenth.
On the sixth and the fourteenth [lunar days], Indrāṇī is situated in the west;
on the seventh and the full moon day, Cāmuṇḍā is in the direction of the wind (the northwest).
On the eighth day conjoined with the new moon, she is within the range of Mahālakṣmīśa;
on the eleventh and the third days, Vaiṣṇavī is indeed in the southeast corner.
On the twelfth and the fourth lunar days, as well as in the southwest, one should not undertake journeys and other such activities while facing the Yoginī Kaumārī.
Aśvinī, Anurādhā, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Mūla, Punarvasu,
Puṣya, Hastā, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā are said to be most auspicious for setting out on a journey.
The five constellations beginning with Hasta, the three Uttaras,
Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Punarvasū.
The group of constellations beginning with Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Mūla, and Viśākhā is remembered as the most excellent for wearing and donning garments.
Three [nakṣatras] are proclaimed as being with their faces downward;
in these, one should establish ponds, tanks, wells, and grassy plots of land.
Digging up a temple, as well as digging for hidden treasure;
the practice of astrology, the commencement of astronomical calculations, and entering into underground caverns.
O Bull-bannered One, one should perform [the rites] directed downwards during the other [asterisms]:
Revatī, Aśvinī, Citrā, Svātī, Hastā, and Punarvasū.
Anurādhā, Mṛga, and Jyeṣṭhā—these are remembered as facing the side;
they are used for the taming of elephants, camels, horses, bulls, and buffaloes.
One may perform the sowing of seeds, as well as going and coming, and the setting in motion of wheels, mechanical devices, chariots, boats, and so forth. (GarP 1.59.22)
One should also perform those actions that are prescribed for the [other] sides during these [asterisms]:
Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, Puṣya, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttarās.
Vāruṇa and Śravaṇa are likewise known as the nine upward-facing [asterisms];
under these, one should perform the royal consecration and the binding of the turban.
One should cause all of these to be erected with their openings facing upward;
likewise, the fourth, sixth, eighth, and ninth are inauspicious.
The new moon day, the full moon day, as well as the twelfth and fourteenth days, and the first day of the dark fortnight—
these are excellent when joined with the son of the Moon (Mercury) on the second lunar day.
The third [lunar day] is auspicious with the son of the Earth (Mars), and the fourth with Saturn;
the fifth is auspicious with Jupiter, and the sixth with Mars and Venus.
The seventh is auspicious with the son of Soma (Mercury); the eighth with Mars and the Sun;
the ninth with Venus; and the tenth is auspicious with Jupiter.
On the eleventh day, Jupiter and Venus [are auspicious]; on the twelfth, Mercury;
on the thirteenth, Venus and Mars; and the fourteenth is most excellent for Saturn.
Both the full moon and the new moon days are most auspicious when Jupiter is present;
the sun burns away the twelfth lunar day, and the moon burns away the eleventh.
Mars shall burn the tenth period, and Mercury shall burn the ninth;
Jupiter burns the eighth, and Venus shall burn the seventh.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) causes burning on the sixth lunar day; indeed, there is no such [burning] at the beginning of journeys and so forth on the first, ninth, fourteenth, and eighth days.
One should avoid setting out on a journey on Wednesday;
likewise, the sixth lunar day in Aries and Cancer, and the eighth lunar day in Virgo and Gemini [are to be avoided].
The fourth lunar day occurs in Taurus and Aquarius; the twelfth in Capricorn and Libra;
the tenth in Scorpio and Leo; and the fourteenth in Sagittarius and Pisces.
These [asterisms] are burnt; indeed, men should not travel during them, as there will be suffering and other afflictions.
When the Sun is in the three Viśākhās and the Moon is in the three Pūrvāṣāḍhās, [these are the times].
O Śiva, the triad of Dhaniṣṭhā is for Mars; the triad of Revatī is for Mercury;
the triad beginning with Rohiṇī is for Jupiter; and the triad of Puṣya is for Venus.
On Saturdays, one should avoid the three [asterisms] beginning with Uttarāphalgunī;
during these conjunctions, calamities, death, disease, and the like may occur.
The Sun is in Mūla, the Moon in Śravaṇa, Mars in the latter Proṣṭhapadās,
Mercury in Kṛttikā, and Jupiter, O Rudra, in Punarvasu.
Pūrvaphalgunī with Venus and Svāti with Saturn—
these are the Amṛta yogas, which accomplish all undertakings.
Is it time that kills? Or is it power? Or is it the undesirable and the dull-witted?
The times beginning with the lunar festival (parvan) should be known by those who are experts in time.
Having combined the syllables and measures of the names of the woman and the man, [divide] by three.
If two remain in the division, there is the destruction of the woman; if one or zero remain, it shall be for the man.
In Viṣkambha, five ghaṭikās are proclaimed; in Śūla, seven;
in Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, six; and in Vyāghāta and Vajra, nine.
On the days of Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti,
one should avoid all ritual actions, for on these occasions death is indeed present.
Hasta and Ārdrā are auspicious when Jupiter is present;
Anurādhā is auspicious for Mercury; Rohiṇī is excellent for Saturn; and Mṛgaśiras is indeed auspicious with the Moon.
Revatī is most excellent for Venus, and Aśvinī is auspicious for Mars;
indeed, when these are joined with Siddhi-yoga, they destroy all defects.
O Bull-bannered Lord, when Venus is in Pūrvaphalgunī and the Moon in Citrā;
and when Mars is in Uttarāṣāḍhā and Mercury in Dhaniṣṭhā, O Hara.
O Rudra, Śatabhiṣā is auspicious on Saturday; likewise, Rohiṇī on Friday;
and Revatī on Saturday, O Śambhu.
The poison-yogas have been fully described.
Puṣya, Punarvasu, Revatī together with Citrā, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, as well as Hasta, Aśvinī, and Mṛga; GarP_1,59.48.
A person should perform the birth rites and other ceremonies under the asterism Śatabhiṣā; likewise, O Rudra,
under Viśākhā, the three Uttarās, Maghā, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī,
and Kṛttikā.
At the time of departure, they bring about death.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Lunar Mansions, Their Deities, the *Dagdhayoga*, and Other Astrological Matters," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 60, Hari said:
The period (daśā) for the Sun is known to be six; for the Moon, fifteen is recorded;
for Mars, eight; and for Mercury, sixteen is recorded by the wise.
Ten years are to be known for Saturn, nineteen for Jupiter,
twelve years for Rāhu, and twenty-one for Venus.
The period (daśā) of the Sun brings about suffering, agitation, and the destruction of the king;
likewise, the period of the Moon bestows prosperity and provides desired food and happiness.
The period (daśā) of Mars brings suffering and causes the destruction of sovereignty and other blessings;
the period of Mercury bestows celestial women, grants sovereignty, and increases the treasury.
The daśā of Saturn brings about the loss of kingdom and suffering for kinsmen;
the daśā of Jupiter bestows sovereignty and grants happiness, dharma, and other blessings.
The daśā of Rāhu brings about the loss of kingdom, disease, and suffering;
the daśā of Venus bestows elephants and horses, as well as the acquisition of kingdom and women.
Aries is the domain of Aṅgāraka (Mars), Taurus is proclaimed as that of Śukra (Venus),
Mercury is to be known as belonging to Gemini, and the Moon belongs to Cancer.
Leo is the domain of the Sun; Virgo is the domain of Mercury;
Libra is the domain of Venus; and Scorpio is the domain of Mars.
The bow (Sagittarius) belongs to the preceptor of the gods (Jupiter), while Capricorn and Aquarius belong to Saturn;
Pisces also belongs to the preceptor of the gods—this is proclaimed as the planetary domain.
If there should be two full-moon days in that [month] with two Pūrvāṣāḍhās occurring, it is to be known as Dvirāṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are for adornment;
deer, snakes, monkeys, cats, dogs, pigs, and birds [are the animals associated with these].
The mongoose and the rat are auspicious on the right during a journey;
likewise, a Brahmin girl, a jackal, a conch shell, a drum, and the earth are favorable for them.
The sight of bamboo, women, and full water-jars during a journey is auspicious;
likewise, jackals, camels, donkeys, and the like are auspicious when on the left side during a journey.
Cotton, medicinal herbs, oil, cooked food, charcoal, serpents, a woman with disheveled hair, red garlands, and a naked person— these and others are seen as inauspicious omens.
I shall describe the characteristics for *hakrā*; one obtains great fruit in the east.
In the southeast there is grief and torment; in the south, one meets with loss.
In the southwest, there is grief and distress; in the west, one obtains sweet food;
in the northwest, one attains wealth; and in the north, there will be quarrel.
Death is declared in the northeast; such is the fruit and non-fruit of hiccough.
Having drawn the solar wheel (ravicakra), Bhāskara appears in the likeness of a man.
In whichever constellation the sun resides, one should place three [units] on its head,
three on its face, and assign one each to its two shoulders.
One should assign one [constellation] to each pair of arms, one to each of the two hands,
five constellations to the heart, and one at the navel.
One should place one constellation at the secret place and place each one at the knees;
the remaining constellations should be assigned to the feet of the Sun.
If the mark is on the foot, the man becomes short-lived;
if it is on the knee, he travels to foreign lands; and if it is located on the private parts, he is an adulterer.

If it resides in the navel, one is content with little; if it resides in the heart, one becomes a great lord (Maheśvara); if it resides in the hand, one becomes a thief; and if it is displaced from its station, one becomes a banner-bearer (standard-bearer).
If the constellation is situated in the shoulder, one obtains wealth; if it is situated in the mouth, one obtains sweet food;
and if the constellation is situated on the head, there will be fine garments.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Planetary Periods and Other Matters in the Science of Astrology," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 61. Hari said:
The Moon situated in the seventh, eleventh, or first house is auspicious in all circumstances;
however, during the bright fortnight, it is likewise auspicious when located in the second, fifth, or ninth house.
Being honored by the worlds, the Moon is regarded like a preceptor;
listen now to those twelve states of the Moon as well.
I shall now describe [the results] for each set of three constellations, beginning with Aśvinī:
[the first] indicates one who was abroad and is seen again; [the second] indicates one in a state of death; [and the third] brings victory.
The state of laughter, the state of play (or sport), and the state of joy; the state of despondency, the state of enjoyment, and the state of fever are thus established.
The trembling state, the state of happiness, and the state consisting of twelve conditions shall occur:
travel abroad, loss, debt, victory, laughter, pleasure, and happiness. (GarP 1.61.5)
Sorrow, enjoyment, fever, trembling, and happiness are the results in sequence;
[the planet] situated in the first house produces contentment, but in the second house there is no peace.
In the third [lunar mansion] there is honor from the king; in the fourth, the arrival of quarrels;
and by the fifth, the moon, there will indeed be the gain of a woman.
In the sixth [month] there is the arrival of abundant grain; in the seventh, pleasure and honor;
in the eighth, danger to life; and in the ninth, the accumulation of a treasury.
In the tenth [lunar day], the accomplishment of one's purpose is certain; in the eleventh, victory;
but with the twelfth moon, there is indeed death—of this there is no doubt.
One should proceed to the east during the seven constellations beginning with Kṛttikā;
one should go to the south during those beginning with Maghā, and to the west during those beginning with Anurādhā.
A northern journey is highly commended during the seven asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā;
Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are likewise well-adorned for such purposes.
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Citrā, Puṣya, Mūla, and Hasta are always auspicious for the giving away of a daughter, for journeys, and for rites such as consecrations.
Indeed, Venus and the Moon, situated in the birth sign or in the second house, bestow auspicious results;
and Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, and the Moon likewise [bestow auspicious results] in each successive sign up to the third house.
Mars, Saturn, the Moon, and the Sun [are auspicious] in the fourth house; Mercury is excellent in the fourth;
Venus and Jupiter are in the fifth, joined with the Moon and Ketu.
Mars in the sixth house in a gentle aspect, Jupiter and the Moon in the seventh, and Mercury and Venus in the eighth are excellent; Jupiter situated in the ninth house is auspicious.
The Sun, Saturn, and Moon are the planets in the tenth house; the remaining ones are in the eleventh.
Mercury is in the twelfth, and Bhārgava (Venus) shall be a giver of happiness.
The crocodile is best with Leo; Aries is most excellent with Virgo; Pisces with Libra, and Cancer with Aquarius.
The Bull is best with the Bow, and the Scorpion with the Twins;
this hexagon [of signs] leads to mutual affection, of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Auspicious and Inauspicious Positions of the Planets," in the section on Astrology (*Jyotiḥśāstra*) within the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Measurement of Hours for the Ascendant (*Lagna*) and Other Matters," in the section on Astrology (*Jyotiḥśāstra*) within the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*: Chapter 63.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 63. Hari said:
"O Śaṅkara, listen as I describe the characteristics of men and women in brief."
His soles are free from sweat, soft, and resemble the interior of a lotus.
Indeed, the feet of the best of kings have closely joined toes and copper-colored nails, beautiful ankles, are free of visible veins, and are as high-arched as the shell of a tortoise.
The feet are rough and pale-nailed, crooked and veiny, shaped like winnowing baskets, withered, and having widely spaced toes.
Suffering and poverty would prevail; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
A shank covered with few hairs, resembling the trunk of an elephant, is excellent. (GarP 1.63.4)
For great-souled kings, there may be a single hair in each pore;
for learned scholars and likewise for those well-versed in the Vedas, there are two hairs in each pore.
Those with three hairs on the forehead are poor; one with fleshless knees is diseased;
and one with few secondary sexual characteristics will be wealthy yet deprived of sons and other kin.
If the penis is thick, one will be poor; if it is crooked, one will be miserable;
if it is uneven, one will be fickle toward women; and if the testicles are symmetrical, one will become a king.
One with pendulous testicles will have a short life and be destitute, while one with small testicles will be poor. A man with pale or dark-colored testicles, however, shall be happy.
Those without wealth have noisy urine; kings have a silent flow. Those rich in enjoyments have symmetrical bellies; those without wealth have bellies resembling jars.
Those with snake-like bellies shall be poor; and by the lines on the forehead, one's lifespan is declared. He on whose forehead three well-aligned lines are seen [is long-lived].
That man who sees two lines lives for sixty years, endowed with happiness and sons;
and by seeing [another] pair of lines, a man lives for forty years.
One with a single line lives for twenty years; those with lines reaching to the ears live for a hundred years.

With seventy lines, the lifespan is one hundred and forty years; with sixty lines, it becomes one hundred and twenty years; and with clearly visible and indistinct lines, a man shall have a lifespan of one hundred years.
One whose lines are deficient lives for forty years;
indeed, by means of broken lines, a man meets an untimely death.
He on whose forehead a trident or even a spear-head is seen shall live for a hundred autumns, endowed with wealth and sons.
O Rudra, he whose line of life (āyūrekhā) is reached from the middle by the index finger and the middle finger shall live for a hundred autumns.
The first line of knowledge indeed follows from the thumb;
the line reaching the base of the middle finger is the life-line (āyūrekhā) beyond that.
If the line of longevity (āyūrekhā) reaches the little finger,
whether it be unbroken or divided, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
O Rudra, he upon whose palm the lines reveal his lifespan shall live for a hundred years as an enjoyer of pleasures;
of this there is no doubt.
If the line of life, starting from the little finger and extending toward the middle finger, reaches it,
it makes a human being sixty years of age.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Male Characteristics in Sāmudrika within the Science of Astrology," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 64— Hari said:
But she whose hair is curled, whose face is perfectly round,
and whose navel spirals to the right— that maiden increases the prosperity of her family.
And she who possesses a golden complexion and red lotus-like hands shall be the devoted wife even of a thousand women.
The maiden who has curly hair and whose eyes are circular will certainly be a partaker of suffering,
and her husband will die.
A maiden with a face like the full moon, possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun,
with large eyes and lips like the *bimba* fruit— that maiden attains happiness.
With many lines there is suffering; with very few, a lack of wealth. Through red lines one attains happiness; through black ones, one goes into servitude.
In affairs of state, she should be a counselor; in ritual acts, a virtuous wife;
in acts of affection, a mother; and in the bedchamber, a courtesan is auspicious.
The woman upon whose palm there appears a goad, an earring, and a wheel shall give birth to a son and obtain a husband who is a lord of men.
But she whose sides are hairy, whose breasts are hairy,
and whose lower lips are sunken, quickly causes the death of her husband.
She on whose palm there is a line forming a wall and an archway,
even if born in the family of a slave, attains the status of a queen.
She whose line of body hair is upturned and continuous,
even if born in a royal family, falls into the state of a slave-girl.
She whose ring finger and thumb do not touch the ground quickly kills her husband and conducts herself according to her own will.
Merely by her movement, an earthquake is produced;
she quickly causes the death of her husband and conducts herself according to her own will.
Through the oil for the eyes, one gains good fortune; through the oil for the teeth, food;
through the oil for the skin, a bed; and through the oil for the feet, a vehicle.
A woman’s auspicious feet are smooth, elevated, and have copper-colored nails;
they are marked with the signs of a fish, a goad, and a lotus, and are characterized by the wheel and the plow.
A woman’s feet are praised when they are free from perspiration and have soft soles;
her shanks are auspicious when hairless, and her thighs resemble the trunks of elephants.
The secret organ is broad, resembling a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, and most excellent;
the navel is praised as being deep, auspiciously spiraling to the right, and hairless;
the three folds of the abdomen belong to a noble woman, and her heart and breasts are free from hair.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Women," within the section on Physiognomy (Sāmudrika) in the Science of Astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra), under the Section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa), in the First Part of the Ancient Section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 65—
Hari said:
I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of men and women as taught by Samudra,
by the mere knowledge of which the past, the future, and the present are understood.
His feet were free from perspiration, with soft soles resembling the interior of a lotus;
his toes were joined together, his nails were copper-colored, and his ankles were concealed by the calves.
When the feet are elevated like a tortoise, with hidden ankles and well-formed heels, they are said to belong to a king;
whereas feet that are shaped like snakes, rough, crooked, and veiny belong to others.
His feet were withered, with pale nails and sparse toes;
they were like dried dye-stuffs, fit only for the road.
O Brahmin, those who cause the destruction of their lineage and those who kill a Brāhmaṇa resemble a stake or a crab;
those who take pleasure in approaching women who should not be approached have shanks with sparse hair.
The shanks are covered with soft hair and are even, possessing the luster of an elephant's trunk; the thighs and knees are symmetrical and well-developed—these are said to be the marks of a king.
Sṛgālajaṅghā was born from Niḥsva; Rauma was born from each one of the kūpakas;
two were born for the kings and the Vedic scholars, and two for the wise ones of prosperity.
Those with three or more [lines] will be destitute men, partakers of misery, and censured;
moreover, those with curly hair—such a man dies while abroad.
One with fleshless knees possesses good fortune; through slightly depressed [knees], one has pleasure with women;
those with protruding [knees] are poor; and with knees covered in flesh, one attains even sovereignty.
A man with a small penis is said by the great ones to have a long life and be wealthy;
one with a large penis is devoid of offspring and abandoned by fortune.
If the penis is bent downwards, one will be deprived of sons and wealth;
if it is curved in another way, one will have sons; but if it is bent downwards, there will be poverty.
If the penis is small and without veins, the man will be happy;
if the penis is joined with thick knots, he will be endowed with sons and other blessings.
One with thighs hidden in a sheath, long and curved, is devoid of wealth;
yet he is strong, fond of battle, and capable of swift movement.
One who is weak and has only one testicle is fickle toward women;
one with symmetrical testicles is declared a ruler of the earth, while one with pendulous testicles lives for a hundred years.
By those [teeth] being prominent, one has a long life; by rough gems [on the teeth], one is a lord;
by white gems [on the teeth], one is destitute; and by dark ones, one partakes in happiness.
Men who pass urine with sound or without sound shall become poor;
likewise, those who discharge it in one, two, three, four, five, or six streams.
Kings are said to be those whose urine flows in a clockwise swirl;
those whose urine is scattered are destitute, yet they bestow preeminent happiness.
Women possess a single stream [of hair] due to their smooth, elevated, and even jewel-like breasts;
those who possess the wealth of a woman-jewel have middling ones, while maidens have depressed ones.
Those with dry breath and very parched breath are proclaimed to be unfortunate;
those with the scent of flowers become kings, while those with the scent of honey possess great wealth.

If there is the smell of fish, the sons will be [procreated] by Śukra; if there is the smell of the body, the offspring will be daughters. If there is the smell of meat, one will be a great enjoyer; if there is the smell of ichor, one will be a performer of sacrifices.
One who has a pungent odor will be poor; one who copulates quickly will be long-lived, while one who copulates slowly will have a short life. One with thick buttocks will be destitute of wealth.
One with fleshy buttocks will be happy; one with buttocks like those of a lion is known to be a sovereign.
A man with a waist like a lion's becomes a king, while one with a waist like a monkey's is destitute.

Those with bellies like a serpent's will be poor; those with bellies resembling cooking pots or jars will be wealthy; those with broad sides will be rich, while those with red and sunken sides will be destitute.
Those with symmetrical armpits are rich in enjoyments; those with sunken armpits are bereft of wealth;
kings have elevated armpits, while those with uneven armpits are deceitful.
Those with fish-shaped navels are said to possess great wealth; those with deep navels are considered happy;
those with broad and deep navels are sharers of suffering.
Indeed, the navel situated in the middle of the *bali* causes suffering from the trident;
a counter-clockwise rotation [of the hair] brings success, while a clockwise one likewise brings wisdom.
A line extending along the side bestows long life; when seated, it makes one a lord of wealth;
below that, it makes one rich in cattle; and the pericarp of a lotus brings sovereignty.
One with a single line on the forehead shall live for a hundred years; one with two lines is said to be a possessor of wealth and enjoyments;
one with three lines becomes a king or a teacher; and one with straight lines is happy.
He avoids forbidden women, possesses a straight trunk, and has kings as his attendants; his flanks are fleshy, soft, perfectly symmetrical, and covered with hairs that curl to the right.
Men with inverted nipples, those who are servants to others, devoid of wealth, and bereft of happiness,
become fortunate if their nipples are not protruding.
Those with uneven and long [breasts] are poor; those with yellowish and fleshy ones are kings.
A heart that is level, elevated, unshakable, fleshy, and broad [is auspicious].
Among kings, those who are base have hair on their heads that is coarse and veiny; one who possesses wealth has a broad chest, while one who is powerful has a chest that is full and robust.
Men with uneven chests are devoid of wealth; likewise, those who meet their end by the sword are destitute.
Those with uneven clavicles are without possessions, as are those whose bones are bound together.
Those with prominent [jaws] possess enjoyments; those with depressed [jaws] are destitute; those with full [jaws] are endowed with wealth.
One with a flat neck is destitute, while one with a veinless and dry throat is happy.

One with a buffalo-like neck will be a hero; one with a deer-like neck will be learned in the scriptures; a king with a conch-like neck will be a consumer of excessive food; and one with a long neck will be a glutton.
A fragrant [tail] with a curved back is auspicious, while the opposite is inauspicious;
one whose armpits resemble the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, which is fragrant and covered in deer-like hair, is most excellent.
Otherwise, however, they are the cause of being devoid of wealth and poverty;
when the two ears are bent, small, joined, and broad, they are auspicious.
In a lord of kings, the arms hang down to the knees, being rounded and fleshy;
in the destitute, they are hairy and short, whereas the best are like the trunk of an elephant.
The fingers of the hand itself are auspicious when provided with weapons and banners;
for the wise they are slender, while for servants they are said to be flat.

Those with thick fingers will be destitute, while those with bent and very thin fingers will likewise be poor; those with hands like those of a monkey will be destitute, and those with hands like those of a tiger will possess strength.
And men whose hands are deep, with well-concealed wrists that are closely joined and fragrant, suffer the loss of paternal wealth. (GarP 1.65.41)
Kings who are devoid of taxes and free from noisy demands are truly wealthy;
those who are concealed and humble are proclaimed to be the possessors of riches.
Those who give with upturned faces are men of uneven character;
those who are masters [of generosity] have hands and palms that appear like lac-dye.
Men who are devoted to the wives of others are considered to be poor;
those with nails like chaff are eunuchs, and those with crooked or cracked nails are likewise impotent.

Likewise, those with deformed nails are penniless, while those with discolored nails are seekers of others' wealth; those with copper-colored big toes are kings, and those with barley-shaped [protrusions] on their big toes are wealthy.
One born with [fingers] arising from the base of the thumb will have a daughter;
one with long finger-joints will be long-lived and fortunate, while one with widely spaced fingers will be destitute.
And he whose fingers are thick, who possesses wealth, and on whose palm three lines indeed arise from the wrist—such a person is a king. (GarP 1.65.47)
A man marked with the yoke and the fish becomes a donor of sacrificial halls;
those shaped like a thunderbolt belong to the wealthy, while those resembling a fish's tail belong to the wise.
In the case of a king, [the marks] resemble a conch, an umbrella, a palanquin, an elephant, or a lotus;
in the case of a lord of treasures, they resemble a water-pot, a goad, a banner, or a lotus stalk.

The hands of those wealthy in cattle have the luster of a rope; those of a lord of men have the luster of a svastika; and in the hand of a king, there are the marks resembling a wheel, a sword, a javelin, a bow, and a spear.
One who is rich in sacrifices has the appearance of a mortar; one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire has the appearance of a sacrificial altar;
and one who is righteous has the appearance of a pond, a temple tank, or a triangle.
The lines at the base of the thumb indicate sons, and those that are fine indicate daughters;
a line extending from the forefinger to the base of the little finger [indicates longevity].
One with a hundred lines lives for a hundred years, while one with a scar on the forehead faces danger from trees;
those with many lines on the chin are destitute, and those with thin chins are devoid of wealth.
Those with fleshy lips are endowed with wealth; those with slightly reddish lips are kings;
while those with lips resembling the bimba fruit that are cracked, rough, and chapped are not.
Teeth that are uneven and lacking in luster are inauspicious; teeth that are glossy and dense are auspicious.
Sharp and even teeth are excellent; a tongue that is red and even is auspicious.
The palate should be known as smooth and long when there is wealth; it is characterized by loss of wealth when it is white, and when it is black, it is rough.
The face should be even, gentle, and well-proportioned.
The face of kings is stainless and smooth; that of the suffering is the opposite;
the face of the unfortunate brings great misery; one obtains a son from the face of a woman.
The face of the wealthy is round; that of those without wealth is long;
the face of the cowardly evildoer is curved; and that of the rogues is square.
The beard of those without sons is sunken and crooked; that of the miserly is short. That of the wealthy is full, lovely, smooth, auspicious, and soft. (GarP 1.65.59)
One whose beard is clumped together and whose tips are not split is a thief;
those with red, sparse, and coarse beards and ears shall meet a violent death.
Those with fleshless, flattened ears will have miserable enjoyments;
those with short ears will be kings, while those with spike-like ears or hairy ears will have their lives cut short.
Kings are proclaimed to be wealthy if they have large ears; those with ears that are smooth, well-knit, long-hanging, and fleshy are sovereigns.
One with sunken cheeks is indeed a consumer of wealth; one with full cheeks is a counselor.
One with a parrot-like nose will be happy, while one with a dry nose lives an exceedingly long life.
One who delights in approaching women who should not be approached will have a nose that is severed at the tip;
one with a long nose possesses good fortune, while a thief has contracted sense organs.
A flat nose indicates death; one with a depressed nose will be devoid of fortune.
However, those with nostrils that have small openings, are well-formed, and are not crooked belong to a lord of kings.
If it occurs in a cruel person, the sneeze will be from the right side; for those who are strong, it may happen only once.
A sneeze produced by a living being (jīva) is compact, resonant, and accompanied by a ringing sound.
Those with eyes that are curved at the corners, resembling lotus petals, partake of happiness;
those who are wicked and sinful have eyes like those of a cat, tawny as honey.
The generals are cruel, with squinting eyes, greenish eyes, and those stained by sin; they are heroes with crooked eyes and elephant-like eyes.
Those with deep-set eyes will become lords, while those with large eyes will be ministers;
those with eyes like blue lotuses will be learned, and good fortune belongs to those with dark eyes.
Indeed, there may be the gouging out of eyes that have black pupils;
those with circular eyes would become sinful, and those with sunken eyes would become destitute.

One with eyes that are moist, large, and wide will possess enjoyments; one with eyes that are very prominent will have a short life; one with eyes that are broad and elevated will be happy; and those with uneven eyebrows will be poor.
One whose eyebrows are thick, long, and closely joined will be wealthy;
one with eyebrows raised like the crescent moon will be destitute; and one with eyebrows that are broken in the middle and drooping will be poor.
Those who are attached to women who should not be approached, yet are abandoned for the sake of obtaining sons,
as well as those with large, protruding foreheads and uneven brows, [are of such a nature].
Men with eyebrows resembling the crescent moon are wealthy;
those with broad, shell-like, and veined eyebrows are doers of evil.
Those with veins that are knotted like swastikas are lords of wealth;
those with sunken foreheads are fit for imprisonment and likewise devoted to cruel deeds.
Those with contracted foreheads are miserly, while those with prominent ones are kings; weeping that is tearless, affectionate, and not dejected brings auspiciousness to men.
Weeping that is copious with tears and piteous, as well as weeping that is harsh, brings happiness; laughter that is without trembling is excellent, while laughter with eyes closed brings misfortune.
One who laughs excessively and wickedly in many ways is indeed like one possessed by madness;
furthermore, those who live for a hundred years have three lines extending across their foreheads.
With four lines there will be kingship and a lifespan of ninety-five;
with a single line, the lifespan is ninety; and those with broken lines are effeminate men.
If [the lines] reach the hairline, the man shall live for eighty years;
likewise, by five, seven, six, or many [lines], he shall live for fifty.
If there are forty [lines] curved, thirty touching the eyebrows,
and twenty curved to the left, the life span will be short due to these minor lines.

Kings have heads shaped like umbrellas, while those with sunken heads are wealthy; those with flattened heads face the death of their father, and those with perfectly rounded heads possess cattle and other riches.
He has a pot-shaped head, delights in sinful acts, and is destitute of wealth and other possessions;
his hair is black, curled, glossy, and grows individually from each pore.
O kings, [the hair] should not have split ends, nor be soft, nor be excessively abundant; likewise, it should not have many roots, nor be uneven, nor have thick tips, nor be tawny.
Those who are destitute and possess extremely coarse, thick, and black hair,
and whose limbs are exceedingly rough, veined, and devoid of flesh— GarP_1,65.85.
All that would otherwise be inauspicious becomes auspicious through this;
it is vast in three respects, profound, long-lasting, and subtle in five respects.
Six parts are elevated, four are short, and this king is red in seven places;
the navel, the voice, and the heart—these three are said to be deep.
For a man, the forehead, the face, the chest,
the eyes, the armpits, and the nose— these six, including the nape of the neck, are the marks of a king.
The shanks, the neck, and the penis are elevated and short;
the back, the four [palms and soles], the palate, the lower lip, and the nails are red.
The corners of the eyes, the feet, the tongue, and the lips—these five are indeed subtle;
likewise, the teeth, the finger-joints, the nails, the hair, and the skin are auspicious.
Long arms, the space between the breasts, long teeth, eyes, and nose—these are declared to be the characteristics of men; now I shall describe the characteristics in women.
The queen's feet are supple and symmetrical; her soles are copper-colored, as are her nails;
her toes are closely set and their tips are elevated—one who attains such a woman shall become a king.
His two auspicious soles are like lotuses, with hidden ankles and well-developed forms;
they are free from perspiration, soft on the surface, and adorned with the marks of a fish, a goad, and a banner.
The feet of a maidservant bear the marks of the vajra, lotus, and plow; otherwise, her shanks are hairless, well-rounded, veinless, and auspicious.
The two knees are auspicious when they are even, without protruding joints, and symmetrical;
the two thighs are auspicious when they resemble the trunks of elephants, hairless, and equal in size.

The secret region of women is vast and supreme, resembling the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree; their hips and foreheads are well-proportioned, and their thighs are auspiciously raised like the shell of a tortoise.
A hidden jewel is a giver of auspiciousness; a heavy hip is auspicious.
Deep, broad, and well-fleshed, it is excellent.
The navel is spiraled clockwise; the waist is adorned with three folds;
the breasts are hairless, full, firm, symmetrical, and auspicious.
Firm and hairy [breasts] are praised, as is a neck that is soft and shaped like a conch shell;
slightly reddish lower lips are excellent, and the face should be fleshy and round.
His teeth were like jasmine flowers; his speech was like that of the cuckoo—polite, free from deceit, and as pleasant as the cry of a swan.
The nose of women that is even, with symmetrical nostrils, is beautiful and auspicious;
the eye, resembling a blue lotus, should reach down to the nose and not be drooping.
The eyebrows are not broad, resembling the crescent moon; and the forehead is auspicious, shaped like a half-moon, not protruding, and hairless.
The pair of ears is well-fleshed, symmetrical, soft, and well-proportioned;
the hairs of the head are glossy, dark blue, soft, and curled.
