For women, the head is considered equally excellent as the sole of the foot or the palm of the hand; likewise, [auspicious marks] such as a horse, an elephant, the śrīvṛkṣa tree, a sacrificial post, an arrow, a barley grain, or a tomara-weapon [are signs of excellence].
With rows of banners and chowries, with mountain-shaped earrings and altars,
and with conchs, parasols, lotuses, fish, svastikas, and excellent chariots.
Women who possess the marks such as the goad and others will be favorites of kings;
their wrists are concealed, and their hands resemble the interior of a lotus.
The palm of a woman's hand should be auspicious, neither sunken nor raised;
marked with lines, it makes a woman one who does not become a widow and who enjoys sensual pleasures.
A line that rises from the wrist and reaches the middle finger on the hand [indicates this].
Whether it be on the palm of the hand or situated on the sole of the foot,
such a mark in women or men leads to sovereignty and happiness.
A line originating from the base of the little finger, extending into the space between the index and middle fingers, makes one live for a hundred years.
If the lines at the base of the thumb are deficient, they indicate a short lifespan;
those that are broad are said to signify sons, while those that are slender signify daughters.
A short, deeply severed [line] indicates a short lifespan, while a long, unsevered one indicates a long lifespan;
such are said to be the auspicious characteristics of women, whereas the opposite is inauspicious.
She whose little finger or ring finger does not touch the ground,
or whose forefinger extends beyond the thumb, is an unchaste woman.
Above, the two calves are provided with two muscular mounds, possessing many prominent veins, covered in hair, and exceedingly fleshy; likewise, the belly is shaped like a water-jar.
A secret organ that spirals to the left, is depressed, or small belongs to those who are miserable; with a short neck one is destitute, and with a long neck there is the destruction of one's lineage.
Women will be broad-hipped and fierce; of this there is no doubt.
When the eyes are squinting and tawny, the virtuous woman has dark and tremulous eyes.
If it strikes the hollows of the cheeks, she is certainly unchaste;
if it hangs down upon the forehead, that woman kills her husband's younger brother.
A woman who has hair on her belly destroys her father-in-law; one with hair on both buttocks destroys her husband;
and she who has hair on her upper lip is certainly not auspicious for her husband.
Breasts that are hairy and unattractive, ears that are uneven,
and teeth that are jagged and irregular— these lead to suffering for you.
Those who eat black meat will suffer from theft; those with long [teeth] bring death to their husbands;
and those with hands resembling carnivorous beasts or like wolves and crows [bring similar misfortune].
Indeed, those with veins that are prominent, uneven, and shriveled are devoid of wealth;
she whose upper lip is excessively elevated is harsh-spoken in quarrels.

The defects in women who are ill-formed have been described, as well as the qualities that follow from them; the characteristics of men and women have been declared, and I shall now speak of that which bestows knowledge thereof.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Men and Women in Sāmudrika," within the section on Astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) in the *Ācārakāṇḍa* of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Hari said: [Chapter Sixty-Six] Hari said:
Through the worship of a stone marked with a discus, one becomes auspicious and free from all defects;
first comes the Sudarśana form, and then the supreme Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
This one with three wheels is Acyuta; he with four wheels has four arms.
He is known as Vāsudeva, then Pradyumna, and thereafter Saṅkarṣaṇa.
The eighth is Puruṣottama; the ninth array consists of ten aspects;
the eleventh is Aniruddha; and the twelfth consists of twelve aspects.
Beyond this, in the realm of Śakra, there is Ananta; marked by one and so forth in sequence, they are the Sudarśanas, who, when worshipped, grant all desires.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone and the deity born of Dvāravatī, where these two meet, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Śālagrāma, Dvārakā, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gayā,
Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, and Sūkara.
The Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, the Candrabhāgā, the Sarasvatī, Puruṣottama, and Mahākāla— these, O Śaṅkara, are the sacred fords (tīrthas).
These indeed remove all sins and bestow liberation upon those who eat;
they are Prabhava, Vibhava, Śukla, Pramoda, and Prajāpati.
Aṅgiras, Śrīmukha, Bhāva, Yuvan, Dhātṛ, as well as Īśvara, Bahudhanya, Pramāthin, Vikrama, and Viṣu.
Citrabhānu, Svabānu, Tāraṇa, Pārthiva, Vyaya, Sarvajit, Sarvadhārī, Virodhin, Vikṛti, and Khara. (GarP 1.66.10)
Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, Manmatha, Durmukha, Hemalamba, Vilamba, Vikāra, Śarvarī, and Plava.
Śubhakṛt, Śobhana, Krodhī, Viśvāvasu, Parābhava, Plavaṅga, Kīlaka, Saumya, Sādhāraṇa, and Virodhakṛt. (GarP 1.66.12)
Paridhāvī, Pramādī, Ānanda, Rākṣasa, Nala,
Piṅgala, Kāla, Siddhārtha, Raudri, and likewise Durmati.
Dundubhi, Rudhirodgārī, Raktākṣa, Krodhana, Akṣaya, Aśobhana, and Śobhana—these years are indeed so named. (GarP 1.66.14)
O Rudra, I shall explain the time for the sake of complete success based on the rising of the five vowels:
the King (Sa), the Queen (Ā), the Neutral (Udātta), as well as Affliction and Death.
One should write the vowels ā, ī, ū, ai, and au within a grid of five fire-squares (pañcāgnikoṣṭhaka),
using lines drawn vertically and horizontally that follow the sequence of the six fires.
One lunar day in the fire-pits [of the diagram], then three, and then the king; these are the Jayā days.
Indifference, death, and affliction follow in order from Mars and Mercury.
Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon, as well as the asterisms beginning with Revatī and ending with Mṛgaśiras, constitute the first digit (kalā). GarP_1,66.18 //
Elsewhere, there are five times five lunar mansions; likewise, the rising [of the breath] occurs in Caitra and the other months.
Furthermore, the first syllable of the names of the two months corresponds to every twelve days.
If the *kalā-liṅga* should remain for five [units], his death will indeed occur;
these are the *kalā*, the lunar day (*tithi*), the day of the week (*vāra*), the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), and the month itself.
And likewise, the arising of the name occurs previously and not otherwise:
Oṃ Kṣaiṃ (Kṣauḥ) Śivāya Namaḥ.
O Śiva, remove the perception of poison and possession from my emaciated limbs;
indeed, the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, which deludes the three worlds, has entered my heart.
The Gaṇa Mṛtyuñjaya, inscribed with yellow pigment (rocanā) and other substances upon birch bark (bhūrja),
when worn on the neck or the arm, bestows victory and other blessings.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Śālagrāma, the Sixty-Year Cycle, Svarodaya, and Jyotiḥśāstra," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[The Jyotiḥśāstra is hereby completed. (Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa—67).
Sūta said:
Having heard [this] from Hari, Hara spoke to Gaurī concerning the knowledge residing within the body.
Mars is proclaimed as fire, the Sun as earth, and Saturn as water;
Rāhu is situated in the station of air and illuminates the right nostril.
The Guru, Śukra, as well as Saumya and Candra as the fourth—
these one should cause to reside in the central channel of one's own self.
When one is engaged in worldly activity (ilā), then one should perform one's duties:
namely, attending to one's station, meditation, trade, and audience with the king.
One should diligently perform other auspicious deeds when the flow is in the right channel (dakṣanāḍī), but [avoid them] during the flow of Saturn, Mars, and Rāhu.
Even so, the arising of misfortunes may occur;
however, the discernment between the auspicious and the inauspicious is indeed known through the *Svarodaya*.
Within the body, the channels (nāḍīs) are manifold in form and very extensive;
from the bulb (kanda) situated below the navel, they have emerged like sprouts.
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated in the center of the navel;
they are arranged like a wheel, and all of them are known to be life-taking.
Among them, three are preeminent: the left, the right, and the middle.
The left is said to be of the nature of Soma, while the right resembles the Sun.
The central channel is Agni, bearing fruit and fulfilling time;
the left channel is indeed of the nature of nectar, established for the nourishment of the world.
When the southern course is joined with the portion of Raudra, it constantly dries up the world;
but when there is a flow of both together, death occurs, which destroys all undertakings.
Upon exhalation, the left [channel] prevails; upon inhalation, the right is traditionally taught.
Likewise, during the flow of the *iḍā*, there is the gentle [state], as well as the states pertaining to the moon and the sun.
One should perform cruel deeds when the vital breath (prāṇa) is situated in Piṅgalā;
for journeys and all undertakings, however, Iḍā is [recommended] for the removal of poison.
In eating, in sexual union, and in battle, Piṅgalā bestows success;
in rites such as eradication and killing, it is Piṅgalā who accomplishes these deeds.
She bestows success in sexual union, in battle, in eating,
in auspicious undertakings, in journeys, and in the performance of rites involving poison.
For the sake of accomplishing peace, liberation, and one's goals, O lords of men, the *iḍā* [channel] should be employed during the flow of both [channels],
while avoiding both cruel and gentle [exhalations].
The wise one should know it to be like poison and should remember it [as such] in gentle and auspicious rites, as well as in matters of gain, victory, and life.
In going and coming, she who is on the left is honored everywhere;
likewise in battle and the like, in eating, in killing, and indeed in union with women.
The auspicious southern channel is recommended for entry during minor rites;
it determines all matters of good and evil fortune, gain and loss, victory and defeat.
If one asks about the living and the non-living, the Middle Way does not succeed;
nor does it succeed in the Left or Right conduct where the Leader is not present as a point of conviction.
If one who is situated in the *tanu* asks [a question], there is success therein without a doubt;
so too when the *vāmadeva*, characterized by desire, flows within the self.
Standing in that portion, one should inquire; success will be fruitless [wherever the auspicious goddess] moves, whether to the left or to the right.
When the Haṃsa has set out according to its portion, fierce deeds are accomplished during the fierce [fortnight], moderate deeds during the mild, and indeed all deeds flow forth during both. 67.23.
Then the yogin, skilled in yoga, should recognize death;
wherever he may stand—whether facing left, right, or straight ahead—he should inquire.
In each such case, one should always observe the rising of the wind in its respective direction:
the wind from the left in front is excellent, while that from the right behind is auspicious.
The left [hand] is said to be Vāmikā, and the right is the auspicious Dakṣiṇā;
likewise, the left is Vāmā and the right is the auspicious Dakṣiṇā.
The living being lives by means of the life-force; whatever is devoid of that becomes stationary.
Whatever task is intended, such as victory and other signs of auspiciousness, [depends upon it].
All of that arises within the *pūrṇanāḍī* through non-conceptualization;
the three fortnights are said to extend from this to the end of the other channels and so forth.
Up until the sixth question, if it is full, the first [alternative] shall win;
but if it is empty, the second shall speak without hesitation.
The wind equal to the left-hand practice arises, bestowing the accomplishment of karma;
when the right-hand path is active, it is uneven and possesses uneven syllables.
Otherwise, when the flow is to the left, if the name indeed consists of an odd number of syllables,
then that warrior attains victory in the midst of battle.
If, indeed, an equal number of syllables arises during the flow of the *dakṣavāta* (right-side wind), one should observe it within the middle channel; of this there is no doubt.
When the vital breath has entered Piṅgalā, one should conquer the battle by means of tranquility;
as long as the movement [of the breath] arises within the channels, one should cause it to reach that direction.
He is not even born to give [anything]; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
However, in the midst of battle, wherever the channel (nāḍī) should always flow— GarP_1,67.34.
One attains victory in that direction; one should predict defeat in an empty [quarter].
One should know there is victory when the movement is "born" (jāta), and one should declare death when it is "dead" (mṛtaka).
He who understands both victory and defeat is a wise man;
for wherever Śiva moves, whether on the left or on the right, that is the path of success.
Having performed that, one attains that state; the journey is continuously auspicious.
When there is a flow of the moon and sun, one should engage in battle.
But whoever, remaining there, asks [the question], that virtuous person will certainly be victorious;
he shall be triumphant as far as the direction in which the wind blows.
There is no doubt that [the result] arises even if Indra stands before one;
the ten nāḍīs beginning with Meṣī, situated on the right and the left, [produce this]. (GarP 1.67.39)
In such and such a manner, as one proceeds through that difficult path with steady care,
the wise know that in the process of emergence one attains emergence, and in the process of withdrawal one attains withdrawal.
Having heard the words of the questioner, one should discern [the deity] by the shape of the bell;
O Śivā, whether on the left or the right, the deity abides within the five elements.
Fire is above and water is below; the wind is situated horizontally;
the earth should be known to be in the middle, while space is everywhere at all times.
Above is death, below is peace; the wise one should effect eradication across the horizontal.
One should know that paralysis occurs in the center, while liberation is everywhere for the all-pervading one.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of Auspicious and Inauspicious Signs in the Svarodaya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 68] Sūta said:
I shall describe the examination of gems. There was an asura named Bala who conquered Indra and the other gods; it is impossible for them to defeat him.
At the sacrifice, when the gods requested him as a victim under the pretext of granting a boon,
Bala, being of supreme courage, gave up his own state as a sacrificial animal; thus slain by the gods, he attained liberation.
Like a sacrificial animal, Bala was slaughtered by them, restrained by the thunderbolt of his own words,
for the sake of the welfare of the gods and for the benefit of the world.
Because that being was purified and his actions were pure,
all the limbs of his body became seeds of jewels.
Then, for the gods, the yakṣas, the siddhas, and the wind-eaters,
there arose a very great crocodile that was born from the seeds of jewels.
As they were falling through the sky with great speed in their celestial chariot,
whatever seed of jewels fell here and there, [it remained].
Whether in the great ocean, in a river, on a mountain, or even in a forest,
each location assumes the character of its contents due to the weight of what is contained therein.
Within them appear jewels that destroy demons, poisons, serpents, and diseases, as well as those which eliminate sins; likewise, there also appear those that are defective.
Vajras, pearls, rubies along with emeralds are mentioned,
as well as the excellent sapphire, lapis lazuli, and topazes.
The karketana gem with its filaments, along with the one called rudhira,
as well as crystal and coral— these have been carefully specified for collection by those who know them.
Shape and color, first the qualities and defects, their results, and the examination—
these, along with the value, are to be understood by those skilled in gems as the essence of all treatises.
Those who are born under an unfavorable birth-constellation (kulagna), or on a defiled day,
are joined with faults and are deprived of an abundance of virtues.
A ruler of the earth who desires prosperity should wear or collect gems that have been purified by examination.
Those who know the treatises, those who are skillful, and those experts who possess the jewels—
they alone are proclaimed to be the knowers of their value.
Since this diamond (vajra) has been declared by the wise to possess great power,
we shall therefore proclaim this examination beginning with the diamond.
In whatever regions of the earth fragments of his bones fell by some means,
there diamonds of various forms appeared, as if from the desire of the wielder of the thunderbolt to conquer that very weapon.
Haima, Mātaṅga, Saurāṣṭra, Pauṇḍra, Kaliṅga, Kosala,
Veṇvātaṭa, and Sauvīra— these eight were the pleasure-resorts of Vajra.

Those born in Himasaila are known to be slightly copper-colored with moon-like luster; those from the banks of the Veṇvā are remembered as being dark like blue lotuses or clouds. Those born in Sauvīra are blackish, while those from Saurāṣṭra resemble dark clouds.

Those from Kaliṅga possess a beautiful radiance like refined gold, and those in Kosala have a yellowish glow. Those originating in Puṇḍra are dark, while in the region of Mataṅga they do not possess an excessively yellowish luster.
If a diamond that is exceedingly light in color, possessed of excellent qualities, perfectly symmetrical on its sides, and free from lines, spots, stains, "crow-feet," and tremors—
indeed, if even a diamond as small as a minute atom seen anywhere in this world possesses a sharp point and edge, then it is truly the unfailing abode of the gods.
In the Vajras, the form of even the deities is declared through the application of colors;
and the differentiation [of the deities] must be made from the colors themselves, for they are based solely upon color.
Green, white, yellow, tawny, dark, and copper-colored— these are naturally beautiful,
being the respective colors of Hari, Varuṇa, Śakra, Hutavaha, Pitṛpati, and Marut.

That of a Brahmin should be as white as a conch shell, a kumuda lily, or crystal; that of a Kshatriya should have the luster of a hare or the brownish-yellow of an eye; that of a Vaishya should resemble the beautiful hue of a plantain leaf; and that of a Shudra should possess a brilliance like a polished sword-blade.
Two types of vajra-colored [complexion] for lords of the earth have been prescribed by the virtuous, but they are not universal;
namely, that which is as red as the fracture of coral or javā flowers, or that which resembles the juice of turmeric.
Because of his lordship over all castes, the king may, at his pleasure, wear the *sārvavarṇika* [staff] made of the wood of any tree; but no one else may ever wear anything other than that.
For the mixture of castes that occurs through the practice of the low and the high is considered less grievous than the mixture of those who possess the diamond-like caste (vajra-varṇa).
A wise person should not practice the adoption of the Vajra [vow] merely by following the classification of the path;
for the manifestation of the excellence of virtuous qualities is the cause of prosperity, while its opposite is the cause for the arising of calamity.
Even if a single horn of it is seen to be split or shattered,
that diamond, though possessed of excellent qualities, should not be kept in the home by those seeking their own welfare.

Even the wielder of the thunderbolt could not swiftly restore the splendor of his vajra, which had its tip shattered by fire, its middle covered with spots of a soiled color, and which was longing for a new support.

That [body] which has a portion appearing like blood, or which may be variegated with red colors—one should not have such a person carried; for it brings an end to life even for one who dies at his own will.
With edges on its sides numbering six, eight, or twelve crores,
with a lofty and perfectly sharp point— these are the qualities of a diamond produced from a mine.

A diamond that is six-cornered, pure, stainless, with a sharp and clear edge, possessed of color, light, well-proportioned, and free from defects— such a diamond, which makes the atmosphere shimmer with the radiance of a rainbow, is not easily found upon this earth.
He who, with body always restrained, bears a thunderbolt that is sharp-pointed, stainless, and free from all defects,
shall experience an increase in his wife, prosperity, sons, wealth, grain, cattle, and sheep every day until the end of his life.
Dangers from predatory beasts, fire, poison, tigers, thieves, and water,
as well as the effects of Atharvan rites, are warded off from afar by him.
If one should possess a diamond free from all defects weighing twenty *taṇḍula* grains,
those learned in the science of gems declare its highest price to be two hundred thousand *rūpaka*s.
Reduced by one-third, then half, then half of that; the thirteenth, the thirtieth, and half a part;
then an eightieth part, a hundredth part, and a thousandth part—this is the application for those who are very small.
The price first prescribed for a diamond made from twelve *taṇḍula* grains was that which applies to one of the highest quality;
this, however, is the determination for one that has gradually lost two [grains] in sequence and is thus reduced by one degree.
Nor is the method for weighing diamonds by means of rice grains alone;
one should calculate a rice grain by means of eight white mustard seeds.
However, among the entire class of gems, it is desired that one should wear that diamond which is endowed with all qualities and floats upon water.
For even if it is damaged by a very slight flaw, whether visible or invisible,
a person obtains a diamond worth one-tenth of its original value.
Even for a diamond with many manifest defects— whether small or large— not even a hundredth part of its true value is prescribed.
Although a diamond with manifest flaws may be seen as an ornament,
its value will be low for the purpose of refining gems.
When that which is endowed with a wealth of virtues becomes obstructed and encounters a defect, it is no use for the king’s ornament; even a gem devoid of virtue serves as no adornment.
A woman desiring the birth of a son should not wear a vajra, even if it possesses excellent qualities,
unless it is devoid of defects such as being long, flat, triangular, or the like.
With iron, topaz, and likewise with hessonite, with beryl and crystal, and also with various kinds of glass; // GarP_1,68.44 //
Skilled people can fashion imitations of diamond;
therefore, they must be examined by wise and expert investigators.
Their testing should be performed with alkaline solutions, abrasives, and whetstones;
for whatever gems exist on earth, as well as other metallic ores.
One may scratch all things with a vajra, yet it cannot be scratched by them;
the heaviness of all jewels is the cause for supporting weight.
The wise describe that [vajra] as the reverse:
birth carves out non-birth, while the diamond-kuruvinda jewels carve out birth.
A diamond scratches another diamond; a diamond is not scratched by anything else.
This includes diamonds, pearls, gems, and whatever other varieties of jewels there may be.
For those [flames] that are obstructed, there is no upward movement;
for some, if it occurs at all, it happens somehow by being diverted sideways.
For those being drawn sideways, that [movement]—
It is struck on its sides.
Even if it has chipped edges, is marked with spots or lines, or is discolored,
a thunderbolt accompanied by a rainbow nevertheless bestows wealth, grain, and sons.
Bearing the mace as described, which is made beautiful by flashes of lightning, the king—
having overwhelmed the majesty of his enemies through his valor— enjoys the lands of all his vassals.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Examination of Gems, Their Specific Varieties, the Vajra, and so forth," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 69.
Sūta said:

Pearls are renowned in the world as originating from elephants, clouds, boars, conches, fish, serpents, oyster shells, and bamboo; among these, those produced from oyster shells are the most abundant.
In that very place, the root alone of a single *ratna* stone is ever set;
however, among those, the experts say that only the one originating from mother-of-pearl is to be pierced, while the remaining ones are said to be unpierceable.

Whether produced from the resin of the *tvaksāra* tree, from the king of serpents, or from a whale; whether born of a conch or produced by a boar—though they are generally freed of their luster, they are nevertheless praised for their auspiciousness.
Regarding the eight origins of pearls proclaimed here by those who know the determination of gems:
among them, that which originates from conch shells is declared the lowest, as is that which is produced from the frontal globes of a lordly elephant.
A conch shell, resembling the color of its own source— the wine— large as a dangling fruit,
yellowish in hue and devoid of luster, emerges from the center of the elephant's frontal globes.
Those kambavas born in the lineage of the preeminent conch Śārṅgamukhāvamarśapīta,
as well as elephants of pure breed, are declared to be the sources of pearls.
From these [pearl-oysters], a pearl is produced that is round and yellowish in color, lacking luster;
it is equal in hue to the back of a *pāṭhīna* fish, well-rounded from the fish, light, and extremely fine.
Fish that move in the midst of the ocean are born from the mouths of aquatic creatures;
it is taught that they possess a color identical to the tips of the boar’s tusks.
Somewhere, somehow, that preeminent king of boars is born upon a region of the earth;
it is declared to possess the luster of the color of hailstones and to originate from the joints of bamboo.
Those bamboos grow in places to be enjoyed by divine beings, not in common areas;
they possess the gait of a peacock and the pure movement of a fish, and in their form, they shine with an exceedingly brilliant color.
Possessing a luster equal to the edge of a sword that has been thoroughly polished and free of all conceptual construction,
one may obtain great jewels of immense radiance, or a kingdom, or even great prosperity that is otherwise difficult to attain.

Those who perform meritorious deeds become endowed with splendor, just as those skilled in ritual procedures, being purified and diligent, strive with effort at an auspicious moment to test the gem-treasure produced from the head of a serpent for the sake of a pearl.
When that great rite of protection is performed while standing upon the palace roof,
then, amidst the deep resonance of great kettledrums and the flashing of streaks of lightning within the intervals, [the sky is filled].
The sky is covered by fresh clouds that hang low, bending under the weight of the rain;
neither serpents, nor demons, nor diseases, nor even the evils of calamities [afflict] him.

Those who destroy the pearl arising from the head of a serpent that remains within its shell do not reach the earth, for it originates from the clouds; rather, the gods carry it away when it has fallen into the hands of a brahmin.
His radiance enveloped the quarters of space, his solar orb discernible in the sky,
having eclipsed all the splendor of fire, the moon, the constellations, and the stars.
Just as it produces light by day, so too during those nights plunged in darkness,
its waters were beautiful with the luster of various jewels and adorned with the four oceans.
It is my conviction that there would be no price for it, even if the entire earth were filled with gold;
for even one who is lowly may sometimes obtain it through the ripening of great merit.
He enjoys that entire earth free from rivalry with co-wives for as long as it endures;
not only does this result from the merit of that king who performs virtuous deeds, but his very birth was also due to the good fortune of his subjects.
Extending for a thousand yojanas all around, it turns away every misfortune;
the row of teeth of that great Asura is like a garland of stars fallen from the sky.
Among those of various colors, the pure-colored milk fell into the water of her husband,
[the milk] of that preeminent jewel of great quality, which was as lovely as the mass of rays from the full moon.
That seed, which had existed previously in other lives, attained its station within oyster shells.
In whatever region of the ocean that beautiful seed of the pearl-gem fell,
there the water, scattered by the clouds, rested within the shell and attained the state of a pearl.
The eight mines are those of Siṃhala, Pāralaukika, Saurāṣṭrika, Tāmraparṇa, Pāraśava, Kauvera, Pāṇḍya, Hāṭaka, and Hemaka.

That which originates from oyster shells, possessing a color that is not too dark, arises through its specific measurements, shapes, qualities, and luster in Vardhana, Pārasīka, Pātāla, Lokāntara, and Siṃhala.
The specific characteristics of its source are inconceivable; therefore, a wise person should strive for the perfection of form and measure.
There is no fixed rule regarding qualities and defects, for all forms exist everywhere.
The price of this pearl, which possesses the luster of mother-of-pearl and is weighed equal to another [standard],
is five thousand and three hundred rūpakas.
That which is less than half a māṣaka is of a price reduced by two-fifths;
that which one may wear for three māṣakas has a maximum price of two thousand [paṇas] as prescribed.
Two [palas] and a half are its value; even with three hundred, it exceeds a thousand.
Its weight, measured at two māṣakas less, is said to have a value of eight hundred.
Experts say that for a coin weighing one and a half *māṣakas* and measuring three hundred and twenty units [in diameter], along with six *guñjās*, the maximum value is two hundred;
for one weighing one and a half [māṣakas]... [text fragment].
The value of that [mantra], when endowed with its qualities, shall be one hundred times [the former].
If it weighs no less than sixteen dharaṇas, they call it Dārvika;
it fetches a price of one hundred and ten [coins], even from the hand of a fool.
Ten times twice (twenty) *dharaṇas* shall constitute at least one *bhavaka*, so say those who know it;
it shall fetch seventy-nine times its own value, provided it is not devoid of the excellence of its qualities.
When it is filled with thirty *dharaṇas*, it is proclaimed as a *śikya* of that [weight];
its value beyond that is determined to be forty.
If it were forty *ra*, she would receive thirty as its price;
if it were fifty *soma*s, its price would be twenty.
Sixty [units] constitute a *nikaraśīrṣa*, and its value is fourteen;
eighty and ninety are proclaimed as *kūpya*;
eleven and nine are their respective values in sequence.

Having taken that entire vessel of food and cooked it with the addition of the juice produced from *jambīra* fruits, one should then grind it with the roots of soft, thin *piṇḍa* plants; thus, one may quickly produce pearls of any desired size, pierced as required.
Having placed it inside a fish-cavity smeared with clay, one should subsequently cook it gently;
then, by means of a cat-cavity (*biḍālapuṭī*), one should cook it in milk, and then cook that which has been cooked in *sudhā* (lime), and finally in pure sour gruel (*cukra*).
Then, through rubbing with a stainless cloth, the pearl becomes pure, endowed with vast qualities and splendor;
so spoke Vyāḍi, who was of great power in the worlds, perfected, compassionate, and intent on the welfare of the wise.
Silver resembling white glass, combined with a hundred parts of gold, should be processed within the mercury;
it becomes pearl, an ornament for the body.
For in this way, skilled people in the land of Siṃhala act whenever there is any doubt regarding the artificiality of a pearl.
One should let it soak for a night in warm, salty oil or water;
or, wrapped in a dry cloth, it should be rubbed with grains of rice.
That which does not undergo discoloration should be known as unadulterated; it is white, of standard proportions, glossy, heavy, translucent, and perfectly pure.
A pearl that is brilliant, well-rounded, and possesses excellent qualities is considered to be of superior merit.

That pearl which possesses weight commensurate with its size, is white, well-rounded, and has a uniform, fine perforation, brings joy even to one who does not buy it; such a pearl is declared to be possessed of excellent qualities.
Thus, when a pearl has attained union through the arising of all these qualities,
not even a single fault or any kind of misfortune shall ever befall its owner.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Examination of Pearls," within the section on the examination of pearls, in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 70.
Sūta said:
Taking the blood— the seed of the finest jewels— from that great-souled and most majestic great Asura, Divākara set out through the sky, which was dark blue like a sword-blade, to wander.

Having encountered the Lord of Laṅkā on the way— whose mind was haughty with the pride of valor and who had incessantly conquered the gods in battles— he was forcibly obstructed by him, just as [the sun] is by Rāhu.

The sun released its rays into that most excellent river, whose deep great pools were agitated by the sight of the lovely rounded hips of the women of Siṃhala, and whose two banks were lined with betel-nut trees.
From that time forward, that Gaṅgā, yielding equal merit and fruit,
attained renown by the name Rāvaṇagaṅgā.
From that time forth, on the nights, her banks, strewn with jewels,
shone as if sharpened within and without by hundreds of golden iron arrows set ablaze.
On its banks there are rubies of brilliant and lovely hue, and in its waters there are lotus-gems;
those arising from *saugandhika* flowers, those born from *kuruvinda* stones, and those produced from crystal are all of great quality.
Some possess a splendor with a color like that of the bandhūka, kuñjāsa, kalendra, gopa, javāsa, māṃsī, or saṃvara;
others are radiant with the hue of pomegranate seeds, while still others have the luster of kiṃśuka flowers.

Having a color identical to that of the *khindura*, the lotus, the blue water-lily, saffron, and even lac-dye, they shine by their own radiance even when the passion is dense; clearly discernible, they possess a manifest beauty in their centers.
Having attained a state of penetration by following the radiance of the sun,
those [crystals] produced from rock-crystal, endowed with excellent qualities, color all their sides from afar by means of a mass of rays.
Some have a luster like a red lotus, its color intensely crimson and blended with the hues of safflower and indigo;
others indeed possess the brilliance of the *aruṣkara* and *kaṇṭakārī* flowers, while still others have the radiance of vermilion.
Some possess the brilliance of the eyes of the male cakora bird, the cuckoo, and the sārasa crane;
others, moreover, have a luster equal to that of the finest blossoming red lotuses.

Jewels originating from the *saugandhika* flower are generally similar to those produced from crystal in their brilliance, hardness, and weight; they possess the lovely luster of blue and red lotuses.
Granted that passion may exist in those born of Kuruvinda gems, it is not at all like that which exists in those produced from crystal;
for even when all are bent down, the latter remain without outward flame yet possess great internal power.
But those kuruvindas which are born in the Gaṅgā of Rāvaṇa bear a deep red hue like that of a ruby, yet possess the luster of crystal.
In the Māndhra country and elsewhere,
none of those who follow the [proper] castes are born who would receive even a small fraction of the price.
In the same way, those originating from crystal in the region known as Tumburu are born with similar properties; indeed, they are recorded as being of little value.
Excellence of color, weight, smoothness, evenness, translucency,
brilliance, and largeness— this is the collection of the qualities of jewels.

Those gems that are cracked, porous, stained with impurities, devoid of luster, rough, and discolored— these are not praised, even if they are equal in all respects regarding their species and qualities.
Whoever, out of ignorance, wears a gem that has been affected by a flaw,
him the host of defects— such as grief, anxiety, death, and loss of wealth— overwhelms.
A wise man should diligently observe that the five types of women who resemble the celestial nymphs (apsarases) may, despite their great beauty, be of inferior birth.
Those originating from Kalaśapura, the Siṃhala and Tumburu regions, and those from Muktapāṇi,
as well as the Śrīpūrṇakas, are similar to the *padmarāga* gems, though they are of different species.
Due to its husk-like coating it is called *kalaśa*; because of its coppery hue it originates from the *tumburu* tree;
likewise, due to its blackness it is born in the land of Siṃhala; and because of its natural state it is named *muktā* (pearl) from the sky.
The Śrīpūrṇaka, being devoid of luster, possesses a distinction that rests solely upon the characteristics of the twice-born;
it nourishes the ruby within its coppery exterior, like the full center of a grain of rice through the process of cooking.
One who appears smeared with oil, or one who loses his luster when rubbed, as well as one whose crown is pressed down by the two fingers and who bears dark streaks along his sides; GarP_1,70.24 //
Having obtained it and having lifted it up according to its nature, he who bears all qualities exceedingly;
or he who, being of equal measure and equal species, may be equal by virtue of his weight—
the wise man, even though born from a mine of jewels, shall be distinguished by his weight and his quality.
If doubt does not vanish, one should rub it on a whetstone;
even after writing it out, they may [rub] each other with what has arisen from their own birth-signs.
Just as it is impossible for anyone to produce a scratch on a ruby or a sapphire by means of either a diamond or a kuruvinda gem, [so too is it impossible to describe the qualities of the Buddha].
Among all gems of a given species, there are never any of a different species that possess an identical color;
nevertheless, the highest degree of differentiation has been taught specifically for the purpose of distinguishing between them.
A gem of inferior birth should not be worn even when strung together with one endowed with excellent qualities;
for a wise man would never wear a thing of low origin, even if it were fastened alongside the Kaustubha jewel.
Just as even a single outcaste, having encountered many twice-born men, slays them without effort,
so too can one of inferior birth cause the ruin of jewels endowed with manifold virtues.
Even when placed in the midst of rivals, and even while existing in a state of negligence,
no calamity whatsoever touches the possessor of a great-quality ruby in this world.
And those calamities arising from the onset of defects do not assail him who,
with disciplined mind, wears a ruby whose beautiful luster is intensified by its excellent qualities.
Whatever price is assigned to a diamond based on its number of grains of rice, once its value has been established,
that same price applies to a highly virtuous ruby of equal weight in māṣakas.
For a precious gem is praised when it is endowed with both color and brilliance;
yet if it lacks even a little of these two, it falls away from its gem-like value.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Examination of Rubies," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 71 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Sūta said:
Taking the bile of the lord of the Dānavas, Vāsuki, the lord of serpents,
went swiftly as if splitting the sky in two.
Then, in the ocean of the sky illuminated by the radiance of the jewel on his head,
he shone like a single, vast silver causeway.
Then, as if destroying heaven and earth with the flapping of his wings,
Garuḍa prepared to strike the lord of serpents.
Suddenly that lord of serpents released it upon the valley of Mount Māṇikya, which was perfumed with the thick fragrance of buds and where *turuṣka* trees were anointed by the goddess Surasā.
Immediately upon his falling, having passed through that same excellent abode near Ramā,
he reached a place on the shore of the ocean belonging to the earth, in the valley at the foot of the excellent Māṇikya mountain.
As that bile was falling away from him, Garuḍa approached and seized it;
then, overcome by fainting, he suddenly released it all through both nostrils.
In that regard, emeralds that possess the luster of the throats of soft-tufted parrots, śirīṣa flowers, the backs of fireflies, young grass,
moss, white water-lilies, young shoots, and the hoods of serpents bring auspiciousness.
Wherever the bile of the lord of the Daityas fell, struck by the arms of the king of serpents,
that region became an inexhaustible mine, exceedingly difficult to attain yet endowed with many virtues.
Whatever is produced in that emerald mine is proclaimed to be for the pacification of all poisons and diseases.
That poison produced by the fangs of a great serpent, which cannot be treated by any collection of mantras or medicinal herbs, is pacified by that [remedy].
Furthermore, whatever else arises there in the mine that is free from defects is proclaimed to be the most excellent among purifying substances.
It appeared intensely green in color, with soft rays of light intermingled and matted together,
as if filled with gold dust within.
Endowed with the qualities of symmetry and color, not lacking in gravity,
it bathes the entire hermitage in radiance through the touch of the sun’s rays.
Having abandoned its greenness,
that within which light has been placed shines like fresh grass due to being struck by the radiance of the newly risen sun.
And that which bestows upon the mind an exceeding clarity when beheld—
the thought of those who know gems is that it is a great mass of emeralds.
Because of the extreme pervasiveness of its color, its interior is clothed in clear rays;
it is thick, glossy, and pure, with a luster equal to the radiance of soft peacock feathers.
With a radiant splendor and a brilliant luster, he shines with a dense form;
yet even so, he retains the very same designation of "virtuous" that he had before.
Variegated, hard, dull, rough, and filled with stones and grit;
smeared with bitumen—emerald of such a kind is defective.
Any gem that has been processed at its joints and is other than emerald should never be worn or purchased by those desiring their own welfare.
The *bhallātakī* and the *putrikā*, due to their similarity in color,
should be recognized as being of different species from the emerald (*marakata*).
Polished with a linen cloth, the figurine loses its brilliance;
indeed, because of the fragility of glass, it is possible to bring about its destruction.
Even for someone who follows an emerald with various forms and qualities of excellence,
the color of the marking-nut (bhallātaka) undergoes a transformation upon its own sound.
There are other Vajras and those who are liberated, as well as any others who are twice-born;
for them, when they are unattached, their radiance becomes upward-moving.
And for some, due to their very straightness, it arises in some way;
yet for those who look askance, it perishes instantly.
While performing the rites of bathing, sipping water, and recitation, as well as the ritual procedures for protective mantras,
they gave gifts of cows and gold, and prepared the necessary implements.
During rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests, and during the worship of gurus, when [the practitioners] were afflicted by various kinds of diseases arising from poison; 71.26.
Wise men should wear this emerald, which is free from defects, endowed with excellent qualities, set in gold, and which shines amidst those moving about in battle.
Whatever price is produced for a ruby when weighed on a scale,
an emerald endowed with excellent qualities fetches even more than that.
And so, while the value of rubies is diminished by their defects,
there would be an even greater loss for this emerald due to its defects.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Examination of Emeralds," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Purvakhanda of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sūta said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 72.
Sūta said:

In that very place, where the young lavalī flowers and sprouts were plucked by the sprout-like fingertips of the Siṃhala maiden, the pair of eyes of the demon— exceedingly beautiful and possessing the luster of a full-blown lotus— fell.
Due to that cause, the coastal land of the ocean shines forth, spreading with waves beautiful on both sides;
it possesses dense jewels of sapphire gems and is marked by lines of blooming *ketaka* groves.

In that place, gems arise from flowers resembling the dark lotus, the plow-bearer (Balarāma), the one who wields the sword (Kṛṣṇa), the bumblebee, the bow-armed one (Viṣ� aṇu), the body of Śiva, and the saffron-colored flower of the throat;
they also arise from the fresh flowers of the *girikarṇikā*. These gems possess a luster identical to their respective sources.
Some were like the clear waters of the ocean, the storehouse of milk;

others were like the luster of water; some resembled a flock of peacocks; some had the appearance of bubbles produced from indigo juice; and others possessed the hue of the throats of intoxicated cuckoos.
In that place, sapphires of great quality are born, uniform in kind and radiant with the beauty of their distinct colors.
Those [images] that are joined with flaws such as earth, stone, rock-cavities, gravel, or cracks,
and those corrupted by defects in color caused by the shadow of a layer of mica, are [unfit].
For from that very source many jewels are born;
the wise, whose intellects are awakened by the scriptures, praise them.
Whatever qualities are seen in a ruby (*padmarāga-maṇi*) when it is worn,
a person obtains those very same qualities by wearing a sapphire (*indranīla*).
Just as there are three origins for rubies,
so too should it be understood without distinction for sapphires.
The very same criteria by which a ruby is examined are also seen to be the criteria for examining a sapphire.
And as much as fire may step over due to the use of a ruby,
an indranīla gem would step over even more than that, by a very great measure.
Nevertheless, no gem whatsoever should ever be placed in fire for the sake of examination or for the increase of its qualities.
If the measure of the fire is not fully understood, and it is corrupted by the defects of burning,
it will lead to misfortune for the master, the performer, and likewise the one who causes it to be performed.
In this world, the wise declare that these— mirror-glass, blue lotus, karavīra, crystal, and others, along with lapis lazuli—
are of different species, though they resemble the sapphire.
The states of being a guru and being harsh should always be understood regarding these [beings],
especially as they increase progressively, like glass and so forth.
Just as a certain sapphire may possess a coppery hue,
so too are both the *karavīra* and the blue lotus copper-colored for the purpose of protection.
That sapphire, in the center of which the radiance of Indra’s bow shines against its blue background, is called an *indranīla*; it is highly precious and rare upon the earth.
That which, due to the predominance of its own color, brings all the hundredfold milk to a state of blueness, is called Mahānīla.
Whatever may be the price of a highly precious ruby weighing one māṣa,
that shall be the price of a highly precious sapphire weighing one suvarṇa.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Examination of Sapphires," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa), within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: The *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 73.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, I shall describe the examination of lapis lazuli, puṣparāga, karketana, and bhīṣmaka, as proclaimed by Brahmā and recounted by Vyāsa.
From the roar of the Daitya, which resembled the tumultuous sound of the ocean agitated at the end of an eon,
there arose beryl— multicolored, the seed of splendor and a luster of delightful hue.
Not far from Mount Vidūra, which possessed lofty ridges,
there was a mine situated along the boundary of Kāmabhūtika.
Because he was born from that sound, he became a source of great virtue;
transcending the world, he became the ornament of the three worlds.
Resembling the roar of that very lord of the Dānavas, and displaying a beautiful form like the rain-clouds at the end of the monsoon,
various Vaidūrya gems shone forth from him like a multitude of sparks.
Taking up the ruby and whatever other jewel colors exist upon the earth,
vaidūrya surpasses them all in the beauty of its hue.
Among them, the best is that which is blue like a peacock's neck or has the luster of a bamboo leaf;
those gems whose beauty resembles the wing-tip of a blue jay are not praised by those learned in the science of jewels.
A virtuous vaidūrya gem provides its master with supreme enjoyments;
one possessed of defects brings about misfortunes. Therefore, one should examine it with great care.
Girikāca, śiśupāla, kāca, and sphaṭika that are streaked with smoke—
these are of different species, though they resemble vaidūrya gems.
One should know *śaileśapālaka* by the absence of lines and its lightness;
*sphaṭika* by its brilliance resembling mountain-crystal and its radiant color.
Whatever is the price of a high-quality sapphire weighing one *suvarṇa*,
that very same price is prescribed for a lapis lazuli gem weighing two *palas*.
Just as there may be various non-genuine stones that possess the same color as a genuine gem,
nevertheless, the supreme method for discerning their differences through inferable characteristics has been taught.
This distinction should always be examined with ease by a wise man;
for the distinction of affection—its lightness and softness—is indeed a universal sign of its true nature.

Being filled with wholesome and unwholesome qualities and bound by various applications of honors, they acquire the emergence of virtues and faults; like jewels that differ in value according to their distinct internal worth.
Gradually passed through and strung with effort by the jeweler,
if the gems are indeed free from defects, they obtain a price six times [their weight].
The value of these jewels, which have come from mines beyond [the known world] and are found near the shore of the ocean, does not hold true everywhere upon the entire earth.
That which was declared by Manu as a *suvarṇa* consisting of sixteen *māṣakas*,
its seventieth part shall serve as the standard for the designation [of a *māṣaka*].
A *śāṇa* is measured as four *māṣas*, and a *māṣaka* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*;
the tenth part of a *pala* is proclaimed to be a *dharaṇa*.
Thus has the procedure for gems been declared for the determination of the value of jewels.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Examination of Vaidūrya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 74 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
When the skin of that enemy of the gods fell upon the Himalayas,
from it there appeared flowers of great quality and brilliant colors.
A stone that is beautiful with a yellowish-white luster is known as padmarāga;
it is called kaukaṇṭaka if it is reddish-yellow.
That which is blood-red yet yellow, clear, and saffron-colored is declared to be of one kind;
that which is neither blue nor white in color, glossy, and delicate is possessed of excellent qualities.
That which is extremely red is indeed known as *padmarāga*;
moreover, that very same [stone], being intensely blue, is called *indranīla*.
For those who know the essence of jewels, its value is indeed proclaimed to be like that of a lapis lazuli gem;
and likewise is the fruit of wearing it, yet for women, it becomes a bestower of sons.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Examination of Topaz," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. [Chapter 75] Sūta said:
Vāyu, having seized the nails of the lord of the Daityas, joyfully cast them into the forests of excellent lotuses;
from that, the karketana gem was produced through the agency of the wind, which is the most honored on earth.
In its color, it shines like blood, Soma, or honey, glowing with a reddish-yellow brilliance like fire;
yet when it is blue, white, harsh, or fractured, it shines as a cause of defects such as disease and the like.
Lustrous, pure, and possessing even color; yellowish-green, heavy, and variegated;
free from flaws, cracks, and insect holes—such karketana gems are supremely purifying.
When it has been wrapped in a golden leaf and heated in the fire until it becomes radiant,
it then destroys disease, dispels the Kali age, prolongs life, sustains the lineage, and bestows happiness.

Those men who bring such a gem of many virtues, a karketana stone, for the sake of auspicious adornment, become honored, possessed of great wealth and many kinsmen; they remain eternally radiant and ever joyful.
Some, having cast off their [true nature], possess a distorted, agitated, and dark luster; they are withered in passion, wavering, turbid, and deformed;
lacking brilliance, intense radiance, noble lineage, and fullness of color, they bear a body resembling that of a karketana gem.
If a karketana gem has its color and form thoroughly examined and possesses the brilliant radiance of the newly risen sun,
then for that supreme jewel, the price declared by those learned in the treatises should be determined as equal to its weight when weighed.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Examination of Karketana Gems," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 76.
Sūta said:
In the northern region of the Himavat, the seed of that enemy of the gods fell;
it attained the status of a source for the most excellent *bhīṣma* gems.
White, resembling conch shells or lotuses, or like the *syonāka* flower, they are radiant;
from that, young, diamond-like, formidable stones emerge.
He who, with faith, wears even a pure *bhīṣmamaṇi*— set with gold and other gems— around his neck or other parts of his body, always attains great prosperity.
Indeed, even when he is nearby, the forest-dwellers—
leopards, wolves, śarabhas, elephants, lions, tigers, and other predators— flee upon seeing him.
Therefore, there is no fear for one who has been fashioned by the lathe of time; they do not mock the Lord.
The Bhīṣma-jewel, endowed with virtues and having properly attained the status of a finger-ring, [remains secure].

Through the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛtṛpti*) becomes lasting for many years. Even the poisons of snakes, birds born from eggs, rats, and scorpions are pacified.
Terrifying fears of water, fire, enemies, and thieves perish.
A wise person should avoid from afar a man who resembles moss or a cloud, who has a yellowish luster yet is devoid of radiance, whose brilliance is dimmed, and who is discolored.
The price for these should be determined by the best of the wise through their knowledge of place and time:
for those produced far away it is much, while for those produced nearby it is little.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Examination of Vaidūrya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 77] Sūta said:

Having gone to the auspicious and excellent mountains, to rivers, and likewise to other locations in the northern regions, he established [the images] by the power of his own nails and arms; and after worshiping the Lord of the Dānavas with manifest splendor in that famous place, they were installed.
Those *pulaka* gems produced in Daśārṇa, Āgadarava,
Mekala, Kāla, Gada, and other regions, which have the color of *guñjā*, collyrium, honey, or lotus stalks,
and which possess a luster resembling *gandharva*, fire, or plantain— these are praised as excellent. 77.2.
Those *pulaka* beads, which bear various patterns resembling a conch, a lotus, a bee, or the sun;
which are free from flaws and are supremely pure;
which are endowed with auspiciousness and variegated with many sections—these bestow prosperity.

Those accompanied by crows, jackals, donkeys, jackals, wolves, and fierce-looking vultures with mouths wet with flesh and blood, which bestow death, must be avoided by the wise; their price is said to be five hundred *palas*.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Examination of Horripilation," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
[The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 78] Sūta said:
Taking the form of the fire-god as desired by the Dānava,
he cast it into the Narmadā river, with some portions remaining in inferior lands.

In that regard, having extracted the gem known as Rudhirākṣa— which is composed of indragopas, has the color of a parrot’s beak, and in its shape is equal in size to a manifest pīlu fruit, and which is fashioned in various ways— it is indeed entirely uniform.

If that film should be as white as the full moon, of an exceedingly pure color, and resembling sapphire on the scale, it is said to produce sovereignty and servants; and when it is ripe, it indeed becomes the color of the divine vajra.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Examination of the Rudhirākṣa Gem," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
*Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa* — 79 Sūta said:
In the lands of Kāvera, Vindhya, Yavana, Cīna, and Nepāla,
Lāṅgalin diligently scattered the fat of the Dānava.
From that, the substance called oil, pure as space, arose as crystal;
it was white like a lotus stalk or a conch shell, yet possessed a slight variation in color.
For it is not equal to jewels, nor does it destroy evil;
yet, once consecrated by an artisan, it immediately obtains some value from that [act]. (GarP 1.79.3)
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Examination of Sphaṭika," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 80 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
Taking his entrails, Śeṣa cast them into the Kelā and other waters of Balarāma;
there, corals of excellent quality were born.

Among those, the primary [gums] are declared to be those with the luster of rabbit's blood, resembling the *guñjā* and *japā* flowers, deep blue, and those of the gods (*devakara*) and hair (*romaka*); their places of origin are the sources of excellent color.
Even if produced elsewhere, it does not possess that primary value due to its connection with exceptional craftsmanship;
for that coral is indeed clear, soft, glossy, and beautifully colored.

O Śaunaka, the examination of the Pulaka, Rudhirākṣa, Sphaṭika, and Vidruma gems has been described for the sake of discerning jewels; they bestow wealth and grain in this world and destroy the fear of poison and affliction.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Examination of Coral," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
[In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 81:
The Examination of Gems, Pearls, and Other Jewels is concluded.]
(Now begins the majesty of the sacred sites.
Sūta said:
I shall describe all the sacred fords; the Gaṅgā is the most excellent among the best of sacred fords.
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, yet she is difficult to attain in three specific places.
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—
Prayāga is the supreme sacred site, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who have died there.
Vārāṇasī is the supreme sacred site where Keśava exists as Viśveśa; by serving the alms-gatherers there, men conquer evil and obtain their desires.
Kurukṣetra is a supreme sacred site, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation through acts such as giving;
Prabhāsa is a supreme sacred site, for Somanātha resides there.
And the beautiful city of Dvārakā, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
the meritorious Prācī Sarasvatī; and the supreme Saptasārasvata.
Kedāra, which destroys all sins, and the excellent village of Śambhala;
Naranārāyaṇa Tīrtha and Badarikāśrama for the sake of liberation.
Śvetadvīpa, the city of Māyā, Naimiṣa, the supreme Puṣkara,
Ayodhyā, Arghyatīrtha, Citrakūṭa, and the Gomatī.
The Vaināyaka Mahītīrtha, the supreme hermitage of Rāmagiri,
Kāñcīpurī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, Śrīśaila, and Setubandhana.
Rāmeśvara is a supreme sacred site (tīrtha), as is the excellent Kārttikeya;
likewise Bhṛgutuṅga, Kāmatīrtha, and the sacred site of Amarakaṇṭaka.
In Ujjayinī is Mahākāla; at Kubjaka is Śrīdhara Hari;
Kubjāmraka is a great tīrtha; and Kālasarpa is the granter of desires.
And Mahākeśī, Kāverī, Candrabhāgā, and Vipāśā;
likewise the holy site of Ekāmra, as well as Brahmeśa and Devakoṭaka.
Know also that the city of Mathurā, the beautiful Śoṇa great river, and the great holy site of Jambū-saras— these are sacred fords.
Where Sūrya, Śiva, Gaṇa, Devī, and Hari reside— in these,
as well as in other such places, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and austerity [yield great fruit].
Worship, ancestral rites, and the offering of funeral cakes—all these become inexhaustible.
The Śālagrāma bestows everything; it is the supreme sacred site of Paśupati.
Kokāmukha, Vārāha, Bhūṇḍīra, and the one known as Svāmī;
Mahāviṣṇu is at Mohadaṇḍa, and Madhusūdana is at Mandāra.
Kāmarūpa is a great holy site where Kāmākhyā resides;
and there is the holy site of Puṇḍravardhana, where Kārtikeya dwells.
Viraja is a great sacred ford, as is the sacred ford of Śrī Puruṣottama;
Mahendra Mountain is a sacred ford, and the Kāverī is another supreme river.
The Godāvarī is a great sacred ford, as is the Payoṣṇī river that grants boons;
the Vindhya mountains are a sin-removing sacred site, and the Bheda of the Narmadā is supreme.
Gokarṇa is a supreme sacred site, as is the city of Māhiṣmatī;
Kālañjara is a great sacred site on earth, and Śuklatīrtha is unsurpassed.
When purification has been performed, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow resides nearby;
there is the Viraja-tīrtha which grants everything, and the supreme Svarṇākṣa-tīrtha.
Nanditīrtha, which bestows liberation and grants the fruit of ten million tīrthas;
Nāsikya, the great tīrtha; and beyond that, Govardhana.
The Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the Bhīmarathī, the Gaṇḍakī, and the Irāvatī;
the holy Bindusaras and the supreme Viṣṇupādodaka.
Meditation on Brahman is the supreme sacred ford; restraint of the senses is a sacred ford;
self-control is the highest sacred ford, and likewise, purity of being is the supreme one.
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford— the lake of knowledge with meditation for its water, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred— attains the supreme goal.
For those people who perceive duality, thinking "this is a sacred ford" and "this is not," going to sacred fords and whatever fruit that entails is prescribed.
For one who knows that "all is Brahman," there is no place whatsoever that is not a sacred ford;
in these [waters], bathing, giving gifts, ancestral rites, and the offering of rice-balls become inexhaustible.
All rivers, all mountains, the sacred ford (tīrtha) frequented by gods and others,
Śrīraṅga— the sacred ford of Hari— and the Tāpī, the most excellent great river.
The Saptagodāvara is a sacred ford, and Koṇagiri is a supreme sacred ford;
there resides the goddess Mahālakṣmī, and the Praṇītā is a supreme river.
On the Sahya mountain, O Lord of the gods, he is Ekavīra;
at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Vindhya, and the Nīla mountain, she is Sureśvarī.
Having bathed at the Kanakhala tīrtha, he shall not be born again. Sūta said:
These and other such tīrthas are indeed bestowers of all things through bathing and other rites.
Having heard this from Hari, Brahmā spoke to Vyāsa, who was accompanied by Dakṣa and others.
After mentioning these holy places, he further spoke of the most excellent of all holy places called Gayā, which is imperishable for all and bestows the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of All Holy Places," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 82 of the Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa].
Salutations to the glorious Gaṇeśa.
(Now begins the glorification of Gayā).
Brahmā said:
O Vyāsa, the supreme majesty of Gayā is the most essential of all essentials.
I shall explain in brief that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; listen.
In former times, there was a most powerful and supreme asura named Gaya;
he performed a most terrible penance that caused distress to all living beings.
The gods, tormented by that penance, went to Hari for the sake of his destruction;
Hari said to them, "It must come to pass through those whose essence is Śiva."
"His great body shall be cast down; so be it," the gods said to Hari.
And once, for the sake of worshipping Śiva, [they took] lotuses from the Ocean of Milk.
Having brought him to the land of Kīkaṭa, the powerful one made him his bed;
deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, he was slain by Viṣṇu with a mace.
Therefore, Viṣṇu Gadādhara stands at Gayā as the bestower of liberation;
his body exists there in the form of a *liṅga*, while Pitāmaha resides in Śuddha.
Janārdana, Kāleśa, and another, Prapitāmaha, as well as Viṣṇu, then declared: "This shall become a sacred field (puṇyakṣetra) established by divine ordinance."
The man who performs sacrifices, ancestral rites, the offering of funeral cakes, ablutions, and other such acts, shall go to heaven and the world of Brahmā; that man shall not go to hell.
Knowing Gayātīrtha to be supreme, the Grandfather performed a sacrifice and honored the Brahmins who had arrived for the purpose of officiating as priests.
Having created great rivers carrying flavorful waters, as well as ponds and the like, he likewise created edible and consumable fruits and the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu).
The Lord gave the sacred field of Gayā, extending five krośas, to the Brāhmaṇas;
however, out of greed for wealth and other gifts during the sacrifices of Dharma, they accepted it.
Then those Brahmins residing at Gayā were cursed:
"May there be no Vedic learning for three generations, and may there be no wealth for three generations! (GarP 1.82.12)
"May there be for you a river carrying water and a mountain of stone";
when thus entreated by them, the Lord Brahmā granted his favor.
For those meritorious people who perform ancestral rites at Gayā go to the world of Brahmā;
by those who honor you, I am always honored.
Knowledge of Brahman, performing the śrāddha at Gayā, dying in the house of a cow,
and residing at Kurukṣetra— this is the fourfold liberation for men.
O Vyāsa, all the oceans, rivers, as well as ponds, wells, and lakes, go to the sacred site of Gayā desiring to bathe; of this there is no doubt.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife—
all sins arising from association with these, perish through the Śrāddha performed at Gayā.
Those who died of natural causes, those killed by animals or thieves,
and those bitten by snakes— all go to heaven through the *śrāddha* performed at Gayā.
The fruit that a man obtains by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā cannot be described by me even in hundreds of millions of years.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Śrī Brahmā said:
Among the Kīkaṭas, Gayā is meritorious; Rājagṛha and its forest are meritorious;
the region of Āraṇa is meritorious; and among rivers, the Punarpunā is meritorious.
Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is in the east, while in the west, south, and north,
the measurement of Gayā is proclaimed to be two and a half krośas.
The sacred field of Gayā extends for five krośas, and Gayāśiras for one krośa;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there, eternal satisfaction is attained.
From Naga, Janardana, and the well, as well as from Uttaramanasa—
this is declared to be Gayashiras, and it is called Phalgutirtha.
In that regard, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one attains the supreme goal for the ancestors;
merely by going to Gayā, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
At Gayā, Janārdana, the God of gods, exists in the form of the ancestors;
by beholding that lotus-eyed one, one is indeed liberated from the three debts.
Having seen the chariot-path at Gayātīrtha, as well as Rudrapada and the others,
Kāleśvara, and Kedāra, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Having seen the divine Grandfather, one is liberated from all sins;
and having seen the Great-Grandfather, one goes to the world free from affliction.
Likewise, by bowing with great effort to that god Gadādhara, Mādhava, the Supreme Person, a man is not born again.
O brahmin sage, by beholding the high-souled Maunāditya, and especially Kanakārka,
while observing silence, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
And by worshipping Brahmā, one shall attain the world of Brahmā;
so too for that man who, having risen at dawn, beholds the Gāyatrī.
By performing the twilight devotions with diligence, one obtains the fruit of all the Vedas;
and by beholding the Sāvitrī at midday, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice.
Having seen Sarasvatī in the evening, one obtains the fruit of giving;
having seen Īśvara situated on the mountain, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Having seen the Lord of Dharma in the Forest of Dharma, one's debt shall be destroyed;
having seen the god Gṛdhreśvara, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Having seen Dhenu in Dhenuvana, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
and having seen Prabhāseśa at Prabhāsa, one attains the supreme goal.
By seeing Koṭīśvara and Aśvamedha, one’s debt shall be destroyed;
by seeing Svargadvāreśvara, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
By beholding Rāmeśvara and Gadālola, one shall attain heaven;
likewise, by beholding Brahmeśvara, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having beheld Mahācaṇḍī at Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one shall obtain all desires;
and having beheld Phalgvīśa, Phalgucaṇḍī, Gaurī, and Maṅgalā, one shall likewise attain them.
One becomes free from debt to the ancestors by visiting Gomaka, the divine Gopati,
Aṅgāreśa, Siddheśa, Gayāditya, and likewise Gaja.
Having beheld Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors;
and having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and beheld the god Gadādhara, a man [attains the same].
What is not sufficient for this regarding men who perform virtuous deeds?
Here, twenty-one generations of men go to the world of Brahmā.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth, whatever oceans and lakes there may be,
they shall all go to Phalgutīrtha once every single day.
On earth, Gayā is meritorious; within Gayā, Gayāśiras is [meritorious];
likewise, Phalgutīrtha is the most excellent, for it is indeed the mouth of the gods.
To the north of the Kanakā river is the Nābhi-tīrtha;
in the center is the meritorious Brahma-sadas-tīrtha, which bestows the world of Brahmā through bathing.
By offering funeral cakes and other oblations at the well, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors;
likewise, by performing a śrāddha at the Akṣaya-vata, the performer leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed at Haṃsatīrtha, a man is liberated from all sins;
likewise at Koṭitīrtha, Gayālole, Vaitaraṇī, and Gomaka.
A person performing a śrāddha at Brahma-tīrtha, Rāma-tīrtha, Āgneya-tīrtha, or Soma-tīrtha leads twenty-one generations of men to the world of Brahmā.
One who performs a śrāddha at Rāmahrada leads his ancestral lineage to the world of Brahmā;
one who performs a śrāddha at Uttaramānasa is not born again as a human being.
At Dakṣiṇamānasa, a performer of śrāddha leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
at Svargadvāra, a man performing śrāddha leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
and one who performs the libation for Bhīṣma on its peak delivers his ancestors across [to liberation].
Likewise, one who performs the śrāddha at Gṛdhreśvara becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
A person faithful to the ancestral rites who gives a cow in the forest shall lead his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
likewise, one who has bathed and beheld the cow shall undoubtedly attain the same by giving a sesame-cow.
Having performed a śrāddha at Aindra, Naratīrtha, Vāsava, or Vaiṣṇava, as well as at a great river, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā.

Having performed bathing, the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) at the Gāyattrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī tirthas, one attains one hundred and one [rebirths].
Such a man leads his ancestral lineage to the world of Brahmā;
restrained and with his mind fixed on the ancestors, he shall emerge from the womb of Brahman.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one shall not enter the confinement of a womb;
by means of the *kākajaṅghā* plant during the libation, the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
By performing a śrāddha at the pond of Mataṅga in the Dharmāraṇya forest, one shall go to heaven;
and by doing so at the Dharmayūpa well, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
"May the deities be my authority and the world-protectors be my witnesses:
having come here, I have performed this expiation for my ancestors upon this funeral pyre."
Having bathed at Rāmatīrtha and performed the Śrāddha ceremony at Prabhāsaka on the rock, the hosts of ancestors are indeed said to be liberated from their state as pretas.
One who performs a śrāddha with meat from an animal nourished by its own mother rescues seven generations of his lineage;
one who performs a śrāddha with the flesh of the muṇḍapṛṣṭha and other such animals leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Indeed, there is no place in Gayā where a sacred ford (tīrtha) does not exist;
throughout the five-krośa Gayā field, wherever one may be, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
A man obtains inexhaustible fruit and leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
he should place his own funeral cake (piṇḍa) into the hand of Janārdana.
"O Janārdana, this ball of rice has been placed by me in your hand;
may it attend upon [my deceased relative] who has gone to the other world, providing inexhaustible liberation."
One certainly attains the world of Brahmā together with one's ancestors at Gayā,
at Dharmapṛṣṭha, and likewise at the lake of Brahmā.
What is given to the ancestors at Gayāśīrṣa and at Akṣayavaṭa becomes inexhaustible;
as do offerings made in Dharmāraṇya, Dharmapṛṣṭha, and Dhenukāraṇya.
Having seen these, one should deliver twenty ancestors belonging to a noble lineage;
this is called the western part of the Great River, known as Brahmāraṇya.
The eastern portion is Brahmasada; the Nāgādri is Bharata’s hermitage.
At Bharata’s hermitage, one who performs the śrāddha rite shall attain the station of Mataṅga.
To the south of Gayāśīrṣa and to the west of the Mahānadī river, that is known as Campakavana; for there indeed lies the Pāṇḍuśilā.
One who performs a *śrāddha* there on the third lunar day at the confluence of the Niścirā,
at the Mahāhrada, and at the Kauśikī, shall obtain inexhaustible fruit.
To the north of the Vaitaraṇī is the third reservoir known as Krauñca;
there, the footprints of Krauñca exist, and one who performs the śrāddha rite there leads his ancestors to heaven.
To the north of Krauñcapāda is the body of water named Niścīra;
where a single visit and a single offering of a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) [yield great merit].
How much more difficult is it to remain permanently established in this very place?
Having touched the waters of the Mahānadī, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
One shall attain imperishable worlds and uplift one's lineage;
when the Sandhyā prayer is recited at the Sāvitra [time], it is as if the twelve-year rite has been performed.
The man who dwells at Gayā during both the bright and dark fortnights purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
Having seen Muṇḍapṛṣṭha at Gayā, the mountain Aravinda, and the third, Krauñcapāda, one is liberated from sins.
And when a lunar or solar eclipse occurs during the period of Makara,
the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā— difficult to obtain even in the three worlds— is accomplished.
A śrāddha offered at the Mahāhrada lake, at the Kauśikī river, especially at the Mūla field, and in the cave of Gṛdhrakūṭa,
yields sevenfold great fruit.
Where the stream of Māheśvarī flows, there one becomes free from debt;
having reached the meritorious Viśālā, a river renowned throughout the three worlds.

The man who performs a śrāddha attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; by departing from this world, he goes to heaven. Having bathed at Māsapada, the performer of a śrāddha obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
By offering a ball of rice at Ravipāda, the deliverance of the fallen occurs;
he who, while staying at Gayā, gives food, by him his ancestors become possessed of a son.
The ancestors, terrified by the fear of hell, long for sons, thinking:
"Whoever shall go to Gayā will deliver us."
Upon seeing his son arrived at Gayā, there shall be a festival for the ancestors;
for he will surely offer us water even by touching it with his feet.
Whether it be one's own son or another person, whenever one causes a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be cast into the Gayā-kūpa in the name of someone, that person shall be led to eternal Brahman.
One who visits ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) shall attain the world of Viṣṇu, Puṇḍarīka;
that river which is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Vaitaraṇī— [he shall cross it].
Having descended indeed into the field of Gaya for the sake of delivering his ancestors, whoever there offers the śrāddha, the funeral cake (piṇḍa), or makes a gift of a cow; ||| GarP_1,83.63 |||
If a son should ever go to Gayā at the turn of time, he would deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage; of this there is no doubt.
One should feed those very Brahmins who have been designated by the priest;
for them is the station of the Brahma-heaven, and likewise the drinking of Soma.
The place was fashioned by Brahmā, and the Brahmins were fashioned by Brahmā;
