all the deities, together with the ancestors, were honored by those who were honored.
One should satisfy the Brahmins at Gayā with offerings to the gods and ancestors according to the prescribed rites;
indeed, it is ordained that Gayā is the place for the abandonment of the body.
He who performs the rite of releasing a bull in the unsurpassed sacred field of Gayā obtains the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
A man of great intelligence, even for his own sake— and likewise for others— should perform the offering of the funeral cakes at Gayā, even if he does so without sesame seeds.
To as many paternal kinsmen, relatives, and friends as there may be,
a funeral cake (piṇḍa) should be offered according to the prescribed rite upon the ground of Vyāsa’s Gayā.
Having bathed at Rāmatīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of [giving] a hundred cows;
and having bathed in the Mataṅgavāpī, he shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Niścirā, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
having bathed at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
By residing at Mahākauśī, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
this river, which purifies the world, has issued forth from the lake of Pitāmaha.
In its vicinity is the well-known Kapilā, known as Agnidhārā;
by bathing there, one who performs the śrāddha rite attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and achieves fulfillment of purpose.
One who is faithful shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice at Kumāradhārā;
furthermore, having approached Kumāra and bowed, one shall attain liberation.
Having bathed in the Somakuṇḍa, a man goes to the world of Soma;
by offering funeral cakes at Saṃvarta’s pond, a man shall become fortunate.
A man whose sins have been washed away goes to Pretakuṇḍa as one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa),
as well as to Devanadī, Lelihāna, Mathana, and Jānugartaka.
At such sacred fords as these, one who offers funeral cakes shall deliver his ancestors;
and by bowing to the gods beginning with Vasiṣṭheśa, one achieves the destruction of debts.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—84.
Brahmā said:

Having performed the *śrāddha* rite according to the rules, one who is intent on going to Gayā should don the dress of a pilgrim (*kārpaṭī*) and perform the circumambulation of the village as well. (GarP 1.84.1)
Then, having gone to another village and partaken of food remaining from a funeral feast (śrāddha),
he should proceed on his way after performing a circumambulation, avoiding the acceptance of gifts.
For one who has merely set out from home toward Gayā,
every step is a stairway for the ancestors to ascend to heaven.
Shaving the head and fasting— this is the rule for all sacred fords,
with the exception of Kurukṣetra, Viśālā, Virajā, and Gayā.
One should perform the śrāddha at Gayā both by day and always by night;
likewise, a śrāddha performed at Vārāṇasī or at the Śoṇanada tīrtha [yields great merit].
By repeatedly performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) at the Mahānadī river, one leads one's ancestors to heaven;
having gone to the northern Mānasa lake, one attains unsurpassed perfection (*siddhi*).
One should perform the śrāddha rite at that place and likewise perform the ritual bath;
he obtains divine desires and the means to liberation in every respect.
Having gone to Dakṣiṇamānasa, one should observe silence and perform the offering of rice-balls and other rites;
at Dakṣiṇamānasa, one obtains the clearing away of the three debts.
With the most excellent of serpents, who inspire joy in the perfected ones (siddhas), cause terror to the sinful,
are licking with their tongues, exceedingly fierce, and unharmed.
The sacred site named Kanakhala is renowned throughout the three worlds;
situated to the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, it is frequented by hosts of celestial sages.

Having bathed there, one goes to heaven; furthermore, a śrāddha offered there becomes inexhaustible. Having bowed to the Sun and performed the proper rites such as offering the piṇḍas, one should do this: GarP_1,84.11: [The verse continues: "O Lord of the world, O Lord of the gods, O Lord of all beings, O Lord of the universe, accept my worship. Having spoken thus, he should offer flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated the Sun three times, he should bow down with palms joined in reverence. Having performed the rites for the ancestors, he should then go to the hermitage of Atri. Having bathed there, he goes to heaven; a śrāddha offered there becomes inexhaustible. Having bowed to the Sun, he should perform this after completing the proper rites such as offering the piṇḍas. Then, having circumambulated the Sun three times, he should bow down with palms joined in reverence. Having performed the rites
Kavyavāha, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman,
as well as the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, and Somapa Pitṛ-deities.
"May my illustrious ancestors come here, protected by you all— those who were born in my lineage and those who are my kinsmen."
I have come to this Gayā for the purpose of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to them;
having offered the cake at Phalgutīrtha, behold the god Pitāmaha.
Then, having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and beheld the god Gadādhara, a man becomes free from debt to his ancestors.
One shall immediately deliver oneself, as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants;
this is the rite prescribed for the first day, and on the second day one should proceed.
One who offers funeral cakes and other oblations at the pond of Mataṅga in Dharmāraṇya shall obtain the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice upon reaching Dharmāraṇya.
The fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices shall be obtained at Brahma-tīrtha;
one should perform the Śrāddha and offer the rice-balls and water-libations in the space between the well and the sacrificial post.
The rite for the ancestors performed with water from a well becomes inexhaustible.
On the third day, having gone to the abode of Brahmā where there is no fire, one should bathe and then perform the libation.
Having performed the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and other ceremonies, they should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) in the space between the sacrificial post and the well;
situated near the cow-pasture, these [ancestors] were established by Brahmā, reaching back to Brahmā himself.
Merely by serving them, the ancestors attain liberation;
by circumambulating the sacrificial post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha on the fourth day and performed the libations for the gods and others,
one should perform the śrāddha at Gayāśīrṣa and at the Rudrapadas and other such sites.
A śrāddha performed at Piṇḍāraka, at Dehimukha, at Vyāsa, at Pañcāgni, at Padatraya, and at the sites of Sūrya, Indu, and Kārttikeya, is likewise inexhaustible.
One should perform the Śrāddha rite for nine deities, or for twelve deities,
on the Anvaṣṭakā days, during the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of a death.
In this place, the śrāddha for the mother is performed separately, whereas elsewhere it is performed together with the husband;
having bathed at Daśāśvamedha and beheld the god Pitāmaha.
Having touched the foot of Rudra, a person does not return here again;
he obtains that fruit which one would attain by giving away the earth filled three times over with wealth.
Having performed a śrāddha at Gayāśiras, he obtains that fruit;
one should offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras even if it is only the size of a śamī leaf.
The ancestors attain divinity; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The wise Mahādeva set his foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha.
By performing austerities there, one obtains great merit;
and whoever offers funeral cakes at Gayāśīrṣa under the names of [specific ancestors], [they attain the highest state].
Those dwelling in hell go to heaven, and those dwelling in heaven attain liberation,
having bathed on the fifth day at Gandālole at the foot of the banyan tree.
Having approached the foot of a banyan tree, one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors; by doing so with either vegetables or warm water, one shall deliver the entire lineage.
When one Brahmin is fed at the Akṣayavaṭa after performing a Śrāddha and beholding his great-grandfather, it is as if ten million have been fed.
One obtains inexhaustible worlds and shall uplift a hundred generations of one's kin;
many sons are to be desired, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā.
"One should either perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) or set free a dark-colored bull, dedicating it to a certain deceased person. Having said this, a certain ghost spoke to a merchant.
"Perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayāśīrṣa in my name;
thus may I be liberated from the state of a preta, and may it grant heaven to the giver as well."
Having heard this, the merchant Gayāśīrṣa offered a rice-ball (piṇḍaka) to the King of the Pretas,
and then, together with his younger brothers, he gave offerings to his own ancestors.
All were liberated; Viśāla, along with his son, became a provider of alms.
In Viśālā, Viśāla became the prince and spoke to the twice-born:
"How may sons and others be mine? they asked Viśālaka, and the brahmins replied, "Everything will be yours through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā."
Then Viśāla, having offered the funeral cakes at Gayāśīrṣa, became possessed of sons;
seeing three men—white, red, and black—in the sky, he spoke to them.
"Who are you? he asked. And one among them, who was white, said to Viśālaka:
"I am your father, the white one; I have gone to the auspicious world of Indra."
"My son's father was a passionate killer of Brahmins and a supreme evildoer;
this grandfather, O Kṛṣṇa, has had sages slaughtered by him."
O giver of funeral cakes, we had both reached the Avīci hell, but now we have been liberated;
having all been set free from there, we go to the supreme heaven.
Having fulfilled his duties and ruled over a vast kingdom, Viśāla went to heaven;
yet those ancestors in my lineage for whom the rites of the funeral cake and water-libations have been omitted—[may they be satisfied by this].

Those whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, those who have just emerged from the womb, those for whom no cremation rite was performed, and likewise others who were not consumed by fire; GarP_1,84.44 //
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather be satisfied by what is offered upon the ground; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme state.
The mother, the paternal grandmother, and likewise the paternal great-grandmother;
as well as the maternal grandfather and the maternal great-grandfather.
The great paternal grandmother, and likewise the maternal grandmother, the paternal great-grandmother, and indeed the great paternal great-grandmother. (GarP 1.84.47)
And may this ball of rice reach others as well, remaining inexhaustible.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Brahmā said:
Having bathed at the Pretaśilā and other such sites, one should offer a pinda with the nectar of Varuṇā’s presence, having invoked the supreme ancestors with these mantras.
"Those who have died in our family and whose destination is unknown—
all of them I shall summon here with water and sesame seeds upon the surface of the *darbha* grass."
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have died in my paternal lineage and those who have died in my maternal lineage, I offer this rice-ball (piṇḍa).
And for those in my maternal grandfather’s lineage whose destination is unknown,
I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
For the sake of the deliverance of all those who have not yet grown teeth and those who were afflicted while in the womb, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
And whatever kinsmen there may be who are devoid of name and lineage—
whether in my own lineage or in another lineage— for whom no destination is known, for their upliftment I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
To those who died by hanging, those killed by poison or weapons,
and those who committed suicide— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
And those who died in a fire, or those killed by lions or tigers,
or even by fanged or horned beasts— to them I offer this funeral cake.
To those who have been consumed by fire, as well as others who have not been consumed by fire,
and to those killed by lightning or thieves— to them I offer this funeral cake.
For the sake of delivering those who have gone to the Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra hells, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
For the sake of delivering those who have gone to the terrible Asipatravana and the Kumbhīpāka hells, I offer this rice-ball.
For the sake of delivering those others who dwell in the world of pretas in places of torment, I offer this rice-ball.
And those who have entered the womb of animals—birds, insects, and reptiles—or those who abide in the womb of trees: to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
To those who have been led by the commands of Yama to dwell in innumerable hells,
I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
To those who wander through thousands of different births by their own karma,
and for whom a human birth is difficult to obtain— to them I give this ball of rice.
May all those who were kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and those who were kinsmen in another birth,
forever attain satisfaction through this offering of funeral cakes.
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas,
may they all always attain satisfaction through this offering of rice balls.
Those who were born in my father’s lineage, as well as in my mother’s lineage,
and those others who have died— my teachers, fathers-in-law, kinsmen, and other relatives.

Those in my family for whom the ancestral rice-offerings have ceased, those deprived of sons and wives, those whose rites have been neglected, as well as those born blind and the lame; [may they all attain peace].
May the funeral offering given by me reach those of my family who were deformed or born prematurely, whether they were known or unknown; may it abide for them inexhaustibly.
May the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, be my witnesses;
having reached Gayā, I have performed the rite of deliverance for my ancestors.
"O Lord Gadādhara, I have come to Gayā for the sake of the ancestral rites;
may you be my witness today that I am now free from the three debts."
The Great River, the Lake of Brahmā, the inexhaustible Banyan tree, Prabhāsa, the rising sun, Gayāśiras,
the Sarasvatī, the Cow of Dharma, and Pṛṣṭha— these are located at Kurukṣetra and Gayā.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 86] Brahmā said:
This which is known as the Pretaśilā at Gayā exists in three places:
at Prabhāsa, at Pretakuṇḍa, and also upon the head of Gayāsura.
This stone, composed of all the gods, is maintained by dharma for the sake of prosperity;
it [liberates] those among men who have fallen into the state of ghosts, such as friends, kinsmen, and others.
Because the auspicious Pretaśilā exists for the sake of their deliverance,
therefore sages, kings, queens, and others always [resort] to this place.
Those who perform the *śrāddha* and other rites on that stone go to the world of Brahmā;
for it is upon the back of the head of the demon Gayāsura that the stone rests.
Therefore, this mountain Muṇḍapṛṣṭha consists of all the gods;
for at the feet of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha are the sources of the Brahma-lakes and other waters.
Among them was a lotus grove, and by that it was characterized;
for there is a mountain named Aravinda, marked by the footprints of Krauñca.
Therefore, Mount Krauñcapāda bestows the world of Brahmā upon the ancestors;
the primordial deities, beginning with Gadādhara, are established there from the very beginning.
Because they were unmanifest in the form of stone, that stone is composed of the gods;
having covered Gayāśiras, the stone remains there due to its great weight.
After some time,
Hari, the primordial wielder of the mace, who is without beginning or end, remained manifest along with Mahārudra and the other gods.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, for the destruction of unrighteousness and the like,
and for the annihilation of the Daityas and Rākṣasas, he previously became a fish, just as he did before.
The Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, the powerful Rāma,
as well as Rāma the son of Daśaratha, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki.
Thus, Gadādhara was manifest yet possessed an unmanifest form;
he was the primordial one, because he was worshipped here at the beginning by the gods, Brahmā and the others.

Therefore, having approached the primordial Gadādhara together with the gods, he who offers [him] water for the feet and so forth, as well as perfumes, flowers, and so forth, [attains the highest state]. (GarP 1.86.13)
The water for the guest-offering (arghya), the vessel, the water for washing the feet (pādya), fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, excellent food offerings (naivedya), and various kinds of garlands.
Garments, crowns, bells, chowries, spectacles, ornaments and the like, as well as alms-food, gifts of food and so forth; // GarP_1,86.15 //
For them, wealth, grain, long life, the perfection of health,
the lineage of sons and so forth, prosperity, knowledge, and desired objects of pleasure [are attained].
A wife, residence in heaven and other realms, and a kingdom obtained after returning from heaven;
being of noble birth, endowed with courage, and crushing enemies in battle.
Freed from slaughter and bondage, he shall attain liberation in the end;
those who perform the funeral rites, the offering of rice-balls, and so forth, go to the world of Brahmā together with their ancestors.
Those who worship Jagannātha, Subhadrā, and Balabhadra,
having attained knowledge and prosperity, go to Puruṣottama along with their sons.
There, in the presence of Puruṣottamarāja, Sūrya, and Gaṇa,
the offering of rice-balls and other oblations to the ancestors bestows the world of Brahmā.
By bowing to Kapardin Vighneśa, one is liberated from all obstacles;
by worshipping Kārtikeya, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
By worshipping the twelve Ādityas, one is liberated from all diseases;
by thoroughly worshipping Vaiśvānara, one shall attain supreme radiance.
Having worshipped Revanta, one obtains unsurpassed horses;
by honoring Indra, one attains great sovereignty, and by worshipping Gaurī, one shall obtain good fortune.
Having worshipped the Vidyā Sarasvatī, having fully honored Lakṣmī and Śrī,
and having duly propitiated Garuḍa, one is liberated from the multitude of obstacles.
By worshipping Kṣetrapāla, one is liberated from the host of planetary afflictions;
by worshipping Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one shall obtain all desires.
By duly worshipping the eight Nāgas, one bitten by a serpent is liberated;
and by honoring Brahmā, one attains the world of Brahmā.
By worshipping Balabhadra, one obtains strength and health;
and by honoring Subhadrā, one attains supreme good fortune.
By worshipping Puruṣottama, one obtains all desires;
by worshipping Nārāyaṇa, one becomes a lord of men.
By touching and bowing to Nārasiṃha, one shall be victorious in battle;
by worshipping Varāha, one shall obtain sovereignty over the earth.
By touching the Mālā and Vidyādhara [images], one attains the station of a Vidyādhara;
by worshipping Ādigadādhara, one obtains all desires.
Having worshipped Somanātha, one shall attain the world of Śiva;
having paid homage to Rudreśvara, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
By bowing to Rāmeśvara, a man becomes as beloved as Rāma;
by praising Brahmeśvara, a man is destined for the world of Brahmā.
By worshipping Kāleśvara, a man becomes a conqueror of death;
and by honoring Kedāra, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having fully worshipped Siddheśvara, one becomes a perfected being (siddha) and shall go to Brahmapura;
indeed, having beheld the primordial Gadādhara together with the original Rudras and others.
Having uplifted a hundred lineages, a man shall lead them to the City of Brahmā;
one seeking dharma shall obtain dharma, and one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth.
One who desires pleasures shall obtain pleasures; one whose aim is liberation shall obtain liberation;
one who seeks a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom; and one who seeks peace shall obtain peace.
Having fully worshipped the primordial Gadādhara, one attains all goals;
a woman desiring sons obtains sons, and she desiring good fortune obtains it.
And she who desires progeny, having obtained offspring, should worship Gadādhara with ancestral rites (śrāddha),
the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the gift of food and water.
By worshipping the primordial Gadādhara, one attains the world of Brahmā;
for among all the sacred fords on earth, the city of Gayā is the most excellent.
Likewise, he who has the form of stone and so forth is indeed the supreme Gadādhara;
for when he is seen, the stone is seen, since everything is Gadādhara.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
(Thus the "Greatness of Gayā" is completed.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 87.
Hari said:
I shall describe the fourteen Manus and their sons, beginning with Suka;
first was Svāyambhuva Manu, and Agnidhra and others were his sons.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
and the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis).
The Jayākhyas, the Amitākhyas, the Śukras, and likewise the Yāmas—
these four groups of twelve each are the drinkers of Soma.
Viśvabhuj, Vāmadeva, and Indra were the sons of Bāṣkali; he was indeed his enemy. That Daitya was slain by Viṣṇu with his great-souled discus.
Then there was Manu Svārociṣa, and his son Maṇḍaleśvara; also Citraka, Vinata, Karṇānta, Vidyuta, and Ravi.
Bṛhadguṇa, Nabhas, Mahābalaparākrama, Ūrjastambha, Prāṇa, Ṛṣabha, and Niścalara; // GarP_1,87.6 //
Datta, Ambha, Liṣṭha, Avarīvan, and Ṛṣya are proclaimed as the seven;
the Tuṣitas are said to be twelve, as are those who are the Pārāvatas.
The wise Indra, the enemy of the gods,
was slain by the Lord Madhusūdana, the doer of much and the ocean of compassion, who assumed the form of an elephant.
The sons of Auttama Manu were Āja, Paraśu,
Vinīta, Suketu, Sumitra, Subala, and Śuci.
Deva, Devāvṛdha, Rudra, Mahotsāha, Ujjita,
Rathaujas, Ūrdhvabāhu, Śaraṇa, Anagha, and Muni.
Sutapās, Śaṅku—these are proclaimed as the seven sages;
they are the Vaśavartins, Svadhāmāns, Śivas, Satyas, and Pratardanās.
Five groups of deities are proclaimed, and each of them consists of twelve;
Indra, Svaśānti, his Śukra, and the Dānava named Pralamba.
Hari Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a fish, slew that Dānava;
then the sons of Tāmasa Manu were Jānujaṅgha and Nirbhaya.
Navakhyāti, Naya, Priyabhṛtya, Vivikṣipa,
Dṛḍheṣudhi, Prastalākṣa, Kṛbandhu, and likewise Kṛta.
Jyotirdhāmā, Pṛthu, Dhṛṣṭakāvya, Caitra, Cetāgni, Hema, and Kau—
these seven sages are proclaimed as the wise ones who delight in the gods.
The Haris, the Devatāmās, and the four groups of twenty-seven [constellations] are his attendants;
Indra, Śibi, his enemy, and the Bhaumarathas are remembered as his [officers].
By Hari, in the form of a tortoise, the asura Bhīmaratha was slain,
as well as Mahāprāṇa, the son of Raivata Manu and a practitioner of spiritual powers.
The forest-dweller, the kinsman, the one without enemies, the one who turns back, the supreme slayer, the pure one,
the one of firm vows, the banner, and the horn— these are described as his [the Sun's] rays by the seers.
Vedaśrī, Vedabāhu, and likewise Ūrdhvabāhu;
Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Satyanetra by name,
and Svadhāman.
Furthermore, there were the Abhūtarajasas, the Devāśvamedhas,
the Vaikuṇṭhas, and the Amṛtas; these are the four classes of deities.
In that assembly were fourteen gods, including the powerful and sovereign Indra;
the tranquil Śatru, the Daitya, was slain by Viṣṇu in the form of a swan.
The sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu were Uru, Puru, Mahābala,
Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyabāhu, and likewise Kṛti.
Agniṣṇura, Atirātra, and likewise the man Sudyumna; Haviṣmān, Uttama, the illustrious Śrīmān, Sva(dhāmā), and Virajas.
Abhimāna, Sahiṣṇu, Madhuśrī, and the Ṛṣis are remembered; as well as the Āryas, the Prabhūtas, the Bhāvyas, the Lekhas, and the Pṛthukas.
Thus, five hosts of the gods of heaven belonging to Aṣṭaka have been described:
Indra, Manojava, Śatru, Mahākāla, and Mahābhaja.
He was slain by Hari, who assumed the form of a horse;
these sons of Vaivasvata Manu were devoted to Viṣṇu.
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti,
Nariṣyanta, Pāṃsu, Nabhas, and Nediṣṭha.
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and Sudyumna were the sons of Manu;
as were Atri, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, Jamadagni, and Kaśyapa.
Gautama, Bharadvāja, and Viśvāmitra as the seventh;
likewise, the forty-nine Maruts are proclaimed.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Sādhyas are three groups of twelve;
likewise, the Rudras are proclaimed to be eleven and the Vasus eight.
The two Aśvins are specified, as well as the ten Viśvedevas;
the ten Āṅgirasa gods and the nine groups of gods likewise.
Śakra was indeed named Tejasvin, and his enemy was known as Hiraṇyākṣa;
then, by Viṣṇu in the form of a boar, he who was called Hariṇya was slain.
I shall now describe the sons of the future Manu named Sāvarṇya:
Vijaya, Cārvavīra, Nirmoha, Satyavāk, and Kṛti.
The most excellent and the most venerable, as well as the very embodiment of speech—
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Vyāsa, Gālava, and the radiant one.
Likewise, Rāma and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga are proclaimed as the seven sages;
also Sutapas and Amṛtābhas, as well as the principal gods.
The host of those gods is recorded as consisting of twenty groups each;
among them, Bali, the son of Virocana, will become Indra.
Having given these three paces to Viṣṇu who was entreating him,
he will abandon prosperity and the station of Indra, and thereafter attain perfection.
Hear now of the sons of the ninth Manu, Dakṣasāvarṇi, who belongs to the lineage of Vāruṇi:
Dhṛtaketu, Dīptiketu, Pañcahasta, Nirāmaya,
Pṛthuśravas, Bṛhadudyumna, Ṛcīka, and Bṛhatguṇa.
Medhātithi, Dyuti, Savasa, Vasu,
Jyotiṣmat, Havya, Kavya, the Ṛṣis, Vibhu, and Īśvara.
Para, Marīci, and Garbha— these three are the possessors of their own true dharmas;
Deśa, Śatru, and Kālakākṣa, and their slayer Padmanābha.
At that time, there will be twelve groups of gods, each consisting of one;
their Indra will be the immensely powerful and wondrous Hara.
Now hear of the ten sons of Dhamaputra, the son of Manu Māsi:
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, and the heroic Bhūriśreṇya.
Śatānīka, Niramitra, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha,
Bhūridyumna, Suvarcas, Śānti, and the powerful Indra.
Ayo, Mūrti, Haviṣmat, Sukṛti, Avyaya,
Nābhāga, Apratimaujas, Saurabha, and likewise the Ṛṣis.
At that time, there will be a host of deities numbering one hundred known as the Prāṇas;
their Indra will be the very powerful one named Śānti.
Bali shall be his enemy, and Hari will cause him to be slain with a mace.
I shall now declare the sons of you, Rudra, who are the eleven-fold [sons]:
Sarvatraga, Suśarman, Devānīka, and Pururguru.
Kṣetravarṇa, Dṛḍheṣu, Ārdraka, Putraka, Haviṣmān, Haviṣya, Varuṇa, and Viśvavistara.
Viṣṇu, Agnitejas, and the seven sages are proclaimed;
likewise, there are the Vihagaṅgamas, the Kāmagas, and those who delight in creative emanations (Nirmāṇarucis).
Each of their groups consists of thirty-three, and Indra is indeed their bull;
his enemy Dhasagrīva, appearing in the form of Śrī, shall cause him to be slain.
Now hear of the sons of Manu, the twelfth son of Dakṣa:
Devavān, Upadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and Vidūratha.
Mitravān, Mitradeva, the heroic Mitrabindu,
Mitravāha, and Pravāha were the sons of Manu, the son of Dakṣa.
Tapasvī, Sutapas, Tapomūrti, Taporati, Tapodhṛti, Dyuti, and another, the seventh, Tapodhana— these are the seven ascetics.
The Svadharmas, Sutapas, Haritas, and likewise the Rohitas,
as well as these Gaṇas of the enemies of the gods— each of these groups consists of ten.
O auspicious one, there Indra will be named Ṛtadhāman, and his enemy will be Tāraka;
Śaṅkara, having become Hari in the form of a eunuch, shall slay him.
Learn from me the sons of Trayodaśa, the Manu Raucya:
Citrasena, Vicitra, Tapas, Dharmarata, and Dhṛti.
Sunetra, Kṣetravṛtti, Sunaya, Dharmapa, Dṛḍha,
Dhṛtimat, Avyaya, Niśārūpa, and Nirutsuka.
The seven sages are proclaimed as being free from delusion and perceivers of reality: Svaromāṇa, Sudharmāṇa, and Sva...
Likewise, the immortals are subject to karma.
There, indeed, are the thirty-three distinct hosts of the gods;
Indra is the lord of heaven, and the enemy of the gods is the Dānava named Tviṣṭibha.
And Mādhava shall slay him in the form of a peacock.
Now hear from me, my son, about the sons of Manu Bhautya, the fourteenth.
Uru, Gabhīra, Dhṛṣṭa, Tarasvin, Grāha,
Abhimānin, Pravīra, Jiṣṇu, Saṃkrandana,
Tejasvin, and Durlabha— these were the sons of Manu Bhautya.
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Māgadha, Śuci,
Ajita, Mukta, and Śukra are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis).
The Cākṣuṣas, the Karmaniṣṭhas, the Pavitras, the Bhrājinas,
and the Vacovṛddhas— these five groups of seven gods have been proclaimed.
The pure Indra is the great Daitya; Hari himself is the slayer of enemies.
He is the one God who, through Viṣṇu in the form of Vyāsa, has indeed manifested fourfold.
Then he composed the Purāṇas and the eighteen branches of knowledge,
as well as the four Vedas with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive treatise on Nyāya.
The Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstra, Āyurveda, Arthaśāstra,
Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda— these indeed are the eighteen branches of knowledge.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Manu and His Lineage," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said:
Hari spoke of the Manvantaras to Brahmā and the others, and to Hara;
Mārkaṇḍeya spoke the hymn to the Pitṛs to Krauñcuki—listen to that. 1.88.1.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: In former times, the Prajāpati Ruci— free from possessiveness and egoism, fearless, and possessed of immeasurable power— wandered over this earth.
Seeing that sage who was without fire, without a dwelling, eating but once a day, and without a hermitage— freed from all attachments— his ancestors spoke to him.
The ancestors said:
"O child, why have you not performed the meritorious act of taking a wife, which is the cause of heaven and liberation?"
Because of intimacy, he was constantly bound by thieves, even without blinking.
A householder who performs the appropriate worship of all the gods, the ancestors,
the sages, and those in need, shall attain the worlds.
By the utterance of "svāhā," he distributes [the offering] to the gods; by the utterance of "svadhā," to the ancestors;
and by the giving of food, he provides for his servants and even for guests.
Therefore, O seer among men, you have by fate incurred this bondage from debts to the gods, as well as from debts to us, and from debts to all living beings day after day.
Without having procreated sons, without having satisfied the ancestors,
and without having performed the Māṇḍya rite, how do you wish to attain the path to heaven?
O son, through injustice, there can be only the awakening to afflictions for you;
having abandoned hell upon death, there will be only affliction in another birth.
Ruci said:
"Possession leads to extreme suffering, to sin, and likewise to a downward rebirth;
therefore, I did not previously take a wife."
A means for resolving one's own doubt is undertaken through momentary consultation;
yet even that does not become a cause for one's own liberation because of attachment to it.
That self which is free from possessions is washed day after day;
indeed, it is better for me that even though it is smeared with the mud of worldly existence, it be cleansed by the waters of knowledge.
The self, marked by the mud of karma accumulated through many births, should be washed by the wise with the waters of knowledge of reality, while their senses remain restrained.
The ancestors said:
"It is indeed proper for one who has restrained the senses to perform the purification of oneself;
however, this is not the path of means by which you, my son, are currently proceeding."
As you dispel your inauspiciousness through the five sacrifices, austerities,
and gifts performed without attachment to their fruits, so too do your previous auspicious and inauspicious karmas [come to an end].
Thus, for one who acts with the understanding that the cause is the Self, bondage does not occur;
nor does that action lead to bondage if it is not performed with excessive attachment.
O child, the karma performed in previous lives— consisting of both merit and demerit for human beings— is indeed exhausted incessantly through experiences composed of pleasure and pain.
In this way, the wise wash away the self and protect it from bondage;
guarded by their own discernment, they are not consumed by the mire of sin.
Ruci said:
"O Grandfathers, ignorance is cooked away in the Veda through the path of ritual action;
why then do you enjoin me to the path of action?"
The Pitṛs said:
"All this is indeed ignorance; this speech regarding action is false.
Nevertheless, there is no doubt that action is the cause for the attainment of knowledge."

That which is performed by the virtuous for the sake of avoiding the non-performance of what is prescribed is indeed restraint for the sake of liberation; any other kind of restraint, on the contrary, leads to a downward state of existence.
O Bhavānī, if you consider this to be better— that "I am washing [my sins]"—
then you too shall be consumed by the sins arising from the non-performance of what was ordained.
Even ignorance becomes beneficial for men, like poison, through the means of its practice; for it does not bind them, even though it is capable of doing so.
Therefore, my child, perform the ritual marriage according to the rules;
let your life from birth not be in vain, failing to attain that which is beyond this world.
Ruci said:
"I am now old; who will give me a wife? For a poor man, the acquisition of a wife is difficult."
The ancestors said:
"O child, our falling and your own descent into the lower realms will surely come to pass; you do not welcome our words."
Having spoken thus, O best of sages, his ancestors suddenly became invisible while he was looking on,
like lamps extinguished by the wind.
The sage Mārkaṇḍeya, of great asceticism, told Kraiñcukya the entire account of Ruci, characterized by his conversation with his father.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Knowledge of Ritual Actions," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: The *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 89.
Sūta said:
Being questioned again by him, Mārkaṇḍeya spoke to the Kraiñcikīnu;
his mind was deeply distressed by those words of his father.
Desiring a maiden, the brahmin-sage wandered the earth; failing to find a maiden and inflamed by his father’s command, he fell into deep anxiety,
his mind exceedingly distressed.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may my marriage be quickly accomplished so that it brings prosperity to my ancestors?"
As that great-souled one was reflecting thus, the thought arose in his mind:
"I shall propitiate this Brahmā, who is born from the lotus, through ascetic penance."
Then, for a hundred divine years, the high-minded one practiced austerities;
remaining there for a long time in the forests, established in his observances,
he then undertook supreme restraints for the sake of propitiation.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, revealed himself and said, "I am pleased; tell me what you desire."
Then, having prostrated before Brahmā, the refuge of the world, he spoke of what he desired to do at the word of the ancestors.
Brahmā said:
"You shall become a Prajāpati; you must create progeny.
O Brahmin, having created offspring and begotten sons, you must likewise establish the sacred rites."
Having performed your duties and thereby attained perfection, you must now,
as your ancestors have instructed, take a wife.
"Indeed, having meditated upon this desire, let the worship of the ancestors be performed;
for they alone, when satisfied, will grant you what you wish. When the grandfathers are content, what would they not give—wives and sons?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the Ṛṣi Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
he performed the libations for his ancestors on a secluded sandbank of the river.
Then the brahmin, becoming single-mindedly disciplined and with his neck bowed low in devotion, respectfully praised the ancestors with these hymns.
Ruci said:
"I pay homage with devotion to the ancestors who dwell as presiding deities,
for they are gratified even by the gods during the śrāddha rites with offerings preceded by the word *svadhā*."
I pay homage here to the ancestors in heaven who are gratified by the great seers with devotion through mental *śrāddha* rites, performed by those desiring both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I pay homage to the ancestors in heaven, whom the perfected ones (siddhas) satisfy at the ancestral rites (śrāddha) with all kinds of divine and unsurpassed offerings.
I pay homage with devotion to the ancestors who are worshipped in heaven by the Guhyakas, who,
through identification with them, attain supreme and ultimate prosperity.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always worshipped on earth by mortals with faith during śrāddha rites, and who bestow the nourishment of desired worlds.
I pay homage here to the ancestors who are always worshipped by Brahmins on earth,
who bestow the status of Prajāpati and grant the attainment of desired objects.

I pay homage to those ancestors who are indeed gratified by forest-dwellers— those whose sins have been washed away by austerity, who are restrained in diet, and who perform ancestral rites with forest-grown offerings.

I pay homage to the ancestors who are constantly gratified by means of meditative absorptions by Brahmins who are celibate lifelong students and practitioners of dharma, whose selves are ever-restrained.
I pay homage to the ancestors whom the Kṣatriyas satisfy with śrāddha offerings; they bestow the fruits of both worlds through all the various rites for the ancestors performed according to rule.
I pay homage to the ancestors who are always worshipped on earth by Vaiśyas,
who are constantly devoted to their own duties with flowers, incense, food, and water.
I pay homage here to the ancestors at the śrāddha ceremony, who are honored with devotion even by Śūdras;
known by the name Sukālins, they satisfy the entire world.
I pay homage here to the ancestors who, in the netherworld (pātāla), are always gratified by great asuras with food of nectar at the śrāddha ceremony, having forever abandoned deceit and pride.

I pay homage to the ancestors who are worshipped with śrāddha offerings in the netherworld (rasātala) by the nāgas, who, desiring all their wishes, honor them according to rule with every kind of enjoyment.
I pay homage here to the ancestors who are always fully gratified by the *śrāddha* offerings,
right there according to the rules, accompanied by the enjoyment of mantras and all forms of prosperity.

I bow to the ancestors who dwell visibly in the world of the gods, on the surface of the earth, or likewise in the intermediate space—those who are worshipped by the enemies of the gods; may they indeed accept what is offered by me.
I bow to the ancestors who are the supreme reality, who dwell in formless celestial chariots,
whom the lords of yogis worship with minds free from impurity as the cause for liberation from afflictions.
I bow to the ancestors who dwell in heaven in embodied form, who partake of the *svadhā* offering when there is an intention for desired fruits,
who are capable of bestowing all things wished for, and who grant liberation when no such intentions are held.
May all those ancestors be satisfied in this [offering], they who grant the desires of those who wish;
whether it be the state of a god, the state of Indra, or even more than that, or elephants, horses, jewels, and great mansions.
May those ancestors who always dwell in the rays of the moon, in the orb of the sun, and in the white celestial chariot,
be satisfied in this rite with food and water, and may they attain nourishment through perfumes and other offerings.
May those ancestors who find satisfaction through the oblation poured into the fire, who eat while residing within the bodies of Brahmins,
and who attain joy through the offering of funeral cakes— may they be satisfied by this food and water.
May those who were fully gratified by the gods with the meat of rhinoceros, by the most desired black sesame seeds that are divine and enchanting,
and by the best of great sages with black vegetables, attain joy here.
And may all the poetic compositions that are most dear to you, which have been honored by me,
be present here within these flowers, perfumes, water, and food offerings prepared by me.

May those ancestors of mine who are honored day by day with offerings, those who are worshiped on earth during the Aṣṭaka festivals at the end of the month, and those who are honored at the end of the year and on auspicious occasions, attain satisfaction here.
Those who shine like the moon and white water-lilies are to be honored among the twice-born; those with the hue of fire and the sun among the kṣatriyas;
likewise, those as bright as gold among the vaiśyas; and those with the luster of indigo among the śūdra folk.

All of them together find satisfaction in this world through my offering of flowers, perfumes, incense, water, food, and the like, as well as by the fire-sacrifice (agnihotra); I bow forever to those ancestors.

Those who, having been gods in former lives, eat the auspicious *kavya* offerings brought for the sake of their complete satisfaction, and who, being satisfied, become the creators of prosperity—may they be satisfied; I bow down to them.
May the *rakṣasas*, spirits, and fierce asuras likewise destroy the inauspiciousness of living beings;
may those primordial ones of the gods, worthy of worship by the Lord of the Immortals, be satisfied in this [rite], for I bow down before them.
May the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Ājyapa,
and Somapa ancestors, thus gratified by me in this śrāddha, attain satisfaction.

May the groups of ancestors known as the Agniṣvātta protect my eastern direction; likewise, may the Barhiṣad ancestors always protect my southern direction. Similarly, may the Ājyapa protect the western, and the Somapa protect the northern direction as well.
May the ancestors always provide protection for me from all sides against Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and likewise from the malice of Asuras.
Viśva, Viśvabhuj, Ārādhya, Dharma, Dhanya, Śubhānana,
Bhūtida, Bhūtikṛt, and Bhūti— these are the nine hosts of the ancestors.
The Auspicious One, the Bestower of Welfare, the Doer, the Healthy One, the Abode of Greater Health,
and the Cause of Healthiness— these six are remembered as his attendants.
Vara, Vareṇya, Varada, Tuṣṭida, Puṣṭida,
Viśvapātṛ, and Dhātṛ— these seven are remembered as the Gaṇas.
The Great One, the High-Souled One, the Honored One, the Possessor of Greatness, and the One of Great Strength—
these five classes of ancestors are likewise destroyers of sin.
One is the giver of happiness, another the giver of wealth, another the giver of dharma, and yet another the giver of prosperity;
thus is the fourfold group of ancestors described.
May those thirty-one classes of ancestors, by whom the entire world is pervaded,
be satisfied here with what has been offered by me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
As he was thus offering praise, a towering mass of splendor suddenly appeared, pervading the entire sky.

Seeing that immense radiance standing there, having completely enveloped the world, Ruci knelt upon the earth and sang this hymn of praise: GarP_1,89.50: "Having seen that immense radiance standing there, having completely enveloped the world, Ruci knelt upon the earth and sang this hymn of praise."
Ruci said:
I always pay homage to those ancestors who are honored, formless, of blazing splendor, meditative, and possessed of divine vision.
I bow to those bestowers of desires, who are the leaders of Indra and the others, as well as of Dakṣa and Mārīci, and likewise of the seven ṛṣis and other beings. GarP_1,89.52
I bow to all those leaders of Manu and the others, as well as the leaders of the sun and the moon, and even to the ancestors within the ocean.
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the constellations and the planets, as well as to wind and fire, the sky, and heaven and earth.
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to Prajāpati, Kaśyapa, Soma, Varuṇa, and the Lords of Yoga.
Homage to the seven Gaṇas likewise in the seven worlds;
I pay homage to Brahmā, the self-born, who possesses the eye of yoga.
I likewise bow to the hosts of ancestors who have Soma as their support and who bear forms of yoga, and to Soma, the father of the worlds.
Likewise, I pay homage to those other ancestors who have the form of fire,
since this entire universe consists entirely of fire and moon.
Those who are in fire, and those who are the embodiments of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni,
as well as those whose nature is the world and likewise whose nature is Brahman.
To all those yogis, my ancestors, with a restrained mind: salutations again and again; may you, who partake of the *svadhā* offering, be gracious.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus praised by him, those best of sages,
the Pitṛs, then emerged, illuminating the ten directions with their splendor.
And he saw them standing before him, adorned with the offerings of flowers, perfumes, and ointments that had been presented to him.
Having prostrated with radiant devotion and once again joining his palms in reverence, Ruci spoke, honoring him individually: "Homage to you! Homage to you! (GarP 1.89.63).
Then the gratified ancestors said to that best of sages,
"Choose a boon," and he, with his neck bowed, spoke to them.
Ruci said:
"The creation of progeny has been commanded to me by Brahmā;
therefore, I desire a blessed, divine wife who will bear me offspring."
The ancestors said:
"Right here, let your most enchanting wife appear instantly;
and from her, O best of sages, a son shall be born to you."
O Ruci, this wise lord of the Manvantara, distinguished by your very name,
shall attain renown throughout the three worlds as Raucya.
He too shall have many sons of great strength and prowess,
high-souled protectors of the earth.
And you, having become Prajāpati and created the fourfold progeny,
shall— once your office has expired and you have known the Dharma— thereafter attain perfection.
And for that person who shall satisfy us with devotion by means of this hymn,
we, being pleased, shall grant enjoyments and supreme meditation, O son.
Therefore, those who desire long life, health, wealth, as well as sons, grandsons, and so forth, should constantly praise [the deities] with this hymn.
He who, standing before the foremost of the twice-born while they are eating at a *śrāddha*, shall recite with devotion this hymn that brings us pleasure— 89.72.
When our supreme presence has been established through the joy of hearing this hymn of praise,
that śrāddha will undoubtedly become inexhaustible for us.
Even if a śrāddha is performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, or if it should be defiled, or if it is performed with wealth acquired through unjust means, or otherwise improperly; 89.74.

Even if offerings are presented by those unworthy of faith, or if they are prepared in such a manner, or even at an improper time or place, or if they are devoid of the prescribed ritual rules; GarP_1,89.75.
Even if a funeral rite (śrāddha) is performed by men out of lack of faith, relying instead on hypocrisy,
it nevertheless serves for our satisfaction through the mere recitation of this [text].
Wherever this hymn, which brings happiness, is recited at a śrāddha ceremony,
our satisfaction there lasts for twelve years.
This auspicious hymn bestows satisfaction for twelve years during the winter season,
and for double that number of years during the cool season.
In the spring, sixteen [recitations] at the time of the śrāddha rite lead to satisfaction;
likewise, sixteen in the summer—this is declared to be the cause of satisfaction.
Even when the śrāddha is performed incompletely, if it is perfected by means of this hymn,
O Ruci, our satisfaction becomes inexhaustible during the rainy season.
Even if recited during the autumn season, it provides for us, through these men, satisfaction lasting for fifteen years when offered at the time of a funeral rite (śrāddha).
In whichever house this remains written at all times,
our presence shall be there whenever a śrāddha is performed.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, this should be recited by you in front of the Brahmins while they are eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha); it brings about prosperity for us.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Ancestors Composed by Ruci," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 90. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, from the middle of that river, there rose up the beautiful and slender-limbed celestial nymph named Pramlocā, who stood near him.
And that supreme Apsaras, Pramlocā, spoke to the high-souled Ruci with very sweet syllables, seeking to propitiate him once more.
An exceedingly beautiful maiden, a woman blessed by my grace,
was born from the high-souled Puṣkara, the son of Varuṇa.
"Accept this woman of excellent complexion, given by me as your wife;
from her, O high-minded one, a son named Manu shall be born to you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"So be it," he replied; then, from that water, he drew forth a beautiful-bodied maiden known by the name Māninī.
And on that riverbank, O best of sages,
that great sage, having brought her there, took her hand according to the prescribed rites.

From her was born his son, possessed of great heroism and great splendor. Sūta said: [Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 91] The son of that [king] was born, endowed with great prowess and great luster. The sages beginning with Svāyambhuva meditate upon Hari through their actions,
being devoted to vows, conduct, worship, meditation, praise, and the chanting of prayers.
It is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego;
it is indeed bereft of space and entirely free from fire.
Indeed, it is devoid of water, abandoned by the Dharma,
deprived of earth, and forsaken by all living beings.
The presiding lord of the elements, likewise the bound controller, the sovereign and all-pervading,
whose form is the nature of consciousness, the overseer of all, and the stainless one.
He is the Great Lord, free from attachment, worshipped by all the gods;
he is the embodiment of splendor, yet devoid of material substance and divested of the quality of passion.
It is eternally free from passion (rajas), distinct from the three qualities (guṇas),
devoid of all forms, and indeed bereft of agency and other such attributes.
It is free from latent impressions, pure, devoid of all defects,
exempt from thirst, and free from that very desire and delusion.
Indeed, it is devoid of old age and death, immovable, free from delusion,
without origin, and entirely devoid of dissolution.
Truth is the Supreme Lord, devoid of all conduct, partless,
free from the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and beyond all names.
The Lord of the gods, whose nature is peace, is the presiding witness over waking and the other states;
he eternally abides in waking and the rest, free from cause and effect.
Thus, he is seen by all; he is embodied, subtle, more subtle than the subtle, supreme;
he is the vision of knowledge, the consciousness of hearing, whose nature is supreme bliss.
Likewise, that which is devoid of the Viśva, free from the Taijasa,
and indeed devoid of the Prājña, is the Fourth (Turīya), the supreme imperishable.
The all-protector, the destroyer of all, whose form is the self of all beings,
indeed devoid of the qualities of the intellect, without support— Śiva, Hari.
It is indeed free from modification, that which is to be known through the Vedāntas,
the supreme being whose form is the Veda, beyond the senses, and auspicious.
The God is devoid of sound and likewise free from taste; He is bereft of touch and devoid of mere form.
Devoid of form and entirely free from smell,
beginningless Brahman extending to the end of the apertures— I am that absolute Brahman alone.
Having understood this, one who has conquered the senses should practice meditation upon Mahādeva;
for that person who practices meditation in this way shall become a human being who is Brahman.
Thus has the meditation of Aśvinī been fully described by me to you.
Now I shall speak of something else; tell me what it is, O Bull-bannered One.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "Meditation on Hari," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 92 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Rudra said:
O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, speak again of the meditation on Viṣṇu,
by the mere knowledge of which a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Hari said:
"I shall explain the meditation on Hari, which destroys the web of Māyā.
O Hara, that meditation is of two kinds, according to the distinction between the embodied and the unembodied."
O Rudra, the formless has been described; now, alas, I shall speak of the formed:
resembling ten million suns, victorious and resplendent in every way.
Hari, white as a jasmine flower or cow’s milk, should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation;
he is endowed with a large and very beautiful conch shell.
Endowed with a discus possessing a fierce mass of flames equal to a thousand suns, he was peaceful, holding a mace in his hand, and possessed a beautiful countenance.
Wearing a highly precious crown blazing with jewels,
the omnipresent God, bearing weapons and holding a lotus, likewise appeared.
Wearing a forest garland, radiant, with symmetrical shoulders and golden ornaments,
well-clothed, pure of body, with beautiful ears, he is seated upon a lotus.
His body was golden, adorned with beautiful necklaces and auspicious armlets;
he was equipped with bracelets and endowed with a forest garland.
Endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, accompanied by Lakṣmī and the lotus-eyed one,
possessed of qualities such as the absence of pride (amimāda) and others, he is the agent of creation and destruction.
He is the object of meditation for sages, for asuras, and for gods; he is exceedingly beautiful, and dwells within the hearts of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
The eternal, undecaying, pure Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Great God who bestows grace upon all, was shimmering with crocodile-shaped earrings.
The destroyer of torment, worthy of worship, auspicious, the destroyer of the wicked;
the soul of all, possessing all forms, omnipresent, and the destroyer of the planetary influences.
Adorned with beautiful finger-rings and possessing brilliantly shining nails,
he is the refuge for all, the bringer of happiness, and Maheśvara of gentle form.
Adorned with every ornament and anointed with beautiful sandalwood paste,
he is accompanied by all the gods and brings joy to all the gods.
He desires the welfare of all the world; he is the Lord of all, the creator of all;
he resides within the solar disc, or within fire, or situated within water.
Vāsudeva, the sustainer of the world, Viṣṇu, is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation;
one should meditate on Hari, the Lord, as the Self, thinking, "I am Vāsudeva."
And those who meditate thus upon Viṣṇu attain the supreme goal;
for in ancient times, Yājñavalkya, having meditated in this way upon Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods, [attained liberation].
Having attained the state of being a teacher of the Dharma, he went to the supreme station;
therefore, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods, you too should meditate upon Viṣṇu.
Whoever recites this meditation on Viṣṇu attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "Meditation on Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 93.
Maheśvara said:
O Slayer of Keśin, O Mādhava, tell me truly how that Dharma which was previously proclaimed by Yājñavalkya may be practiced, O Hari.
Hari said:
Having approached Yājñavalkya, who was residing in Mithilā,
the sages paid him homage and questioned him exhaustively regarding the duties of the social classes and other matters.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu, he who had conquered his senses spoke to them.
Yājñavalkya said:
In that land where the black antelope roams, learn from me the laws,
together with the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences.
The Vedas are the fourteen repositories of knowledge and of Dharma;
the exponents of the Dharmaśāstras are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, and Aṅgiras.
Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, Parāśara,
Āpastamba, Uśanas, Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati.
Gautama, Śaṅkha-Likhita, Hārīta, Atri, and likewise I—
these, having propitiated Viṣṇu, became teachers of Dharma.
Whatever substance, endowed with faith, is given to a worthy recipient at the proper place and time by means of the right method— all that possesses the defining characteristic of Dharma.
Sacrificial rites, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the practice of Vedic study—this is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga.

An assembly of four who know the Vedic dharma, or even one consisting of those learned in the three Vedas—whatever such an assembly declares shall be one's own duty; or else, a single person who is the most excellent among those who know the inner self.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are the castes; however, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with those at the cremation ground are indeed performed with mantras.

The rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) occurs during the fertile period; the rite of male-conception (*pumsavana*) before the fetus moves; the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) in the sixth or eighth month; and the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) upon delivery.
On the eleventh day [after birth], the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month, the first outing;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food; and one should perform the tonsure ceremony according to family custom.
In this way, the sin arising from the seed and the womb is pacified;
these rites for women are to be performed silently, except for the marriage ceremony, which is accompanied by mantras.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Castes as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Yājñavalkya said:

The initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [of age]; for a Kṣatriya, in the eleventh; and for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth—or according to some, according to family custom.
Having initiated his disciple with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) at the beginning,
Kuru should teach him the Veda and instruct him in the rules of purity and conduct.
During the day and at the twilights, one should void urine and feces with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) placed over the ear while facing north; however, if it is at night, one should face south.
Having risen with his penis still held,
the one who observes the great vow should perform purification that removes both odor and residue, using earth and water drawn from a source.
With his knees joined together, seated in a clean place facing north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
The bases of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand,
are respectively the *prajāpati*, *pitṛ*, *brahman*, and *daivata* tirthas.
Having sipped water three times and wiped the mouth twice,
one should touch the sense-organ openings with water that is natural, free from impurities, and devoid of foam and bubbles.
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; women and Śūdras are purified by water merely touching the lips once.
Bathing with mantras dedicated to the water-deities, sprinkling [the body], the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma),
the worship of the Sun, and the recitation of the Gāyatrī with full conviction.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras, preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Praṇava; this is the threefold regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).
Having restrained his breath and sprinkled himself with water using the three verses addressed to the Waters,
he should sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the stars rise in the west.
One should thus remain standing during the morning twilight until the sun appears;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-ritual at both twilights.
Then he should salute the elders, saying, "I am so-and-so," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study.
When summoned, he should study and report everything to him;
he should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, a sacred thread, and a girdle;
he should go about for alms among blameless Brahmins for the sake of his own livelihood.
The practice of begging for alms by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should be characterized by desire at its beginning, middle, and end, respectively.
Having performed the fire-ritual, he should eat with humility, by the permission of his guru,
preceded by the *āpośāna* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it.

Established in the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), a Brahmin shall not eat food from a single source except in times of distress; however, he may eat at a *śrāddha* feast as much as he desires, provided he does not violate his vow.
One should avoid honey, meat, and likewise food that has been cooked [the previous day], and so forth.
He is a guru who, having performed the prescribed rites, imparts the Veda to him.
"He who initiates him and gives him [instruction] is proclaimed as the Ācārya;
he who teaches a single portion is the Upādhyāya, and he who performs the sacrifice is called the Ṛtvij."
These are to be honored according to their seniority, yet the mother is more venerable than them all.
For each Veda, the period of celibate studentship (brahmacarya) shall be twelve years or five.
Some say it lasts until the time of initiation; others say until the tonsure ceremony in the sixteenth year, or until the sixteenth, twenty-second, or twenty-fourth year.
The ultimate time limit for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas has passed;
beyond this, these individuals fall, being deprived of all religious duties.
Those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī and become Vrātyas cannot be purified except by the Vrātyastoma sacrifice;
for they undergo a second binding with the girdle of muñja grass before their mother.
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are these twice-born ones;
[they are the rightful performers] of sacrifices, of austerities, and of auspicious deeds.
The Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good for the twice-born;
with honey and milk, the twice-born man should satisfy the gods.
He should daily recite the Rigvedic verses for the ancestors with honey and ghee;
likewise, the twice-born man should recite the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvāṅgirasa.
He indeed gratifies the ancestors and the gods daily with clarified butter and nectar,
as well as with dialogues, Purāṇas, Nārāśaṃsī verses, and songs.
He who daily studies the Itihāsas and the sciences according to his ability satisfies the ancestors and the gods with meat, milk, rice, and other offerings.
Satiated themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires;
whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain its fruit.
A twice-born man who has completed his vow becomes a sharer in the fruits of the gift of land and of austerity through Vedic study;
however, a lifelong celibate student shall dwell in the presence of his teacher.

In the absence of these, one who has conquered the senses should, by this same rite, effect the [destruction] of the body in his son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire. He attains the world of Brahmā and is not born again in this world.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Castes as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Śrī-Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī-Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 95:
Yājñavalkya said:
"O sages of firm vows, listen to the duties of the householder;
having given wealth to the preceptor and bathed with his permission," (GarP 1.95.1).

Having completed the religious life of celibacy, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks— one who has belonged to no other man before, who is pleasing, not a sapinda relative, and younger than himself.
One who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same ṛṣi-lineage or gotra;
likewise, she who is beyond the fifth degree on the mother's side and the seventh degree on the father's side.
A bridegroom who is of the same caste, learned in the Vedas, wise, free from defects, and renowned for ten generations within a great family of Vedic scholars; GarP_1,95.4 //
As for what is said regarding the taking of a Śūdra wife by the twice-born,
that is not my opinion, because in such a case, he himself is born from her.
Three wives in the order of the castes, likewise two, and one respectively, are the lawful wives for the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya; for one born as a Śūdra, she alone is his own.
The Brāhma marriage consists of giving away a girl, adorned according to one's means, after having invited [the groom];
the son born of that union purifies twenty-one persons on both sides.
Having received the divine [gift] from the officiating priest at the sacrifice, the Ārṣa [gift] consists of a pair of cows;
the first-born [son] purifies fourteen generations, and the one born later purifies six.
Having said this, that body born from [the merit of] giving to a seeker while practicing dharma together shall purify six generations of one's lineage along with oneself.
The Āsura [form] is from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden.
The first four [forms of marriage] are for a Brāhmaṇa; likewise, the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa for a Kṣatriya; the Āsura for a Vaiśya; and the last one is censured for a Śūdra.

The hand should be taken in marriage from women of the same caste; a Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow, and a Vaiśya woman should take up a goad during the wedding of one born of the first two castes.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother—
each subsequent one among these gives the daughter in marriage upon the failure of each preceding, provided they are in their natural state.
By not giving her away during her fertile seasons, one incurs the guilt of killing an embryo;
in the absence of such givers, the maiden may choose her own husband.
A maiden is given only once; he who takes her away incurs the punishment of a thief.
One who abandons an unblemished wife is liable to punishment, but one may abandon a wife who is extremely corrupt.
If a woman is childless, her brother-in-law,
a kinsman (sapiṇḍa), or one of equal lineage (samānodaka), having been consecrated with clarified butter, may approach her during her fertile period with the intention of obtaining a son.
One should proceed until the conception of a fetus occurs; otherwise, one would become fallen.
By this procedure, the son born shall belong to the owner of the field.
One should cause the unfaithful wife to dwell deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms-food,
humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
Soma gave them purity, and the Gandharva gave them melodious speech;
Agni gave them complete fitness for sacrifice, since women are indeed sacrificially pure.

If there is infidelity during the fertile period, purification occurs through menstruation; however, they must undergo abandonment of the fetus, as well as in cases of killing the fetus or the husband, and likewise for other great sins.

Even a woman who drinks liquor, is diseased, hateful, barren, wasteful of wealth, or speaks unpleasantly, as well as one superseded by a co-wife, must be maintained; otherwise, there would be a great loss of merit.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish;
she who, whether her husband is dead or living, does not approach another man [is a true wife].
Through this, he attains fame and rejoices with Umā;
abandoning a pure woman, he should provide for her a third share until his death.
The word of the husband must be carried out by women; this is the supreme duty of a woman.
Of the sixteen nights of a woman's fertile period, she should approach her husband on those that are even-numbered.

A celibate student (*brahmacārī*) should avoid the sacred days (*parvan*), as well as the first three nights; likewise, when approaching his wife, he should avoid her when she is emaciated, and avoid the constellations Maghā and Mūla.
One who possesses self-control, recollecting the power of women, shall surely procreate a son endowed with auspicious marks and free from disease, or he may act according to his desire.
One should be devoted solely to one's own wife, for women must be protected from all sides by the husband,
brothers, father, kinsmen, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and brothers-in-law.
Women should be honored by their kinsmen with ornaments, clothing, and food;
they should keep the household utensils in order, be skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure.
She should always perform prostration at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law;
she should avoid play, bodily adornment, social gatherings, festivals, and looking at herself in a mirror.
A woman whose husband has been sent away should avoid laughter and traveling to the houses of others;
her father should protect her in childhood, and her husband alone in youth.
In old age, the son protects her, and otherwise, her kinsmen do so;
she should not remain without her husband, whether by day or by night.
In the performance of religious rites, one should employ the eldest wife and never the youngest;
a husband should cremate a virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire.
She should take a wife and establish the sacred fire according to the prescribed rules without delay;
having attained fame in this world, she shall go to heaven for the benefit of her husband.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Duties of a Householder as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter Ninety-six of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Yājñavalkya said:

I shall now declare the supreme rules concerning those born of mixed castes and others, such as householders; for from a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Mūrdhāvasikta, and from a Vaiśya woman, a Viṭ.
One born of a Śūdra woman from an Ambaṣṭha is a Niṣāda or a Parvata;
one born of a Vaiśya woman from a Kṣatriya is a Māhiṣya, designated as a Mleccha.
From a Vaiśya father on a Śūdra mother, a Karaṇa is born; this is the rule recorded for women married to men of different castes.
From a Kṣatriya father on a Brāhmaṇī mother, a Sūta is born, and likewise from a Vaiśya father, a Vaidehaka.
But from a Śūdra is born a Cāṇḍāla, who is despised by all castes;
from a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya woman bears a Māgadha, and a Śūdra woman bears a Kṣattṛ.
A Vaiśya woman indeed gave birth to a son, the Āyogava, by a Śūdra; and from a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, the Rathakāra is born.
Those born from the inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) orders should indeed be known as non-existent and existent [respectively].
Through the excellence of birth, one is to be known as a twice-born (dvija) in the seventh or even the fifth generation.
Upon the reversal of actions, there is equilibrium as before, with the higher and lower states;
the householder should perform the rites prescribed by the Smṛtis every day in the marriage fire.

Or even apart from the time of giving, having performed the funeral rites for the body in the Vedic sacrificial fires, the twice-born man, having completed the rules of purification, [should proceed].
One should perform the morning twilight devotion preceded by the cleansing of the teeth;
having offered oblations into the fire, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras dedicated to all the deities.
A householder should master the meaning of the Vedas and various treatises,
and he should approach the Lord for the sake of attaining success in yoga, protection, and other such goals.
Having bathed, he should likewise gratify and worship the gods and the ancestors,
as well as the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas, according to his ability.
For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should recite the spiritual knowledge (vidyā) pertaining to the self;
[one should also perform] the rites of bali, svadhā, oblations (homa), Vedic study (svādhyāya), and hospitality toward guests.
One should perform great sacrifices for the spirits, ancestors, gods, Brahmā, and humans;
one should cast what has been offered into the fire for the deities and present the bali-offering to the spirits.
One should scatter food on the ground for dogs, outcasts, and crows;
food should be given daily to the ancestors and to human beings, as well as water.
One should perform one's daily recitation every day and should not cook food for oneself alone;
[one should provide for] children, women living in the father's house, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, and young girls.
Having fed his guests and dependents, he should eat the remnants of the meal with his wife according to the rite of the Prāṇāgnihotra, consuming the food without disparaging it.
One should eat food that is measured, ripened, beneficial, and prepared with the first portion for children and others;
it should be consumed both before and after with the *āpośāna* rite.
A twice-born man should prepare food that is both unblemished and immortal;
he should give it to guests and to people of the various castes according to his ability and in due order.
A guest is not to be turned away even in the evening; there is no doubt about this. Alms should be given with respect to a mendicant who observes virtuous vows.
One should feed all those who have arrived, and a great bull to a *śrotriya*.
However, every year, the *snātaka*, the teacher, and the king are to be honored.
Likewise, one's beloved, a bridegroom, and the officiating priests at a sacrifice;
furthermore, a traveler is declared to be a guest, as is a Śrotriya who has mastered the Vedas.
These two are worthy of honor for a householder who desires the world of Brahmā;
he should not take pleasure in food prepared by others, except when invited by those whose conduct is blameless.
One should avoid restlessness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating;
and one should follow a learned guest (śrotriya) as far as the boundary of the village once he has been satisfied.
One should spend the remainder of the day with learned men, beloved ones, and kinsmen;
then, having performed the evening twilight devotions and offered oblations into the fire, one may take food.
One should act together with devoted servants and contemplate one's own welfare;
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should honor a Brahmin with wealth and other offerings.
The path must indeed be yielded to the elderly, the afflicted, and those carrying heavy loads;
sacrifice, study, and giving are the duties of both the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya.
Receiving gifts is the additional duty for a Brahmin, as are officiating at sacrifices and teaching;
for a Kṣatriya, however, the primary duty is the protection of the subjects.
Agriculture, trade, commerce, and cattle-rearing are prescribed for the Vaiśyas;
service to the twice-born is prescribed for the Śūdra. A twice-born man should not neglect his sacrifices.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
self-control, forbearance, straightforwardness, and generosity are the means for the practice of dharma for all.
One should practice a conduct that is consistent, straightforward, and free from deceit;
he who possesses more than a three-year supply of food is worthy to drink the Soma.
One whose food supply lasts for a year may perform the rites pertaining to the *Prakṛta* and *Saumika* sacrifices;
likewise, the Soma sacrifice may be performed every year, as may the animal sacrifice at each solstice.
The *Agrayaneṣṭi* and the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices should be performed with diligence;
if these are impossible, the twice-born man should perform the *Vaiśvānarī* sacrifice.
One should not perform a deficient rite when the necessary materials are available, for it yields no fruit;
by performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra, one is born as a Caṇḍāla.
One should not take what is obtained for the sake of sacrifice; otherwise, one might become a vulture or even a crow.
One may possess grain in a granary or a jar, or have enough for three days, or perhaps only for tomorrow.
Or he may live by gleaning ears of grain; each subsequent mode among these is superior.
He should not strive for wealth that conflicts with his Vedic study, nor from whatever source it may come.
One who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from kings, pupils, or those for whom he performs sacrifices;
however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, motivated by selfish motives, heretics, and those who act like herons.
Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails kept short, and remaining pure,
he should not eat while his wife is looking on, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing.
One who has mastered the Veda should never speak unpleasantly;
being disciplined, he should carry a staff and a water-pot, and perform circumambulations of the gods.
But one should not urinate in a river, in the shade, in ashes, in a cow-pen, in water, or on a path;
nor should one face fire, the sun, cows, the moon, the twilight, water, women, or the twice-born.
One should not look at fire, the sun, or a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse;
nor should one void urine or feces, nor sleep with the head toward the west.
One should not cast spittle, blood, feces, urine, or poison into water;
