one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step across it.
One should not drink water from one's cupped hands, nor should one awaken a sleeping person;
one should not play with dice against gamblers, nor should one lie down with those who are diseased.
One should avoid forbidden acts, the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river [by swimming],
and staying upon hair, ashes, chaff, embers, or skull-bones.
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter through any place other than the gate;
one should not accept gifts from a king who is greedy and who acts contrary to the scriptures.
The commencement of the study of the chapters (adhyāya-upākarma) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇā,
or under the asterism Hasta when the medicinal herbs appear, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the day of Rohiṇī in the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
one should perform the formal dismissal of the Vedas (chandasām utsarga) outside, near water, according to the prescribed rule.
There is a three-day suspension of study upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative;
likewise upon the commencement (upākarma) and the conclusion (utsarga) of the Vedic term, and when a scholar of one's own Vedic branch has died.
In the event of thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor,
one should complete the Veda and likewise study the Āraṇyaka for a full day and night.
On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, or the eighth day; during an eclipse of Rāhu;
on the junctions of the seasons; or after eating, or having accepted food offered at a śrāddha ceremony.
When the interval is filled by cattle, frogs, mongooses, dogs, snakes, cats, and pigs, that constitutes a day and night; likewise for the descent and the ascent of Śakra.
When there is the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, or the chanting of the Sāman;
or when one is near impure substances, a corpse, a Śūdra, an outcaste, a cemetery, or someone who has fallen from their status.
In an impure place, or when one is oneself impure; during a downpour of lightning and thunder;
after eating while the hands are still wet; inside water; at midnight; or during an excessive windstorm.
During a lightning strike, when there is a rain of dust, at the terrifying sight of a meteor shower at twilight,
when running, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at one's house.
Traveling in a donkey-cart or camel-cart, riding an elephant, horse, or boat, or climbing a tree or a mountain—
these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interdictions for study.
One should not step over a Veda-reciter, nor one's teacher, nor the shadow of a king, nor another's wife, nor blood, excrement, urine, spittle, or the remains of unguents.
Brahmins and those whose nature is that of Kṣatriyas should never be treated with contempt;
one should discard remnants of food, excrement, urine, and water from the feet from afar.
One should follow the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; one should not touch another's vital points (marmans).
One should not engage in censure or physical punishment, yet one may strike a son or a disciple.
A householder should always practice righteousness and never act contrary to it;
he should not engage in disputes with his mother, father, guests, or wealthy persons.
One should not bathe in the waters of others without first removing five lumps [of earth];
however, one may bathe in rivers, springs, divine pools, and lakes.

One should avoid the beds and other belongings of others, and one should not eat [the food] of a miser, a prisoner, an enemy, or one who does not maintain the sacred fires, except in times of distress.
[One should not eat the food] of flute-makers, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, those initiated into a group,
physicians, the sick, the angry, the impotent, and those who live by the stage.

[One should avoid] those who are cruel, fierce, fallen, or outcaste; those who are hypocritical or eat the leavings of others; those who sell the scriptures, as well as those who are ruled by women or who perform sacrifices for an entire village.
[One must avoid] cruel people, kings, dyers, ungrateful persons, those who live by killing,
flatterers, liars, and likewise sellers of Soma.
One should never eat the food of bards or goldsmiths, nor meat that has been prepared in vain, nor food containing hair or insects. (GarP 1.96.64)
One should avoid food that is stale, leftover, touched by a dog, defiled by a fallen person, touched by a woman in her courses, publicly proclaimed [for sale], or insufficient.
Food smelled by a cow, the leavings of birds, or that which has been intentionally touched by the foot;
and among Śūdras, those who are slaves, cowherds, family friends, or sharecroppers [are permitted].
Food may be eaten from a barber and even from one who offers himself [as a servant];
food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or has been kept for a long time.
One should also avoid preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk that are not oily, as well as the milk of camels, one-hoofed animals, and women.
One should avoid the flesh of carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, and the parrot; as well as the cranes, single-hoofed animals, swans, balākas, cranes, and ṭiṭṭibhas.
One should avoid eating kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, and fried pastries in vain,
as well as the curlew, web-footed birds, wagtails, and wild animals or birds.
Having intentionally eaten a blue jay, a fish, or a blood-footed bird, or having intentionally eaten dried meat, a man shall observe a fast for three days.
Having eaten onions, garlic, and the like, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
however, eating meat after having worshipped the gods and ancestors at a Śrāddha ceremony entails no fault.

That person of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rules shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal's body; having abandoned meat and attained his desires through prayer, he then goes to Hari.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrāddha as Taught by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 97] Yājñavalkya said:
I shall proclaim the purification of substances; listen to that, O most excellent ones:
[the purification] of gold, silver, and lotuses, as well as of conch-shells, ropes, leather, and so forth.
The purification of vessels and seats is prescribed with water;
that of the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles with hot water, and that of grain and other such items by sprinkling.
By planing wood, horn, and the like,
and by scrubbing sacrificial vessels with warm water and cow urine, woolen and silken cloths are purified.
One who gazes at the face of a woman while eating alms-food, or food that has been cooked again, or food made of earth,
or food defiled by hair, flies, or insects, likewise destroys his cows.
Purification occurs by throwing ashes; the purification of the ground is by sweeping and so forth;
[the purification] of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, and water.
Iron and bronze are always pure when unknown; they are purified by ashes and water.
That which has been smeared with impurities is cleansed by earth and water once the odor and the stain have been removed.
Water on the earth that is naturally pure, which satisfies the cattle, is likewise [pure]; so too is meat fallen from dogs, *caṇḍālas*, carnivorous beasts, and the like.
A ray of light, fire, dust, a shadow, a bull, a horse, the earth, and the winds;
the droplets from a horse or a goat, as well as drops from sipping water, are pure.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road,
and after putting on another garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
After sneezing, spitting, sleeping, putting on a garment, or shedding tears—in these five instances one should not sip water for purification; instead, one should touch the right ear.
For the gods, beginning with Agni, reside in the right ear of the Brahmin.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Purification of Substances as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Yājñavalkya said:
Now I shall declare the rules for giving; listen to me, O you of excellent vows!
Among others, the Brāhmaṇas are superior, and among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior still.
One should know that even among those [ascetics], the knower of Brahman who is endowed with austerity is the most worthy recipient;
cows, land, grain, gold, and so forth should be given with reverence to such a worthy recipient.
One who is devoid of both learning and austerity must not accept gifts;
by accepting them, he leads both the giver and himself downward.
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions;
even when requested, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith.
A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, well-behaved, covered with a cloth,
accompanied by a bronze vessel and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given as a gift.
The horn [of the calf] is made of ten suvarṇas, the hoof of seven palas,
and the bronze vessel for the calf is declared to be fifty palas in weight.
With a golden pippala-leaf vessel, either a male calf or even a female calf should be given;
and her offspring shall also be granted, free from disease.
The donor attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on the stone;
moreover, if it is made of *kāśīlā*, he delivers his lineage up to the seventh generation.
As long as two feet and the face of the calf are visible at the birth canal,
for that long the cow should be known as the Earth, until she releases the fetus.
Having given a cow for milking or even one that does not yield milk, in any manner whatsoever—
provided it is healthy and not afflicted— the donor is glorified in heaven.
Massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods,
washing the feet of others, and clearing away the remnants of food from twice-born men are equal to the gift of a cow.
By giving whatever is desired to a twice-born man, one attains heaven;
by giving land, lamps, food, clothing, and clarified butter, one shall go to the abode of Śrī.
By giving a house, grain, an umbrella, a garland, a tree, a vehicle, clarified butter, water,
a bed, and ointment, one is honored in the heavenly world.
The giver of the Veda attains the world of Brahmā, which is difficult even for the gods to reach;
for he has indeed bestowed the Vedas, their meanings, the sacrificial scriptures, and the treatises on Dharma.
Even by having it written down for a price, one may attain the world of Brahmā;
for the Lord created this as the root of the universe in the beginning.
Therefore, with every effort, one should compile a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas;
or, having written down the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, he who bestows them [upon others].
One obtains merit equal to the gift of the Veda and a twofold increase in prosperity;
[one avoids] Lokāyata, fallacious reasoning, and the speech of commoners and barbarians.
A twice-born man must not listen to this, for it leads that twice-born man downward;
he who is capable yet does not accept [this teaching] shall attain the worlds of the giver.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, perfumes, and water should not be refused; even from one of evil deeds, that which is brought unasked may be accepted.
Except from unchaste women, eunuchs, and outcasts, as well as from enemies;
for the sake of honoring the gods and guests, for the purpose of satisfying the ancestors,
and for his own subsistence, he may accept gifts from anyone.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Laws of Giving as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 99.
Yājñavalkya said:
Now I shall describe the ritual for the *śrāddha*, which destroys all sins:
[it is performed] on the new moon, the eight lunar days (*aṣṭakā*), at times of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), during the dark fortnight, and during the two solstices.
Material wealth, the excellence of a Brahmin, the equinox, the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign,
the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Gajacchāyā conjunction, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Devotion to the *śrāddha* rite and the proper times for the *śrāddha* have been proclaimed;
among all gods, the fire is supreme, and a young *śrotriya* learned in the Vedas is likewise esteemed.
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman, one who knows the Trimadhu and Trisuparṇa hymns,
a sister’s son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, a sacrificer, a father-in-law, and a maternal uncle.

Those who have performed the Triṇāciketa rite, daughters' sons, disciples, relatives, and kinsmen; those established in ritual action, those established in austerity, those who maintain the five fires, and celibate students.
Brahmins devoted to their fathers and mothers are the deities of the śrāddha;
likewise, one who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, and one born of a remarried woman [are excluded].
Those who have broken their vows of celibacy, those who are devoid of proper conduct,
and all those who are not devotees of Viṣṇu— none of these are ever worthy of the śrāddha rite.
One should issue the invitation on the previous day; the twice-born guests should remain self-restrained, and having had their hands washed, one should seat them upon their seats in the forenoon.
In rites for the gods as well as for the ancestors, one should place [the vessels] according to one's ability in their respective places:
two in the eastern direction for the gods, three in the northern direction for the ancestors, and one each separately for both.
The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; or rather, the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed for them as well.
Having given water for washing the hands, one should also provide *kuśa* grass for the purpose of the seats.
Having invoked [the deities] and being permitted by them, one should scatter barley over the food with the verse "viśve devāsaḥ," and then place it in a vessel containing a purifier (*pavitra*).
Having poured milk with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," and likewise barley grains with "yavo 'si," he should pour them directly into their hands with the mantra "yā divyāḥ."
Likewise, having offered scented water, lamps, garlands, and rows of lights,
he should then perform the rite for the ancestors by keeping them to his left and circumambulating them counter-clockwise.
Having offered double-folded *kuśa* grasses and having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā," the learned [priest] should then recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ."
If the purpose is barley, it should be performed with sesame seeds; one should perform the *arghya* offering and so forth as before.
Having offered the *arghya*, one should place their remnants into a vessel according to the prescribed rule.
Saying, "You are the place for the ancestors," he places the vessel face down on the ground;
then, taking food soaked in ghee, he asks, "I shall offer it in the fire."
Being thus addressed with "Do so," he, having offered oblations into the fire according to the ritual for the ancestors (pitṛyajña),
should, with a concentrated mind, place the remnants of the offering into the vessels.
Having given food upon whatever vessels are available, and especially upon those made of silver, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra: "The earth is the vessel."
Having performed [the ritual] with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should place his thumb upon the twice-born [brāhmaṇa];
likewise, he should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis and the verses beginning with "madhu vātā."
Having recited [the mantra] as desired, one should speak; they too should eat while remaining restrained in speech.
One who is free from anger and haste should offer the desired food, consisting of sacrificial oblations.
Having recited the purificatory mantras until satisfied, as well as the previous recitations, one should take up food and say, "Are you satisfied? and then consecrate the remainder with a mantra.
He should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once for each [deceased];
then, taking all the food together with sesame seeds, he should face the south.
One should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remnants of the meal, as in the Pitṛyajña rite;
likewise, one should offer them for the maternal grandfathers, and thereafter provide water for sipping (ācamana).

Then, having caused the benediction to be recited, he should offer the water for imperishability (akṣayyodaka). Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability, he should utter the word "svadhā."
"Permitted by those present, let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors;
when the Brahmins have said, 'Let there be *svadhā*,' he should then pour water upon the ground."
While offering water for the Viśvedevas, he should say: "May they be pleased! and likewise:
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny."
"May our faith not depart, and may we have much to give"—
uttering such dear words repeatedly, he should bow down and dismiss [the preceptor].
With the words "vāje-vāje," they should perform the dismissal with affection, starting with the ancestors,
into that vessel where the remnants of the offerings were previously poured.
Having turned that paternal vessel face upwards, he should dismiss the Brahmins;
having followed them clockwise, he should eat what was partaken of by the ancestors.
He should remain celibate for that night together with his wife;
having thus performed the circumambulation, he should also [offer] the Nāndīmukha rites for the elders.
One should offer oblations mixed with large jujube fruits (*karkandhu*) that have been soaked in water;
the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of the invocation to the gods (*daiva*), consists of a single portion of food, and employs a single purifying blade of grass (*pavitraka*).
Devoid of the *āvāhana* and *agnaukaraṇa* rites, and performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*),
one should dismiss the Brahmins with the words "May [the offerings] wait upon [you]" in place of the usual "May it be inexhaustible" (*akṣayya*).
One should say, "Be pleased," and they should reply, "We are pleased.
One should prepare four vessels mixed with fragrant water and sesame seeds.

For the sake of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*) with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ"; one should perform the remainder as previously prescribed.
This Sapindikarana rite for a woman is also performed as an Ekoddista;
for one whose Sapindikarana occurs before the completion of a year, [the following applies].
A twice-born man should also give food along with a water-pot for a year;
he should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to cows, goats, Brahmins, or into fire or water.
By means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) one indeed [attains the fruit] for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
likewise by fish, deer, sheep, birds, goat, and spotted deer.
The ancestors here are satisfied by the offerings of the meat of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively, for each successive month as the months increase.

One should undoubtedly give [offerings] on the thirteenth day of the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism; by giving śrāddha in this manner starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight, one obtains daughters and other blessings.
For those slain by the sword, however, [an offering] is given on the fourteenth day;
[it bestows] heaven, progeny, vigor, valor, as well as land and strength.
He obtains preeminence among sons, good fortune, prosperity, leadership, auspiciousness,
the power of a rolling wheel, as well as success in trade and other such pursuits.
Health, fame, freedom from sorrow, the supreme goal,
wealth, knowledge, perfection of speech, base metals, as well as cattle, goats, and sheep.
He who duly offers a śrāddha for horses and longevity during the period beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī shall obtain these desires.

O twice-born ones, garments and other such gifts certainly gratify the man who performs the śrāddha rite, as well as his longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, and the joys of heaven and liberation. (GarP 1.99.44)
Just as the Grandfather (Brahmā) always bestows a kingdom out of affection, so does he grant it.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Śrāddha as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Yājñavalkya said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 100.
Yājñavalkya said:
Learn now the symptoms of one afflicted by Vināyaka:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men.
The assembly became dejected and their undertakings fruitless due to this omen;
likewise, the king lost his kingdom, and the pregnant queen lost her husband and her son.
On an auspicious day, one should perform his ceremonial bath according to the prescribed rites,
after he has been anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Then, for one whose head has been anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, auspicious blessings should be recited by virtuous brahmins.
One should cast earth, yellow pigment, perfumes,
and guggulu into the waters that have been drawn from a lake by four people of a single caste using jars.
Likewise, it should be placed upon a red bull-hide seat;
it is remembered by the sages as the thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed purifier.
With that I consecrate you; may the purifying waters cleanse you.
May King Varuṇa grant you fortune, and may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune.
Indra and Vāyu have granted you fortune, and the Seven Sages have granted you fortune; whatever misfortune is in your hair, at your parting, or upon your head—[may it depart].
May the waters on your forehead, ears, and eyes always destroy those [obstacles].
For one who has bathed, [one should apply] mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood.
And holding kuśa grass with his left hand, he should offer oblations at the head [of the victim], reciting:
"Mita and Samita, as well as Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa."
And at the end, having spread *kuśa* grass everywhere upon the ground at a crossroads, one should offer [oblations] to Kuṣmāṇḍa and the prince, accompanied by the word *svāhā*.
Rice grains both prepared and unprepared, as well as rice mixed with minced meat, variegated and fragrant flowers, and the three kinds of liquor; 100.12.
Radishes, fried cakes, and likewise garlands of onions,
curd, milk-rice, cooked rice, and flour mixed with jaggery along with modakas.
Having brought all these together and placed them on the ground with the head [of the image] facing that way,
one should worship Ambikā and offer the arghya with palms joined in reverence.
Having performed the rite for averting evil with *dūrvā* grass, mustard flowers, and *putrajanman* blossoms,
he should pray to the virtuous Ambikā.
Grant me beauty, grant me glory, O Blessed One; grant me fortune. Grant me sons, grant me prosperity, and grant me all my desires.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins with white garments and ointments;
having likewise worshipped the planets, one should give a pair of garments to the preceptor.
Thus, one who is devoted to the worship of the Sun shall obtain the auspicious fruit of his actions.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Gaṇapati as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Yājñavalkya said:

One who desires prosperity, one who desires peace, or one afflicted by the malevolent gaze of the planets should perform the planetary sacrifice (*grahayañña*) according to the rules; these are the planets as they are remembered by the wise.
The Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter,
Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu are remembered as the host of planets (graha-gaṇāḥ).
Learn of the colors from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, lead, and bell-metal.
Red, white, and likewise red; yellow, yellow, white, and black;
black, black—in this sequence are the colors, and from them the substances and the sages.
One should arrange the colors for the planets and draw them upon a cloth for the purpose of the fire oblation;
one should bathe and offer oblations with the substances appropriate for the planets according to the prescribed rite,
and gold, garments, and beautiful flowers should be presented as gifts.
Fragrances, offerings, and guggulu incense should be presented;
there, oblations (caru) should be performed with mantras for each respective deity.

One should offer oblations with these very mantras in their proper sequence: "With the black one," "This [sacrifice]," "O gods," "Agni is the head," "The summit of heaven," and "Awake! (RV 10.87.1; 6.16.13; 1.22.5; 8.44.16; 1.95.4; 10.184.1).
"Bṛhaspate paridīya," "sarve annāt parisutam," "śanno devīḥ," "kayā naś ca," and "ketuṃ kr̥ṇvan"— these [mantras] are used in sequence.
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, then pippala,
audumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in their respective order.
It should be offered oblated with honey and ghee, as well as combined with curd;
likewise, jaggery-rice, milk-porridge, sacrificial food (haviṣya), and milk-rice made from ṣaṣṭika rice.
One should offer curd-rice, sacrificial oblation, cakes, meat, and various kinds of food to the planets according to their sequence; thereafter, one should present vessels to the planets.
A cow, a conch, as well as an ox, gold, a garment, a horse,
a black cow, iron, and a goat— these indeed are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) in sequence;
for by worshipping the planets constantly, one obtains results such as sovereignty and the like.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Pacification of Planets as Taught by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 102.
Yājñavalkya said:
I shall describe the stage of the forest-dweller; let the great sages listen to it.
Having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
The forest-dweller shall remain celibate, maintaining the sacred fires and the domestic fire, being patient;
he shall worship the fires, the ancestors, the gods, and guests with food grown without the use of a plow.

But the self-possessed one, wearing a beard, matted hair, and body hair, being self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, and abstaining from accepting gifts, should satisfy his dependents.
Devoted to sacred study, habituated to meditation, and delighting in the welfare of all beings,
he may take possession of wealth either once a day or once a month.

In the month of Āśvayuja, one should abandon what has been prepared; one should employ the time with vows and other observances, eating either once a fortnight or once a month, and become one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow should sleep on the ground and subsist on fruits and the like;
in the summer he should stand amidst five fires, and during the rains he should lie upon the bare earth.
In the winter, one should spend the day practicing yoga while wearing wet clothes.
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood paste—
toward both of them, as well as toward everyone else, he remains without anger and perfectly content.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of Forest-Dwellers as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 103—
Yājñavalkya said:
O best of beings, listen as I shall proclaim the dharma of a monk:
having performed a sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee, whether from the forest or from the home.
Even at the end of the Prājāpatya vow, having consigned the sacred fires into himself, he—
intent on the welfare of all beings, peaceful, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot— [should live].
Having renounced all pleasure gardens, one should resort to a village for the sake of alms;
one should wander for alms with vigilance, not being conspicuous in the evening.
In the village of Rohita, free from greed and possessing only what is necessary for sustenance,
one may become a Paramahaṃsa or a single-staffed ascetic (ekadaṇḍī), beginning with the observances of self-restraint (yama).
A practitioner of perfected yoga who casts off the body attains immortality even here;
a householder who is a donor, fond of guests, and possessed of knowledge is liberated even through the performance of a *śrāddha*.

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Forest-Dwellers and Renunciants as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 104] Yājñavalkya said:

Upon the emergence of the banner from hell—the exhaustion of sinful karma—the killer of a Brahmin shall become a dog, a donkey, or a camel; the drinker of liquor shall likewise become a frog or a yak.

A thief of gold becomes a worm or an insect; one who violates the teacher’s bed becomes grass and the like; one who has contracted consumption becomes black-toothed; and one with deformed nails becomes a śipiviṣṭa.
All these [sins] may arise from the sequence of killing a Brahmin, or they may all belong to the child;
one who steals food becomes deceitful, and one who steals speech becomes mute.
One who steals grain has an extra limb; a slanderer has a putrid nose;
one who consumes oil becomes an oil-drinker; and a backbiter has a foul-smelling mouth.
Having purchased a Brahmin’s daughter as a maiden, one becomes a Rākṣasa in the forest; having stolen jewels, one is born into a low caste; and one who steals leaf-vegetables becomes a peacock.
Having stolen a cluster of flowers, one becomes a muskrat; having stolen grain, one becomes a mouse;
having stolen fruit, one becomes a monkey; and by stealing livestock, as well as milk, one becomes a goat or a crow.
The meat-eater becomes a vulture, the one with white leprosy a cotton-clad ascetic, and the stealer of salt a cricket;
having obtained the fruit according to their karma, they reach the state of animals through the passage of time.
Those lowest of men, fallen from their auspicious marks, are born into poverty;
thereafter, having become free from stain, they arise as yogins in a great family.
They are born endowed with auspicious marks and possessed of wealth and grain.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ripening of Karma as Taught by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 105]:
From the non-performance of prescribed duties and from the practice of those that are censured...
And from the lack of restraint of the senses, a man undergoes a fall.
Therefore, one should diligently perform expiation for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world will become serene.
In this way, the world is appeased and one's own self is purified; through expiations, there is the destruction of evil. Those who do not perform expiation and are devoid of remorse [fall].
Indeed, those who commit evil go to the hells of Mahāraurava and Raurava,
as well as Tāmisra and Lohaśaṅku, which is filled with a foul stench.
The Haṃsābha, the Lohitoda, the Sañjīvana, the river-path,
the Mahānilaya, the Kākolam, the Andhatāmisra, and the Vāpana.
Indeed, due to their lack of merit, the sinful go to Avīci and Kumbhīpāka;
namely, the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, the adulterer, and the violator of the Guru’s bed.
Censuring the guru and censuring the Vedas—these two are indeed equal to the killing of a Brahmin—as is the eating of forbidden food and the performance of crooked actions. (GarP 1.105.7)
Tasting the mouth of a woman during her menses is equal to drinking liquor;
stealing a horse, a gem, or similar valuables is equated with the theft of gold.
Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, with virgins, with women of one's own kin,
with women of the lowest castes, and likewise with women of the same lineage, is recorded in tradition as equal to violating the bed of one's guru.
The father’s sister, the mother’s [sister], the maternal uncle’s wife, even the daughter-in-law,
the mother’s co-wife, the sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter— GarP_1,105.10.
One who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru's bed;
his penis shall be cut off, and he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing.

The killing of a cow, the state of being a *vrātya*, theft, the non-discharge of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, the sale of forbidden goods, and the supersession of a younger brother by an elder brother; GarP_1,105.12 //
Teaching for wages, receiving instruction from a paid teacher, adultery, abandoning an elder brother who is unmarried, usury, and the manufacture of salt; GarP_1,105.13 //
For one born of a true Śūdra, Vaiśya, or Kṣatriya, there is living by censured means,
atheism, the violation of vows, and the sale of a bull or a cow on a spit.
Abandoning one's father, mother, or friends; the sale of a pond or a grove; the defilement of a maiden; and officiating at the sacrifice for one who marries before his elder brother.
Giving away one's daughter to that very person, crookedness, the breaking of vows, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and consorting with women who drink liquor; GarP_1,105.16 //
Abandoning one's Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's children; likewise, abandoning one's kinsmen; engaging with improper scriptures; and the selling of one's wife or oneself.
Minor sins have also been described; now learn the expiation for them:
carrying a skull as his banner and subsisting on alms, he shall proclaim his deed.
A killer of a Brahmin shall attain purification after twelve years by eating sparingly;
or else, he may offer his own body, starting from the hair, with the mantra "Svāhā to the hairs."
Or one may offer oblations ending with the marrow, using their respective mantras in due order;
through the protection of a Brāhmaṇa, purification shall occur, and by performing it thus, there is indeed purification.
Having rescued a bird, a cow, or a Brahmin from danger, or even having been killed for the sake of a Brahmin,
one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic Saṃhitā three times in the forest.
Or, having resorted to the Sarasvatī river, he should bestow his wealth upon a worthy recipient;
one who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
Or, like one who kills an embryo according to its caste, even if he has not actually killed her, one who approaches an Ātreyī with the intent to kill her should perform the great vow.
If a Brāhmaṇa is engaged in a sacrificial session, one should observe double the penance;
for one who has drunk *surā*, purification is attained by drinking liquor, water, ghee, and cow urine.
Or else, wearing bark garments and matted hair, he should consume ghee that has the color of fire;
the slayer of a Brahmin should perform this vow and is worthy of undergoing the purificatory rites once again.
Likewise, a Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks wine by drinking blood, feces,
or urine is excluded from the world of her husband and shall become a vulture, a sow, or a dog.
A twice-born man who has stolen gold, having given a mace to the king and having made his deed known, becomes pure by being slain by him.
Or, by giving gold equal to his own weight, the twice-born man shall attain purification;
or he should sleep secretly upon an iron bed with an iron woman.
Having cut off his penis and testicles, he should cast them away in the south-western direction;
one who has violated the Guru’s bed must perform the Prājāpatya penance for a year.
Or, for three months, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa vow while reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā;
a killer of a cow should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and remain self-controlled for one month.
One who sleeps in a cow-pen and follows the cows is purified by the gift of a cow;
furthermore, purification from minor offenses (upapātaka) may be achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Or by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by performing the Parāka penance,
a man shall give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh in the case of killing a Kṣatriya.
Alternatively, he who has killed a Vaiśya should observe the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for three years, or he should observe this same vow for one year,
or he should give one hundred and one cows.
A killer of a Śūdra should give this for six months, or else ten cows;
having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the vow prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
For killing a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a domestic animal, or a frog,
the sinner should drink milk for three days or perform the Kṛcchra penance or even more.
For an elephant, five dark-colored bulls should be given; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for donkeys, goats, and rams, a bull; and for a crane, a three-year-old bull.
For cutting down trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred Ṛks should be recited;
and a student observing celibacy becomes an *avakīrṇin* by approaching a woman.
By sacrificing an ass dedicated to Nirṛti as an animal victim, one becomes purified;
for eating honey and meat, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance and the remaining vows.
If one sent on a mission should die, the preceptor shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances;
having acted contrary to the preceptor's will, he becomes pure only after propitiating him.
One may win over enemies by means of gifts of grain and the like, or even through acts of affection;
if a Brahmin dies while such assistance is being rendered, there is no sin.
One who has been falsely accused of a great sin or a minor sin by another should subsist on water for one month, reciting [mantras] with his senses restrained.
One who approaches his brother’s wife without being authorized should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having approached a woman in her courses, he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights.
Dwelling in a cow-pen for one month as a celibate student, subsisting on a milk-vow and devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one is liberated from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

One who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy of them (vrātyas) should perform the kṛcchra penance three times; likewise, one who causes the Veda to be forgotten, one who abandons those who have sought refuge, and one who eats barley for a year [must do the same].

One who has traveled in a donkey-cart or a camel-cart, or who has bathed naked, slept during the day, or had sexual intercourse with a woman during the day, should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Having treated a guru with contempt, having uttered "huṃ" against him, or having defeated a Brahmin in debate,
one should appease that person and then fast for a day, O sages.

If a staff is raised against a Brahmin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if it is brought down, it is an *atikṛcchra*, having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the offense.
An expiation must be prescribed in cases where no specific atonement has been stated;
for women, the abortion of a fetus and the reviling of their husband are causes for falling [from caste].
This is the fault when [the moon] is near a planet; therefore, one should avoid her from afar.
One who is known to have committed a fault should perform the vow with the permission of his guru.
But one whose offense is not publicly known should perform the secret vow;
having fasted for three nights and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, even a killer of a Brahmin [is purified].
Having offered a milch cow into the pure water,
he should subsist on air for a day while reciting the verse beginning with "lomabhyaḥ svāhā."
Having recited [the mantra] over water, one should offer forty oblations of clarified butter;
having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses, one becomes pure.
A drinker of liquor, a stealer of gold, and one who has violated the Guru’s bed are liberated by standing in water and reciting the Rudra-hymn and the Sahasra-śīrṣa hymn.
One should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins;
one becomes pure by drinking water consecrated with the syllable Oṃ and the Soma-plant.
Having observed a fast, a twice-born man who has consumed semen, feces,
or urine is purified of the sin committed through ignorance once the three daily twilight prayers (sandhyā) have been performed.
Indeed, by reciting the Rudra-ekādaśa, the destruction of sin occurs for the twice-born;
[he should be] devoted to the study of the Vedas, peaceful, and intent upon the performance of the five great sacrifices.
Alas! Sins do not touch one who has quickly remembered [the Lord] and cast them away;
by reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times, one becomes pure, except for the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
Celibacy, compassion, patience, meditation, truthfulness, sincerity,
non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-restraint— these are remembered as the *yamas*.
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ,
austerity, freedom from anger, devotion to the guru, and purity— these are recorded as the observances (niyamas).
Having consumed the five products of the cow—cow’s milk, curd, urine, dung, and ghee—one should fast on the following day; thus one performs the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
With each of the *sāntapana* substances taken separately over six days, followed by a day of fasting,
this seven-day rite is known as the *mahāsāntapana*.
The *parṇakṛcchra* is declared to consist of leaves of the *udumbara*, lotus, and *bilva*, along with *kuśa* water,
each practiced individually on successive days.
One should drink hot milk, ghee, and water, each for one day respectively;
followed by a fast for one night—this is the purifying Taptakṛcchra penance.
By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for,
and by fasting, the quarter-kṛcchra is declared.
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold Prajāpatya penance is said to be the Atikṛcchra when one subsists on only as much water as fills the palm of the hand.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days;
and fasting for twelve days is declared to be the *parāka*.
Taking one of each— oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley meal— daily, along with one day of fasting, is called this "Saumya Kṛcchra."
Through the practice of these for three nights each, one by one in sequence,
this is to be known as the "Tulāpuruṣa" [vow], lasting fifteen days.
One should eat morsels of food in increasing amounts during the bright fortnight, equal to the size of a peacock's egg;
one should decrease them by one each day during the dark fortnight; thus one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Alternatively, one may subsist for a month on exactly two hundred and forty morsels of food; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having bathed at the three sessions of the day, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance consisting of morsels (*piṇḍa*);
one should recite purifying mantras and consecrate the morsels with the *gāyatrī*.
For sins that have not been specifically prescribed, purification is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon.
But one who performs the kṛcchra penance with a desire for dharma enjoys great prosperity.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Discernment of Expiations Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—106.
Yājñavalkya said:
I shall proclaim the purification for the deceased; listen to that, O you who are firm in your vows.
One who has not yet reached two years of age should be buried; one should not perform the water libation thereafter.
Having followed [the body] as far as the cremation ground accompanied by other kinsmen,
they should recite the *Yamasūkta* while chanting it over a common fire (*laukikāgni*).
If he has maintained the sacred fires, he should be cremated according to the ritual procedure for those who have established the fires;
then, from the seventh or the tenth day, the kinsmen approach the waters.

Facing the direction of the ancestors (the south), they should perform the water-libation rites for themselves with the mantra "May our sin be burnt away by this," and likewise for their maternal grandfathers, teachers, and the wives of teachers.
The paternal kinsmen, the maternal relatives, the son, the friend, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, and the officiating priest—
restrained in speech, they pour water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage.

But they should not perform water-libation rites for heretics or those who have fallen from their caste, nor for those who have not observed the vow of celibacy, for *vrātyas*, nor for women who follow their lusts.
Women who drink liquor and those who commit suicide are not entitled to the period of impurity or the water-offering;
therefore, one should not weep, for the stability of life is impermanent.
The ritual should be performed according to one's ability; thereafter, having chewed neem leaves, one should go toward home, restrained at the door of the house.
Having sipped water (ācamana), they should then touch fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds;
then, having touched them, they should enter [the house], placing their feet slowly upon a stone.

Regarding rites such as entering [the funeral pyre], even from touching a deceased person, purification for those who merely witness it occurs instantly; for others, it comes through bathing and self-restraint.
Eating food that has been purchased or obtained, they should sleep separately on the ground;
for three days, food should be offered to the deceased by one who performs the piṇḍayajña.
Water should be kept in the open air for one day, and milk in an earthen vessel;
the Vaitāna and Āvasathya rites, as well as the rituals enjoined by the Vedas, must be performed.
From birth until the time of the tonsure ceremony, impurity is declared to last for one night;
from the initiation of vows (upanayana) until the instruction in the sacred formulas (vratādeśa), it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, it lasts for ten nights.
Impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) is said to last for three nights or ten nights;
however, in the case of a child less than two years old, the impurity (sūtaka) belongs to both parents, while for a stillbirth it belongs to the mother alone.
Between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days:
ten for the [lowest] castes, twelve for the [middle] castes, and likewise fifteen for the [highest] castes.
Likewise, there is a period of impurity for thirty days in the case of a *preta*;
however, purification occurs immediately for those who have not given away their daughters in marriage and for young children.
And [this applies] toward the preceptor’s resident pupil, a Vedic scholar, a maternal uncle, and a learned priest;
as well as toward non-legitimate sons and wives who have gone over to another man.
Likewise, on the day of death, there is purification for those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, as well as for those who commit suicide, provided it occurs immediately thereafter.
O Lord of the Earth, there is no impurity for kings who have been killed by poison and the like,
nor for those engaged in a sacrificial session, those observing a vow, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman.
In matters of giving, marriage, sacrifice, battle, or national upheaval,
as well as in times of dire distress, immediate purification is prescribed.
Time, fire, action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, recitation, remorse, and fasting—
these are the causes of purification for all.
For those who perform improper acts, the giving of gifts purifies them, just as the current of a river purifies;
however, in times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even that of a Vaiśya.
Fruit, Soma, linen, creepers, curd, milk, ghee, water, sesame, boiled rice, meat broth, alkali, honey, lac, and cooked oblation; GarP_1,106.23 //
Clothing, stones, liquor, flowers, vegetables, clay, leather, sandals, the skin of the black antelope, silk, salt, and even meat; ||| GarP_1,106.24 |||
A Vaiśya following the prescribed conduct should not sell oil-cakes, roots, or perfumes;
however, for the sake of dharma, he may sell sesame seeds at a rate equal to the quantity of grain.
A twice-born man, even when fallen into distress, should not sell salt and such items;
yet, by accepting gifts from a low person, the twice-born is not defiled, just as the sun is not.

In that same way, one should engage in agriculture and other such labors; likewise, horses are not to be sold. Having observed that [the people] are hungry, distressed, and devoid of a means of livelihood, the king should provide a righteous livelihood for the Brahmins and others.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Impurity and its Removal as Spoken by Yājñavalkya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—107.
Sūta said:
Parāśara spoke to Vyāsa concerning the dharma of the castes, stages of life, and so forth:
"In every kalpa, through the process of destruction and creation, beings and other entities indeed undergo decay."

Revelation (śruti), tradition (smṛti), and the conduct of the virtuous—whatever is performed by those who act according to the Vedas; the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the duties for the Brāhmaṇas and other classes have always been proclaimed by Manu and others.
In the Kali age, charity is the dharma; in the Kali age, one should abandon the agent [of action].
However, an evil deed committed therein bears fruit within a year through a curse.
Through right conduct, one shall obtain everything: the six duties day after day—twilight prayers, bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and the worship of gods, guests, and others.
At that time, there will be unprecedented Brahmins of excellent vows and unprecedented ascetics;
and a Kṣatriya, having conquered the armies of his enemies, shall protect the earth.
Trade, agriculture, and so forth belong to the Vaiśya; devotion to the twice-born belongs to the Śūdra.
One falls [from one's status] through eating what is unfit to be eaten, through theft, and through approaching those who should not be approached.
A twice-born man practicing agriculture should not yoke an exhausted ox;
having performed his bath, yoga, and other rites for half the day, he should feed the Brahmins.
One should perform the five sacrifices, cause the cruel [deed] to be censured, and one who is possessed by sin should not sell sesame or clarified butter; this is the sacrifice of the slaughterhouse.
Having given a sixth part to the king, a twentieth to the deities,
and a thirty-third to the Brahmins, the cultivator is not defiled by sin.
Farmers, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have not given [grain] from the threshing floor become thieves;
a Brāhmaṇa is purified in three days after the birth or death of a deceased person.
A Kṣatriya [becomes pure] after ten days, a Vaiśya after twelve days, and a Śūdra at the end of a month;
a Brāhmaṇa reaches purity after ten days, and a Kṣatriya after twelve days.
A Vaiśya is purified in fifteen days, while a Śūdra is purified in a month;
those who share the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) but have separate doors and dwellings are considered heirs.
Upon birth and upon death, there shall be impurity for them;
it lasts ten nights in the fourth generation, six nights in the fifth, and ten nights in the case of a male.
In the sixth [month], purification occurs after four days; in the seventh, after three days;
and for a child who dies in a foreign land, there is immediate purification, because [the impurity] ceases upon death.
For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and for those who have just emerged from the womb,
there is no cremation with fire, no offering of funeral cakes, and no libation of water.
If a woman’s fetus miscarries or is aborted,
the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had remained in the womb.
Until the naming ceremony, purification occurs immediately; from birth until the tonsure ceremony, it lasts for a day and night;
until the initiation vows, it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, it lasts for ten days.
The flow [of menses] may continue until the fourth day; the discharge [of the embryo] occurs on the fifth or sixth.
There is no impurity resulting from celibacy, the Agnihotra sacrifice, or the avoidance of social contact.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female and male slaves, servants,
one who maintains the sacred fire, a Vedic scholar, and a king are proclaimed to be immediately pure.

The mother is purified after ten days; the father becomes pure by bathing upon birth. Upon birth, impurity (sūtaka) arises from physical contact; the father becomes pure by performing ritual sipping (upaspṛśya).
In the intervals between weddings, festivals, and sacrifices, or during periods of death or birth impurity,
it is ordained that one should avoid anything other than what was previously intended.
Birth is purified by death; for one born [during an impurity], it is like death.
For those who have perished in cattle-raid and similar calamities, however, the birth-impurity lasts for one night.
One is purified by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) for carrying a destitute or deceased person;
however, from carrying a deceased Śūdra, one shall remain impure for three nights.
There is no funeral consecration for one who commits suicide, one killed by poison, one strangled, or one bitten by a worm;
having touched a cow-killed person or one bitten by a worm, one is purified through the Kṛcchra penance.
She who abandons a blameless and non-degraded husband during his youth shall remain a woman for seven births and experience widowhood again and again.

By having sexual intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period, one incurs the sin of killing a child; likewise, a sow-like woman, those who have violated their vows, and those from whom the rites of food and water have been withdrawn are women who should not be approached.
The legitimate son (aurasa) and the son born of the wife (kṣetraja)—both being born of the father—are the givers of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to their father.
For one who has superseded his elder brother (parivitti), there shall be a Kṛcchra penance, and for the girl [who was given in marriage], likewise a Kṛcchra.
The donor should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*;
this applies in the case of those who are humpbacked, dwarfs, eunuchs, those with stammering speech, and the mentally dull.
There is no fault in marrying again if the husband is born blind, deaf,
mute, lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste.
In five calamities, another husband is ordained for women;
a woman who dies together with her husband shall dwell in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on the body.
A man bitten by a dog or similar animal becomes pure through the recitation of the Gāyatrī;
however, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and has been killed by Cāṇḍālas or others must be cremated with the fire of the world (lokāgni).
Having washed its bone with milk, one should burn it with one's own fire while reciting mantras;
but if he has died while away from home, one should again fashion an effigy out of kuśa grass and burn it.
Having spread six hundred palāśa sticks upon a black antelope skin,
and having placed a śamī stick at the head [of the skin], one should place the lower fire-drill (araṇi) at the penis.
One should place the *kaṇḍa* in the right hand and the *upabhṛt* in the left;
one should place the mortar on the side and the pestle on the back.
Having cast the grinding stone into his belly, he should place the rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds in his mouth;
the *prokṣaṇī* vessel in his ear, and the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) in his two eyes.
One should place pieces of gold in the ears, eyes, mouth, and nostrils;
by means of the implements of the Agnihotra sacrifice, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
With the mantra "asau svargāya lokāya svāhā," he should offer a single oblation of clarified butter;
[he should avoid] the swan, the crane, the curlew, the ruddy goose, and the cock.
One who kills a peacock or a ram is purified in a day and night;
having killed all kinds of birds, one is purified in a day and night.
Having killed all four-footed animals, one should recite [the mantra] while fasting for a day and night;
having killed a Śūdra, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance, but the killer of a Vaiśya, the Atikṛcchra;
for killing a Kṣatriya, the Cāndrāyaṇa; and for a Brāhmaṇa, one should undergo the Dvāviṃśa or Triṃśa.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Dharma as Spoken by Parāśara," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 108] Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the Essence of Ethics (Nītisāra), which is based upon the treatises on statecraft (Arthaśāstra) and other sciences;
it is beneficial for kings and others, meritorious, and bestows longevity, heaven, and other rewards.
A man desiring success should always cultivate association with the virtuous;
there is no benefit from the wicked, either for this world or for the next.
One should avoid conversation with the base, yet one may look upon the non-cruel; one should avoid conflict with a friend and intimacy with one who serves an enemy.
Through instructing foolish disciples, through supporting wicked women,
and through association with the corrupt, even a wise man comes to ruin.
One should avoid from afar a foolish Brāhmaṇa, a warrior (Kṣatriya) who does not fight, an inert Vaiśya, and a Śūdra who is well-versed in the syllables of the Veda.
At the proper time, one should form an alliance with an enemy; at the proper time, one should wage war even against a friend.
Relying on the necessity of the task at hand, the wise man bides his time.
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake while others sleep; indeed, Time is difficult to overcome.
In due time it takes away vitality, and in due time it dwells within the womb;
Time brings forth creation, and Time again shall withdraw it.
Time, whose movement is subtle and eternal, is here conceived as twofold:
by way of its coarse aggregate-movement and by way of its internal subtle movement.
Bṛhaspati, the omniscient, spoke this Essence of Ethics to the Lord of the Gods,
by means of which Indra became all-knowing, slew the Daityas, and attained heaven.
Royal sages and brahmins should perform the worship of gods, brahmins, and others;
they must perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), which destroys even the greatest sins.
One who cultivates association with the excellent, holds virtuous discourse with the learned,
and maintains friendship with those free from greed, does not come to grief.
One should never engage in slander, nor for the sake of another's wealth, nor in jesting with others' wives, nor in dwelling in the house of another.
Even a stranger who brings benefit is a kinsman, while even a kinsman who brings harm is a stranger; a disease born of one's own body is harmful, whereas medicine from the forest is beneficial.
He is a kinsman who is intent on one's welfare; he is a father who provides nourishment;
that is a friend in whom there is trust; and that is a country where one may live.
He is a servant who is obedient; that is a seed which sprouts;
she is a wife who speaks kindly; he is a son who lives.
He lives who possesses virtues; he lives who possesses dharma. For one who is devoid of virtue and dharma, his life is fruitless.
She is a wife who is skillful in the home; she is a wife who speaks kindly;
she is a wife whose life is her husband; she is a wife who is devoted to her husband.
She is constantly bathed and fragrant, always speaks kindly,
eats little, speaks little, and is perpetually endowed with auspiciousness.
She is constantly devoted to the Dharma, always dear to her husband,
ever pleasant in speech, and always desirous of him during the proper season.
Endowed with these initial rites, she increases all good fortune;
he who has such a wife as this is not a mere mortal, but a lord of the gods.
He whose wife is misshapen-eyed, dejected, fond of quarreling, and always speaking with increasing harshness—his is not old age; that is not old age, but true decay.
He whose wife has taken refuge with another and desires the house of a stranger, being of wicked conduct and devoid of shame—for him, that is true old age; it is not merely the aging of the body.
She whose wife is discerning of virtues, follows her husband, and is content with even the smallest thing—she is truly beloved; others are not beloved, though they may claim to be so.
A wicked wife, a deceitful friend, a servant who speaks back, and living in a house with snakes—these are nothing but death; of this there is no doubt.
Abandon association with the wicked; cultivate the company of the virtuous.
Perform meritorious deeds day and night, and constantly contemplate impermanence.
A woman who has a neck like a serpent’s, whose speech is like that of a hooded snake, who is fierce, dark, agitated in her song, and whose eyes are overwhelmed with blood;

who is like a tiger, whose face is terrible in anger, and who is as formidable as a crow’s tongue with flickering flames of fire—such a woman, though clever, who wanders into others' homes, whose mind is deluded, and who is devoid of passion, must not be served.

Attachment arises by the power of fate sometimes toward one's own child, toward an ungrateful person, toward fire, and even toward a golden image that has stolen Sītā; but passion for courtesans never arises at all.
When a serpent is seen in one's home, when a disease has been diagnosed by a physician,
and when the body is subject to the stages of life such as childhood and so forth— who, surrounded by these times, can attain steadfastness?

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of Ethics as Spoken by Bṛhaspati," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 109 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Sūta said:
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
and one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of the self.
Indeed, dwelling in hell is better than living in a home of evil conduct;
for from hell one's sin is exhausted, but from a wretched home one does not turn back.
The wise man moves with one foot while standing firm on the other;
he should not abandon his former dwelling without having examined his new destination.
One should abandon a country of wicked conduct; one should abandon a residence that is fraught with calamities;
one should abandon a miserly king; and one should abandon a friend who is full of deceit.
Of what use is wealth that has fallen into the hands of a miser? Of what use is knowledge that is crowded with many deceitful graspings?
Of what use is beauty devoid of virtue and prowess? Of what use is a friend who turns his back at the time of misfortune?
Many companions never seen before all become friends to one who stands firm in his position;
but for one deprived of wealth and fallen from his station, even his own kin become enemies at the wrong time.
One should recognize a friend in times of adversity, a hero in battle, one who is pure in private, a wife when wealth has vanished, and a guest who is dear even during a famine.
Birds abandon a tree whose fruit is exhausted; cranes leave a dried-up lake; courtesans forsake a man devoid of wealth; ministers desert a fallen king;
bees abandon a withered flower; and deer flee from a forest consumed by fire. Indeed, every person acts out of necessity; for who is truly dear to anyone?
Win over the greedy by giving wealth, the praiseworthy with a gesture of joined palms,
the fool by following his whims, and the wise man with truthfulness.
For gods, virtuous men, and the twice-born are pleased by sincerity;
others [are pleased] by food and drink, while the wise are pleased by the gift of honor. (GarP 1.109.11)
One should win over the superior by prostration, the deceitful by sowing dissension, the base by giving small gifts, and an equal by means of equal prowess.
For whatever the disposition of each person may be, the wise man, speaking what is beneficial for that very person and having gained their confidence, should quickly bring them under his influence.
One should never place trust in rivers, clawed beasts, horned animals, those with weapons in hand, women, or royal families.
A wise person should not disclose the loss of wealth, mental anguish, misconduct within the home, deception, or insults.
Association with the base and the wicked, a total lack of respect, affection for others' homes, and residing in the houses of others— these destroy a woman's virtuous conduct.
In whose family is there no fault? Who has not been afflicted by disease?
Who has not encountered misfortune? And whose prosperity has remained uninterrupted?
What man on earth has not become arrogant upon attaining wealth? Whose misfortunes have not arrived? Whose mind on earth has not been shattered by women? Who indeed is beloved by kings?
Who has not come within the range of Time? What wealth has attained lasting dignity? Or what man, having fallen into the snare of the wicked, has escaped in safety? (GarP 1,109.18)

How could a wise person perform that action in which there is no friend, kinsman, or relative, nor even a sense of self; where, even when successful, no fruit is seen, and in failure, there is great suffering? (GarP 1,109.19)
One should avoid that country where there is no honor, no joy, no kinsmen,
and no acquisition of knowledge whatsoever.
Acquire that wealth which brings no fear from kings or thieves,
and which one does not abandon even when dead.
The heirs indeed divide among themselves that which was acquired through life-threatening labors once he has died;
yet whatever evil deed was committed out of a desire for wealth, that alone becomes the inheritance of the one who is afflicted by his own transgression.
Wealth that has been accumulated and stored, which is grasped again and again like the hoard of a miserly rat, leads only to suffering.
Naked, wretched, and harsh, with begging bowls marked upon their hands,
they demonstrate here in this world such a fruit for one who does not give.
Miserable people instruct others and beg, saying "Give!"—such is the state of one who does not give; may you never become like that.
That wealth which has been accumulated through hundreds of sacrifices, yet is not bestowed upon a virtuous person when requested—
wealth thus miserly guarded— is eventually spent in the houses of thieves or kings.
The wealth of a miser goes neither to the gods, nor to the brahmins, nor to his kinsmen, nor even to himself; rather, it goes to fire, thieves, and the king.
May you never, under any circumstances, pursue those goals that are achieved through excessive hardship, by transgressing the Dharma, or by bowing down before an enemy.
For lack of practice is the ruin of knowledge; for women, it is wearing shabby clothing;
for diseases, it is eating when food is digested; and for an enemy, it is deceitfulness.
The punishment for a thief is execution; for a bad friend, it is speaking little;
for women, it is sleeping separately; and for a Brahmin, it is not being invited [to a feast].
Wicked people, artisans, servants, evil drums, and women become gentle when struck; they are not fit recipients for honor.
One should know that servants are to be tested by sending them on errands, kinsmen by the onset of misfortune,
a friend in times of calamity, and a wife when one's wealth has been exhausted.
The food of women is said to be twofold, their wisdom fourfold,
their resolve sixfold, and their desire eightfold.
One should not conquer sleep with dreams, nor should one conquer a woman with desire;
one should not conquer fire with fuel, nor should one conquer thirst with wine.
Desire for women flourishes through meals containing meat, unctuous foods, intoxicants, perfumes and ointments, delightful garments, and garlands. (GarP 1,109.35)
Even regarding celibacy, it must be said that the stirrings of passion arise when one beholds a pleasing man;
for the womb of a woman becomes moistened upon seeing such a person.
Upon seeing a well-dressed man, whether he be a brother or a son, the womb of women becomes moist; this is indeed the truth, the absolute truth, O Śaunaka.

Rivers and women are of a similar nature; in their independence regarding movement and other such acts, rivers cause banks to fall with their waters, and women cause families to fall with their faults.
A river erodes its bank, and a woman ruins her family;
for both women and rivers, the movement is independent and playful.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor are beautiful-eyed women with men.
There is no satiety for the learned, for those who are beloved, for those who speak kindly, nor for pleasures, sons, life, or excellence.
A king is never satiated by the accumulation of wealth, nor does the ocean reach satiety with water;
a wise man is not satiated by what is spoken, and the eye is never satiated by the sight of a king.
For those supreme men who live by their own labor for the sake of Dharma, who always delight in their wives according to the scriptures,
who have conquered their senses, and who are fond of guests, liberation is found even in the home.
For one of virtuous deeds, heaven shall consist of women who are pleasing to the mind, beautiful in form, and well-adorned, as he dwells upon the rooftops of palaces.
Neither by gifts, nor by honor, nor by honesty, nor by self-control,
nor by weapons, nor by sacred texts— women are difficult to manage in every way.
Slowly one should acquire knowledge, slowly wealth, and slowly one should climb a mountain;
slowly one should pursue pleasure and virtue—these five things, step by step.
Worship of the gods and the like is eternal; the giving of gifts to Brahmins is eternal;
knowledge endowed with virtue is eternal; and a true friend is eternal.

Those who do not study knowledge in their childhood, and those who, established in youth, are destitute of wealth and wives—they are to be pitied in this world of living beings; they wander about in human form like wild beasts.
A student of the scriptures should not set his mind on recitation or eating;
for the sake of knowledge, he should travel even to the farthest distance with the speed of Garuḍa.
Those who, being afflicted by desire, did not study the sciences while they were young, and whose wealth was lost in their youth,
are treated with contempt in old age and burn like a lotus in the winter cold.
Reasoning is unstable and the scriptures are diverse; there is no sage whose view is not divided.
The reality of Dharma is hidden in a cave; the path is that which has been traveled by the great multitude.
The internal mind is discerned through facial expressions, gestures, gait, physical movements, speech, and the changes in the eyes and face.
A wise person infers even what has not been spoken, for the fruit of intelligence is the knowledge of another’s gestures;
a meaning once uttered is grasped even by a beast, and horses and elephants carry out what is shown to them.
One fallen from wealth should go on a pilgrimage; one fallen from truth shall indeed go to the Raurava hell;
one fallen from yoga should resort to truth and fortitude; and one fallen from his kingdom should resort to hunting.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
[Chapter 110 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
He who abandons certainties and pursues uncertainties loses his certainties;
for that which is uncertain is already lost.
Knowledge in the hands of a man devoid of the instrument of speech is like a weapon in the hands of a coward;
it produces no satisfaction in his body, just as beautiful wives bring no joy to a blind man.
The power to enjoy food when there is food to eat, the power for pleasure with excellent women,
and the power to give when there is wealth— these are not the fruits of minor austerity.
The Vedas have the Agnihotra sacrifice as their fruit; virtuous conduct has auspicious character as its fruit;
wives have pleasure and sons as their fruit; and wealth has giving and enjoyment as its fruit.
A wise man should marry a girl born of a noble family even if she is ugly, but never one who is not of noble birth, even if she is beautiful and has shapely hips.
For what is the use of even that object which is associated with misfortune?
Who indeed would take the jewel from the crest of a serpent?
One should accept an oblation even from a family of impure conduct; a well-spoken word even from a child;
gold from filth; and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
Nectar should be taken even from poison, gold even from filth,
the highest knowledge even from a low person, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
There can be no friendship with a king, nor is a snake ever without venom;
there is no family that remains stainless where women are born.
One should appoint a devoted person to the family; one should engage a son in the sciences;
one should involve an enemy in calamities; and one should enjoin a loved one to dharma.
Servants and ornaments should be employed only in their proper places;
for a crest-jewel never truly shines when placed upon the foot.
The crest-jewel, the ocean, fire, the bell, the unbroken sky,
or else the protector of the earth— [these are placed] on the head or at the foot through negligence.
Like a cluster of blossoms, there are indeed two destinies for a man of spirit:
either at the head of all the world, or fallen upon the ground in the forest.
If a gem fit for a collection of golden ornaments is set in tin, it neither cries out nor does it shine; rather, the blame falls upon the one who employed it.
Between horses, elephants, and iron; between wood, stone, and cloth;
and between women, men, and water—there is a vast difference.
For even when one whose conduct is steadfast is treated with contempt, it is impossible to destroy all his virtues;
for even when fire is cast downward by a villain, its flame never goes below.
A noble steed does not endure the stroke of the whip; a lion does not [tolerate] the trumpeting of elephants;
nor does a hero endure the terrifying sound directed at him by an enemy.
If, by fate, one is deprived of wealth or suddenly fallen from his station, he should not desire the service of wicked people, nor indeed the base;
for even when tormented by hunger, a lion does not eat grass for the sake of food, but generally drinks the warm blood of elephants.
He who desires to reunite with a friend who has once proved treacherous embraces death itself, just as a female mule conceives a fetus.
The offspring of an enemy, even if they speak sweet words, must not be overlooked by wise men;
for at the right time, they bring about calamity like dreadful vessels of poison.
One should eliminate an enemy by means of an enemy who has been won over by a favor,
just as one extracts a thorn stuck in the foot with a thorn held in the hand.
One should never think of those who are constantly intent on doing harm;
they will fall of their own accord, like trees growing on a riverbank.
For those things that are actually harmful appear in the form of benefits, and those that are beneficial take on the appearance of harm;
these always lead to the ruin of one who is dependent on fate.
Indeed, a mind that is free from sin arises when it is appropriate for the task at hand;
moreover, when destiny is favorable, a person experiences well-being in all circumstances.
In matters of investing wealth, in the acquisition of knowledge,
in eating, and in worldly dealings, he should always be free from shame.
A wealthy man, a learned Vedic scholar, a king, a river, and a physician as the fifth—
if these five are not found in a place, one should not establish a residence there.
Where the five— worldly conduct, fear, shame, courtesy, and a disposition toward generosity— are not found, one should not dwell there for even a single day.
A king who knows the divisions of time, a river, and a virtuous person as the fifth—
wherever these are not found, one should not make one's dwelling.
"O Śaunaka, it is said that there is no finality in knowledge in any single place;
everyone does not know everything, and an omniscient one does not exist anywhere."
There is no one here in this world who is all-knowing, nor is there anyone on earth who is utterly ignorant;
rather, he who understands according to his inferior, superior, or middling knowledge is a wise man by virtue of that.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: [Chapter 111 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] The Sūta said:
I shall now describe the characteristics of both the king and his servants;
for a protector of the earth must always examine them all thoroughly.
Devoted constantly to truth and righteousness, he protects the kingdom;
having conquered the enemy armies, he should protect the earth through dharma.
One should gather flower from flower, but one should not cause the destruction of the root;
like a garland-maker in the forest, and not like a charcoal-burner.
