Milk-mongers who consume milk do not eat its transformation [curd];
likewise, kings may enjoy another's kingdom, but they should not corrupt it.
Just as one who milks a cow for its milk should not cut off its udder,
so too a kingdom, when oppressed by excessive exploitation, does not prosper.
Therefore, with every effort, one should protect the earth;
for the protector, the earth shall bring fame, long life, glory, and strength.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu, a righteous king who is devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins and has conquered his senses is capable of protecting his subjects.
Having attained unstable sovereignty, a king should direct his mind toward Dharma;
for in an instant wealth may perish, and riches and the like are not under one's own control.
Truly, sensual pleasures are enchanting; truly, worldly prosperities are delightful;
yet life itself is indeed as fickle as the flickering glance from the corner of a woman's eye.
Old age stands like a tigress, threatening [all], and diseases prevail in the body like enemies;
life flows away like water from a broken jar, yet no one in this world practices what is beneficial for themselves.

O humans, why do you act without hesitation? Perform what is beneficial for others and what is conducive to your own welfare from the outset, so that you may rejoice when struck by the arrows of Madana with the slow, lingering glances of passionate women.
Do not commit sin; remain ever devoted to the twice-born and Hari. Life passes away completely, faltering under the guise of Death, which has become like a water-clock.
He who looks upon the wives of others as his own mother, upon the wealth of others as a clod of earth,
and upon all living beings as himself— he is a wise man.
For this very purpose, O best of Brahmins, do kings desire sovereignty:
that their word shall not be obstructed in any of their undertakings.
For this purpose indeed do kings accumulate wealth;
having protected themselves, they bestow that wealth upon the twice-born.
The sound of the syllable *oṃ* causes the kingdom of the brahmins to flourish;
through that practice, the king prospers and is not afflicted by diseases.
Even sages who are incapable [of worldly activity] accumulate material goods;
how much more so, then, a protector of the earth who nurtures his subjects like his own children?
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who has wealth is esteemed in this world; he who has wealth is a wise man.
Friends, sons, wives, and well-wishers abandon one who is destitute of wealth;
yet they resort to him once again when he possesses riches, for in this world, wealth is indeed a person's kinsman.
For a king who is devoid of the treatises is indeed blind;
he sees through his spies, whereas one bereft of the treatises does not see at all.
He whose sons, servants, ministers,
and priests have their senses asleep will not possess his kingdom for long.
He by whom these three— sons, servants, and kinsmen— are won,
has conquered the earth with its four oceans along with all other kings.
He who transgresses those things established by scripture and those supported by reason—
that king indeed perishes both in this world and in the next.
Upon encountering adversity, a king should not give way to mental anguish;
with an even mind and a serene soul, he should remain equanimous toward both pleasure and pain.
The steadfast, having encountered hardship, do not become despondent;
does not the moon rise again after entering the mouth of Rāhu?
"Fie, fie upon those humans who are pampered by the pleasures of the body! Do not cause distress to this very body which is already emaciated by poverty.
For it is heard that the noble sons of Pāṇḍu, though lacking wealth, abandoned their suffering and attained happiness once again."
Having mastered the science of the Gandharvas, instrumental music, and the arts of courtesans,
as well as the science of archery and the treatises on statecraft, the king shall protect the world.
That king who becomes angry with a servant without cause takes upon himself the madness of poison released by a black serpent.
One should always restrain the gaze from fickleness and refrain from false speech toward a human being, a learned brahmin, and indeed among one's own circle of servants.
A king who acts with negligence, being arrogant toward his servants and kinsmen,
is always quickly overcome by his enemies within his own realm.
A king should never constantly utter the sound "huṃ" nor knit his brows;
that base king who punishes his servants without fault shall lose all the pleasures and enjoyments of this world.
Enemies are overcome by those who remain engaged in battle while acting with ease.
Exertion, daring, fortitude, intelligence, power, and prowess—
against one whose enthusiasm is sixfold in this way, even a god trembles.
When an action has been performed with diligence and yet success is not found, destiny alone is the authority; nevertheless, human effort must always be exerted.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. [Chapter 112] Sūta said:
Servants are to be known as being of three kinds— superior, inferior, and middling—
and they should be appointed to the three corresponding types of tasks according to their fitness.
I shall now describe the examination of servants; for whatever quality belongs to each [servant], that I will fully declare, exactly as it has been told.
Just as gold is tested by four means—by rubbing, cutting, heating, and striking—so too should a servant be examined by four: by his speech, his conduct, his character, and his work.
One who is endowed with noble birth, good conduct, and virtue, devoted to truth and righteousness,
handsome, and very serene, is appointed as the superintendent of the treasury.
One who examines value and form shall become a gem appraiser;
one who thoroughly understands strengths and weaknesses is appointed as a commander-in-chief.
One who knows the truth of gestures and physical expressions, who is strong, pleasant to behold,
vigilant, and capable of subduing others, is called a *pratīhāra*.
Intelligent, eloquent, wise, truthful, and with senses subdued—
he who has thoroughly examined all the scriptures is indeed a virtuous scribe.
One who is intelligent, wise, and capable of discerning the minds of others,
who is resolute, and who speaks exactly as instructed— such a person is appointed as a messenger.
One who knows all the treatises on the Smṛtis, is learned, has conquered his senses,
and is endowed with the qualities of heroism and valor, is appointed as the Superintendent of Dharma.
One who is hereditary from his father and grandfather, skillful, learned in the scriptures, truthful in speech, pure, and firm— he is called a cook.
One who has practiced Ayurveda, whose appearance is pleasing to all,
and who is endowed with long life, virtuous conduct, and good qualities— he alone is ordained as a physician.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, is devoted to the practice of recitation and sacrifice,
and is constantly intent on bestowing blessings— such a person is the royal priest.
The king should always avoid employing as officials a scribe, a reciter, an accountant, an opponent, or one who is characterized by laziness.
The mouth of the wicked man, like that of a serpent— tongue-tied, causing agitation, cruel, and utterly terrible— is intended solely for doing harm.
A wicked person should be avoided, even if he is adorned with learning;
is a snake not terrifying, even when decorated with a jewel?
Who indeed does not feel fear toward a wicked person who displays anger without cause?
For the poison of a great serpent and the unbearable, harsh speech of such a malicious one would always fall together upon his mouth.
He who would slay a servant who is equal in purpose, equal in capability, one who knows his vital points, who is industrious,
and who takes half the kingdom, is himself not slain.
Those who possess valor yet speak with gentle and measured words, who have conquered their senses and are devoted to truth, are beneficial servants;
however, those whose conduct is the opposite of this both before and after [the task] are not beneficial servants.
Free from laziness, well-contented, and vigilant;
equanimous toward pleasure and pain—such steadfast servants are rare in the worlds.
One who lacks patience and self-control, who is cruel-minded and a reviler,
who is hypocritical, deceitful, and treacherous, who is full of envy, incapable, and terrified by fear— he must certainly be abandoned by the king.
Well-maintained missiles and various kinds of weapons should be brought into the fortress; thereafter, one should strike down the enemy.
Then, for six months or even a year, the lord of men should maintain peace while observing his own accumulated strength; thereafter, he should strike down the enemy again.
O Lord of the Earth, he who appoints fools [to office] incurs these three consequences for himself:
infamy, loss of wealth, and indeed, a fall into hell.
Whatever action he performs, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
by that the king increases, even subtly, through the work of his servants.
Therefore, a lord of the earth should always employ a wise man for the accomplishment of virtue, pleasure, and wealth, indeed for the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Science of Politics Spoken by Bṛhaspati," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—113.
Sūta said:
One should employ those who possess virtues and avoid those devoid of virtue;
for all virtues belong to the wise, while faults belong exclusively to the fool.
One should always sit with the virtuous, one should form associations with the virtuous, and engage in debate and friendship with the virtuous; one should never perform any action with the wicked.
One should remain even while in prison with those who are wise, discerning, knowers of the Dharma, and speakers of truth; one should not dwell in a kingdom with the wicked.
One who leaves tasks unfinished is joined with misfortune;
therefore, one should cause all tasks to be completed without remainder.
Just as one should milk a honey-bee for its essence without killing the flower,
so should a king milk both the earth and the cow with regard for their calves.
Just as the six-legged bee gathers honey from flowers in due order,
so should a king, having acquired wealth, make a store.
An anthill, a honeycomb, and the moon during the bright fortnight;
likewise, royal wealth and alms—each increases little by little.
Seeing the depletion of what has been earned and the accumulation of what has been given away,
one should make each day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and virtuous deeds.
Even in the forest, faults arise for those possessed by passion; even in the home, the restraint of the five senses is asceticism.
For one who engages in blameless action and from whom passion has departed, the home is a grove of asceticism.
Dharma is protected by truth; knowledge is protected by yoga;
the alms-bowl is protected by cleaning; and the family is protected by modesty.
Better is dwelling in the Vindhya forest, better is death while fasting, better is lying upon a bed infested with snakes or falling into a well,
and better is entering the midst of terrifying waters swirling in eddies than to say to one's own kin, "Give me even a small amount of wealth."
Wealth is not exhausted by enjoyment when one’s fortune has declined; for as long as previously acquired merit remains, riches never perish.
Knowledge is the ornament of Brahmins, the king is the ornament of the earth,
the moon is the ornament of the sky, and good character is the ornament of everything.

These sons of kings, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the others—heroes equal to the moon, true to their vows, possessing bodies like the sun, and protected by Keśava—are now situated among malevolent planets, fallen under the power of the wretched, and have gone forth to live on alms. For who is capable of anything? By the force of destiny, the lines of karma cause one to wander.
Salutation to that Ear, by whom Brahmā was confined within the vessel of the cosmic egg like a potter’s clay; by whom Viṣṇu was cast into the great peril of the thicket of his ten incarnations;
by whom Rudra was made to wander for alms with a skull held in the hollow of his hands; and by whom the Sun is made to revolve eternally in the sky.
The donor was Bali, the beggar was Murāri, and the gift was the earth in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas;
having given it, only imprisonment as the fruit was obtained. Homage be to you, O Fate, who acts according to your own will!
Even if Lakṣmī were his mother and Janārdana himself were his father,
punishment would always fall upon him for harboring such evil thoughts and acting accordingly.

Wherever, in whatever manner, and in whatever way one’s well-determined karma was performed in the past, that very same thing one has personally instilled within oneself must be experienced in the interim.
Suffering is ordained by oneself; happiness is ordained by oneself.
Indeed, from the time one takes up the bed of the womb, one experiences the results of previous lives.

For a man cannot escape the consequences of the karma he has created, whether by fleeing into the atmosphere, into the midst of the ocean, or by entering a cleft between mountains; nor can he escape it even if held upon his mother’s head or cradled in her lap.

With poison as its triple rampart, the ocean as its moat, the *rākṣasas* as its warriors, and the supreme science of polity (*artha-śāstra*) taught by Uśanas as its sustenance— that Rāvaṇa has perished through the power of Time.
In whatever age, at whatever time, whether by day or by night,
and in whatever muhūrta or moment [it occurs], it is exactly so and not otherwise.
They travel through the atmosphere or enter into the surface of the earth;
they sustain all the directions, yet nothing is perceived that has not been given.
Knowledge previously studied, wealth previously given, and actions performed in the past—these indeed run ahead of one who runs. (GarP 1.113.24)
In this world, karmas are the primary factor; even though Janakī was born under an auspicious asterism and a favorable planet, and at a moment fixed by Vasiṣṭha, she became a vessel for suffering.
When Rāma has thick calves, when Lakṣmaṇa moves with a sound,
and when Sītā has thick hair— those three have become vessels of suffering.
A son does not go [to hell] by the karma of his father, nor does a father by the karma of his son;
they go by what they themselves have done, bound by their own actions.
In bodies produced by karma, physical and mental diseases fall here like arrows released by firm archers.
Otherwise, a wise man seeks his goal with an intellect pregnant with the teachings of the scriptures;
like a master, he ordains his previously performed karma in such a way that it does not act otherwise.
Whether a child, a youth, or an old man, whoever performs good or evil deeds,
he experiences the fruit thereof in that very state of existence, life after life.
Even a man who does not look forward, even a person living in a foreign land,
is led by the wind of his own past actions to wherever that fruit awaits.
A human being obtains the wealth that is destined to be obtained; even a god is not able to prevent it.
Therefore, I do not grieve, nor is there any wonder in me, for the line upon my forehead does not change—that which is ours cannot belong to others.
A snake in a well, an elephant on one's shoulder, and a rat running in its hole—a man flees even more swiftly than these; but from whom can one escape the consequences of one's own karma?
True knowledge does not become diminished; even when being given away, it increases.
Like water contained within a well, it indeed becomes abundant.
Those who have attained prosperity through righteousness are truly virtuous, whereas those who have attained it through unrighteousness are not;
for in this world, both dharma and artha are great, and one should remember this for the sake of achieving one's purpose.
If the very same sufferings that a wretched person undergoes for the sake of food were instead undertaken for the sake of the Dharma, one would no longer be a vessel for affliction.
Of all forms of purity, purity regarding food is preeminent;
he who is pure by means of the objects of food is truly pure, whereas one is not made pure by clay or water alone.
Truthfulness is purity, purity of mind is purity, restraint of the senses is purity,
compassion toward all beings is purity, and water-purity is the fifth.
For one who possesses truth and purity, heaven is not difficult to attain;
indeed, he whose speech is truthful excels even the horse sacrifice.
Indeed, even with a thousand applications of clay and a hundred rinsings with water,
one of evil conduct whose consciousness is corrupted by inner disposition is not purified.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
He does not rejoice in honors nor does he become angry at insults;
one who, when provoked, would not speak harshly—this is the characteristic of a virtuous person.
When a wise and pleasant man who is poor hears beneficial words at the proper time, no one is satisfied with him.
That which cannot be obtained by mortals through the power of mantras, through heroism, through wisdom, or through human effort— what cause for lamentation is there in that?
"Obtained by me without being asked, and having gone again at my command; it has gone back to where it came from—what cause for lamentation is there in that?"
On a single tree, various birds always gather together at night;
at dawn, they depart for other directions—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
When all those traveling together as a single caravan are headed for the same destination,
what cause for lamentation is there if one among them travels more quickly?
O Śaunaka, beings have an unmanifest origin, a manifest middle state, and an unmanifest end;
what cause for lamentation is there in this?
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has arrived does not live on, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
One obtains only what is to be obtained; one goes only where it is to be gone;
one encounters only those sufferings and joys that are to be encountered.
A person obtains each of those things; what will idle talk accomplish?
Just as flowers and fruits, even without being prompted, do not bypass their own proper time, so too does previously performed karma.
Neither moral conduct, nor lineage, nor learning, nor wisdom, nor virtues, nor purity of seed [matters];
rather, the fortunes previously acquired through austerity bear fruit for him in due time, just like trees.
In that place where death is the slayer, and in that place where there is prosperity and wealth,
he goes of his own accord, impelled by his own past actions.
Action performed in the past follows its doer,
just as among thousands of cows, a calf finds its mother.
"In this way, karma performed in the past follows its doer.
O fool, enjoy the fruit of your own good deeds; why do you lament?"
Just as an action previously performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
so indeed does the doer follow it in another birth.
A base person sees the faults of others even when they are as small as mustard seeds, yet even when seeing his own faults as large as bilva fruits, he does not see them.
O twice-born one, for those possessed of passion, hatred, and the like, there is no happiness anywhere;
indeed, upon reflection, I see that true happiness exists only where there is peace.
Where there is attachment, there is fear; attachment is a vessel for suffering.
Sufferings have their root in attachment; when that is abandoned, there is great happiness.
The body itself is the abode of both suffering and happiness;
both life and the body are born together with birth itself.
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.
After happiness comes suffering, and after suffering comes happiness;
for human beings, happiness and suffering revolve like a wheel.
That which has passed is gone; if it were still far away, it would exist as something present. One who understands this is not afflicted by grief.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: [This is followed by the beginning of the one hundred and fourteenth chapter of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.]
No one is anyone's friend, nor is anyone anyone's enemy;
friends and enemies alike arise solely from specific causes.
By whom was this jewel-mine created: the two syllables "mitra" (friend), which provide protection from sorrow, protection from fear, and are a vessel for joy and trust?
By whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" are uttered even once,
the girdle has been fastened by him for the journey toward liberation.
Men do not place such trust in their mother, nor in their wives, nor in a uterine brother, nor even in their own son,
as they do in a friend born of their own nature.
If one desires eternal joy, one should completely avoid these three faults:
gambling, the investment of wealth, and looking at another's wife in their absence.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a wise man.
Lust, which finds perverse pleasure, does not exist among those who are self-controlled;
for just as there is a means of slaughter, so too does punishment follow.
Even the course of the wind at the end of an eon, or of a horse, or of the great ocean, can be understood;
but the course of one who is not free from passion cannot be understood.
There is no opportunity, there is no privacy, and there is no man who solicits her;
for that reason, O Śaunaka, the virtue of chastity arises in women.
Indeed, one woman always serves another, even if she is devoted to her husband, due to the lack of men. (Garuda Purāṇa 1.114.10)
Whatever secrets a mother, afflicted by passion, may commit, they should not be considered by her sons as violations of moral conduct.
Sleep dependent on others, following the activities of another's heart, constant mockery and laughter, even freedom from grief,
the body staked as a wager with its throat torn by the hooves of lecherous men, and a livelihood sustained by intense longing— such is the life of a courtesan, highly esteemed in this world.
Fire, water, women, fools, serpents, and royal households—these six must always be approached with caution; they can take one's life instantly.
What is surprising if a Brahmin, skilled in the Vedic scriptures, should be a learned scholar? What is surprising if a king, skilled in the science of governance, should be righteous?
What is surprising if a woman, endowed with beauty and youth, should be virtuous? But it is truly a marvel if a man, even though he is destitute, should never commit an evil deed.
One should not reveal one's own vulnerabilities to others, but should discern the vulnerabilities of others;
one should conceal one's own limbs like a tortoise and observe the conduct of others.
Dwelling in the depths of the netherworld, situated within high walls—
if women were not obtainable through the mere parting of one's hair, by whom would they not be won?
For one who knows the vital points, who is sharp, and who is like a thorn to his own kin— even though he shares the same nature—
does not afflict as much as an external enemy who has established enmity.
He is truly wise who wins over the fool with sweets, the disciplined with discipline,
a woman with wealth, the gods with austerity, and all the worlds through excellent gathering.

Those who desire a friend through deceit, righteousness through impurity, the cultivation of prosperity through the torment of others, knowledge through ease, or a woman through mere manliness— truly, they are not wise.
If a foolish man should cut down a fruit-bearing tree for the sake of its fruit,
his undertaking will indeed be fruitless, and he shall incur a great transgression.
O Brahmin, I do not believe that a man who drinks liquor can truly be an ascetic, one who possesses the means for practice, one who has exerted himself from afar, or even a virtuous woman. 114.21.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one trust even a friend;
for a friend, when provoked to anger, might reveal all one's secrets.
Trusting in all beings and being virtuous toward all beings—one should conceal one's own nature within oneself; this indeed is the characteristic of a holy man.
Whatever action has been performed, it follows the doer;
therefore, even while engaged in any activity whatsoever, one should maintain a resolute mind.
An elderly woman, fresh liquor, dried meat, the three radishes,
curd at night, and sleeping during the day— a wise man should avoid these six.
For a poor man, social gathering is poison; for an old man, a young woman is poison;
poorly taught knowledge is poison; and food eaten during indigestion is poison.
Song is dear to the unimpeded; a high seat is dear to the base;
giving is dear to the poor; and a young woman is dear to a man.
Excessive drinking of water, eating hard food, the suppression of natural urges, the wasting of the bodily constituents,
sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night— by these six, diseases dwell within men.

Early morning sunlight, excessive sexual intercourse, smoke from cremation grounds, warming the palms over a fire, and looking at a woman during her menses— these indeed cause one’s very long life to be diminished.
Dried meat, old women, the morning sun, fresh curd,
sexual intercourse at dawn, and sleep— these six are immediately life-taking.
Freshly clarified butter, grapes, a young woman, a meal of milk,
warm water, and the shade of a tree— these six instantly take away one's life.
Water from a well, the shade of a banyan tree,
and the breasts of women are warm during the cold season and cool during the hot season.
Three things immediately increase strength: oil massage for children, wholesome food, and rest;
while three things immediately take away strength: travel, sexual intercourse, and fever.
One should never eat dried meat or drink milk together with one's wife or friends, nor with kings; for such acts cause separation in an instant.
Even the Goddess Śrī abandons one who wears tattered clothes, who bears stains upon his teeth, who eats excessively, who speaks harsh words,
and who sleeps at sunrise or even at sunset— even if he holds the discus in his hand.
Constant cutting of grass, scratching the ground, rubbing the feet, impurity of the teeth, wearing soiled garments, and roughness of the hair;

sleeping during the two twilights, sleeping naked, excessive eating and laughing, and playing musical instruments upon one's own body or a seat—these would bring about the loss of even Keśava’s own fortune.
A well-washed head, well-massaged feet, attendance upon beautiful women, moderation in eating,
not sleeping naked, and avoiding sexual intercourse on forbidden days— these six bring back prosperity that has long been lost.
Indeed, by wearing any flower— especially the pāṇāḍara—
upon one's head, misfortune (alakṣmī) is destroyed.
The western shadow of a lamp, the shadow of a bed or a seat,
and whatever auspiciousness resides at the bathing place of a washerman— therein Fortune herself abides.
One who desires long life should avoid the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, an elderly woman, fresh curd, and the dust raised by a broom. (GarP 1.114.40)
One should know that the dust raised by elephants, horses, chariots, grain, and cows is auspicious; however, one should recognize it as inauspicious when raised by donkeys, camels, goats, and sheep.
The dust of cows, the dust of grain, and the dust arising from the body of a son—
this dust is highly auspicious and is the destroyer of great sins.
The dust of goats, the dust of donkeys, and the dust raised by brooms—
this dust is a great evil and a cause of great sin.
The wind from a winnowing basket, water from the tips of fingernails, the water used for wiping after bathing,
water from the hair, and the dust from a broom destroy previously accumulated merit.
One should not pass between two Brahmins, nor between a Brahmin and a fire, nor between a husband and wife, nor between two masters, nor between a horse and a bull.
What wise person would place their trust in women, kings, fire, serpents, the study of one's own scriptures, the service of enemies, or the tasting of sensual pleasures?
One should not trust the untrustworthy; one should not over-trust even the trustworthy.
Danger arising from misplaced trust cuts away even the very roots.
If one remains trusting after having made peace with an enemy,
he is like one who has fallen asleep at the top of a tree and only awakens when he has already fallen.
One should not be excessively mild, nor should one be excessively harsh in action;
for the mild is overcome by the mild alone, and the cruel by the cruel alone.
One should not be excessively straight, nor likewise excessively soft;
for there, the straight trees are cut down, while the crooked ones remain standing.
Fruit-bearing trees bend, and virtuous people bow;
but dry trees and fools break apart and do not bend.
Just as unwanted sufferings come and go, so should a man treat those who seek him out, like a cat that pounces upon its prey.
The noble always act with abundance both before and after;
the ignoble act in the opposite manner. Therefore, conduct yourself as you wish.
A secret counsel with six ears is leaked; one with four ears is maintained;
but even Brahmā does not discover the end of a counsel that has only two ears.
What is the use of a cow that neither gives milk nor bears calves? What is the purpose of a son who is born but is neither learned nor righteous? (GarP 1.114.55)
By even a single good son who is wise, endowed with learning,
and a lion among men, a family is illuminated, just as the sky is by the moon.
By even a single fine tree, when in bloom and fragrant,
the entire forest is made to smell sweet, just as a family is by a noble son.
For one virtuous son is better than a hundred devoid of merit;
the moon alone dispels the darkness, not even a thousand stars.
One should pamper [the son] for five years, and for ten years one should discipline him;
but when the sixteenth year has arrived, one should treat the son like a friend.
Being born, he takes away the wife; growing up, he takes away the wealth;
dying, he takes away the life-breaths. There is no enemy equal to a son.
Some are tigers with the faces of deer, and some are deer with the faces of tigers;
for when one does not recognize their true nature, there is indeed distrust at every step.
There is one fault for those who possess patience; a second does not exist:
that people consider one endowed with patience to be weak.
One should approve of this alone, for enjoyments are indeed subject to momentary destruction;
moreover, the thoughts of one who is discerning toward those he holds dear are truly undisturbed.
O Śaunaka, when the father has died, the eldest brother is equal to a father;
for he becomes the father of them all and the protector of them all.
He conducts himself with impartiality toward all his youngest [dependents],
whether they live together with him in shared enjoyments or are like his own sons.
For the combination of many things of little substance is indeed formidable;
a rope woven from blades of grass can even bind an elephant.
For he who, having stolen the property of another, bestows it as a gift, that donor goes to hell; the fruit of that act belongs to the owner of the wealth.
By the destruction of the property of the gods, by the seizing of the property of Brahmins,
and by the transgression against Brahmins, families fall from their noble status to that of being non-noble.

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
The ancestors and the gods do not eat the offerings of one who is mean-spirited,
a husband of a low-caste woman, one conquered by his wife, or one in whose house lives a paramour.
Know that one who is ungrateful, ignoble, long-simmering in anger, and dishonest—these four are *caṇḍālas*; the fifth is he who is born as such by birth.
An enemy of weak intellect must not be neglected even if he is small out of contempt;
for even a tiny fire, if not extinguished, reduces the entire world to ashes.
It is my conviction that he who is peaceful in his youth is truly peaceful;
for when the bodily elements are wasting away, in whom does tranquility not arise?
O best of Brahmins, since prosperity is common to all like public roads, one should not become filled with joy thinking, "This is mine. (GarP 1,114.74)
The body is dependent on the mind and subject to the elements; when the mind is destroyed, the elements go to destruction.
Therefore, the mind must always be protected; when the mind is healthy, the elements flourish.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Great Essence of Ethics," in the section on Conduct within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—115] Sūta said:
One should avoid from afar a bad wife, a bad friend, a bad king, a bad son, a bad daughter, and a bad country.
Dharma has gone forth into exile, asceticism has wavered, and truth has departed far away; the earth yields fruitless results, people are deceitful, and the Brahmins are addicted to greed.
Mortals are under the sway of women, women are fickle, and base people have risen to high positions. Alas, what a misery is life indeed in the Kali age! Blessed are those people who are already dead.
Blessed are those who do not witness the ruin of their country, the destruction of their family, their wives' infidelity, or their son's addiction to vice.
There is no peace with a bad son; how can there be delight in a bad wife?
There is no trust in a bad friend; there is no security of life in a bad kingdom.
The food of others, the property of others, the beds of others, the wives of others,
and dwelling in the house of another— even from Śakra himself, these will take away one’s prosperity.
Sin is transmitted among men through conversation, through physical contact, through social association, through eating together,
and through sharing seats, beds, and vehicles.
Women are ruined by beauty; asceticism is destroyed by anger;
cattle perish by wandering at will; and the best of the twice-born is ruined by the food of a Śūdra.
From sharing a seat, from sharing a bed, and from mixing in the same row for a meal, sin transfers from one person to another like water from one jar to another. (GarP 1.115.8)
There are many faults in pampering and many virtues in striking;
therefore, one should strike both a disciple and a son, but not pamper them.
For embodied beings, time is old age; for mountains, water is old age;
for women, lack of enjoyment is old age; and for garments, the sun's heat is old age.
The base desire strife; the mediocre desire peace;
the excellent desire honor, for honor is the wealth of the great.
For pride is the root of wealth; when pride exists, what is the use of riches?
For one whose pride and arrogance have fallen away, what is the use of wealth or even of life?
The base desire wealth; those of middle rank desire both wealth and honor;
the best desire honor alone, for honor is indeed the wealth of the great.
Even in the forest, lions do not bow to anyone, nor do they look for meat when they are hungry;
those born into noble families, though deprived of wealth, do not undertake base occupations.
No consecration or ritual refinement is performed for the lion in the forest;
for one whose strength is ever-magnificent, the sovereignty of the king of beasts is his by himself.
A negligent merchant, a deceitful person, a proud monk, a dissolute man, a poor lover,
an unlovely woman, and one who speaks unpleasantly— these do not undertake their respective tasks.
A donor who is poor, a miser who is wealthy, a son who is disobedient, service to a wicked person,
and death while helping others— these five arise as the misdeeds of a man.
Separation from a beloved, humiliation by one's own kin, a remaining debt, service to a wicked person,
and friends who turn their faces away due to one's poverty— these five intense fires burn even without physical fire.
And among those thousands of anxieties, four anxieties are like the edge of a sword:
being insulted by the low-born, a wife who is hungry, a wife who is disaffected, and the obstruction of one's own kin.
Subjugation, a son, wealth, knowledge, health, association with the virtuous,
a beloved wife who is obedient— these five are the uprooters of suffering.
The deer, the elephant, the moth, the bee, and the fish—these five are slain by five [senses] alone;
how can that one destroyer not be slain who indulges in all five with all five?
One who is impatient, harsh, arrogant, poorly dressed, or has come uninvited— these five types of brahmins are not to be honored, even if they are equal to Bṛhaspati himself.
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death—
these five are distinguished for the embodied being at the very moment of birth.
In climbing mountains, in water, in a herd of cows, in subduing the wicked,
and in rising from a fall— these five qualities are traditionally held to be excellent.
The shadow of a cloud, affection for a rogue, intimacy with another's wife—
these five things, as well as youth and wealth, are indeed unstable.
In this world, life is unstable; wealth and youth are unstable;
sons, wives, and the like are unstable; but Dharma, fame, and glory are stable.
A hundred-year lifespan is exceedingly short; night takes half of it away.
Even that remaining half is rendered fruitless by the exhaustion of disease, grief, and old age.
The lifespan of humans is limited to a hundred years; half of that is spent at night, and more than half of what remains passes in childhood.

A small portion is spent in the suffering of separation from kin and death, while another is consumed in service to kings. What is the use of pride for those who possess only the remainder, which is as fickle as the heart of a wave upon the water?
In this world, death, consisting of day and night, moves about in the form of old age;
it devours all beings just as a serpent swallows the wind.
Whether walking or standing, waking or sleeping, if one does not act like a beast for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, [one has failed]. (GarP 1,115.30)

What difference is there between a beast and that man-beast whose intellect is devoid of discernment regarding what is harmful and beneficial, who has been subjected to much deliberation during the time of sacred learning, yet whose mind finds satisfaction merely in filling its belly?
He whose fame is not celebrated for heroism, austerity, or generosity,
nor for learning or the acquisition of wealth, is merely his mother’s excrement.

That which is lived even for a moment by men renowned for their wisdom, prowess, and fame, and whose honor remains unbroken—that indeed, the knowers declare, is called true life; for even a crow lives long and eats the offerings of others.
What is the use of life devoid of wealth and honor? What is the use of a friend who is full of fear and suspicion?
Practice the vow of a lion; go forth and do not despair! Even a crow lives for a long time and eats the offerings of others.

He who here shows no compassion toward himself, his teacher, his circle of servants, the destitute, nor toward the affairs of his friends—what is the fruit of his life in the world of men? Even a crow lives long and consumes offerings.
He whose days come and go devoid of the three aims of life does not truly live, even though he breathes like the bellows of a blacksmith.
The fruitfulness of one whose conduct is self-dependent lies in not being dependent on others;
those whose actions are dependent on others are dead even while they live.
Indeed, base men are easily satisfied; a handful of grain for mice is easily filled. Yet the dissatisfied base man is satisfied even with very little.
The shadow of a cloud, fire from grass, service to the lowly, water on a road,
a courtesan’s passion, and affection for a wicked person— these six are like bubbles.
The world does not find happiness through speech that is devoid of substance;
for life has pride as its root—when pride withers, whence can there be happiness?
The strength of the weak is the king; the strength of the child is crying;
the strength of the fool is silence; indeed, the strength of the thief is falsehood.
For in whatever measure a person masters the scripture, to that same extent his intelligence shall increase and his specialized knowledge shall shine forth.
For in whatever way a person directs his mind toward what is wholesome,
in that very way he becomes beloved by the world everywhere.
A person is ruined by these three: greed, negligence, and misplaced trust.
Therefore, one should not be greedy, nor negligent, nor should one trust.
One should fear as long as the danger has not yet arrived;
but once the intense danger has arisen, one should indeed remain fearless.
A remainder of debt, a remainder of fire, and likewise a remainder of disease increase again and again; therefore, one should not leave any remainder.
One should return a favor for a favor, and an injury for an injury;
I see no fault in this, for one should practice evil toward the wicked.
One should avoid such a friend who destroys one's interests in one's absence but speaks pleasantly in one's presence; he is likewise an enemy composed of deceit.
For even a virtuous person perishes through association with the wicked;
even clear water is made turbid by mud.
He eats as a true twice-born one eats; such is the determination regarding the sharing of the remnants.
Therefore, with every effort, the twice-born should be honored with diligence.
That is truly enjoyed which is the remnant of what has been eaten by the twice-born; he is wise who commits no evil;
that is true friendship which is performed in one's absence; and that is dharma which is practiced without hypocrisy.
That is no assembly where there are no elders; they are not elders who do not speak the Dharma.
That is not Dharma for us where truth is absent; that is not truth which is pierced by deceit.
Among men, the Brahmin is supreme; among radiant things, the sun;
among all limbs, the head; and among vows, truth is the highest.
That is auspiciousness where the mind is serene; that is true life which is not service to another;
that is truly earned which is enjoyed by one's own kin; and that is the roar of warriors which is [the slaying] of enemies in battle.
That woman should not give way to intoxication; he is happy who is abandoned by craving.
That is a true friend in whom there is trust; that man has conquered his senses.
In that regard, where respect and affection have been abandoned and friendship has vanished,
only that [self-praise] is to be commended by which one's own self is made the object of praise.
One should not search for the source of rivers, of *agnihotra* sacrifices, of the *Bhārata*, or of a water-jar; for a fault is never removed by tracing it back to its origin.
Rivers end at the salt ocean; sexual union ends with the exhaustion of women;
gossip ends with slander; and wealth ends with the threefold suffering.
Royal fortune ends with a Brahmin’s curse; spiritual luster ends with sin;
residence in a cowherd settlement ends with a ritual sipping of water; and a lineage ends with a woman, O Lord.
All dwellings end in decay; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death.
If he wishes for [the deceased] to return, he should follow him no further than a short distance;
he should turn back at the edge of water or from a tree of glossy appearance.
One should not dwell where there is no leader, nor where there are too many leaders;
one should not dwell where a woman is the leader, but one may dwell where a fool is the leader.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.
One should abandon a barren wife in the eighth year, one whose children have died in the ninth,
one who gives birth only to daughters in the eleventh, and one who speaks unpleasantly immediately.
Because men do not desire them, out of fear of their own attendants,
and because they have transgressed the bounds of propriety regarding wealth, women remain dependent upon their husbands.
A wise person should avoid from afar a weary horse, an elephant in rut, cows that have recently calved, and frogs in waterless places.
For those distressed by worldly affairs, there is neither friend nor kinsman; for those distressed by desire, there is neither fear nor shame;
for those distressed by anxiety, there is neither happiness nor sleep; for those distressed by hunger, there is neither strength nor vigor.
Whence can there be sleep for the poor man, for one who is a servant to others,
for one addicted to another's wife, and for one who steals another's property?
The man who is free from debt and free from disease sleeps happily; likewise, he who eats with ample space and is not overly attached to his wife sleeps happily.
A lotus rises high above the water;
a servant becomes arrogant when his master is powerful.
For a lotus remaining in its place, the sun and Varuṇa are friends; yet for that very same lotus when displaced from its place, they cause its withering and drying up.
Those who are friends to one established in his own position become his enemies;
the sun loves the lotus in the water, yet it causes the drying up and uprooting of the land.
Those who remain in their proper place are honored, and those established in their station are honored;
but when they have fallen from their place, men—like hair, teeth, and nails—are no longer honored.
Conduct reveals one's family; speech reveals one's country;
eagerness reveals affection; and the body reveals one's diet. (GarP 1.115.74)
Rain upon the ocean is in vain; food for one who is already satiated is in vain;
a gift to the wealthy is in vain; and good deeds performed by a base person are in vain.
Even one who is far away is near if he dwells in another's heart;
but even one who is nearby is far away if he has departed from the heart.
A distorted face, a dejected voice, perspiration on the body, and great fear—
those very signs that appear at death are present in the beggar.
Better is the birth of one who dwells on a mountain peak— such as that of Kubja, Kīṭaghāta, or one expelled by the wind— than a life of begging.
Since Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, assumed the form of a dwarf after being entreated [by Bali],
who else could be more exalted than he, such that even his purpose does not incur diminution?
The mother is an enemy and the father is a foe to those children who have not been taught;
they do not shine in the midst of an assembly, just as cranes do not shine among swans.

Knowledge is indeed a beauty superior to that of a handsome form; knowledge is wealth well-guarded; knowledge is the achiever of good deeds and the maker of one beloved by the people; knowledge is the teacher of teachers.
Knowledge is the destroyer of the suffering of kinsmen; knowledge is the supreme deity; knowledge is honored among kings; for a man devoid of knowledge is but a beast.
Whatever wealth and property is seen within the interior of the house should be taken away entirely; however, the knowledge [of this spell] shall not be carried off by others.
In former times, Viṣṇu recounted the *Śaunakīya*, the *Nītisāra*, and all the *Vratas*; there, Śaṅkara heard them,
from Śaṅkara Vyāsa heard them, and from Vyāsa they were heard by us.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Essence of Ethics and Other Teachings Spoken by Śaunaka," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa— 116] Brahmā said:
O Vyāsa, I shall describe the vows by which Hari becomes the bestower of all;
when Hari is worshipped on every month, asterism, lunar day, and weekday.
By means of eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, offering fruit, and so forth,
one bestows wealth, grain, and the like, as well as sons, sovereignty, victory, and other such blessings.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), Vaiśvānara and Kubera, when worshipped, grant wealth;
likewise, Poṣya Brahmā and Śrī, when honored on the first day, as well as Aśvinī, [grant prosperity].
On the second [tithi], Yama; on this [occasion], Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa bestows wealth.
On the third, the three deities—Gaurī, Vighneśa, and Śaṅkara.
On the fourth day, Hari is worshipped as the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha); on the fifth, Kārttikeya;
on the sixth, Ravi; and on the seventh, Bhāskara, the bestower of wealth.
On the eighth and ninth days of the month of Durgā, one should worship the Mothers and the deities who grant the objects of the directions;
on the tenth day, Yama; and on the eleventh, the Moon and the Sages.
On the twelfth day Hari [is worshipped], on the thirteenth Kāma, on the fourteenth Maheśvara, and on the fifteenth Brahmā and the Pitṛs, who bestow wealth.
On the new moon day, the days of the week beginning with Sunday (Bhāskara) are to be worshipped;
likewise, the lunar mansions and the astrological conjunctions, when honored, bestow all things.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Vows for Lunar Days and Other Occasions," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 117] Brahmā said:
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, known as Vyāsānaṅga-trayodaśī,
one should use a tooth-stick made from *mallikā* wood and worship Śiva with *dhuttūra* flowers.
One should offer an oblation to Anaṅga and then consume honey during the Pauṣa month.
One should worship Yogeśvara with bilva leaves and flowers from the kadamba tree;
the tooth-stick should be made of sandalwood or similar wood, and the food offering should consist of kṛsara and other such items.
O Sage, having worshipped Naṭeśvara with kunda flowers and a garland of pearls in the month of Māgha,
one should use a tooth-stick made of *plakṣa* wood and offer *pūrikā* as the food offering.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship Vīreśvara with marūbaka flowers;
sugar, vegetables, and maṇḍa [should be offered], and a tooth-stick made from mango wood should be used.
In the month of Caitra, one should worship Su-rūpa and consume camphor at night;
for tooth-cleaning, one should use the wood of the *aṭa* tree, and as an offering, one should present *śaṣkulī*.
In Vaiśākha, the worship of Śambhu is performed with *damanaka* and *aśoka* flowers;
for the one of great form (*mahārūpa*), the food offering (*naivedya*) consists of rice cooked with jaggery (*guḍabhakta*) and *puṭṭabara*.
One should chew a tooth-stick and likewise offer nutmeg;
one should worship Pradyumna in the month of Jyeṣṭha with campaka flowers and chew a tooth-stick made of bilva.
Likewise, for one who has committed the sixth offense against the teaching of Umāpati, one should worship with agallochum, a tooth-stick, and apāmārga grass. GarP_1,117.8 //
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer *karavīra* flowers to Śambhu, the wielder of the trident;
by consuming fragrant substances and offering clarified butter and other items, one performs the purification of the *karavīra* flower.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Sadyojāta with bakula flowers and cakes;
and in Āśvina, one should worship Madanaka, the lord of the Gandharvas, and Surādhipa.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Rudra with Campaka flowers, golden water-lilies, and by offering victor-modakas, while using a tooth-stick made of Khadira wood.
The tooth-stick should be from the *badarī* tree, and the tenth meal consists of *madana* fruits;
one who provides milk and vegetables should worship Śiva with lotuses at the end of the year.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame, rice, and other grains, along with perfumes and other substances, into the fire while Rati, Muktamananga, and [the deity] seated upon the golden mandala are present.
Having performed worship with songs and instrumental music throughout the night,
one should present to a twice-born man a bed, a vessel, an umbrella, a garment, and a pair of sandals.
A man who devoutly feeds a cow and a twice-born shall have fulfilled his purpose. This entire concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for all vows should be understood as being of this nature;
and the fruit thereof shall consist of prosperity, sons, health, good fortune, and heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Vow of Anaṅga-Trayodaśī," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—118. Brahmā said:
I shall describe the vow of Akhaṇḍa-Dvādaśī, which brings about absolute liberation.
Having fasted on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should subsist on cow products.
On the twelfth lunar day, one should worship Viṣṇu and, for four months, give a vessel filled with five kinds of grain to a Brahmin, reciting this: GarP_1,118.2 //
O Viṣṇu, whatever vow has been performed by me throughout seven births,
may it remain unbroken for me here, O Blessed One, through your grace.
O Supreme Person, just as you alone are the entire world in its undivided totality,
so too do all these undivided portions truly belong to me.
One who performs the vow by offering vessels of roasted barley flour mixed with ghee at the beginning of Caitra and the beginning of Śrāvaṇa,
having fulfilled the vow, shall become a partaker of women, sons, and heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Akhaṇḍa-dvādaśī Vow," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—119.
Brahmā said:
I shall describe the Agastyārghya-vrata, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it should be performed when the sun has not yet entered Virgo, during the three days of the [solar] transit.
O Sage, having worshipped the image made of kāśa flowers in the water-jar, one should indeed offer the arghya to Agastya while keeping a vigil at nightfall.
Having worshipped with curd, unbroken grains, and other offerings, and having fasted with fruits and flowers,
[one should offer] that which is endowed with five colors and provided with gold and silver.
One should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented with the mantra "Agastyaḥ khanamāna," using a vessel filled with seven kinds of grain and smeared with curd and sandalwood paste.
Resembling a jasmine flower, born from fire and wind,
son of Mitra and Varuṇa, O pot-born one, homage be to you!
A Śūdra, a woman, and others should abandon grain, fruit, and liquids by this very [rite];
one should give a water-pot along with gold and a sacrificial fee to a twice-born man;
and having performed it for seven years, one should feed seven twice-born men, thereby becoming a partaker of all [merits].
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Vow of the Arghya Offering to Agastya," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—
120] Brahmā said:
I shall now describe the Rambhā-tṛtīyā, which bestows good fortune, prosperity, sons, and other blessings;
one should fast on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Then, with bilva leaves and holding kuśa grass water in his hand, he should worship Gaurī;
in the month of Pauṣa, he should worship the Daughter of the Mountain at the Kadamba tree and other such sites with marubaka flowers.

One who gives camphor and the like, one who gives *kṛsara* (rice and peas), one who uses jasmine for his tooth-stick, one who offers the *Subhadrā* [flower] in the month of Māgha, one who offers white water-lilies (*kalhāra*), one who consumes ghee, and one who gives *maṇḍaka* cakes; // GarP_1,120.3 //
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship Gomatī with a tooth-stick made of *gītī* wood;
having fashioned a tooth-stick from *kunda* flowers, one who possesses life-force should offer *śaṣkulī* cakes.
In the month of Caitra, one should worship Viśālākṣī with *damanaka* flowers;
offering *kṛsara*, consuming curd, using the *tagara* tree for the tooth-stick, and one should worship Śrīmukhī.
In Vaiśākha, one who gives a banyan tree should worship with *karṇikāra* and *aśoka* flowers;
in Jyeṣṭha, the giver of a plot of land should worship Nārāyaṇī with hundred-petaled lotuses;
indeed, he becomes a possessor of cloves; and in Āṣāḍha, one should worship Mādhavī.
One who eats sesame seeds with bilva leaves and offers milk-rice and *vaṭaka* cakes,
and uses an udumbara tooth-stick and *tagara* [flowers], attains prosperity in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Māllika, one should worship with the best of milky tooth-sticks;
in Bhādrapada, one should worship with lotuses, offering horns and giving food to the hungry.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should cause the princess to consume jīraka with japā flowers at night; in Kārtika, one should worship her with food offerings consisting of kṛsara.
One who subsists on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should worship Padmaja with jasmine flowers;
at the end of the year, one should honor Brahmins together with their wives with offerings of rice cooked in ghee.
Having worshipped Umāmaheśvara, one should offer molasses and other gifts;
having kept a vigil at night with garments, umbrellas, gold, and so forth,
and giving cows and other items in the morning accompanied by songs and instrumental music, one attains everything.
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Rambhā-Tṛtīyā Vow," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—
121] Brahmā said:
He declared that one should perform the Cāturmāsya vows on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī),
or on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, after having worshipped Hari with all [one's being].
"O Lord Keśava, since you are pleased with me, may this vow which I have undertaken in your presence attain its fulfillment without obstacle."
O Lord Janārdana, if I should die while this vow, once undertaken, remains unfulfilled, may it become complete for me through your grace.
Having worshipped in this manner, one who desires to perform the vow of Hari should undertake the observance, worship, recitation, and so forth; thus, all evil is brought to destruction.
Having bathed and performed worship, one should undertake vows, ritual worship, recitation,
and so forth; he who, having bathed, worships Viṣṇu for four months by eating but one meal a day, goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from all impurity.
One who has abandoned liquor, meat, and wine, who knows the Vedas, and who worships Hari,
attains the world of Viṣṇu— free from oil— by performing even a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance dedicated to Viṣṇu.
By fasting for one night, one becomes a celestial deity dwelling in a vimāna;
by eating only at every sixth meal-time, a man shall go to Śvetadvīpa after three nights.
Through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance one attains the abode of Hari and liberation unasked;
through the Prājāpatya, the world of Viṣṇu; and by performing the Parāka vow, one reaches Hari.
One who subsists on barley meal and barley gruel as alms, one who eats milk, curd, and ghee,

one whose food consists of cow’s urine and barley gruel, one who consumes the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one who eats vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like, and one who avoids savory juices— such a person is a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Cāturmāsya Vow," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 122 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Brahmā said:
I shall now describe to you the vow known as the month-long fast, which is the most excellent of all.
A forest-dweller, an ascetic, or a woman may perform this month-long fast.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
one should undertake this vow for a period of thirty days.
"O Viṣṇu, from this day forward, until your rising,
I shall worship you without fail for exactly thirty days."
O Viṣṇu, if I were to die during the interval between the twelfth days of the bright fortnights of the months of Kārttika and Āśvina, may there be no violation of my vow for me.
One who observes the vow should worship Hari while bathing at the three periods of the day with perfumes and other offerings;
however, one should avoid anointing the limbs and applying perfumes within the temple of the deity.
Then, having performed worship on the twelfth day, one should provide a meal for the twice-born;
thereafter, the performer of the month-long fast for Hari should break his fast.
One established in the vow who faints midway should consume milk and other such substances;
by means of milk and the like, the vow is not destroyed, and one shall attain both enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Vow of Monthly Fasting," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—123* Brahmā said:

I shall describe the vows for the month of Kārttika: having bathed, one should worship Viṣṇu, subsisting for the month on a single meal per day, or eating only at night, or by means of food obtained unasked.
Whether by means of milk, vegetables, fruits, and the like, or again by fasting,
one who is liberated from all sins and has attained his desires shall go to Hari.

The vow of Hari is always excellent; among those, it is superior during the southern transit of the sun (dakṣiṇāyana); better than that is the Cāturmāsya, and better than that is the Bhīṣmapañcaka in the month of Kārttika.
Then, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one should observe the most excellent vow;
having bathed, one should worship Hari three times a day with barley and other offerings for the sake of the ancestors and others.
Remaining silent, he should sacrifice with clarified butter and other substances, or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water;
then, having bathed [the image], he should anoint it with camphor and other fragrant unguents.
For five days, the twice-born should burn incense of guggulu resin smeared with ghee;
as for the food offering, it should be milk-rice (paramānna), while he recites the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva; one should offer clarified butter, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth, with the eight-syllable mantra ending in svāhā. (GarP 1.123.7)
On the first day, one should worship the feet of Hari with lotuses;
on the second, the region of the knees with bilva leaves; and on the next, the navel with fragrant substances.
On the fifth day, one should worship the head with *bilva* and *javā* flowers;
one should sleep on the ground with *mālatī* flowers and consume cow dung in due order.
Cow’s urine, curd, and milk—these constitute the *pañcagavya* on the fifth day;
one should observe the night-vow (*nakta*) on the fifteenth day, and by becoming a practitioner of this vow, one shall partake in both enjoyment and liberation.
One should regularly observe the Ekādaśī vow during both fortnights;
it destroys the flood of sins and the hellish state, bestows everything, and grants the world of Viṣṇu.
When the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), and the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī) meet at the end of the night,
Hari is eternally present wherever that Ekādaśī occurs.

Where the tenth and eleventh lunar days coincide, even if Asuras and others are present there, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day; one may do so even during periods of birth-impurity or death-impurity.
O Sage, one should observe the fast on the fourteenth day mixed with the first day of the lunar fortnight, and likewise on the full moon and new moon days when they are mixed with the first day.
One should observe the second [lunar day] mixed with the third, and likewise the third;
one should always observe the fourth joined with the fifth, and the fourth conjoined with the next;
the fifth unassociated with the sixth, and the sixth joined with the seventh.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Vow of Bhīṣmapañcaka and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa—
124] Brahmā said:
I shall describe the Śivarātri vow and the narrative that grants all desires,
just as Gaurī once questioned Bhūteśa regarding this supreme observance.
Īśvara said:
On that fourteenth day of the dark fortnight which falls between the months of Māgha and Phālguna,
Rudra, when worshipped through keeping a vigil, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the twelfth day, Hara when joined with Kāma and Keśava should be worshipped;
when worshipped by those who have fasted, he likewise delivers one from hell.
In Arbuda, there was a wicked Niṣāda king named Sundarasena;
accompanied by hunters, he went to the forest to kill deer.
Having failed to obtain deer and other prey, afflicted by hunger and thirst on the mountain,
he remained awake at night, stationed in a grove by the shores of a lake.
There, while protecting his own *liṅga* and casting his body aside,
leaves fell upon the head of the *liṅga* itself, which he did not perceive.
He threw water upon the linga to settle the dust,
but by a lapse of attention, a single arrow fell from his sprout-like hand.
Having gone to the ground on his knees, he touched and grasped the liṅga;
in this manner, there was bathing, touching, worship, and a vigil.
Having returned home in the morning and eaten the food provided by his wife,
he died at the appointed time and was led away, bound with nooses by the messengers of Yama.
Then, having been defeated in battle by my hosts, he was set free;
together with the dog, that pure one became a member of my retinue at my side.
Thus, from ignorance one gains merit, but from knowledge one gains imperishable merit;
having worshipped Śiva on the thirteenth day, the observer of vows should undertake the restrictive observance.
"O Lord, tomorrow morning on the fourteenth day, I shall keep vigil during the night;
I will perform worship, charity, austerity, and fire-offerings according to my own ability."
Having remained without food on the fourteenth day, O Śambhu, I shall eat on the following day for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; O Lord of Īśvara, be my refuge.

Having bathed [the deity] with the nectar of the five products of the cow at that time, and having taken refuge in the Guru, one should worship Hara with perfumes and other offerings, saying: "Oṃ, salutations, salutations to Śiva."
One should offer oblations of sesame, rice, and grain, along with a sacrificial porridge mixed with ghee;
having performed the fire sacrifice and offered the final oblation, one should listen to sacred stories accompanied by song.
At midnight, at the third watch, and again at the fourth,
having likewise recited the root mantra, one should ask for forgiveness at dawn.
O Lord, by your grace, this vow has been performed by me without obstacle;
forgive me, O Protector of the worlds.
O Lord of the three worlds, take [it] away! // GarP_1,124.17 //
Whatever merit has been performed by me today and offered to Rudra— O Lord,
through your grace,
my vow has been completed today.
"O Illustrious One, be gracious to me; please go toward my home.
By the mere sight of you, I am purified—of this there is no doubt."
One should feed those established in meditation and give gifts such as clothing and umbrellas;
O God of gods, Lord of beings, you who bestow grace upon the worlds!
"May the Lord be pleased with that which has been given by me with faith";
having thus asked for forgiveness, the observer of the vow should perform the twelve-year penance.
Having obtained fame, fortune, sons, sovereignty, and other blessings, one shall go to the city of Śiva;
one should perform the vigil here during all twelve months.
One who observes the vow and gives lamps after feeding twelve people shall attain heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vow of Śivarātri," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 125] The Grandfather (Brahmā) said:
King Māndhātṛ became a universal monarch by fasting on the eleventh day;
one should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.
The eleventh day mixed with the tenth was fasted upon by Gāndhārī;
her hundred sons were destroyed. Therefore, one should avoid that [fast].

"Where the eleventh day is joined with the twelfth, there Hari is present; where the eleventh day is joined with the tenth, there the asura is present. When doubt arises due to the contradiction of many statements..."
In that case, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as the fast; the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī).
Even if there is but a single digit (kalā) of the eleventh day (ekādaśī), it should be observed as a fast, and likewise the twelfth day.
The eleventh, the twelfth, and especially the thirteenth—
when these three lunar days are conjoined, that auspicious tithi should be accepted, for it removes all sins.
O twice-born one, having fasted on the eleventh day, or indeed on the twelfth,
one should observe it as mixed with the third [day], but never when it is joined with the tenth.
Keeping a vigil at night, listening to the Purāṇas,
and worshipping Gadādhara while fasting on two Ekādaśīs,
King Rukmāṅgada attained liberation; others as well have attained it through the Ekādaśī vow.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 126] Brahmā said:
I shall now describe that supreme mode of worship which brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation, by means of which the world indeed attained the highest goal. GarP_1,126.1 //
Having arranged the general mandala, one should place Dhātṛ at the gateway,
as well as Vidhātṛ, Gaṅgā, and the great river Yamunā.
One should worship Dvāraśrī and Daṇḍa, as well as Pracaṇḍa and Vāstupuruṣa;
and in the center, one should worship Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, and Ananta.
The earth, the Dharma, as well as knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty;
likewise, the four beginning with non-dharma (adharma), the bulb, the stalk, and the lotus.
The pericarp, the filaments, the quality of purity (sattva), the quality of passion (rajas), and the quality of darkness (tamas);
likewise, the spheres of the sun and other luminaries, as well as the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vimalā.
Having worshipped Durgā, Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, and Kṣetrapāla in the corners, and having honored the seat and the form while recollecting Vāsudeva and Bala; ||| GarP_1,126.6 |||
Then one should worship the great-souled Aniruddha, Nārāyaṇa,
as well as his limbs such as the heart and so forth, and his weapons such as the conch and so forth.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 127.
Brahmā said:
In ancient times, during the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, when the moon was conjoined with the solar asterism (the Sun’s mansion),...
Likewise, one Ekādaśī was observed as a fast by Bhīma.
Having performed this wondrous vow, he became free from his debt to the ancestors;
this is the famous Bhīmadvādaśī, which increases the merit of living beings.
Even without being performed under a specific lunar mansion, this [rite] destroys such acts as the killing of a Brahmin;
it destroys great sin just as a wicked king destroys his own realm.
Just as a bad son ruins a family, as a bad wife ruins her husband, as unrighteousness ruins righteousness, and as a bad minister ruins a king; so too [does a bad companion ruin a practitioner].
Just as knowledge is [overcome] by ignorance, purity by impurity, faith by lack of faith, and truth by falsehoods; // GarP_1,127.5 //
Just as heat might destroy snow, so does the accumulation of wealth lead to misfortune;
just as giving becomes a mere recitation, and austerity becomes a source of pride.
Just as [one loses] a son through lack of training, cattle through being led too far, tranquility through anger, and wealth through not guarding it. (GarP 1.127.7)
Just as knowledge leads to wisdom through dispassion, and just as a fruit is obtained through desirelessness,
so too has this auspicious Dvādaśī been proclaimed for the destruction of sin.
The three Puṣkaras— namely, the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher's wife— when committed simultaneously, destroy [all other sins].
Nor indeed are the sacred field of Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, or Prabhāsa;
nor the Kālindī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, or even the Sarasvatī.
Indeed, all sacred fords are equal to the Ekādaśī;
there is no gift, no recitation, no fire-offering, nor any other meritorious deed anywhere that can compare to it.
On one side is the gift of the entire earth, and on the other is the day of Hari;
yet even compared to that, this single Ekādaśī is superior and possesses great merit.
Having fashioned an image of the Lord Varāha out of gold,
one should place it upon a new vessel made of copper, which is set atop a water-pot.
O Brahmins, having performed worship with great effort—using gold, lamps, and other offerings—to that which contains all seeds and is wrapped in white cloth; 127.14.
Salutation to the Boar for the feet; salutation to the one in the form of a boar for the waist;
to the one with a deep voice for the navel; to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa for the chest.
One should worship the arm with the words "to the thousand-headed one," the neck with "to the Lord of All," the mouth with "to the Soul of All," and the forehead with "to the Source."
The hairs [of the body] are worthy of worship for the hundred-rayed one; having worshipped the Discus-bearer according to the rite, one should keep a vigil at night.
Having heard this Purāṇa, which sets forth the majesty of the God,
one should give it in the morning to a virtuous Brahmin who is a petitioner.
Having presented his retinue along with a golden boar as an offering,
the observer of the vow, not being excessively satiated, should afterwards perform the breaking of the fast.
Having acted thus, a man should know that he shall not become a suckling again;
by fasting on the meritorious Ekādaśī, he is indeed released from the three debts,
and having performed all vows and other rites, he attains his heart's desire.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 128—
Brahmā said:
O Vyāsa, I shall describe the vows by which Hari, the giver of all, is pleased;
for that restraint ordained by the scriptures is called a vow, and it is considered to be austerity (*tapas*).
The specific observances for this vow are self-restraint and the like;
one should bathe daily at the three sessions of the day, sleep on the ground, and keep the senses conquered.
One should avoid conversing with women, Śūdras, and outcasts;
furthermore, one should offer oblations with the five purifiers according to one's ability.
A man of virtuous deeds should perform all these difficult penances;
however, for the sake of preserving his hair, he should observe a vow of double the duration.
One observing a fast should avoid bell-metal, black gram, lentils, chickpeas, millet, leafy vegetables, honey, and food belonging to others.
Flowers, ornaments, garments, incense, perfumes, and ointments—these may be spoiled by fasting; likewise, the cleansing of the teeth and the application of collyrium may be spoiled.
Having used a tooth-stick and the five products of the cow, one should observe the morning vow;
[one must avoid it] by drinking water repeatedly and by chewing betel-leaf.
The fast is impaired by sleeping during the day and by sexual intercourse;
[the virtues are] forbearance, truthfulness, compassion, generosity, purity, and restraint of the senses.
Worship of the gods, offering oblations into the fire, contentment,
and non-stealing— this common duty is remembered as tenfold in all vows.

Eating at night when the stars are visible is called *nakta*; eating at night when they are not visible is called *anakta*. One should consume one *pala* of cow urine and half a thumb’s measure of cow dung.
One should provide seven palas of milk and three palas of curd;
one should provide one pala of ghee and one pala of kuśa-water.
With the Gāyatrī, with "gandhadvārām," with "āpyāyasva," and with "dadhigrahaḥ," and with "tejo 'si" and "devasya," one should perform the Brahmakūrca vow.
The establishment of the sacred fires, the consecration of temples, sacrifices, gifts, and vows;
the Vedic observances, the ritual release of a bull, the tonsure ceremony, and the girdle initiation—these are [the rites].
One should avoid auspicious rites and consecrations during the intercalary month (malamāsa).
The lunar month is that which runs from new moon to new moon, while the solar month consists of thirty days.
The solar month is based on the sun's transit [of a zodiac sign], while the sidereal consists of twenty-seven [days];
the solar month is for marriage, whereas the civil (sāvana) duration is for sacrifices and the like.

The pairs [of tithis] are the second and third, the fourth and fifth, the sixth and seventh, the eighth and ninth, the tenth and eleventh, and the twelfth joined with the eleventh; likewise the fourteenth and the full moon. GarP_1,128.16 //
Even when the new moon occurs on two lunar days, it yields great fruit;
however, this same [conjunction] occurring in reverse order is most terrible and destroys previously accumulated merit.
The menstrual flow of women does not destroy a vow that has already been commenced by the practice of austerity;
however, they should perform other physical acts, such as giving gifts, themselves.
If a violation of the vow should occur through anger, negligence, or greed,
one shall not eat for three days and the shaving of the head must take place.
If the body lacks the capacity [to perform the vow], one should have the son or others perform the vow;
if a Brahmin observing the vow faints, one should cause him to drink water and other [restorative] substances.
