Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Definitions of Vows," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 129—
Brahmā said:
O Vyāsa, listen now as I describe the vows beginning with the Pratipad;
this is known as the Śikhivrata, by which one attains the station of Vāsava (Indra).
Having undertaken the practice of eating only one meal a day, and having completed it, he should bestow a Kapila cow;
and at the beginning of Caitra and other months, he should perform the worship of Brahmā according to the rules,
with offerings of perfumes, flowers, gifts, and delightful garlands and the like.
One should worship the God with offerings of sesamum and shall obtain all desires;
likewise, by offering flowers for a year on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika.
A man who gives flowers and other offerings will possess beauty;
by worshipping Śrīdhara with splendor on the third day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, he shall partake in beauty.
One should perform the sacrifice on a bed that is not empty and give fruit to a twice-born man;
having given the bed, one should pray: "Salutation to Śrīdhara and to Śrī."
On the third lunar day, one should worship Umā, Śiva, and Agni;
sacrificial food should be offered as the oblation, and likewise, *damanaka* flowers should be presented.
He obtains the fruit beginning with the month of Caitra; this has been proclaimed to me by Umā:
he who avoids salt on the third lunar day starting from Phālguna.
Upon its completion, one should give a bed and a house furnished with household utensils,
having honored a Brahmin couple, saying, "May Bhavānī be pleased."
One shall dwell eternally in the world of Gaurī; it is the supreme bestower of good fortune.
Gaurī, Kālī, Umā, Bhadrā, Durgā, Kānti, and Sarasvatī.
Maṅgalā, Vaiṣṇavī, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Nārāyaṇī are the [goddesses] in sequence; beginning from the third day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one shall obtain non-separation [from her husband].

On the fourth lunar day at the beginning of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one who observes the vow while abstaining from food gives sesame seeds to a Brahmin and himself consumes water mixed with sesame.
The completion occurs within two years, and one shall attain the beginning and end free from obstacles.
"Gaḥ svāhā" is this root mantra, joined with the *praṇava* (OM).
Glaiṃ glāṃ [is for] the heart; gāṃ gīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ [are for] the head and the crest-lock;
gūṃ [is for] the armor; goṃ and gaiṃ [are for] the eyes; and goṃ [is used] in the rites of invocation and so forth.
Āgaccholkāya, Gaṇandholka, Puṣpolka, Dhūpakolkaka, Dīpolkāya, Maholkāya; and then the offering and the cleansing.
The Gāyatrī mantra for Sidedholka is prescribed as the Nyāsa for the thumb and the other fingers:
"Oṃ, may we know Mahākarṇa; may we meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa; may that Danti inspire us. (GarP 1.129.15)
One should worship these Gaṇas likewise with offerings of sesame seeds and oblations:
"Svāhā to the Gaṇa, to Gaṇapati, and to Kūṣmāṇḍaka."
Homage indeed to Amogholka, the one with a single tusk, who has the form of the destroyer of Tripura;
Oṃ, homage to the one whose mouth is formidable with dark (or white) teeth and who causes trembling in battle.
At the end of "svāhā" for Padmadaṃṣṭa, the mudrā is indeed dancing among the Gaṇas;
with clapping of hands and laughter, there shall be the fruit of good fortune and other benefits.
Likewise, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Gaṇeśa;
for a year, one obtains learning, prosperity, fame, long life, and a lineage of sons.
Having fasted on a Monday and on the fourth lunar day, one should worship Gaṇa;
by reciting, offering oblations, and remembering the Vidyā, one shall go to heaven and attain liberation.
He who worships on the fourth day of the bright fortnight with offerings of sugar-candies, *laḍḍukas*, and *modakas*,
and performs the propitiation of Vighna, shall attain all his desires and good fortune.
One should worship the son and others with *damana* flowers; the fourth [day] is called *damana*. With "Āṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," ending in the dative case, one should worship Gaṇa.
In whichever month one may offer oblations, recite mantras, or maintain mindfulness,
one attains all desires and achieves the destruction of all obstacles.
One should worship Vināyaka, Mūrtika, and the others with these names;
he too attains a good rebirth, as well as the happiness of heaven and liberation.
Worshipped by the hosts, Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭrin, Tryambaka,
Nīlagrīva, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, and Vighnarājaka.
Smoky-colored, with the crescent moon on his forehead, the tenth Vināyaka is Gaṇapati with an elephant’s face;
one should worship this host in the twelve-spoked [mandala].
Whether performed individually or collectively, one who observes Madhavī shall obtain all desires on the auspicious fifth day of the months of Śrāvaṇa, Āśvina, Bhādrapada, and Kārttika.
Vāsuki and Takṣaka, Kālīya and Maṇibhadraka,
Airāvata and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Karkoṭaka and Dhanañjaya.
Indeed, these— Āyuḥ, Ārogya, Saṃpad, Ananta, Vāsuki, Śaṅkha, Padma, and Kambala— are bathed with ghee and other substances.
Likewise, every month, [he should worship] the nāgas Karkāṭaka, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhaka, Kālīya, Takṣaka, and Piṅgala.
One should worship the eight Nāgas during the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada; one shall attain liberation and go to heaven.
During the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, however, they should be drawn on both sides of the door and worshipped.
On the fifth day, one should worship the Nāgas and offer oblations to the Mahoragas;
milk and clarified butter should be given as the food offering, which removes all poisons.
The Nāgas hold hands of protection, and thus the fifth day is for the extraction of those bitten by snakes.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Fifth Vow for the Extraction of Poison from the Bitten," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—130. Brahmā said:
In this manner, one should worship Kārttikeya in the month of Bhādrapada;
all acts such as ritual bathing and giving gifts performed during this month are said to be inexhaustible.
On the seventh [day], one should cause the Brahmins to eat food and worship the Sun with:
"Oṃ, to Khakholka, may there be immortality; be ever united with what is dear, Svāhā! (GarP 1,130.2).

On the eighth day, one should perform the breaking of the fast after consuming black pepper; by bathing with self-restraint on the seventh day and worshipping the Sun, one becomes a partaker of heaven.
One should give fruits to the Brahmins, saying, "May Mārtaṇḍa be pleased," and one should cause [the recipient] to eat dates, coconuts, or citrons.
"May all my desires be fulfilled in every respect. (Thus ends the Phala-saptamī.
Having worshipped the deity on the seventh day, one should then feed [the brahmins] with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins, he himself should then drink milk;
what is known as food to be chewed, sucked, licked, and boiled rice should likewise be offered.
One who desires wealth, sons, and so forth should abandon this [food] and eat only rice;
subsisting on air, one should conquer hunger and observe the Vijaya-saptamī vow.
One who desires objects of pleasure should worship the Sun today, and by fasting, one should cross over intoxication.

He who avoids wheat, mung beans, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, bronze vessels, stone-ground flour, honey, meat-spirits, liquor, meat, ointments for the body, collyrium, and sesame seeds— his desired goal is fulfilled on each of the seven seventh days.
(Thus ends the Vijaya-saptamī vow.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Saptamī Vows," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa, within the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—131.
Brahmā said:
O Brahmin, having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
one should worship Dūrvā, Saurī, Gaṇeśa, and Śiva with fruits and flowers.

With all fruits, rice, and other offerings, [one should say] "Salutation to Śambhu" and "Salutation to Śiva. O Dūrvā grass, you are born of nectar; indeed, as the eighth [day], you possess all desires.
"One is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin by eating food that has not been cooked over fire" (thus ends the Dūrvā-aṣṭamī vow).
And on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, when the moon is in conjunction with Rohiṇī, there is worship of Hari at midnight.
Even when overlapped by the seventh lunar day, this [vow] destroys the sins of three lifetimes.
One should fast and worship with mantras, and break the fast at the end of the lunar day.

Salutations again and again to Govinda, who is Yoga, the Lord of Yoga, the Master of Yoga, the Source of Yoga. (This is the mantra for bathing. Salutations again and again to Govinda, who is Sacrifice, the Lord of Sacrifice, and the Master of Sacrifice. GarP_1,131.5.

(At the time of worship: Salutations again and again to Govinda, the All, the Lord of All, the Master of All. (At the time of lying down: Salutations again and again to Govinda, the Whole, the Lord of the Whole, the Support of the Whole, the Source of the Whole.
One should worship the deity on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), as well as Rohiṇī together with the Moon;
and having taken water in a conch shell along with flowers, fruits, and sandalwood.
Having gone to the ground on his knees, he should present the *arghya* offering to Candra:
"O you who were born from the Ocean of Milk,
O you who arose from the eye of Atri!"
O Lord of the Moon, together with Rohiṇī, accept this water offering from me for the sake of Śrī,
Vasudeva, Nanda, and Bala.
Then one should offer the *arghya* accompanied by fruit to Yaśodā,
and [offerings] to Ananta,
Vāmana, Śauri, Vaikuṇṭha, and Puruṣottama.
Vāsudeva, Hṛṣīkeśa, Mādhava, Madhusūdana,
Varāha, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Nṛsiṃha, and Daityasūdana.
Dāmodara, Padmanābha, Keśava, he whose banner bears the eagle; Govinda, Acyuta, the divine Ananta, the unconquered.
[He praised] Viṣṇu, who is beyond the senses, the seed of the universe, the cause of creation, preservation,
and destruction, without beginning or end, the Lord of the three worlds, and Trivikrama.
Nārāyaṇa, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
wearing divine yellow garments, and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
To Hari, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, the abode of the universe, the Lord of Śrī, the bearer of Śrī—
that very God whom the goddess Devakī bore from Vasudeva.
"Salutation to that one whose self is Brahman, for the protection of the earthly Brahman;
having recited these names, one should again pray for the sake of [attaining] the goal."
Save me, O Lord of the gods of gods! O Hari! From the ocean of saṃsāra!
Save me, O Lord, destroyer of all sins,
from the ocean of suffering and grief!
O delight of Devakī! O Lord of Śrī! O Hari!
O Viṣṇu, you rescue from the ocean of saṃsāra those of evil conduct who remember you even once, time and again.
O God, I am exceedingly wicked; protect me from this ocean of sorrow!
O Lotus-eyed One, I am submerged in the great ocean of ignorance.
Save me, O Lord of the gods of gods!
There is no protector other than you.
You took birth as Vāsudeva for the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, who acts for the welfare of the world;
may there be peace, may there be auspiciousness, and may he possess wealth, fame, and sovereignty.
(Thus ends the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī Vrata.
Thus concludes the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī Vrata," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—132.
Brahmā said:
He who eats only at night until the eighth day, and at the end of the year gives a cow as a gift, goes to the station of Indra;
this is called the Sadgati vow.
O Goddess, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa, that which is called the Mahārudra was indeed well performed for my pleasure; its fruit is ten thousandfold.
When the eighth lunar day falls on a Wednesday during both fortnights,
then on that day this vow is the supreme narrative.
In that [consecration], those who perform the ritual restrictions shall not have their prosperity impaired;
[this applies] except for two finger-breadths from the eight handfuls of rice.
Indeed, a human being desiring liberation, with true devotion and faith,
should eat the cooked food placed within a leaf-cup made of mango leaves and encircled by *kuśa* grass.
If one worships a wise man with the fivefold offerings at a body of water, he shall obtain the desired fruit, provided it is accompanied by *kalambikā* and *amlīkā*.
According to one's capacity, one should give a sacrificial fee consisting of a water-pot filled with rice;
the seed-syllable should be "Buṃ Budhāya," ending with "svāhā" and preceded by "kamala" and so forth.
On the petals and in the center of the limbs, one should visualize the dark-complexioned [Viṣṇu] bearing arrows and a bow;
the meritorious narrative of Budhāṣṭamī must certainly be heard by those of virtuous conduct.
In the pure city named Pāṭaliputra, there was an excellent brahmin named Vīra;
his wife was Rambhā, and their son was the eminent Kauśika.
His daughter was named Vijayā, and Vṛṣa became the guardian of the city;
taking her with him, Kauśika went to the Gaṅgā in the summer and took his pleasure there.
While he was engaged in play, his bull was forcibly carried off by cowherds who were thieves;
rising up from the Ganges, he wandered through the forest in distress.
Vijayā went for water together with her mother, and she too went;
then, thirsty and seeking lotus stalks, he arrived at the lake.
Having seen the worship and other rites performed for the celestial women, he was filled with wonder;
approaching them, he requested food, saying, "I am hungry, along with my younger brother."
The women said, "We shall perform the vow; you too, O Kuru, perform the vow.
For the sake of a wife and for the sake of wealth and drink, they both worshipped Budha.
Taking two leaf-cups, they ate the food that had been offered;
when the women had departed, those two givers of wealth saw wealth and drink.
Having taken what was given by the thieves, he arrived home at nightfall;
and having bowed to the sorrowful Vīra, he slept comfortably that night.
Seeing a young maiden, he said out of grief, "To whom should my daughter be given? and due to his virtuous conduct and the true fruit of his vows, he replied, "To Yama."
When his parents had gone to heaven, Kauśika undertook a vow for the sake of sovereignty;
having given the great kingdom of Ayodhyā to Yama, he gave his sister as well.
Yama also said to Vijayā, "Become a housewife in my city; do not open [the door] when Yama has gone elsewhere. She did not do so.
Not seeing her own mother, she saw her standing in the torments of the noose.
Then, having become anxious and learning of the vow spoken by Kośika which bestows liberation, she performed it;
thereafter, the mother was liberated. Therefore, one should observe this vow.
By the power of his merit, he went to heaven and dwelt there in happiness.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Budhāṣṭamī Vow," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—133.
Brahmā said:
Those who drink eight buds of the *aśoka* tree under the asterism Punarvasu on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra shall never encounter sorrow.
O Aśoka, beloved by Hara,
born in the month of Madhu,
I drink [of you] while tormented by grief; make me forever free from sorrow.
(Thus ends the Aśokāṣṭamī vow.
Brahmā said:
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, when it is joined with the Uttarāṣāḍhā nakṣatra...
That is called Mahānavamī; bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts performed on it become inexhaustible.
On the ninth day alone, one should worship Durgā;
this is the great vow of supreme merit, practiced by Śaṅkara and others.
On the sixth lunar day and others, for the sake of conquering enemies,
one should always feed a maiden while engaged in recitation and fire-offerings, even if she has not been requested.
"Durgedurge rakṣiṇi svāhā"—this is the mantra for worship and other rites;
the nine goddesses consist of the long vowels and other mātrās, ending with "namaḥ."
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the six syllables beginning with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* upon the heart and other limbs,
from the thumb to the little finger, one should indeed worship Śivā.
On the eighth day, nine houses made of wood—or even just one—should be constructed;
within that, the Goddess should be fashioned from gold or even silver.
One should worship [the deity] on a trident, a sword, a book, a cloth painting, or a mandala;
[the deity] holds a skull-cup, a shield, a bell, a mirror, and makes the threatening gesture with the hand.
She holds a banner, a hand-drum, and a noose in her left hands,
as well as a spear, a mallet, a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, and a goad.
The arrow, the discus, and the dart are joined with the *durgā* weapon;
the remaining sixteen hands should hold [the other implements], excluding the collyrium and the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).
Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā,
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Aticaṇḍikā.
And the ninth is Ugracaṇḍā, whose form is like the fire in the center;
she is yellow, reddish-brown, black, blue, smoky, and white.
Pāta is said to be white, and Ālīḍha is likewise green;
his mount is a buffalo, which seizes him by the hair with the tip of its sword-like horn.
Having recited the ten-syllable mantra, he cannot be bound by anyone.
Then one should worship a sword fifteen finger-breadths long, or a trident;
or else one should worship it upon a *liṅga*, or on sandals, or even in water.
One should maintain a diverse worship and observe a fast on the eighth day;
at the end of the night, one should cause a five-year-old buffalo or goat to be slaughtered.
Having offered that blood and other substances according to the rite with the mantra "Kālikālī," one should likewise offer to Pūtanā in the southwest and to the evil Rākṣasī in the northwest.
One should offer the carakī plant in the northeast and the vidārī plant in the southeast.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Mahānavamī Vow," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 134] Brahmā said:
And here the mantra of Mahākauśika is proclaimed, which yields great fruit.
(The Mahākauśika Mantra): Oṃ, homage to Mahākauśika!
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, quiver, quiver; lala lala, kulva kulva, culva culva, khalla khalla, mulva mulva.

Gulva gulva tulva pulla pulla dhalva dhulva dhuma dhuma dhamadhama māraya māraya dhakadhaka jñāpaya jñāpaya vidāraya vidāraya kampa kampa kampaya kampaya pūraya pūraya āveśaya āveśaya oṃ hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ haṃ vaṃ vaṃ huṃ taṭataṭa madamada hrīṃ oṃ hūṃ to the Nairṛta!
One should say, "Homage to Nirṛti; [this] must be given.
One should offer the bali-oblation consecrated with the Mahākauśika mantra.
In front of him, the king should bathe after fashioning an earthen umbrella;
having struck it with a sword, he should offer it to Skanda and Viśākha.
Likewise, at night, worship should be performed for the Mothers and the Goddesses:
Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍikā,
Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, and Kapālinī.
"O Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā—homage be to you!
Maidens and young women should likewise bathe the Goddess with milk and other substances."
One should honor the twice-born, the poor, and the heretics with gifts of food;
and during chariot processions, one should honor them with banners, leaves, flags, and garments.
This worship on the Mahānavamī day bestows victory, sovereignty, and other blessings.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the first part known as the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa*, in the section on conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*), the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals and Mantras of Mahākauśika on the Great Ninth Day" (*Mahānavamyāṃ Mahākauśikamantrakṛtyādivivaraṇa*).
[Chapter 135 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Brahmā said:
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the man observing the vow should worship the Goddess with a single meal; O Brahmins, he should mutter the Vīra-mantra one hundred thousand times.
(Thus ends the Vīranavamī vow.
Brahmā said:
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship the Goddess with *damanaka* flowers.
Longevity, health, and good fortune, and being unconquered by enemies.
(Thus ends the Navamī-vrata of Damanaka.
Brahmā said:
On the tenth day, one who eats only a single meal and, at the conclusion of the vow, gives ten cows [is purified].
And by giving golden directions, one becomes the sovereign of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
(Thus ends the Daśamī-vrata of the Directions.
Brahmā said:
On the eleventh day, worship of the sages should be performed, which is beneficial to all.
Possessing wealth and sons, he is glorified in the world of the ṛṣis at the end.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya,
Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
In the month of Caitra and others, one should perform worship with garlands made of *damanaka* flowers;
the eighth day is called Aśokā, and likewise the ninth day is called Vīrā.
The tenth lunar day of the ten directions is called Damanā, as are the ninth and the eleventh.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ṛṣyekādaśī Vow," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 136] Brahmā said:
I shall now describe the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is when the eleventh and twelfth lunar days are conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism.

That lunar day is declared to be Vijayā; worship of Hari and other rites performed on it become inexhaustible, whether by means of eating once a day, eating only at night, or likewise eating only what is unasked for.
One should not become a performer of the twelve-day rite merely by fasting or by begging for alms;
likewise, one must avoid bell-metal, meat, honey, greed, and false speech.
On the twelfth lunar day, a man should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, sleeping during the day, the application of collyrium, stone-based flour, and lentils.
The twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, when conjoined with the Śravaṇā asterism, is to be known as the Great Twelfth; it yields great fruit for one who observes a fast.
A bath at the confluence of rivers on a Wednesday yields great fruit;
one should worship a golden image of Vāmana within a water-filled pitcher containing jewels.
Covered with a pair of white garments and provided with an umbrella and a pair of sandals, one should then worship the head [of the image] with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva. (GarP 1.136.7)
Likewise, salutations to Śrīdhara for his face; salutations indeed to Kṛṣṇa for his throat;
salutations to Śrīpati for his chest; and to the wielder of all weapons for his arms.
The wise one should worship Vyāpaka with "Oṃ namo vyāpakāya" on the belly, Keśava on the stomach, Trailokyapati on the penis, and Sarvabhṛt with "Oṃ namaḥ sarvabhṛte" on the shanks.
"Salutation to the Self of All for the feet; the food offering consists of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should offer jars and sweetmeats (modaka), and keep a vigil throughout the night."
Having bathed, sipped water for purification, and performed worship, one should speak with hands joined in reverence:
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, known by the names Budha and Śravaṇa!"
"Having brought about the destruction of the flood of sins, become the bestower of all happiness!
May the Lord of the Gods of gods be pleased; let one give water-pots to the Brahmins.
Whether on a riverbank or elsewhere, one who performs this shall attain all desires. (GarP 1.136.12)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Śravaṇadvādaśī Vow," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 137] Brahmā said:
On the thirteenth day of the month of Kāma, he should be worshipped with *damanaka* and other offerings;
accompanied by Rati and Prīti, he is indeed free from sorrow and adorned with jewels.
(Thus concludes the Madanaka-trayodaśī vow.
Likewise, he who does not eat for one year on the fourteenth and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights becomes a partaker of liberation through the worship of Śiva. (GarP 1.137.2)
(Thus ends the vow of the fourteenth and eighth days dedicated to Śiva.
Having fasted for three nights, one should give a beautiful mansion on the full moon day of Kārttika;
one attains the world of the Sun through this auspicious Dhāmavrata. GarP_1,137.3 //

That which is given to the ancestors on the new moon day, such as water and other offerings, becomes inexhaustible; likewise, one who eats only at night while worshipping the days by their names partakes in all [the merits] of those days.
(Thus end the lunar-day vows. O brahmin seer, those which indeed correspond to the twelve lunar mansions in each month—
At the end of their names, a person should properly worship that which has not fallen among them.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Keśava under the asterism Kṛttikā and so forth;
for four months, one should offer oblations of ghee and present *kṛsara*.
At the beginning of Āṣāḍha, one should feed Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared with that same [grain];
one should observe the practice of eating only at night, accompanied by bathing in the water of the five products of the cow and the offering of food.
Before the dismissal, all the substance offered is called *naivedya*;
once the Lord of the World has been dismissed, it becomes *nirmālya* in an instant.
The foremost experts in the Pāñcarātra tradition partake of the food offering themselves;
in this manner, at the end of the year, one should perform a special worship.
Homage, homage to you, O Acyuta!
May there be the destruction of my evil, and may my merit increase.
May my sovereignty, wealth, and so forth be forever inexhaustible for me; likewise, may my lineage be indeed imperishable.
O Acyuta, just as you are higher than the highest, having become the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest,
so likewise grant my desired wish, O immeasurable remover of sins, which has always been performed by me.
O Acyuta, O Ananta,
O Govinda, be gracious regarding that which is desired.
O Puruṣottama, you whose nature is immeasurable, make that [merit] inexhaustible.
By fasting on the eleventh, eighth, and fourteenth days for a year, a man shall indeed attain longevity, prosperity, and a favorable rebirth for seven years.
On the seventh [lunar day], one should worship Viṣṇu, Durgā, Śambhu, and Ravi in succession;
being stainless, one attains their world and all desires.
By eating a single meal, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for,
and by fasting, they worship all the deities with vegetables and other offerings.
Everyone shall attain enjoyment and liberation on all lunar days. On the first day (pratipad), Agni, the giver of wealth, and the Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, are worshipped.
On the second [tithi] Śrī and Yama, on the fifth Pārvatī with Śrī, on the sixth the Nāgas, and on the seventh Kārttikeya; on the seventh [again], Bhāskara is the bestower of wealth.
On the eighth day, O lords of sages, the Mothers [are worshipped]; on the ninth, Takṣaka;
on the tenth, Indra; and on the eleventh, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
On the twelfth day Hari is worshipped, on the thirteenth Kāma, on the fourteenth Maheśvara, and on the fifteenth Brahmā and the other ancestors.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of Vows Concerning Lunar Days, Weekdays, Asterisms, and so forth," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa—
138] (Thus the Vows are completed).
Hari said:
"I shall proclaim the lineages of kings and the histories of those lineages.
From the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu, Brahmā was born; and from his thumb, indeed, Dakṣa was born."
From him came Pitṛ Vivasvān, and from Vivasvān his son Manu; [from Manu were born] Ikṣvāku, Śaryāti, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Praṣadhraka.
Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Diṣṭa, and Śaśaka were also [his sons]. Manu had a daughter named Ilā, and Sudyumna was his son.
From Budha, upon Ilā, was born King Purūravas, O Rudra;
and from Sudyumna were born three sons: Utkala, Vinata, and Gaya.
From the killing of a cow, Abhṛcchradra was born; Pṛṣadhra, however, was the son of Manu. From Karūṣa, Kṣatriyas were born who became renowned as the Kārūṣas.
Diṣṭaputra, however, became a Vaiśya, and he was Nābhāga;
from him came the son Bhalandana, and from Bhalandana came Vatsaprīti.
From him was born Pāṃśu, from him the king Khanitra, and from him Kṣupa;
from Kṣupa was born a son named Viṃśa, and from Viṃśa was born Viviṃśaka.
From Viviṃśa came Khanīnetra, and Vibhūti is known as his son;
from Vibhūti was born Karandhama, and from him was born Avikṣita.
Marutta was the son of Avikṣita, and from him Nariṣyanta is remembered;
Tama was born from Nariṣyanta, and from him came Rājavardhana.
From Rājavardha was born Sudhṛti; Sudhṛti’s son was Nara; from Nara came the son Kevala; and from Kevala was born Dhundhumān.
From Dhundhumāra was born Vegavān, and Budha was the son of Vegavān;
from Budha was born Tṛṇabindu, as well as Kāñcī and Elāvilā.
Alambusā bore Viśāla to Tṛṇabindu;
from Viśāla was born Hemacandra, and from Hemacandra came Candraka.
From Candra came Dhūmrāśva, and from Dhūmrāśva likewise came Sṛñjaya;
from Sṛñjaya was born Sahadeva, and Kṛśāśva became his son.
From Kṛśāśva was born Somadatta, and from him came Janamejaya;
his son was Sumanti—these were indeed the kings of Vaiśālī.
Śaryāti had a daughter named Sukanyā, who became the wife of Cyavana.
Śaryāti’s son was named Ananta, and from Ananta was born Revata.
Raivata was the son of Revata; from Raivata, Revatī was born.
Dhṛṣṭa’s son was Dhārṣṭaka, whose field was indeed Vaiṣṇava (or Vaiṣyaka).
And so it came to pass.
Nābhāga’s son was Neṣṭha, and Ambarīṣa was his son;
from Ambarīṣa came Virūpa, and from Virūpa came Pṛṣadaśva.
And his son was Rathīnara, who was devoted to Vāsudeva.
Ikṣvāku had three sons: Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍaka.
From Ikṣvāku was born Vikukṣi; Śaśāda [was named] because he ate a hare.
From Śaśāda came Purañjaya, whose son was known as Kakutstha.
From Anenas came Kakutstha, and Pṛthu was the son of Anenas;
Viśvarāta was the son of Pṛthu, and Ārdra was born from Viśvarāta.
From Ārdra was born Yuvanāśva; from Yuvanāśva came Śāvasta;
from Śāvasta was Bṛhadaśva, and his son was Kuvalāśvaka.
From Dṛḍhaśva was born the renowned Dhundhumāra;
from Dṛḍhaśva were born Candrāśva, Kapilāśva, and Haryaśva.
From Haryaśva was born Nikumbha, and from Nikumbha came Hitāśva;
from Hitāśva came Pūjāśva, and from him was born Yuvanāśva.
From Yuvanāśva and Bindumatī was born Māndhātṛ;
he had three sons: Mucukunda, Ambarīṣa, and Purukutsa.
And fifty maidens were the wives of the sage Saubhari;
from Yuvanāśva and Ambarīṣa came Harita, and from Yuvanāśva [came] Harita.
From Purukutsa, by the Narmadā river, was born a son named Trasadasyu;
from him Anaraṇya was born, and Haryaśva was also born from Anaraṇya.
His son was Vasumanas, and Tridhanvan was his offspring;
Trayyāruṇa was his son, and Satyarata was his son.
He who was known as Triśaṅku then became Hariścandra;
from Hariścandra came Rohitāśva, and from Rohitāśva came Harita.
Cañcu was the son of Harita, and Vijaya was the son of Cañcu;
from Vijaya was born Ruruka, and from Ruruka, Vṛka was born as his son.
From Vṛka, King Bāhu was born; and from Bāhu, Sagara is recorded to have been born.
From Sagara and Sumati, O Hari, sixty thousand sons were produced.
In Keśinī there was only one, known by the name Asamañjasa.
His son was the learned Aṃśumat, and his son was Dilīpa;
from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha, who brought the Gaṅgā to the earth.
From Śruta was born Bhagīratha’s son Nābhaga; from Śruta, it is said, came Nābhāga, from whom Ambarīṣa was born, and from Ambarīṣa came Sindhudvīpa.
Sindhudvīpa’s son was Ayutāyu, whose son was Ṛtuparṇa;
from Ṛtuparṇa came Sarvakāma, and Sudāsa was his son.
And the son of Sudāsa was known by the name Mitrasaha;
his son, born of Damayantī, was known as Kalmāṣapāda.
Aśvaka was his son, and from Aśvaka, Mūlaka was born;
after him came King Daśaratha, and his son was Ailavila.
Viśvasaha was his son, and Khaṭvāṅga was his offspring;
from Khaṭvāṅga came Dīrghabāhu, and Aja was the son of Dīrghabāhu.
His son was Daśaratha, and four sons are recorded as his offspring:
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata, who were all possessed of great strength.
Kuśa and Lava were born from Rāma; Tārkṣya and Puṣkara from Bharata;
and Citrāṅgada and Candraketu were born from Lakṣmaṇa.
Subāhu and Śūrasena were born from Śatrughna;
Kuśa’s son was Atithi, and Niṣadha was indeed the son of Atithi.
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and Nabha is recorded as the son of Nala;
Puṇḍarīka was the son of Nabha, and Kṣemadhanvan was his son.
Devānīka was his son; from Devānīka came Ahīnaka; from Ahīnaka came Ruru; and Pāriyātra was the son of Ruru at the sacrifice.
From Pāriyātra came Dala at the sacrifice; Dala’s son is remembered as Chala.
From Chala came Uktha, from Uktha came Vajranābha, and from him came Gaṇa.
From the Gaṇa was born Uṣitāśva; from him Viśvasaha arose.
Hiraṇyanābha was his son, and his son is known as Puṣpaka.
From Puṣpa was born Dhruvasandhi; from Dhruvasandhi came Sudarśana;
from Sudarśana came Agnivarṇa; and from Agnivarṇa came Padmavarṇa.
From Padmavarṇa was born Śīghra, and from Śīghra his son Maru was born;
Prasuśruta was the son of Maru, and Udāvasu was his son.
From Udāvasu came Nandivardhana; from Nandivardhana, Suketu;
from Suketu was born Devarāta, and from him the son Vṛhaduktha.
From Bṛhaduktha came Mahāvīrya, and Sudhṛti was his son;
from Sudhṛti came Dhṛṣṭaketu, and from Dhṛṣṭaketu came Haryaśva.
From Haryaśva was born Maru; from Maru was born Pratīndhaka;
from Pratīndhaka came Kṛtiratha, and Devamīḍha was his son.
From Devamīḍha came Vibudha; from Vibudha came Mahādhṛti;
from Mahādhṛti was born Kīrtirāta, and his son was Mahāroma.
From Mahāromṇa came Svarṇaroman; Hrasvaroman was his son.
From Hrasvaroman came Sīradhvaja, and Sītā was his daughter.
His brother was Kuśadhvaja; from Sīradhvaja came Bhānumān; from Bhānumān came Śatadyumna; and from Śatadyumna, Śuci is recorded as having been born.
Ūrja was the son of Śuci, and Sanadvāja was his offspring;
Kulī was born from Sanadvāja, and Anañjana was the son of Kulī.
From Anañjana was born Kulajit, and his son was Adhīnemika;
Śrutāyu was his son, and Supārśva was his offspring.
From Supārśva was born Sṛñjaya; from Sṛñjaya was born Kṣemāri;
from Kṣemāri was born Anenā, and his son is known as Rāmaratha.
From that Rāmaratha came Satyaratha; Upaguru is recorded as being from Satyaratha;
from Upaguru came Upagupta, and Svāgata was from Upagupta.
Svanara was born from Svāgata, and Suvarcas was his son; Supārśva was the son of Suvarcas, and Suśruta was born from Supārśva.
Jayas was born from Suśruta, and from Jayas, Vijaya arose;
the son of Vijaya was Ṛta, and Sunaya was the son of Ṛta.
From Sunaya was born Vītahavya, and from Vītahavya, Dhṛti is remembered [as the son].
Bahulāśva was the son of Dhṛti, and from Bahulāśva, Kṛti is remembered [as the son].
In both lineages of Janaka, the reliance upon yoga has been described.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Solar Lineage," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 139] Hari said:
The lineage of Sūrya has been told; now hear from me the lineage of Soma.
Brahmā was the son of Nārāyaṇa, and from Brahmā arose Atri.
Atri’s wife was Soma, who was the beloved of the preceptor of the gods;
from Soma, Tārā gave birth to Budha, and Purūravas was the son of Budha.
Then, from Budhaputra and Urvaśī, six sons were born: Śrutātmaka, Viśvāvasu, Śatāyu, Āyu, Dhomān, and Āvasu.
The son of Amāvasu was named Bhīma, and the son of Bhīma was Kāñcana.
Suhotra was the son of Kāñcana, and Jahnu was born from Suhotra.
From Jahnu was born Sumantu; from Sumantu came Apajapaka. Balakashva was his son, and from Balakashva, it is recorded, Kuśa was born.
From Kuśa were born Kuśāśva, Kuśanābha, Amūrtarayas, and Vasu;
from Kuśāśva was born Gādhi, and Viśvāmitra was his son.
The maiden Satyavatī was given in marriage to the twice-born Ṛcīka;
from Ṛcīka was born Jamadagni, and Rāma was his son.
From Viśvāmitra were born the sons Devarāta, Aduchandas, and others;
from Āyus came Nahuṣa, and from him were born Anenas, Raji, and Rambhaka.
From Kṣattravṛddha was born King Suhotra;
from Suhotra were born three: Kāśya, Kāśau, and Gṛtsamada.
From Gṛtsamada was born Śaunaka; likewise, from Kāśya came Dīrghatamas.
From him [Kāśya] came Vaidya Dhanvantari, and Ketumān was his son.
Bhīmaratha was the son of Ketumān, and Divodāsa was his son;
from Divodāsa came Pratardana, who was renowned there as Śatrujit.
Ṛtadhvaja was his son, and from Ṛtadhvaja came Alarka;
from Alarka Sannati was born, and Sunīta was the son of Sannati.
Satyaketu was the son of Sunīta; Vibhu was the son of Satyaketu;
Suvibhu was the son of Vibhu; and Sukumāra was the son of Suvibhu.
From Sukumāra was born Dṛṣṭaketu, and Vītihotra was his son.
Bharga was the son of Vītihotra, and Bhargabhūmi was his son.
"These high-souled Kāśis were indeed Vaiṣṇavas;
Raji had five hundred sons who were destroyed by Śakra."
Pratikṣattra was born from Kṣattravṛddha, and Saṃjaya was his son;
Vijaya was the son of Saṃjaya, and Kṛta was the son of Vijaya.
From Kṛta was born Vṛṣadhana, and Sahadeva was his son;
from Sahadeva came Adīna, and from Adīna came Jayatsena.
From Jayatsena was born Saṃkṛti, and from Saṃkṛti came Kṣattradharmā;
then, in order, were born Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Ayāti, and Vikṛti.
The sons of King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, were well known;
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu.
Druhyu, Anu, Pūru, Śarmiṣṭhā’s son Vārṣaparvaṇi, Sahasrajit, Kroṣṭu, Manu, and Raghu were the sons of Yadu.
From Sahasrajit was born Śatajit; from him indeed came Haya and Haihaya.
Anaraṇya was the son of Haya, and Dharma was born from Haihaya.
From Dharma was born Dharmnetra; from Dharmnetra came Kunti. From Kunti was born Sāhañji, and Mahiṣmān was his son.
Bhadraśreṇya was his son; Durdaṃma was the son of Bhadraśreṇya; Dhanaka was born from Durdaṃma, and Kṛtavīrya was the son of Dhanaka, O Jānaki.
From Kṛtavīrya was born Arjuna, who had mastered the sacred fires, accomplished his duties, possessed vital energy, and was endowed with great strength;
from Arjuna came Śūrasenaka.
Jayadhvaja, Madhu, Śūra, Vṛṣaṇa, and Pañca were his five brothers of like vows.
From Jayadhvaja was born Tālajaṅgha, and from Tālajaṅgha came Bharata.
Madhu was the son of Vṛṣaṇa, and from Madhu came the lineage of Vṛṣṇi; Kroṣṭu was born as the son of that great-souled one, and Āhi was his son.
From Āhuḥ was born Uśaṅku; from him, while he was still known as Citraratha, came Śaśabindu. From Citraratha [descended] his wives, and he indeed had one hundred thousand sons.
And he had ten lakhs of sons, the foremost of whom were Pṛthukīrti and the others:
Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthujaya, Pṛthudāna, and Pṛthuśravas.
From Pṛthuśravas was born Tama; from Tamas was born Uśanas. His son was named Śitagu, and from him came Śrīrukmakavaca.
Rukma, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Pālita, and Hari—these were the sons of Śrīrukmakavaca; likewise, Vidarbha was born from Jyāmagha.
And from his wife Śaibyā, he begot Kratha and Kauśika from Vidarbha; from Romapāda came Babhru, and from Babhru likewise came Dhṛti.
Kauśika’s son was Ṛci, and from him, it is said, came King Caidya;
Kunti was his son, and Vṛṣṇi is recorded as the son of Kunti.
Vṛṣṇi’s son was Nivṛti, and likewise Nivṛti’s son was Daśārha;
Vyoma was the son of Daśārha, and Jīmūta was his offspring.
From Jīmūta was born Vikṛti; from him Bhīmaratha arose;
from him Madhuratha was born, and Śakuni was his son.
Karambhi was the son of Śakuni, and his son is remembered as Devavān; from Devakṣattra, who was devoted to the gods, Madhu is said to have been born.
Kuruvaṃśa was the son of Madhu, and Anu was born from the Kuru lineage;
Puruhotra was indeed the son of Anu, and Aṃśu was born from Puruhotra.
From Aṃśu was born Sattvaśruta, and from him indeed came King Sāttvata;
from Sāttvata were born Bhajina and Bhajamāna, and Andhaka was the son of Sāttvata.
Mahābhoja, Vṛṣṇi, Divyāvanya, Devāvṛdha,
Nimivṛṣṇi, Bhajamāna, and likewise Ayutājit.
Śatajit, Sahasrājit, Babhru, and the divine Bṛhaspati;
from Mahābhoja came Bhoja, and from that Vṛṣṇi came Sumitraka.
From him came Svadhājit; likewise, from him came Anamitrāśin. Nighna was the son of Anamitra, and from Nighna, Śatrājit was born.
Another renowned son was Prasena; likewise, from Anamitra came Śibi. Satyaka was the son of Śibi, and from Satyaka came Sātyaki.
Sañjaya was the son of Sātyaki, and Kuli was his son;
Yugandhara was the son of Kuli—these are proclaimed as the descendants of Śibi.
In the lineage of Anamitra was Vṛṣṇi; his son was Śvaphalka, whose son was Citraka.
From Śvaphalka and Gāndinī was born Akrūra, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
From Upamadgu came Akrūra, and from him Devadyota was born;
Devavān and Upadeva are recorded as the two sons of Akrūra.
Pṛthu and Vipṛthu are recorded as the sons of Citra; Śuci is remembered as the son of Andhaka; Kukura was the son of Bhajamāna, and likewise Kambalabarhiṣa.
Dhṛṣṭa was born from Kukura; from him came Kāpotaromaka. His son was Viloma, and Tumburu was the son of Viloma.
From him Dundubhi was born, and from him Punarvasu is remembered;
his [sons] were Āhuka and Āhukī, and there was also a daughter of Āhuka.
Devaka and Ugrasena were born; from Devaka was born Devakī, as well as Vṛkadevā, Upadevā, Sahadevā, and Surakṣitā.
Vasudeva married Śrīdevī and Śāntidevī;
Devavān and Upadeva are known as the two sons of Sahadevā.
Ugrasena’s sons were Kaṃsa, Sunāman, Vaṭa, and others;
from Bhajamāna came Vidūratha, and from Vidūratha was born Śūra.
Then Śami was the son of Sūra, the son of Vidūratha;
Pratikṣattra was the son of Śami, and Svayaṃbhōja was his son.
Hṛdika was born from Svayaṃbhū, and Kṛtavarman was his son;
Deva and Śatadhanu were born from Śūra, the son of Devamīḍhuṣa.
Ten sons were born to Māriṣā, beginning with Vasudeva;
and [there were also] Pṛthā, Śrutadevī, Śrutakīrti, and Śrutaśravas.
Rājādhideva gave Pṛthā, the daughter of Kunti, to Śūra;
she was given by Kunti to Pāṇḍu, and upon her, [sons were begotten] by Dharma, Anila, and Indra.
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Pārtha, Nakula, and Sahadeva were born to Mādrī from the two Aśvin deities; formerly, Karṇa was born to Kuntī.
From Śrutadevī was born Dantavakra, who was indeed difficult to overcome in battle; and from Kaikaya, five sons beginning with Santardana were born of Śrutakīrti.
To Rājādhidevī were born Vinda and Anuvindaka;
and from Damaghoṣa, Śrutaśravas gave birth to Śiśupālaka.
Rohiṇī, the daughter of Puru, was the wife of Madirānaka-dundubhi;
Devakī and others were the daughters of Bhadrā. From Rohiṇī, Balabhadra was born.
Sāraṇa and the others, as well as Śaṭha, were born from Balabhadra by Revatī;
Niśaṭha and Ulmuka were born from Devakī, and thus six were born.
Kīrtimān, Suṣeṇa, the noble Bhadrasena,
Ṛjudāsa, and Bhadradeva— he, Kaṃsa, indeed slew them all.
Saṃkarṣaṇa was the seventh, and Kṛṣṇa himself was the eighth;
furthermore, Hari had sixteen thousand wives.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Lakṣmaṇā of the lovely smile,
and the eminent Jāmbavatī— these eight gave birth to many sons.
Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, and Sāmba were the principal [sons];
from Pradyumna was born the mighty Aniruddha by Kakudminī.
From Aniruddha and Subhadrā was born a king named Vajra;
Pratibāhu was the son of Vajra, and Cāru was his son.
Vahni was born in the lineage of Turvasu; Vahni’s son was Bharga. From Bharga, Bhānu was born as a son, and the son of Bhānu was Karandhama.
Learn from me the lineage of Maru, the son of Karandhama, and that of Druhyu. The son of Druhyu was Setu, and Āraddha was his offspring.
From Āraddha was born Gāndhāra, and from Gāndhāra came Gharma;
Ghṛta was the son of Gharma, and Durgama was the son of Ghṛta.
O Pracetas, listen to me regarding the lineage of Aṅga himself;
Sabhānara was the son of Aṅga, and from him Kālañjaya was born.
From Kālajya was born Sṛñjaya, and from Sṛñjaya came Puruñjaya;
Janamejaya was his son, and Mahāśāla was his offspring.
Mahāmanas is remembered here as the great Śāla king of Aśvina;
from Aśvina was born Śibi, and Vṛṣadarbha was the son of Śibi.
The son of Mahāmanojātītikṣu was Ruṣadratha;
Hema was born from Ruṣadratha, and Sutapas was born from Hema.
From Bali were born Sutapas, as well as Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Andhra,
Paiṇḍra, Bāleya, Anapāna, and Aṅgata.
From Anapāna came Diviratha, and from him Dharmaratha was born;
from Dharmaratha came Romapāda, and Caturaṅga was his son.
Pṛthulākṣa’s son was Campa; from Pṛthulākṣa came Campa’s son, Haryaṅga, and his son was Bhadraratha.
His son was Bṛhatkarman, from whom Bṛhadbhānu was born;
Bṛhanmanas was the son of Bṛhadbhānu, and his son was Jayadratha.
The son of Jayadratha was Vijaya; the son of Vijaya was Dhṛti;
the son of Dhṛti was Dhṛtavrata; and from Dhṛtavrata came Satyadharman.
His son was Adhiratha, and Karṇa was his son.
Now hear from me about Vṛṣasena and the descendants of Karṇa belonging to the Puru lineage.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lunar Dynasty," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Hari said:
Janamejaya was the son of Purośca; from Janamejaya came Namasyu. His son was Abhayada, and from Abhayada was born Sudyu.
Sudyu’s son was Bahugati, and Saṃjāti was his offspring;
Vatsajāti was the son of Saṃjāti, and Raudrāśva was his son.
R̥teyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, Kakṣeyu, Kṛteyuka,
Jaleyu, and Santateyu were the excellent sons of Rodrāśva.
Ratināra was the son of Ṛteyu, and his son was Pratiratha;
Medhātithi was his son, and his son is recorded as Ainila.
Duṣyanta was born to Ainila, and his son Bharata was begotten upon Śakuntalā; from Bharata, Vitatha was born.
Vitatha’s son was Manyu, and it is remembered that Manyu’s son was Nara.
Nara’s son was Saṃkṛti, and Garga was indeed the son of Saṃkṛti.
From Garga was born Manyu, and from him Śini was born as a son;
from that son of Manyu, who was possessed of great heroism, was born Urukṣaya.
From Urukṣaya came Trayyāruṇi, and from Vyūhakṣatra, who was born of Manyu, came Suhotra; his sons were Hastin, Ajamīḍha, and Dvimīḍha.
From Ajamīḍha was born Purumīḍha, and from him came Kaṇva;
from Kaṇva Medhātithi was born, from whom the Kāṇvāyana twice-born ones descended.
From Ajamīḍha came Bṛhadiṣu; his son was Bṛhaddhanu;
his son was Bṛhatkarman; and his son was Jayadratha.
From Jayadratha was born Viśvajit, and Senajit was his son;
Rucirāśva was the son of Senajit, and Pṛthusena was his son.
Pārā was the son of Pṛthusena, and from Pārā the king Dvīpa was born;
Sṛmara was the son of that king, and Sukṛti was the son of Pṛthu.
Vibhrāja was the son of Sukṛti; from Vibhrāja was born Aśvaha;
from him came Kṛtyā; and Brahmadatta was his son, whose son was Viṣvaksena.
From Dvimīḍha came Yavīnara, and from Yavīnara came Dhṛtimat;
from Dhṛtimat came Satyadhṛti, and his son was Dṛḍhanemi.
Supārśva was the son of Dṛḍhanemi; likewise, Sannati was born from Supārśva. Kṛtu was the son of Sannati, and from Kṛtu, Ugrāyudha was born.
From Ugrāyudha was born Kṣemya, and Sudhīra was his son;
from Sudhīra came Purañjaya, and his son was Vidūratha.
From Ajamīḍha and Nalinī was born the king named Nīla;
from Nīla was born a son named Śānti, and Suśānti was his offspring.
From Suśānti was born Puru, and Arka became his son;
from Arka came Haryaśva, and from Haryaśva was born Mukula.
From Mukula, the Pāñcāla, were born Yavīnara, Bṛhadbhānu, Kampilla, and Sṛñjaya; and from Śaradvat was born the great Vaiṣṇava.
Divodāsa was the second son of this Śaradvat through Ahalyā;
his son was Śatānanda, and from that virtuous one was born Satyadhṛti.
Kṛpa and Kṛpī were born to Satyadhṛti through Urvaśī due to the loss of his virility; Kṛpī became the wife of Droṇa and gave birth to the preeminent Aśvatthāman.
From Divodāsa was born Mitrayu, and from Mitrayu came Cyavana;
from Cyavana was born Sudāsa, and Saudāsa was his son.
Sahadeva was his son; from Sahadeva came Somaka;
Jantu was born from Somaka, as was another great son, Pṛṣata.
From Pṛṣata was born Drupada; from him Dhṛṣṭadyumna arose.
From Dhṛṣṭadyumna came Dhṛṣṭaketu, and from Ajamīḍha, Ṛkṣa was born.
From Ṛkṣa, Saṃvaraṇa was born; Kuru was born from Saṃvaraṇa.
Sudhanus, Pīkṣin, and Jahnu were the sons of Kuru.
From Sudhanus was born Suhotra; from Suhotra was born Cyavana;
from Cyavana was born Kṛtaka, who was likewise the Vasu Upāricara.
Bṛhadratha was his successor, as were Satya and others, the sons of Vasu;
from Bṛhadratha came Kuśāgra, and from Kuśāgra, Ṛṣabha was born.
From Ṛṣabha was born Puṣpavān; from him was born King Satyahita. From Satyahita came Sudhanvan, and from Sudhanvan came Jahnu.
From Bṛhadratha was born Jarāsaṃdha, and Sahadeva was his son;
from Sahadeva came Somāpi, and Śrutavat was the son of Somāpi.
Bhīmasena, Ugrasena, Śrutasena, Aparājita, and another named Janamejaya were born; and from Jahnu, Suratha was born.
From Suratha came Sārvabhauma;
from Vidūratha [came] Jayasena; and Āvadhīta was the son of that Sārvabhauma.
Ayutāyu was his son, and Akrodhana was his son; Atithi was the son of Akrodhana, and Ṛkṣa was the son of Atithi.
From Ṛkṣa came Bhīmasena; from Bhīmasena came Dilīpa;
from Dilīpa came Pratīpa; and from Pratīpa came Devāpi.
Śaṃtanu and Bāhlīka—these three were brothers, all kings.
From Bāhlīka was born Somadatta; from him came Bhūri and Bhūriśravas.
Śala was born to Śantanu by Gaṅgā as a great and righteous Bhīṣma;
while Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya were born to Śantanu by Satyavatī.
Ambikā and Ambālikā were the two wives of Vicitravīrya;
from them were born Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, and likewise Vidura from his servant-woman.
Vyāsa begot a hundred sons, headed by Duryodhana, upon Gāndhārī; and five were born to Pāṇḍu.
Prativindhya, Śrutasoma, Śrutakīrti,
Śatānīka, and Śrutakarman— these five were born in order from Arjuna by Draupadī.
Yaudheyī, Hiḍimbā, Kauśī, Subhadrikā,
Vijayā, and Reṇumatī— these five bore sons in succession.
Devaka, Ghaṭotkaca, Abhimanyu, Sarvaga, Suhotra, Niramitra, and Parīkṣit, who was born of Abhimanyu.
Janamejaya will follow him; now hear of the kings who shall come after him.
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lunar Dynasty," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—141. Hari said:
Śatānīka, Aśvamedhadatta, Adhisomaka,
Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, Uṣṇa, and then King Citraratha.
Śucidrava, Vṛṣṇimant, Supeṇa, Sunīthaka,
Nṛcakṣus, Mukhābāṇa, Medhāvī, and Nṛpañjaya.
Pāriplava, O sages, Medhāvī, Nṛpañjaya,
Bṛhadratha, Hari, Tigma, Śatānīka, and Sudānaka.
Udāna, Ahni, Nara, Daṇḍapāṇi, Nimittaka, and Kṣemaka; then Śūdra was the father, and from him came the son.
But the Bṛhadbalas declare that there were kings born of the Ikṣvāku lineage;
after Bṛhadbala came Urukṣaya, and after him Vatsavyūha.
From Vatsavyūha were born Sūrya, his son Sahadeva,
Bṛhadaśva, Bhānuratha, Pratīcya, Pratītaka,
Manudeva, Sunakṣatra, Kinnara, and Antarikṣaka.
Suparṇa, Kṛtajit, the righteous Bṛhadbhrāja,
Kṛtañjaya, Dhanañjaya, Saṃjaya, and Śākya as well.
Śuddhodana, Bāhula, Senajit, Kṣudraka, Sumitra, and Kuḍava; now hear from Sumitra about the Māgadhas.
Jarāsaṃdha, Sahadeva, Somāpi, Śrutaśravas,
Ayutāyu, Niramitra, Sukṣatra, and Bahukarmaka.
Śrutañjaya, Senajit, Bhūri, and likewise Śuci; Kṣemya, Suvrata, Dharma, Śmaśrula, and Dṛḍhasenaka.
Sumati, Subala, Satyajit, Viśvajit,
and Iṣuñjaya— these are remembered as the kings of the Bārhadratha lineage.
Consequently, kings will become unrighteous and like Śūdras;
for the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the imperishable, is the creator of heaven and the other realms.
Dissolution is of three kinds: occasional, natural, and absolute.
In dissolution, the earth goes into the waters, the waters into fire, and the fire into heat.
The wind merges into the wind, and the ether into the ether;
it goes into the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), the intellect (buddhi) into the mind (mati), the individual soul (jīva) into the living soul, and that [living soul] into the Unmanifest Self.
The Self, the Supreme Lord, Viṣṇu, the one Nārāyaṇa, and Nara are imperishable;
everything else, including heaven and the rest, is indeed perishable.
Kings and others have met their destruction; therefore, one should avoid sin.
One should practice the Dharma steadfastly, so that by abandoning sin, one may go to Hari.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Vision of the Future Royal Dynasties," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—142.
Brahmā said:
The Lord Hari, having descended, protected Viṃśa and the others for the sake of destroying the dharma of the Daityas and for the protection of the Vedic dharma and other traditions.
The Unborn One assumes incarnations in the form of a fish and so forth;
having become a fish, he slew the Daitya Hayagrīva, who was a thorn to the horses.
Having brought forth the Vedas, Keśava protected Manu and the others;
and for their welfare, he became a tortoise and supported Mount Mandara.
Indeed, during the churning of the ocean of milk, the divine Dhanvantari appeared,
rising up while bearing a water-pot filled with nectar.
He taught the eight-limbed Āyurveda to Suśruta;
and Hari, assuming the form of a woman, caused the gods to drink the nectar of immortality.
Then the Boar, having descended, slew Hiraṇyākṣa;
he supported the earth and protected the gods.
Then Narasiṃha, having manifested, slew his enemy Hiraṇyakaśipu and the Daityas, and protected the Vedas, the Dharma, and other sacred traditions.
After that, Paraśurāma, the lord of the world born of Jamadagni, became Hari;
twenty-one times he made the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas.
He slew Kārtavīrya in battle and gave the earth to Kaśyapa;
having performed a sacrifice, the mighty-armed one remained on Mount Mahendra.
Then, from Daśaratha, the fourfold Madana was born as his sons: Rāma, and his younger brothers Bharata and the others. Rāma was destined for greatness.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Jānakī, Rāma’s wife,
as well as Rāma himself, acted for the benefit of his mothers in order to fulfill his father’s word.
Having arrived at Śṛṅgavera, Citrakūṭa, and the Daṇḍaka forest,
he then cut off the nose of Śūrpaṇakhā and [slain] Khara and Dūṣaṇa.
Having slain the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, the night-stalker who had abducted Sītā,
he installed his younger brother Vibhīṣaṇa in the city of Laṅkā.
Having established [Rāvaṇa] in the kingdom of the rākṣasas through Sugrīva, Hanumān,
and others, he ascended the Puṣpaka chariot together with Sītā, who was devoted to her husband.
Accompanied by the well-disposed Lakṣmaṇa, he indeed returned to his own city, Ayodhyā;
there he ruled the kingdom and protected the subjects, including the gods and others.
She protected the Dharma by performing sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha;
she took her pleasure with the lord of the earth, Rāma, according to her desire.
While Sītā remained in Rāvaṇa’s house, she did not resort to Rāvaṇa;
in deed, thought, and speech, she was always devoted to Rāghava.
That Sītā was indeed devoted to her husband, just like Anasūyā;
listen as I tell you of the greatness of a woman devoted to her husband.
In former times, there was a leper named Kauśika living in Pratiṣṭhāna;
his wife worshipped her husband, though he was so afflicted by disease, as if he were a god.
Though rebuked, she regarded her husband as a deity;
when told by her husband, that courtesan brought the prostitute, having taken an excessive fee.
Then, on the road, that twice-born man [Māṇḍavya], who was not a thief but had been impaled on a stake under the suspicion of being a thief,
was afflicted by extreme suffering in the darkness.
Mounted upon his wife's shoulders, Kauśika caused him to move;
enraged by the touch of his feet, Māṇḍavya spoke to him.
"His death shall occur at sunrise, by him who has kicked me with his foot.
Hearing that, his wife said: "The sun will not rise."
Then, due to the absence of sunrise, it became perpetual night for many years; consequently, the gods fell into fear.
They went to Brahmā for refuge, and the Lotus-born One said to them:
"Indeed, the power of his asceticism shall be quelled by this very splendor."
Due to the greatness of the devoted wife, the sun does not rise;
and because of its failure to rise, there is likewise the destruction of you mortals.
Therefore, for the sake of desiring the rising of the sun, you must indeed propitiate Anasūyā, the ascetic and devoted wife of Atri, who is his consort.
Having gone there, the devoted wife Anasūyā propitiated them;
and by performing the ritual at sunrise, she restored her husband to life.
Indeed, Sītā was even more distinguished than the devoted wife Anasūyā.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Vision of the Ten Incarnations," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 143 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
I shall now recount the Rāmāyaṇa, which, when heard, destroys all sins.
From the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu, Brahmā was born; Marīci became his son.
From Marīci came Kaśyapa; from him, Ravi; from him, Manu is remembered. From Manu came Ikṣvāku, and in his lineage, King Raghu is remembered.
From Raghu was born the powerful King Daśaratha;
he had four sons of great strength and prowess.
Rāma was born of Kausalyā; Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, was born;
and Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna were the two sons born of Sumitrā.
Rāma, devoted to his father and mother, obtained a collection of divine weapons from Viśvāmitra; thereafter, he indeed slew the Yakṣī Tāṭakā.
In the sacrifice of Viśvāmitra, the powerful one indeed slew Subāhu;
then, having gone to the sacrifice of Janaka, he married Jānakī.
The hero Lakṣmaṇa took Ūrmilā; Bharata took the daughter Māṇḍavī;
and Śatrughna indeed took Kīrtimatī, as well as both daughters of Kuśadhvaja.
Having gone to Ayodhyā with their father and the others, Rāma and the rest remained there;
Śatrughna and Bharata went to their maternal uncle Yudhājit.
When those two had departed, that best of kings prepared to bestow the kingdom;
he was then entreated by Kaikeyī for his son Rāma.
Rāma desired to dwell in the forest for fourteen years,
together with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, for the sake of his father’s welfare.
Having abandoned his kingdom like a blade of grass, he went to Śṛṅgaverapura;
leaving his chariot at Prayāga, he proceeded to the Citrakūṭa mountain.
Due to his separation from Rāma, the king ascended to heaven;
having performed the funeral rites, Bharata, accompanied by his army, returned and spoke to Rāma.
"Having returned to Ayodhyā, O high-minded one, rule the kingdom!
But he did not wish for it, having instead given his sandals to Bharata for the sake of the kingdom.
Then, having been dismissed, Bharata protected the kingdom of Rāma;
remaining devoted in Nandigrāma, he, observing his vow, did not enter Ayodhyā.
Rāma also departed from Citrakūṭa and went to the hermitage of Atri;
having paid homage to Sutīkṣṇa and Agastya, he arrived at the Daṇḍaka forest.
There, a rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā arrived seeking to devour them;
having had her ears and nose cut off by Rāma, she was then driven away.
Impelled by him, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and Triśiras likewise arrived with an army of fourteen thousand rākṣasas.
Rāma also dispatched them to the city of Yama with his arrows;
for Rāvaṇa, urged by the Rākṣasī, had indeed come to carry her away.
Then, having first assumed the form of a deer while carrying his triple staff,
Rāma, urged on by Sītā, slew Mārīca.
As he was dying, he cried out, "Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having been called by Sītā, arrived, and Rāma beheld him.
Having gained an opportunity and taken Jānakī upon his lap, Rāvaṇa said, "Surely Sītā has been abducted by the illusory power of the rākṣasīs."
Having pierced through Jaṭāyu, the powerful one then went to Laṅkā and held her,
who was protected there, within the shade of an Aśoka tree.
Having arrived, Rāma beheld the leaf-hut empty;
then the Lord, grieving for Jānakī, began to search for her.
Having performed the funeral rites for Jaṭāyus and having gone toward the southern direction as directed by him,
Rāghava then formed a friendship with Sugrīva.
Having pierced seven palm trees with a straight-knotted arrow,
he then pierced Vālin, the lord of the monkeys, at Kiṣkindhā.
Rāma, staying himself on Ṛśyamūka, made Sugrīva his ally;
Sugrīva then dispatched monkeys who were like mountains.
To search for Sītā in the eastern and other directions,
they went to the western, northern, and eastern quarters and returned full of joy.
And those who, searching for Jānakī, were wandering toward the southern direction through forests,
mountains, islands, and the sandy banks of rivers.
Indeed, not seeing Jānakī and having resolved upon death,
Hanumān, that elephant among monkeys, learned [the truth] from the words of Sampāti.
He leapt across the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, which was a hundred yojanas wide;
there he beheld Jānakī situated within the Aśoka grove.
She was threatened by the rākṣasīs and by the rākṣasa Rāvaṇa,
who said to her, "Become my wife," while she remained thinking only of Rāghava.
Having given his ring to Sītā, the monkey spoke words of well-being to her:
"I am the messenger of that Rāma; do not grieve, O Maithilī."
"And give me a token of recognition by which Rāma will remember me.
Having heard that, Sītā gave the jewel from her braid to Hanumān.
"O monkey, you must speak in such a way that Rāma may lead [us] quickly.
Having said, "So be it," Hanumān shattered the divine grove.
Having slain Akṣa and other Rākṣasas, and having himself come to their imprisonment,
he saw [them] with all the arrows of Indrajit and spoke to Rāvaṇa.
"I am Hanumān, the messenger of Rāma; give Maithilī back to Rāma!
Having heard this, he became enraged and set his tail ablaze.
The mighty monkey, his tail ablaze,
having burned Laṅkā, returned to the side of Rāma.
Having eaten the fruit in Madhuvana, he informed [Rāma] that Sītā had been seen;
he also gave the jewel from her braid to Rāma, and Rāma went to the city of Laṅkā.
Accompanied by Sugrīva, Hanumān, Aṅgada, and Lakṣmaṇa,
Vibhīṣaṇa also came to seek refuge with Rāghava.
Rāma consecrated that younger brother of Rāvaṇa as the sovereign of Laṅkā;
and having constructed a bridge over the ocean with Nala, Rāma crossed it.
And standing upon Mount Suvela, he beheld the city of Laṅkā;
then those heroic monkeys—Nīla, Aṅgada, Nala, and the others—[did likewise].
Then Dhūmra, Dhūmrākṣa, Vīrendra, Jāmbavat and others, along with Mainda,
Dvivida, and their leaders, shattered the city of Laṅkā.
Having slain the Rākṣasas of massive bodies, who resembled heaps of black collyrium, as well as all the other Rākṣasas along with the monkeys, Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, remained.
And Vidyujjihva, Dhūmrākṣa, Devāntaka, Narāntaka,
Mahodara, Mahāpārśva, Atikāya, and Mahābala.
Kumbha, Nikumbha, Matta, Makarākṣa, Akampana, Prahasta, the heroic Unmatta, and the exceedingly powerful Kumbhakarṇa.
The mighty Rāghava, with his weapons and other means, indeed cut down the son of Rāvaṇa;
having severed the multitude of his arms, he struck down Rāvaṇa.
Then, having taken the pure Sītā and remaining in the Puṣpaka chariot,
he arrived at Ayodhyā, the most excellent city, together with the monkeys.
Thereupon he ruled the kingdom, protecting his subjects like his own children;
having performed ten horse-sacrifices, he performed the ritual immersion at Gayāśiras.
Having performed the funeral rites for the funeral cakes according to the rules and having bestowed gifts, Rāghava,
upon seeing his two sons Kuśa and Lava, consecrated them both in the kingdom.
Rāma ruled the kingdom for eleven thousand years;
thereafter, Śatrughna slew Lavaṇa and the actor Bharta.
Having bowed to the sages, Agastya and others, and having heard the origin of the Rākṣasas,
he went to heaven together with the people residing in Ayodhyā, his purpose fulfilled.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Rāmāyaṇa," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—144.
Brahmā said:
I shall proclaim the *Harivaṃśa*, the supreme majesty of Kṛṣṇa;
from Vasudeva and Devakī were born Vāsudeva and Bala.
For the sake of protecting righteousness and the like, and for the destruction of unrighteousness and the like,
Kṛṣṇa, having drunk deeply from her breasts, brought Pūtanā to her end.
Then the cart was overturned, and the twin *arjuna* trees were shattered;
the serpent Kāliya was subdued, and Dhenuka was struck down.
Having held up Mount Govardhana and been worshipped by Indra,
Hari fulfilled his burden-lifting task and made a solemn vow.
For the protection of Arjuna and others, Ariṣṭa and the rest were struck down;
the Daitya Keśin was slain, and the cowherds and others were fully satisfied.
Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, and the wrestler Kaṃsa were struck down from their platforms;
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and others were the eight supreme wives of Hari.
Indeed, that great-souled one had sixteen thousand other wives;
their sons, grandsons, and so forth numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
And from Rukmiṇī was born Pradyumna, who slew Śambara;
his son was Aniruddha, the husband of Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa.
Wherein a great battle took place between Hari and Śakra,
and Bāṇa’s thousand arms were severed, leaving him with only two.
By him Narakasura was slain, by whom Pārijāta was carried away; Bala and Śiśupāla were killed, as was the monkey Dvivida.
After Hari had departed, Aniruddha begot a son named Vajra, who became king;
he made Sandīpani his preceptor and restored his son to him,
while Ugrasena was appointed as the protector of Mathurā and the guardians of the celestial realms.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Harivaṃśa," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 145] Brahmā said:
I shall fully proclaim the Bhārata, which brought about the removal of the earth's burden;
for Kṛṣṇa, fighting on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas and others, accomplished this task.
From the lotus at Viṣṇu’s navel was born Brahmā; Brahmā’s son was Atri, and from Atri came Soma. From him was born Budha, and from him, through Ilā, Purūravas was born.
In that lineage, Yayāti was born; [from him came] Bharata and Kuru. In his lineage was Śantanu, and from Śantanu, a son was born to Gaṅgā.
Bhīṣma was endowed with all virtues and had reached the further shore of the Brahmavaivarta.
Two sons were born to Śantanu by Satyavatī;
the Gandharva Citrāṅgada slew the son Citrāṅgada.
Another Vicitravīrya became the husband of the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
when Vicitravīrya had ascended to heaven, [Pāṇḍu] was born from Vyāsa through that [wife].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the son of Ambikā, Pāṇḍu the son of Ambālikā, and Vidura was born to a maidservant; from Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī bore [sons].
There were hundreds of mighty warriors, headed by Duryodhana;
meanwhile, five sons were born to Pāṇḍu from Kuntī and Mādrī.
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, Nakula,
and Sahadeva— these five possess great strength and prowess.
The enmity between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas arose indeed through the workings of destiny;
the Pāṇḍavas were oppressed by the fickle Duryodhana.
Those heroes, though burnt in the house of lac, were liberated by means of their own stainless wisdom.
Then, having slain the Rākṣasa Baka, those great-souled ones entered the dwelling of a Brāhmaṇa in that city of Ekacakrā.
Then, having learned that the Svayaṃvara of Draupadī was taking place in the kingdom of the Pañcālas and that her hand would be won by valor as the bride-price, the Pāṇḍavas married her.
With the consent of Droṇa and Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra then bestowed half of the kingdom upon them;
they subsequently obtained it in Indraprastha, the most excellent of cities.
Then, having constructed the assembly hall, those of firm vows performed the Rājasūya sacrifice;
meanwhile, in Dvāravatī, Arjuna obtained his beloved Subhadrā,
the sister of Vāsudeva, with the consent of the Slayer of Mura.
The divine chariot Nandighoṣa, the unsurpassed bow of Agni,
that divine weapon named Gāṇḍīva renowned throughout the three worlds,
inexhaustible arrows, and likewise impenetrable armor.
With that bow, the heroic Pāṇḍava Bībhatsu, endowed with great prowess and having Kṛṣṇa as his companion, offered libations to the Fire-god.
Having conquered the kings during his world-conquest and taken their jewels,
he joyfully presented them to his great brother Yudhiṣṭhira, who was skilled in statesmanship.
The righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounded by his brothers,
was defeated by the sinful Duryodhana through a game of dice involving deceit— a game played according to the counsel of Karṇa and Duḥśāsana and the will of Śakuni.
Then, for twelve years, they performed great austerities in the forest,
accompanied by Dhaumya and Draupadī as the sixth, surrounded by a multitude of sages.
Taking refuge in Virāṭa’s city in disguised forms,
those highly wise ones lived there for one year, protecting him from that seizure of cattle.
Having departed, those heroes respectfully requested their own kingdom from King Duryodhana; they asked for five villages as half of the realm.
Endowed with strength and surrounded by seven divine akṣauhiṇīs, they did not reach Kurukṣetra, yet they waged war there.
Duryodhana and the others, joined by eleven [forces] and exerting themselves,
engaged in a tumultuous battle resembling the war between the gods and the asuras.
Bhīṣma was the commander-in-chief at the outset of Duryodhana’s army,
and Śikhaṇḍin was that of the Pāṇḍavas; between them there occurred a most terrible battle, day and night, with weapons against weapons, arrow against arrow.
Covered by hundreds of arrows from Śikhaṇḍin and Arjuna, Bhīṣma awaited the northern solstice and meditated upon the Lord who wields the mace.
Having spoken many kinds of teachings and having gratified his numerous ancestors,
he became absorbed in the stainless state of bliss, freed from all sin.
Then the valiant Droṇa went forth to fight with Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
that battle lasted for five days and was exceedingly terrible.
Where those protectors of the earth were slain by Pārtha in battle,
even Droṇa, having encountered an ocean of grief, attained heaven.
Then Karṇa went to fight with Arjuna,
the great-souled one; after engaging in a great battle for two days, that heroic man was submerged in the ocean of Pārtha’s weapons and subsequently attained the world of the Sun.
Then Śalya went to fight with the wise Dharmarāja;
within half a day, Śalya was slain by arrows resembling blazing fire.
Then the valiant Duryodhana, seizing his mace with speed,
rushed toward Bhīma like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
Then, having been struck down by the hero Bhīma with his mace,
Aśvatthāman, the son of Droṇa, went to the sleeping army during that night.
Remembering the slaughter of his father, he struck with the strength of his arms;
then the valiant one slew Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the sons of Draupadī as well.
While Draupadī was weeping, Arjuna, having conquered Aśvatthāman with the Aiṣika weapon, seized that supreme crest-jewel.
Yudhiṣṭhira, having comforted the women who were overwhelmed with grief,
bathed and offered libations to the gods, the ancestors, and the grandfathers.
Then, comforted by Bhīṣma, he ruled over a great kingdom;
he worshipped Viṣṇu with an Aśvamedha sacrifice performed according to the rules and accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Having installed Parīkṣit on the throne and heard of the destruction of the Yādavas in the Mausala [Parvan],
the king chanted the Thousand Names.
Then Vāsudeva, accompanied by his brothers Bhīma and the others, went to Viṣṇu’s heaven;
he did so again for the purpose of deluding the Buddhas, the enemies of the gods.
Furthermore, Kalki Viṣṇu will appear again in the village of Śambhala;
mounted upon a horse, he will then reduce all the worlds to ashes.
Indeed, for the protection of the gods and others, for the removal of unrighteousness,
and for the sake of slaying the wicked, he takes on incarnations.
Just as Dhanvantari, born from the churning of the ocean of milk,
indeed proclaimed the Ayurveda for the sake of the life of the gods and others.
By hearing the Bhāratas and the incarnations from the high-souled Śuśruta, the son of Viśvāmitra himself, a man shall go to heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Mahābhārata and Other Works," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 146 of the Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa] Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, I shall now explain the etiology of all diseases in their true essence,
just as it was previously proclaimed by the eminent sages, beginning with Ātreya.
Disease, evil, fever, affliction, disorder, corruption,
malady, consumption, distress, ailment, and affliction— these are synonymous terms.
The etiology, the premonitory symptoms, the clinical signs, the therapeutic suitability, and the pathogenesis— thus the knowledge of diseases is traditionally taught as fivefold.

They say that the "source" (nidāna) is designated by various synonyms— such as sign (nimitta), cause (hetu), sphere (āyatana), condition (pratyaya), arising (utthāna), and reason (kāraṇa)— by which the prior form is characterized.

A disease that is about to arise, not yet dominated by a specific derangement of the humors, has unmanifest signs due to its subtlety; such are the symptoms of diseases according to their respective natures.
That very [substance], when it has attained manifestation, is designated as "form" (rūpa);
it is the manifesting of configurations, the sign, the characteristic mark, the token, and the shape.
The application of medicines, food, and lifestyle regimens— which are contrary to the cause, the disease, and the perverted [symptoms], yet produce the opposite effect— brings about happiness.
One should recognize the alleviation of a disease as that which is known as "sātmya" (wholesome);
its opposite is "anupaśaya," designated as "asātmya" (unwholesome) for the disease.
Just as a disease is produced by a specific morbid humor and its subsequent spreading,
that manifestation is designated as *samprāpti* (the full onset).
It is differentiated according to the distinctions of number, type, predominance, strength, and time, just as it will be stated here that there are eight types of fever.

Regarding the various combinations of the humors (doṣas), one should determine the predominance of a disease based on whether it arises from independence or dependence [of one humor over others]. GarP_1,146.11 //

The specific strength or weakness [of a remedy] is determined by the totality or deficiency of its constituent parts, such as the root and so forth; likewise, the time for administering medicine according to the disease is determined by the portions of night, day, and the half-meal intervals, in accordance with their respective purity.
Thus has the meaning of the diagnosis been stated; it shall now be taught in detail:
for all diseases whatsoever, the diagnosis is the provoked humors (malas).
The cause of their provocation is said to be the indulgence in various unwholesome things;
the threefold unwholesome application of these three has been previously described.

Through the consumption of bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, and dry foods in immoderate quantities, as well as through running, physical exertion, staying awake at night, and speaking in an excessively loud voice; // GarP_1,146.15 //

The wind (samīraṇa) becomes aggravated by physical exertion, sexual intercourse, grief, anxiety, exercise, and coitus; it is provoked at the end of summer, at the end of the day, at the end of the night, and at the end of a meal.
Bile [is aggravated] by pungent, salty, sharp, hot, and acrid substances, by anger, and by burning foods;
and during autumn, midday, the middle of the night, and at times of internal heat.
By means of substances that are sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, obstructive to the channels, and cold;
and by means of comforts such as pleasant sitting, sleep, indigestion, and daytime sleeping, which promote corpulence—// GarP_1,146.18 //
When food that has been eaten is undigested due to the absence of proper emesis and other such measures,
and when phlegm (śleṣman) is aggravated during the forenoon and the early part of the night, I shall describe the resulting complications.
Furthermore, there is a combination (sannipāta) of all [the humors] due to their becoming mixed,
as well as from eating food that is contaminated, undigested, irregular, incompatible, and so forth.
With spoiled liquor and water, dried vegetables, raw radishes, oil-cake, meat that is stale, putrid, dried, or emaciated; GarP_1,146.21 //

Due to those various factors that produce the three humors (doṣas), from the transformation of food, from the corruption of the bodily constituents (dhātus), from wind (vāta) arising before [the meal], and from the disturbance caused by the possession of dual spirits (dvigraha-āveśa); GarP_1,146.22 //
Due to the consumption of spoiled food, by malefic planets afflicting the natal star,
from various improper yogas, from the indulgence in sinful acts,
from the complications of women's childbirth, and likewise from improper medical treatment; // GarP_1,146.23 //
Thus provoked for each specific disease,
the humors (doṣas), following the course of the ailment, quickly resort to an elixir (rasāyana) and undergo transformation within the body.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of All Diseases," in the section on Conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Dhanvantari said:
*Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—147* Dhanvantari said:
I shall now declare the diagnosis of fever for the sake of awakening understanding regarding all fevers:
Fever is the lord of diseases, a malevolent force, the king of death, a devourer, and the end-maker;
it was born from the upward-turning eye of Rudra, who was enraged at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
That torment, consisting of delusion and characterized by suffering, arises from one's own misconduct;
cruel in nature, it persists through various births under diverse names.
Pākala is the affliction among elephants, abhitāpa among horses, alarka among dogs,
