indramada among clouds, nīlikā in the waters, jyotis among medicinal herbs, and that which is called ūṣara in the earth.
In the case of a fever arising from phlegm (kapha), there occurs nausea, vomiting, cough, stiffness, coldness in the skin and other parts,
and pustules appearing on the limbs.

At the appropriate time, there is either the manifestation or the increase of all [symptoms] according to their respective natures; the alleviation [of symptoms] is as described in the section on etiology, while the opposite constitutes non-alleviation.
Loss of appetite, indigestion, stiffness, and lethargy;
burning in the heart, improper digestion, drowsiness, and lassitude;
and the failure of the bladder to discharge its contents due to the suppression of the natural urges—these are the complications.
Excessive salivation, nausea, loss of appetite, a mouth with a taste for fluids, clarity of the urine, heat and heaviness of the limbs, excessive urination,
lack of digestion, and absence of emaciation are the symptoms of *āma-jvara* (fever with undigested toxins).
Hunger, emaciation, lightness of the limbs, mildness of fever,
and the discharge of the humors— these are the signs of a fever free from *āmaja* (undigested morbid matter) after eight days.
Just as [the symptoms] correspond to their own specific signs in a combined fever, even when born from a combination of fevers,
there occur headache, fainting, vomiting, burning of the body, dryness of the throat and mouth, loss of appetite, and pain in the joints;
along with sleeplessness, agitation, horripilation, yawning, and excessive talkativeness— these arise from wind combined with bile.

Fever born of phlegm and wind has as its symptoms: burning heat, loss of appetite, pain in the joints and head, spitting, labored breathing, cough, discoloration of the skin, coldness, numbness, darkness before the eyes, vertigo, drowsiness, and a sense of being embraced by a cold embrace.
Coldness, stiffness, sweating, burning sensations, instability, thirst, cough, the discharge of phlegm and bile,
delusion, drowsiness, a coated tongue, and a bitter taste in the mouth— these are to be known as the symptoms of a fever born of phlegm and bile.
In this [fever], there is burning with all the symptoms occurring again and again;
it becomes cold, great sleep during the day, and wakefulness at night.

There is either constant sleep or no sleep at all; indeed, there is either great perspiration or none at all; singing, dancing, laughter, and so forth, as well as the cessation of natural activities, [occur].
The eyes are tearful, turbid, reddened, sunken, and have disheveled eyelashes;
there is pain in the calves, the sides, the head, the joints, and the bones, as well as vertigo.
The ears are ringing and painful, or indeed become extremely cold;
the tongue is scorched and rough, and the joints of the limbs feel heavy and tremble.
Spitting up blood and bile, rolling of the head, excessive thirst,
and the appearance of dark-red circular patches on the trunk.
Heartache, a sense of impurity, little or excessive activity, a glossy appearance of the mouth, loss of strength, loss of voice, and delirious speech; // GarP_1,147.17 //

One should call that *sannipāta* condition "abhiṇyāsa" (prostration), characterized by a long duration of the maturation of the humors (*doṣapāka*), constant drowsiness, and a continuous rattling in the throat, as well as the destruction of vitality (*hataujas*).
When the wind (vāyu) is obstructed in the throat, the bile (pitta) is intensely compressed within;
then, due to its mobile nature and lightness, it moves toward the external pathways.
Consequently, in a fever arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), there occurs yellowness of the eyes.

When the humors have increased and the digestive fire has been destroyed, the fever characterized by all symptoms combined is a *sānnipāta* fever; it is incurable, whereas otherwise it is difficult to cure.
Otherwise, that which arises from a combination of humors— wherein the *pitta* remains separate—
produces a burning sensation either in the skin or in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), whether preceding or following [the other symptoms].
Similarly, when wind and phlegm are cold, the burning sensation and other symptoms arising from them are difficult to overcome;
in that case, the phlegm is liquefied and dried up by the pitta during the onset of the cold stage.
When the bile (pitta) has subsided, fainting, intoxication, and thirst arise;
furthermore, at the end of the burning sensation and other symptoms, drowsiness, lassitude, and vomiting occur in succession.
Sweat is produced in four ways: from external contact, from possession, from curses, and from malevolent spells; that born of injury arises from burning sensations and the like.
And due to that fatigue, the wind (vāyu), generally vitiating the blood,
produces a fever accompanied by pain, distress, dejection, and discoloration.
[It is] born from planetary possession, medicine, poison, anger, fear, grief, and desire.
In this [disease], there is also a sudden onset of seizures, weeping by day,
fainting caused by the smell of medicinal herbs, headache, vomiting, and emaciation.
From poison arise fainting, diarrhea, a dark discoloration, burning sensations, and vertigo;
from anger, trembling and headache; and from fear or grief, delirium.
From desire arise delusion, aversion, burning, the loss of shame, sleep, intellect, and fortitude;

in the onset of possession (graha) and other states, these symptoms belong to the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), with wind (marut) predominating in form and the other two [humors] in their respective functions.
Those two terrible fevers of *sannipāta* arising from anger within anger, or from bile (*pitta*), or born of curses and malevolent spells, are considered most unbearable. (GarP 1.147.30)
And it is tormented and consumed by the mantras of the *abhicāra* rites;
first the body is afflicted here and there, and then by eruptions and disorientation.
The fever of one seized by constant fainting increases day by day;
thus fever is seen to be of eight kinds, yet it is also twofold in brief.
It is bodily or mental, mild or sharp, internal or external in its locus;
it is natural or morbid, curable or incurable, and associated with phlegm (sāma) or free from phlegm (nirāmaka).
Previously, there was heat in the body and heat in the mind;
however, due to the movement of the winds through yoga, it becomes cool when joined with phlegm (śleṣman).

When fever is associated with pitta, there is a burning sensation; when it is mixed, the symptoms are mixed; furthermore, when it is localized internally, there will be excessive complications in the fever, internal agitation, and the retention of waste products.
Furthermore, external fever with external intensity has been established;
it is naturally produced by wind and the other humors in succession during the rainy season, autumn, and spring.
The other type is the modified (vaikṛta), which is difficult to cure; generally, the natural (prākṛta) fever arises from wind (anila).
In the rainy season, the vitiated wind produces a fever accompanied by bile (pitta) and phlegm (śleṣman).
In autumn, one should treat the pitta, and its attendant, the kapha;
because of their nature and because of the seasonal excretion [of waste], there is no danger from fasting in that season.
In spring, phlegm (kapha) increases, and subsequently wind (vāta) and bile (pitta) may also arise;
fever caused by strong [doshas] with minor complications is curable.

In every respect, a fever characterized by abnormal symptoms is declared incurable from the outset; likewise, the intensity of complications, weak digestion, and excessive urination [indicate the same].
There is no discharge, no wasting away, and no appearance of hunger or fever;
yet there is an excessive force of fever, thirst, delirium, labored breathing, and vertigo.
The onset of impurities and internal agitation are the signs of the fever being matured;
once it has reached its full digestion, one should avoid the opposite [of treatment] and observe fasting for seven nights.
Fever is said to be of five kinds according to the strength or weakness of the humors and the season; it is most frequently taught to arise from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
The continuous, the constant, the quotidian, the tertian, and the quartan fevers; these impurities pervade the channels that carry the bodily humors, urine, and feces.
Heating the entire body, increased by [the qualities of] equanimity and so forth, they are powerful, heavy, and, being dependent on the *rasas*, affect him without distinction.
They would constantly produce an unbearable, feverish heat that is without rival;
then, it would swiftly exhaust the impurities, the fever, and the bodily constituents.
In all its aspects, through the purity or impurity of the tastes and so forth, [the effects] arise sequentially from wind,
bile, and phlegm after seventeen, twelve, and ten days respectively.
"Generally, one follows the boundary for both liberation and destruction"—this is the opinion of Agniveśa; however, the traditional teaching of Hārīta is as follows.
The seventh, ninth, and likewise the eleventh lunar days are doubled;
this is the boundary of the three defects, leading both to liberation and to destruction.
Due to purity or impurity, fever may persist here for even a long time,
especially in those who are emaciated, afflicted by disease, and consumers of improper diet and other such habits.
Even a minor fault, having acquired strength from any one of the [three] humors such as wind (vāta),
becomes an adversary because it is characterized by irregular increase and decrease.
The disturbed humor (doṣa), characterized by irregular decrease and increase, produces fever;
being powerful, it manifests at its own time, causing fever in those individuals.
Furthermore,
when its opposing forces have been weakened and its defects exhausted, the fever subsides and becomes subtle, dissolving right within the bodily constituents such as the rasa.
Because the channels that carry the vital fluids are constricted, distorted, and near-closed, he experiences emaciation, discoloration, dullness, and other such conditions.
The defect of pervading the entire body does not quickly arise;
by that [practice], the virtuous are constant, while the opposite occurs through its reverse.
The irregular fever, characterized by an irregular onset and associated with the time of night,
is generally a disorder residing in the blood that produces a continuous fever.

At the junction of day and night, it occurs once; on another day, it relies upon that [junction]. In that [state], the channel carrying flesh and the channel of fat are involved in the third-day fever.
Grāhī arises from pitta and vāta in the head, from kapha and pitta in the trika (the sacral region), and from vāta and kapha in the back; it is known to recur with an interval of one day.
The fourth [type of seizure] resides in any one of the impurities—fat, marrow, or bone;
indeed, another [type] residing specifically in the marrow manifests its power.
Due to wind (vāyu), it first enters the elbows and calves from the head;
having reached the bones and marrow, it is the fourth type of reverse fever (caturthaka-viparyaya).

It causes fever for three days in three ways, but releases it for one day; this occurs through the relative strength or weakness of the humors (*doṣas*) arising from various other activities and conditions.
Due to the non-inversion of past actions, one should observe a fast for seven nights;
likewise, fever arises from the mind and from karma at various times.
Because it moves through the profound elements, because it arises from a combination [of all three humors],
and because the humors are equal in their intensity, the quartan fever is difficult to treat.
Because in these subtle fevers, which are extremely remote [from the core],
the humors (doṣa) move slowly and in small quantities through the channels of the blood and so forth over a long period of time.
Because it consumes the body entirely and produces feverish distress and other symptoms,
when its progression has been interrupted by effort, the fever is observed as being accompanied by heat.
Irregular and characterized by irregular undertakings, it follows the course of the night;
its movement becomes increasingly slow and its power diminishes accordingly.
In due time, that provoked humor (doṣa) causes fever, and it does so after a long or even a very long interval, according to the respective tastes and other factors it encounters.
Just as a seed sown on the ground and moistened with water does not wait for time to sprout, so too does the seed of a fault [produce its result].
Just as one who has taken poison brings its force into the internal seat,
so too does the poison of the faults of time, having gained strength through the lapse of time, further provoke the humors.
In this way, irregular fevers such as the *satata* and others arise;
there is nausea, heaviness, dejection, breaking pain in the limbs, and yawning.
Loss of appetite, vomiting, and labored breathing occur in every fever when the rasa-dhatu is affected; additionally, there is spitting of blood, thirst, dryness, heat, and the eruption of pustules.
When [the fever] is based on blood, there is burning heat, passion, dizziness, intoxication, and delirium;
when it is based on the internal heat (pitta), there is thirst, exhaustion, stool that is touched by heat, internal burning, vertigo, and darkness.
When the fat is located within the flesh, there is foul odor, twitching of the limbs,
perspiration, excessive thirst, vomiting, a foul smell in the mouth, or an inability to endure [these symptoms].
In the bone stage, there is incoherent speech, exhaustion, loss of appetite, and the breaking of the bones;
there is the aggravation of the humors, awakening, labored breathing, convulsions of the limbs, and moaning.
Internal burning with external coldness, labored breathing, and hiccups indeed affect the marrow;
there is the vision of darkness, the cutting of the vital points (marmans), and stiffness of the penis.
When semen flows, death occurs when it is dependent upon the semen;
however, in the case of the opposite, five other conditions arise that become increasingly difficult to cure.
As if smearing the limbs with phlegm and heaviness,
accompanied by mild fever, delirium, and coldness— this is *pralepaka*.
He suffers from a constant mild fever, is parched, and moves with difficulty due to cold;
his limbs are stiff, he is dominated by phlegm (śleṣman), and he becomes one who consumes the strength of his own body.
One who passes urine that has the color of a variety of turmeric and resembles its paste is indeed known as the variety of fever named Hāridraka; it is considered to be fatal.
When the phlegm and wind are equal in a person whose bile is diminished,
the fever that arises from the day becomes sharp, while the fever arising at night becomes mild.
When the body has had its strength taken away by the sun during the day and has been further dried up by physical exertion,
a fever caused by wind (vāta) will inevitably occur in the early part of the night.
When the phlegm and bile are situated in the stomach while the self (ātman) resides therein,
half of the body becomes cold and half becomes hot.
When bile is deposited in the body and phlegm is situated at the extremities,
the body becomes hot while the hands and feet become cold.
That which resides in the lymph and blood is curable; so is that which has reached the flesh and fat.
That which has reached the bones and marrow is difficult to cure, as it destroys the luster of its respective limbs.
Unconscious and afflicted by the force of the fever, he looks about as if filled with rage;
he constantly voids feces that are foul-smelling, hot, and expelled with great force.

The body becomes light, free from fatigue, delusion, and fever; there is a burning sensation in the mouth, excellence of the sense organs, and absence of pain; there is perspiration, sneezing, a natural inclination of the mind toward yoga, a desire for food, and itching on the head—these are the signs of the departure of fever.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Fever and Other Topics," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 148—
Dhanvantari said:
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the etiology of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease),
[caused] by excessively hot, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and burning substances.
When excessively consumed along with other such foods as *kodrava* and *uddālaka*,
the pitta provoked by pitta-disorders causes the liquid blood to faint (become turbid).
Having attained a state of mutual similarity with them, they pervade the body through the corruption of bile and blood, as well as from their conjunction and their toxic influence.
Among those [humors] that follow the variations of odor and color, it is designated by the term "rakta" (blood);
it originates from the spleen and the liver as the seat of blood.
Heaviness of the head, loss of appetite, a desire for cold things, a sensation of fumes,
sour eructations, vomiting, nausea after vomiting, cough, dyspnea, vertigo, and exhaustion.
Redness is not beneficial; there is a fish-like odor from the mouth, and you are free from fever.
There is a reddish-yellow or greenish hue in the eyes and other parts. (GarP 1,148.6)
In this [state], there will be an inability to distinguish between blue, red, and yellow colors;
one will possess the nature of intoxication even while dreaming.
When provoked, it flows upward through the nose, eyes, ears, and mouth; downward through the penis, womb, and anus; and through all the pores of the skin.

Since disorders arising from phlegm (kapha) and others located in the upper body are cured by purgation, many medicinal substances are prescribed for pitta; indeed, purgation is the most excellent medicine for it.
Wherever phlegm (kapha) persists as a secondary consequence, there too a purgative is required;
for those who have sweet decoctions, mild emetics that are beneficial for clearing phlegm are appropriate.

Those things which are pungent, bitter, or astringent, or which by their very nature increase phlegm, as well as downward-moving [drugs] and palliative treatments, are not conducive to longevity; therefore, emesis is the means for achieving success in such cases.
Emesis for pitta is a mild remedy and not a drastic one;
it is suitable for a person whose strength remains continuous and whose pitta has been pacified.
Astringent [tastes] are beneficial for him, as are sweet ones exclusively;
however, that which is afflicted by both phlegm and wind is incurable and merely palliative.
Because it is contrary [to the natural order] and because no medicine can cure it, it is unbearable;
indeed, there is no purificatory treatment whatsoever for this one who is so contrary.
In the case of rakta-pitta, purification is prescribed in the reverse order;
likewise, pacification and cleansing are desired here.
Indeed, when the humors are combined, emesis is beneficial in every respect;
for in that case, the movement of the humor is observed to be like a Śiva-weapon hitting its mark.
And the complications resulting from their transformation are established therein.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Raktapitta," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa— 149] Dhanvantari said:
Since cough is a disease that acts quickly, it shall therefore be explained here.
Five types of cough are recognized: those caused by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, chest injury (kṣata), and wasting (kṣaya).
All of them will be neglected until their destruction, each succeeding one being more powerful than the last; the symptom of those yet to come will be itching in the throat and loss of appetite.
There, the downward-moving wind, having turned upward and reached the chest, spreads through the throat, causing dryness of the ears, mouth, and throat.
Filling the channels of the veins, they then cause the limbs to twitch;
making the eyes roll as if to close them, the afflicted voice suffers and the sides are oppressed.
It proceeds with a crooked sound like that of a cracked bell-metal vessel,
causing pain in the heart, sides, and head, as well as delusion, agitation, and loss of voice.
It causes a dry cough accompanied by great force, pain, and sound;
with horripilation, one expectorates dry phlegm with difficulty, after which the condition subsides. (GarP 1,149.6)
From pitta arise yellow eyes, a bitter taste in the mouth, fever, and dizziness;
vomiting of bile and blood, thirst, hoarseness, a sensation of fumes, and intoxication.
In the Kāsavega type, there is continuous [vomiting] like the appearance of celestial lights;
due to phlegm, there is slight pain in the chest and head, while the heart feels numb and heavy.
There is a coating in the throat born of intoxication, as well as catarrh, vomiting, and loss of appetite;
there is horripilation and the discharge of thick, oily phlegm. (GarP 1,149.9)
When these various acts of rashness, such as fighting and the like, are performed beyond one's physical capacity, the wind (vāyu) becomes exhausted; then, the powerful bile (pitta) follows after it.
The provoked [wind] causes coughing, by which the phlegm—yellow, dark-brown, dry, knotted, and greatly increased—is expectorated along with blood. (GarP 1,149.11)
One should spit with a throat that is aching and as if split apart,
and with a chest pierced as if by sharp needles and afflicted by colic.

Afflicted by a painful touch like a piercing thorn, accompanied by splitting pain, oppression, and burning heat, he suffers from aching joints, fever, labored breathing, thirst, loss of voice, and trembling. (GarP 1.149.13)
Then, moaning like a pigeon, he suffers from pain in his sides;
due to phlegm and other humors, he vomits, and his digestive power, strength, and complexion decline.
In one who is emaciated, there is the presence of blood and urine, as well as labored breathing and stiffness of the back and waist;
these are the symptoms of Rājayakṣman when the vāyu and other humors are aggravated in a person who is running [or exerting himself].
In the seat of consumption (yakṣman), they produce a cough and then expectorate phlegm that resembles putrid pus—
thin, mixed, and greenish-red.
The heart feels as if it is being slept upon, pricked, and even cooked;
suddenly there is a desire for heat and cold, excessive eating, and a loss of strength.
The mouth becomes glossy, clear, and curved; the eyes become beautiful to behold;
and then all the symptoms of wasting appear in him.
Thus, this cough born of wasting (kṣayaja) destroys the bodies of those already emaciated;
however, it may be palliable in those who are strong. Likewise, the cough born of injury (kṣataja) is also palliable, provided both types are recent.

These two shall also be effective by their inherent power; furthermore, there is a separate sequence for the *sādhya* and other [categories], as well as all those who are mixed, those who are emaciated, the aged, and the elderly.
Since diseases such as cough, dyspnea, consumption, vomiting, and loss of voice arise from neglect,
one should therefore conquer them with urgency.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Cough," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—150] Dhanvantari said:
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the etiology of the disease of dyspnea (śvāsa);
dyspnea arises from the increase of cough or from the aforementioned factors that aggravate the humors (doṣas).
Even from dysentery, diarrhea, vomiting, poison, jaundice, and fever;
from dust, smoke, wind, injury to the vital organs, or even by cold water—
The five types [of asthma] are the minor (kṣudraka), the intermittent (tamaka), the interrupted (chinna), the great (mahān), and the fifth, the upward-moving (ūrdhva);
in these, the wind, obstructed by phlegm, remains pervasively throughout the body.
Vitiating the channels that carry breath, water, and food,
[the wind] situated in the chest produces asthma arising from the stomach (āmāśaya).

Its premonitory symptoms are pain in the heart and the flanks, upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), abdominal distension, and a splitting sensation in the temples; in this condition, excessive eating leads to exhaustion.
Impelled by that wind, the wind itself, impelling the minor [wind],
being turbid, moves against the natural direction through the vessels, agitating the phlegm.
Seizing his head and neck and pressing upon his chest and sides, [the disease] causes severe coughing, wheezing, delusion, loss of appetite, and a thick nasal discharge.
He produces a breath of intense force that afflicts the vital breath;
he faints from its impulse, and finds momentary relief at the end of each spitting.
Lying down with great difficulty, he pants; when seated, he seeks relief;
his eyes are wide open, his forehead is covered in sweat, and he is in intense agony.
With a parched mouth, frequent sighing, a desire for warmth, and trembling,
it increases through clouds, water, cold, eastern winds, and phlegmatic conditions.
That *astamaka* fever, though generally palliable, may be curable in a strong man;
however, the first type of it does not subside with cold treatments for one suffering from fever and fainting.
Afflicted by the pain of the tearing of vital organs (marmans) as if from coughing and labored breathing,
he suffers from perspiration, fainting, abdominal distension, and the sensation of a burning and bursting in the bladder.
With his gaze cast downward and his eyes bleary, one eye reddened with affection;
his mouth parched, lamenting in distress, his luster vanished and his consciousness lost.
Gasping with a most tremendous and piteous sound, he chokes and pants,
tossing about incessantly like a frenzied bull in rut.
His knowledge and discernment were lost, his eyes and face were bewildered;
he rolled his eyes, his urine and feces were obstructed, and his speech was faltering.
With a parched throat and intense pain in the ears, temples, and head, he who breathes out long and upward but cannot draw it back down; GarP_1,150.16 //
With his mouth and ears obstructed by phlegm and afflicted by the enraged wind,
he gazes upward, rolling his eyes aimlessly in all directions.
When his vital points are being severed, he laments with his speech obstructed;
these [omens] are unmanifest when they succeed, but when manifest, they certainly take away life.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Cough," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—151] Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, I shall now describe the etiology of hiccup; listen to that. Its single cause, premonitory symptoms, number, and its nature according to the bodily humors shall be explained.
Hikkā is of five types: bhakṣyodbhavā, kṣudrā, yamalā, mahatī, and gambhīrā;
it arises there from wind (marut) due to improper and hurried consumption.
Afflicted by food and drink that is dry, sharp, coarse, and unappeasing,
the vital breath produces hiccup characterized by a low sound and accompanied by hunger.
That [hiccup] which occurs equally with meals and drinks is born of food;
however, when the wind is provoked by exhaustion, it brings about the minor hiccup.
Flowing out from the base of the collarbone, it indeed possesses a slow velocity;
it increases with physical exertion and becomes mild immediately after eating.
That hiccup which proceeds with slow and twin-like impulses increases in intensity at the beginning and reaches its peak at the end.
One should identify that as Yamalā when she shakes her head and neck;
she is characterized by delirium, vomiting, diarrhea, rolling of the eyes, and yawning.
That [suffering] is characterized by the twin [cough], rapid [breathing], hiccups, and indigestion;
it belongs to one whose pair of eyebrows and temples are destroyed, and whose eyes have lost their hearing [clarity].
Paralyzing the body, speech, memory, and consciousness, it torments the seeker and strikes at his vital points. (GarP 1,151.9)
Bowing from behind with envy, the Mahāhikrā proceeds;
she possesses great spears, great sounds, great speed, and great strength.
And from the heart or from the navel, she proceeds as before.
Possessing such a form, she may perform great yawning and stretching;
however, one who is profound may accomplish it through a profound cause.
One should avoid the first two [types of women], as well as any woman with abnormal genitalia,
one who has excessive discharge, one who is pregnant, one who is elderly, and one who is promiscuous.
For one whose body is wasted by diseases and emaciated by the cessation of food, even all other ailments lead to destruction; yet they do not act with such swiftness as this.
Hiccups and labored breathing—these two indeed take up residence at the time of death.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Hiccup," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—152] Dhanvantari said:
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the etiology of the disease of consumption (yakṣma),
which is followed by many diseases and preceded by many diseases.
Rājayakṣmā, kṣaya, śoṣa, and rogarāj—thus it is called;
for in ancient times, this was the king of the stars, the twice-born, and the monarchs.
And because it is both a king (rājan) and consumption (yakṣman), it is considered *rājayakṣman*;
furthermore, it is called *kṣaya* because it causes the wasting away of the body and its medicinal remedies, and because it arises from that [wasting].
Because it dries up the bodily fluids and other constituents, emaciation is called the "king of diseases," as it is like a king.
Rashness, the suppression of natural urges, and the depletion of semen, vitality, and unctuousness [lead to this condition].
The abandonment of the proper rules for food and drink are its four causes;
by these, the wind (vāyu) is provoked, which then needlessly excites the bile (pitta) throughout the entire body.
Having entered the joints of the body, they afflict those vessels;
they either block the openings of the channels or likewise discharge excessively through them.
It causes pain in the middle, the upper, the lower, and the lateral parts of the heart;
its form will be a severe catarrh and fever.
Excessive salivation, sweetness in the mouth, softness of the fire and the eyes, a state of greed for food and drink, and the perception of the pure as impure; GarP_1,152.8 //
The falling of flies, grass, hair, and so forth into food and drink generally causes nausea,
vomiting, loss of appetite, and a decline in strength even after one has bathed.
Excessive whiteness of the hands, thighs, chest, feet, face, belly, and eyes;
a goad on the arms; a tongue [like a whip]; and the sight of loathsomeness in the body.
A fondness for women, liquor, and meat; loathsomeness; veiling the head;
the growth of nails, hair, and bones; and being overcome in a dream—these [are the signs]. 152.11.
Falling victim to chameleons, snakes, monkeys, beasts of prey, or birds; and climbing upon hair, bones, husks, ashes, or other such refuse.
The sight of empty villages and regions, of water drying up, of celestial lights in the sky, and of trees blazing with forest fires; GarP_1,152.13 //
When located in the trunk (koṣṭha), it causes rhinitis, dyspnea, cough, pain in the throat and head, loss of appetite,
upward breathing, emaciation, and downward vomiting.
When pain and awareness are present at the sides and located at the joints, fever arises;
these eleven symptoms are produced by *rājayakṣman*.
One should recognize their complications as pains that destroy the throat,
yawning, body aches, spitting, sluggish digestion, and foul breath.
In that condition, due to vāta, there is pain in the head and sides, along with body aches;
due to pitta, there is constriction of the throat and loss of voice, as well as [pain] in the feet, shoulders, and hands.
Burning sensation, diarrhea, vomiting of blood, foul breath, fever, intoxication, loss of appetite, vomiting, cough, heaviness in the head and body—these arise from phlegm (kapha). (GarP 1.152.18)
Excessive salivation, catarrh, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice,
and weak digestion arise from the humors (doṣas), due to the dullness of the digestive fire and the predominance of swelling, coatings, and phlegm.
When the openings of the channels are blocked and the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) have become very slight,
a burning sensation arises in the seat of the mind, and indeed other complications (*upadravas*) occur.
Food mixed with sour juices is digested right within the digestive tract;
generally, for those whose constituent elements are diminished, food does not lead to the nourishment of the limbs.
For its essence does not serve for blood or flesh;
rather, being supported on all sides, it exists solely as that which is wasting away.

When the signs are slight and the disease is extremely diminished, one should avoid treating it if there is a wasting of the six organs; otherwise, one should certainly treat it even in all other cases.
Due to the individual or combined humors, and from the depletion of all the fat, hoarseness of voice occurs;
his voice becomes weak, dry, and faltering.
Due to Vāta, there is a throat with the appearance of a parrot's color that is relieved by unctuous and warm treatments;
due to Pitta, there is a burning sensation in the palate and throat, and constant dryness occurs.
The throat feels as if it is being smeared with phlegm, and the mouth makes a wheezing sound;
when all the symptoms are present simultaneously and mutually contradictory, that is the state of *kṣaya* (wasting).
There is excessive smoky appearance and the symptoms of phlegm arise;
wasting diseases (kṣaya) in this condition are difficult to cure, and one should avoid those that are slight in all respects.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Phthisis," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari spoke: The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—153. Dhanvantari declared:
Now, O Suśruta, I shall explain the causes of anorexia;
anorexia arises from the humors (doṣas) localized in the tongue and the heart.
The fifth [type of taste] arises from the combination [of all three humors] and from mental distress.
The mouth becomes astringent, bitter, and sweet, respectively, in cases of wind (vāta) and the other humors.

Just as the mind [becomes] devoid of its natural flavor when afflicted by grief, anger, and the like, so too does it become corrupted by each of the individual defects of vomiting, or by all of them together, or by other [defects] as the fifth.

The *udāna* wind expels all the faults that have been accumulated and are fit for elimination; his afflictions quickly subside, and in due course, there arises a distaste for the indulgence of sensory pleasures.
The navel and back ache quickly, and one vomits food from the sides;
thereafter, one vomits frothy matter that is thin, scanty, and slightly astringent.
Accompanied by the emission of sounds, it occurs with great difficulty or with forceful urgency;
caused by wind (vāta), it is characterized by coughing, dryness of the mouth, and affliction of the voice.
Due to bile (pitta), it resembles alkaline water, smoky, greenish-yellow, and is accompanied by blood;
it is sour, pungent, and bitter, and is characterized by thirst, fainting, burning sensations, and suppuration.
From *kapha*, it is unctuous, thick, yellow, and mixed with honey-like phlegm;
it is sweet, salty, copious, persistent, and causes horripilation.
One who possesses swelling of the face, sweetness in the mouth, drowsiness, nausea, and cough—
having manifested all these symptoms— is to be abandoned in every respect.
Everything is loathsome to him through seeing, hearing, and so forth;
and in diseases born of wind and the like, or from food corrupted by worms, there occurs pain, trembling, and nausea— these especially arise when the disease is caused by worms.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Anorexia," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—154] Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, I shall now describe to you the etiology of heart disease and other ailments;
indeed, five types of heart diseases are recognized, including those caused by worms.
Due to wind, emptiness is excessively experienced, and one weeps aloud;
the heart is split, parched, and rigid, accompanied by a sense of emptiness and vertigo.
Sudden dejection, grief, fear, lack of interest in sound, trembling, fainting from shivering, obstruction of breath, and scant sleep; GarP_1,154.3 //

From pitta arise thirst, fatigue, and a burning sensation; from phlegm (kapha) there is sweating and a sequence of sourness; indeed, vomiting of sour bile and a fever characterized by a sensation like smoke [are the symptoms].
Due to phlegm, the heart becomes stiff and heavy as if filled with pebbles;
there is coughing, weakness of the bones, spitting, drowsiness, laziness, loss of appetite, and fever.
In heart disease caused by the three doshas and worms, there is darkening of the eyes,
entering into darkness, nausea, swelling, itching, and discharge of phlegm.
And here, the heart is constantly torn as if by a saw,
as one attempts to treat this terrible disease that brings death so swiftly, indeed so very swiftly.
Thirst arises from wind, bile, and phlegm; loss of strength occurs from the combination of all three (sannipāta);
and the sixth type arises from a complication (upasarga), wherein wind and bile are the causes.
For when it is provoked in all [the humors], due to the complete drying up of the bodily constituents (dhātu),
it causes dizziness, trembling, burning sensations, delusion, and heartache throughout the entire body.
Thirst arises when the vessels carrying blood to the root of the tongue, the throat, the internal membranes, the palate, and the fluids are dried up; this is their general characteristic.

Dryness of the mouth, lack of thirst for water, aversion to food, loss of voice, roughness of the throat, lips, and palate, and exhaustion upon protruding the tongue [are the signs]. Garuḍa Purāṇa 1,154.11.
From wind arise incoherent speech, mental derangement, excessive belching, and likewise disease; from it also come emaciation, wretchedness, ringing in the ears,
and dizziness of the head.
From pitta arise loss of the sense of smell, bad taste in the mouth, impairment of hearing, and loss of strength;
there is an increase of coldness, acidity, and froth, as well as fainting and a bitter taste in the mouth. (GarP 1,154.13)
Redness of the eyes, constant emaciation, burning sensation,
and excessive coughing occur when the phlegm is provoked from the rasa-dhatu and the wind (vāta) enters the water-carrying channels.
Because of that, the channel, filled with phlegm, becomes parched like mud;
the throat feels as if covered with bristles, and there is drowsiness and sweetness in the mouth.
Distension of the abdomen, heaviness of the head, numbness, vomiting, anorexia, lassitude, and indigestion— this is the fever characterized by all symptoms.

From the suppression of blood arising from [excessive] sexual pleasure, or from the suppression of wind and bile, thirst occurs in one who has suddenly resorted to cold water after being overcome by heat. (GarP 1,154.17)

That which has moved upward from heat, that which arises from bile, that which is produced by excessive drinking or intoxication, that which has a sharp onset, and that which results from the improper cooking of medicated fats— these constitute [the types of vomiting].
Thirst arising from phlegm is caused by the consumption of unctuous, pungent, sour, and salty foods;
that which is characterized by the symptoms described for the depletion of rasa is of the nature of depletion (kṣayātmikā).
The intense thirst that arises from other long-term diseases and afflictions such as consumption, delusion, and fever is known as being of the nature of an *upasarga* (epidemic).
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Amlapitta," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—155] Dhanvantari said:
I shall declare the etiology of alcoholism (madātyaya) and other related disorders as spoken by the sages:
[it is caused by substances that are] sharp, sour, dry, subtle, pungent, habit-forming through excessive use, and light.
Wine is expansive and clear; its opposite is fat.
Furthermore, qualities that are sharp, arising, and manifest during the day cause the agitation of the mind.
Beings are brought to the end of their lives by poison acting with intensity;
likewise, liquor, through its qualities such as sharpness and so forth, destroys the qualities of vitality, mildness, and vigor.
Established in the first and even the second stage of intoxication, which are abodes of joy, he brings his agitated mind to a state of non-action through ten qualities.
Struck by false conceptualization, the fool is deluded into thinking this is happiness;
having reached the junction between the mediocre and the superior, intoxication becomes his royal throne.
Like an unrestrained serpent, one might do anything; therefore, this ground is for those who are beyond reproach, yet it is the abode of immoral conduct.
He alone is the supreme guide through the difficult terrain of the many paths;
yet, remaining inactive, he lies face down here, established in the third intoxication.
Even after death, the evil-souled one has gone to an even more wretched state—
[losing] dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, honor and misfortune, and what is beneficial and harmful.
Afflicted by thirst and delusion, joined with emaciation,
delusion, and so forth, he falls downward into madness, wandering, and fainting, accompanied by epilepsy.
Those who are strong, having eaten their fill and being great eaters, do not become excessively intoxicated.
From wind (vāta), from bile (pitta), from phlegm (kapha), or from all three combined, the disease of alcoholism (madātyaya) arises.
Their common characteristics are profound delusion, pain in the heart,
violent tearing [of the body], thirst, somnolence, exhaustion, fever, and loss of appetite.
Obstruction of the frontal passages, dimness of vision, cough, labored breathing, insomnia, excessive perspiration, constipation, swelling, and confusion of the mind; // GarP_1,155.12 //
He is overcome as if by a dream, and though spoken to, he does not reply;
from bile (pitta) there arises fever with a burning sensation, perspiration, delusion, and constant confusion.
In the case of phlegm (śleṣman), there is vomiting, nausea, sleepiness, and heaviness of the abdomen;
in the case of all three combined (sarvaja), all symptoms are present. Having understood this, one who drinks wine [should do so with care].
Suddenly, both may become beautiful yet destroyers of one another and emaciating; this would especially occur for him due to a severe wind.
There is destruction [of tissues], spitting of phlegm, dryness of the throat, excessive sleepiness,
intolerance of sound, distraction of the mind, and indeed wind-pain in the limbs.

Heart disease, throat ailments, delusion, dyspnea, thirst, vomiting, and fever—these afflict one who does not turn away from intoxicants; however, he who has conquered his self and acts with conscious discernment shall be freed from them.
He is never afflicted by physical or mental disturbances; for him, those three diseases—arising from passion, delusion, and unwholesome food—shall cease to exist.
The blockage of the channels that carry fat, blood, and moisture gives rise to intoxication,
fainting, and prostration, which occur in order of increasing severity.
In this state, intoxication arises from all defects, as well as from blood, liquor, and poisons;
due to the infinity of its power, it has reached a semblance of movement, being flickering and deceptive in its manifestations.
In intoxication arising from wind (vāta), the body becomes rough, dark, and reddish;
through bile (pitta), one is prone to anger, has a reddish-yellow complexion, and is fond of quarreling.
In dreams, he utters incoherent speech and the like due to phlegm, for he is intent on meditation;
through the derangement caused by the combination of all [humors], there is stiffness of the blood and affliction of the limbs.

The symptoms of bile (pitta) are present at the outset; here, there is a distorted sense of one's own authority, excessive perspiration, trembling, and great sleepiness, along with exhaustion that exceeds all others.
One should discern wind and the other humors within the blood and other tissues by their excellence of characteristics:
[if the blood] is reddish, blue, or black, or if one enters into darkness as it were, [these indicate the presence of wind].
One awakens quickly; there is pain in the heart, trembling, dizziness, coughing, a dusky-red complexion, and fainting—these are the symptoms when [the disease] is of the nature of wind (māruta).
Seeing the sky as red or yellow due to bile, one enters into darkness;
and upon awakening, one is afflicted by sweat, burning heat, and thirst.
With a complexion like that of a broken earthenware pot, yellowish-blue in hue, and eyes agitated by red and blue,
one whose vision is clouded by phlegm perceives the sky as resembling a mass of clouds and enters into it.
After a long time, I awoke from that darkness, my heart and chest overflowing with tears,
while my limbs remained heavy and motionless,
as if bound by the duties of royalty.
Possessing every kind of deformity due to these three defects, he is like another demon of epilepsy;
he quickly casts one down motionless, even without loathsome movements.
When the humors have produced the onset of intoxication and fainting in embodied beings,
they subside by themselves through renunciation, or are quelled by medicines.
Exceedingly powerful, they arrested the activity of speech, body, and mind; together with their renunciation, they fell down, taking refuge in the destruction of the vital breaths.
Because of that, men become like wood, resembling the dead;
they would die quickly, very quickly, if medical treatment were not applied.
One should quickly turn back a man who is sinking in renunciation, which is like a fathomless ocean with its surging waters teeming with crocodiles.
Driven here and there by the activities of pride, anger, and passion, one applies logic equally to what is appropriate and inappropriate; this is not the case with intoxication.
Having distinguished between the vessel of the region of the throat, the natural capacity, or the age, one drinks in accordance with that; thereafter, one drinks the nectar.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Alcoholism and Other Disorders," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa— 156] Dhanvantari said:
Now, O Suśruta, I shall explain the etiology of hemorrhoids—
those peg-like growths that always arise within the flesh of living beings.
Therefore they are called *arśāṃsi* because they obstruct the path of the anus;
the *doṣa*, having corrupted the skin, flesh, and fat, produces various forms.
They say that fleshy sprouts arising from food, drink, and so forth produce hemorrhoids;
in brief, they are divided into two types according to whether they are congenital or arise from another [previous] life.

And the fissures at the tips of the dried [flesh], which are located along the region of the anus, measure four and a half finger-breadths; within that, three [fissures] are situated at a distance of one and a half finger-breadths.
The channel flowing toward the childhood [state] is the emitter (visarjinī) within their midst;
it is external in its non-concealment, located one finger-breadth outside the anus and so forth.
Beyond that, the body hairs there are a measure of one and a half finger-breadths;
the reason for this is that, although they arise simultaneously [with the body], their seeds were scorched during childhood.
The production of the seeds of hemorrhoids occurs due to the misconduct of the mother and father,
from the provocation of the deities, or otherwise from a derangement of the humors (sānnipāta).
Thus, all diseases arising from one's lineage are declared to be incurable;
those that are congenital are especially so, being rough and hideous to behold.

Those [discharges] which are directed inward, pale, and accompanied by severe complications should be treated individually according to their own nature, based on the specific doṣa, combination, or accumulation.
The [tumors] caused by wind and phlegm are dry, while those caused by bile are moist;
the causes for the provocation of the humors are as previously stated regarding clothing and so forth.
When the impurity is excessively accumulated in the fire [of the stomach], this [disease] arises again through sexual intercourse,
from the agitation of drinking, or from eating food that is irregular, hard, or coarse.

From the friction caused by the breaking of the ground arising from the buttocks, eyes, neck, and lips, and from contact with excessively cold water and continuous, forceful straining; // GarP_1,156.12 //
From the suppression of the urge to void urine or feces, or from their forced expulsion, there arises disgust, diarrhea, and indeed *grahaṇī*; that too is a complication.
Furthermore, from excessive physical exertion, uneven terrain, and other such activities,
as well as from the miscarriage of an immature fetus or the pressure caused by the growth of a fetus, [women may suffer].
By these and other such factors, the apāna wind becomes agitated within the waste;
it then resides in the folds of the anus, which are filled with fluid, active, and radiant in form.
The premonitory symptoms of that [jaundice] are as follows: weakness of the digestive fire, constipation, a sense of sinking in the bones, cramps in the calves,
and vertigo.
There is swelling of the eyes that have become congested, or there may be retention of feces;
the wind (vāyu), being obstructed, generally moves below the navel. (GarP 1.156.17)
Bloody, cutting [the flesh], he contracts with difficulty while gasping;
there is rumbling in the intestines, flatulence, and an abundance of caustic eructations.
There is abundant urine, scanty feces, loss of appetite, a smoky sensation in the stomach, pain in the head, back, and chest, lethargy, and loose stools.

Lust for the objects of the senses, anger arising from the experience of suffering, apprehension, dysentery, swelling, and [afflictions] such as jaundice, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen; GarP_1,156.20 //
These very [defilements] increase when those whose names have not been struck down are born;
for pride, being turned back by them, obstructs the downward path.
It agitates the other winds throughout all the sense organs and the body,
likewise drying up the urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and wind.
Then, having stolen the fire, they all for the most part become afflicted by hemorrhoids;
they are emaciated, utterly devoid of energy, dejected, wasted, and lusterless.
Lacking essence and shorn of luster like a tree consumed by fire,
he was seized by agonizing and violent diseases that afflict the vital organs as described for those afflicted by *yakṣma*.
Likewise, by cough, thirst, distaste in the mouth, dyspnea, and catarrh;
and by exhaustion, aching of the limbs, vomiting, sneezing, swelling, and fever.
Afflicted by impotence, deafness, numbness, and gravel-like pain,
emaciated, with a broken voice, he meditates repeatedly, spitting and suffering from loss of appetite.
One suffers from pain in all the joints, bones, heart, navel, anus, and groin;
with a straining anus, one passes bile resembling the color of a blue crane (*balāka*).
One voids excrement that is dried up, with mucus at the tip, alternating between cooked and raw,
pale-yellow like bile, stained like turmeric, and slimy.
The anal papillae are characterized by an excess of wind (vāta), being dry, accompanied by a tingling sensation,
swollen, reddish like glowing embers, rigid, uneven, and rough in appearance.
Mutually dissimilar, crooked, sharp, and gaping-mouthed,
they resemble the pods of the *śimbī*, the *kharjūra* date-palm, the *karkandhū* jujube, and the cotton plant.
Some resemble kadamba flowers, while others are like mustard seeds;
they cause excessive pain in the head, sides, shoulders, calves, thighs, groins, and other parts.
They cause sneezing, belching, constipation, oppression of the heart, and loss of appetite;
they bring about cough, dyspnea, irregularity of the digestive fire, ringing in the ears, and vertigo.
Afflicted by these, one passes stool that is knotted, scanty, accompanied by sound, and characterized by dysentery; it is mixed with mucus and froth, and is difficult to evacuate.
His skin becomes black, and his feces, urine, eyes, and face become bound [with darkness];
indeed, for him, there arises the occurrence of abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement (plīhodara), and prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā).
Those dominated by bile (pitta) have blue mouths and a reddish, yellowish, or blackish luster;
they have thin tips, exude fluid, are spread out, small, soft, and flaccid.
Resembling the tongue of a parrot, pieces of liver, or the mouth of a leech,
they cause burning, wasting, fever, perspiration, thirst, fainting, loss of appetite, and delusion.
They possess heat, are fluid, blue, hot, yellow, red, and of pale complexion;
they have a barley-corn-like waist, and their skin, nails, and other features are green, yellow, or turmeric-colored.
Those [tumors] dominated by phlegm (śleṣman) have large roots, are dense, cause little pain, and are white;
they are protruding, enlarged, glossy, rigid, round, heavy, and stable.
They are slippery, motionless, smooth, abundant with itching, and pleasant to the touch;
they resemble the seeds of the *karīra* and *panasa* fruits, as well as cow’s teats.
They cause distension and pain in the groins, excision-like cutting in the pubic region, bladder, and navel, along with cough, dyspnea, nausea, excessive salivation, loss of appetite, and catarrh.
They cause great hardship, heaviness of the head, coldness, and an alkaline taste;
they produce disorders such as impotence, weak digestion, vomiting, and diarrhea.
The flows of fat, lymph, phlegm, abundant feces, excrement, and blood do not leak out nor do they break apart; likewise, the skin and other parts become pale and oily.
Due to the combination of symptoms and the accumulation of associated disorders, these hemorrhoids possess all the characteristics;
they are blood-dominant, located in the anus, and endowed with a yellowish appearance.
Resembling the sprouts of the banyan tree and similar to guñjā berries or coral,
they are exceedingly corrupt and hot, afflicted by severe constipation.
Blood flows forth suddenly due to its excessive discharge,
and he who resembles a peacock is afflicted by the sufferings arising from the loss of blood.

His complexion, strength, and vigor will be diminished; his vitality will be destroyed and his senses will become turbid due to [the consumption of] mung beans, kodrava, citron, karīra, chickpeas, and the like.
The powerful wind (vāyu), aggravated by dry and constipating factors in the seat of feces,
obstructs the downward-carrying channels while drying up the lower parts.
Feces may cause a severe obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine;
by that, intense pain arises in the abdomen, back, heart, and sides. (GarP 1,156.48)
There is distension of the abdomen, diarrhea, nausea, and cutting pain;
furthermore, there is intense colic in the bladder and the occurrence of swellings on the cheeks.
Due to the upward movement of the wind (pavana), there arise vomiting, loss of appetite, fever,
heart disease, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa), urinary retention, and dysentery.
Deafness, excessive headache, dyspnea, pain in the head, cough, chronic catarrh,
mental disorders, thirst, asthma, bile-related diseases, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, and so forth.
And these extremely severe diseases born of wind arise; this is the ultimate affliction, characterized by hemorrhoids, death, and upward movement of the bodily humors.
For those whose digestive tracts are overcome by wind (*vāta*), [the hemorrhoids] arise even without those [causes];
however, the innate defects (*doṣa*) are located within the inner layer of the rectum.

Those [diseases] that are established are incurable; those born from the combination of two [humors], as well as those located in the second *vala*, are managed by means of the strength of the digestive fire and other factors.
They say those [afflictions] which have persisted for more than a year are difficult to cure;
likewise, those that have arisen on the outer layer of skin and are aggravated by a single doṣa.
Hemorrhoids that have not been present for long are easily curable;
those occurring on the penis and other such parts will be described according to their respective locations, as well as those born near the navel.
The Vyāna wind, having taken up the phlegm along with the slimy and soft tissues of a mole, produces hemorrhoids on the exterior of the skin.
They know that [condition] to be like a wedge, firm and hard, and like a leather peg;
there is pricking pain from Vāta and blackness at the edges from Pitta.
The sliminess, the knottedness, and the discoloration of the phlegm [occur];
therefore, a wise person should quickly exert effort toward the pacification of hemorrhoids,
for they swiftly cause disease.
If one should perform this, it causes the disease of bound bowels (baddhagudodara).
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Wounds," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—157] Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, I shall now declare the etiology of diarrhea (atisāra) and dysentery (grahaṇī);
it is of six types, caused by the humors individually, by all of them combined, and by fear and grief.
That diarrhea arises all the more intensely from the excessive drinking of water,
as well as from dried foods, muscle fat, oil, sesame flour, and sprouted grains.

Due to the consumption of alcohol, parching substances, or excessive quantities of food; from the derangement caused by excessive unctuousness; and from parasites, noise, and antagonistic factors, the wind (vāyu) becomes provoked in such a person.

It causes the downward wind (apānavāyu) to disperse, and by striking the digestive fire with that very wind, it activates the functions of the stomach, the bowels, and the liquefaction of feces and excrement.
The symptoms of that impending diarrhea manifest as a breaking pain in the heart,
the rectum, and the abdomen, along with perspiration of the limbs and constipation of the waste.
In that condition, there is distension and indigestion; due to wind, it is free from fever,
and one voids very small amounts of stool that are soundless and full of mucus.
The urine is rough, frothy, and clear, or it is repeatedly drawn up; likewise, it has the appearance of burnt meat, is slimy, and causes cutting pain.
With a parched and prolapsed anus, his hair standing on end and sighing deeply,
he has eaten food turned yellow by bile, appearing like turmeric or the color of young grass.
Accompanied by phlegm, it is reddish, extremely foul-smelling, and characterized by thirst, fainting, perspiration, and a burning sensation;
it is accompanied by pain in the anus, heat, and suppuration, and is thick.
There, the discharge is slimy, followed by small amounts of mucus with a flow;
it is accompanied by horripilation, distress, and heaviness in the bladder, anus, and abdomen.

Even when [the ritual] has been performed, he remains untouched by attachment; the soul of all, possessing all characteristics, he would cause that which was done to melt away when the mind is agitated by fear.
Then the wind (vāyu) is obstructed, causing heat, liquidity, and a sense of floating;
they say the symptoms of vāta and pitta are equal [in this state], and it is the same due to grief.

Diarrhea (atīsāra), in brief, is of two types: with undigested matter (sāma) and without undigested matter (nirāmaka). When it arises from blood, it is a disorder of the nutrient-fluid (rasa); due to heaviness, one voids [stools] in water that are foul-smelling, accompanied by flatulence, constipation, pain, and excessive salivation. 157.13.
The opposite of this is the "tasteless" (nirāma) type caused by phlegm, in which no one sinks [into death];
however, in cases of diarrhea, if one does not exert sufficient effort [in treatment], it leads to the disease of malabsorption (grahaṇī).
For him, there may be diarrhea caused by the excessive accumulation of the effects of extinguished digestive fire,
whether it be with mucus (*sāma*) or without mucus (*nirāma*), which is discharged as digested matter.
That diarrhea is characterized by excessive discharge and is naturally prone to rapid action;
it occurs through the decay of undigested matter, yet when digestion has occurred, it is not at all matured.
Cirakṛt is a disorder of the *grahaṇī* that causes the accumulation and discharge of waste;
it may cause sudden diarrhea or frequent, intermittent colic.
It arises in four ways: from each of the individual *doṣas* and from their combined aggravation (*sannipāta*).
The limbs lose their former strength, the vital breath becomes sluggish over time,
there is excessive salivation, a bad taste in the mouth, loss of appetite, thirst, fatigue, and vertigo.
Distension of the abdomen, vomiting, a ringing sound even in the ears, emaciation, nausea, suppressed eructation, and fever are the general symptoms [of poisoning]. (GarP 1.157.19)
Fainting, headache, constipation, swelling of the hands and feet,
drowsiness, dryness of the palate due to wind (vāta), darkness of vision, and ringing in the ears [occur].
It causes pain in the sides, thighs, groins, and neck, as well as acute cholera-like cramps;
it increases all types of diseases and wards off hunger and thirst. (GarP 1.157.21)
When digested, it causes flatulence; when eaten, one attains well-being.
From wind (vāta), there arises suspicion of heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, and jaundice.
After a long time, he repeatedly voids excrement that is painful, liquid, dry, hard, and accompanied by sound and froth; his anus is afflicted with dyspnea and coughing.
From the yellow [dosha], one produces a liquid that has a yellowish-blue luster or a yellow appearance;
the person is afflicted by foul-smelling and sour eructations, burning sensations in the heart and throat, loss of appetite, and thirst.
Due to phlegm, there is suffering in digestion, mental distress, vomiting,
loss of appetite, burning of the mouth, spitting, coughing, nausea, and catarrh.
The heart feels as if weighed down by torpor; the abdomen is motionless and heavy;
eructations are foul and sweet; and there is a sense of exhaustion accompanied by a feeling of horripilation.
When [the stool] is mixed with mucus and bound together by heavy and sour substances, it flows out;
even though the patient is not emaciated, there is weakness, and in the case of the "all-originated" type, all these symptoms are observed.

The three impurities, thirst and the rest, which are declared to be the humors (doṣas) in the division of the constituent parts, are also its [the body's] grahaṇī disorders; they are the cause of its destruction.
Diseases of wind (vāta), urinary stones, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal dropsy, fistula-in-ano,
hemorrhoids, and chronic diarrhea— these eight are the great diseases that are very difficult to overcome.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of the Essence of Diseases," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 158.
Dhanvantari said:
Now, therefore, listen, O Suśruta, to the etiology of urinary obstruction (mūtraghāta).
The bladder, the neck of the bladder, the penis, the waist, the scrotum, and the anus [are its locations].
The rectal cavities are said to have a single channel and are situated within the pelvic bones;
for even though the bladder is downward-facing, it is connected by the openings of the urine-carrying vessels.
They fill the sides with smooth (subtle) fluids that flow incessantly;
having entered by those very same [channels], they produce twenty types of disorders.
Urinary obstruction and urinary disorders (prameha) afflict the vital organs with difficulty;
accompanied by pain in the bladder, groin, and penis, one voids urine in very small quantities repeatedly.
In the wind-born type, the urine is passed with difficulty; in the bile-born type, it is yellow and accompanied by constant burning and pain;
in the phlegm-born type, it is reddish, and there is heaviness and swelling of the bladder and penis.
When the wind, having turned back from the opening of the bladder and drying it up, is accompanied by desire and suppressed, then all impurities become entirely pervasive throughout the whole body.
Then, from urine mixed with bile, phlegm, or semen,
a terrible stone (aśmarī) is gradually formed, just as bile forms the gallstone (rocanā) in a cow.
All [types] of this disease have phlegm as their basis; furthermore, its premonitory symptom is distension of the bladder and excessive pain all around its vicinity.

Obstruction of urine, difficulty in urination, fever, and loss of appetite are the general symptoms; there is pain in the navel, the perineal suture (sīvanī), the bladder, and the head of the bladder.
The urine will become voluminous, and likewise when the passage is obstructed;
once it has been bound and re-bound, one may void it easily, clear and resembling cow-dung stones (gomedaka).
From its agitation, there arises blood and flesh on the path, and pain occurs;
therein, afflicted by the onset of wind (vāta), the patient gnashes his teeth and trembles.
It seizes the penis and excessively pains the navel;
it voids feces accompanied by wind and passes urine drop by drop repeatedly.
His urinary stone (aśmarī) is dark and rough, as if covered with thorns;
due to the bile (pitta), the bladder (vasti) feels burning and hot, as if it were being cooked.
The stone (aśmarī) shaped like the kernel of a bhallātaka fruit is red, yellow, or white;
the bladder feels as if it is being pricked, and it is cold and heavy due to phlegm (śleṣman).
The stone (aśmarī) is large, smooth, honey-colored, or white;
these occur in children, and most frequently in them alone.
Due to the smallness of the accumulation in the seminal receptacle, one experiences ease in its grasping and discharge;
however, a large seminal stone (śukrāśmarī) arises from the retention of semen.
The wind, having seized the semen—whether displaced from its site or not yet discharged—within the two testicles, dries it up; that semen thus becomes a stone (*aśmarī*).
It causes pain in the bladder, difficulty in urination, and produces a white swelling;
as soon as it arises, it dries up and dissolves away.
When this [urinary tract] is afflicted by fever and cough, there occurs gravel (śarkarā) just like a stone (aśmarī);
or that [stone], split by the wind (vāyu), becomes gravel when the wind moves downward.
It exits together with urine; when [the process] is reversed, it undergoes digestion.
By the suppression of urine, the enraged wind (marut) becomes obstructed at the opening of the bladder.
Accompanied by retention of urine, pain, and sometimes itching on the left side,
one should incise the *sthūlaviplutā* hemorrhoid after exposing and elevating the bladder to the edge of the rectum.
When the bladder is afflicted, it causes pain and burning there, as well as throbbing and cramping;
furthermore, urine is discharged drop by drop.
This obstruction of the flow is also known as *vātabasti*;
it is difficult to overcome, and the second type, characterized by powerful wind (*anila*), is even more difficult to overcome.
The wind, having taken refuge within the passage of the feces and the bladder,
forms a firm, stone-like, elevated knot that is devoid of strength.
Vātāṣṭhīlā is that which causes the discharge of feces, urine, and flatus;
it is a morbid wind that has become coiled within the bladder, producing intense pain.
When the urine is obstructed, one suffers from wandering pain, stiffness, cramps, and heaviness;
or else one voids the urine in very small quantities, or only intermittently.
When urine is suppressed for a long time, it results in what is called *vātakuṇḍalika*;
the urine does not flow out, or it is obstructed, and that condition is known as *mūtrātīta*, characterized by little pain.
When, due to suppression, the urine is obstructed by wind and turned upward,
it then fills the abdomen below the navel.
Due to the impairment of the digestive fire or by the wind (*vāyu*), it may cause intense pain, distension, weakness, and the retention of waste, as well as the retention of urine. (GarP 1.158.29)
In one who has little urine, the [urine] that has been discharged remains in the bladder, the navel, or the anus,
and then flows out slowly, either with pain or without pain.
If the discharge of urine occurs in an interrupted manner, that is harmful to the teacher and the penis;
there will suddenly be thirst in the mouth and a steady, slight pain within the bladder.
A knot that causes pain equal to that of a urinary stone is called *mūtragranthi* (urinary glandular tumor);
it occurs when, during urination, a man who has approached a woman has his semen drawn upward by the *vāyu*.
When one urinates while displaced from the proper position, the urine flows either before or after [the discharge];
resembling ash-water, that is called *mūtraśukra*.
When the wind causes upward movement (udāvarta) of feces in those who are dry and weak,
and it enters the urinary tract mixed with feces, then [the following occurs].
If the urine droplets have an equal odor [to the stool], one should diagnose that as *vighāta*.
This occurs due to bile disorders, physical exertion, consumption of pungent and sour foods, flatulence, and so forth.
When the urine is located in the bladder due to aggravated wind (vāyu), it causes a burning sensation;
first it turns the urine, and then it becomes either mixed with blood or purely bloody.
They call that *uṣṇavāta* which is hot again and again and difficult to endure;
it occurs when pitta and vāyu are located in the bladder of one who is parched and whose body is exhausted.
If pitta and kapha,
or both of them, are congealed by vāta, they produce a wasting of urine accompanied by pain and burning, which is called by that [same] name.
Then, with difficulty, one voids urine that is yellow, red, white, or thick; it is accompanied by burning and may have the color of the powder of *rocanā* or conch shell. GarP_1,158.39 //
They say that when it is dry or possesses all colors, it is called *mūtrasāda*.
Thus have the diseases arising from the urine been described in detail.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Urinary Retention and Dysuria," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 159—
Dhanvantari said:

I shall now declare the etiology of urinary disorders (prameha); listen, O Suśruta! There are twenty types of prameha, among which ten arise from phlegm (śleṣman) and [the remaining] from bile (pitta).
Six and four [types] arise from wind (anila), and they carry fat, marrow, and phlegm;
one who has *hāridramēhin* passes pungent feces resembling turmeric.
In *mañjiṣṭhameha*, the urine is like water mixed with madder;
in *raktameha*, it is warm, salty, and blood-colored.
The *vasāmehin* passes urine frequently mixed with or resembling fat;
the *majjamehin* passes urine frequently resembling or mixed with marrow.
One suffering from elephantiasis (hastimehin) passes urine incessantly like a rutting elephant, devoid of force,
accompanied by semen, and obstructed.
The patient suffering from *madhumeha* becomes like honey; it is said to be of two types:
when the wind (*vāyu*) is provoked by the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), or when its path is obstructed by the humors (*doṣa*).
Covered by the symptoms of the doshas, he displays the signless state;
in one moment diminished and in the next moment full, he becomes difficult to cure.
If neglected for a long time, every [type of urinary disorder] indeed develops into madhumeha;
and because it is sweet among the urines, one generally voids urine like honey.
All of these are designated as madhumeha (diabetes mellitus) because of the sweetness of the body;
furthermore, there are indigestion, loss of appetite, vomiting, drowsiness, cough, and nasal catarrh.
Complications arise in cases of phlegm-born urinary disorders (meha):
pricking pain in the bladder and penis, tearing of the scrotum, and fever.
Burning sensation, thirst, acidity, fainting, and diarrhea are the symptoms arising from pitta;
while upward movement of wind (udāvarta), trembling, palpitations, and restlessness are those born of vāta. (GarP 1,159.11)
Pain, sleeplessness, emaciation, dyspnea, and cough arise;
[the skin diseases] śarāvikā, kacchapikā, jvālinī, vinatā, and alajī [also occur].
Masūrikā, sarṣapikā, putriṇī, savidārikā,
and vidradhi— these are the ten types of carbuncles resulting from the neglect of urinary disorders (prameha).
Due to the binding action of *kapha* upon food, its movement therein generally proceeds [slowly];
it is sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, slimy, and cold.

New grain, liquor, soup, meat, sugarcane, molasses, milk, and curds—these should be avoided when staying in one place for more than a night; likewise, one should refrain from lying down [in such a place]. GarP_1,159.15.
Corrupted by *prameha*, the *kapha* takes refuge in the bladder;
having vitiated the body's moisture, sweat, fat, muscle-fat, and flesh, it causes [the disease].
When phlegm and the other [humors] are excessively diminished, the wind (vāyu) brings the bile (pitta) and blood, which have taken refuge in the urine,
toward the urinary bladder (vasti), and it likewise causes their depletion.
The cognitions of what is curable or incurable and so forth arise from that very [ignorance];
likewise, when a fault is equal, they are rendered equal because of its supremacy.
Their general characteristic is the production of copious and turbid urine;
even though the specific humors (*doṣas*) and affected tissues (*dūṣyas*) may differ, [the disease remains the same] due to the particularity of their combination.

The distinction among the types of urinary disorders (meha) is determined by differences in the color and other qualities of the urine. [In the case of Udakameha, the urine is] clear, very white, cold, odorless, and resembles water.
In *mehatyudakameha*, the urine is slightly turbid and slimy;
in *ikṣumeha*, it is extremely sweet like the juice of sugarcane.
In the case of *sāndramēha*, one urinates what has become thick and stale;
the one with *surāmēha* urinates what is like liquor—clear on top and thick at the bottom.
With his hair standing on end, the one suffering from *śukrameha* passes urine that is thick and white like flour,
resembling semen or mixed with semen.
The one suffering from *sikatāmeha* voids impurities in the form of sand;
the one suffering from *śītameha* voids urine that is very copious, sweet, and extremely cold.
In śanairmeha, the patient voids urine very slowly and in small quantities;
in lālāmeha, the urine is slimy and mixed with threads of saliva.
In *kālameha*, one voids urine that is dark blue in color and appearance, smelling like an alkaline solution and having the touch of an alkaline liquid, resembling ink.
They arise at the joints and vital points (marmans), as well as in fleshy regions;
they are elevated at the edges and depressed in the center, accompanied by a lack of moisture and intense pain.
A pustule shaped like a shallow bowl (śarāva) is known as śarāvikā;
that which is shaped like a tortoise and accompanied by burning pain should be recognized by the wise as kacchapikā.
A large, blue pustule is known by the name Vinatā;
it burns the skin upon its appearance, being flaming and a giver of great suffering.
Alopecia (alajī) is red or white, covered with pustules, and is dreadful;
whereas masūrikā should be known as having the shape and form of a lentil (masūra).
A large pustule shaped like a mustard seed, located on the tongue, causing a burning sensation and great pain, is known as *putriṇī*; it may be large or small and is extremely subtle.
Round like the root-tuber of the vidārī plant and hard, it is called vidārikā;
however, when it possesses the symptoms of an abscess (vidradhi), it should be known as vidradhikā.
The *putriṇī*, *vidārī*, and *duḥsahā* arise from an abundance of fat;
others, characterized by a predominance of *pitta*, arise immediately from a deficiency of fat.
Those pustules may arise according to the respective aggravation of the humors (doṣas);
even without urinary disorder (prameha), these are produced by vitiated fat (medas).
And they are not perceived as long as the color is absent—
whether it be yellow or red— devoid of the premonitory signs of *meha*.

One who passes urine that resembles blood, they know that to be *raktapitta*. Excessive sweating, body odor, looseness of the limbs, an addiction to lying down, eating, and sleeping, a burning sensation in the heart, eyes, tongue, and ears, coarseness and intensity [of the body], and the excessive growth of hair and nails [are its signs]. (GarP 1,159.36)
A fondness for cold, dryness of the throat and palate, sweetness in the mouth, and a burning sensation in the hands and feet are the signs of an impending group of urinary disorders (meha);
moreover, ants run toward one's urine.
In urinary disorders (prameha), there is thirst and a sweet discharge; in diseases of honey-like sweetness (madhvāmaya), various morbidities may arise.
Alternatively, due to over-saturation, it may originate from phlegm (kapha), or when the humors are diminished, it may be of the nature of wind (vāta).
The complete forms of *kapha*-type and *pitta*-type urinary disorders, as well as those arising from sexual excess, which have sequentially transferred to the *pitta* type, are palliable;
however, if there is no fatal destiny (*diṣṭa*), such a urinary disorder may be curable.
