Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Prameha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 160—
Dhanvantari said:
I shall describe the etiology of abscesses (vidradhi) and of abdominal tumors (gulma); listen, O Śuśruta!
[They arise] from the consumption of stale, excessively hot, dry, parched, and burning foods.
—The Great Purāṇa of the Glorious Garuḍa, Chapter 160.1.
Dhanvantari said:
"O Śuśruta, listen as I describe the diagnosis of abscesses (vidradhi) and abdominal tumors (gulma).
[They arise] from consuming stale, excessively hot, dry, parched, and burning foods."
Through crooked postures in bed and various corrupting factors that vitiate the blood,
the skin, flesh, fat, bones, and marrow become corrupted, taking refuge in the abdomen.
That swelling which occurs both externally and internally, characterized by great piercing pain and intense agony, whether it be circular or elongated, is known as the disease *vidradhi* (abscess).
Due to the humors (doṣas), whether individually or combined, and due to blood that has not flowed out,
it moves here and there in the body, being hard, knotted, and stagnant.
In the interim, there occurs a severe and deep swelling that increases the size of the abdominal lump;
it exudes fluid like an anthill, and a loss of digestive fire (agnimāndya) arises.
In the navel, bladder, liver, spleen, lungs, heart, abdomen, and groins—
when the heart trembles, there is exceedingly intense pain in each of those respective locations.
It arises with a dark-red head, ripens irregularly, has an uneven shape, and is accompanied by loss of consciousness, vertigo, distension, discharge, crawling sensations, and sound. (GarP 1,160.7)
From pitta, it is reddish-copper or black, accompanied by thirst, delusion, fever, and burning;
from kapha, it is pale, itchy, and characterized by frequent onset, suppuration, and swelling.

The fever arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta) is characterized by impurity, coldness, stiffness, yawning, loss of appetite, heaviness, long duration, and lack of digestive transformation; it is a mixed type.
And by implication, the characteristic of *viḍbheda* (diarrhea) here consists of both external and internal symptoms:
it is dark, covered with eruptions, dusky, and accompanied by intense burning, pain, and fever.
The symptoms of bile manifest externally through blood, and likewise internally in women;
the cause of the disease arises from blood produced by injuries from weapons and the like.
Blood arising from a wound, driven by the wind (vāyu) and inciting bile (pitta),
produces an abscess (vidradhi) characterized by pitta and blood, accompanied by many complications.
Thus, the classification of complications is understood according to the difference in their locations:
for if [the wind] is blown into the navel, it reaches the bladder and causes dysuria.
There is obstruction of inhalation and exhalation, enlargement of the spleen, extreme thirst,
constriction of the throat, and a crushing pain in all the limbs and the heart when [the humor] is located in the *kloman*.
Delusion, fainting, coughing, as well as a piercing pain in the heart, and the arising of humors in the interior of the belly, the sides, and the abdomen.
Likewise, there is pain in the hip joints, the groin, the waist, and the back,
as well as in the sides, and obstruction of the wind in the anus.
One should determine their state of being unripe, ripening, or suppurated as one does for swellings;
when ripened, they discharge from above the navel through the mouth, while others do so from the anus.
One should know that a swelling arising from the anus, the chest, or the navel is a *vidradhi* (abscess) caused by the excessive moisture of the *doṣas*;
that which arises from the combination of all three (*sannipāta*) causes a displacement of its own seat.
For when it is ripe, the abdominal tumor (nābhivasti) located there may burst either internally or externally;
and for one who is emaciated, the internal suppuration of a greatly increased [tumor] is afflicted by complications.
In that case, there shall be an abscess for sinful men and sinful women;
and when the fetus has died within the womb, a dense swelling shall arise.
When the breast is afflicted, there is either pain or the symptoms of an external abscess;
however, because of the subtlety of their blood, this does not occur in women who are virgins.
The enraged wind, its movement obstructed, strikes the base of the penis;
reaching from the scrotum and groin, it flows through the channel leading to the testicular sac.
By compressing [the scrotum], it causes an enlargement of the vessels in the testicles;
the humors reside there within the fatty tissues, and that disease, known as *vṛddhi*, is of seven types.
In both types of urinary obstruction, due to Vāta, [the swelling] occurs either externally or internally;
it is filled with wind, rough to the touch, dry, and causes a burning sensation from the Vāta.
Resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, it is characterized by burning, heat, and suppuration due to pitta;
due to kapha, it is intense, heavy, unctuous, itchy, hard, and slightly painful.
A swelling covered with vesicles is black; a swelling from blood has the symptoms of enlargement;
and an increase of fat, like phlegm, is soft and resembles a palm fruit.
For one who has the habit of retaining urine, as he goes there, his urine—
free from desire, full of fortitude, and flowing gently— undergoes no agitation.
There is difficulty in urination, and below it, a circular swelling of the scrotum,
caused by those who provoke wind (vāta) through excessive consumption and immersion in cold water.
When embodied beings are agitated by the retention of feces and urine, by the contortions of their limbs,
and by their vital energies being disturbed, they become internally emaciated.
When the wind becomes disordered, it may drive that blood downward;
then, situated at the joint of that very moment, it produces a swelling resembling a tumor.
If it is neglected, there occurs the growth of a tumor, various pains such as flatulence, and manifold diseases;
being intensely compressed within, it moves with a sound, and swelling up, it returns again to the head.
This [condition], characterized by an increase in blood, is incurable; it has a form similar to *vātavṛddhi*, with veins that are dry, black, and reddish, resembling a window covered by wool.
The wind (vāta), having become aggregated through contact with the eight distinct humors and the defect of the menstrual flow (ārtava),
produces the eighth [type of disorder] in women.
One who has been emaciated by fever, fainting, diarrhea, and such acts as vomiting, or one who is afflicted by cold and hungry, may become strong. (GarP 1,160.34)
He who, afflicted by [diseases], drinks food and drink or undergoes fasting, immersion in water, and so forth,
while harboring lowly conceptions and provoking [the humors].
Without practicing oleation and sudation, one might resort to drying treatments;
or, having been purified, one might suffer a loss of purification, or experience tremors.
His humors (malas) are either dominated by wind (vāta), or they are indeed separate from it;
or else, all of them, combined with blood, follow the course of the body's channels due to the wind.
The wind, having obstructed the upward and downward pathways, indeed causes colic;
it is perceivable by touch, arises from a gulma, is hot, and has the form of a knot.

Due to excessive straining, the destruction of phlegm and feces, or the obstruction of the channels, the wind (vāyu) takes up residence in the abdominal cavity; through its dryness, it attains a state of hardness.
That which is independent is defective in its own substratum; that which is dependent is defective in another's substratum.
Therefore, phlegm is like a lump, indeed mixed with impurities.
The Gulma located in the bladder, navel, heart, or sides is so called;
when born of Vāta, it is characterized by headache, fever, and rumbling in the spleen and intestines. (GarP 1,160.41)
The piercing pain is like that of a needle; there is diarrhea with the loss of stool, and urine is passed with difficulty.
Furthermore, there is swelling in the limbs, face, and feet, as well as a deficiency of digestive fire.
Due to the mobility of the wind (*anila*), it causes roughness, blackness of the skin, and other such conditions;
being of undetermined configuration, it produces various kinds of pain.
Like a thicket swarming with ants, it throbs and is pushed about;
from pitta arise burning, sour eructations, fainting, diarrhea, perspiration, thirst, and fever. (GarP 1,160.44)
A yellowish discoloration appears on all limbs, and there is the manifestation of swelling from internal tumors;
the phlegm diminishes and flares up, as if burning its own seat.
From *kapha*, there is numbness, loss of appetite, malaise, fever in the head, coryza, lethargy, nausea, and a whitish or blackish discoloration of the skin and other parts. (GarP 1.160.46)
The abdominal tumor (gulma) is deep-seated, hard, heavy, and like a fetus situated within the womb;
the killers here run about from that very place, remaining in their own locations.
Generally, those tumors (gulma) arising from the combination of two [humors] involve a mixture of sexual fluids;
that born from all three is characterized by intense pain and burning, rapid suppuration, and is thick and elevated.
That blood-gulma (raktagulma) is indeed incurable; it arises only in women who, during their menses, suffer from colic or have a diseased womb.
Or if a woman indulges in excessive wind-inducing practices, the provoked wind obstructs her menstrual flow,
which is established to occur every month in the womb.
She undergoes nausea, longings, and the appearance of breast milk, and she acts according to her desires; she causes the fetus to develop and manifests its physical form within the womb.
Gradually, through contact with the wind (vāyu), pitta produces an accumulation of blood in the female reproductive organs;
from that, it generates the types of gulma mentioned for vāta and pitta.
Furthermore, there is intense pain in the uterus and in the seat of the blood,
as well as vaginal discharge, foul odor, and frequent sensations of trickling and aching.
Sometimes a gulma arises like a pregnancy; all of these originate from sexual passion.
A gulma ripens after a long time, whereas an abscess (vidradhi) does not increase further once it has begun to suppurate.
It ripens very quickly, for it has its basis in vitiated blood;
because it causes rapid burning, it is therefore called *vidradhi*.
There is a burning sensation in the bladder, pain in the spleen, a loss of digestive fire, complexion, and strength, or else the onset of the natural urges. (GarP 1,160.56)
Conversely, in the case of the opposite, there is no excessive pain in the external parts of the abdomen;
rather, there is discoloration, coughing, or a pronounced protrusion on the outside.
They describe *ānāha* as a condition characterized by distension in the abdomen accompanied by excessive, very severe pain,
along with the upward and downward obstruction of wind (*vāta*).
Dhana is like a gooseberry (aṣṭhī) and is knotted; aṣṭhīlā is elevated.
Pratyaṣṭhīlā is joined with all the characteristics [of aṣṭhīlā] and has that same shape.
Likewise, wind arising from the receptacle of digested food (pakvaśaya), due to its basis in intense pain,
causes excessive belching, constipation, lack of satiety, and rumbling in the intestines.
Flatulence, distension, and loss of the power of digestion shall be the signs of an impending gulma.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Abscesses and Gulma," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, I shall now declare the etiology of abdominal enlargements; listen to that.
Indeed, all diseases arise when the digestive fire is weak, but abdominal enlargements especially so.
Others are born with diseases such as anīrṇāmaya due to the accumulation of impurities; their upward and downward vital airs being obstructed, they become agitated and fail to flow properly.
Having vitiated the prāṇa and apāna breaths, they cause them to enter the joints of the flesh;
having distended the abdomen, they produce abdominal enlargement (udara) in eight distinct varieties.
Afflicted by the individual humors, by all of them combined, or by splenomegaly, inguinal hernia, ulcers, and edema,
they suffer with dry palates and lips, and with swelling in all their feet, hands, and bellies.
Men whose physical activity, strength, and appetite have vanished, whose bellies are distended as if blown up,
and who resemble hungry ghosts (pretas)— these are the signs of what is to come.
Hunger is destroyed, everything is digested with a burning sensation as if there were a loss of appetite;
that man who does not recognize when food is digested consumes what is unwholesome.

The strength of the body wastes away; one pants even when inactive and makes little effort; the intellect turns away from its objects, and there is also emaciation due to grief and other such symptoms.

For one suffering from abdominal disease, there will be constant pain in the back and joints even with light and small meals; moreover, due to the decay caused by old age, there will be a loss of strength. (GarP 1,161.8)
Independence, lassitude, the production of impurities, weak digestion,
burning sensations, swelling, and flatulence occur when water is present within the *āmāśaya*.
Death occurs everywhere in water; lamentation therein is fruitless.
Like a window, the belly gurgles through the networks of veins.
If one suppresses the urge by means of mantras, it may vanish;
however, when the wind is obstructed, there arise pains in the heart, waist, navel, anus, and groin.
The wind should exit with a sound, carrying urine that is scanty;
there should be no excessive restlessness, and the man's mouth should be tasteless.
In that regard, in vātodara (wind-bellied condition), there is swelling in the hands, feet, face, and abdomen, as well as pain in the flanks,
sides, belly, waist, back, and breaking pain in the joints.
Dry cough, aching of the limbs, heaviness in the lower body, accumulation of impurities,
a dark-red discoloration of the skin and other parts, and a loss of the sense of taste in the mouth [are the symptoms].
His abdomen is pierced by pins, covered with blue and black veins,
distended, and it produces a strange sound within the belly.
In this condition, the wind (vāyu) produces painful sounds and movement in every way.
In pitta-type abdominal enlargement (pittodara), there is fever, fainting, a burning sensation, and a bitter taste in the mouth.
There is giddiness, diarrhea, yellowness of the skin and other parts, and a greenish abdomen;
the vessels and other features become yellowish-copper colored, accompanied by perspiration, heat, and a burning sensation.
In cases of *śleṣma* (phlegm) abdominal enlargement, there is smoky fuming, softness to the touch, rapid suppuration, burning pain, lassitude, perspiration, swelling, and heaviness.

Drowsiness, distress, loss of appetite, labored breathing, coughing, paleness of the skin and so forth, abdominal enlargement, and blurred vision; the abdomen is glossy and covered with white and black veins.
When water increases excessively, it becomes hard, cold to the touch, heavy, and stable;
it provokes the three *doṣas* through those various impurities that give rise to the three *doṣas*.
Corrupted by all manner of vitiating factors, the accumulated impurities,
becoming impassioned, reach the digestive tract and undergo transformation, resulting in emaciation, fainting, and vertigo.
They produce a most dreadful abdominal swelling that possesses all three characteristics and suppurates quickly;
it increases even further when exposed to cold winds.
From overeating, from agitation, from activities such as traveling or drinking, from unwholesome drinks and the like, and from vomiting, disease, or emaciation; // GarP_1,161.23 //
The spleen, situated on the left side, increases when displaced from its natural location;
having grown from blood or from the lymph-chyle (rasa) and other tissues, it produces pain.
That [fetus] is like a hard, protruding stone, elevated like the back of a tortoise;
as it gradually grows, it causes distension within the womb.
Accompanied by dyspnea, cough, thirst, a bad taste in the mouth, flatulence, fever,
jaundice, fainting, vomiting, burning of the skin, and delusion.
It has a reddish luster, a variegated luster, and is adorned with blue and yellow;
it is accompanied by upward-moving wind, constipation, delusion, thirst, distress, and fever.
Due to heaviness, loss of appetite, and hardness, through obstruction, delusion, and transference,
the liver (yakṛt) may also become displaced from the right side like a spleen.
When the liver has become cooked, there is always bound feces in the rectum;
he may be afflicted by hemorrhoids, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), or other such ailments.
The provoked *apāna* wind binds the feces, bile, and phlegm within the abdomen; thus obstructed, it causes fever and pain.
Cough, dyspnea, heaviness in the thighs, headache, pain in the navel and flanks, retention of waste, loss of appetite, vomiting, and the accumulation of impurities and wind in the abdomen.
The abdomen is covered with a network of firm, blue, and reddish veins;
and from above the navel, it generally takes on the shape of a cow’s tail.
When the abdomen is pierced by bone fragments, other splinters, or similar objects,
the liver and other organs are cooked, and their contents flow out through those openings.
If there is indeed pain in the rectum, then there will be a very small amount of fecal matter;
it may have a foul odor and be slimy, yellowish, or reddish.
Then, having filled the belly with the remainder, it begins its terrible growth;
it increases below the navel and quickly attains the nature of water.
When the form of the *doṣas* is aggravated and pervaded by dyspnea, thirst, and vertigo, they call this *chidrodara*; others, however, call it *paristrāvī*.

For one who has begun drinking oils and the like, who suddenly indulges in unwholesome food, who drinks excessive water, whose digestive fire is weak, and who is emaciated or excessively thin; GarP_1,161.37.
The wind, obstructed from its own path, and the phlegm, saturated with water, cause that very water to increase;
from that minute quantity, it becomes a mass of drops.
Due to that anger, his belly became afflicted with thirst, pain in the anus and groin,
cough, dyspnea, and loss of appetite, and it was covered with veins of various colors.
Filled with water, soft to the touch, and characterized by similar agitation and trembling,
it arises covering the channel, firm and unctuous within the belly of the crane.
And when all the vital points (svasthāna) have been displaced from their positions during equanimity,
the digestive fires (pāka), becoming liquefied, cause even the joints, channels, and orifices to become fluid.
When perspiration is indeed obstructed, those [humors] situated within become faint;
filling that very abdomen, they produce the disease of the belly.
A fetus situated in the stomach that is round and struck does not produce sound;
likewise, one that is weak, terrible, or touched by a channel perishes.
The disappearance of the veins in the abdomen is said to be the sign of all types of abdominal enlargement (udara), namely:
those caused by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), the spleen (plīha), the combination of humors (sannipāta), and water (udaka).
An abdominal enlargement (udara) that has produced fluid within a fortnight and is accompanied by the complication of obstruction is considered,
by its very nature, to be almost entirely the most difficult to treat.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—162.
Dhanvantari said:
Listen, O Suśruta, as I speak to you regarding the diagnosis of pale swelling (pāṇḍuśotha):
when the humors (malas), with pitta predominant, are provoked by the aforementioned causes of provocation, [they produce this condition].
If, propelled and repelled by the powerful wind, it remains stationary, reaching the ten vessels and pervading the entire body; GarP_1,162.2 //
Vitiating the skin, blood, phlegm, and flesh while residing in the nutrient fluid (rasa),
it produces various kinds of colors on the skin within the layers of the skin and flesh.
Turmeric itself is *hāridra*, and among those [diseases], this one has reached an excessive paleness;
that fierce disease strikes, and because of it, there is heaviness (*gaurava*).
There is a loosening of the contact between the elements and a decay of qualities arising from the immature state;
consequently, one's blood, fat, and bones become deficient in essence, and the sense faculties become flaccid.
With limbs as if dissolving, with a heart melting away,
and with a face like the peak of a mountain of arrows, he experienced a state of numbness there through his saliva.
One who suffers from deficient thirst, aversion to cold, decayed greed, and extinguished digestive fire;
one with diminished strength, fever, dyspnea, earache, as well as vertigo. // GarP_1,162.7 //
It is of five types, arising from each of the humors individually, from all of them combined, or from eating clay;
its premonitory symptom is a throbbing in the heart and dryness of the skin.
Loss of appetite, yellowish urine, absence of perspiration, and scanty urination occur;
when fat and wind are in equilibrium, there is intense pain and a moistness of the limbs in that condition.
Darkness of the eyes, blackness of the hair, nails, feces, urine, and eyes, swelling, bad taste in the nose and mouth, dryness of the stool, and fainting at the sides [of the chest]. GarP_1,162.10 //

In the case of pitta, there is a greenish-yellow appearance in the veins and other parts, fever, darkness of vision, thirst, emaciation, fainting, foul odor, a desire for cold things, and a bitter taste in the mouth. (GarP 1.162.11)
Diarrhea, acidity, burning sensation, moisture in the heart due to phlegm, drowsiness, salivation, horripilation, and loss of voice [are the symptoms]. (GarP 1,162.12)
Cough and vomiting arise from the accumulation [of humors]; when its specific signs have vanished, it is extremely difficult to endure.
When provoked by wind and bile, the phlegm becomes pungent, or when by phlegm, it becomes sweet.

Having corrupted the fat and other tissues through dryness, it causes the discharge of blood and brings about the depletion of the bodily channels, following the same procedure as previously described.
When jaundice arises from consumption (kṣaya), there is discharge from the navel, feet, mouth, and penis;
one passes stool that is broken, mixed with blood, and accompanied by phlegm, as if containing worms.
If one who suffers from a bile disease consumes [substances] that increase bile, jaundice (kāmalā) will arise;
the bile, having emerged from the stomach and intestines, burns the blood and flesh and carries them away.
The urine and eyes are turmeric-colored, the mouth and excrement are red;
he suffers from burning sensations, indigestion, and thirst, has the appearance of a frog, and his sensory faculties are weak.
In one afflicted by *pāṇḍuroga*, there may arise a swelling accompanied by *pitta*;
and through neglect, swellings and other such conditions lead to the difficult-to-cure *kumbhakāmalā*.
When jaundice occurs with a greenish-yellow complexion, there is anemia;
when wind and bile are predominant, there is vertigo, thirst, sexual excitement toward women, and mild fever.
Drowsiness, or loss of digestive fire—these they call *halīmaka*;
excessive laziness is the premonitory symptom of these conditions.
Swelling (śotha) is declared to be the primary [symptom]; therefore, it is described as follows:
the vitiated wind (vāyu), along with bile (pitta), blood (rakta), and phlegm (kapha), leads the corrupted [humors] outward through the vessels (śirā).
For when their movement is obstructed by these [doshas], they produce a swelling that relies upon the skin and flesh;
because it is a compact accumulation, they call that swelling *utsedha*. Thus, from this collection [of doshas], it is known as *śotha*.
Due to the specific distinctions of all causes, it consists of nine types according to the variations in form;
[it arises] from various individual humors (doṣas), from all [humors combined], from physical injury, and even from poison.
When that very [mark] is led across all the limbs, it may arise from desire;
they know it to be of three kinds through its broad, elevated, and knotted specific characteristics.
The general cause of swellings is the arising from the humors (doṣas), particularly in one who has been quickly depleted by disease, physical labor, fasting, and the like. GarP_1,162.25.
When one consumes in excess that which is extremely cold for the guru, or salt, alkaline, pungent, sour, vegetables, water, sleep, and staying awake; GarP_1,162.26.

Obstructing the flow of urine, dried meat, indigestion, fatigue, sexual intercourse, walking on foot, or even traveling in a jolting vehicle—all these cause [the food] to digest with difficulty. (GarP 1.162.27)
Dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, menorrhagia, fever, constipation, lassitude, vomiting, hiccup, anemia, and erysipelas; GarP_1,162.28.
Those [doshas] located in the upper part cause swelling in the upper body; those in the bladder cause it in the lower part; those in the middle cause it in the middle;
and those that pervade the whole body cause swelling throughout the entire body, following the specific location of their respective substrates.
Its premonitory symptoms are sneezing, distension of the vessels, and heaviness of the limbs;
due to Vāta, the swelling is mobile, dry, with rough hair, and reddish or dark in color.

There is a sensation like that of a conch shell, distension of the bladder and intestines, swelling, piercing pain in the flesh and fat, numbness, upward movement of Vāta, exhaustion, and the body quickly rises when pressed. (GarP 1,162.31)
The ointment should be pacified by massages; it is mild at night and intense during the day.
When that area is smeared with a paste of bark and mustard seeds, it experiences a tingling sensation.
Having a yellow, red, or blackish luster and arising from bile, it causes emaciation;
it either does not subside quickly or first burns the body in its middle part.
Thirst, burning fever, perspiration, vertigo, exhaustion, intoxication, and delusion; longing for food, diarrhea, a foul odor, intolerance to touch, and softness of the body.
It is itchy, pale-haired, with hard skin, cold, heavy, unctuous, smooth, and stable; it causes pain, drowsiness, vomiting, and loss of digestive fire.

And by means of malice, through wounds such as being cut or pierced by weapons and the like, and by cold winds, sour winds, and those arising from *bhallātaka* and *pikaccha* plants; // GarP_1,162.36 //
From contact with liquids or dried substances, there may arise an edematous swelling accompanied by spreading (visarpa),
characterized by intense heat, a reddish appearance, and generally possessing the symptoms of pitta.
Poisoning arises from the crawling over or urination by venomous creatures,
and even from the bites, teeth-marks, or scratches of non-venomous creatures.
Due to contact with things defiled by feces, urine, semen, or impurities;
from the touch of the wind from a poison-tree; and from being dusted with a mixture of poisons (*gara-yoga*). // GarP_1,162.39 //
A swelling that is soft, mobile, hanging down, rapid in onset, and causing burning pain and distress is curable when recent; it is incurable if accompanied by complications, as previously stated.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Pandu-sophen (Pāṇḍu-sotha)," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [Śrīgaruḍa-mahāpurāṇam—163] The glorious Dhanvantari spoke:
O Suśruta, listen as I shall hereafter describe the etiology of visarpa and other diseases;
visarpa occurs due to the obstruction [of channels] by the vitiated doṣas, resembling a swelling.
They say that this [place] is the external support; therein, due to fear or exhaustion, it becomes increasingly difficult to master, and the fault therein is according to its respective nature.
Aggravated especially by provocative and burning factors, they quickly enter the body here; for though they reside within, they manifest externally.
Due to the onset of thirst, the irregular movement of the bodily urges,
and the rapid loss of digestive fire and strength, the poison spreads externally.
Among those, the one caused by Vāta has symptoms identical to those of Vāta-fever;
it is characterized by swelling, throbbing, piercing pain, splitting sensations, exhaustion, distress, and horripilation.
From pitta, it has a rapid course, exhibits the symptoms of pitta-fever, and is excessively red;
from kapha, it is accompanied by itching, is unctuous, and has a pain similar to that of kapha-fever.
Those arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) and endowed with all their symptoms,
if neglected, are covered with eruptions (sphoṭa) possessing the characteristics of all [the humors] and bear the marks of ulcers; they also discharge sweat.

Accompanied by fever, vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, and vertigo arising from wind and bile, as well as glandular swellings, loss of digestive fire, darkness before the eyes, and anorexia; (GarP 1,163.8)
It causes all the limbs to become as if strewn with glowing embers;
whatever region the erysipelas (visarpa) spreads to, that very place becomes afflicted.
Dark like extinguished embers, blue or red, it accumulates there;
due to its rapid movement, it quickly becomes like a boil scorched by fire.
When the wind is exceedingly strong, it causes a spreading erysipelas (visarpa) that follows the vital points (marman);
it causes pain in the limbs, robs one of consciousness and sleep, and excites labored breathing.
And having reached such a state, that man suffers from hiccups; at times, seized by pain in his vital organs, he lies upon the ground or sits upon beds and seats.
Then, struggling, afflicted, and with his mind and body deluded, he experiences a sleep from which he is difficult to awaken; this is called agnivīsarpa.
The wind, obstructed by phlegm, pierces that phlegm in many ways;
or, in one whose blood has increased, it pierces the blood located in the skin, vessels, sinews, and flesh.
Having corrupted [the blood], it becomes long-lasting, thick, and coarse in nature; it produces a chain of glandular swellings accompanied by reddened edges, intense pain, and fever.
Accompanied by dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, dryness of the mouth, hiccup, vomiting, giddiness,
delusion, discoloration, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, and loss of digestive fire— this is Granthivīsarpa, born from the provocation of Kapha and Vāta.
From the combination of kapha and pitta arise fever, stiffness, drowsiness, lethargy, headache,
exhaustion of the limbs, convulsions, delirium, anorexia, and vertigo.
Fainting, loss of digestive fire, cracking of the bones, thirst, heaviness of the sense organs,
the evacuation of undigested matter (āma), and a coating of the channels— this [disease] spreads throughout the body.
Generally,
it affects the stomach, does not cause excessive pain, and is covered with eruptions that are extremely yellow, red, and pale.
It is glossy, black, dark-blue in luster, dirty, swollen, and heavy;
it suppurates deeply, generally becomes moist upon contact with heat, and breaks open.
When the flesh is cooked and sloughed away, revealing the network of tendons and veins, and when it spreads everywhere, exhibiting all the aforementioned symptoms and affecting the entire skin,
smelling like a corpse— this erysipelas they call Kardama.
Provoked by injury from an external cause and impelling the blood along with bile,
the wind (vāyu) produces erysipelas (visarpa), which is covered with eruptions resembling horse-gram (kulattha).
[The disease] characterized by eruptions, swelling, fever, pain, and burning, with dark-red blood [is known as visarpa].
Those caused by each of the doshas individually are three [types], and those arising from two doshas are curable provided they are without complications.
Those who are incurable, those from whom all vital functions have departed,
those whose vital organs (marman) have been overwhelmed, those whose sinews, veins, and flesh are decayed, those who are putrid, and those who smell like a corpse.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vīsarpa," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 164] Dhanvantari said:
Through improper diet and conduct, especially those that are antagonistic, and by practicing the censuring of the virtuous, killing, and the seizing of property and so forth; // GarP_1,164.1 //
Driven instantly by past sinful deeds, those impure ones enter the channels and, joined with them, reach the skin, fat, blood, and flesh.
Corrupting and drying up [the tissues], they exit from there and cause discoloration of the skin; the experts call this *kuṣṭha*.
Whatever has been neglected over time, all that enters the cavities of the body;
having reached the internal and external constituents (*dhātu*), it causes them all to become moistened and leads to their decay.
It assails, in due order, the worms that are accompanied by sweat, moisture, and contraction, as well as the subtle and dreadful ones, along with the body hair, skin, sinews, and vessels.
One should treat external leprosy (kuṣṭha) as if it were covered in ashes;
leprosy is said to be of seven types, arising from the humors (doṣa) individually, in pairs, or combined together.
Although all [types of leprosy] arise from the three humors, they are designated according to whichever one is predominant;
thus, Kāpāla leprosy is caused by Vāta, Audumbara by Pitta, and [the third type] by Kapha.
One should also examine the types known as maṇḍala and ṛṣya, which arise from wind and bile;
as well as carma-kuṣṭha, ekakuṣṭha, kiṭima, sidhma, alasa, and vipādikā.
Dadru and śatāruṣī arise from vāta and śleṣman; puṇḍarīka, along with visphoṭa, pāmā, and carmadala, arise from śleṣman and pitta.
From all [these causes] arises *kākaṇaka*; the first triad [of causes] produces *dadru* along with *kākaṇaka*;
and *puṇḍarīka*, *aryajihva*, and the others constitute the seven great leprosies (*mahākuṣṭha*).
Excessive smoothness or roughness of touch, perspiration or lack thereof, discoloration of the skin,
burning sensation, itching, numbness, pricking pain, horripilation, swelling, and darkness [of vision] occur in the skin.
Excessive pain in wounds, rapid onset, and long duration; dryness even in those that have healed; and excessive provocation by even a slight cause [are signs of vitiated blood]. (GarP 1.164.12)
Horripilation and blackness of the blood are the primary symptoms of leprosy;
that which resembles a blackish-red skull, being dry, rough, and thin, [is the first sign].
Covered with hair that is discolored and spread over a wide area,
accompanied by intense pricking pain— that is known as the uneven *kāpāla* leprosy.
One should call the *kuṣṭha* that has the appearance of an udumbara fruit "audumbara";
it is described as circular, very thick, and characterized by excessive burning pain.
The udumbara fruit should be unblemished, free from cracks, and like a worm;
it should be firm, true, heavy, oily, white-red in color, and possessed of its own natural impurities.
A circular patch (maṇḸala) is described as being characterized by mutual adhesion, swelling, excessive itching, discharge, and worms, and as being smooth with a yellowish luster.
Vicarcikā is characterized by itching, pustules, a darkish hue, and moisture;
it is rough, with reddish edges and a dark center that is elevated.
That which is described as having the appearance of a deer's tongue is called ṛṣyajihva; it is infested with many worms.
That which has the touch of an elephant's hide or a donkey's skin is said to be the leprosy known as carma.
Furthermore, *kiṭima* is painless, resembling the scales of a fish,
dry, the color of fire, painful to the touch, itchy, and rough-black.
Rough on the outside yet smooth within, it sheds dust when rubbed;
it has a soft touch, is thin and glossy, transparent, and free from perspiration or spots.
Generally, there is emaciation of the upper body, the skin is covered with pustules and itching,
and *vipādikā* (cracking of the feet) occurs in the hands and feet due to excessive redness.
It was filled with intense pain and deep itching, covered with reddish pustules,
and possessed the color of long-stretching *dūrvā* grass or the *atasī* flower.
It is described as being shaped like a sugarcane field, characterized by scabies, itching,
thick roots, burning pain, discharge of blood, and many ulcers.
It generally causes burning, moisture, and pain throughout one's entire life;
it is a pale, blood-stained circular patch, accompanied by itching, a burning sensation, and pain.
When covered with raised eruptions that are red like water on a lotus leaf,
that indeed becomes a *puṇḍarīka* [leprosy], being strewn with white and reddish pustules.
Visphoṭa eruptions, pustules, scabies, itching, and exudative pain—
these are characterized by being small, dark-red, and dry, and they generally appear on the buttocks, hands, and elbows.
Accompanied by cracking sensations and touch-sensitivity, characterized by itching, redness, and excessive burning, it has red scales;
this is *carmadala*, also known as *kākaṇa*, which involves intense burning pain.
The *kākaṇa* coin is reddish-brown and black, resembling the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
it possesses all the black marks, which arise from their respective causes.

One should prescribe treatments according to the specific humors by means of the signs and actions prescribed for each; however, one should abandon the case of *kuṣṭha* that follows its own predominant humor or that involves all the humors.
Whatever has been described regarding leprosy (kuṣṭha), as well as that which resides in the bones, marrow, and semen,
and that which is considered difficult to cure when involving fat— these are palliable if they have reached the skin, flesh, and bones.
That which arises from phlegm and wind is not difficult to treat, as is that which is located in the skin and free from impurities;
however, when it is firmly established in the skin, there occurs discoloration and roughness of the body.
In the blood and flesh, there is perspiration, heat, and swelling; furthermore, eruptions appear on the hands and feet, and due to distress, they are especially prevalent in the joints.
Through constant application, there may be a breaking down of the fat;
however, there is no excessive perception [of the disease] in the marrow, bones, eyes, vital force, and voice.
When the semen is infested with worms, there is injury to one's own wife and offspring;
all the other symptoms [of the preceding types] occur as before, as they do in the case of [semen affected by] deer and other animals.

White leprosy (*śvitra*), also known as *kilāsa*, arises solely from the vitiation of the bodily tissues; it is a severe condition characterized by a lack of discharge and is supported by the emergence of all three humors (*dhātu*).
From wind (vāta), it is dry and reddish; from bile (pitta), it is copper-colored like a lotus petal and accompanied by burning;
from phlegm (kapha), it is white, thick, and heavy, and it destroys the body hair.
One should recognize that [the swelling] is accompanied by itching and, in sequence, involves blood, flesh, and fat;
both types are difficult to cure merely by their color, and each subsequent one is more severe than the last.
Leucoderma that is not white-haired, abundant, or confluent with one another, which is fresh, and produced from a source not burnt by fire, is curable; otherwise, it is to be rejected.
One who desires accomplishment must especially avoid vitiligo, even if it has arisen only recently on the private parts, the palms of the hands, or the lips.
Diseases generally arise from indulgence in physical contact, the same food, and similar associations,
as well as from sharing a bed or seat, and from the use of the same clothing, garlands, and ointments.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Kuṣṭha Disease," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—165.
Dhanvantari said:
Worms are said to be of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal;
the external ones are of four types, according to their origin from impurities, phlegm, blood, or feces.
Therein, twenty kinds of external [parasites] arise from impurities;
they are the size of sesame seeds in shape and color, and they dwell in the hair and clothing.
Those known as lice and nits are many-legged and minute;
they are of two kinds, which produce pustules on the abdomen and cause itching and swellings.
The internal causes of leprosy arise from phlegm (śleṣman), while those originating externally arise from sweet foods, molasses, milk, curd, fish, and freshly cooked rice. GarP_1,165.4 //
Arising from phlegm in the stomach, they grow large and spread everywhere;
some resemble broad leather straps, while others are like earthworms.
Having the appearance of sprouts of mature grain, they are slender, long, and minute;
white and with a coppery luster—thus, by name, they are of seven kinds.
The entrail-eaters, the belly-twisters, the heart-eaters, the great rectums,
the excreters, the darbha-flowers, and the fragrant ones— they all cause [these afflictions].
Nausea,
salivation, indigestion, loss of appetite, fainting, vomiting, fever, abdominal distension, emaciation, sneezing, and catarrh.
Minute creatures born from blood reside in the locations of the blood-carrying vessels;
they are footless, circular, and copper-colored, and some are invisible due to their extreme subtlety.
Keśāda, Romavidhvaṃsa, Romadvīpa, and Udumbara—
these six, along with Saurasamātṛ, share the same function as Kuṣṭha.
In the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), ulcers arise from feces that spread upward; when they have increased, they may become directed toward the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya).
Then, following the odor of his eructations, exhalations, and feces,
there appeared [worms] that were broad, round, thin, or thick, and dark-brown, yellow, white, or black.
These five types of worms— namely the kakerukas, makerukas,
sausurādās, those called śūlas, and the lelihās— indeed produce [these ailments].
Cracking of the anus, colic, constipation, emaciation, roughness, pallor,
horripilation, loss of digestive fire, and itching in the rectum— these occur when [the humors] move along the wrong channels.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Worms," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Dhanvantari said:
*Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—166* Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, I shall declare to you the etiology of wind-diseases; listen to that.
For in every way, the recounting of what is useless is indeed an obstacle.
He whose body is not seen by the wicked wind, who is without distinction [in all things],
he is Viśvakarman, the soul of the universe, the universal form, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati).
He is the creator, the sustainer, the all-pervading Viṣṇu, the destroyer, death, and the end-maker;
since it has been said that he is thus, one should always strive for this with diligence.
When the recognition of the defects has been stated, one should determine the natural and modified actions according to the classifications of the doshas, both in brief and in detail.
Each of these fivefold heroic activities is here subject to modification;
their classification is now declared along with their causes and characteristics.
When the wind (vāyu) becomes agitated by those things that deplete the bodily constituents (dhātu), it cannot be properly pacified;
it then fills even more those very same channels (srotas) within the cavities of the body.
Then, having concealed the opening from those [channels] filled with defects,
your wind, becoming enraged once, produces colic, constipation, and rumbling in the intestines.
It certainly causes obstruction of the spleen, loss of voice, stiffness of the eyes, back,
and waist, as well as other various painful afflictions in the body.
Vomiting arising from the stomach, dyspnea, cough, cholera,
itching, obstruction, perspiration, and other such diseases [are treated] above the navel.
He caused impairment of the sense organs such as hearing, cracking and roughness of the skin,
intense pain, labored breathing, diseases from poison, and discoloration.
It causes obstruction within the intestines, loss of appetite, emaciation, and dizziness;
it forms a knot in the flesh and fat, and produces roughness upon the skin and other parts.
The vital points of the body are excessively tormented as if struck by a staff or a fist;
one perceives intense pain located in the bones and joints of the thighs. (GarP 1,166.12)
When the marrow is affected, there is instability in the bones; when the bone is affected, there is insomnia and pain;
and when the semen is affected, there is either premature ejaculation or its morbid alteration.
Residing within the respective embryos and located in the semen, it causes distension and depletion in the head;
situated there, when provoked, it produces swelling and difficult dysuria.
The wind located in the joints causes a sensation like touching a water-filled leather bag, dryness, and,
when residing in all the limbs, produces pricking pain, piercing, throbbing, and breaking sensations.
Stiffening, convulsing, sleepiness, breaking of the joints,
and trembling— when the enraged [wind] repeatedly enters all the channels (dhamanīs),
it then convulses the limbs; this disease is known as ākṣepaṇa (convulsive seizure).
When the wind, having been repelled below, moves upward again, then,
having seized the heart, it causes pain in the head and the temples.
He should contract his limbs on all sides, or cause his jaw to bend;
he breathes with great difficulty, and his two eyes are closed.
Free from attachment and accompanied by *upatantraka*, he coos like a pigeon;
when that very breath is joined with the wind in the heart, it is located in the depressed nose.
He repeatedly attains a state of health and repeatedly becomes unwell;
that [fever] arising from injury is considered the most difficult to treat.
Then, when his wind (vāyu), its continuity severed, pervades the entire body, there occurs the cessation of perspiration, and he is again subjected to stretching.
It causes the disappearance [of consciousness], a paralysis of the eyes,
yawning, exhaustion, and the loosening of the teeth, destroying all effort.
There is external pain in the sides, stiffness of the jaw, back,
and head, extension of the body outward, and [pain] in the back, heart, and head.
At that time, the chest is heaved upward or the shoulder is bent;
there is discoloration of the teeth and the mouth, and indeed an absence of perspiration from the limbs.
They describe the patient suffering from wind-disease as having external extension and lockjaw,
when the vital airs, driven by the wind, reach the feces, urine, and blood.
The defects of his body extended from head to foot;
though he remained as nothing more than a pale mass, the extent of his wounds had greatly increased.
Health may be restored during a paroxysm of the limbs by means of all types of shaking;
likewise, it occurs through scraping the tongue, eating hot food, or from excessive pride.
When the wind (vāyu), located at the root of the jaw, becomes aggravated,
it causes stiffness of the jaw and produces either the state of having the mouth wide open or the state of having the mouth tightly closed.
By that [wind], there occurs a paralysis of the jaw, making chewing and speaking difficult;
the wind also causes the tongue to become paralyzed through the stiffening of the speech-carrying vessels.
Through that, there is stiffness of the tongue and an inability to consume food, drink, or speak;
it arises from carrying heavy loads on the head or from speaking excessively and laughably.
From uneven pillows and from chewing hard foods, the wind increases;
and by those [factors], the wind, becoming turbulent, rises upward.
She distorts his face, causing him to laugh loudly and stare;
then she renders his power of speech feeble and makes his eyes rigid.
Loosening of the teeth, loss of voice, loss of hearing, inability to perceive objects, lack of sense of smell, destruction of memory, terror, and labored breathing arise. (GarP 1.166.33)
Spitting, pain in the sides, the closing of one eye, intense pains above the collarbone, or even the paralysis of half the body; GarP_1,166.34 //
Some call this condition *ardita*, while others call it *ekāṅga*;
it arises by resorting to the blood and affects the vessels that support the head. GarP_1,166.35 //
That seizing of the head which is rough, painful, and black is incurable;
likewise, when the wind (vāyu) seizes the body as well as the tendons (snāyu).
It destroys one side of the body; that is called pakṣāghāta (hemiplegia). One half of the entire body becomes incapable of action and devoid of sensation.
Some know [the condition] as disease of a single limb, while others recognize it as pain in the armpits;
when the *vāyu* resides throughout the entire body, there is obstruction and stiffness of all limbs.
A hemiplegia caused by pure vāta is considered most difficult to cure;
it is difficult when associated with another [dosha], and incurable when aggravated by the cause of wasting (kṣaya).

One whose channels are obstructed by undigested matter (āma) and who, being afflicted by phlegm, causes the limbs to become rigid, suffers from daṇḍāpatānaka; indeed, this condition is entirely incurable.
The wind arising from the root of the shoulder, having contracted the vessels located there,
produces *bāhuka* by causing a throbbing sensation externally.
That which is at the base of the fingers, the tendons on the back of the arms, and that which causes the loss of function in the arms—this is called the *vipūcī*. GarP_1,166.42 //
When the wind (vāyu) residing in the waist displaces the tendons (kaṇḍarā) of the thigh, then the person becomes lame;
he becomes a cripple through the destruction of both thighs.
One who trembles at the start of movement and walks as if limping should be known as a *kalāyakhañja*,
whose connection of the joints has been released.
Through the consumption of cold, hot, liquid, dry, heavy, and unctuous substances;
likewise through indigestion, physical exertion, agitation, unctuousness, and staying awake at night; // GarP_1,166.45 //
At the appropriate time, phlegm that has been excessively accumulated over a long period breaks apart and, having overcome the other humors, enters the body.
Then the bones of the thighs are filled within by congealed phlegm;
that bone bathes the thigh with that [phlegm] and likewise with cold wind.
One characterized by a darkened body, stiffness of the limbs, drowsiness, fainting, loss of appetite, and fever—
others call that *urustambha* (stiffness of the thighs), while others call it *bāhyavāta*.
A swelling of wind and blood with great pain in the middle of the knee should be known as *kroṣṭukaśīrṣa*, resembling the head of a large jackal.
When, due to unevenly placed footwear or from fatigue,
the wind (vāta) seizes the ankle, that condition is called vātakaṇṭaka.
When the wind (māruta) afflicts the heels, the fingers, the navel, or the throat, it seizes them with a twisting pain; that condition is called gṛdhrasī.
When both feet become numb and yet experience a tingling sensation,
that should be known as *pādaharṣa*, arising from the provocation of phlegm and wind.
When the wind, conjoined with bile and blood, causes a burning sensation in the feet—
especially while walking— one should designate that as *pādadāha* (burning of the feet).
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vātavyādhi," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa— 167] Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, I shall declare to you the etiology of vātarakta; listen to that.
[It arises] from incompatible foods, eating before the previous meal is digested, anger, sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night.
Vāta-śoṇita generally arises in those who are delicate, those who indulge in improper diet and lifestyle, and those who are corpulent and sedentary.
Due to the suppression of fire and impurity, when the blood of men is vitiated,
the wind (vāyu), increased by wind-inducing factors and cold things, becomes enraged and moves into a wrong path.
Obstructed by such blood, it becomes vitiated at that very moment;
likewise, the wind causes pain in the anus, as well as phlegm and vātaśoṇita (blood disorder caused by wind).
Having first stabilized it, one should generate [the wind]; afterwards, it flows everywhere.
Specifically, its characteristic is that it becomes suspended due to vomiting and other such conditions.
Likewise, there will be a disease called *sāmbuda*, which is equal to leprosy (*kuṣṭha*),
appearing in the knees, calves, thighs, hips, shoulders, hands, feet, and the joints of the limbs.
Itching, throbbing, piercing pain, splitting sensations, heaviness, and numbness—
having occurred again and again, they subside, only to manifest repeatedly once more.
Sometimes, taking his stand at the base of the feet or even the hands,
he rushes through the entire body like an enraged rat through its burrow.
First, that which resides in the skin and flesh arises;
thereafter, after some time, it becomes deep-seated and invades all the bodily constituents (dhātus).
In the regions of the waist and other restrained areas, there is swelling and suppuration that is coppery, dark, or reddish;
it is knotted together, and that wind [afflicts] the bones and marrow.
Moving with great speed, he courses within as if cutting [the body] apart and making it wheel-like;
moving everywhere throughout the body, he makes it lame or crippled.
When wind (vāta) is predominant, there is excessive pain, throbbing, and breaking sensations;
the swelling is dry, blackish, or dark-brown, and it fluctuates in size.
Constriction of the vessels, fingers, and joints, stiffness of the limbs, and intense pain;
aversion to cold, lack of relief from it, rigidity, tremors, and numbness [are the symptoms].
In the case of blood (rakta), there is swelling with excessive pain and pricking, which becomes copper-colored and tingling;
it is not relieved by either unctuous or dry applications, and is accompanied by itching and moisture.
In the case of pitta, there is a burning sensation, confusion, a sweet taste in the mouth, fainting, intoxication, thirst,
intolerance to touch, pain, vomiting, emaciation, suppuration, and excessive heat.
In cases of kapha, there is a sense of stiffness, heaviness, numbness, oiliness, and coldness;
there is itching and dull pain, and from the combination [of doshas], all the symptoms appear together.

One should treat blood-bile (raktapitta) arising from a single humor, as well as that born from two humors which is palliable; however, one should quickly abandon that most dreadful form arising from all three humors.
The wind (māruta), having quickly struck the blood in the limbs and joints of the extremities, causes them to obstruct one another; thus, by means of agonizing pains, it takes away the vital breaths.

In the fivefold vital air (prāṇa), which is of the nature of wind, [diseases arise] from dryness, restlessness, and leaping; from overeating and injury; and from the forceful provocation of natural urges and their suppression.
When aggravated, it causes impairment of the eyes and other senses;
furthermore, chronic catarrh, burning sensations, thirst, cough, dyspnea, and so forth arise. (GarP 1.167.20)
Residing in the throat, shoulders, and head, it causes constriction of the throat, loss of impurities, vomiting, anorexia, chronic catarrh, and diseases such as goiter.

The *vyāna* [vital air] is vitiated by excessive walking, bathing, sporting, and activities involving sensory objects, as well as by discordant foods, dry substances, fear, joy, despair, and the like.
The loss of virility, energy, and strength; grief, mental agitation, and fever; all forms of piercing pain, horripilation, and a state of deep sleep.

The *samāna* [vāyu], through irregular, undigested, cold, or mixed foods, causes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), and other ailments, as well as a general exhaustion of all the limbs. (GarP 1,167.24)

And when corrupted by sleeping and staying awake at improper times and other such factors, it produces diseases such as colic, abdominal tumors, and dysentery, which have their basis in the undigested food (āmāśaya).
The *apāna* [vital energy] is disturbed by dry and heavy food, suppression of natural urges, excessive straining, and the over-indulgence in riding in vehicles, sitting, rising, and walking.
When provoked, it causes all diseases localized in the colon (pakvāśaya),
as well as many others such as disorders of urine and semen, hemorrhoids, and prolapse of the rectum.
The entire body is pervaded by lassitude, numbness, and heaviness;
due to the unctuousness of the time of awakening, there is coldness, swelling, and loss of digestive fire.

One should know that state to be free from *āma* when itching and dryness have been eliminated and there is a corresponding alleviation; liberation [from the disorder] occurs through the reversal of symptoms such as drowsiness.
The obstruction of wind by wind is said to have many varieties;
when obstructed by pitta, there is burning, thirst, colic, giddiness, and darkness.

From pungent, hot, sour, and salty [foods], there is a burning sensation and a desire for cold; from coldness, heaviness, and colic, there is a lack of digestive fire; and from pungent substances, ghee, and milk, [these symptoms arise] in excess.
When [the fever] is covered by phlegm (kapha), there is a desire for jumping, exertion, dryness, and heat;
when covered by phlegm, there is aching of the limbs, nausea, heaviness, and loss of appetite.

In the stage of blood-dominance (raktāvasthā), there is always a burning pain and intense distress arising from the skin and flesh; the swelling becomes intensely red, and circular patches (maṇḍalas) appear.
The swelling becomes hard with flesh, as do nausea and pustules;
there arises a tingling sensation as if ants are crawling over it.
The swelling on the limbs is movable, soft, cold, and causes loss of appetite.
That [vāta] caused by fat should be known as difficult to cure, like "rich vāta" (āḍhyavāta);
when the skin is covered [by fat], there is a sensation of touch that is neither hot nor cold.
But when it is enveloped by marrow, there is irregular yawning and a sense of being constricted.
One experiences pain and pressure, yet finds relief through manual manipulation;
however, when there is swelling caused by the obstruction of semen, no such excessive movement is felt.
When food has been eaten, pain occurs in the stomach; once it is digested, a cutting sensation certainly arises.
When the bladder is obstructed by urine, there will be suppression of urination and distension.
When the openings are obstructed, there is a blockage; then, as it cuts through its own location, the man, overcome by fever, falls quickly and suffers fainting.
When the vitiated semen has been suppressed by another [act], it may be discharged after a long time;
or, when the bodily wind (vāyu) is obstructed by all the tissues (dhātus), there is pain in the hips, groins, and back.
When the wind moves in reverse, the heart is severely oppressed;
when the vital breath (prāṇa) is obstructed by bile (pitta), there is vertigo, fainting, pain, and a burning sensation.
In the case of Vyāna, however, there is pain, lassitude, loss of voice, and burning throughout the body;
furthermore, there is a gradual loss of movement and activity, along with a fever accompanied by piercing pain.
In the *samāna* [vāyu], there is injury from heat, cessation of perspiration, excessive thirst, and a burning sensation;
in the *apāna*, however, there is a yellowish coloration of the excrement.

When the vital breath (prāṇa) is obstructed by phlegm, there is an increase of impurities, a burning sensation, as well as constipation and dysuria; furthermore, there is a ringing sound in the ears and a blockage of the channels.
Spitting, perspiration, and the obstruction of inhalation and exhalation;
in the *udāna* [vital breath], there is heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, and the suppression of speech and voice.
In drinking [alcohol], there is a loss of strength and complexion, a stiffening of the joints and bones, heaviness in all limbs, and an excessive increase in bulk. (GarP 1,167.45)
When the *samāna* [vāyu] is obstructed, there is ignorance regarding actions, absence of perspiration, and weak digestion;
when the *apāna* is obstructed, there is the retention of all urine and the cessation of the passage of feces.
Thus, they know the disease of vāta-rakta to be of twenty-two kinds;
likewise, the vital breaths (prāṇa and so forth) mutually invade one another in their respective order.
All these, as well as the twentyfold obscuration of knowledge— namely,
nausea, suppression of breath, catarrh, and stiffness of the head.
When the apāna is obstructed by the prāṇa, there occurs heart disease and dryness of the mouth;
when the prāṇa is obstructed by the udāna, there will indeed be a loss of strength.
By means of careful investigation, the physician should differentiate all obstructions,
taking into account the locations of the bodily humors (vātās), as well as the increase or decrease of their functions.
Pitta is the mutual covering for the five [winds] beginning with prāṇa;
and there is the abiding of pitta and the others when they are mixed, as well as by those [elements] combined together.
Likewise, one should carefully observe those [diseases] caused by combinations of pitta and the other humors, which are manifold in their mixtures,
according to the emergence of their respective symptoms.
One should repeatedly observe even firm symptoms that gradually subside;
specifically, *prāṇa* is said to be life and *udāna* is said to be strength.
From the affliction of these two, there occurs the destruction of both lifespan and strength.
The winds, whether obstructed, unknown, known, or displaced from their positions,
may become difficult to master even with great effort, or they may cause affliction.
Abscesses, splenic disorders, heart disease, abdominal tumors, loss of digestive fire,
and other such conditions arise as complications when those [doshas] are obstructed and neglected.
O Suśruta,
this introduction has been uttered by me as spoken by Ātreya,
for the sake of discerning all diseases and for the increase of the lifespan of men and others.
Having thus understood [the nature of] diseases and so forth, one should indeed perform medical treatment;
the *triphalā* [mixture], combined with honey, clarified butter, and jaggery, destroys all diseases.
Alternatively, triphalā combined with the three pungents (savyoṣā) destroys all diseases;
or else, it may be combined with śatāvarī, guḍūcī, agni, and viḍaṅga.
Śatāvarī, guḍūcī, agni, śuṇṭhī, mūṣalī, balā,
punarnavā, bṛhatī, nirguṇḍī, and nimba leaves.
Or, Triphalā, processed seven times with the juice of Bhṛṅgarāja, Āmalaka, and Vāsaka, or even just once, [should be taken].
The previously mentioned powder, bolus (modaka),
pill (vaṭikā), ghee, oil, or decoction, prepared according to their availability, cures wasting diseases;
[the dosage] may be one pala, half a pala, one karṣa, or even half a karṣa.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vatarakta," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa— chapter 168—
the section on Diagnosis (Nidāna) is complete.
Dhanvantari said:
I shall declare the essence of yoga, proven and effective in removing all diseases;
listen, O Suśruta, in brief, for the sake of the life of living beings.
From the consumption of food that is astringent, pungent, bitter, sour, or dry, and from anxiety, sexual intercourse, physical exertion, fear, grief, and staying awake at night; // GarP_1,168.2 //
Due to loud speaking, excessive burden, and the over-exertion of physical labor,
the wind becomes provoked when the rain falls, when food is digested, and at the end of the day.
From consuming food that is hot, sour, salty, alkaline, or pungent, and from eating when the previous meal is undigested;
and from indulging in intense heat, fire, the sun's glare, intoxicants, and anger. (GarP 1,168.4)
The bile of an embodied being becomes aggravated at the time of digestion, at midday, at the end of the rainy season, during the summer months, and also at midnight.
From eating food that is excessively sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, heavy, and cold, and also from the consumption of fresh grain, slimy substances, and the meat of marshy animals; 1,168.6.
Through lack of physical exercise, daytime sleep, and the pleasures of reclining and sitting, the derangement of *kapha* arises; it also becomes aggravated after eating and during the spring season.
Roughness of the body, contraction, piercing pain, and stiffness, as well as numbness, horripilation, rigidity, and emaciation; // GarP_1,168.8 //
Darkness of complexion, looseness of the limbs, and an increase in exhaustion and fatigue are the signs of wind (vāyu);
one should declare a disease associated with these to be of the nature of wind (vātātmaka).
Burning heat, perspiration, moisture, agitation, passion, and exhaustion;
pungency, acidity, the stench of corpses, sweat, fainting, excessive thirst, and vertigo.
A person [afflicted] with the symptoms of bile experiences a yellowish or greenish complexion,
while oiliness, sweetness, slowness of action, and rigidity [are experienced] in the body.
Stiffness, lack of satiety, a sense of congestion, swelling, itching,
heaviness, and an excessive inclination toward itching and sleep are the symptoms arising from kapha.
One should recognize a disease arising from two doṣas through the combination of their respective causes and symptoms;
that which arises from all causes and possesses all three symptoms is of the sannipāta type.
The body of embodied beings is said to be the substratum of the humors (doṣas), elements (dhātus), and wastes (malas).
Their equilibrium is health; the opposite results from their decrease or increase.
Fat, blood, flesh, fat-tissue, bone, marrow, and semen are known as the constituents (dhātus);
wind, bile, and phlegm are the humors (doṣas); and feces, urine, and so forth are the impurities (malas).
Vāyu is cold, light, subtle, destructive of the voice, stable, and powerful;
pitta is sour, pungent, and hot, and when undigested, it is a cause of disease.
Sweet, salty, unctuous, heavy, and excessively slimy is the phlegm (śleṣman);
the wind (vāyu) resides in the rectum and the hips, while the bile (pitta) is situated in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya).
The seat of *kapha* is the stomach, the throat, or the joints of the head;
pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes provoke the wind (*samīraṇa*).
Bitter, sour, and salty [tastes] increase bile; sweet, hot, and salty increase phlegm. These same tastes, when applied in their opposite qualities, serve to pacify them.
For those who are ill, they lead to relief; for those in good health, they are the cause of well-being.
It should be known as beneficial for the eyes, sweet, and an increaser of the rasa-dhātu;
it is predominantly sour, pleasing to the mind, and likewise a stimulant of digestion and a digestive aid.
Bitter [taste] destroys fever and thirst, is purifying and drying;
it increases pitta, is scraping, astringent, constipating, and desiccant. (GarP 1,168.21)
Substance is the supreme basis for taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation;
it persists through the interval between taste and transformation, and it is the swift substratum of all substances.
Cold, hot, and salty are considered the potencies (vīrya) of tastes;
furthermore, the post-digestive transformation (pāka) of tastes is of two kinds, being either pungent or [sweet].
The excellence of the physician, the medicine, the patient afflicted by disease, and the attendant—these are the four factors of medical treatment; their opposites lead to failure.
Having understood the place, time, age, digestive fire, similarity of constitution, medicine,
body, mental state, strength, and disease, one should perform the medical treatment.
A mountain with abundant water is marshy (*anūpa*), causing the provocation of phlegm and wind;
another type, the arid (*jāṅgala*) mountain, has sparse vegetation and is characterized by an excess of diseases of blood and bile.
A location endowed with mixed characteristics is known as common.
One is called a child until sixteen, middle-aged until seventy, and thereafter old.

Kapha, pitta, and vāta are generally said to be addressed by treatments that avoid alkali, fire, and surgery, respectively; such measures are employed when the patient is emaciated or advanced in age.

Nourishment should be administered for the emaciated, reduction for those with a corpulent body, and protection for those of moderate build; these are considered the three types of bodily constitutions.
One should diligently recognize strength through steadfastness, exertion, and contentment;
such a person is unchanging, possesses great energy, and is one of great daring.
When drinks, food, and so forth, even if they are contrary to one's [usual] nature,
are conducive to one's well-being, that is called "equilibrium" (sāmya).
From the mother's consumption of phlegm-increasing foods, a man with a phlegmatic constitution is born;
likewise, from wind-increasing or bile-increasing foods, and from wholesome eating that maintains the equilibrium of the humors, [the corresponding types are born].
A man who is emaciated, coarse, and has sparse hair, whose mind is fickle,
who delights in much speech, and who dreams of sunlight, is of a windy (vāta) temperament.
One who has premature grey hair, is fair-skinned, perspires easily, is irascible yet wise,
and perceives luminous objects even in dreams, is said to have a pitta constitution.
A man of phlegmatic constitution (śleṣmaprakṛti) has a steady mind, a clear voice, subtle features, and glossy hair; in dreams, he beholds water and rocks.
A person who possesses a combination of two or three *doṣas* is to be known by their mixed characteristics;
even when other *doṣas* are present, that which is predominant is considered the primary constitution (*prakṛti*).
The digestive fire (*jāṭharānala*) is of four types— dull, sharp, irregular, and even— arising from a predominance of phlegm (*kapha*), bile (*pitta*), and wind (*anila*), or from their equilibrium.
One should maintain equilibrium when it is balanced, suppress Vāta when it is disturbed;
counteract Pitta when it is sharp, and purify Śleṣman when it is dull.
It is the source of all diseases, causes indigestion, and destroys the digestive fire;
its symptoms consist of undigested matter (āma), sourness, flatulence, and constipation, and it is of four types.
From indigestion (āmadoṣa) arises cholera (viṣūcikā), as well as heart disease, lethargy, and other ailments;
in such cases, one should induce vomiting with water mixed with vacha and salt.
From sourness (amlāt), there arise the absence of semen, vertigo, fainting, and thirst;
in that case, drinking cold water and resorting to [medicinal] wind are indicated for the undigested state.
One should avoid body aches, heaviness of the head, diseases arising from defects in food and the like, sleeping during the day, and fasting in that condition. (GarP 1,168.41)
In cases of *śūla* (piercing pain) and *gulma* (abdominal tumors), which indicate the obstruction of the channels of feces and urine,
sudation therapy should be administered, and salt water should be given for drinking.
Undigested food, sourness, and flatulence caused respectively by phlegm, bile, and wind—
the wise man, having smeared the abdomen with asafoetida, the three pungents, and rock salt, [should treat them].
One should practice sleeping during the day, for it destroys all forms of indigestion;
since a mass of diseases arises from unwholesome food, one should therefore abandon unwholesome food.
Warm water as an after-drink, or honey, acts as a digestive aid;
however, milk is generally incompatible with karīra, curd, and fish.
Bilva, śoṇā, gambhārī, pāṭalā,
and gaṇikārikā constitute this great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla), which stimulates digestion and destroys phlegm and wind.
Śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, the two types of bṛhatī,
and gokṣura constitute the minor pentad of roots (kanīya-pañcamūla), which removes wind and bile and is aphrodisiac.
Both [these formulations] consist of ten roots and remove fevers caused by the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta);
they are recommended for cough, dyspnea, drowsiness, and pain in the flanks.
With these oils and ointments, one may conquer gray hair through external application;
water should be four times the quantity of the [herbal] decoction, and the resulting oil should be four times the quantity of the paste.

The oil and milk should be equal in quantity, and the paste should be one-fourth the amount of the oil. The cooking with these processed medicinal herbs should be the same for enemas (basti) and internal potions (pāna).
One should likewise prepare the cooking so that it is "rough" for massage (abhyaṅga) and "mild" for nasal medication (nasya).
One should know that health consists of the gross body and senses, along with the intellect presiding over them; one should treat such a person as long-lived.
He who perceives objects through his senses in a distorted way is subject to death;
as is he who hates his physician, friends, and teachers, and who treats his loved ones as enemies.
He whose ankles, knees, forehead, jaw,
or likewise his cheeks have fallen away or been displaced from their positions will soon give up his life.
One should abandon that man whose left eye sinks, whose tongue is dark, whose nose is deformed, whose lips are black and displaced from their position, and whose mouth is black.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Terminology of the Medical Science," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*,
Dhanvantari said:
I shall now describe the rules for after-drinks (anupāna) for the purpose of distinguishing between what is beneficial and what is harmful:
red śāli rice destroys the three doṣas and wards off thirst and excess fat.
Mahāśāli rice is supremely aphrodisiac; kalama rice alleviates phlegm and bile;
cold and heavy, white ṣaṣṭika rice generally destroys the three doṣas.
Śyāmāka is drying, parching, dry, increases vāta, and subdues kapha and pitta; priyaṅgu, nīvāra, and koradūṣa are proclaimed to be like it.
Barley, when soaked many times, is cooling and removes phlegm and bile;
wheat is aphrodisiac, cooling, heavy, sweet, and destroys wind.
Mudga beans conquer phlegm, bile, and blood; they are astringent, sweet, and light.
Māṣa beans possess great strength, are aphrodisiac, remove bile and phlegm, and are heavy.
Rājamāṣa is non-aphrodisiac, it destroys phlegm and bile, and relieves afflictions caused by wind (vāta).
Kulattha removes asthma, hiccups, heart disease, phlegm, abdominal tumors (gulma), and wind.
Makuṣṭhaka is cooling and constipating, and it destroys hemorrhagic fever, insanity, virility, blood, phlegm, and bile; while Caṇaka is known to increase wind (vāta).
Masūra is sweet, cooling, constipating, and subdues kapha and pitta;
likewise, kalāya is rich in all these qualities and is extremely wind-increasing.
Āgkī is known to destroy kapha and pitta and is likewise considered to be semen-enhancing; atasī should be known as increasing pitta, while siddhārtha conquers kapha and vāta.
Sesame is alkaline, sweet, and unctuous; it provides strength, is hot, and increases pitta.
Various types of grain are strength-depleting, dry, and cold.
Citraka, iṅguda, nālīka, pippalī, madhuśigru, cavya, caraṇa, nirguṇḍī, tarkārī, and kāśamardaka; // GarP_1,169.11 //
The bilva fruits destroy kapha and pitta, kill worms, and are light and digestive stimulants.
Varṣābhū and mārka destroy vāta and kapha, and eliminate the [three] doṣas.
The castor plant (eraṇḍa) is bitter in taste; black nightshade (kākamācī) removes the three doṣas;
cāṅgerī destroys phlegm and wind; and mustard (sarṣapa) gives rise to all the doṣas.
In the same way, *kausma-sumbha* and *rājikā* increase wind and bile;
*nāḍīca* destroys phlegm and bile; and *cucu* is sweet and cooling.

The lotus leaf (*padmapatra*) destroys the [three] humors, while the *tripuṭa* greatly increases wind (*vāta*). The *vāstuka*, containing alkali (*kṣāra*), destroys all the humors and is an excellent appetizer.
The taṇḍukīya, vipahara, and likewise others such as pālaṅkya;
radish (mūlaka) causes the [three] doṣas, but when steamed it alleviates wind and phlegm.
Indeed, that which is beneficial for the throat when ripe is considered the foremost remedy for all disorders;
likewise are karkoṭaka, vārtāka, padola, and kāravellaka.
Kūṣmāṇḍa removes leprosy, urinary disorders, fever, dyspnea, cough, and disorders of pitta and kapha;
it pacifies all the doṣas, is beneficial for the heart, and cleanses the bladder.
Kaliṅga and alābu destroy bile but produce wind;
trapuṣa and urvāruka increase wind and phlegm while warding off bile.
Vṛkṣāmla destroys kapha and vāta; jambīra alleviates kapha and vāta;
pomegranate destroys vāta and is constipating; the fruit of the nāgaraṅga is heavy. (GarP 1,169.20)
Keśara and mātuluṅga are digestive stimulants that alleviate kapha and vāta;
māṣa removes vāta and pitta, while its skin is unctuous, hot, and dispels wind.
Sāramāmalaka is aphrodisiac, sweet, pleasing to the heart, and slightly sour; it stimulates the appetite after a meal, is meritorious, and is like nectar. Harītakī is comparable to immortality.
The *akṣa* fruit is laxative and destroys phlegm and wind; it likewise conquers the three doṣas.
The sour *tintiḍī* fruit removes wind and phlegm and acts as a laxative.
The lakuca is unwholesome; the bakula is sweet and conquers phlegm and wind;
the bījapūraka destroys abdominal tumors, wind, phlegm, asthma, and cough.
The wood-apple (kapittha) is astringent, destroys the [three] humors, and when ripe, is heavy and removes poison;
