it increases phlegm and bile, while the immature fruit, when full-grown, increases bile.
Ripe mango increases wind and bestows flesh, semen, complexion, and strength;
jambu fruit subdues wind, subdues phlegm and bile, is constipating, and causes flatulence.
Tinduka destroys phlegm and wind; Badara removes wind and bile; Bilva causes constipation and increases wind; Priyāla dispels wind.
They say that the rājādana fruit, the moca, the panasa,
and that which comes from the coconut increase semen and flesh, and are sweet, unctuous, and heavy.
Grapes, madhūka, dates, and saffron conquer vātarakta; pippalī, when ripe and sweet, is supreme for removing dyspnea and pitta.
Fresh ginger is appetizing, aphrodisiac, digestive, and removes phlegm and wind;
likewise, dry ginger, black pepper, and long pepper are considered conquerors of phlegm and wind.
One should know that black pepper is non-aphrodisiac; this is the consensus of medical authorities.
Asafoetida destroys abdominal tumors, colic, and constipation, and removes wind and phlegm.
Yavānī, dhanyaka, and jājī are supreme for removing vāta and kapha;
rock salt (saindhava) is known to be beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and a pacifier of the three doṣas.
Sauvarcala salt destroys constipation, is heating, and cures pain in the heart;
viḍaṅga is heating, relieves colic, is sharp, and subdues wind (vāta).
Romaka salt increases wind (vāta), is sweet, appetizing, moistening, and heavy;
it cures heart disease, anemia, and throat ailments, while yavakṣāra kindles the digestive fire.
Fire is illuminating and sharp; alkali (sarjikṣāra) is a digestive solvent.
Water from the sky destroys the bodily humors, is light, beneficial for the heart, and removes poison.
Water from rivers is not to be drunk; it increases wind, is dry, and is light.
Water from lakes is sweet and light. Water from ponds removes wind and phlegm, while water from tanks is known to increase wind.
Water from mountain springs is pungent, fire-producing, dry, light, and destroys phlegm; it is digestive and increases bile.
Water from wells increases bile, while water from ponds and tanks destroys bile. Garuḍa Purāṇa 1,169.37.
That which is graced by the rays of the sun during the day and by the rays of the moon at night,
being entirely free from all defects, is equal to the water of the sky.
Warm water removes fever, dyspnea, fat, wind, and phlegm;
boiled and cooled, it destroys the three *doṣas*; and that which has been left overnight increases the *doṣas*.
Cow’s milk subdues wind and bile, is unctuous, heavy, and a rejuvenative;
that of the buffalo is even heavier and more unctuous than cow’s milk, and it destroys the digestive fire.
Goat's meat cures bloody diarrhea, removes cough, dyspnea, and phlegm;
it is beneficial for the eyes, life-prolonging, and serves as a nasal therapy for women suffering from internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta).
Curd is supreme for removing wind, is aphrodisiac, and increases pitta and kapha;
however, whey produced from churning destroys the humors and cleanses the channels.
Freshly extracted butter (navanīta) removes the afflictions of malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, and facial paralysis;
however, products such as inspissated milk (kilāṭa) and the like are heavy and causes of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
But buttermilk, as described by the ancient sages, cures malabsorption, edema, hemorrhoids, anemia, diarrhea, and abdominal tumors; it pacifies the three doṣas.

Ghee from a cow is aphrodisiac, sweet, and removes wind, bile, and phlegm; it is beneficial for the intellect and the eyes, and when processed with medicinal ingredients, it conquers all three humors.
Clarified butter (ghṛta) that has been processed [with medicinal herbs] destroys epilepsy, insanity, and fainting;
one should know that the ghee of goats and other animals possesses qualities similar to cow’s milk.
Urine removes phlegm and wind and destroys all worms and poisons.

Oil produced from sesame seeds removes paleness, abdominal diseases, skin disorders, hemorrhoids, swelling, abdominal tumors, and urinary disorders; it subdues wind and phlegm, is strengthening, and promotes the growth of hair.
Sesame oil destroys worms and jaundice, and removes phlegm, fat, and wind;
linseed oil is not beneficial for the eyes, yet it removes bile and destroys wind.
Honey produced from flowers is said to destroy phlegm and bile, to be beneficial for the hair, and to nourish the skin and ears;
it is proclaimed to alleviate the three doṣas, yet it is also declared to increase wind (vāta).
Sugarcane cures hiccup, dyspnea, worms, vomiting, urinary disorders, thirst, and poison; it destroys hemorrhaging and pitta, and is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and increases kapha.
Phāṇita (unrefined molasses) is bilious and parching; *tavara* and *surā* are light; *matsyaṇḍikā* (crystallized sugar) is aphrodisiac, unctuous, sweet, and conquers blood disorders, bile, and wind.
Fresh jaggery (guḍa) alleviates wind and bile, is parching, subdues wind, and increases phlegm;
however, old jaggery is highly wholesome, pacifies bile, and clarifies the blood.
Gaḍaśarkarā, being unctuous, removes blood and bile and acts as an aphrodisiac;
wine produces all types of *pitta*, yet it conquers *kapha* and *vāta* due to its acidity.
Those varieties originating from Sauvīra are sharp and cause hemorrhaging and bile disorders;
however, gruel made from fried rice is digestive, appetizing, and wholesome.
Light gruel that facilitates the downward movement of wind, purifies the bladder,
and contains curd, pomegranate, and the three pungents (vyoṣa), as well as jaggery, honey, and long pepper, [is beneficial].
This rice-gruel is well-prepared for treating cough, asthma, and dysentery;
milk-rice (pāyasa) generates phlegm and is strengthening, while rice-and-pulse porridge (kṛsarā) destroys wind (vāta).
Well-washed, strained, unctuous, pleasantly warm, light, and appetizing;
prepared with bulbs, roots, fruits, and grains, it is nourishing and heavy.
Soup that is well-prepared, light, and served lukewarm is beneficial;
likewise, boiled and squeezed vegetables, seasoned with fats and other ingredients, are wholesome.
Soup made from pomegranate and *āmalaka* kindles the digestive fire and subdues wind and bile;
soup made with *āmalaka* alone destroys asthma, cough, catarrh, and phlegm.
Soup made from barley, jujube, and horse-gram is beneficial for the throat and subdues wind;
that made from mung beans and āmalaka is constipating and destroys phlegm and bile.
Curd with jaggery subdues wind; roasted flour (saktu) is parching and increases wind.
A cake filled with ghee kindles the digestive fire, while *śaṣkulī* is aphrodisiac, heavy, and nourishing.
Edible flour-balls mixed with meat are known to be nourishing;
those prepared with oil are detrimental to vision, and those steamed in water are difficult to digest.
Mandakas are considered wholesome when very hot, while guḍas are considered wholesome when cold;
water as a post-drink destroys fatigue, thirst, and other such ailments.
Protection is provided by means of food, drink, and so forth; one becomes entirely free from disease.
[The poison] is not hot, resembles the color of a peacock's throat, and causes discoloration.
The odors, touch, and tastes will be intense, and the consumer will suffer mental anguish;
upon smelling it, there will be eye disease that is incurable even by the best of physicians;
trembling, yawning, and so forth—this is the characteristic of poison.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Subsequent Drinks (Anupāna) and Other Matters," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: [Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—170] Dhanvantari said:
Fever is known to be of eight types: those arising from individual [humors], combinations of two, all three combined, and those caused by external factors.
To alleviate thirst and fever, one should administer water that has been boiled with *mustā*, *parpaṭaka*, *uśīra*, *candana*, *udīcya*, and *nāgara*, and then cooled.
One should first administer this digestive (pācanaka) remedy, which removes fever, consisting of nāgara, devadāru, dhānyaka, and the two types of bṛhatī, to one suffering from fever.
A decoction prepared from āragvadha, abhayā,
mustā, tiktā, and granthika is digestive and beneficial for fever accompanied by undigested toxins (āma) and pain.
Equal parts of *madhūka* pith, rock salt, *vaca*, black pepper,
and long pepper should be finely ground with water and administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*) to restore consciousness.
A decoction prepared from trivṛt, viśālā, triphalā, kaṭukā,
and āragvadha, combined with alkali, is a purgative that should be drunk to alleviate all fevers.
A decoction made from mahauṣadha, amṛtā, musta, candana, uśīra, and dhānyaka,
when combined with sugar and honey, destroys tertian fever.
Having tied it with seven red threads around the waist at the root of the Apāmārga plant on a Sunday,
one certainly destroys tertian fever.
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, a childless ascetic has died;
one should offer him water with sesame seeds, and the fever lasting for one day will be released.
Oils prepared with the decoction and paste of *guḍūcī*, as well as those of *triphalā*, *vāsaka*,
*mṛdvīkā*, and *balā*, are effective destroyers of fever.
A decoction of *dhātrī*, *śivā*, *kaṇā*, and *vahni* is the ender of all fevers;
now I shall describe the medicine that removes fever and diarrhea.
A decoction prepared from *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *bilva*, *nāgara*, *utpala*, *dhānyaka*, *pāṭhā*, *indrayava*, *bhūnimba*, *musta*, and *parpaṭaka*,
along with *mahauṣadha* (ginger), cures acute diarrhea accompanied by fever.
A decoction made from *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, *musta*, *bhūnimba*, *amṛta*,
and *vatsaka* removes all fevers and destroys all types of diarrhea.
Milk boiled with musta, parpaṭaka, divya,
and ginger, along with śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā.
Balā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, bilva, and so forth, along with pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka—
this [mixture] is beneficial when combined with food for all those suffering from diarrhea.
A decoction of *bilva* and mango stones, combined with sugar and honey, cures diarrhea;
likewise, a preparation of *kuṭaja* bark mixed with *kaṇā* (long pepper) is beneficial for diarrhea.
A decoction of vatsaka, ativiṣā, viśva, and kaṇā,
when administered, is effective for diarrhea accompanied by blood and characterized by colic due to undigested matter (āma).
Now, regarding the treatment of *grahaṇī*:
since *grahaṇī* destroys the digestive fire (*agni*), clarified butter (*havis*) cooked with the decoction and paste of *citraka* is a destroyer of *grahaṇī*.
It cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*), edema (*śotha*), abdominal enlargements (*udara*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), colic (*śūla*), and hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and it stimulates the digestive fire.
One should add here the five salts: sauvarcala, saindhava, viḍaṅga, audbhida, and likewise sāmudra.
Know that medicine for hemorrhoids consists of three types: surgical instruments, caustic alkali, and fire; yet among these, freshly extracted buttermilk is indeed the destroyer of hemorrhoids.
For the destruction of hemorrhoids, one should eat gudūcī combined with pippalī and abhayā fried in ghee,
along with sour loṇikā.
The combination of sesame, sugarcane juice, and milk destroys hemorrhoids and skin diseases;
likewise, pañcakola with black pepper and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) stimulates the digestive fire.
Harītakī, when eaten regularly with ginger, jaggery,
or even combined with rock salt, stimulates the digestive fire.
A decoction made from triphalā, amṛtā, sātīkā, bhūnimba,
and nimba, when mixed with honey, destroys anemia (pāṇḍuroga) along with jaundice (kāmalā).

A bolus (*modaka*) composed of *trivṛt*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *śyāmā*, long pepper (*pippalī*), sugar, and honey, brings an end to *sannipāta* disorders and removes hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*). (GarP 1.170.24)
While clothing is available, as well as hope and the means of life,
why does one suffering from blood-bile, consumption, or cough fall into despair?
A decoction of *āṭarūpaka*, grapes (*mṛdvīkā*), and *pathyā*, mixed with sugar and abundant honey,
cures cough, dyspnea, and hemorrhagic disorders (*raktapitta*).
Vāsā juice mixed with sugar and honey, when drunk, conquers blood-born [diseases].
Sallakī, badarī, jambu, priyāla, āmra, arjuna, and dhava,
as well as milk enriched with honey, each separately prevent the flow of blood.
Having drunk ghee prepared with the fresh juices of *nirguṇḍī*— including its roots, fruits, and leaves—
one who was emaciated by consumption shines like a god, free from all disease.
Harītakī, pippalī, śuṇṭhī,
and marica combined with jaggery is declared to be a cough-destroying modaka that eliminates thirst and loss of appetite.
When thirty palas each of kaṇṭakārī and guḍūcī have been boiled down to a decoction,
one prastha of ghee prepared in that liquid will cure cough and kindle the digestive fire.
Black *dhātrī*, sugar, and ginger, combined with honey, destroy hiccup;
one suffering from hiccup or asthma should drink *bhārgī* with *viśvā* along with warm water.
In cases of hoarseness of voice, one should hold a piece of khadira wood smeared with oil in the mouth;
or one may take a pathyā fruit combined with pippalī, or combined with nāgara.
One should drink the powder of *viḍaṅga* and the three myrobalans (*triphala*) with honey to cure vomiting;
or one may drink a decoction of *āmra* and *jambū* mixed with honey.
Triphalā dispels all vomiting and draws away thirst; when drunk with honey, it also cures vertigo, fainting, and heart disease.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are beneficial when drunk for dispelling epilepsy, planetary afflictions, and the like;
likewise, the juice of the kūṣmāṇḍa gourd mixed with ghee and yaṣṭīmadhu serves that same purpose.
One should consume aged ghee prepared with the juice of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*; it destroys insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy.
Ghee cooked with a decoction and paste of *aśvagandhā*, along with four times the amount of milk, destroys wind-disorders, acts as an aphrodisiac, improves the complexion, and promotes virility.
One who drinks the powder of *nīlī* and *muṇḍīrikā* combined with honey and clarified butter, along with a decoction of *chinnā*, overcomes even the most difficult cases of *vātarakta*.
Five *pathyā* fruits with jaggery cure leprosy, hemorrhoids, and wind disorders;
likewise, the fresh juice, paste, powder, or decoction of *gaḍacī* [is effective].
Ghee boiled with milk and the decoction and paste of black *guḍūcī* is the ender of *vātarakta* (gout) and the pacifier of skin diseases, ulcers, and the like. (GarP 1.170.40)
Guggulu combined with triphalā removes vātarakta and fainting;
and guggulu taken with cow’s urine destroys ūrustambha.
A decoction of ginger and gokṣuraka relieves the pain and colic of vāta associated with āma.
[Likewise, a decoction] of the ten roots (daśamūla), amṛtā, eraṇḍa, rāsnā, ginger, and devadāru [is effective].
A decoction combined with black pepper and jaggery destroys edema of the heart;
it is declared to be a bolus that cures cough and destroys thirst and loss of appetite.
When one *prastha* of ghee is prepared with thirty *palas* each of the juices of *kaṇṭakārī* and *guḍūcī*, it cures cough and heart disease and acts as a digestive stimulant.
A decoction combined with black dhātrī, sugar, ginger, black pepper, and rock salt,
when taken with castor oil, destroys heavy vāta accompanied by āma.
Balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī, and gokṣura,
along with hiṅgu and varṇa, when drunk, alleviate vāta-type colic.
One should cause [the patient] to drink [a decoction] prepared with triphalā, nimba, yaṣṭīmadhu, kaṭukā, and āragvadha,
mixed with honey, for the alleviation of burning sensations and pain.
Water boiled with the three myrobalans (triphalā) and liquorice (yaṣṭīkā) destroys the pain of indigestion (pariṇāma).
Iron filings (maṇḍūra) purified with cow’s urine and combined with the powder of the three myrobalans,
when licked with honey and ghee, destroys colic born of the three humors (tridoṣaja).
Trivṛt, black myrobalan, and yellow myrobalan taken in parts of two, four, and five respectively,
made into pills with an equal amount of jaggery, remove diseases caused by the obstruction of feces.
This powder of *harītakī*, alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), *pippalī*, and *trivṛt*, mixed with ghee, should be drunk; it destroys upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
Trivṛt, harītakī, and śyāmā, processed with the milky sap of snuhī and formed into pills,
when drunk with urine, are excellent for breaking up abdominal distension.
Ghee prepared with a paste of trikaṭu, triphalā, dhānyaka, viḍaṅga, cavya, and citraka, when properly processed, cures vātagulma.
Long pepper root brought with milk removes pain in the heart;
one should drink half that amount of sauvarcala salt and ghee prepared with the ashes of cow dung.
Or by means of *kaṇā*, stone-splitting [medicines], powdered *śilājatu*,
rice-gruel, or even jaggery, one who suffers from dysuria lives.
One afflicted by disorders of wind (vātaroga), accompanied by pain and difficulty in urination (mūtrakṛcchra), should drink a decoction of *amṛtā*, *nāgarī*, *dhātrī*, *vājigandhā*, and *trikaṇṭaka*.
Barley alkali, equal in measure to sugar, removes all types of urinary distress;
likewise, the juice of *nidigdhikā* mixed with honey destroys urinary distress.
Salt with the pastes of the three myrobalans (triphalā) is known to remove urinary obstruction;
when urine is obstructed, one should insert camphor powder into the penis.
A decoction derived from the root of *śigru* is pungent and hot, and it causes the passage of stones.
The juice of *dhātrī* combined with honey and *niśā* removes all types of *meha*.
A decoction of *triphalā*, *dāru*, *dārvī*, and *aṣṭa* taken with honey destroys *meha*.
One who desires to increase corpulence should gradually abandon sleeplessness, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and anxieties.
One who eats barley or śyāmāka grain with honeyed water will become stout;
conversely, by drinking hot food or gruel with its scum, one becomes lean of body.
Sacā, vyajīraka, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, sauvarcala,
and āmalā, when drunk with honey, destroy blood disorders, eliminate phlegm, and stimulate all the digestive fires.
One suffering from abdominal enlargement should drink one *prastha* of ghee prepared with four parts water, two parts urine, and a paste of *citraka*, along with milk.
One should increase the dose by ten [morsels] each day for ten days, adding one *paippālika* morsel per day along with milk; likewise, one should decrease it again in the same manner.
One who eats sixty-day rice with milk for a thousand days of this [practice] will experience nourishment,
longevity, and the destruction of splenic enlargement.
Ghee prepared with the decoction and paste of *punarnavā* removes swelling;
it should be consumed with cow’s urine, or *pippalī* taken with milk,
or *abhayā* in equal parts with jaggery, or *viśva* (ginger), by one suffering from edema.
By drinking castor oil produced from the *eraṇḍa* plant, combined with milk prepared with *balā*,
a person shall conquer intestinal hernia (*antravṛddhi*) accompanied by flatulence and pain.
A paste made from myrobalan (pathyā) combined with black salt and castor oil is a supreme remedy for curing hemorrhoids.
Glandular swellings (gaṇḍamālā) are destroyed by nasal drops made from the root of nirguṇḍī;
furthermore, fomentation with smuhī and gaṇḍīrī destroys tumors (arbuda).
By applying a paste of *hastikarṇapalāśa*, along with *dhattūra*, castor oil plant, *nirguṇḍī*, *varṣābhū*, *śigru*, and mustard seeds, one cures goiter.
An ointment [made from these] destroys elephantiasis that has arisen long ago and is extremely severe;
*śobhāñjana*, rock salt, and asafoetida destroy abscesses.
Śarapuṅkhā mixed with honey is a healer of all wounds;
likewise, an application of nimba leaves heals swelling and wounds.
Triphalā, khadira, dāru, and nyagrodha cleanse wounds;
a physician should irrigate a fresh wound accompanied by pain with these.
Having diagnosed traumatic wounds, the physician should apply ghee mixed with liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhuka*), slightly warmed, together with honey.
One should employ cooling treatments that destroy the heat of pitta and rakta;
a decoction made from bamboo bark, castor root, gokṣura, and vanidā [is recommended].
Asafoetida and rock salt, when drunk, cause the blood located within the abdominal cavity to flow out;
or [it may be done] with the ununctuous broth of barley, jujube, and horse-gram.
One should eat food or drink gruel mixed with rock salt;
the juice of karañja, ariṣṭa, and nirguṇḍī destroys worms in wounds.
Guggulu combined with the powder of triphalā and made into pills acts without restriction; it destroys constipation and heals wounds.
Alternatively, an ointment prepared with the fresh juice of dūrvā grass, or with kampillaka,
or with the paste of the bark of dāruharidrā, is a primary healer of wounds.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Treatment for Fever and Other Diseases," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—171.
Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, listen to the treatment for diseases such as sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa):
having incised the sinus with a surgical instrument, the procedure for sinuses is the same as that for wounds.

One should conquer fistula-in-ano, malignant ulcers, pain, and hemorrhoids by using equal parts of guggulu, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the three acrids (vyopa) combined with clarified butter.
Oil extracted from the juice of *nirguṇḍī* removes sinus ulcers and malignant wounds;
it is beneficial for skin diseases such as *pāmā* when used for drinking, massage, and nasal drops.
Guggulu combined with one part each of triphalā, kṛṣṇā, and three, five, and one [parts] respectively,
is beneficial for those suffering from glandular swellings, edema, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano.
When a vein is pierced in the middle of the *dhvaja*, purification occurs in cases of venereal disease (*upadaṃśaka*);
however, suppuration must be guarded against with great effort, for it causes the destruction of the penis.
One should drink a decoction of paṭola, nimba, triphalā, and guḍūcī along with guggulu and khadira; thus the secondary venereal disease (upadaṃśa) is destroyed.
One should burn *triphalā* together with *sāmasī* and honey in a cauldron;
this ointment for *upadaṃśa* heals the ulcer instantly.
Ghee cooked with the pastes and decoctions of triphalā, nimba, bhūnimba, karañja, khadira, and other such herbs is the supreme remedy for upadaṃśa.
Having recognized that it has been broken at the outset, one should sprinkle it with cold water;
once it has healed, an ointment should be applied, and a bandage provided with *kuśa* grass should be fastened.
Black gram, meat, as well as clarified butter, milk, vegetable broth, and pure water—
these nourishing foods and drinks should be given to the patient with a fracture.
One who consumes a paste made of garlic, honey, ghee,
and sugar will experience the rejoining of bones that are severed, split, or fallen away before long.
Aśvattha, triphalā, vyoṣa,
and varā, taken in equal parts and combined with an amount of guggulu equal to their total weight, is an effective remedy for healing fractured joints.
In all types of kuṣṭha, emesis, purgation, and bloodletting [are indicated];
likewise, [the use of] vacā, vāsā, paṭola, nimba, and the bark of kaliṅgī.
A decoction drunk with honey, combined with madana, removes wind;
a purgative should be administered using trivṛt, karṇaphala, and trikaṭu.
Oil prepared with realgar and black pepper destroys leprosy;
this ointment is effective for all types of leprosy, as is rice cooked with *śivā* and five kinds of molasses.
Kuṣṭha applied as an ointment with the milky sap of the karañja and gaja plants along with cow’s urine,
or an application of karavīra after being anointed with oil, removes leprosy.
Haridrā, malaya, rāsnā, guḍūcī, iḍagaja,
āragvadha, and karañja— this ointment is supreme for removing skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Realgar, viḍaṅga, vākucī, and mustard seeds,
ground with urine along with karañja, constitute this ointment that destroys skin diseases like the sun.
This ointment, made from viḍaṅga, eḍagaja, vacā, kuṣṭha, niśā, sindhūttha, and sarṣapa,
ground with urine and sour gruel, destroys ringworm and skin diseases.
Seeds of *prapunnāṭa*, *dhātrī*, resin of *sarja*, and *snuhī* ground with *sauvīra* salt—
this is the supreme ointment for ringworm.
One should grind the leaves of *āragvadha* with sour gruel;
this destroys ringworm, skin scabs, leprosy, and even vitiligo.
Vāgujī taken warm with milk conquers skin diseases for one who subsists on a milk diet.
Sesame, ghee, triphalā, honey, vyōṣa, bhallātaka, and sugar—
these seven taken in equal parts are aphrodisiacs, purifying, destroyers of disease, and grant freedom of action.
The powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and kṛṣṇā, licked with honey, destroys skin diseases, worms, urinary disorders, sinus ulcers, and fistulas. (GarP 1.171.23)
He who eats abhayā, ariṣṭa, ariṣṭā, āmalaka, and niśā shall conquer all forms of leprosy after one month; of this there is no doubt.
The resin of the *khadira* tree burnt in ten thousand jars,
along with the juice of *sākṣadhātrī*, honey, and *mūlaka*, is an elixir that destroys leprosy.
Having drunk a decoction of dhātrī and khadira combined with vāgajī, one quickly destroys vitiligo as white as a conch shell or the moon; of this there is no doubt.
By drinking bhallātaka oil for a month, a person shall conquer disease;
likewise, khadira water, when consumed through drinking and other means, becomes a conqueror of leprosy.
One should eat a karṣa of a large quantity of *somarājī* fruit that has been soaked in a decoction of *malapūka*, while abstaining from salt; one should then drink a decoction of *akṣa* and *phalgu*.
When applied as a paste, aparājitā, vāsā, śuddhā, triphalā, paṭola, and karañjaka destroy even incurable leucoderma.
If one consumes neem and black cane as a medicated ghee prepared with their decoction and paste, that becomes "vajraka" [medicinal oil]; it cures leprosy, and one lives for a hundred years.
One should cook oil with four times as much of the natural juice of dūrvā grass;
by mere anointing, itch, eczema, and scabies are destroyed.
Oil prepared with the bark of *druma*, *arka*, and *kuṣṭha*, the salts,
cow’s urine, *gambhārikā*, and *citraka* removes skin diseases, ulcers, and other such ailments.
(Now, the treatment for *amlapitta*): Likewise, *dhātrī*, *nimbaphala*, and *citraka* with cow’s urine;
[and] with *vāsā*, *amṛtā*, *parpaṭikā*, *nimba*, *bhūnimba*, and *mārka*.
A decoction of triphalā and kulattha, taken with honey, destroys amlapitta.
A bitter decoction of the three fruits (triphalā), patola, and sugar,
or combined with licorice (yaṣṭīmadhu), when drunk, conquers fever, vomiting, and acid dyspepsia (amlapitta).
Vāsā-ghṛta, Tikta-ghṛta,
and Pippalī-ghṛta should be administered in cases of amlapitta, as should guḍakūṣmāṇḍaka.
Long pepper combined with honey destroys acid bile;
a bolus of long pepper and jaggery is wholesome for removing phlegm and weak digestion.
Having ground ajājī together with dhanvyāka, one should cook it in one prastha of ghee;
this removes phlegm, bile, and loss of appetite, and cures weak digestion and vomiting.
(Thus concludes the treatment for *amlapitta*.

A decoction made from long pepper (*pippalī*), immortality-plant (*amṛta*), neem (*bhūnimba*), *vāsaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *parpaṭa*, and *khadira-ariṣṭaka* removes the pain of eruptive boils (*visphoṭa*) and fever. (GarP 1,171.38)
Ghee combined with the juice of triphalā and trivṛt should be administered for the purpose of purgation to pacify erysipelas and fever.
A decoction known as the "Eightfold" (aṣṭaka), prepared from khadira, triphalā, arishta, paṭola, amṛta, and vāsaka, conquers measles and smallpox.
Rubbing with the powder of garlic destroys skin diseases such as leprosy, erysipelas, boils, and itching,
and it also eliminates mosquitoes.
Having excised with a surgical instrument skin-warts, joint-gems, moles, and black birthmarks,
one should cauterize them completely with alkali and fire.
An ointment of *paṭola* and *nīlī* destroys the disease known as *jvālāgardabha*. A medicated oil (*tala*) boiled with *guñjā* fruits and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* [is likewise effective].
It destroys throat ailments, leprosy, and diseases caused by wind (vāta).
The marrow of *arka* seeds, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nālīcchā*, and *bhṛṅgarāja*,
along with iron powder and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), when aged and cooked, produce black hair.
Two *prasthas* of milk mixed with sugar, one *pala* of *madhuka*,
and one *kuḍava* of oil, when cooked together, form an errhine (*nasya*) that removes gray hair.
For diseases of the mouth, one should hold a gargle of triphalā;
likewise, house-soot, barley-alkali, pāṭhā, vyōpa, and rasāñjana [are used].
One should hold in the mouth a powder of *tejovatī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *lodhra*, and *citraka*, mixed with honey; this cures diseases of the neck, teeth, and mouth.
The tender sprouts of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *jambū*,
and *mālatī* constitute the excellent "five sprouts" (*pañcapallava*) decoction for rinsing the mouth.
The lukewarm juice of garlic, ginger, śigru, pāṭalī,
radish, and rudantī is excellent for filling the ears.
If the ear is afflicted with severe pain, accompanied by noise and discharge,
one should pour lukewarm goat's urine mixed with powdered rock salt into it.
Oil cooked with the juice of *jātī* leaves overcomes putrid ear disease;
likewise, mustard oil with ginger, when applied warm, relieves earache.
Milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), citraka and harītakī,
ghee-jaggery confection (sarpirguḍa), the six-ingredient preparation (ṣaḍaṅga), and vegetable soup (yūṣa) serve to alleviate chronic catarrh (pīnasa).
Diseases arising in the eyes and the abdomen, as well as catarrh, ulcers, and fever—
these five are pacified within five nights by fasting (*laṅghana*).
The filling of the eyes with the juice of *dhātrī* removes inflammation;
likewise, honey combined with rock salt (*saindhava*), or the juice of *śigru* and *dāru* along with *añjana*, [achieve the same].
An external plaster made from ground turmeric, devadāru, rock salt, pathyā, añjana, and white clay, when applied, cures eye diseases.
By applying a paste of *abhayā* from a dead tree combined with *triphalā* and milk,
or by holding warm, slightly salted ground leaves of *śuṇṭhī* and *nimba* over the eye, swelling, itching, and pain are briefly relieved.
Abhaya, akṣa, and amṛta, taken in one, two, and four parts respectively,
and licked with honey and ghee— or as a decoction— destroy all eye diseases.
This ointment, prepared with sandalwood, the three myrobalans, betel nut, and the roots of the palāśa tree,
ground with water, removes all darkness [of ignorance].
Black pepper ground with curd is an ointment that removes night-blindness;
likewise, ghee boiled with milk along with the decoction and paste of the three myrobalans (triphalā) [is effective].
This, when drunk at the onset of night, will quickly destroy cataracts:
long pepper, the three myrobalans, grapes, iron powder, and rock salt.
An ointment made from pills ground with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* is recommended;
it destroys blindness, cataracts, and other eye diseases.
The three pungents, the three myrobalans, black salt, rock salt,
realgar, rucaka salt, conch-shell navel, jasmine flowers, and neem.
Rasāñjana, bhṛṅgarāja, ghee, honey, and likewise milk—
having ground these together, this pill is a destroyer of all eye diseases.
The root of a burnt castor plant, ground with *kākī* and applied as a paste, quickly destroys headache; or else, [the paste made from] the flower of the *mucukunda*.
Oil boiled with one hundred palas each of castor root, *cakrā*, and *vyāghrī*—
when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), it removes diseases of wind and phlegm, cataracts, and disorders of the upper [head].
Sugar-cane with jaggery, or long pepper with rock salt—
these are [recommended] for all diseases such as arm-stiffness and for all upward-moving disorders.
In the case of Sūryāvarta, medical treatments such as nasal therapy (nasya) should be administered.
A decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) combined with ghee and rock salt, used as a nasal drop, destroys the piercing pain in the limbs and relieves the headache of Sūryāvarta. (GarP 1.171.67)
A woman suffering from *vātāsṛgdara* (menorrhagia or dysmenorrhea caused by wind) should drink a mixture of *sauvarcala* salt, cumin, *madhūka*, and blue lotus, combined with curd and honey.
In cases of Pitta-type fever, one should administer the fresh juice of Vāsaka, or the juice of Guḍūcī,
or the paste of Āmalakī seeds with water, along with sugar and honey.
For the sake of pacifying *pāṇḍu* and *pradara*, one should drink the sweet juice of the *āmalaka* root, or even that of the *kārpāsa* [cotton] plant, with rice-water.
The root of *taṇḍulīyaka* together with *rasāñjana* and honey,
when drunk with rice-water, conquers all forms of dysentery (*asṛgdara*).
Likewise, the root of *kuśa* drunk with rice-water conquers dysentery.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Treatment for Nāḍīvraṇa and Other Diseases," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 172.
Dhanvantari said:
O Suśruta, listen as I shall describe the treatment for diseases of women and other ailments; in disorders of the female reproductive tract, treatment that conquers Vāta is most highly recommended.
Vacā, upakuñcikā, jātī, kṛṣṇa, āvāsaka, saindhava, ajamodā, yavakṣāra, citraka, and sugar [should be combined]. (GarP 1.172.2)
Having ground and mixed it with water and other liquids, one should eat it fried in ghee;
this cures pain in the womb and the flanks, heart disease, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids. (GarP 1,172.3)
By applying an ointment of *badarī* leaves, the dilation of the womb is pacified;
and by applying an ointment of *lodhra* and *tumbī* fruit, it brings about firmness to the womb.
Ghee cooked with the five sprouts, piṣṭāhva, and mālatī flowers,
and processed by the sun, causes the flow of blood and destroys foul odors from the vagina.
Having consumed sour gruel, a *japā* flower, a leaf of *jyotiṣmatī*, ground *dūrvā* grass, and *citraka* mixed with sugar; ||| GarP_1,172.6 |||
The powder of *dhātrī*, *añjana*, and *abhayā*, when drunk with water, removes [uterine] dust;
likewise, *lakṣmaṇā* taken with milk, or used as a nasal drop during the fertile period, bestows a son.
Half an *āḍhaka* of milk, clarified butter, and *aśvagandhā* bestow a son;
even a barren woman shall obtain a son by drinking [the milk] with clarified butter, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and *kesara*.
Milk boiled with the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *urubūka*, and *gokṣuraka*,
combined with sugar, is an excellent remedy for the colic of a pregnant woman.
By applying a paste made individually from pāṭhā, aṅgali, siṃhī, āmra,
and kūṭaja to the navel, the bladder, or the vulva, a woman gives birth easily.
In the case of a Sūta woman, there is pain in the heart, head, and bladder known as *arkaṇḍa* (or *kvalla*);
in that condition, she should drink barley-alkali with whey or lukewarm water.
A decoction prepared from the ten roots (daśamūlī), taken with clarified butter, removes diseases of the abdomen;
likewise, the powder of śāli rice mixed with milk acts as a galactagogue.
For the purification of breast milk, she should consume the fresh juice of the vidārī tuber as well as the root of the cotton plant,
while subsisting on a diet of mung bean soup.
One should administer a linctus composed of kuṣṭha, vacā, abhayā, brāhmī, and madhuka, mixed with honey and ghee,
to a child to produce a healthy complexion, long life, and beauty.
In the absence of breast milk, one should drink goat's milk or cow's milk possessing those same qualities.
For one suffering from inflammation caused by fire, fomentation with earth heated by fire should be applied.
One should drink *leha* (electuary) made from *mustā*, *viṣā*, and *āragvadha* in cases of vomiting and fever;
[an electuary] made from *mustā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *viṣā*, *bilva*, and *kūṭaja* cures diarrhea.
Honey, trikaṭu, and citron prevent hiccup and vomiting;
kuṣṭha, indrayava, siddhārtha, niśā, and dūrvā conquer skin diseases.
Bathing with a decoction of mahāmuñjī, tikta, and kośātaki removes the afflictions of the planets;
likewise, anointing with *saptacchada*, turmeric, and sandalwood [provides protection].
The wearing of conch, lotus, seed-rosaries, rudrākṣas, coral, iron, and so forth;
and with the mantra "Oṃ kaṃ ṭaṃ yaṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Vainateya," peace for children is attained through sprinkling and the offering of oblations.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Bālamrahā, accept this offering; release the child! Svāhā!
One pala of śirīṣa root drunk with rice-water removes poison;
and [the same amount] of white varṣābhū plant drunk with rice-water cures snakebites.
Curd, clarified butter, rice-gruel, household smoke,
turmeric, as well as flour, a drink, and honey— these, along with rock salt, are a destroyer of poison.
A decoction of the root of *aṅkoṭa* drunk with clarified butter destroys poison;
that medicine which destroys old age and disease is an elixir (*rasāyana*).

One who desires the medicinal qualities of a rejuvenative tonic (*rasāyana*) should consume *abhayā* (chebulic myrobalan) in sequence with *sindhu* (rock salt), honey, sugar-cane juice, ginger, and long pepper, along with honey and jaggery, during the rainy season and the other seasons respectively.
At the end of a fever, one should consume a single *abhaya* and two *vibhītaka* fruits;
having eaten these, along with a quartet of honey, clarified butter, and *dhātrī*, it effects a lifespan of a hundred years.
Yellow *aśvagandhā* taken with milk or ghee cures all diseases;
the fresh juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇī* and *vidārī* is like nectar.
Having consumed sesame, dhātrī, and bhṛṅgarāja, one shall live for a hundred years.
So too by consuming trikaṭu, triphalā, citraka, guḍūcī, and śatāvarī.
Powdered viḍaṅga and iron, taken with honey, destroy diseases;
so too do triphalā, pippalī, śuṇṭhī, guḍūcī, and śatāvarī.
Powdered *vidanga* and *bhringaraja*, and so forth, when processed [with appropriate substances], removes all diseases;
having licked this powder with *vidari*, honey, and ghee, one may approach ten women.
One should cook ghee with the paste of *śatāvarī* and ten times its amount of milk;
when combined with sugar, long pepper, and honey, it is known as a digestive tonic (*jāraka*).
Pratimarṣa, avapīḍa, nasya, pravapana,
and śirovirecana— these are declared to be the fivefold treatment (pañcakarma).
The six seasons are traditionally reckoned in order by pairs of months beginning with Māgha;
one should practice the service of fire and consume preparations of honey and milk.
Likewise, one should not sleep during the day in the spring when accompanied by women;
during the rainy season, one should avoid sleeping and other such activities, as well as the rays of the autumnal moon.
Śāli rice, mung beans, rainwater, boiled milk,
and likewise the leaves of nimba, atasi, kusumbha, śigru, and mustard are wholesome.
Indeed, oils extracted from the roots of *jyotiṣmatī* remove worms,
skin diseases, urinary disorders, and pains in the head caused by wind and phlegm.
Pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, jujube, karamarda, priyāla, jambīra, nāgagra, āmrātaka, and kapittha. // GarP_1,172.35 //
Bitter substances (pittala) subdue wind (anila) but provoke phlegm (kapha). Water [is used] with *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *kuṭaja*, and *akṛtabandhana*.
Dhāmārgava should always be combined with these for emetic purposes;
likewise, madana, indrayava, and vacā are used for emesis in the forenoon.

The digestive tract is soft due to pitta, harsh due to the predominance of vāta and kapha, and moderate when the doṣas are in equilibrium; in these three conditions, one should administer the purgative trivṛt.
Saindhava salt combined with sugar and honey, nagara, and trivṛt;
or harītakī and vihaṅga taken with cow’s urine—these are purgatives.
Castor oil and a decoction of triphalā in double the quantity [should be used];
when the humors are dominated by vāta, one should first feed the patient and then induce vomiting.
One should make a nozzle from bamboo or similar material, measuring six, eight, or twelve finger-breadths in length;
its aperture should be like that of the karkandhu fruit, and it is used as a bladder for one lying on their back.
This same procedure is declared for the administration of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha);
the dosage is three and a half, six, and nine palas respectively for the mild, medium, and superior types.
Pathyā, akṣa, vātryoka, and dvicaturbhāga, which destroy diseases when processed with a decoction of śatavārī, bhṛṅgarāja, sindhuvāra, and other such plants.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Treatment for Women's Diseases and Other Topics," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 173.
Dhanvantari said:
I shall now describe the substances beginning with the sweet that remove [excessive] passion:
śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, goat's milk, cow's milk, ghee, meat broth, and honey.
Marrow, śṛṅgāṭaka, yavaka, ervāru, gīkṣura,
gambhārī, lotus seed, grapes, dates, and balā.
Nārikela, ikṣu, ātma-ja, vidārī,
priyālaka, madhuka, tāla, and kṣmāṇḍa— this is the primary sweet group (madhura-gaṇa).
When consumed excessively on its own, it pacifies fainting and burning sensations, clarifies the six sense faculties,
yet produces worms and increases phlegm.
One should apply treatments such as the application of jaggery for dyspnea, cough, hoarseness of voice, tumors, goiters, and elephantiasis.
The pomegranate, the āmalaka, the mango, the wood-apple, the karamarda, the citron, the āmrātaka, the jujube, and the tamarind fruit. 173.6.
Curd, buttermilk, fermented rice water, lakuca, and sour vetasa—
this sour and salty taste, when combined with ginger, is digestive and promotes the digestion of food.
Sour [taste] causes moistening, generates wind, is exhilarating, causes burning, and promotes downward movement; however, when consumed in excess, it certainly causes the trembling of the teeth.
It causes coldness of the body and burning of the voice, throat, mouth, and heart;
having ripened wounds that are cut or split, it is activated by the fire element.
Salts such as yavakṣāra and sarjikā constitute the saline group;
they are purifying, digestive, moistening, and they cause disintegration and spreading.
That single rasa, which obstructs the channels and produces softness, when consumed excessively, causes itching of the limbs, swelling of the abdomen, discoloration,
blood-wind disorders (raktavāta), blood-bile disorders (pittarakta), and ailments such as pain in the generative organs. (GarP 1,173.11)
Vyoṣa, śigru, mūlaka, devadāru, and kuṣṭha;
garlic, valguja fruit, mustā, guggulu, and lāṅgalī.
The pungent [taste] is digestive, purifying, and an ender of leprosy, itching, and phlegm;
it removes obesity, lethargy, and worms, and counteracts semen and fat.
However, when consumed excessively on its own, it causes vertigo, burning sensations, and other ailments.
Kṛtamāla, kīra, haridrā, indrayava, as well as svādukaṇṭaka, vetra, the two types of bṛhatī, and śaṅkhinī.
Guḍūcī, candravantī, trivṛt, maṇḍūkaparṇī, kāravellaka, vārtāku, karavīraka, and vāsaka; // GarP_1,173.15 //
Rohiṇī, conch powder, karkoṭa, jayantī,
jātī, vāruṇaka, nimba, jyotiṣmatī, and punarnavā.
The bitter taste is scarifying, as well as appetizing and digestive;
it is purifying, destroys fever and thirst, and overcomes fainting, throat afflictions, and the like.
For that [practice], when indulged in excessively, causes the complete drying up of feces, urine, and moisture;
it produces lockjaw, convulsions, pain, headaches, ulcers, and other such ailments.
Triphalā, sallakī, jambu, āmrātaka, vacā and so forth;
tinduka, vakula, śāla, pālaṅkī, mudga, and cillaka.
Astringent [taste] is grasping, fixing, stiffening, moistening, and drying;
when consumed excessively by itself, it causes pain in the heart,
as well as dryness of the mouth, fever, flatulence, stiffness of the neck, and other such ailments.
Turmeric, kuṣṭha, salt, meṣaśṛṅgī, the two types of balā,
kacchurā, sallakī, pāṭhā, punarnavā, and śatāvarī.
Agnimantha, brahmadaṇḍī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, eraṇḍa,

as well as barley, jujube, horse-gram, and so forth— consuming one karṣa each of these, or the ten roots (daśamūla) either individually or combined, likewise removes wind-disorders and excessive bile.
Śatāvarī, vidārī, bālaka, uśīra, candana,
dūrvā, vaṭa, pippalī, badarī, and likewise sallakī.
Plantain, blue lotus, lotus, udumbara, and patolaka;
furthermore, this is the group that removes phlegm, consisting of turmeric, jaggery, and kuṣṭha.
Śatapuṣpī, Jātī, Vyoṣa, Āragvadha, and Lāṅgalī;
among unctuous substances, ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow are considered the most excellent.
Likewise, ghee is recommended for those desiring intelligence, memory, wisdom, and digestive fire;
pure ghee is prescribed for disorders of pitta, while that mixed with salt is for disorders of vāta.
It should also be administered when there is an excess of phlegm, combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali,
for those suffering from tumors, sinus ulcers, worms, phlegm disorders, fat disorders, and wind disorders.
Oil should be administered for the sake of lightness and firmness to those individuals with hard bowels,
as well as to those whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) have been depleted by exposure to wind and sun, carrying heavy loads, sexual intercourse, or physical exercise.
When the pathways of the channels are obstructed by dryness, afflictions, depletion, excessive fire, or wind,
one should perform the treatment for the female reproductive tract after burning away the network of vessels in cases of headache.
The dose for the best [patient] is one *pala*; for the middling, three *akṣas*;
and for the lowest, half a *pala*, in the case of oils, decoctions, and medicinal herbs.
Warm water should be given with ghee, while it is recommended separately for oil;
however, in cases of thirst associated with *sneha* or *pitta*, a person should drink warm water.
The downward movement of wind, bright and excellent stools, and unctuousness—this is considered the state of one who is properly lubricated.
For one who is dry, lubrication should be administered; for one who is excessively lubricated, drying measures should be applied.
Sudation is desired for disorders of wind and phlegm, whether the wind or the phlegm predominates, using *śyāmāka* grain, *koradaṣa*, *ānata*, buttermilk, oil-cake, and parched barley flour.
One should not apply sudation to those who are excessively obese, dry, weak, or fainting.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of Yoga, Samādhi, and Other States," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 174] Dhanvantari said:
I shall now describe ghee, oil, and other substances that cure diseases; listen, O Suśruta!
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, vacā, somā, brāhmī, and brahmasuvarcalā.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with equal parts of *abhayā*, *guḍūcī*, *aṭarūpaka*, and *vāgujī*, each weighing one *akṣa*.
One *prastha* of the juice of *kaṇṭakārī* combined with one *prastha* of milk—
this is known as *Brāhmī-ghṛta*, which is supreme for producing learning and intelligence.
Triphalā, citraka, balā, nirguṇḍī, nimba, vāsaka,
punarnavā, guḍūcī, bṛhatī, and śatāvarī.
With these [ingredients], ghee should be prepared as available to alleviate all diseases.
One should cook half an āḍhaka of oil in a decoction of one hundred parts of *balā*,
using the pastes (*kalka*) of madhūka, mañjiṣṭhā, candana, utpala, and padmaka.
With small cardamom, long pepper, kuṣṭha, cinnamon, cardamom, aloe-wood,
and saffron, along with fragrant substances, aśvagandhā, and the life-promoting (jīvanīya) herbs, all these should be infused in one āḍhaka of milk.
Cooked with a mild fire, this should be placed in a beautiful silver vessel;
it cures all disorders of wind (vāta) that reside within all the bodily constituents (dhātu).
This oil, known as Rājavallabha, which is strengthening and beneficial for the voice,
should be prepared by combining one prastha of śatāvarī juice with an equal amount of milk.
Śatapuṣpā, devadāru, māṃsī, śaileyaka, balā,
candana, tagara, kuṣṭha, manaḥśilā, and jyotiṣmatī.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with these pastes, each weighing one karṣa;
[this is for] those who are hunchbacked, dwarfish, or lame, and for those who are deaf, marked by moles, or afflicted by leprosy.
For those whose limbs are broken by wind, those who fail in sexual intercourse, those whose bodies are worn out by old age, and those with bloated faces and parched mouths; GarP_1,174.11 //
This oil, which brings an end to the families of diseases, quickly destroys all those winds located in the skin, as well as those situated in the vessels and the tendons.
This Nārāyaṇa oil, spoken by Viṣṇu, is a destroyer of disease;
one should prepare it separately as an oil or a ghee with each of the medicinal herbs individually.
An expansion [of the ritual] may be performed with *śatāvarī*, *guḍūcī*, or *citraka* combined with *gocanā*;
or with *nirguṇḍī* or *kaṇṭakārī*, using their juices and other substances.
Or with the dwelling-place of the frog, or with vāsaka, the three fruits (triphalā), brāhmī, śṛṅgaka, bhṛṅgarāja, and kuṣṭha; || 174.15 ||
A pill, a bolus, or even a powder made from *musalī*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *khadira*, *vaṭa* and other such [trees],
destroys all diseases.
Combined with clarified butter, honey, or even water, sugar, jaggery, and the like,
as well as salts and pungent spices, it cures diseases of the head according to what is available.
Or else, one may use citraka, arka, trivṛt, yavānī, hayamāraka,
sudhā, bālā, gaṇikā, saptaparṇa, and suvarcikā.
Having gathered *jyotiṣmatī*, the wise physician should cook it with oil;
this "flowing" oil (*niṣyandana-taila*) should be administered copiously for fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇdara*).
This great oil, beginning with *citraka*, is supreme for cleansing and healing, bestows all complexions, and shatters all diseases.
Ajamodā, red lead, yellow orpiment, the two types of turmeric, the two alkalis, sea-foam, fresh ginger, and resin produced from the Śara tree; GarP_1,174.21 //
With *indravāruṇī*, *apāmārga*, plantains, and *syandana*—sesame oil combined with these and goat’s urine [should be used]. (GarP 1,174.22)
One should cook this Ajamoda oil with cow’s milk over a gentle fire; it removes scrofula (gaṇḍamālā). GarP_1,174.23 //
One who is skilled should cook [the medicine] when it is raw and purify it once it is cooked;
one should then effect healing and softening with this oil.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of Brāhmī Ghee and Other Remedies," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—175.
Rudra said:
Thus Dhanvantari, who is Viṣṇu, spoke to Suśruta and the others; Hari, in turn, spoke to Hara regarding various medicinal formulations that destroy diseases.
Hari said:
O Śaṅkara, in all fevers, fasting should first be practiced,
as well as drinking boiled water and staying in a windless place.
O Lord, fevers indeed go to destruction through the application of fire and fomentation;
likewise, a decoction of *guḍūcī* and *mustaka* removes fever caused by wind (*vāta*).
Listen now to [the remedy] for fever caused by pitta: ghee prepared with *durālabhā*, along with *śuṇṭhī*, *parpaṭa*, *mustā*, *bālaka*, *uśīra*, and *candana*.
A decoction with ghee cures fever born of phlegm; likewise, one with ginger and dūrvālabhā cures it, as does one with vālaka; and one with ginger and parpaṭa cures all fevers.
A decoction of *kirātatikta*, *nāgarī*, *guḍūcī*, ginger, and *mustaka* will alleviate fever caused by pitta; now hear another excellent formulation.
A decoction made from vālaka, uśīra, pāṭhā, kaṇṭakārī, mustaka,
and likewise suradāru, is a fever-destroyer.
O Śaṅkara, that [mixture] of dhanyāka, nimba, and mustā with honey,
combined with paṭola leaves, guḍūcī, and triphalā, [is beneficial].
This [mixture] derived from *harītakī*, *pippalī*, *āmalaka*, and *citraka*, when drunk, removes all fevers, stimulates hunger, and subdues wind (*vāta*).
A powder, or a decoction of dhānyaka, uśīra, parpaṭa,
āmalakī, and guḍūcī, mixed with sandalwood and honey, [removes] fever.
It shall be the subduer of all fevers; now hear [the remedy] that removes *sannipāta* fever:
with *haridrā*, *nimba*, *triphalā*, *mustaka*, and *devadāru*.
Water boiled with the decoction of *kaṭurohiṇī*, *paṭola*, and *patra* should be drunk; it subdues fever born from the three *doṣas*.
Having consumed the powder of *nāgabalā* along with *kaṇṭakārī*, *nāgara*, *guḍūcī*, and *puṣkara*, one will overcome dyspnea, cough, and other such ailments.
In cases of fever caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, hot water prepared with *viśva*, *parpaṭaka*, *uśīra*, *musta*, and *candana* should be given to the thirsty patient.
One should give very cold water, which cures thirst, vomiting, fever, and burning sensations;
a decoction of the five roots beginning with Bilva (*bilvādi-pañcamūla*) should be used in cases of Vātika fever.
Long pepper root, guduchi, and ginger are digestive;
this decoction, when administered in a fever caused by vata, is supremely pacifying.

A decoction of *parpaṭa* and *nimba*, taken with honey, destroys fever caused by *pitta*; yet, even when this treatment is being administered, if consciousness does not return to the patient, [one should proceed further].
One should cauterize either the feet or the forehead with an iron rod.
A decoction of *tikta*, *pāṭhā*, *parpaṭa*, *viśālā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *trivṛt*,
taken with milk, is a purgative that cleanses all fevers.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of Various Formulas for Removing Fever," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Lord said: The Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa—176. The Blessed One said:
Beautiful hair grows upon a bald man within seven nights from the application of burnt elephant tusks mixed with goat’s milk and *rasāñjana*.
Oil prepared with one-fourth part of the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* and combined with powdered *guñjā* causes the growth of hair.
Anointing with ela, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, and murā is auspicious;
likewise, taking the fruit of guñjā as an ointment cures *candralupta*.
By applying a paste of powdered mango seeds, the hair indeed becomes fine;
and a paste of *karañja*, *āmalaka*, *elā*, and lac removes redness.
By applying a paste of mango stone marrow and *āmalaka*, the hair indeed becomes firmly rooted,
thick, long, glossy, and does not fall out.
Oil prepared with viḍaṅga and gandhapāṣāṇa is excellent;
likewise is that prepared with four times the amount of cow’s urine, or with manaḥśilā alone.
By massaging the head, one brings to an end the appearance of hair-whorls and lines produced on the scalp;
likewise, conch powder that has been heated nine times and rubbed onto lead [produces the same effect].
O Bull-bannered Lord, the hair becomes smooth and deep black.
[One should take] *bhṛṅgarāja*, iron powder, *triphalā*, and *bījapūraka*.
Indigo, oleander, and jaggery— boiled together with these in equal proportions,
this great medicine, when applied as an ointment, turns white hairs black here on earth.
The marrow of the mango stone, the three myrobalans, blue vitriol, and *bhṛṅgarāja*,
along with aged, processed iron powder and sour gruel, produce black hair.
Having ground the seeds of *cakramarda*, *kuṣṭha*, the root of *eraṇḍa*,
and very sour *kāñjika* together, an ointment applied from this mixture cures diseases of the head.
Saindhava salt, vacā, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, nāgeśvara,
śatapuṣpā, and devadāru— with these, oil is prepared.
Combined with a fourth part of cow-dung juice,
it brings an end to severe earache by filling the cavity with that powder.
O Śiva, by filling the ears with sheep’s urine and rock salt,
there shall be a destruction of foul odors in the ears, as well as of worms, discharges, and the like.
By filling [the area] with the juice of *mālatī* flower petals as a medicinal application,
or even with a full stream of cow's urine, the discharge of pus is destroyed.
Kaṣṭha, māṣa, marīca, tagara, honey, pippalī, apāmārga, aśvagandhā, bṛhatī, and white mustard seeds; GarP_1,176.16.
Barley, sesame seeds, and rock salt, used as an ointment for the feet, are auspicious;
they cause the growth of the penis, the arms, the breasts, and the ears.
Likewise, pungent oil, *bhallātaka*, *bṛhatī*, and the fruit of the pomegranate [serve the same purpose].
Anointed with the processed bark-fibers, the linga increases by means of that.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Growth of Hair and Other Matters," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 177—
Hari said:
Indeed, the juice of *sobhāñjana* leaves mixed with honey, when applied to the eyes, removes diseases from them; there is no doubt about this.
Eighty sesame flowers, jasmine blossoms,
uśīra, nimba, āmalaka, ginger, long pepper, and taṇḍulīyaka.
One should grind this into a pill with rice-water, dry it in the shade, and apply it suddenly as a collyrium to the eyes with honey; this removes timira and other eye disorders.
One should grind the marrow of the *bibhītaka* seed, conch-shell navel,
realgar, neem leaf, and black pepper with goat's urine.
The flower [of *puṣpākṣī*] destroys night-blindness, as well as *timira* and *paṭala*;
[one should take] four parts of conch-shell and half of that amount of realgar.
Having ground together rock salt and half that amount of this [substance] with water,
one should make pills that have been dried in the shade and apply them as an ointment to the eyes.
The great medicine [consisting of] trikaṭu, triphalā, and the fruits of karañja destroys cataracts (timira), film (paṭala), and piciṭa.
Having ground rock salt and the two types of turmeric with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
the mere application of that collyrium destroys cataracts and other such ailments.
The root of the *āṭarūṣaka* plant ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
when applied as an ointment to the eyes and eyelids, destroys eye pain.
Soma juice and the root of *badarī* drunk together remove pain in the eyes;
likewise, rock salt, pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), and the root of *apāmārga* [are effective].
O Śaṅkara, by rubbing [the substance] with milk and sour gruel in a copper vessel and applying it as an ointment, even Piñjaṭa himself is destroyed.
Oṃ dadru sara kroṃ hrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ, dadru sara hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ uṃ ū sara krīṃ krīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ.
By means of this mantra, women indeed come under one's control through the application of collyrium.
The root of *bilvaka* and *nīlikā*, ground together and used as an ointment—
by merely applying this, cataracts (*timira*) are indeed destroyed.
Kaṭuka (long pepper), tagara, haridrā, āmalaka, and vacā,
ground with khadira and applied as a collyrium, remove eye diseases.
One who performs *dhauti* with the mouth full of water, washing the eyes with a large measure,
is constantly liberated from all eye diseases at dawn.
An application prepared with the root and leaf of white *eraṇḍa*,
along with a sprinkling of goat’s urine and heat, cures the flickering of the eyes caused by wind (*vāta*).
An ointment made from sandalwood, rock salt, old palāśa leaves, harītakī,
a layer of flowers, indigo,
and *vakrikā* removes [cataracts].
The root of *guñjā* rubbed in goat’s urine removes cataracts; likewise, [the eye disease] of silver, copper, and gold is removed by rubbing with a rod held in the hand.
O Rudra, rubbing [this] as an unguent destroys the disease of jaundice;
smelling the fruit of the ghoṣā plant after it has been drunk destroys jaundice.
Dūrvā grass, pomegranate flowers, lac, and harītakī— these,
when taken as a fresh juice, indeed destroy nasal polyps and blood disorders caused by vāta.
O Bull-bannered One, O Blue-and-Red One, by grinding the root-fiber of the *jāṅgalī* plant and administering its juice as a nasal drop (*nasya*),
hemorrhoids are destroyed in an instant.
Cow’s ghee, resin of the *sarja* tree, *dhanyāka*, rock salt, *dhuttūraka*, and red ochre— beeswax processed with these, O Rudra, [is used for sealing].
Oil with [these ingredients] cures wounds on the lips that are cracked or torn;
likewise, chewing and holding a *jātī* leaf in the mouth cures diseases of the mouth.
By eating the seeds of the kesara flower, loose teeth shall become firm.
Muṣṭaka, kuṣṭha, elā, yaṣṭika, honey, and vālaka— [these are used for this purpose].
By eating this dhanyāka, remove the foul odor from the mouth,
whether it be caused by astringent, pungent, or bitter vegetables.
For one who uses this regularly, the foul odor of the mouth shall cease,
and all dental injuries will indeed come to an end.
The practice of holding gargles and mouthfuls of sour gruel mixed with oil removes diseases of the mouth caused by burning from betel-leaf powder; may it be auspicious.
And for one who has abandoned phlegm, [the remedy] is like chewing ginger, as well as citron leaves, cardamom, licorice, and long pepper. (GarP 1,177.28)
Likewise, having licked the powder of these [herbs] along with a *jātī* leaf,
or chewing the root of *śephālikā*, removes throat-pain (*galashuṇṭhi*).
By drawing blood from the vessels of the nose, the *śaṃśakara-jihvikā* [disease] is destroyed.
The juice of *śirīṣa* seeds, combined with four parts of turmeric, [is the remedy].
O Lord of Beings, when this has been cooked, it serves as a nasal medication (nasya) that cures diseases of the head;
by the mere application of this nasal medication, diseases of the throat are destroyed instantly.
The destruction of tooth-worms occurs from chewing the root of *guñjā*;
likewise, a decoction of *kākajaṅghā*, *snuhī*, and *nīlī*, mixed with honey, [achieves the same].
O Śiva, a ghee prepared with *karkaṭapāda* and mixed with milk destroys the worms that infest the teeth and those born within them. (GarP 1.177.33)
And by that, having been treated with an emollient, the teeth should not produce a grinding sound;
or else, having smeared them with pure *karkaṭapāda* or *aśiva*.
Indeed, by applying a paste of the fruits of *jyotiṣmatī* ground with water for three weeks,
along with white *abhayā*, the stains and spots on the teeth are removed.
Lodhra, saffron, mañjiṣṭhā, loha, kāleyaka,
barley, and rice— these, combined with yaṣṭīmadhu, [should be used].
An application of paste made from [these ingredients] ground with water makes the faces of women beautiful.
Furthermore, one *prastha* of oil prepared with two parts of goat’s milk [is likewise beneficial].
Alternatively, by using one *karṣa* each of red *candana*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *lakṣāṇā*,
together with *yaṣṭīmadhu* and saffron, one’s facial radiance will be produced within seven days.
Powdered ginger and long pepper, along with *guḍūcī* and *kaṇṭakārikā*—
water boiled with these, when drunk, indeed stimulates the digestive fire.
O Lord of the First, one should likewise consume *kaga* to alleviate wind-pain and consumption;
[as well as] *karañja*, *parpaṭa*, *uśīra*, *vāhatī*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
Gokṣura boiled with water and drunk removes fatigue;
it brings about the destruction of burning sensations, bile, fever, consumption, and fainting.
Honey, clarified butter, and powdered long pepper, boiled and mixed with milk, when drunk, will cure heart disease, cough, and irregular fever. (GarP 1.177.42)

O Bull-bannered Lord, for all medicinal herbs used as decoctions, one should take exactly half a karṣa; however, O Vṛṣabhadhvaja, the specific dosage should be understood according to the patient's age.
Milk drunk together with the juice of cow dung,
as well as the juice of *kākajaṅghā*, will destroy irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*).
Milk boiled with ginger (maśuṇṭhi) may arise as a fever-curer for a woman;
likewise, liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka), musta, rock salt (saindhava), and the fruit of bṛhatī [are effective].
O Śiva, by giving these things, as well as by the gift of a horse, a man shall obtain sleep;
likewise, O Śiva, sleep shall come through the gift of pepper, a lamp, and a tethering post for a horse.
The root of *kākajaṅghā*, when placed on the head, induces sleep;
likewise, oil prepared with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and resin (*sarjarasa*) is effective.
Combined with cold water, this ointment destroys feverish heat;
likewise, it removes the burning sensation born from blood-fever and inflammation.
Śṛka-śaivāla-mantha, śuṇṭhī, pāpāṇabheda, śauvāñjana, gokṣura, or indeed varuṇacchanna; GarP_1,177.49.
Having given the root of *Saubhāñjana* and water boiled with these,
along with *hiṅgu* and barley-alkali, when drunk, it destroys wind disorders (*vāta*).
O Śiva, long pepper, long pepper root, and likewise marking-nut—
water boiled with these, when drunk, acts as a supreme remover of colic.
Ant-hill earth prepared with the roots of *aśvagandhā* and *kā* [i.e., *kākajaṅghā*],
O Rudra— by rubbing with this, *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs) is pacified.
The root of bṛhatī, indeed, when ground with water and drunk,
certainly causes the breaking up of obstructed wind (saṃghātavāta).
The root of fresh *tagara* taken with buttermilk will indeed destroy *jhiñjinīvāta*,
just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
The consumption of *asthisaṃhāra* with a single meal,
or even with meat broth, cures wind disorders and heals fractured bones.
Coated with ghee, dried, and combined with goat's milk;
by applying this [ointment] to the feet, one would destroy [the enemy], and there should be no doubt in this matter.

By applying a plaster of honey, clarified butter, rock salt, beeswax, molasses, red ochre, bdellium, and resin (sarjarasa), along with the cracked [parts], there is purification of the *kloma*. (GarP 1,177.57)
O Bull-bannered Lord, a foot smeared with pungent oil and heated over a smokeless fire, when rubbed with clay, becomes level.
Sal resin, beeswax, cumin, and myrobalan—
an ointment of clarified butter processed with these indeed removes the pain of burns from fire.
Sesame oil heated by fire, combined with barley ash,
will destroy a burn wound when applied as an ointment many times.
Buffalo butter, burnt sesame seeds ground with flour, and *bhallātaka*—
by means of nasal drops and external application, these destroy wounds and pain in the heart.
O Hara, O Śaṅkara, O Bull-bannered Lord, a wound caused by a weapon has been filled with camphor, cow’s milk, and ghee,
and it has been bound with a white-colored bandage;
yet it still touches upon suppuration and pain.
The wound from the sword-stroke was filled with the very sap of its root;
healed by the application of the two [medicines] and filled with clarified butter, it became free of scars.
The roots of śarapuṅkhā, lajjālukā, and pāṭhā,
ground with water and applied as a paste, cause wounds inflicted by weapons to subside.
The root of *kākajaṅghā*, dried for exactly three nights,
indeed destroys suppuration, putrefaction, and pain in a wound when applied with *rohita*.
Sesame oil mixed with water and the root of the *apāmārga* plant— by the application of its sprinkling,
the pain arising from a blow shall perish.
O Śaṅkara, by grinding together harītakī, rock salt, and ginger with water and consuming them,
indigestion is indeed destroyed.
The root of the nimba tree tied around the waist will cure pain in the eyes;
the root of the śaṇa plant, burnt together with betel, removes [pain] in the penis.
Haridrā steamed with rice, white mustard root, and the seeds of the citron— this ointment made from these ingredients in equal parts,
when applied for seven nights, will produce a beautiful body.
O Bull-bannered Lord, by administering a nasal drop (*nasya*) made from the leaf of white *aparājitā* with the juice of *nimba* leaves,
or with the essence of honey, there shall be liberation from *ḍākinīs*, the Mothers, and *brahmarākṣasas*.
The root of white jayantī, collected under the Puṣya asterism,
along with the roots of white aparājitā, arka, and citraka—
having made a pill from these, a woman becomes subjugated by means of a forehead mark (tilaka).
O Rudra, one should know that equal parts of long pepper, iron powder, ginger, and emblic myrobalan, along with rock salt and honey-sugar, [constitute this formulation].

By eating [the substance] for seven days in portions the size of an udumbara fruit, a man shall become strong and live for two hundred years. "Oṃ ṭha ṭha ṭha"—when employed in all rites for subjugation, this mantra fulfills all desires. (GarP 1,177.73)
Having collected it, O Śaṅkara, the wise man should burn that dwelling of the crow; the ashes from the funeral pyre, when placed upon the head of the enemy, [bring him ruin].
O Rudra, listen to that supreme yoga which causes him to be expelled:
indeed, one should cast excrement onto the skin of a wild rat.
Having smeared the name of the person [targeted] with the blood of a black crow, one should indeed cause the obstruction of their excrement by tying it to a thread fastened around the waist.
Then, O Hara, having been cast into the very center of a withered lotus petal,
both that woman and that man are devoured by flocks of crows.
Sugar, honey, ghee, milk, sesame, and *gokṣuraka* in equal parts—
O Rudra, that shall destroy the enemy;
O Hara, this is the rite of eradication.
If one offers a hundred oblations of the wood of the owl, the black crow, and the *bilva* tree,
mixed with blood, while reciting the names of two individuals,
a great enmity will arise between them; of this there is no doubt.

The flesh of a Rohita fish, processed with bear’s milk, is prepared into an oil; by its massage, diseases are dispelled. Furthermore, by the application of sandalwood water as a nasal drop (nasya), the regrowth of hair occurs.
If that man takes the root of the *lāṅgalikā* plant in his hand and applies it as an ointment to his body, he dispels the pride of old age.
O Śiva, O Lord, one may extract the life-force even from blazing serpents dwelling in their holes by means of peacock blood alone.
Indeed, the body of a serpent or a python, when burnt in a funeral pyre, has its ashes cast before one's enemies; this shall cause their defeat.
By this mantra, that [substance] is thrown, causing great destruction for the enemy:
*oṃ ṭha ṭha ṭha cāhīhicāhīhi svāhā / oṃ udaraṃ pāhihi pāhihi svāhā*. (GarP 1,177.84)
If the impurity from Sudarśanā is collected under the Puṣya asterism and cast into the middle of the house, serpents will avoid it.
O Śiva, a wick made from the root of the *arka* plant, ignited by the sun-fire (*arkāgni*) and combined with mustard oil,
destroys the snakes of the path.
Cat flesh, excrement, and yellow orpiment,
processed with goat urine— when smeared with this, a mouse will drive away other mice.
O Rudra, one who has been liberated in the temple [attains this]; there is no need for deliberation here. [One should offer] fruitless *arjuna* flowers, *bhallātaka*, and *śirīṣa*. (GarP 1.177.88)
Lac, resin of the Sarja tree, Viḍaṅga, and Guggulu—
incense made from these is a destroyer of flies and mosquitoes.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of Eye-Collyrium and Other Remedies," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
Hari said: The *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—178.
Hari said:
One should give *brahmadaṇḍī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *priyaṅgu*, and *nāgakeśara* combined with betel leaf to women while reciting this mantra; thus they come under one's control:
*oṃ nārāyaṇyai svāhā*. (GarP 1.178.1)
He to whom betel is given shall become submissive through this excellent mantra:
Oṃ hariḥ hariḥ svāhā. (GarP 1.178.2)
Godanta and yellow orpiment, combined with *kākajihvā* and reduced to powder, should be applied to the head of whomever one desires; that person shall become submissive.
White mustard seeds and the remains of an offering (*nirmālya*) cause the destruction of whatever is in the house.
If the root of the *vaibhītaka* or the *śākhoṭaka* tree, joined with its leaf,
is placed at the door of a house, there will certainly be quarreling therein.
One should grind the flesh of a wagtail together with honey;
by smearing it on the womb during the period of menstruation, a man shall become a slave.
Having fumigated with agallochum, guggulu, and blue lotus combined with jaggery, one will become beloved at the king’s gate.
One who sees with a tilaka made from the root of the *śvetāparājitā* ground together with *rocanā* shall bring even those in the royal palace under one's control.
Kākajaṅghā, vacā, kuṣṭha, nimba leaves, and saffron,
combined with one's own blood, cause a man to become submissive.

Having taken the auspicious blood of a wild cat, one should steep it in *karañja* oil; then, over a fire of *rudrākṣa* wood, one should cause soot to fall using a lotus leaf. From that collyrium, one becomes invisible.
Oṃ, homage to the wielder of the sword and vajra, the great general of the yakṣa army, svāhā!
Oṃ rudraṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, the swift vidyā of the excellent spear! Oṃ, O Mothers, paralyze [them], svāhā!
Having recited this knowledge-mantra, which wards off thieves, one thousand times,
the root of the mahāsugandhika plant, when placed upon the waist, will cause semen to be immobilized.
Oṃ, homage to all sentient beings! Homage! Grant success, grant success! Svāhā!
Having consecrated a *karavīra* flower seven times with this mantra, one should wave it before women; in an instant, she will indeed come under one's control.
One should grind brahmadaṇḍī, vacā, and leaves together with honey;
by anointing her limbs with this, a woman desires no other husband.
The crest of the *brahmadaṇḍī* plant thrown into the mouth causes the immobilization of semen;
the root of *jayantī* held in the mouth bestows victory in legal disputes.
The root of *bhṛṅgarāja*, ground and mixed with semen,
will surely bring a man under one's control once it has been used as an ointment for the eyes.
One should offer the Aparājitā flower together with a blue lotus along with betel-leaf;
this is the supreme means of subjugation.
On the big toe, the foot, the ankle, the knee, and likewise the hip;
on the navel, the chest, the belly, the armpit, the throat, and the cheek.
The crescent moons are situated on the lips, the eyes, the forehead, and the head;
in women they are located above during the bright fortnight and below during the dark fortnight, while in men they are situated in the reverse order.
O Rudra, on the left side and the right side, respectively,
the sixty-four arts (*kalā*) that cause melting and so forth are proclaimed in the *Kāmaśāstra* as the means of subjugating women;
through embracing and other such acts, they bring young women under control.
With a forehead mark (*tilaka*) made of *rocanā*, *gandhapuṣpa*, *nimba* flowers, *priyaṅgu*,
saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and sandalwood (*candana*), one shall bring the world under one's control.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Goddess Gaurī, grant me good fortune, sons, mastery, and so forth.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Goddess Lakṣmī, [grant] all good fortune that enchants the three worlds.
O Rudra, by the application of a paste of fragrant turmeric and saffron,
as well as incense and sweet-smelling flowers, one shall bring others under control.
Dūrvā grass, vacā, kuṣṭha, saffron, and śatāvarī,
combined with sesame oil and applied as a paste to the vagina, make a man submissive.
O Rudra, if a woman fumigates her vulva with the smoke of neem wood, she will become fortunate; even a slave shall become her husband.
Buffalo butter, lac, liquorice,
and saubhāgya— by smearing these on the vulva, one gains good fortune, and likewise, the husband becomes a slave.
Licorice, cow’s milk, and likewise thorny milkweed—
these should be taken in equal parts with warm water;
when reduced to one-fourth, this brings about the excellent conception of a fetus.
One should soak the seeds of the citron (mātuluṅga) with milk;
by drinking that, one obtains a fetus—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
One desiring a son should cause [the woman] to drink the seeds of the *mātuluṅga* and the roots of the *eraṇḍaka* combined with clarified butter.
Paśvagandhā boiled in the milk of a dead animal produces urine.
One should grind the seeds of the palāśa tree with honey;
if a woman in her menses drinks this, she will be freed from menstrual flow and pregnancy.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 179— Hari said:
Having boiled yellow orpiment, barley-alkali, patrāṅga, red sandalwood, nutmeg,
vermilion, and lac, one should smear the teeth with it.
Having cleansed the teeth with a decoction of *harītakī*, one should apply an ointment;
O Rudra, there is no doubt that the teeth of a man will become red or white.
One should boil radish roots over a mild fire and fill the ears with its juice;
by filling the ears with this, ear discharge is destroyed.
Having taken an arka leaf, one should warm it slowly over a mild fire;
having squeezed it, one should fill the ears with the juice, and the earache will be destroyed.
One should cook oil with *priyaṅgu*, *madhuka*, *dhātakī*, rows of *utpala*,
*mañjiṣṭhā*, *lodhra*, *lākṣā*, and the fresh juice of *kapittha*;
by filling [the vagina] with it, the discharge of women will be destroyed.

The alkali of dried radish and ginger, asafoetida, great medicinal root (musta), white flowered leadwort (saptaparṇa), sweet flag (vacā), costus, deodar, drumstick tree, and rasāñjana; GarP_1,179.6 //
Sauvarcala salt, barley-alkali, as well as sarjaka and rock salt,
likewise granthi, viḍa salt, and musta— these, mixed with honey, [should be used] in a fourfold proportion.

Likewise, the juice of the citron and the juice of the plantain, when combined with those [other ingredients] and cooked in oil, will quickly remove discharges and the like; of this there is no doubt.
By filling the ears with pungent oil (kaṭutaila), the destruction of worms occurs;
likewise for turmeric, nimba leaves, long pepper, and black pepper.
O Hara, grind together viḍaṅga, bhadramusta, and as the seventh, viśvabheṣaja,
with cow’s urine and form them into pills;
one pill cures indigestion, while two remove cholera.
Patola taken with honey, or likewise with cow’s urine, destroys eye disease; this "Śaṅkarī" wick also cures all ailments of the eyes.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 180,
Hari said:
