One should powder together equal parts of vacā, māṃsī, bilva, tagara, padmakesara, nāgapuṣpa, and priyaṅgu;
a mortal who is fumigated with this may roam the earth like a god of love.
One should combine camphor and devadāru with honey; by applying that very mixture as an ointment to the penis, one shall indeed bring a woman under one's control.
During sexual intercourse, a man should restrain his own organ;
he should smear the left hand of the woman with the [substance] from his left hand.
Once smeared, the woman comes under his control and desires no other man.
Oṃ, O Raktacāmuṇḍā, bring such-and-such a person under my control, bring them! Oṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hraḥ phaṭ.
Having recited this mantra ten thousand times, O Śaṅkara, one will become a subduer by means of a tilaka made with yellow orpiment mixed with one's own blood. (GarP 1.180.4)
Saindhava salt, black salt, sauvīra salt, fish gall,
honey, ghee, and sugar— by applying this to the vulva of women, [they become fragrant].
The man who engages in sexual intercourse [with his wife] and will not go to another woman [should take] Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Vacā, Māṃsī, Somarājī, and Phalgu.
Having made buffalo butter into a paste, the best of physicians should grind it together with the roots and leaves [of the aforementioned plants] using milk and clarified butter.
Having purified a pill, one should insert it into a woman's womb;
even if she has given birth ten times, she will become a virgin again.
Mustard seeds, *vacā*, and the fruits of the *madana* tree, along with cat dung and *dhattūra*, combined with a woman's hair; [GarP_1,180.9]
This incense removes quartan fever and destroys the fevers of ḍākinīs;
it consists of arjuna flowers, bhallātaka, and viḍaṅga.
A fumigation made from *balā*, resin (*sarjarasa*), *sauvīra* salt,
and mustard seeds destroys mosquitoes, as well as snakes, lice, and flies.
From the powder of *bhūtalā* and by filling the vagina with it, there shall be a paralysis;
furthermore, from smearing it upon the vagina, a stiffening of the vulva occurs.
Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 181— Hari said:
Betel leaf, ghee, honey, and salt, when combined with milk in a copper vessel,
are an excellent remedy for removing pain in the eyes.

One should lick a mixture of *harītakī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*), soaked in honey and ghee, for cough, asthma, and hiccups. (GarP 1.181.2)
A person should lick the powder of pippalī and triphalā with honey;
thus, chronic catarrh, cough, and even the most severe dyspnea are destroyed.
O Bull-bannered One, one should lick the ash of *samūla-citraka* mixed with the powder of *pippalī*, combined with honey, to cure asthma, cough, and hiccup.
Blue lotus, sugar, madhuka, and padmaka in equal parts,
mixed with rice-water, will alleviate disorders of blood.
Ginger, sugar,
and honey combined together form a pill that grants a voice like that of a cuckoo immediately upon consumption.
Having rubbed with this substance— yellow orpiment, conch powder, and the ash of plantain leaves—
this is the best method for removing body hair.
Salt, yellow orpiment, and the fruits of the *tumbinī*,
combined with lac resin, is an excellent means for removing body hair.
One should grind together lime, yellow orpiment, conch-shell ash, realgar,
and rock salt with goat’s urine.
At that very moment, from the mere application [of this], the removal of body hair is excellent.
[The ingredients are] conch-shell, *āmalaka*, *patra*, and the flowers of *dhātakī*.
Having ground that [substance] together with milk, one should hold it in the mouth for seven days;
the teeth will become glossy, white, and of stainless luster.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 182— Hari said:
Curd is generally forbidden during autumn, summer, and spring;
however, curd is praised in winter, the cool season, and the rainy season.
If sugar is drunk with fresh butter after a meal, it produces intelligence.
O Hara, a man who should eat one *pala* of old jaggery will become endowed with strength and be able to unite with a thousand women.
Having powdered kuṣṭha and combined it with ghee and honey, one should consume it at the time of sleep; this destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
O Śaṅkara, having made a powder of Atasī, Māṣa, and Godhūma,
a wise man should smear his body with Pippalī and ghee;
thus he becomes like Kandarpa himself for all eternity.
Having eaten a preparation made of barley, sesame, *aśvagandhā*, *muśalī*, *saralā*,
and jaggery, a young man shall become strong.
By drinking asafoetida, black salt, and dry ginger with boiled water,
the colic known as *pariṇāma-śūla* and indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) are destroyed.
One should grind dhātakī and somarājī together with milk;
by this, one who is weak shall become stout—of this there is no doubt.
A strong person should lick fresh butter mixed with sugar and honey;
by subsisting on milk, one suffering from consumption shall attain nourishment and incomparable intelligence.
Crushed crab mixed with milk, when drunk, cures consumption and fever;
likewise, *bhallātaka*, *viḍaṅga*, alkali of barley, and rock salt [have this effect].
Realgar and conch powder, likewise cooked in oil, certainly causes the hair to fall out; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having taken the juice of the mālūra fruit, one should grind a leech in it;
by smearing the hands with this, there is an excellent suppression of fire.
Having taken the juice of the *śālmalī* tree and placed it in donkey urine, one should scatter it at the beginning of the fire; for by this, the supreme quelling of fire is achieved.
Taking the belly of a female crane together with the fat of a frog, one should have a pill made from it; then the wise man should cast it into the fire.
By the application of this method, there is indeed the supreme suppression of fire.
Having chewed muṇḍī bark, vacā, musta, marica, and likewise tagara,
one should immediately lick fire with the tongue.
Having powdered *gorocanā* and *bhṛṅgarāja* in equal parts with clarified butter, there will indeed be the stopping of divine waters by means of this mantra:
*Oṃ agnistambhanaṃ kuru kuru*. (GarP 1,182.15)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One! Paralyze the water! Saṃ saṃ saṃ! Ke-ka ke-kaḥ! Caracara!
This is the mantra for paralyzing water; O Śiva, it paralyzes the water.
If one buries a vulture bone, a cow bone,
or likewise a discarded flower offering at the door of an enemy, that person shall meet his death.
One should apply five red flowers of distinct species,
combined with saffron and endowed with one's own blood.
O Rudra, having ground one pala of yellow pigment (rocanā) together with a flower, this mark (tilaka) applied by a woman or a man brings about subjugation.
Brahmadaṇḍī under the Puṣya asterism, when consumed in food or drink, brings about subjugation;
one should drink warm water boiled with one pala of Yaṣṭimadhu.
O Maheśvara, this mantra— *oṃ hrūṃ jaḥ*— indeed removes constipation and heartache;
O Rudra, it destroys [all ailments].
The poison produced by all scorpions.
Long pepper, fresh butter, ginger, rock salt, black pepper, curd, and costus, when used as a nasal drop or taken by mouth, will remove poison. (GarP 1.182.22)
O Śiva, by drinking and applying as an ointment this mixture of triphalā, fresh ginger, kuṣṭha, and sandalwood combined with ghee, there shall be destruction of poison.
The eyes of a pigeon, yellow orpiment, and realgar—
by the application of these, one destroys poison as Vainateya destroys serpents.
O Bull-bannered One, this application of rock salt and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), combined with curd, honey, and clarified butter,
destroys the poison of a scorpion.
O Rudra, having boiled *brahmadaṇḍī* and sesame seeds, one should drink the powder of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*); this destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and obstructed blood.

Having drunk milk mixed with honey, one should stop the discharge of blood; one should also smear the vulva and the navel with the root of *āṭarūpaka*. A woman will give birth easily; there is no need for doubt in this matter. (GarP 1.182.27)
O Bull-bannered One, by drinking sugar mixed with honey along with rice-water, the pacification of bloody diarrhea occurs.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—183. Hari said:
O Lord whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, by drinking a decoction of black pepper, ginger, and the bark of *kuṭaja*, *grahaṇī* disease shall be destroyed.
One should grind long pepper, the root of long pepper, black pepper, tagara, vacā,
the resin of devadāru, and pāṭhā together with milk.
By this very application, dysentery is indeed destroyed;
an ointment made from long pepper and sesame flowers removes jaundice.
Harītakī combined with an equal amount of jaggery and mixed with honey,
O Rudra, acts as a purgative;
of this there is no doubt.
Triphalā, citraka, citra, and likewise kaṭukarohiṇī—
this indeed is an excellent purgative that removes ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
One should boil *harītakī*, *śṛṅgavera*, *devadāru*, and *candana* with goat’s milk, along with the root of *apāmārga*;
or by using *jayantī*, one shall destroy *ūrustambha* within seven nights.

One should have fine powders made from ananta-śṛṅgavera; by using pills composed of guggulu and an equal amount of jaggery, one destroys wind disorders, those located in the tendons, and even sluggish digestion.
Having extracted the *saṅkhapuṣpī* flower along with its leaves and root, one should drink it with goat’s milk to remove epilepsy. *GarP_1,183.8*
One should drink aśvagandhā and abhayā together with water;
blood-bile (raktapitta) shall be destroyed—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Having made a powder of *harītakī* and *kuṣṭha*, one should fill the mouth with it;
then, by drinking cold water, all vomiting is prevented.

Guduchi, padmaka, arishta, dhanyaka, and red sandalwood destroy fever caused by pitta and kapha, vomiting, burning sensations, and thirst, and they stimulate the digestive fire. Om Hum Namaḥ. (GarP 1.183.11)
Having bound *śaṅkhapuṣpī* to the ears, one shall indeed remove fever with this mantra:
*oṃ jambhinī stambhinī mohaya sarvavyādhīn me vajreṇa ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ sarvavyādhīn me vajreṇa phaṭ*. Thus. (GarP 1,183.12)
Having recited [the mantra] over eight hundred flowers and placed them in his hand, he should touch the fingernail; O Rudra, this cures quartan fever as well as other fevers.
Jambū fruit, turmeric, and the slough of a snake—
this incense cures all fevers and also [removes] the quartan fever.
One should cook oil with *karavīra*, *bhṛṅgapatra*, salt, *kuṣṭha*, and *karkaṭa* along with four times as much urine;
when applied as an ointment, it indeed removes scabies, eczema, leprosy, and ulcers.
O Rudra, by drinking long pepper with honey, as well as by eating sweet food and by consuming surana, the spleen disease is destroyed.
One should insert long pepper and turmeric combined with cow’s urine into the opening of the anus; this will eliminate hemorrhoids.
Goat’s milk and ginger, when drunk together, destroy splenomegaly and other ailments;
likewise do rock salt, viḍaṅga, somarājī, and mustard seeds.
One should grind the two types of *rajanī* and poison with cow’s urine;
by applying that as an ointment with *nimba* leaves and so forth, leprosy is destroyed.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 184— Hari said:
An ointment of *rajani*, plantain, and alkali destroys *sidhma*.
Likewise, one part of *kuṣṭha* and two parts of *pathyā*,
when well-ground with warm water, destroy pain in the waist.
Haritaki, fresh butter, sugar, and long pepper, when taken together, will remove the discoloration of the eyes; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
One should cook ghee with the leaf of the *āṭarūṣaka* over a gentle fire;
having then made it into a powder, this ointment is supreme for removing the disease of hemorrhoids.

Having drunk guggulu combined with the three myrobalans (triphalā), fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) shall be destroyed. One should likewise cook a decoction of cumin (ajājī) and ginger (śṛṅgavera) with whey (maṇḍa). GarP_1,184.4 //
Yavakṣāra combined with salt destroys dysuria;
likewise, sugar also acts as a destroyer of dysuria.
The fire from a funeral pyre, the excrement of a wagtail, the froth of a horse, and *saubhāñjana* as a collyrium for the eyes— when a man is fumigated with these,
O Śiva, he becomes invisible even to all the gods, let alone to human beings.
Having burned sesame seeds and barley, one should make them into soot and apply it;
together with that very oil, one who has been burnt by fire will become well.
An ointment made from *lajjālu* and *śarapuṅkhā*, mixed with clarified butter, destroys fire.
Oṃ namo bhagavate ṭha ṭha chindhi chindhi jvalanaṃ prajvalitaṃ nāśaya nāśaya huṃ phaṭ. (GarP 1,184.8)
The root of *nirguṇḍī* tied to the hand quickly removes fever;
likewise, having cut the root of white *guñjā* into seven pieces [and tying them], [the same result follows].
By tying it in the hand, one destroys hemorrhoids without a doubt;
with Viṣṇukrāntā and goat's urine, there is protection against thieves, tigers, and the like.
One should perform all the rites using the roots of *brahmadaṇḍī*;
indeed, the powder of *triphalā* taken with clarified butter is a destroyer of leprosy.
Clarified butter prepared with *punarnavā*, *bilva*, and *pippalī*,
when drunk, removes *hikkā*, asthma, and cough, and for women, it promotes conception.
Or one may eat the seed of the *narī* plant cooked with milk and clarified butter, combined with ghee and sugar; from that, semen shall become inexhaustible.
Viḍaṅga, madhuka, pāṭhā, māṃsī, sarjarasa,
as well as rāsnā, triphalā, apāmārga, and manaḥśilā.
One should grind *udumbara* and *dhātakī* with sesame oil and smear it upon the female organ and the male organ; thus, the man and woman will become mutually fond of one another.
"Salutations to you, O Lord, the Giver of Boons! O Attractor, O Attractress, O Enchanting One, svāhā!"—with this [mantra], O Śaṅkara, one should then smear the linga with oil from the womb.
Punarnavā, amṛtā, dūrvā, kanaka, and aindravāruṇī—
their juices should be rubbed together with the juice of jasmine seeds.
Having placed the mercury in the middle of a crucible, its killing (māraṇa) is proclaimed;
milk combined with honey and clarified butter destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
Honey, clarified butter, jaggery, copper, and the juice of *kāravella*—from heating these together, silver is produced; now hear the method for making gold.
One should wear the yellow *dhārtarūṣa* flower and one *pala* of lead;
and from the branch of the *lāṅgalikā*, gold shall arise through fire.
By lighting a lamp with oil from *dhattūra* seeds,
one who is seated in meditative absorption will not be seen by anyone standing in the sky.
Just as a frog is naturally drawn to a clay bull,
so too one who is joined with the limbs of Śaṅkara sniffs the incense and roars;
he indeed displays wonder like a bull— of this there is no doubt.
And at night, with mustard oil and the insect known as a firefly,
a lamp ignited from these two blazes like a mass of flames from the mouth of Agni.
O Rudra, having burned the powder of a muskrat, one should apply it as an ointment;
if one applies it correctly, the victim is instantly consumed by fire.
Liberation occurs through sandalwood; by drinking it or applying it as an ointment, one becomes happy.
If one personally anoints the eyes with the ichor of an elephant in rut,
one will be victorious in battle and shall become a great hero.
Having indeed seized the fangs of a water-snake, one should cast them into the mouth [of the victim];
then he remains within the water without hesitation, just as if on dry land.
One should combine together the eyes and fangs of a crocodile, as well as bones and blood, along with fat and oil; having smeared oneself with that,
one should remain in water for three days.
The eyes of a crocodile, the heart of a tortoise,
the fat and bones of a mouse, and likewise the fat of a porpoise—
by applying these together as an ointment, one may remain in water as if in a house.
Iron powder drunk with buttermilk becomes a remedy for jaundice;
likewise, the root of *taṇḍulīyaka* and *gokṣūra*, drunk with milk, [has the same effect].
The root of the *jātī* plant, taken with buttermilk, removes diseases of the mouth when it is yellowish;
likewise, the root of the *kola* plant cures indigestion.
Satakra, kuśa grass, or even the root of markaṭī,
or indeed the root of vākucī with sour gruel (kāñjika), cures dental diseases.
Likewise, O Śiva, the root of indravāruṇī drunk with water removes poison and the like; or, by drinking the root of surabhikā, that [poison] shall be destroyed.
Powdered *guñjā* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), or *balā*, *atibalā*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and sugar combined with honey, when applied as a paste, removes diseases of the head.
When drunk, it causes a barren woman to conceive; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
[One should take] the root of white Aparājitā combined with Pippalī and Śuṇṭhikā. (GarP 1.184.34)
When ground into a paste, it destroys headache when applied as a head-ointment;
by drinking the top shoots of *nirguṇḍikā*, one shall destroy *gaṇḍamālā*.
One should eat the alkali derived from *ketakī* leaves together with jaggery;
or, having drunk *śarapuṅkhā* with buttermilk, one shall destroy the spleen disease.
The resin of the *mātulaṅga* (citron), combined with jaggery and clarified butter,
truly destroys pains born of wind and bile when used as a drink.
Ginger, black salt, and asafoetida, when drunk, remove heart disease.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter in the section on medical science within the Ācārakāṇḍa, in the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—185. Hari said:
"Āṃ gaṇapataye"—this is the mantra of Gaṇapati, which bestows wealth and knowledge.
Having recited this eight-thousand-verse [text] and then bound his topknot, one will achieve victory in legal disputes; by reciting it a hundred times, one becomes dear to people.
O Rudra, one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of black sesame seeds smeared with ghee; within three days, the king will become submissive.
Having fasted on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days and having worshipped Vighnarāja,
one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains one thousand and eight times;
he shall remain unconquered in battle, and all shall serve him.
Having recited it eight thousand times, and then indeed eight hundred times, one should bind the topknot; thus there will be victory in the royal court and in legal disputes.
Any man who, at the time of dawn, places the syllable *hrīṃ* together with the *visarga* on the foreheads of women, certainly brings them under his control.

Having placed [the mantra] in the abode of the woman with a well-concentrated mind, one should make the passionate woman full of longing; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. GarP_1,185.7 //
Whoever, being pure and with a restrained mind, performs ten thousand oblations,
women will always come under his control at the mere sight of him.
When a tilaka is made with realgar, patraka, gorocana,
and saffron, women come under one's control.
By making a forehead mark (tilaka) with bhrṅgarāja, sahadevā, vacā, and white aparājitā, one may bring the three worlds under one's control.
A man who makes a tilaka mark with a wick-candle prepared from both gorocanā and fish gall,
using his left little finger,
brings the entire three worlds under his control; of this there is no doubt.
O Mahādeva, gorocanā is infused with the blood of the *dhātus*;
having made a tilaka with these, whatever man she gazes upon—
At that very moment, one should bring him under control; there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
Nāgeśvara, śaileya, cinnamon bark, leaf-mace, and harītakī; sandalwood, kuṣṭha, sūkṣmailā, and red śāli rice combined together.
O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, beloved of Pārvatī, this incense, which acts as a subduer through the arrows of Smara, destroys the afflictions of love at the time of sexual union.
A man who, having taken his own semen with his left hand,
anoints the left foot of a passionate woman, shall become dear to her.
O Mahādeva, by smearing the liṅga with rock salt, pigeon excrement, and honey, one will indeed become the subduer of women.
Taking any five red flowers whatsoever,
one should grind them together with an equal amount of *priyaṅgu* in a single mixture. By smearing this upon the *liṅga*, a woman shall come under one's control.
Hayagandhā, mañjiṣṭhā, mālatī flowers,
and white mustard— by being smeared with these, one becomes dear to women.
The root of *kākajaṅghā*, when drunk with milk, cures consumption.
For one who consumes *aśvagandhā*, *nāgabalā*, jaggery, and black gram,
his form becomes like that of those moving in the prime of youth.
O Rudra, either iron powder combined with the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā), or the powder of the three myrobalans alone, when consumed with honey, cures the pain known as pariṇāma-śūla.

O Śiva, drinking boiled water mixed with the alkaline ash of a snail, as well as deer-horn burnt by fire combined with cow's clarified butter, when drunk, brings about the destruction of pains in the heart and the back. GarP_1,185.21.
Asafoetida, black salt, ginger, and the great medicine (mustard) of Śiva—
water boiled with these, when drunk, indeed removes all types of colic.
The root of the *apāmārga* plant, combined with sea salt and taken as a relish,
shall be a remedy for colic caused by indigestion.
O Rudra, O Śaṅkara, the sprout of a banyan tree rubbed with rice-water and drunk with *takra* brings about the destruction of diarrhea.
O Lord of Beings, half a karṣa of aṅkoṭa root ground with rice-water, when drunk, cures all types of diarrhea and dysentery.
Powdered long pepper, ginger, and *kuṭaja* bark, combined with jaggery and drunk in gradually doubling doses, destroys the disease of *grahaṇī*. (GarP 1.185.26)
O Śiva, a pill made from the root of white Aparājitā, turmeric, beeswax, rice, Apāmārga,
and Trikaṭu certainly destroys the great disease of cholera; of this there is no doubt.
O Śaṅkara, the powder of each of these— triphalā, aguru, bhūteśa, śilājatu, and harītakī— when mixed with honey and drunk, brings all types of urinary disorders (meha) to an end.
One *prastha* of *arka* (calotropis) milk, and likewise one *prastha* of sesame oil;
one *pala* each of realgar, black pepper, and vermilion.
Having made it into a powder, one should then dry it in the heat of the sun in a copper vessel;
when drunk with the milk of the *snuhī* plant and rock salt (*saindhava*), it shall alleviate colic.
Trikaṭu, triphalā, and black sesame oil at night, as well as realgar,
neem leaves, jasmine flowers, and goat’s milk.
Then one should grind that urine with conch-shell and sandalwood;
having made a wick from these, one should then apply it as collyrium to the eyes.
The film of the eye, cataracts, ophthalmia, and disorders such as *timira* are destroyed;
indeed, the powder of *vibhītaka* with honey is a destroyer of asthma.
The powder of long pepper and the three myrobalans, combined with honey and rock salt, cures all diseases, fever, asthma, consumption, chronic catarrh, and heart ailments. (GarP 1.185.34)
One should indeed saturate the powder of *devadāru* twenty-one times with goat’s urine; one should then apply it as an ointment to the eyes.
By this, night-blindness, cataracts, and even the absence of eyelashes shall be destroyed.
O Rudra, from the application of this collyrium made of pippalī, ketakī, haridrā, āmalaka,
and vacā mixed with milk, all eye diseases shall be destroyed.
O Śiva, O Hara, if the roots of *kākajaṅghā* and *śigru* are held in the mouth after chewing them,
the destruction of dental worms will surely occur.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Application of Mantras, Tantras, and Medicine," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Hari said:
The essence of *guḍūcī* drunk with honey cures urinary disorders (*prameha*).
Likewise, the root of *gohālikā* drunk combined with sesame, curd, and clarified butter [has the same effect].
O Śaṅkara, boiled *niruddhamūtra* brings back [the flow of urine];
likewise, when drunk with *sauvarcala* salt, it indeed removes hiccup.
O Rudra, the root of *gorakṣakarkaṭī* ground with cold water and drunk for only three days will destroy urinary gravel.
Having ground the root of *Mālatī* collected during the summer season and prepared it with goat’s milk mixed with sugar,
one will remove urinary obstruction and indeed cure jaundice and gravel.
The root of the *dvijayaṣṭi* plant ground with rice-water and applied as a plaster removes *gaṇḍamālā* and even the incurable *galagaṇḍa*.
By smearing with the powder of *rasāñjana* and *harītakī*, a person shall destroy diseases; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O Rudra, by applying a paste of the root of *karavīra* and a paste of *pūgaphala*, the disease of men is destroyed; I shall now tell you another yoga.
By applying a plaster of *dantī* root, *haridrā*, and *citraka*, hemorrhoids (*bhagaṇdara*) shall be destroyed; I shall now describe another formulation:
O Lord of Umā, for hemorrhoids whose blood has been sucked out by leeches.
If cat bone is rubbed with a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and applied as an ointment, then blood will not flow; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Haridrā, processed many times with the milky sap of Snuhī,
forms a pill that destroys hemorrhoids when applied as an ointment, O Bull-bannered Lord.
Ghoṣā fruit and rock salt, ground together, are a supreme remedy for hemorrhoids.
O Śiva, cow’s ghee prepared with three parts of water from the lye of *palāśa* wood,
when drunk along with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), destroys hemorrhoids.
The burnt fruit of the *bilva* tree destroys hemorrhoids caused by blood;
likewise, one may eat black sesame seeds mixed with fresh butter.
O Bull-bannered One, powdered ginger combined with barley-alkali and an equal amount of jaggery certainly increases the digestive fire when taken at dawn.
Water boiled with ginger, when drunk, indeed stimulates the digestive fire;
likewise, O Rudra, *harītakī*, rock salt, *citraka*, and long pepper [have this effect].
Their powder, when drunk with warm water, produces extreme hunger;
likewise, pork eaten with clarified butter also produces extreme hunger.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 187— Hari said:
O Śiva, one should grind the leaves of the *hastikarṇapalāśa* into powder;
this powder, freed from all diseases, [should be taken] in a quantity of one hundred palas.
O bull-bannered Rudra, by consuming it with milk for seven days,
a man shall become a possessor of the Vedas, possessing the gait and prowess of the king of beasts.
O Rudra, by constantly consuming milk, one becomes sixteen years of age, endowed with a lifespan of a thousand years, and possesses a complexion like that of a ruby.
Milk combined with honey and clarified butter bestows longevity;
when consumed together with honey, it grants a lifespan of ten thousand years.
It makes a man a retainer of sacred learning and beloved by women;
when eaten daily with curd, it becomes a maker of a body as firm as a diamond.
A man who has consumed that [mango], combined with *kāñjika* sour gruel, shall live for a thousand years, endowed with streaks of hair.
Honey processed with the three myrobalans (triphalā) indeed makes one's divine body free from wrinkles and grey hair for a hundred years, and bestows clear vision.
A blind man may indeed see by consuming this powder mixed with clarified butter;
when applied as an ointment combined with buffalo milk, it produces black hair.
O Bull-bannered One, even for one who is bald, hair grows back by means of a powder mixed with oil; it destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
By merely rubbing it on, one is liberated from all passion;
by applying collyrium made from goat's milk and powder for a month, one gains divine vision.
Having taken the seeds of the *palāśa* tree in the month of Śrāvaṇa and freed them from their husks,
one should consume their powder with fresh butter.
Having bowed to the Lord Hari, one should daily consume half a *karṣa* of each of the sixty types of grains from the Purāṇa, while drinking wholesome water; O Hara,
such a person shall live for thousands of years, free from wrinkles and grey hair.
Having collected the root of Bhṛṅgarāja under the Puṣya asterism,
one should prepare its powder and consume it with Sauvīra.
By practicing this for only one month, a man becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair;
he shall live for five hundred years and possess the strength of an elephant.
O Rudra, by consuming it under the asterism of Puṣya, he will become a possessor of the memory of the Vedas.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Yoga for Longevity," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: [Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇam—188] Hari said:

A wound shall become free of pus and, being devoid of infection, the blow shall be filled with healing; by rubbing the root of the *apāmārga* plant with both hands, its juice prevents the flow of blood from the blow when applied as a filling. (GarP 1,188.1)
O Rudra, the root of the lāṅgalikā plant and likewise that of the ikṣu-darbha;
when the opening of the wound is smeared with these,
O Śaṅkara, even a foreign object that has been embedded for a long time will emerge from the wound through that very path.
The root of *bālamūla* or the root of *meṣaśṛṅgī*, rubbed with water and applied as an ointment,
heals a chronic wound or sinus tract that has been present for a long time.
Eaten together with buffalo meat and kodrava grain,
the powder of *hiṅgu* root, when administered, removes sinus ulcers.
The fruit of the *brahmayaṣṭi* ground with water and smeared [on the body], or rubbed [over it] with that same [mixture], destroys blood disorders; of this there is no doubt.
Barley ash, viḍaṅga, and sulphur,
as well as the powder of these along with ginger, should be mixed with blood.
O Śiva, that which is smeared with the [excrement] of a chameleon destroys an abscess;
likewise, the seeds of *saubhāñjana* together with linseed and lampblack [effect the same].
O Śaṅkara, all these, including yellow mustard seeds,
ground with non-sour buttermilk, will indeed destroy *granthika*.
The root of white aparājitā ground with rice-water;
by administering it as a nasal drop (nasya), there shall be the dispersal of the host of bhūtas.
Anointment with Agastya flowers together with long pepper indeed removes colic.
O Śiva, a plaster made from snake-skin, asafoetida, nimba leaves, barley,
and white mustard seeds destroys malevolent spirits.
Gorocanā, marīca, pippalī, saindhava, honey,
and añjana— when prepared with these, O Śiva, it shall be a remover of grahas and bhūtas.
Incense made from guggulu and an owl's tail-feather will ward off the seizing spirits;
one who is afflicted by quartan fevers shall be freed from them when draped in black cloth.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wounds," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 189 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Hari said:
By filling the eyes with the juice of white *aparājitā* flowers, the cataract (*paṭala*) is destroyed; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O blue-and-red one, crusher of gods and asuras, by chewing the root of the *gokṣuraka* plant itself, the pain of dental caries shall be destroyed. *GarP_1,189.2*
If a woman, having fasted, drinks the root of the white *arka* plant with cow’s milk on the first day of her menses,
it cures her abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and colic.

A woman who has purified herself after her menses, having fastened a white *arka* flower— taken according to the prescribed rite and previously consecrated with mantras— around her waist, will give birth.
Take the root of either the *palāśa* or the *apāmārga* held in the hand;
it removes all fevers and drives away spirits, ghosts, and the like.
O Supreme Lord, the root of the scorpion-plant (vṛścikamūla), drunk in the morning with water that has stood overnight,
will destroy burning fever.
When this is tied upon the crest-lock, it shall ward off diseases lasting for a single day;
when drunk with water that has stood overnight, it shall remove all poisons.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever gives the root of the *lajjāluka* plant along with one's own semen enters into enmity; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever grinds the root of *pāṭhā* with cow’s ghee and drinks it, all poison shall be destroyed; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Just as one might [apply] the root of *śirīṣa* with water that has stood overnight, so too,
by filling the ears with the juice of the root of red *citraka*, the disease of jaundice (*kāmalā*) will be destroyed; there is no doubt about this.
The root of the white *kokilākṣa* plant, combined with goat’s milk and drunk for three weeks, will indeed bring about the destruction of the disease of consumption (*kṣayaroga*).
One should drink the flower of the coconut combined with goat’s milk;
by this, his threefold vāta of blood is destroyed.

One should take the root of the *sudarśana* plant, well-prepared with a garland, and bind it around the neck; this destroys the afflictions of the *tryāhika* and other fevers, as well as the influence of planets and spirits.
O Rudra, the flower and the very root of the white guñjā,
when placed in the mouth, shall remove many kinds of poison.
Bound on the hand, it wards off arrows; bound on the neck, it removes the afflictions of malevolent planets and the like.
Bound on the waist on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, O Nīlalohita, it takes away the fear of lions and other wild beasts.
O Lord of Beings, one should wear the root of *viṣṇukrāntā* tied to the ear with a silk thread;
indeed, there will be no fear of crocodiles or other such dangers.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—190. Hari said:
The root of Aparājitā combined with cow’s urine, when drunk, quickly removes scrofula; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord, O Rudra, the root of indravāruṇī drunk according to the prescribed rite,
combined with jiṅginī, eraṇḍa, and śūkaśimbī,
and administered with cold water, removes pain in the arms and neck.
Buffalo butter, *aśvagandhā*, long pepper, *vacā*, and the two types of *kuṣṭha*—this ointment removes pain from the penis, the channels, and the breasts. (GarP 1.190.3)
A paste made from the powder of *kuṣṭha* and *nāgabalā* combined with fresh butter, when applied,
will make the thighs and buttocks of young women beautiful and well-rounded.
If the root of *indravāruṇikā* is uprooted and cast from afar with the name of someone, that person’s spleen disease (*plīha*) will perish.
The root of white punarnavā, when drunk with rice-water, destroys abscesses; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
The alkali of plantain leaves prepared with water— by consuming it,
all diseases of the abdomen are destroyed.
Taking the root of the plantain tree and combining it with jaggery and clarified butter,
when cooked over a fire and consumed, it removes the worms residing in the stomach.
If one regularly consumes the powder of nimba leaves and āmalaka at dawn, his leprosy will be destroyed.
Harītakī, viḍaṅga, haridrā, white mustard seeds,
the roots of somarāja and karañja, and raudhava—
these, ground with cow’s urine, are indeed destroyers of the disease of leprosy.
One part of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and two parts of *śivā* (harītakī), along with the seeds of *somarāja*, when eaten with *pathyā* (harītakī), cure ringworm (*dadru*).
A decoction of *amlātaka* with cow’s urine, mixed with salt and rubbed in a bronze vessel until it becomes coarse,
destroys *kuṣṭha* and *dadru* when applied as an ointment.
Turmeric, yellow orpiment, dūrvā grass, cow’s urine, and rock salt—
this ointment destroys ringworm, scabies, and likewise artificial poison.

O Rudra, the seeds of Soma-rāja combined with fresh butter and tasted with honey indeed remove white leprosy; there is no need for hesitation regarding this when accompanied by a diet of buttermilk and rice. GarP_1,190.14
O Rudra, a paste made from the root of white aparājitā ground with its own water and applied for a month destroys white leprosy.
O Bull-bannered Lord, scabies and the disease called *durnāman* are destroyed by the application of buffalo butter, vermilion, and black pepper.
O Lord, the dried root of *gāmbhārī* boiled with milk and consumed destroys *śuklapitta*.
O Rudra, by rubbing the seeds of radish with the juice of apāmārga, a paste is formed; by that ointment, sidhma is destroyed.
Turmeric combined with the juice of plantain and sugarcane removes *sidhma* (leucoderma).
O Mahādeva, by anointing [the body] with the alkali of plantain and *apāmārga* mixed with castor oil, [the same result is achieved].
Sidyma is destroyed instantly.
Kūṣmāṇḍa, Nala, and alkali, along with cow’s urine in accordance with reality,
and turmeric ground with water, should be cooked over a gentle fire.
O Bull-bannered Lord, one should apply an ointment made by wrapping [the body] in buffalo dung to achieve the beauty of her limbs. (GarP 1.190.21)
By rubbing the body with a mixture of sesame, mustard, the two types of turmeric, and kuṣṭha, a man who was foul-smelling shall become fragrant. (GarP 1.190.22)
Manohara, daily [using] dūrvā grass, kākajaṅghā,
and the flowers of arjuna along with jambū leaves, as well as lodhra— this ointment will remove the foul odor of the body. (GarP 1.190.23)
A powder made from *lodhra* flowers and gold dust is appropriate;
for one whose body has been rubbed with this, the afflictions of summer shall not prevail.
Sprinkling with milk at dawn destroys the affliction caused by heat;
moreover, an ointment made from *kākajaṅghā* serves as a cosmetic for the body.
Licorice, sugar, the juice of vāsaka, and honey—
when drunk together, this cures hemorrhaging, jaundice, and anemia.
The juice of vāsaka mixed with honey, when drunk, removes *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders);
when water is drunk at dawn, it removes even severe *pīnasa* (nasal catarrh).
O Maheśvara, the powder of *bibhītaka*, *pippalī*, and rock salt, when drunk with *kāñjika* vinegar, destroys hoarseness of voice.
One should consume powdered āmalaka with cow's milk;
likewise, realgar, the root of balā, kola leaves, and guggulu [should be taken].
O Maheśvara, a wick made from these— namely, *jātipatra*, *kolapatra*, and realgar— and burned in a fire of *badarī* wood,
when used for smoking, removes cough; of this there is no doubt.
The powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and long pepper (pippalī), consumed with honey at the beginning of a meal, quickly removes thirst and fever when taken with honey.

Water boiled with the root of the *bilva* tree, honey, and *guḍūcī*, when drunk, removes the three types of vomiting; of this there is no doubt. *Dūrvā* grass ground with rice-water, when drunk, is a cure for vomiting.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—191. Hari said:
The root of punarnavā, gathered under the Puṣya asterism,
when its water is drunk, ensures that no serpents remain within one's dwellings.
O Bull-bannered One, he who wears an image of Tārkṣya fashioned from the teeth of a bear shall not be seen by serpents for as long as he lives.
O Rudra, he who drinks the root of the śalmali tree with water under the Puṣya asterism—there, the nāgas shall have their fangs removed; of this there is no doubt.

Under the Puṣya asterism, one should catch snakes by binding them with the root of the *lajjālukā* plant tied to the hand; or even by means of an ointment—there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
The root of the white *arka* tree, gathered under the Puṣya asterism, when drunk with cold water,
destroys the venom of biting insects as well as poison derived from the *karavīra* and other such sources.
The root of mahākāla ground with sour gruel (kāñjika) indeed removes the poison of voḍra and ḍuṇḍubha snakes when applied as a paste.
The root of *taṇḍulīyaka* ground with rice-water and drunk together with ghee removes all poisons.
The root of the blue water-moss (nīlīlajjālukā) ground with rice-water, when drunk, destroys the poison of that biting insect; this may be done either once or for both [the patient and the carrier].
The fresh juice of the kūṣmāṇḍaka fruit, when drunk together with jaggery, sugar,
and milk, indeed destroys the poison of a stinging insect.
Likewise, sugar mixed with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu) should be drunk along with the root of kodrava and with harītakī to remove delusion (moha).
And the milk of a female camel, when drunk in three mouthfuls of cool water over the course of three nights, removes the poison of mice.
For one whose mouth has been burned by betel, the flow of saliva ceases;
by drinking ghee with sugar, the intoxication from drinking liquor is indeed removed.
O Maheśvara, water well-decocted with the root of *kṛṣṇāṅkola* and drunk from it causes the poison of *gara* to perish within three nights.
O Mahādeva, warm cow’s ghee combined with rock salt will destroy the pain arising from a scorpion sting.
Kusumbha, saffron, yellow orpiment, realgar, karañja, meat, and the root of the arka plant, O Śaṅkara. (GarP 1.191.15)
O Śiva, by eating these, the poison of men shall perish;
and by the offering of lamp oil, O Śiva, the poison born of the bites of insects shall likewise perish— of this there is no doubt.
The poison of a scorpion at the site of the bite is destroyed by ginger combined with *tagara*;
likewise, the poison of a honeybee is eliminated by applying these as a paste.
One should apply a plaster of śatapuṣpā and rock salt with clarified butter;
or else, the seeds of śirīṣa, rubbed with milk, should be used.
O Mahādeva, by anointing with that [ointment], the poison born of a dog is destroyed;
likewise, the poison born of a frog is destroyed by sprinkling water on a blazing fire.

O Lord whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, the poison of those who are swollen shall be destroyed by drinking milk mixed with *dhattūra* and *karasa*, along with jaggery and other ingredients.
Water boiled with the bark of the *vaṭa*, *nimba*, and *śamī* trees— by sprinkling that [water] upon the mouth and teeth, the pain caused by poison shall indeed be destroyed.
O Lord of Umā, by anointing with devadāru and by anointing with red ochre (gairika),
as well as with nāgeśvara, the two types of daridra, and likewise with mañjiṣṭhaka—
the poison of spiders (lūtā) shall be destroyed through these ointments.
The seeds of the karañja, as well as the leaves of the varuṇa, along with sesame and mustard seeds, will indeed destroy poison; there is no doubt about this.
O Hara, if ghee and *kumārī* leaves mixed with salt are administered,
the itching of horses' bodies will be destroyed within ten days.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Prathamāṃśa) of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 192— Hari said:
Eight parts of *citraka*, sixteen parts of *śūraṇa*,
four parts of *śuṇṭhī*, and likewise two parts of black pepper.
Take three parts of pippalī root, four parts of viḍaṅga,
eight parts of muśalī, and four parts of triphalā;
with twice as much jaggery (guḍa), one should prepare boluses (modaka) from these here.
Indeed, its consumption cures indigestion, as well as jaundice, anemia, and jaundice with icteric tinge; it also wards off diarrhea, weak digestion, and enlargement of the spleen.
Bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, pāṭalā, pāribhadraka,
prasāraṇī, aśvagandhā, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā.
Balā, atibalā, rāsnā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, punarnavā,
eraṇḍa, śārivā, parṇa, guḍūcī, and kapikacchukā.
One should boil ten palas of these [drugs] in pure water;
with that decoction reduced to one-fourth, one should cook it in a vessel of oil.
Having given either goat's or cow's milk four times the quantity [of the oil],
one should cause śatāvarī and rock salt to be added in an amount equal to the oil.
I shall now describe those substances which are to be ground; listen to that.
Śatapuṣpā, devadāru, balā, parṇa, vacā, and aguru.
One pala each of kuṣṭha, māṃsī, saindhava, and punarnavā—
this oil should be administered for drinking, as nasal drops, and likewise for massage.
It destroys heart-pain, side-pain, and scrofula;
it cures epilepsy and gout, and the man shall become possessed of a beautiful body.
O Hara, even a mule would conceive a fetus; how much more so a human woman?
This oil should be administered for all disorders of Vāta, including those of horses, elephants, and men who are afflicted by Vāta.
Sesame oil prepared with asafoetida, tumburu, and ginger is indeed the best for filling the ear; it is supreme for removing earache.
One should add the alkali of dried radish and ginger, as well as asafoetida and dry ginger;
then, having added four times the amount of buttermilk, one should cook this oil.
Deafness, earache, pus discharge from the ears,
and worms are all destroyed by filling the ears with this oil.
The alkali of dried radish and ginger, realgar, dry ginger,
*śatapuṣpā*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *dāruśigru*, and *rasāñjana*.
Sauvarcala salt, barley alkali, sea salt, and rock salt,
as well as granthika, viḍa salt, and musta, along with honey and four times the amount of fermented gruel (śukta).
The juice of mātuluṅga and the juice of kadalī as well—oil should be cooked with these; it is supreme for removing earache.
Deafness, ringing in the ears, and a terrible discharge of pus from the filling of these ears with this oil shall destroy the worms within.
O you who have the moon as your crest-jewel, this excellent alkaline oil, which removes impurities from the mouth and teeth, brings about their immediate destruction. GarP_1,192.19 //
Sandalwood, saffron, spikenard, camphor, and clove; and the fruits of jasmine, kaṅkola, betel nut, and cloves.
Aloeswood, musk, costus, tagara,
pādikā, gorocanā, priyaṅgu, balā, and likewise nakhī.
One should prepare oil from sarala, saptaparṇa, lac, āmalakī, and likewise from padmaka.
It is the supreme remover of perspiration, impurities, foul odors, itching, and skin diseases;
O Rudra, one may approach a hundred women, and even a barren woman obtains a son.
Yavānī, citraka, dhānyaka, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), cumin, as well as sauvarcala, viḍaṅga, pippalīmūla, and black mustard; GarP_1,192.24 //
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with these [herbs] combined with eight *prasthas* of water;
it indeed destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and swelling, and truly kindles the digestive fire.
Black pepper, trivṛt, kuṣṭha, yellow orpiment,
realgar, devadāru, the two types of haridrā, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, and sandalwood.
Viśālā, karavīra, the milky sap of arka, and the juice of cow dung—
of these, one karṣa each should be taken, and half a pala of poison should be added.
One should cook one *prastha* of *saṭuka* oil with eight times its amount of cow urine in an earthen or iron vessel,
heating it slowly over a mild fire.
Scabies, eczema, ringworm, and even eruptive boils are destroyed by this massage, and a state of softness is produced. (GarP 1.192.29)
One should rub even extensive vitiligo with this oil;
even long-standing vitiligo will be destroyed at that very moment.
Patola leaves, kaṭukā, mañjiṣṭhā, śārivā, niśā,
the leaves of jātī, śamī, and nimba, along with madhuka— these, boiled together, [form] ghee.
O Auspicious One, by applying these as a paste, even discharging wounds become free from pain;
[the herbs are] Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Vacā, Soma, Brāhmī, and Brahmasuvarcalā.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with equal parts (*akṣa*) of *abhayā*, *guḍūcī*, *āṭarūṣaka*, and *vākucī*.
One *prastha* of the juice of *kaṇṭakārī* combined with one *prastha* of milk—
this is known as *Brāhmī-ghṛta*, which is supreme for producing memory and intelligence.
By using agnimantha, vacā, vāsā, pippalī, honey,
and rock salt for seven nights, one is sung of by the kinnaras as if [one were] one of them.
Apāmārga, guḍūcī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śatāvarī,
śaṅkhapuṣpī, abhayā, and viḍaṅga, taken in equal parts with ghee,
when consumed for three days, shall make a man a bearer of eight hundred granthas.
If vacā is consumed for one month with water, milk, or clarified butter,
it makes a man wise, endowed with the power of retaining what he has heard.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, if one drinks one *pala* of vacā root mixed with milk,
it will instantly endow a person with great wisdom.
Water boiled with bhūnimba, nimba, triphalā, parpaṭa,
paṭolī, mustaka, and vāsaka destroys [these ailments].
Eruptions and redness [of the eyes] will occur; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Kataka fruit, conch shell, rock salt, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and vacā [are the remedy]. (GarP 1,192.40)
A wick made from these— phenī, rasāñjana, honey, viḍaṅga, and realgar—
destroys kāca, timira, and likewise paṭala.
Two *prasthas* of *māṣaka* and one *droṇa* of water should be boiled down until a quarter remains; with this, one should cook one *prastha* of oil.
Having added one āḍhaka of sour gruel (kāñjika), one should cause these ground ingredients to be administered:
punarnavā, gokṣuraka, rock salt (saindhava), the three acrids (tryūṣaṇa), and vacā.
Salt, *suradāru*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*,
when used as a nasal drop or taken by drink, certainly remove even the most severe earache.
O Maheśvara, from massage one may overcome deafness and all diseases;
likewise, two palas of rock salt, ginger, and the five-fold citraka [should be used].
Then one should cook five *prasthas* of *sauvīra* and one *prastha* of oil;
this cures menorrhagia, hoarseness of voice, splenic disorders, and all wind-related ailments.
The udumbara, the vaṭa, the plakṣa, the two kinds of jambū, and the arjuna;
the pippalī, the kadamba, the palāśa, the lodhra, and the tinduka.
Oil prepared with a decoction of madhūka, āmra, sarja, badara, padmakeśara, śirīṣa seeds, and kataka destroys ulcers— even those of long standing— when applied as an ointment. (GarP 1.192.48)
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—193. Hari said:
Onion, cumin, kuṣṭha, aśvagandhā, ajamodaka, vacā, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), and salt constitute an excellent powder. GarP_1,193.1 //
Clarified butter processed with the juices of *brāhmī* and combined with honey,
when consumed for seven days, shall produce a supreme and stainless intellect.
Siddhārthaka, vacā, hiṅgu, karañja, and devadāru;
mañjiṣṭhā, the three myrobalans (triphalā), viśva, śirīṣa, and the two types of rajanī.
Priyaṅgu, nimba, and the three pungent substances (trikaṭu), rubbed together with cow’s urine,
are beneficial when used as nasal drops, an ointment, and likewise for massage.
It removes epilepsy, poison, insanity, consumption, misfortune, and fever;
it destroys fear from malevolent spirits and brings success at royal courts.
Nimba, kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, śigru, mustard,
as well as devadāru, paṭola, and coriander, rubbed together with buttermilk.
One should indeed lead the body, its limbs smeared with oil, through the process of rubbing;
thus, scabies and leprosy shall perish, and it certainly destroys itching.
Sea salt, rock salt, alkaline salt, black mustard, common salt, and soot;
likewise, pungent substances, iron filings, trivṛt, and suraṇaka— these taken in equal parts and cooked over a gentle fire with curd, cow’s urine, and milk.
One should drink this powder, which increases strength and digestive fire, with warm water;
whether the previous meal is digested or undigested, one may then eat excellent meat and other foods with ghee.

This powder relieves pain in the navel, pain in the bladder, and that which arises from abdominal tumors (gulma) or the spleen; it removes all types of pain, kindles the digestive fire, and is supremely beneficial for pain resulting from the transformation of food (pariṇāma-śūla). GarP_1,193.10.
Abhayā, āmalaka, drākṣā, pippalī, kaṇṭakārikā,
śṛṅgī, punarnavā, and śuṇṭhī— when consumed together, these indeed destroy cough.
Abhayā, āmalaka, drākṣā, pāṭhā, and vibhītaka,
when eaten together with an equal amount of sugar, will act as a remover of fever.
Triphalā, jujube, grapes, and long pepper cause purgation;
likewise, harītakī taken with warm water and salt causes purgation.
Turtles, fish, horses, buffaloes, cows, jackals, monkeys, cats, peacocks, crows, boars, owls, and cocks. GarP_1,193.14 //
O Haṃsa, one should offer as incense the feces, urine, flesh, hair, or blood of these [animals] for the pacification of those afflicted by fever and those who are insane.
O Lord of Umā, these varieties of medicinal herbs have been described;
they destroy diseases just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is the medicine; when remembered, he brings about the cessation of disease.
Whether meditated upon, worshipped, or praised, there is no need for doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—194. Hari said:
I shall proclaim the auspicious Vaiṣṇava armor, which removes all diseases,
by means of which protection was formerly afforded to Śambhu as he destroyed the Daityas.
Having prostrated before the Lord Īśāna, who is unborn, eternal, and free from ailment;
the God Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, all-pervading and imperishable.
Having paid homage to Janārdana, I bind this amulet,
which is unfailing, incomparable, all-encompassing, and the warder-off of all suffering.
May Viṣṇu protect me from the front; may Kṛṣṇa guard me from behind;
may Hara protect my head, and Janārdana my heart.
May Hṛṣīkeśa protect my mind; may Keśava protect my tongue; may Vāsudeva protect my eyes; and may the all-pervading Saṅkarṣaṇa protect my ears.
May Pradyumna protect my sense of smell, and Aniruddha my skin; may Vanamālī protect the region of my throat, and Śrīvatsa protect my lower parts.
May the Discus protect my left side, warding off the Daityas;
and may the Goddess Gadā protect my right side, repelling all the Asuras.
May the pestle protect my belly; may the plow protect my back.
May the Śārṅga bow protect my upper body, and may Nandaka protect my shanks.
May Śaṅkha protect my heels, and Padma both my feet;
for the sake of accomplishing all purposes, may Garuḍa always protect me.
May Varāha protect me in the water, and Vāmana in difficult terrains;
may Narasiṃha protect me in the forest, and may Keśava protect me everywhere.
May the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha bestow gold upon me;
may Kapila, the teacher of Sāṃkhya, bring about the equilibrium of my bodily constituents.
May the unborn Lord, who dwells in Śvetadvīpa, lead us to Śvetadvīpa;
may he, the crusher of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, destroy all our enemies.
May Viṣṇu always draw away the impurity from my body;
may Haṃsa, Matsya, and Kūrma protect me in every direction.
May the god Trivikrama sever all my sins;
likewise, may the god Nārāyaṇa protect my intellect.
May the remainder [of my merit] produce stainless knowledge that destroys ignorance;
may Vaḍavāmukha destroy whatever defilement has been committed by me.
May the Lord Dattātreya bestow supreme happiness upon my feet and my head;
may he grant it to me along with my sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
May Rāma destroy all my enemies with his axe;
may the mighty-armed son of Daśaratha, the slayer of demons, protect me forever.
May Rāma, the joy of the Yādavas, who destroyed Pralamba, Keśin, Cāṇūra, Pūtanā, and Kaṃsa, slay my enemies with his plow; may that childhood state of Kṛṣṇa grant me all my desires.
Terrified by fear, I see a man who is black and tawny, a terrible darkness of gloom, like the Ender (Antaka) himself with a noose in his hand. GarP_1,194.19 //
Then I went for refuge to the lotus-eyed Acyuta;
I am blessed and forever fearless, for the Blessed Lord Hari belongs to me.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all calamities,
and having donned the Vaiṣṇava armor, I wander upon the surface of the earth.
I am invincible to all beings, for I am composed of all the gods;
this is through the remembrance of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
May there be constant success for me according to the mantra as it has been uttered:
"Whoever looks at me with their eyes, and whoever I look at with my eye—
may Viṣṇu bind the eyes of all those who are evil and wicked."
May the spokes of that discus which belongs to Vāsudeva indeed sever my sins and strike down those who would harm me.
Among the rākṣasas and piśācas, in wildernesses and forests,
in disputes, on royal roads, at gambling matches, and in quarrels.
When crossing a river in a terrible situation, when life-threatening danger has arrived,
in the event of fire, thieves, or falling [from a height], and for the warding off of all malevolent planets.
In cases of panic caused by lightning, snakes, or poison, or indeed during illness and the perils of obstacles,
one should constantly recite this mantra whenever fear arises in the body.
This mantra of the Blessed One is the supreme among mantras;
it is the renowned secret armor that destroys all sins and evils,
a great and profound creation manifested through his own *māyā*, as vast as the end of an eon.
O you who are without beginning or end, O seed of the world, O lotus-navelled one, homage be to you! Om, to Time, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to the Person of Time! Oṃ, svāhā to Kṛṣṇa!
Oṃ, svāhā to the one whose form is Kṛṣṇa!
Oṃ caṇḍāya svāhā!
Oṃ caṇḍarūpāya svāhā!
Oṃ pracaṇḍāya svāhā!
Oṃ, to the one of fierce form, svāhā!
Oṃ, to the all-pervading one, svāhā! Oṃ, to the one of all forms, svāhā!

Oṃ, homage to Bhuvaneśa, the sustainer of the three worlds! Here, *viṭi siviṭi siviṭi svāhā*. Oṃ, homage to Ayokhetaya! O you, command [them]—the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Antāpasmārakas, Chardanas, and Duddharṣaṇas; [command them] regarding all fevers such as those occurring every day, every two days, every three days, every four days, or at every hour, as well as fevers by day, fevers by night, fevers at the junctions of time, and all other fevers.
This body of mine is the food for spiders, insects, thorns, *pūtanās*, serpents, and for poisons both stationary and mobile; make it wholesome!

*Sphuṭa sphuṭa sphuṭa prakoṭa laphaṭa vikaṭadaṃṣṭra*—may he protect me from the east! *Oṃ hai hai hai hai*, you who are struck by the time of a thousand suns, victory! Protect me from the west! *Oṃ nivi nivi*, you whose form is like the blazing flame of a fire!

O Mahākapila, protect me from the north! Oṃ vili vili mili mili, Garuḍi Garuḍi, Gaurī-Gāndhārī, may you utterly destroy the poison, the delusive poison, and the most terrible poison! Svāhā! Protect me from the south! Behold me! Protect me, protect me from all fears and calamities caused by spirits! Victory! Victory! Be victorious! By that, the fear of enemies, pride, and the sound of musical instruments shall be diminished; may the Unfallen One, the dispeller of fear, grant fearlessness from every quarter.
May they all enter his entire belly, just as rays of light enter the setting sun;
may Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and Hari— destroy all my fevers.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vaiṣṇava Armor," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—195. Hari said:
Listen to that vidyā which grants all desires within seven nights:
Homage to you, the Blessed One Vāsudeva; we meditate upon him.
Salutations to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, and to Saṅkarṣaṇa;
salutations to the one who is pure consciousness and whose form is supreme bliss.
To him who delights in the Self, who is peaceful, whose vision of duality has ceased,
and who is all your own forms— to you, therefore, salutations again and again.
Salutations to you, the great Hṛṣīkeśa, whose form is infinite;
in whom this world exists, from whom it arises, and before whom it is born.
Salutations to You, that Brahman, who bears the earth made of clay;
whom mind, intellect, senses, and vital breaths neither touch nor know;
who moves within and without like the sky—I bow to You.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Great Puruṣa, the Lord of the great elements! O Supreme Lord, whose pair of lotus-feet are adorned with the pollen of the lotuses that are the modesty and grace of all sentient beings, and who possess the knowledge known as Dharma—homage to you!
By means of this knowledge, Citraketu attained the state of a Vidyādhara.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 196— Hari said:
"O Maheśvara, having conquered all his enemies by reciting the vidyā known as Viṣṇudharma, he attained the status of Indra; I shall now declare that [vidyā] to you."
One should place the syllables beginning with Oṃ in sequence upon the feet, knees, thighs, abdomen, heart, chest, mouth, and head.
Having recited "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" and likewise the reversal [of the mantra],
one should then perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
One should place [the letters] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *ya*, on the joints of the fingers and thumbs;
one should place the syllable *oṃ* at the heart, and the entire mantra upon the head.
One should utter this mantra-assignment: "Oṃ, to Viṣṇu," placing the syllable *oṃ* between the eyebrows, the syllable *śi* at the eyes and so forth, up to the head. (GarP 1.196.5)
One should meditate upon the supreme Self, which is endowed with all powers;
may Hari protect me, and in the form of the Fish, may he protect me in the water.
May Trivikrama protect me in the sky, may Vāmana protect me on land,
may Narasiṃha protect me in the forest, and may Rāma protect me on the mountain.
May Varāha protect me on the earth; may Nārāyaṇa protect me in the sky;
may Kapila protect me from the bondage of karma, and Datta protect me from disease.
Hayagrīva [attains his state] from the deities; Kumāra from Makaradhvaja;
the god Nārada from the worship of others; and Kūrma indeed always [arises] in the south-west.
May Dhanvantari protect me from unwholesome food, Nāga from the power of anger, Yajña from all diseases, and Vyāsa from ignorance. (GarP 1.196.10)
May the Buddha protect [us] from the assembly of heretics; may Kalkī protect us from sin. May Viṣṇu protect us at midday; may Nārāyaṇa protect us in the morning.
May Madhu-han protect me in the afternoon, and Mādhava in the evening;
may Hṛṣīkeśa protect me at nightfall, and Janārdana at dawn.
May Śrīdhara protect me at midnight, and Padmanābha at the dead of night;
may they, bearing the discus, the mace Kaumodakī, and arrows, slay our enemies and the Rākṣasas.
May the conch and the lotus, as well as the Śārṅga bow and Garuḍa, who adorn his sides, protect the intellect, the senses, the mind, and the vital breaths from enemies.
May Śeṣa, whose form is that of a serpent, protect me always and everywhere;
and may Nārasiṃha protect me always in the intermediate directions and the cardinal points.
And whoever, while maintaining this, beholds anyone with his eye,
that person shall become submissive, free from sin, released from disease, and go to heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said: The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—197.
Dhanvantari spoke:
I shall fully proclaim the Gāruḍa, which was indeed uttered by Garuḍa for Kaśyapa; it is the Gāruḍa taught by Sumitra, which destroys poison.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these classes within earth and the other elements are indeed the lords of the mandalas.
The deities residing within the five principles (pañcatattva) are attained by the servants of Viṣṇu;
they are distinguished by long vowels and are devoid of neuter genders.
Śiva is said to possess six limbs: the heart, the head, and the crest (śikhā) in due order;
the armor, the eye, and the weapon. Nyāsa is the establishment [of these] in their respective locations.
At the end of the mantra that bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhiprada*), there is the fire of time (*kālavahni*) below the wind (*anila*);
it is conjoined with the sixth vowel and further endowed with the half-moon (*ardhendu*).
The divisions of the higher and lower are said to be above and below Śiva;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon all the limbs with the letter *ra*, according to the prescribed rule.
By reciting [the mantra] upon the heart, the palm of the hand, the body, the ear, and the eye,
one shall attain all perfections (siddhis) equal to those of the Four-faced One.
One should visualize the earth as square, very extensive, and yellow in color, presided over by the deity Indra; in its center is the maṇḍala of Varuṇa.
In the center is a lotus likewise arranged, with a very cool half-moon,
possessing the luster of sapphire and gentle, or else an āgneya-maṇḍala.
One should visualize a triangle joined with svastikas, blazing with garlands of flames;
it has the appearance of crushed collyrium, is circular, and is adorned with a dot.
One should meditate upon the nectar of space, which has the appearance of waves of milk, possesses the luster of pure crystal, and is flooding the entire world.
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are stationed in the earthly circle;
Karkoṭaka and Padmanābha are established in the watery region.
In the southeast, one should also place Kulika and Takṣaka, as well as Mahābja and Karkaṭaka; these five elements are situated within the wind-maṇḍala.
One should likewise assign Jayā and Vijayā to the joints of the fingers, from the thumb to the little finger, in both direct and reverse order.
Having assigned the six limbs of Śiva to the locations of one's own mouth and so forth,
one should assign them to the little finger and the other fingers, to the heart and the other centers, to the crest-lock, and to the two hands.
One should first perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) upon the joints of the fingers in sequence; then follows the placement of the elements (bhūta), and likewise the limbs of Śiva.
Preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, joined with the name itself—
this is declared to be the rule for all mantras regarding installation and worship.
The first syllable of their names is proclaimed as this mantra;
it is the mantra that brings about the presence of the eight classes of nāgas.
Oṃ svāhā; preceded by the five elements in their proper order, this is Tārkṣya himself, the accomplisher of all rites.
Having performed the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*) upon the body with the vowels, one should again perform the placement [of the consonants];
one should contemplate the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as blazing, which effects the purification of the self.
Afterwards, one should contemplate the seed-syllable, which consists of nectar at the end of the year;
having thus performed the nourishment, one should contemplate it upon the crown of one's own head.
One should offer the earth, shining with the luster of molten gold,
filled with all the worlds and accompanied by the guardians of the quarters, at one's feet.
The wise one should place this blessed Earth within his own body;
he should meditate upon her as being of a dark complexion, and she becomes twice the size of the earth.
Having placed within the space between the navel and the neck the triangular mandala of the Sun, blazing and filled with garlands of flames reaching as far as the world of Brahmā; GarP_1,197.24 //
One should meditate upon the sharp mandala of Vāyu, which has the appearance of crushed collyrium, pervading and abiding within the entire [body], situated within the form of one's own self.
Situated above the topknot, it is divine, possessing the luster of pure crystal,
pervading the immeasurable great void, and like nectar.
Having first performed the ritual placement of the elements (*bhūtanyāsa*) and that of the serpents (*nāga*) in their proper order,
the mantras ending in the letter *la* and joined with the nasal bindu are applied according to the sequence of the elements.

Then one should offer the seed-syllable of Śiva and then meditate upon the mandala. The wise knower of the ritual procedure, at the time of performing the rite, should contemplate that specific color of the mandala which has been declared according to the sequence for each individual.
Then, one should constantly meditate upon Tārkṣya, adorned with fluttering black serpents as his wings, for the sake of neutralizing both stationary and mobile poisons.
Having surrounded [the body] with planets, spirits, piśācas, ḍākinīs, yakṣas,
rākṣasas, and nāgas, one should install Śiva within one's own body.
The placement (nyāsa) of the nāgas and the two elements is declared to be twofold;
having meditated thus, one should perform the ritual actions of the self-principle (ātmatattva) and so forth in their proper sequence.
Having first offered the three principles (tritattva), and thereafter the principle of Śiva (śivatattva),
just as [they are] in the body, so too in the deity, [one should offer them] upon the joints of the fingers.
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body in both direct and reverse order,
[one should place] the bulb (kanda), the stalk (nāla), as well as the lotus (padma), and likewise virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), and the others.
One should worship with the letter at the end of the class conjoined with the second vowel;
"śauṃ" in the center of the pericarp, and on the head, conjoined with the letter *ra*.
One should place the groups [of consonants] beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa* starting from the east;
likewise, two by two, they should be placed at the ends of the petals and the ends of the filaments, beginning from the east.
One should assign the vowels to the filaments and worship the sixteen [deities] ending with Īśāna;
the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā have been declared, and thereafter one should assign the three principles (tattvas).
Then one should invoke Śiva upon the head; thereafter, one should install the Lord together with his limbs (the retinue) there in the pericarp, preceded by the ritual sequence.
One should worship Earth on the western petal, Water situated on the northern,
Fire on the southern petal, and Vāyu on the eastern.
One should first visualize one's own seed-syllable in the form of a physical image as previously described;
*yaṃ* is the root of the wind in the southwest, while *ra* resides in fire.
One should always worship Vaṃ as Īśa, and one should worship Oṃ situated in the heart;
one should worship those subtle elements (tanmātras) and the gross elements (bhūtamātras) only outside.
Thereafter, having meditated upon the limbs of Śiva, one should then worship them:
having worshipped the heart in the southeast, the head in the region of Ishana (the northeast).
One should place the *śikhā* in the southwest (*nairṛtya*), assign the *kavaca* in the northwest (*vāyavya*),
place the *astra* on the outside, and position the *netra* in the north (*uttara*).
One should worship the seed-syllables on the tips of the petals and at the tip of the pericarp;
the eight nāgas, beginning with Ananta and ending with Kulīra, are situated there in sequence.
The mantra-practitioner should always worship [the deities] individually according to the prescribed rite, following the sequence starting from the east and ending with Īśa.

This rite is prescribed for the lotus in the heart according to the ritual rules, as well as upon stone and other materials within the prepared maṇḍala; it applies to both the daily and occasional rites.
One should constantly contemplate the Self as assuming forms at will, captivating to the mind,
flooding the entire world, and the agent of creation and destruction.
Blazing with garlands of flames as far as the world of Brahmā,
he has ten arms, four faces, tawny eyes, and holds a trident in his hand.

For the sake of accomplishment in all rites, one should meditate upon Bhairava—who has terrifying fangs, is exceedingly fierce, possesses three eyes, and bears the moon upon his crest—as well as Garuḍa. (GarP 1.197.48)
For the purpose of destroying the nāgas, he manifested the terrifying and formidable Garuḍa;
his two feet were established in the netherworld (pātāla), and the directions were supported by his wings.
One should contemplate the seven heavens upon his chest, the cosmic egg resting at his throat,
and his head extending from the east to the northeast.
And the triad of powers situated within the crest of Sadāśiva,
Śiva who is higher than the highest, Tārkṣya himself, the manifest leader of the worlds.
Three-eyed and of fierce form, the destroyer of venomous serpents,
a devourer with a terrifying mouth— Garuda, whose very body is composed of mantra.

In all ritual acts, one should contemplate [the deity] as blazing like the fire of time (kālāgni). Having thus performed the rite of placement (nyāsa), whatever one contemplates in the mind, that shall come to pass.
Whatever may be the goal to be accomplished, a man indeed becomes like Garuḍa; by his mere sight,
pretas, bhūtas, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas,
as well as quartan fevers and other ailments, are destroyed.
Dhanvantari said:
Thus he spoke to Garuḍa, and Garuḍa spoke it to Kaśyapa;
listen now to that knowledge just as Maheśvara spoke it to Gaurī.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—198.
Bhairava said:
Now I shall declare the Nityaklinnā Tripurā, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation:
Oṃ Hrīṃ, come, O Goddess! Aiṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ, [you who are] the cause of the line!
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Kledinī Bhaṃ, likewise with Madanakṣobhiṇī.
One should worship with "aiṃ yaṃ yaṃ krīṃ" by means of the line of qualities (*guṇarekhā*), and with "hrīṃ" within the heart of passion (*madanāntara*).
One should worship Nirañjanā with "aiṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ," Vāgīśvarī within the line of passion, and Khanetrāvalī; and one should worship Vegavatī upon the seat of the great corpse (*mahāpretāsana*).
Oṃ hrīṃ kraiṃ naiṃ kraiṃ, salutation to the eternally intoxicating flow, krīṃ!
Aiṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Tripurā!
Oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ, the western face; oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, and likewise the northern.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ: the southern and upper faces, and the western one.
Oṃ Hrīṃ: salutation to the noose (pāśa), Krīṃ: to the goad (aṅkuśa), Aiṃ: to the skull-cup (kapāla).
Ādyaṃ Bhayaṃ: Aiṃ Hrīṃ; likewise for the head (śiras) and the crest-lock (śikhā), as well as the armor (kavaca).
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Krīṃ, phaṭ to the weapon! GarP_1,198.1
In the east, one should invoke Kāmarūpa, Asitāṅga Bhairava, and Brahmāṇī; in the south, one should invoke Caṇḍa, Ruru Bhairava, and Māheśvarī. GarP_1,198.2 //
Likewise, in the west, "Homage indeed to Caṇḍa";
in the north, "Homage to Kaumārī, to Ulkā, and to Krodha," and to Vaiṣṇavī.
In the southeast corner, [offer] to Aghora and Unmattabhairava, and to Vārāhī;
in the southwest corner, to Sāra, Kapālī, Bhairava, and Māheśvarī.
In the northwest corner, one should worship Jālandhara, Bhīṣaṇa, Bhairava, and Cāmuṇḍā;
in the northeast corner, one should worship Vaṭuka, Saṃhāra, and Caṇḍikā.
Then one should worship Rati, Prīti, Kāmadeva, and the five-arrowed god;
through meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings, the Goddess is always accomplished.
The eternal Tripurā shall destroy disease through the sequence of Jvālāmukhī;
I shall now describe the sequence of Jvālāmukhī—she, the auspicious one, is to be worshipped in the center.
Nityāruṇā, Madanāturā, Mahāmohā by her very nature,
Mahendrāṇī, Kalanākarṣiṇī, and likewise Bhāratī.
Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Aparājitā.
Vijayā, Ajitā, Mohinī, Tvaritā,
Stambhinī, Jṛmbhiṇī, and Kālikā are to be worshipped outside the lotus;
one should also worship the sequence of Jvālāmukhī, which brings about the removal of poison and other afflictions.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—199.
Bhairava said:
Now I shall describe the Cūḍāmaṇi for the sake of purifying [the results of] auspicious and inauspicious [actions];
having recollected the Sun, the Goddess, Gaṇa, and the Moon, a person should draw it.

Alternatively, one may count the [auspicious] banners and so forth in their proper order, starting from the directions and positions indicated by the three lines appearing like cow-urine or as stated in the *praśrava* verses.
The banner, smoke, the lion, the dog, the bull, the donkey, the elephant, and the crow should be known as the eighth; one should install them with their respective names and mantras.
Seeing a banner at the place of the banner, there is thought of sovereignty, wealth, and so forth;
smoke situated at the place of the banner brings thoughts of minerals and yields profit.
When a lion is situated in the position of the banner, there will be the acquisition of wealth and so forth;
when a dog is situated in the position of the banner, there will be concerns regarding female slaves, pleasure, and the like.
Seeing a bull in the position of the banner (dhvajasthāna) indicates anxiety regarding one's status and brings gain;
seeing a donkey in the position of the banner will result in suffering, affliction, and the like.

Seeing an elephant at the location of the banner (dhvaja) portends anxiety regarding one's position and victory; likewise, seeing a crow at the location of the banner portends anxiety regarding afflictions and the loss of wealth.
Having seen a banner in the place of smoke, there is first suffering and then wealth;
likewise, having seen smoke in the place of smoke, there will be strife, suffering, and so forth.
When a lion is situated in the smoky quarter, there will be mental anxiety, loss of wealth, and so forth;
when a dog is situated in the smoky quarter, there will be victory, gain, and the like.
