Seeing a bull in the place of smoke, one gains women, cattle, horses, wealth, and so forth;
seeing a donkey in the place of smoke, there is disease as well as the loss of wealth.
If an elephant is seen in the place of smoke, there is the attainment of a kingdom, victory, and so forth;
if a crow is situated in the place of smoke, there is the destruction of wealth and kingdom.
Seeing a banner in the position of Leo, one should predict the acquisition of a kingdom and so forth;
when Dhūmra is situated in the position of Leo, there is the attainment of a daughter, wealth, and the like.
When the lion is situated in the place of the lion, there is victory and meeting with friends;
when the dog has gone to the place of the lion, there is anxiety regarding women and the acquisition of a village.
Seeing a bull in the place of the lion brings gain of houses, fields, and wealth;
seeing an elephant in the place of the lion brings the lordship of a village.
Seeing an elephant in the place of the lion, one obtains health, long life, happiness, and so forth;
when a crow is situated in the place of the lion, there is the acquisition of daughters, grain, virtues, and the like.
Seeing a banner in the position of the dog indicates anxiety regarding one's station, as well as happiness and other such matters;
when Dhūmra is situated in the position of the dog, there is quarrel and the destruction of one's undertakings.
If the lion is situated in the place of the dog, there will be failure in one's undertakings;
if the dog is situated in the place of the dog, there will be loss of wealth.
Seeing a bull in the place of a dog, a sick person is liberated from disease;
seeing a donkey in the place of a dog, there shall be fear of quarrel.
If one sees an elephant in the place of a dog, there will be a reunion with one's son and wife;
however, if a crow stands in the place of a dog, there will be suffering and the destruction of the family.
Seeing a banner in the position of Taurus, there is honor from the king, happiness, and so forth;
when Dhūmra is situated in the position of Taurus, there is honor from the king, happiness, and so forth.
When Leo is situated in the place of Taurus, there is good fortune, wealth, and so forth;
when Canis Major (Śunī) is situated in the place of Taurus, strength, prosperity, and desire are said to arise.
Seeing a bull in the position of the Bull [sign] brings fame, contentment, happiness, and so forth;
seeing a donkey in the position of the Bull will result in great gain and other benefits.
Seeing an elephant in the position of Taurus, there will be union with women, elephants, and the like;
if a crow is situated in the position of Taurus, there will be the attainment of one's place and honor.
Seeing a banner in the place of the donkey, there will be disease, grief, and so forth;
when smoke is situated in the place of the donkey, there will be fear of thieves and the like.
When the lion is situated in the place of the donkey, there is honor, prosperity, victory, and so forth;
when it is situated in the place of the dog or the donkey, there is suffering and the loss of wealth.
Seeing a bull in the place of a donkey indicates happiness and union with loved ones;
seeing a donkey in the place of a donkey, one should predict suffering, affliction, and the like.
If an elephant is seen in the place of the donkey, there will be happiness, sons, and so forth;
but if a crow is situated in the place of the donkey, there will be quarrel and indeed disease.
Seeing a banner in the position of the elephant, one gains women, victory, fortune, happiness, and so forth;
when Dhūmra is situated in the position of the elephant, there is an acquisition of wealth and grain.
If a lion is situated in the place of the elephant, there is the attainment of victory and success;
if a dog is situated in the place of the elephant, there is health, happiness, and prosperity.
Seeing a bull in the place of an elephant indicates the acquisition of wealth, honor, and so forth;
seeing a donkey in the place of an elephant indicates suffering first, followed by happiness.
Seeing an elephant in the position of the elephant brings fields, grain, happiness, and so forth;
when a crow is situated in the position of the elephant, there is the acquisition of wealth and grain.
Seeing a banner in the place of the crow, there will be the destruction of one's purpose;
when Dhūmra is situated in the place of the crow, the misery of the Kali age shall come to pass.
If a lion is situated in the place of a crow, there will be conflict and indeed suffering;
if a dog is situated in the place of a crow, there will be fear of the destruction of the home and so forth.
Seeing a bull in the place of a crow portends fear of displacement from one's position and the like;
seeing a donkey in the place of a crow portends the loss of wealth and defeat.
If one sees an elephant in the place of the crow, there will be wealth, fame, and so forth;
if a crow is situated in the place of the crow, there will be departure to a foreign land and the like.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—200.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, I shall describe the conquest of the winds, which brings victory and reveals the path to victory;
it is the quartet of auspicious factors known as wind, fire, water, and Indra.
The wind should be present on both the left and the right and should be abundant;
fire should flow upwards, while Varuṇa should be below.
Mahendra, situated in the center, moves to the left during the bright fortnight and to the right during the dark fortnight,
for three days at a time, starting from its rising.

If the rising occurs on the path of the sun and the setting occurs by way of the moon, then there will be prosperity on the first lunar day and other such times; however, if this is reversed, there will be misfortune.
The collections of virtues increase; otherwise, obstacles are appropriate.
O fair-faced one, sixteen transits are proclaimed for both day and night.
And when the wind, having remained for half of each watch (prahara), should transition, then the loss of health is to be known; the wind thus wanders within embodied beings.
When the wind is situated in the right nostril during eating and sexual intercourse,
one who holds a sword in hand and is filled with desire shall conquer enemies in battle.
Going toward the left is the most excellent in all undertakings;
when the wind blows from that direction, it is an auspicious omen for one who has come into being.
In the Māhendra, Vāruṇa, or Vāta [wind], no calamity whatsoever arises;
there is drought when the wind blows to the right, and rain when it blows to the left.
Thus ends the two hundredth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 201 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Dhanvantari said:
I shall proclaim the Ayurveda of horses, which defines the characteristics of all purposes regarding the horse:
one with a crow’s beak, black tongue, tree-like face, and a hot palate.

One with protruding teeth, one with missing teeth, one with horns, one with gaps between the teeth, one with a single testicle, one whose testicles have descended, one covered in a sheath, one with cloven hooves, and one with breasts. GarP_1,201.2 //
Mārjārapāda, Vyāghrābha, Kuṣṭhavidradhisannibha, Yamaja, Vāmana, and Mārjāra with tawny eyes; GarP_1,201.3 //
A horse possessing these defects should be abandoned; the best horse is born in Turaṣka, the middling is five cubits in height, and the lowest is three cubits.
Those mounts that are not crowded together, as well as those with short ears,
which have a brindled luster, are not lacking in power, long-lived, and do not become dejected.
Through the worship of Revanta, through fire-offerings (homa), and by providing portions for the twice-born, [one is protected].
[The materials used are] sarala wood, neem leaves, guggulu resin, mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
One should tie sesame seeds, *vacā*, and *hiṅgu* around the neck of the horse.
Wounds are said to be of two kinds: those of exogenous origin and those arising from internal humors.
That which arises from wind (vāta) ripens slowly, while that born of phlegm (śleṣman) ripens quickly;
that caused by bile (pitta) is characterized by burning in the throat, and that from blood (śoṇita) is mildly painful.
For the purification of malignant wounds caused by external factors such as insects, weapons, and the like,
one should use castor root, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāruharidrā*), *citraka*, and ginger.
Garlic or rock salt, nourished with buttermilk or sour gruel;
or a bolus of sesame flour mixed with curd and rock salt;
or a bolus combined with nimba leaves—these serve to cleanse and heal wounds.
One should prepare a powder by combining patola, nimba leaves, vacā, citraka, pippalī, and śṛṅgavera in one place.
From drinking this, worms, phlegm, and sluggish wind are destroyed.
Likewise, neem leaves, cloth, lac, the three myrobalans, and khadira [are used].
Then, having boiled it and strained out the blood, the wise one should administer it for three days alone for the pacification of the horse's skin disease.
In cases of leprosy with ulcers, mustard oil is beneficial;
likewise, a decoction of garlic and other ingredients is for the purpose of pacifying [the disease] through drinking and as food.
In cases of those combined with other types of Vāta, one should immediately administer a nasal drop (nasya) there, prepared either with the juice of mātuluṅga or with the juice of māṃsī.
On the first day, two *palas* [are given], increasing by one *pala* each day until eighteen *palas* are reached on the final day.
In the lowest [grade], there should be eight palas; in the middle, there should be fourteen.
During autumn and the heat of summer, one should neither give nor cause [the gift] to be given at all.
In diseases caused by Vāta, [one should apply] oil combined with sugar, ghee, and milk;
in Kapha disorders, pungent oils with the three acrids (vyoṣa); and in Pitta disorders, [oil] with the decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
A horse that eats rice, *ṣaṣṭika* grain, and milk is not to be despised;
a horse with a golden complexion, resembling a ripe jambu fruit, is not to be despised.
At the half-watch [of the night], one should feed the horse Guggulu;
one should quickly feed it milk-rice (pāyasa) and milk, so that the horse becomes well-steadied.
In the case of a disorder involving wind (vāta), one should give milk and śāli rice with meat broth;
in the case of bile (pitta), one should give them with honey, mung bean soup, and ghee.
In cases of phlegm (kapha), one should administer mung beans or kulattha, which are pungent and bitter;
for deafness, illness, or excessive eating, guggulu is indicated when the three doṣas are involved.
For all diseases, one should administer one pala of dūrvā grass on the first day;
thereafter, one should increase it by one karṣa daily until it reaches five palas.
Regarding both drink and food, eighty palas is the maximum;
sixty for those of middling capacity, and forty for those who enjoy pleasures.
In cases of ulcers, skin diseases, and lameness, it should be combined with a decoction of triphalā;
in cases of weak digestion and swelling, it should be joined with cow's urine.
In cases of wounds involving wind and bile, or in such diseases, cow's milk mixed with ghee should be administered;
and for those who are emaciated, food combined with meat should be given for the purpose of nourishment.
Five palas of well-ground *guḍūcī* should be given to horses in the morning,
mixed with ghee, during the autumn and summer seasons.
That very [medicine], which destroys disease, bestows nourishment, and increases strength and splendor,
should be given to the horse, either mixed with milk or otherwise.

By means of the medicinal preparations of *guḍūcī*, one should take four, three, or two *palas* respectively for the superior, middling, and inferior [qualities of the patient], as well as for *śatāvarī* and *aśvagandhā*.
When, without any apparent cause, the gait of the mounts becomes uniform and they suddenly die, one should declare that to be an *upasarga*.
Through fire offerings and other rites, by protecting [the patient], by feeding Brahmins, by the performance of bali offerings,
and by pacification rituals, as well as by the administration of harītakī and other medicines, the pacification of calamities shall occur.
Harītakī, combined with cow’s urine, oil, and salt,
should be taken starting with five fruits, then increasing by five each time until reaching a full hundred;
the maximum dose is one hundred, or eighty, or sixty.
I shall proclaim the Ayurveda of elephants; the medicinal preparations (kalpas) mentioned are beneficial for elephants.
For an elephant, the dosage is fourfold; by means of these, one destroys the diseases of elephants.
The pacification of planetary portents and diseases, as well as rites for peace,
are accomplished by honoring the gods and Brahmins with jewels and giving away a tawny cow.
Having fasted, the physicians should tie a garland onto the two tusks of the elephant,
as well as *vaca* and white mustard seeds consecrated with the mantra.
One should protect the elephant by worshipping the Sun and others, Śiva, Durgā, Śrī, and Viṣṇu;
one should offer oblations to the spirits and bathe it with four jars [of water].
One should give consecrated food and sprinkle the elephant with ashes;
this auspicious and pure protection against spirits will always guard the elephant.
Triphalā, pañcakola, daśamūla, viḍaṅga, śatāvarī, guḍūcī, nimba, vāsaka, and kiṃśuka.
Beneficial for destroying diseases of elephants, it is dry and astringent;
thus has been stated the essential summary of what is taught in the two Āyurvedas.

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Ayurveda of Elephants and Horses," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hari said: [The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—202] Hari said:
Furthermore, O Śiva, a single fresh root of *punarnavā* or *apāmārga*,
when placed fresh from its source into the female organ, removes pain in the private parts;
it also removes the pains of childbirth and the distress of young women.
The root of the *bhūmikūṣmāṇḍa* plant, or even rice powder,
when drunk with milk for seven days, will cause women to produce abundant breast milk.
The root of *rudra*, *indra*, and *vāruṇī*, when applied as an ointment, destroys pain in a woman's breasts;
moreover, a cake (*polikā*) cooked in ghee should certainly be prepared.
O Maheśāna, when it is eaten, it destroys the pain of the womb;
when applied as a paste with the root of *kāravella*, it emerges [from the womb].
The female organ enters [the male]; no deliberation is required here.
[One should apply] roots of indigo and paṭola with clarified butter and sesame water.
O Rudra, their ground [roots] indeed act as a plaster that extinguishes the glow of Jvālāgardabha;
likewise, Pāṭhā root ground with rice-water, when drunk, [achieves the same].
Likewise, drinking *kuṣṭha* will remove evil diseases;
indeed, water from a bellows mixed with honey, when drunk, [removes] that which has entered within.
O Śiva, O Rudra, lac, which is like clarified butter, when drunk together with milk, effects the cessation of the torment of evil diseases. GarP_1,202.8.
It removes the disease of menorrhagia; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O Śiva, the powder of *dvijayaṣṭī* and *trikaṭuka*, when drunk, removes [the ailment]. (GarP 1.202.9)
O Maheśvara, remove the blood-tumor (*raktagulma*) of women by means of a decoction of sesame seeds;
and [remove] that which is bound within the flowers of young women.
The bulb of the red lotus, mixed with sugar and sesame seeds,
when drunk along with sugar by women, causes the miscarriage of the fetus.
The cessation of blood flow occurs through the consumption of cold water;
O Rudra, [blood flow] that has been discharged is [stilled] by drinking boiled *kāñjika* prepared with *śarapuṅkhā*.
Asafoetida combined with rock salt quickly induces labor in women;
likewise, the root of the citron (mātuluṅga) tied around the waist induces labor.
At the root of the *apāmārga* plant, according to the name of the pregnant woman, if it is uprooted in its entirety, there shall be a son; otherwise, a daughter.
When the root of the Apāmārga plant is placed upon the head of women, the pain of labor will be destroyed; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O Śiva, O Hara, when filled with camphor, madanaphala, and madhuka, the womb of even an old woman becomes excellent; how much more so, then, that of a young woman?
The child upon whose forehead a tilaka is made with that which is called gorocanā,
and to whom sugar and kuṣṭha are given to drink, shall be free from fear— O Śiva— the child shall be safe from poisons, spirits, seizing demons, and diseases.
O Rudra, the constant wearing of conch-shell, nābhi, vacā, kuṣṭha, and iron provides protection for children against afflictions.
Palāśa powder, taken with honey, cow’s ghee, āmalaka, and viḍaṅga,
makes a man of great intelligence as soon as it is drunk.
Within one month, O Mahādeva, he becomes free from old age and death.
O Rudra, the seed of the *palāśa* tree, taken in equal parts with ghee, sesame, and honey,
and consumed for seven days, brings old age to its complete destruction.
Having consumed the powder of *rudrāmalaka* mixed with honey, oil,
and ghee for one month, a man shall become youthful and attain mastery over speech.
Indeed, the powder of auspicious *āmalaka* fruit, taken with honey or water at dawn, will strengthen the nose; it is auspicious when consumed, O Śiva.

Having consumed the powder of *kuṣṭha* with clarified butter and honey in the morning, a man will indeed possess a body fragrant like that of a celestial being and shall live for a thousand years. (GarP 1.202.24)
O Maheśvara, split black gram grains that are husked, soaked in ghee, dried, and indeed cooked with milk— GarP_1,202.25.
O Mahādeva, having consumed [the substance] with honey, clarified butter, and milk, one may desire a hundred women; at that very moment it shall come to pass—of this there is no doubt.
And mercury becomes auspicious when treated with castor oil and sulfur;
sprinkled with water from the three times, it bestows strength through its consumption. (GarP 1.202.27)
Milk prepared with dehusked mung beans and seeds of *śimbā*,
when drunk with the oil of *apāmārga*, brings about desire for a hundred women.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of Various Applications of Medicinal Herbs," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 203— Hari said:
To that cow who hates her own calf, one should give her own milk mixed with salt;
then her calf will become dear to her.
Indeed, a dog’s bone tied around the neck, as well as that of a buffalo or a cow, causes the entire mass of worms to fall away; of this there is no doubt.
The hoof-print of a cow or a goat shall appear from the consumption of the root of the guñjā plant.
O Śiva, the juice of the *varuṇa* fruit, when churned with the hand,
causes the swarm of worms in four-footed and two-footed beings to fall away.
O Rudra, one should heal a wound by filling it with *jayā*;
likewise, the drinking of elephant urine indeed wards off afflictions caused by cows and buffaloes.
Lentils and rice seeds,
ground with buttermilk and drunk with the milk of a cow, a buffalo, or a bull, will be beneficial for a man.
O Śiva, if the leaf of the *śarapuṅkhā* plant is given with salt,
it destroys the bursting of the limbs caused by water and the loss of the manes of horses.
O Hara, if even a single leaf of *ghṛtakumārī*, given with the proper ritual characteristics (*salakṣaṇa*),
is applied to the mane of a horse, its itching will undoubtedly cease.

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Application of Various Medicinal Herbs," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 204 of the Śrīgaruḍamahāpurāṇa].
Sūta said:
Thus Dhanvantari spoke the science of medicine to Suśruta;
now I shall state the names of the medicinal herbs in brief.
Sthirā, vidārigandhā, śālaparṇī, aśumatī,
lāṅgalī, kalasī, kroṣṭupucchā, and guhā are considered [the eight drugs] known as the *guḍūcī* group.
Furthermore, *punarnavā* is *parṣābhū*, *kaṭhillī*, and *kāruṇā*;
likewise, *eraṇḍa* is *uruvūka*, *āmarda*, and *vardhamānaka*.
Jhaṣā is to be known as nāgabalā; śvadaṃṣṭrā is considered to be gokṣura;
śatāvarī is varā, bhīru, pīvarī, indīvarī, and varī.
Vyāghrī, bṛhatī, kṛṣṇā, haṃsapādī, and madhusravā are synonyms for dhāmanī; kaṇṭakārī, kṣudrā, siṃhī, and nidigdhikā are synonyms for the same.
Vṛścikā, tryamṛtā, kālī, viṣaghnī, sarpadaṃṣṭrikā, markaṭī, ātmaguptā, ārṣeyī, and kapikacchukā are synonyms. (GarP 1,204.6)

*Mudgaparṇī*, *kṣudrasahā*, *māṣaparṇī*, *mahāsahā*, *tyajā*, and *parā* are to be known as the great [plants]; they are designated by the names *daṇḍa*, *yonī*, and *aṅka*. *Nyagrodha* is to be known as *vaṭa*, while *aśvattha* is considered *kapila*.
The *plakṣa*, *gardabhāṇḍa*, *parkaṭī*, and *kapītana* are synonyms;
furthermore, the *pārtha*, *kakubha*, and *dhanvin* are to be known by the names of Arjuna.
The *nandīvṛkṣa* is a sprouting tree and is said to be a promoter of nourishment;
the *vañjula* is known as the *vetasa*, and the *bhallāta* is also called *aruṣkara*.
Lodhra is also known as sāravaka, dhṛṣṭa, and tirīṭa;
furthermore, the bṛhatphalā is to be known as mahājambū, while the other is bālaphalā.
The third is *jalajaṃbū*, which is also celebrated as *nādeyī*;
it is also known as *kaṇā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *upakuñcī*, *śauṇḍī*, and *māgadhikā*.
Pippalī has been described by those who know it; its root is known as granthika.
Marica is to be understood as ūṣaṇa, while śuṇṭhī is viśva and mahauṣadha.
One should know that *vyoṣa* consists of the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), and it is also celebrated as *tryūṣaṇa*.
*Lāṅgalī*, *halinī*, *śreyasī*, and *gajapippalī* are synonyms for the same.
*Trāyantī* and *trāyamāṇā* are synonyms; *utsā* is known as *suvahā*.
*Citraka* is called by the names *śikhī*, *vahnī*, and *agni*.
*Ṣaḍgranthā*, *ugrā*, *vacā*, *śvetā*, and *haimavatī* are known as synonyms.
*Kuṭaja*, *vṛkṣaka*, *śakra*, *vatsaka*, and *girimallikā* are synonyms for the same plant.
One should recognize the seeds of Kaliṅgendrayavāriṣṭa;
mustaka is known by the name megha, and kauntī should be understood as hareṇukā.
Elā is said to be of two kinds, *bahulā* and *sūkṣmailā*, as well as *truṭi*;
likewise, *padmā*, *bhārṅgī*, *kāñjī*, and *brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā* are to be known [as synonyms].
Mūrvā is known as madhurasā, tejanī, and tiktavallikā;
mahānimba and bṛhannimba are synonyms for dīpyaka, which is yavānikā.
Viḍaṅga is known as krimiśatru; rāmaṭha is indeed called hiṅgu.
Ajājī is to be understood as jīraka, and kāravī as upakuñcikā.
Kaṭukā, tiktā, and likewise kaṭukarohiṇī are to be known [by these names]. Tagara is nata, vakra; and coca is tvaca and varāṅgaka.

Kumāra said:
Now, O Kātyāyana, I shall explain grammar in brief for the sake of discerning established words and as a means for the linguistic development of beginners.

A word (pada) is known as that which ends in a nominal suffix (suP) or a verbal suffix (tiṅ). There are seven case-inflections (vibhakti) of the nominal suffixes; those beginning with su, au, and jas are declared to be the first [case], which consists of the nominal stem (prātipadika).
In the case of address, when the gender and so forth are expressed, the meaningful nominal stem—excluding verbal roots and suffixes—is [the base] in the object and the agent. GarP_1,205.3.

The second case (dvitīyā) should be used for the accusative (amauśas), as well as for that which is the object of an action; the second case is prescribed for the object, and also when joined with the particles antarā and antareṇa.
The third case ending, consisting of *ṭā*, *bhyām*, and *bhis*, is prescribed for the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).
That by which an action is performed is the instrument; he who performs it is the agent.

The fourth [case-ending] occurs after the suffixes *ṅe*, *bhyām*, and *bhyas* when the factor of action (*kāraka*) is the recipient (*sampradāna*). That for whom one has the desire to give, or whom one maintains [a feeling toward], or who finds pleasure [in receiving], is the recipient (*sampradāna*).

The fifth case ending (pañcamī) occurs after [a word] with the suffixes ṅasi, bhyām, and bhyas, when it functions as the *apādāna* kāraka—that from which one departs, from which one takes, or from which one receives danger. (GarP 1,205.7)
The sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) occurs after the suffixes ṅasi and os when the primary sense is the relationship with an owner;
the seventh case (saptamī) occurs after the suffixes ṅi and sup, and that [seventh case] pertains to the locus (adhikaraṇa).
The substratum (ādhāra) and the locus (adhikaraṇa), as well as that which is intended or unintended when used with verbs meaning "to protect" (rakṣ),
are traditionally taught to be the ablative (apādāna).
The fifth case (pañcamī) occurs in connection with *pary-upa*, as well as with *itarat*, *ṛte*, and words denoting directions other than one's own;
the second case (dvitīyā) occurs in connection with *ena* and with those termed *karmapravacanīya*.
The prefixes *pari*, *pra*, and *ati* are used in the sense of desire (*vīpsā*), suchness (*itthambhāva*), and a mark (*cihna*).
*Anu* is said to be used with the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*) and in the sense of inferiority (*hīna*). *Upa* is also used in the sense of inferiority.
The second and fourth case endings are used for the action of motion in the sense of movement;
however, when the object is inanimate, both case endings are used in the sense of disregard regarding the object of the verb *man* (to think).
The use of *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed [with the dative];
likewise, the fourth case is used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*), as well as after words expressing an action (*bhāvavācin*) when they have the sense of the infinitive suffix *-tum*.

The third case (instrumental) occurs in connection with "saha" (with); the seventh case (locative) occurs when denoting a limb, a qualifier, time, or a state; and the sixth case (genitive) also occurs in connection with these.
With *svāmī*, *īśvara*, and *adhipati*, the sixth case is used when expressing a witness, an heir, or offspring;
when expressing a selection from a group, two cases are used; and when employing a cause (*hetu*), the sixth case is used.
Likewise, when used with a verb meaning "to remember," with the verb *kṛ* in the sense of "preparation," and with verbs meaning "to injure" in the sense of the object,
the suffix *kṛt* denotes the agent as the object.
The sixth case (genitive) is not used for the agent or the object when used with past passive participles (*niṣṭhā*).
A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is of two kinds: namely, the noun and likewise the verbal root (*dhātu*).
From the roots *bhū* and *vādi*, the suffixes *tiṅ* and *la* arise; indeed, ten types of *lakāra* are traditionally taught.
*Ti*, *tas*, and *jhi* constitute the first person; *si*, *thas*, and *tha* the middle person; and *mi*, *vas*, and *mas* the highest person (*uttamapūruṣa*).
The *parasmaipada* endings are *mi*, *vas*, and *mas*; the *ātmanepada* endings are *ta*, *ātām*, and *jha*.
The first person consists of *ti*, *tas*, and *anti*; the middle person consists of *si*, *thas*, and *tha*; and the last person consists of *mi*, *vas*, and *mas*. 1,205.19.
The substitutes for *iḍ*, *bahis*, and *mahi* are derived from the verbal root, as well as those beginning with *ṇic*;
even when a noun is employed [as the subject], the first person [of the verb] shall occur.
The second person is said to be used with *yuṣmad* (you), and the first person with *asmad* (I/we);
the roots beginning with *bhū* are declared to be *dhātus*, as are those ending in *san* and so forth.
The suffix *laṭ* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) for the present tense; *liṭ* for the past; *laṅ* optionally for the remote past;
and *loṭ* and others for the benedictive after a verbal root.
The imperative mood (*loṭ*) is prescribed at the very beginning of an injunction;
it may also be used for addressing, as well as for invitation, entreaty, inquiry, request, and benediction.

The *liṅ* occurs for the past that is beyond the senses; the *liṭ* occurs for the past; the *lṛṭ* occurs for the future; and likewise, [the *luṭ*] occurs for the future not belonging to the current day, derived from the verbal root.
The conditional (lṛṅ) is prescribed for the donor when there is non-occurrence of the action; the subjunctive (leṭ) is proclaimed in the sense of the optative (liṅ).
The kṛt suffixes occur in all three [voices]: in the impersonal (bhāva), the passive (karman), and the active (kartṛ).
The suffixes -tavya, -anīya, and those beginning with -tṛ are similar to [the agentive suffix] -ta.
Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Grammar," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

I shall state the examples of established usage, preceded by the rules of phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*) and so forth: "O Brahmins, you have come; behold this most excellent [teaching]; may he be the bull among fathers. (GarP 1.206.1)
The letter *ḷ* is renowned as *seva*; by means of wisdom, it is the plow-pole (*lāṅgalīṣā*).
The letter *tav* is the water of the Gaṅgā; it is also *ṛṇa*, *arṇa*, and *prārṇa*.
One who is afflicted by cold, a goldsmith, one who serves Indra, one who serves Suka,
a son-in-law, one who sits on a seat, one who acts for the sake of his ancestors, and one who is bound by a debt— one should conquer these in the science of policy.
The leader, salt, and cows—these are not lords;
rather, know that the two skillful ones here are the temple of the Goddess.
"These horses are his six"—that is not speech; "the six petals"—that is the practice; "it moves, it does not transcend"—that is water; that is the cremation ground.
"O Sugata, you cook here; O Bhagavat, you cover [the fire];
from you comes the crackling sound, and it is remembered that you cross over [the world]. (GarP 1,206.6)
You write upon that wheel; you lie down, yet you are unlike others;
you traverse the interior of the cosmic egg, and you always perform worship.
Who acts with difficulty? Who does what? Who abides in the fruit?
Who lies down? Who is impotent? And who attains dignity?
"Who is here? Who indeed is it? "The gods say so; they say, 'O, go!
"Viṣṇu, who is self-born, goes, as does Gīṣpati and Dhūrpati."
This [world] would go toward us, and that [other world] goes toward its own vision and sound;
likewise, the shadow of a hut is but a shadow, and other junctions (*saṃdhi*) are of such a nature.
Six types of compounds have been enumerated: that which is the *dvija*, the *karmadhāraya*, the *dvigu*, the *trivedī*, the *grāma*, and this one is known as the *tatpuruṣa*.
That which is caused by it, that which has it as its object, fear of a wolf, or wealth [acquired]—
one who knows the truth, being skilled in knowledge, [should analyze these] as a *bahuvrīhi* or an *avyayībhāva*.
The suffix *bhāva* is used in relation to feminine nouns; however, as previously stated, *dvandva* compounds include gods, sages, and humans.
Examples of *taddhita* derivatives include *pāṇḍavaḥ*, *śaivaḥ*, *brāhmaṃ*, and *brahmatā* and so forth.
The words *deva*, *agni*, *sakhi*, *pati*, *aṃśu*, *kroṣṭu*, and *svāyambhuva* are masculine;
likewise, *nā*, *praśasta*, *cara*, *gaura*, and *glau* are masculine when ending in *-aj*. GarP_1,206.14 //
Halanta, Aśvayuj, Kṣmābhuj, Marut, Kravyād, Mṛgāvidh,
Ātman, Rājan, Yuvan, Panthān, Pūṣan, Brahmahan, and Halin.
Viḍve, dhā, uśanā, anaḍvān, madhuliṭ, kāṣṭhataṭ,
likewise vanavāri, asthi, vastu, jagatsāma, and ahanī.
The neuter nouns ending in *a*, *i*, and *u* are like clarified butter (*sarpi*), vapour (*vapū*), and fire (*teja*).
Also included are *jāyā*, *jarā*, *nadī*, *lakṣmī*, *śrī*, *strī*, *bhūmi*, and *vadhū*.
Furthermore, *bhrū*, *punarbhū*, *dhenu*, *svasṛ*, and *mātṛ* are feminine; likewise, *vāk*, *sraj*, *diś*, *ut*, *kruddh*, *yuvati*, and *kukubh* are generally feminine.
Dyu and divau, as well as prāvṛṣ, are [names for] the rainy season; sumāna is used for the uṣṇih meter in the feminine.
Now I shall tell you of those words which, through their connection with qualities, substances, or actions, take feminine gender. GarP_1,206.19 //
Śuklakīlāpa, Śuci, Grāmaṇī, Sudhī, Paṭu, Kamalabhū, Kartṛ, Sumata, Bahava, and Sunau. GarP_1,206.20 //
Truth, fire, and likewise man; indeed, he who does not eat [the forbidden], Dīrghapāt;
all, the universe, both, and those two; one, the other, and whichever of the two.
Ḍatara, ḍatama, nema, tva, sama, as well as sima and itara; and likewise pūrva, adhara, dakṣiṇa, uttara, and avara. (GarP 1.206.22)

Furthermore, this [distinction] between "para" (the other) and "antara" (the internal), as well as whatever is expressed by "kim" (who/what) and "adas" (that), consists of the forms derived from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which are halved according to their status as first or last and their degree of brevity.
Likewise, *katipaya*, *dvau*, and so forth— all such words—
as well as *śṛṇoti* and the like, *juhoti*, *jahāti*, and *dadhāti*.
He blazes and praises; he desires a son and desires wealth; he breaks and dies; he wishes to accumulate and wishes to lead.
All abide in all, for all; from all, it has gone everywhere;
and in all of all, as well as in everything—thus are Viśva and the others.
"Former, former things, from the former, in the former, and the former have been declared.
Sūta said:
"The forms ending in nominal and verbal suffixes have been shown merely by their names in their established forms."
Kātyāyana, having heard it from the youth, spoke at length.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The First [Section on] Conduct," in the first part of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—207.
Sūta said:
Having bowed to my teacher Vāsudeva, to Gaṇeśa, to Śambhu, and to Sarasvatī,
I shall explain prosody according to the distinctions of meters, measures, and syllables for those of limited intellect.
The groups (gaṇas) consist of three syllables each: *ma*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, *ja*, *ra*, *sa*, and *ta* at the beginning, middle, and end of all [feet].
In the Āryā meter, there are four groups of four syllables each at the beginning, end, and throughout the middle.
A syllable ending in a consonant, those ending in a visarga, a long vowel followed by a conjunct consonant,
and one at the end of a quarter-verse (pāda) when accompanied by an anusvāra— these are said to be heavy (guru), consisting of two mātrās.

When there is no sequence in the yoga, nor even a slight lightness in what is heavy, there may be the designations of *śloka*, *cāryā*, and so forth; the pause (*yati*) is known as the break (*viccheda*).
A quarter is to be known as a fourth part; even is that which is even, while uneven is that which is odd.
A meter is even, half-even, or uneven; the third [type] is the uneven.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Definition of Technical Terms and Designations in Prosody," in the section on Conduct (*Ācārakāṇḍa*) within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
The *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 208.
Sūta said:

In the Āryā meter, there are eight gaṇas; the *ja* gaṇa always occurs in the odd positions. In the sixth position, there may be a *ja*, *na*, or *la* gaṇa, provided that the sixth syllable is not the second syllable of a word.

In the first half, there are seven short syllables; then in the second half, five [short syllables] followed by a foot of three gaṇas. This is Pathyā; Vipulā occurs when there is a deviation from the fire (three) and the wind (two).

In the middle of the [verse], the *capalā* consists of two *jagaṇas* and two *jagaṇas*; it is called *mukhacapalā* when [the first *jagaṇa*] is at the beginning, and *jaghanacapalā* when it is in the second half; these are the characteristics of the *āryā* meter.
If the characteristics of the first half of an Āryā are found in both halves, it is a Gīti;
if they are found from the second half onwards, it is an Upagīti; and by reversal [of these positions], it becomes an Udgīti.
The Āryāgīti has a heavy syllable at the end; this is the characteristic of the Gotījāti class.

If there are six *kalās* in the odd quarters and eight in the even ones, provided they are not contiguous; in the *vaitālīya*, the even quarter should not depend on the following one, and the *ra-la-gu* (r, l, and a heavy syllable) [constitute the cadence].
The two preceding [feet] are as before; this is considered to be the *aupacchandasika* meter.
When there are *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* [in the first quarter], it should be known as *āpātalikā*;
then, when the second [quarter] has *la* dependent on another (*parāśrita*) in all its feet, it is *dakṣiṇāntikā*.
When the *udīcyavṛtti* occurs on the odd [pādas] and the *prācyavṛtti* on the even [pādas],
with the fifth syllable occurring simultaneously in the fourth quarter, it is the *pravṛttaka*.

The *cāruhāsinī* consists of the union of the first quarter with a northern [syllable], while the *yugmapādaikapādikā* occurs when there is an odd-numbered foot; this is the summary of the *vaitālīya*.
One should not eat [this] at the beginning; these two would not exist if the fourth and subsequent gaṇas were present.
Pathyāvakra occurs with *ja* in even [pādas], while otherwise it is Viparītādi.
In that [meter], there are *na*, *sa*, *ca*, *pa*, *la*, *vi*, *pu*, and *la* with a seventh light syllable;
or, according to Saitava, it consists of *ma*, *ra*, *u*, *ta*, *u*, followed by four *ga*s (the ocean).
That which consists of sixteen *la* syllables and possesses immovable stability is called *mātrāsamaka*.

Likewise, when there is a *na*, *ma*, *la*, *ta*, *tha*, *ga*, and finally a *ja* and *na*, or alternatively, four *ga*s followed by two *la*s, it is a *viśloka*; or else, from that same [pattern], doubling the *ga*s results in a *dvānavāsikā*.
In the [syllables] five, eight, and nine, there should be a *la*; *citrā* consists of sixteen parts.
That which is taught as having equal and unequal *mātrās* is called *padākulaka*.

In the petals, it is determined that the measure is always such that there are no syllables without the *la* [mora], no *la* moras without the heavy syllables (*guru*), and no heavy syllables without the *la* [moras]. GarP_1,208.15 //
In the first half, the *śikhā* consists of twenty-eight *tala*s; in the second, it consists of thirty. From this *khañja*, its reversal occurs.
In the first two feet there are sixteen *gaṇas* of *anaṅgakrīḍā*, and in the last foot there are thirty-two *la*s;
with twenty-seven *ti*s and *lā*s, it is called *rucirā* when both halves are identical.
The meters measured by morae (mātrāvṛtta) have been explained; now I shall indeed speak of the meters measured by syllables (varṇavṛtta).

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Āryā and Other Metres," in the section on Prosody within the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—209.
Sūta said:
She is to be known as Śrīrukthā by the *genus* (gaṇa) *utyukthā*, which consists of two long syllables (*gurudvaya*).
A woman with the *mo* [syllable] is a *nārī*; one with *ro* is a *mṛgī*; one with *magau* is a *kanyā* of the *pratiṣṭhā* [meter].
O cowherd, *paṅkti* is well-established; *tanumadhyā* is known as *tayau*.
With two *na*s and two *ya*s, it is *bālalalitā*; indeed, these are the *gāyatrī* meters.
Masagair is Madalekhā; uṣṇik is the meter known by the wise.
Bhau-gau is celebrated as Citrapadā; Vidyunmālā consists of ma-ma-ga-ga.
The *māṇavaka* consists of the sequence bha, ta, la, ga; the *haṃsaruta* is known as ma, na, u, ga; the *samānikā* is ra, ja, ga, la; and the *pramāṇikā* is ja, ra, la, ga.
Any other [meter] besides these two is called *vitāna*; this is declared to be the *anuṣṭubh* meter.

With *ra*, *na*, *sa*, and *ma* [syllables], there is the *halamukhī*; with *na*, *u*, *ma*, and *śiśubhṛtā*, it becomes the *bṛhatī* meter; it is said that *smau* followed by *ja* and *ga* is the *virājitam*.
Paṇava consists of ma, na, ya, ga;
mayūrasāriṇī consists of ma, ra, ja, ra, ga; and rukmavatī consists of bha, ma, sa, ga.
The *manoramā* meter born of men consists of *ma*, *ta*, *ma*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ga*;
the *paṅkti* meter is declared to consist of *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, *ga*, and two *ga*s; and the *upasthita* consists of *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, *ga*, and two *ga*s.
That which consists of *ja*, *ta*, *ga*, *na*, *ja*, *ga*, preceded by *gu* (two *ga*s), is the *indravajrā*.

Upajātis consist of various combinations of these [meters] at the beginning and end; Sumukhī is na, ja, ja, with a ga and a la; Dodhaka is bha, bha, bha, with two gas; and Śālinī is ma, ta, ta, with two gas.

The *Abdhiloka* consists of five and six syllables; it has a pause at the fifth and sixth [syllables], and its feet are described as *vā*, *tū*, *rmā*, *ma*, *ta*, *tā*, *ga*, *ga*, *śrī*, *bhā*, *tau*, *na*, *na*, and *gā*. GarP_1,209.10 //
The *maganā* is said to have the playful grace of a bee;
*rathoddhatā* consists of *na*, *ra*, *la*, and *ga*; and *svāgatā* consists of *ra*, *na*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga*.
Vṛttā consists of *na*, *na*, *sa*, *ga*, and *ga*; *samadrikā* consists of *na*, *na*, *ra*, *la*, and *ga*.
*Śyenikā* consists of *ra*, *ja*, *ra*, *la*, and *ga*; *śikhaṇḍita* consists of *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, *ga*, and *ga*. Thus has the *triṣṭubh* meter been fully described by the high-souled Piṅgala.
*Vaṃśastha* consists of *ra-na-bha-sa*, while *jaga-jara* is *vaṃśasthavila*.
From that, *jaga-ra* is *indravaṃśā*; with four *ta*s, it is known as *toṭaka*.
*nabha-bhrau* is *drutavilambita*, and *nanama-ya* is *puṭa*.
This Muditavadanā, whose face is joyful, is described as having eight, four, and five [syllables], and likewise as having nine, seven, and six [syllables]. GarP_1,209.14 //

But that *stragviṇī* is considered to have the syllables *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and *sa* in its feet, with a *rasa* (six) gaṇas, and it is variegated with flowers, its movement surging with water. *GarP_1,209.15*
The *bhujaṅgaprayāta* metre is proclaimed to consist of four *ya*s;
*prayaṃvadā* consists of *na*, *bha*, and *ja*s; and *maṇimālā* consists of *ta*, *ya*, *ta*, and *ya*.
With *ga*, *bha*, and *ja* gaṇas, it is *sannidrā*; with *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, and *ra*, it is *lalitā*;
with *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *sa*, it is *pramitākṣarā*; and with *na*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*, it is *ujjvalā*.
The Vaiśvadevī consists of the meters ma-ma-u and ya-ya-u; its pause occurs after five syllables.
The Jaladharamālā consists of sa-ma-bha-sa; its pause occurs at the fourth and last (twelfth) syllables.

The *praharṣiṇī* metre consists of *na*, *ta*, *ta*, *ga*, and *kṣa*; it has a pause after the fourth and sixth syllables (*rasaiḥ*). The *manajaragāḥ* (with *ma*, *na*, *ja*, *ra*, *ga*) have pauses at the third, seventh, and tenth syllables (*vahnibhiḥ daśabhiḥ*).
*Rucirā* consists of *ja*, *bha*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*, with a pause (*yati*) after four and seven syllables;
*Mattamayūra* consists of *ma*, *ta*, *ya*, *sa*, and *ga*, with a pause after seven and four syllables.
*Mañjubhāṣiṇī* is *sajasā jsau*; *Sunandinī* is *sajasā magau*;
*Candrikā* is *nanau tatau gaḥ*, with a pause at the seventh and sixth syllables.

The *Aparājitā* meter is said to consist of seven syllables with no restriction (*asambādhā*), a pause (*yati*) at the fifth syllable (*matanasā*), and the sequence *na-na-ra-sa-la-gu* (with pauses at the fifth and twelfth syllables). GarP_1,209.22.

This *praharaṇakalikā* consists of *na*, *na*, *bha*, and *na*, followed by *la* and *ga*; likewise, *vasantatilakā* consists of *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, *ja*, *ga*, and *gu*. *Siṃhonnatā* consists of *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, *ja*, *ga*, and *gu*. GarP_1,209.23 //
The *śarkarī* meter is established when the feet consist of the syllables *bha, ja, sa, na, ga, ga, i, ndu, va, da, na, tha, su, ke, śa, ra, m*, and *na, ra, na, ra, la, ga*. GarP_1,209.24.
The fourteenth [syllable] shall be light; the *śreṣṭhā* consists of a *ga*, a *sa*, and a *la*;
it has a pause at the sixth and seventh syllables, and likewise a pause at the eighth and seventh syllables in the *sraksrā*.
The *mālinī* consists of a cluster of eight *ma* syllables; when it has a *na*, a *na*, and a *ya*, it becomes the *nanamā*.
When it has a *va*, a *sa*, a *u*, a *ra*, and a *ya*, it is the *vasusvarayatiḥ*. And with a *na*, a *ja*, and *bha-jra-s*, it is the *prabhadraka*.

That which consists of *elā*, *sayau*, *nanau*, and *yaḥ*, along with the eight syllables of *citralekhā* and *svarāṣṭaka*; and that which consists of *marau* and *mayau*—this is called the *ati-śarkarī*.

From *svarā* comes *kha*; *vṛṣabhagajajṛmbhita* consists of *bha*, *na*, *na*, *ga*, *na*, *ga*; *vāṇinī* consists of *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *ra*, with a *ga* at the end; this has been declared as the *aṣṭi* meter by Piṅgala.
The *śikhariṇī* consists of six, eleven, and seven syllables; its structure is na-sa-bha-la-ga with a caesura at the eighth and fifth syllables.
The *pṛthvī* consists of eight, eight, and six syllables; its structure is ja-sa-ja-sa-ya-la-ga.

*Vaṃśapatrapatita* consists of ten vowels [and the following consonants]; *Bhramaravilasita* has *la*, *ga*, *na*, *bha*, and *la*; and *Hariṇī* consists of six, four, and seven [mātrās], with *na*, *sa*, *ma*, *ra*, *sa*, *la*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*).
Mandākrāntā consists of six *gaṇas*, four *ma*s, one *bha*, one *na*, one *ta*, one *ga*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*).
Nardaṭaka consists of one *na*, one *ja*, one *bha*, one *ja*, two *la*s, a *ga*, and a *yati*. GarP_1,209.31.
Kokilaka consists of seven, six, and four [mātrās]; atyaṣṭi is as before. Kusumitalatā has five, six, and seven [mātrās] with the gaṇas ma, ta, ya, and ya; dhṛti has twelve [mātrās].

Śārdūlavikrīḍita consists of ra, sa, ra, ta, ya, ma, na, sa, ra, and ga (17 syllables), with pauses at the sixth, ninth, and twelfth syllables; Meghavisphūrjita consists of ma, sa, ja, sa, ta, ta, and ga (19 syllables), with pauses at the twelfth and seventeenth syllables.
Chanda is said to be Atidhṛti; after that, Kṛti occurs. [Its definition is:
seven horses (m), seasons (j), Suvadanā (bha), bha, ra, ma, na, ya, bha, la, and a heavy syllable (g).
In the Vṛtta meter, when there are two *ra* (r) gaṇas and two *ja* (j) gaṇas in each quarter, with a *ga* (g) and a *la* (l), it is called Kṛti.

When there are three *sa* (s), *na* (n), *ga* (g), and *ra* (r) gaṇas, it is Sragdharā; and when there are *ma* (m), *na* (n), *bha* (b), *na* (n), *ta* (t), *tri* (three *ra*s), and *ya* (y), it is Prakṛti.

With *dig* (ten), *arka* (twelve), *bhadra* (sixteen), *bhr* (four), *nrau* (two nasals), *naranā* (three nasals and one nasal), and *go* (nine), it is *yathākṛti*; with *na*, *ja*, and *bha* (one, two, and one heavy syllable), it is *aśvalalita*; and with *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *bha*, *la*, and *ga* (one, one, one, one, one light, and one heavy), it is so.
When the *mattākrīḍa* consists of eight *baṇas*, ten *mas*, *na*, *na*, *la*, *la*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*) in the body of the verse, it is called *vikṛti-chinnā-saṃkṛti*.

In the *krauñcapadā* meter, there are five, seven, and twelve syllables in the first foot; then *bha*, *ta*, *nu*, *i*, *na*, *sa*, *bhā*, *bha*, *na*, and *ya* constitute the groups [of syllables]; and in the second foot, there are five, five, eight, and seven syllables, followed by *bha*, *ma*, *u*, *sa*, and *bhau*.
Nine and nine [syllables] are declared to be *atikṛti*; indeed, *utkṛti* is said to be [ten and ten].
With eight, eleven, seven, and seven [syllables], there is *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita*.
With nine rasas and six laghus, the caesura is called apavāha; with six guhas (rasas), five bāṇas, and six monās, the gaṇas are sa, ga, and ga.
This Daṇḍaka is a fall into fierce conduct; therefore, one should not go there.
From this [Daṇḍaka], by increasing the *ra* at the end, there arise the Vyāla, Jīmūta, and other varieties.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Equal Meters and Other Verses," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 210] Sūta said:
If there are *sa*, *sa*, *sa*, *la*, and *ga* in the odd quarters (*pāda*), and *bha*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* in the even ones, it is *Upacitraka*;
likewise, *bha*, *bha*, *bha*, and *ga* constitute *Drutamadhyā*.
In the odd quarters, *ga* is [the first syllable], and in the other [even quarters], the groups *na*, *ja*, and *jya* are prescribed.
In the *viṣama* (odd) feet, the *vegavatī* consists of the gaṇas sa, ga, and bha; in the *sama* (even) feet, they are bha, bha, ga, ga.
In the *viṣama* feet, the *ketumatī* consists of ta, ja, ra, and ga; in the *sama* feet, they are ma, sa, ja, ga, and a guru.
Thus there arises the *bhadravirāṭ*. However, in the *viṣama* feet, it is *sajau* (sa, ja).
In the *sagaṇa* [meter], if the even feet consist of *bha*, *ra*, *na*, *ga*, and *ga*, it is called *ākhyānakī*;
likewise, if the odd feet consist of *ta*, *ja*, *ja*, *ga*, and two *gurus*, it is [the same]. (GarP 1.210.4)

Viparītākhyānaka consists of the syllables ja, ta, ja, ga, and ga in the odd positions; likewise, ta, ta, ja, ga, and ga in the even positions, with a 'ga' at the end—thus it has been illustrated by Piṅgala.
They say that when the first foot is odd (viṣama), it is Puṣpitāgrā with the syllabic sequence na-na-ra-ya;
when even (sama), it is Vaitālīya with the sequence na-ja-ja-ra-ga.
The other [type] is called Aparavaktra, and the next is Aupacchandasika.
Vāṅmatī is that [meter] which consists of the gaṇas ra, ja, ra, ja, and ra in uneven [pādas].
Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Half-Samavṛtta Metres and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Chapter 211 of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*].
Sūta said:
The first quarter consists of eight syllables, the second of twelve syllables,
the third of sixteen syllables, and the fourth of twenty syllables.
For the general characteristic of that which is below is indeed established by means of the *padacaturūrdhva* meters.
The *āpīḍa* is declared to consist entirely of *sarvalas*, with two [syllables] occurring at the end of each preceding quarter-verse.
In the second [verse], when the feet consist of eight syllables, it is the *kalikā*; in the first [verse] it is the *arkaja*.
Then, in the third [verse], when there are likewise eight syllables per foot, it is the *lavalī*.
This is declared to be the *amṛtadhārā* when there are four feet of eight syllables each.
(Thus ends the section on *padacaturūrdhva* meters.

In the first [quarter], there are *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *la*; in the second, *na*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*; in the third, *bha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ga*; and in the fourth, *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*.
Saurabhaka would be as before, with *ra*, *na*, *bha*, and *ga* in the third foot;
and Lalita would be like Adgatā, with *na*, *na*, *sa*, and *sa* in the third foot.
(Thus ends the section on Udgatā.
Upasthitapracupita consists of: in the first foot, ma, sa, ja, and bha;
in the second, ga and ga; in the third, sa, na, ja, ra, and ga; and in the fourth, na, na, and sa.
Nine *najas* should be in the fourth [foot], and the remaining feet are as before.
In the third foot there is a specific rule: the meter *Nau-sanau-nasau* (na, u, sa, na, u, na, sa) constitutes a *Vṛtta*.
If there is a *ta* and a *ja* in the third foot, and the rest is as before, it is the *Ārṣabha*;
if the first foot is as before and the remaining feet have *ta*, *ja*, and *ra*, it becomes the *Śuddhavirāj*.
(Thus ends the section on the *upasthitapracupita* meter.

Alternatively, a verse (*gāthā*) may consist of feet with an uneven number of syllables, such as five or six, up to eleven; in this case, it is not called a *chandas*, but rather a *gāthā*, as in the case of the *daśadharmaka* and other such verses. (GarP 1,211.9)

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Irregular Meters and Other Topics," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—212.
Sūta said:
In the *prastāra* method, first place a *la*; then, for the subsequent [syllables], place one equal to the preceding;
when the number is even in the process of finding the missing [syllable], place a *la*, and when it is even in the half-measure, if it is odd, place a *guru*.
The reverse-order quality is to be taken; that which was taught twice is to be subtracted once.
In the case of the form "two," the number is zero; in the case of "zero," it is said to be doubled.
When halved that many times, it is multiplied by that [number], and finally, it is diminished by two twice over.
In the other [directions], it is full; in the other [directions], it is full; thus Meru would be level when spread out.
The number of fingers and the number of metrical feet, starting from the first finger and moving upwards, are doubled and then diminished by one; this is declared as the *Chandaḥsāra*.
Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Prosody," in the first section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 213 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Sūta said:
O Śaunaka, just as Brahmā spoke to Vyāsa after hearing it from Hari,
so shall I tell you that conduct beginning with the duties of the Brāhmaṇas, which bestows all things.
Having understood the Śruti and the Smṛti, one should perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti;
if the Śrauta rite is not prescribed, then one should perform the Smārta rite.
If one is unable to perform even that, the wise person should practice the conduct of the virtuous;
for the Śruti and Smṛti are the eyes of the Brahmins for perceiving their duties.
The supreme dharma is that declared in the Śruti; the secondary is that contained in the Smṛti scriptures;
and that which is attained through the conduct of the virtuous—these are the three eternal dharmas.
Truthfulness, charity, compassion, freedom from greed, knowledge, sacrifice, worship, and self-restraint—
these eight are the purifiers and the characteristics of the conduct of the virtuous.
The bodies and sense organs of those ancestors were composed of light;
they are not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
The primary dwellings and the religious practices of the social classes have been proclaimed;
truth, sacrifice, austerity, and charity—this is the characteristic of dharma.
Non-appropriation of what is not given, charity, study, silent recitation,
knowledge, wealth, austerity, purity, birth in a noble family, and freedom from disease.
The cause for the cessation of saṃsāra proceeds from dharma alone;
from dharma come happiness and knowledge, and from knowledge liberation is attained.
Sacrificing, studying, and giving according to the scriptures are declared to be the eternal common duty of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts from a pure person—
these three modes of livelihood, the sages say, are for those of the highest caste.
Living by the sword, protecting living beings,
and tending cattle, agriculture, and trade are recorded as the means of livelihood for a king and a Vaiśya, respectively.

For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born; for the twice-born, service according to their respective order; and for the religious student (brahmacārin), residence with the teacher, service to the sacred fires, and the study of the Veda.
Having bathed three times [daily], having caused [the teacher] to bathe, he should subsist on alms for his teacher; his stay [with him] lasts until the end of life.
Wearing a girdle, with matted hair, carrying a staff, or shaven-headed, he should take refuge in his teacher.
He should perform the Agnihotra ritual and maintain his livelihood through his own duties;
he may engage in sexual intercourse with his lawful wife on occasions other than the sacred festival days.
The performance of worship and other rites for the gods, ancestors,
and guests, and the steadfast adherence to the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti— this is the dharma of the householder.
Wearing matted hair, maintaining the sacred fire, sleeping on the ground, wearing deerskin,
dwelling in the forest, and subsisting on milk, roots, wild rice, and fruits.
Abstaining from prohibited foods, bathing three times a day, maintaining the observances of a vow,
and honoring the deities and guests— this is the dharma of the forest-dweller.
The renunciation of all undertakings, subsisting on alms-food, dwelling at the foot of trees, freedom from possessiveness, absence of malice, and equanimity toward all living beings.
The capacity for experiencing pleasure and pain through contact with the pleasant and unpleasant;
internal and external purity; restraint of speech; and the practice of meditation.
The withdrawal of all the senses, constancy in concentration and meditation,
and the complete purification of one's being— this is called the dharma of the wandering mendicant.
Non-violence, speech that is pleasant and true, truthfulness, purity, forbearance,
and compassion are said to be the common dharma for both those belonging to the social orders (varṇas) and those bearing the marks of religious orders (liṅgins).
All those who act according to what has been taught attain the supreme goal.
From the time of awakening until sleep, I shall describe to you the dharma of the householder.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as physical austerities rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Having risen at the end of the night, having performed purification and being composed,
one should, untiring at all times, bathe and perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).
One should perform the morning twilight devotion preceded by the cleansing of the teeth;
and during the day, one should void both urine and feces while facing the north.
And at night he should perform [the rites] facing south, and during both twilights just as during the day;
whether in shade or in darkness, by night or by day, the twice-born man [should act].
However, as for how one who is face-to-face should act during dangers that threaten life:
[one should do so] on auspicious ground consisting of cow dung, charcoal, anthills, or ploughed earth.
One should not void urine or feces in the shade of trees that provide livelihood for travelers,
nor within water, nor in a temple, nor at an anthill, nor on a spot where mice dwell.
One should avoid taking earth from the dwellings of others, from what has been left over after purification, or from a cremation ground.
One should apply one application of earth to the penis, and two applications of earth to the left hand.
Two [clods] should be given for both; this is declared to be the purification with urine:
one for the penis, three for the anus, and likewise ten for the left hand.
Five [handfuls] for the feet, ten for each hand, and seven handfuls of earth;
the first application of earth is recorded as being the measure of half a prasṛti.
The second and third [periods] are proclaimed to be half of that;
he who, while seated, is unable to void excrement or urine [should wait].
He should always perform half of his own prescribed purification;
for purification performed by day, half of that is prescribed for the night, or else a quarter.
But while these are prescribed for one who is healthy, one who is afflicted should perform them according to their strength:
fat, semen, blood, marrow, saliva, feces, urine, earwax, and excrement.
Phlegm, tears, rheum from the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of men;
one should perform purification only as much as one considers necessary for cleanliness.
The number of purifications is not limited by specific injunctions;
indeed, purification is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.
External purification is said to be by means of earth and water, while internal purification is the purity of one's disposition.
First, one should sip water three times; then, one should wipe the mouth twice.
Having wiped [the mouth] with the base of the thumb, one should touch the mouth three times;
thereafter, immediately after, one should touch the nose with the thumb and the forefinger.
Again and again, one should touch the eyes and ears with the thumb and ring finger;
the navel with the little finger and thumb, and the heart with the palm.
Then, with all [the fingers], he should touch the head, and subsequently the two arms with the tips;
by reciting the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas three times, he should gratify them in due order.
First, he wipes twice with the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*, then that brings happiness;
[he recites] the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, and the *Vedāṅgas*, the *Vedāṅgas*, in due order.
One should touch the ether in the mouth, the wind in the nostrils, the sun in the eyes, the directions in the ears,
the knot of the vital breaths at the navel, and Brahmā in the heart.
Having touched the head with the Rudra [mantra], one gratifies [Rudra]; then the crest with the Ṛṣis;
and the arms with Yama, Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vasudhā, and Anala.
Having sprinkled water on his feet, he should meditate on Viṣṇu and Indra;
on both hands, Agni and Vāyu; and on the joints of the fingers, Sūrya, Candra, and the mountains.
The Gaṅgā and other rivers are those lines situated in the middle of the hand;
when the time of dawn has arrived, one should perform purification according to the rules.
Thereafter, one should perform the bath preceded by the cleansing of the teeth;
for when the mouth is stale, a man is always impure.
Therefore, with every effort, one should indeed perform the cleansing of the teeth using the *kadamba*,
*bilva*, *khadira*, *karavīra*, *vaṭa*, or *arjuna* trees.
The *yūthī*, *bṛhatī*, *jātī*, *karañja*, *arka*, and *atimuktaka*;
the *jambū*, *madhūka*, *pāmārga*, *śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, and *asana* trees.
Trees such as the *kṣīrī* and the *kaṇṭakī*, which are pungent, bitter, and astringent, are recommended for cleaning the teeth; they bestow wealth, health, and happiness.
Having washed and eaten, and having discarded [the remains] in a clean place, one should then perform ācamana;
likewise on the new moon day, as well as on the sixth, ninth, and first lunar days.
One should avoid using a tooth-stick on the day of the sun (Sunday),
as well as when a tooth-stick is unavailable or on a prohibited lunar day.
One should perform the cleansing of the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of these.
They praise the morning bath as beneficial, bringing about both visible and invisible results.
The pure-souled one, bathing in the morning, performs the recitation of mantras and other rites;
yet the body is extremely impure and endowed with nine apertures.
This [impurity] flows day and night; therefore, the morning bath is a means of purification, producing clarity of mind and increasing beauty and good fortune.
One should perform that which pacifies grief and suffering, like a bath in the Gaṅgā,
today under the constellation Hasta, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
And in the Daśapāpaharā, having not given away the impurity of one's gifts, there is indeed contrary conduct, violence, and the pursuit of another's wife. (GarP 1.213.57)
Harsh speech, falsehood, slander, incoherent talk,
speaking of the property of others, and thinking of what is undesirable in the mind.
For the purpose of destroying the afflictions of these ten states, I perform this bath in the Gaṅgā;
for forest-dwellers and householders, the morning bath is performed briefly.
The ascetic should bathe three times a day, while the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) does so once;
having sipped water and invoked the sacred ford (tīrtha), he should bathe while remembering the imperishable Hari.
It should be known that there are thirty million Rākṣasas named Mandehas;
these evil-minded beings desire to devour the rising sun.
He who does not perform the twilight worship slays the sun;
[the gods] consume him with water purified by mantras, which takes the form of fire.
The junction of day and night is indeed called *saṃdhyā*;
that *saṃdhyā* lasts for two *nāḍikās*, as long as visibility remains.
At the conclusion of the Gandhyā rite, however, the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed to be performed by oneself;
for the fruit that results from performing the oblation oneself is not produced by another.
Whatever is offered by a sacrificial priest, a son, a teacher, a brother, a sister’s son, or a husband,
that indeed is as if offered by oneself.
Brahmā is indeed the Gārhapatya fire; the three-eyed Lord is the Dakṣiṇāgni;
Viṣṇu is the Āhavanīya fire; and Kumāra is called Satya.
Having performed the fire oblation at the proper time, he should then recite the solar mantras with a concentrated mind, as well as the Sāvitrī and the Praṇava, according to the prescribed rule.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, in the seven *vyāhṛtis*,
and in the three-footed *sāvitrī*, no fear exists anywhere.
The person who, having risen at dawn, constantly recites the Gāyatrī,
is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
She is described as being white in color, likewise clothed in silk garments;
the auspicious goddess holds a rosary and is seated upon a lotus throne.
Having invoked according to the rule with this sacrificial formula, "Thou art splendor," this *yajus* was formerly seen by the gods who desired the vision of the Divine Eye.
Having invoked her who resides within the solar disc and also abides in the world of Brahmā,
and having recited the mantra there, one should then dismiss her with a salutation.
One should perform the worship of the deities precisely in the forenoon;
for there is no god higher than Viṣṇu, therefore one should always worship him.
A wise person should not conceive of the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva as being distinct.
In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, and fire; GarP_1,213.74.
Gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise the king as the eighth—
these one should constantly behold and worship by circumambulating them from left to right.
First, the study of the Veda; then reflection, practice, recitation, and its impartation to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold.
He who, having had the meaning of the Vedas, the sacrificial treatises, and the treatises on dharma transcribed for a price, gives them away, goes to the world of the Vedas.
Whoever, having written down the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, bestows them [upon others],
obtains merit equal to the gift of the Veda, doubled.
And likewise, in the third portion, one should accomplish the welfare of those to be supported:
mother, father, teacher, brother, offspring, the destitute, and those who have sought refuge.
The guest who has arrived and the sacred fire are declared to be among those who must be supported;
the maintenance of those to be supported is praised as a means for attaining heaven.
One should therefore make every effort to provide for the group of those dependent on one;
it is better that a single person lives, being supported by many.
Other men, though living, are as good as dead, for they are merely fillers of their own bellies;
yet even a dog possesses the capacity to fill its own belly.
From wealth that has increased and been accumulated from here and there,
all activities proceed, like rivers from mountains.
The earth containing all mines of jewels, grains, livestock, and women are designated as "wealth" (artha) because they serve the purpose of accomplishing one's aims.
A Brahmin should live in times of no distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury.
Wealth should be known to be of three kinds: white, variegated, and black;
its division should be understood as sevenfold and distinct.
Wealth obtained through inheritance, that given out of affection, and what is acquired together with one's wife—
these three kinds of property belong equally to all social classes.
The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa is seen to have three characteristics:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the constant acceptance of pure gifts.

They say that for a Kṣatriya as well, there are three specific types of wealth: that obtained for the sake of purification, that received from taxes, that acquired through fines, and likewise that born of victory.
Distinct wealth is seen even for the Vaiśya, which is of a different nature;
for the Śūdra, it consists of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, [obtained] through favor from these [higher castes].

A twice-born man may personally engage in the activities of usury, agriculture, and trade, or have them performed by another; even when performing these himself during times of distress, he incurs no sin.
Many means of livelihood have been proclaimed by the seers;
yet among all of these, they consider usury to be the most superior.
Due to drought, fear of kings, or afflictions such as rats, there may be obstacles to agriculture and similar pursuits; however, such obstacles do not exist in lending on interest.
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark, by night or by day,
in heat, rain, or cold, its growth does not cease.

The prosperity that accrues to those who travel to foreign lands and subsist on various kinds of merchandise arises for one who correctly engages in lending at interest and remains established in that practice.
One who has obtained a gain should worship the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins;
when they are satisfied, they undoubtedly pacify that fault of his.
A merchant should give what pertains to trade, such as clothing, gold from the Gaṅgā, and so forth; a farmer should give food, drink, vehicles, beds, and seats.
Having given twenty [cows] to kings, and a hundred such as cattle and gold,
the self-possessed man should make a collection by means of a quarter of that, using barley-gruel.
With one half [of the income], he should support himself while performing the obligatory and occasional rites;
with a quarter, he should increase the root capital for the purpose of trade.
Knowledge, craftsmanship, prosperity, service, cattle-herding, trade, agriculture,
living by alms, and usury— these are the ten means of livelihood.

Wealth acquired through receiving gifts belongs to the Brāhmaṇa; that acquired by conquest with weapons belongs to the Kṣatriya; wealth acquired by righteous means belongs to the Vaiśya; and wealth acquired through service belongs to the Śūdra.
A river with abundant water, vegetables, clay, leaves, fuel, and *kuśa* grass,
as well as the Vedic recitation of the Brahmins— these are the supreme wealth of the learned.
But there is no fault in accepting what is offered unasked;
the gods know that to be nectar (amṛta), therefore one should never reject it.
Desiring to offer the teacher’s property and intending to honor the deities and guests,
he may accept gifts from all quarters, but he should not derive personal satisfaction from them.
A twice-born man may accept [gifts] from a virtuous person or even from one who is not virtuous;
for one who possesses good qualities and has few faults does not sink, whereas one devoid of qualities indeed sinks.
Having thus maintained himself by means of the activity of his senses,
the best of the twice-born should perform purification from others through penance (*prāyaścitta*).
And in the fourth part [of the day], one should collect earth for the purpose of bathing, as well as sesame, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth; the bath should be performed in natural water.
Daily, occasional, optional, that which is auxiliary to ritual acts, and that which removes impurities;
along with cleansing, sipping water, and immersion—these are proclaimed as the eight types of bathing.
A man who has not bathed is unfit for recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites;
therefore, the morning bath is proclaimed as the obligatory daily bath (nityasnāna).
Having touched a Cāṇḍāla, a corpse, excrement, and so forth, or having touched a woman in her menses, one must bathe;
when one who is fit for bathing bathes, that is indeed an occasional (naimittika) bath.
Bathing such as the *puṣyasnāna* and others, as prescribed by the rules of the astrologers, is designated as optional (*kāmya*); one should not perform it without a specific desire.
One who desires to recite purifying mantras and wishes to honor the deities and guests should perform a bath; that is proclaimed as the constituent part of the ritual act.
The practice there is for the purpose of removing impurities, and not otherwise;
[it is performed] at lakes, at bathing-places dug by the gods, at sacred fords, and at rivers.
Since bathing itself is an action, it is therefore called "action-bathing" (*kriyā-snāna*);
the limbs are purified by water, and one obtains the fruit of bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
Through cleansing, bathing, and mantras, sin is swiftly destroyed;
this includes daily rites, occasional rites, and the removal of impurities that forms part of ritual action.

In the absence of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), however, one should perform the rite with hot water or water drawn from others; water drawn from the earth is meritorious, and more so than that is water from a spring.
The merit from that is even more essential than that; therefore, it is said that nothing should be withheld.
The water of a sacred ford is more meritorious than that, but the water of the Ganges is the most meritorious of all.
The water of the Ganges quickly purifies sin committed until the end of one's life;
so too does the water present at Gayā and Kurukṣetra.
Therefore, one should know that other water from the Gaṅgā is supreme;
[it is so] at the birth of a son, during auspicious conjunctions, and likewise at the transit of the sun.
Bathing at night upon the sighting of Rāhu is commended, but not otherwise;
as is the bathing performed at every dawn, during the twilight, and when the sun has risen.
That which is equal to the Prājāpatya penance destroys even great sins;
it is the same fruit that would accrue by performing the Prājāpatya for twelve years.
One who bathes at dawn, endowed with faith for a year,
obtains those vast enjoyments that are comparable to the eclipses of the moon and sun, if he so desires.
One should always bathe in the morning during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna;
indeed, he who, having reached the month of Māgha, bathes in the morning and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya), [attains great merit].
In this way, one dispels even a most terrible sin within a mere month,
[even if committed] against one's mother, father, brother, friend, or teacher.
He for whose sake one should immerse oneself [in the water] shall receive a twelfth part [of the merit];
Viṣṇu is especially pleased by *āmalaka* fruits on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*).
A man desiring prosperity should always perform his bath with *āmalaka* fruits;
[otherwise, he may encounter] distress, ill repute, short life, wealth, or even death.
Health and the attainment of all desires result from anointing oneself with the sun and other [planets];
likewise for one who has fasted, observed the vow, and had his hair and nails trimmed by barbers.
Fortune remains pleased only so long as she does not touch the oil;
having bathed in this manner, a man should satisfy the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should contemplate with a focused mind:
"May my ancestors come; may they accept this handful of water."
One should likewise offer three handfuls at a time with cupped hands into the southern sky;
having put on dry clothing, those standing on dry ground should do so upon strewn kusha grass.
Those who know the ritual rules should perform the libation, but never into a vessel;
for whatever is harsher than water or more impure than meat, [that is what remains].
"May all that which is unpeaceful and defiled depart;
having taken water with this mantra using the left hand. (GarP 1.213.132)
One should cast that toward the southwest for the destruction of demons;
[this removes] whatever sin arises from eating forbidden things and whatever from accepting improper gifts.
Whatever evil deed I have committed through the actions of speech, mind, or body,
may Indra, Varuṇa, and Bṛhaspati together purify that for me.
"May Savitṛ, Bhaga, and the sages beginning with Sanaka,
as well as the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied," so saying— GarP_1,213.135.
Performing a concise libation, he should cast three handfuls of water;
free from envy, he should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
One should worship all the gods with mantras characterized by those [deities], such as those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Savitṛ, Mitra, and Varuṇa, while offering salutations.
One should place the flowers individually with a salutation;
then one should worship Viṣṇu, who consists of all the gods, as well as Bhāskara.
Whoever offers flowers or even water with the Puruṣasūkta,
by him this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, becomes worshipped.
One should also worship Janārdana with other Tantric mantras;
first, the arghya offering should be presented, and after that, the unguent.
Then [he should perform] the offering of a handful of flowers, incense, and sacrificial fruits;
likewise, bathing within the water, as well as the ritual sprinkling and sipping of water.
One should consecrate the water for the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta three times, doing so constantly.
This is declared by the great-souled ones to be the procedure for bathing;
for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, bathing with mantras is prescribed.
For a Śūdra, however, it is ordained that he should listen in silence with a salutation;
teaching is the Brahma-sacrifice, while the libation is the Pitṛ-sacrifice.
A human sacrifice is for the gods, while a sacrifice to the spirits consists of honoring guests;
[the merit of feeding a guest] is tenfold in a cow-pen and more than a hundredfold in a fire-sanctuary.
In sacred fields of accomplishment, at holy fords, and in temples of the deities,
[one attains] an infinite [merit] in the presence of Viṣṇu, equal to hundreds of thousands of millions.
And likewise, in the fifth part,
a distribution according to reality is prescribed for the ten million ancestors, gods, and humans.
He who, having first given to the Brahmins, eats together with his friends,
attains heaven after death by practicing the gift of food.
One should first eat what is sweet, salt and sour in the middle,
and pungent, bitter, and astringent flavors, as well as milk, at the end.
