One should completely avoid leafy vegetables grown on the ground at night,
and one should never be addicted to the consumption of a single taste.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is remembered as nectar; the food of a Kṣatriya is remembered as milk; the food of a Vaiśya is indeed just food; and the food of a Śūdra is remembered as blood.
One should dwell here on the new moon day, or for at least one year.
Therein both Śrī and Lakṣmī dwell; of this there is no doubt.
In the belly is the Gārhapatya fire, and in the region of the back is the Dakṣiṇa fire.
The Āhavanīya fire is in the mouth, and the Satya fire is on the head;
he who knows these five fires is called one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni).
The body is said to be water and Soma, as well as various kinds of food;
for Prāṇa is indeed Agni and likewise Āditya—the enjoyer of these three is truly one alone.
May this food serve for my strength, as well as for that of the earth, the waters, fire, and wind;
through its transformation, may there be unimpeded happiness for me as well.
Then, having wiped his hands, he should consume betel;
with a well-composed mind, he should listen to the historical narrative (itihāsa).
One should study the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth during the sixth and seventh parts of the day; thereafter, having bathed, a man should perform the evening twilight worship.
O twice-born one, this practice has been declared by me for the day;
the wise man who reads or hears this *Ācāra* shall go to heaven.
For it is remembered, O twice-born one, that Keśava is the performer of dharma through right conduct (*ācāra*).
Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa—
214] Brahmā said:
Now I shall describe the procedure for bathing, since all ritual actions have their root in bathing:
clay, cow dung, sesame seeds, darbha grass, and fragrant flowers.
At the time of bathing, one who is restrained and pure, seeking to bathe,
should place those [substances] ending with scented water upon the ground in a secluded spot.
Having divided that clay and the cow dung into three parts,
the wise man should then wash his feet and likewise his hands with water and the clays.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, with his topknot tied, having sipped water properly and remaining silent,
he should worship the water while circumambulating it to the right, reciting the verse beginning with "uruṃ rāja."
One should cause that water to swirl with the three verses beginning with "ye te śatam."
Oṃ. For King Varuṇa has made a wide path for Sūrya to follow. May the speakers be established as those who possess hearts of wisdom. Homage to Agni-Aruṇa; may the noose of Varuṇa be praised away.
Homage to Varuṇa.

Oṃ! Those hundred and those thousand great sacrificial nooses of yours, O Varuṇa, which are spread out—may Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, all the gods, and the Maruts of beautiful praise release us from them today, Svāhā!
Having formed the *añjali* with the mantra "sumitriyā naḥ," one should pour water over the left hand, sprinkle it twice behind, and then cast it away.
Oṃ! May the waters and plants be friendly toward us;
may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate.
Having first washed both feet and the hips with three handfuls of earth each,
and having rinsed his mouth and offered salutations to the water, he should then proceed.
Oṃ, Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]; he established his foot in three places; it is gathered in his dust.
Afterwards, even though one is already pure, one should sip water while reciting the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One should indeed cleanse one's limbs with clay while reciting the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and one should immerse oneself facing the sun while reciting the verse "āpo asmān."
Oṃ! May the Waters, our mothers, purify us; may those who are rich in ghee cleanse us with ghee.
For these goddesses carry away every impurity; from them, I emerge bright and purified.
Then, having submerged and emerged slowly from the vessels without becoming agitated,
and having smeared them with cow dung while reciting the verse *mānastoke*, he should proceed.
Oṃ! Do not harm us in our honor, nor in our children, nor in our life, nor in our cattle, nor in our horses.
O Rudra, do not slay our heroic men who are full of wrath; we, possessing oblations, invoke you forever.
Then one should consecrate [the disciple] with the Varuṇa mantras in their proper order:
with the two verses beginning "imaṃ me varuṇa," and also with "tvanno" and "satvanno."
And [he recites] "O waters, you are the path to cross" (*āpo vṛṇītamasī*) and "May they release me at the purificatory bath" (*muñcantv avabhṛthe*);
and "Om, O Varuṇa, hear this my call, and be merciful to me today; seeking your protection, I implore you. (GarP 1.214.15)
Oṃ. I approach you with prayer, worshipping you; for that the sacrificer hopes by means of oblations.
O Varuṇa, be mindful here without anger; do not steal away our long life.
Oṃ. Do you, O Agni, who know, appease the wrath of the divine Varuṇa on our behalf.
Most worthy of sacrifice, the best of bearers, blazing brightly, release us from all enmities—*svāhā*!
Oṃ! Be such a protector for us, O Agni, most near to us at the dawning of this very dawn.
Bestowing gifts, ward off Varuṇa [from us]; grant us favor; be easy for us to invoke.

Oṃ! O Waters, O Plants, from injury, from sin, and from the king—therefore, O Varuṇa, release us. Since we have invoked you, O Slayer of Sin, as "Varuṇa," for that which we have sworn by you, therefore, O Varuṇa, release us.
Oṃ! O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us, untie the lowest, and release the middle one.
Then, O Āditya, may we be sinless before you and before Aditi.
Then, release me even from Varuṇa;
O wife of Yama, having been measured out from every sin,
you move about again as one purified by the final bath, ever protected.

O goddess, that which was created by the gods for the sake of mental travel, fashioned for the sake of equality, O you who protect from the flowers of the gods, protect us from the slight delusion of the intellect.
Having thus consecrated himself, having immersed himself and sipped water again,
he should cause [the disciple] to drink from a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting these purifying mantras that do not contain the word "aliṅga."
With the three verses beginning with "āpohiṣṭhā," with this verse "idamāpo haviṣmatīḥ," with the two verses beginning with "devīrāpaḥ," and with the three-verse hymn beginning with "āpodevāḥ."
"drupadādiva," "śanno devīḥ," "apām rasaḥ," "āpo devīḥ," and the "pāvamānyaḥ"— these nine initial verses shall purify you today.
The Lord of Consciousness (Citpati) moves slowly, having submerged himself in meditative absorption;
likewise, he recites the verses beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇā" and other Pāvamānī hymns.

One should, according to one's ability, employ the *Taratsamā*, the *Śuddhavatī* verses, and the purificatory hymns (*pavitrāṇi*), as well as many meritorious hymns to Varuṇa (*vāruṇyāḥ*), according to one's capacity.
Accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī*,
one should perform the consecration at the beginning and at the end in the proper sequence.
The cleansing rite is prescribed for one who remains standing in the midst of water;
one should recite the mantra within the water and perform the Aghamarṣaṇa three times.
One should recite three times the verse beginning with "drupadādyāḥ" and the three-verse hymn beginning with "ayaṃ gauḥ," as well as other mantras prescribed by tradition, while remaining composed.
A wise person should recite the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava; or he should repeat the Praṇava, or meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Water is the abode of Viṣṇu, and he alone is called the Lord of Waters (Appati);
these [elements] are his very bodies, therefore one should indeed meditate upon him within the waters.
Having immersed oneself repeatedly in the waters with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," one should indeed recite this Gāyatrī dedicated to Viṣṇu for the purpose of constant remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Oṃ! May this water carry away its own impurity, washing away the redness;
may it be as nectar for the Hotṛ priest, and a non-terrifying remedy for the swelling.
May the purifying waters release me from that sin. May the waters rich in oblation, the measurers, appear; may he who possesses the oblation come forth.
May the divine Asura possess the oblation; may Sūrya possess the oblation.

O divine waters, that wave of yours which is fit for the oblation, endowed with power, and sweet as the Ādityas—O deities, grant that to the gods who are pure and bright. Of those [waters], you are the distributor of the portion, the most excellent, the first, and the highest, O waters, through the greatness of the ocean and the power of the sun.
May the divine waters, rich in sweetness, full of food, and possessing royal power, accept these sesame seeds.

With those [waters] by which one sprinkles for Mitra and Varuṇa, and with which one leads Indra to food—may the divine waters, who are the source of the two worlds, grant us well-being. Of the essence of the waters, I shall take that which is most excellent, which exists in the sun and is perfectly concentrated.
O divine waters, rich in sweetness, rise up from your place for the sake of my kinship with offspring; from that place let the plants, along with their seeds, spring forth.
May the Soma-loving ancestors purify me; may the father, powerful with his life-span, purify me with the cleansing filter.
May the grandfathers purify me, and may the great-grandfathers purify me.
Through the purifier, may I attain full life; through the rays, may I attain all life.
O Agni, may you prolong our lives; grant us vigor and food from the skin of the trees. May the divine folk purify me; may they purify me with mind and thought.
May all beings purify themselves; O Jātavedas, purify me!
Purify me with the filter, O radiant God, with your bright light;
O Agni, according to your wisdom, [purify] my mental powers.
O Agni, may the Brahman purify me with that filter of yours which is spread within your flame;
[may he do so] as Pavamāna, the dweller in light,
the all-seeing one, with his filter.
May that which is the purifier purify me;
O divine Savitṛ, by both means— the filter and the impulse.
We purify this with the power of Brahman.
O Goddess, purifying and belonging to all the gods, you take hold of these [waters]; may they, worthy of honor, flow toward us. Rejoicing with her in our communal feasts, may we be masters of riches.
May the Lord of Speech purify me with the flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun.
Whatever desire I may have for you who are purified by that strainer, may I be able to accomplish it.
May the divine Savitṛ, the Lord of Speech, purify me with the flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun.
O Lord of the Purifier, may I be able to accomplish that desire of yours which belongs to you who are purified by the purifier.
This spotted cow has stepped forth; we have restored the mother and the father, ten times a hundredfold. May this [cow] go to the Lord of Heaven.
May the divine Savitṛ purify me with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun.
O Lord of the strainer, may I be able to accomplish whatever desire I have while being purified by you who are purified by the strainer.
Om. The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Like an eye stretched across the sky.
Having bathed in this manner and put on two unwashed, uncut garments,
he should then wash his hands with earth and water, thoroughly rinsing them.
Furthermore, having sipped water, one should sip again with the mantra during bathing and eating;
likewise, one should recite the *drupadā* three times and also the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
Having sipped water and bathed himself, and having sipped water three times after eating,
he should then worship the Sun with his hands joined in *añjali* and holding flowers over his head.
Having cast water and stirred it, [he recites] "ud u tyam," "citram," "taccakṣur devahitam," and also "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat."
With arms raised and concentrated in mind, he should mutter these [mantras] while looking at the sun;
likewise, he should worship the Maker of Day with the Gāyatrī according to his ability.
With the *anuvāka* beginning with "vibhrāṭ," with the *sūkta* of Puruṣa,
with the *śivasaṅkalpa*, and likewise with the *maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa*.
Furthermore, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) should be performed according to one's ability with the Divākīrtya hymns and other solar mantras proclaimed by all the gods.
Or, for the sake of accomplishing the recitation, one should recite the Adhyātmavidyā according to the prescribed rule;
having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times, [one should worship] Śrī, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Kṣiti.
One should fully satisfy Vāc, Vāgīśvarī, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi,
as well as Umā, Arundhatī, Śacī, and Mātṛ.
Jayā and Vijayā, Sāvitrī and Śānti as well, Svāhā, Svadhā, Dhṛti, and likewise the supreme Aditi.
One should offer libations to the wives of the sages and to maidens, as well as to the deities associated with specific desires;
one who desires all auspiciousness, however, should offer libations to Sarvamaṅgalā.
Saying, "May this world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
be satisfied," he should cast three handfuls of water and perform the libation while making his desired wishes.
Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Bathing," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 215 of the Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
I shall now fully describe the libation (tarpaṇa) which grants satisfaction to the gods and the ancestors.
Oṃ, may the Modās be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the Pramodās be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the Sumukhas be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the ill-faced ones be satisfied. Oṃ, may the obstacles be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the makers of obstacles be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the Vedic meters be satiated. Oṃ, may the Vedas be satiated. Oṃ, may the medicinal herbs be satiated.
Oṃ, may the eternal one be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the other teachers be satisfied. Oṃ, may the year with its constituent parts be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the gods be satisfied. Oṃ, may the apsarases be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the devāndhakas be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the oceans be satisfied. Oṃ, may the nāgas be satisfied. Oṃ, may the mountains be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the river-dwelling humans and yakṣas be satisfied!
Oṃ, may the rākṣasas be satisfied! Oṃ, may the piśācas be satisfied!
Oṃ, may the Suparṇas be satisfied. Oṃ, may the elements be satisfied. Oṃ, may the fourfold assembly of beings be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Dakṣa be satisfied. Oṃ, may Pracetas be satisfied. Oṃ, may Marīci be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Atri be satiated. Oṃ, may Aṅgiras be satiated. Oṃ, may Pulastya be satiated.
Oṃ, may Pulaha be satiated. Oṃ, may Kratu be satiated. Oṃ, may Nārada be satiated.
Oṃ, may Bhṛgu be satisfied. Oṃ, may Viśvāmitra be satisfied. Oṃ, may Raivata be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Cākṣuṣa be satisfied. Oṃ, may Mahātejas be satisfied. Oṃ, may Vaivasvata be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Dhruva be satisfied; Oṃ, may Dhava be satisfied; Oṃ, may Anila be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Prabhāsa be satisfied.
Wearing the sacred thread around the neck:
Oṃ, may Sanaka be satisfied;
Oṃ, may Sanandana be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Sanātana be satisfied. Oṃ, may Kapila be satisfied. Oṃ, may Āsuri be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Voḍhu be satisfied. Oṃ, may Pañcaśikha be satisfied. Oṃ, may Kavyavāha, the carrier of offerings for humans, be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Anala be satisfied. Oṃ, may Soma be satisfied. Oṃ, may Yama be satisfied.
Oṃ, may Aryaman be satisfied.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder:
*Oṃ*, may the Agniṣvātta ancestors be satisfied;
*Oṃ*, may the Somapa ancestors be satisfied.
Oṃ, may the ancestors who sit upon the sacrificial grass be satisfied.
Homage to Yama!
Homage to Dharmarāja!
Homage to Death!
Homage to the Ender!
Homage to Vaivasvata!
Homage to Kāla!
Homage to the Destroyer of All Beings!
Homage to Audumbara!
Homage to Dadhnya.
Homage to Nīla.
Homage to Parameṣṭhin.
Homage to Vṛkodara!
Homage to Citra! Homage to Citragupta! // GarP_1,215.4 //
May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied.
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the ancestors. Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the grandfathers.
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the great-grandfathers. Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the mothers.
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the grandmothers.
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the great-grandmothers. Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the maternal grandfathers.
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the maternal great-grandfathers.
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the elder paternal grandfathers; may they be satisfied. May those below, those above, and those in the middle—our Soma-loving ancestors—arise!
May those who have gone to the life-force, who are free from cruelty and knowers of the Truth (Ṛta), protect us, O ancestors, in our invocations.
The first añjali is offered to the father by pronouncing his lineage:
*oṃ aṅgiraso naḥ pitaro dṛh / atharvāṇo bhṛgavo dṛh*.
May we abide in the good-will of those worthy of sacrifice, and may we share in their auspicious benevolence.
Oṃ! May the gentle Pitṛs, the Agniṣvātta-s, come to us by the paths traveled by the gods; rejoicing with the *svadhā* offering at this sacrifice, may they speak for us and protect us.
Oṃ! You who carry strength, nectar, clarified butter, milk, and sweet juice, overflowing with nourishment—you are the *svadhā* offering; satisfy my ancestors!
Oṃ! To the fathers, *svadhā* and obeisance! Oṃ! To the grandfathers, *svadhā* and obeisance!
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the great-grandfathers. Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the maternal grandfathers. Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the maternal great-grandfathers.
Oṃ, svadhā and obeisance to the elder paternal grandfathers.
[Recite] "pitāmahasya dṛ. Oṃ, the ancestors have eaten; the ancestors have rejoiced; the ancestors, being satisfied, [are] pure (sva).

Come hither, O Pitṛs, and drink; take your seats upon the three worlds and the sacred abodes. O Jātavedas, Lord of the chariot, through the purity of your presence, accept this well-prepared sacrifice with the *svadhā* offerings.
Om! For the one who follows the cosmic order (*ṛta*), the winds blow sweetly and the rivers flow with honey.
May the plants be sweet for us; may the nights and the dawns be full of sweetness; may the earthly realm be rich in honey.
May heaven be honey for us, our father; may the lord of the forest be full of honey for us; may the sun be honeyed; and may the cows be honeyed for us.
The offering of the joined palms (añjali) to the great-grandfather:

"Oṃ, homage to you, O ancestors, for the sap; homage to you, O ancestors, for the vigor; homage to you, O ancestors, for the life-force; homage to you, O ancestors, for the svadhā-offering; homage to you, O ancestors, for the terrible; homage to you, O ancestors, for the wrath."
Homage to you, O ancestors; O ancestors, give us a house.
Homage to you, O ancestors; we offer this garment to you, O ancestors. [This is done] three times with cupped hands for the maternal grandfathers.
Then he saw his mother and the others.
And those born in our family who died childless or without a lineage—
may they be satisfied by this water squeezed from my garment which I have given.
Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Libation to the Devas and Others," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—
216] Brahmā said:
I shall now proclaim the Vaiśvadeva, the supreme characteristic of the *homa* offering.
Having kindled the fire and sprinkled water around it, [one recites]: "Oṃ! I send the flesh-eating Agni far away; let him go to the realm of King Yama, carrying off the impurities.
Let this other Jātavedas remain right here and, knowing the way, carry the oblation to the gods."

Oṃ! O Purifier, Vaiśvānara! Here is the seat. O Great Brahman, whose form is the splendor refined within the womb of the two kindling woods (araṇī), I awaken Vaiśvānara for a moment during the three watches of the day.
Oṃ! May both [worlds] come to us from afar through Vaiśvānara. Like Agni with his own radiance, he has his back upon the sky;
he has his back upon the earth; he has entered the waters and the plants. Vaiśvānara, Agni, has by his power taken his place upon them. Homage!
He spent six divine nights there.
Oṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati!
Oṃ, svāhā to Soma!
Oṃ, svāhā to Bṛhaspati!
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni and Soma!
Oṃ, svāhā to Indra and Agni!
Oṃ, svāhā to Heaven and Earth!
Oṃ, svāhā to Indra!
Oṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Oṃ, svāhā to Brahmā!
Oṃ, svāhā to the waters!
Oṃ, svāhā to the herbs and trees! Oṃ, svāhā to Grahi!
Oṃ, to the gods and goddesses, svāhā!
Oṃ, to Indra, svāhā! Oṃ, to the attendants of Indra, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Yama! Oṃ, svāhā to the servant of Yama! Oṃ, svāhā to all beings who roam during the day!
Oṃ, svāhā to the ancestral spirits who dwell upon the earth!
Oṃ, to those beings who roam about, wretched and blinking in the midst of the world—to them I give this offering, desiring prosperity; may the Lord of Prosperity grant me prosperity.
Oṃ! May the Lord of the Cāṇḍālas grant [this] to the cāṇḍālas, the outcasts, and the crows.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Vaiśvadeva," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Brahmā said:
Now I shall briefly describe the ritual of the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vidhi) for the twice-born;
whether one is impure or pure, or even if one has fallen into any state whatsoever.
Whoever should remember the lotus-eyed one is pure both externally and internally.
The Gāyatrī is the metre; Viśvāmitra is the seer; it has three feet.
The oceans are its belly; the moon and sun are its eyes;
fire is its mouth.
Viṣṇu is the heart;
Brahmā and Rudra are the head;
Rudra is the tuft of hair.
The application (*viniyoga*) is as follows:
*Oṃ bhūḥ* for the feet; *bhuvaḥ* for the knees.
*Svaḥ* in the heart;
*mahaḥ* in the head;
*janaḥ* in the crest-lock.
Tapaḥ at the throat;
Satya at the forehead;
Oṃ, salutation to the heart.
Oṃ bhūḥ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ svaḥ, huṃ to the armor.
Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ, phaṭ to the weapon! GarP_1,217.3
Oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ svaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam; that is the three-footed [Gāyatrī].
Oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūrbhuvaḥ svarom.
Oṃ sūryaśca, etc.
Oṃ *āpaḥ punantu* and so forth;
Oṃ *agniśca* and so forth. (GarP 1.217.4)
Oṃ! May the boon-granting goddess come;
she who is the deity Brahmā in the forenoon, the twilight named Gāyatrī, with reddish limbs and red garments.
Mounted upon a boar and a swan, she is seated upon the glorious Puṣkara.
Holding a water-pot, peaceful, and wearing a rosary of beads,
may the boon-granting goddess, white in form, come at midday.
And Māheśvarī Sāvitrī is adorned with white garments and other ornaments;
she is mounted upon the shoulders of a bull and holds a trident and the gesture of granting boons.
May the boon-granting goddess Sarasvatī come in the afternoon;
she resembles the flax flower, belongs to Viṣṇu, and has Garuḍa as her vehicle.
Clad in yellow garments and endowed with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
she is described as white in color and seated within the solar mandala.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, adorned with white flowers:
"Oṃ, you waters are indeed refreshing; grant us strength. (RV X.9.1) GarP_1,217.10 //
For the sake of great joy and for the eye:
Oṃ, may you cause us here to partake of that essence of yours which is most auspicious.
Like mothers who do not fail, Oṃ! To him whose abode you quicken, to him may we come with speed; O Waters, give us life.
Oṃ, may the waters and the plants be friendly to us; Oṃ, may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate.
Oṃ, as one released from a wooden post, as one bathed and cleansed of impurity, as clarified butter purified by a strainer—may the waters cleanse me from mental sin.
Oṃ. From the heat of the fervor (tapas), when it was kindled, arose both the Cosmic Order (ṛta) and Truth (satya).
From that, night was born;
from that, the ocean; from the ocean, the waves; and from the ocean, the waves, the year (saṃvatsara) was born.
Ordaining days and nights for all that blinks, the Controller,
the Ordainer, fashioned the sun and the moon as before; he fashioned heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and likewise the sky.
For the Gāyatrī [mantra], Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Savitṛ is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for silent recitation (japa).
Oṃ! His rays bear up that god who knows all beings.
For all to see, [he has raised] the Sun.
Om! The brilliant face of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
Sūrya has filled heaven, earth, and the mid-region; he is the soul of all that moves and stands still.
Oṃ! That eye, beneficial to the gods, has risen in the east, bright and shining.
May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns;
may we hear for a hundred autumns.
"Oṃ! He who has eyes on all sides, and faces on all sides, arms on all sides, and feet on all sides;
he, the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them together with his arms and wings.
O gods who know the way, who know the path, whose minds are focused on the goal—O Lord of the mind, place this sacrifice to the gods in the wind, Svāhā! One should mutter this. GarP_1,217.12 //
"O Goddess who dwells upon the mountain, since a peak has arisen on the northern part of the earth,
you have been granted permission by Brahmā; go as you please."
Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Sandhyā Ritual," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 218—
Brahmā said:
O Vyāsa, I shall describe the Śrāddha ceremony, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
First, one should invite Brahmins, especially those who are celibate students (brahmacārins).

With the sacred thread over the right shoulder (pradakṣiṇopavīta), one should invite the gods; with it over the left shoulder (vāmopavīta), one should invite the ancestors. One should wash their feet while reciting the appropriate mantras.
"Oṃ, welcome to you"—this is the question.

When they have replied, "Oṃ, a very warm welcome," [the host says], "Oṃ, svāhā! This water for the feet and this arghya offering for all the Viśvedevas. Thus, he offers water along with unbroken kuśa grass at the feet of the Brahmins representing the gods, using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods).
Then, facing south with the sacred thread over the left shoulder, [he offers] to our fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers belonging to such-and-such gotras...

Saying, "Obeisance to Nāmaśarman; may this water for the feet and this *arghya* be *svadhā*," one offers water together with bent *kuśa* grass and flowers at the feet of the Brahmins representing the ancestors and others, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*. (GarP 1.218.4)
In the same manner for the maternal grandfather and others.
[One says] "This is the water for sipping, svāhā, svadhā," and places it in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa; [one says] "This is your arghya," and offers flowers into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa.

Saying "Oṃ, may this seat be successful; here it is successful," and reciting the seven *vyāhṛtis*: "Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam," one should first seat the Brahmins representing the gods facing east, and the Brahmins representing the ancestors facing north.
[One should offer: "Oṃ, to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis..."
"Salutation! To Svadhā! To Svāhā! May they be ever-present!"—thus one should recite three times.

Oṃ. Today, in this place, in the month of [name], when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of [name], on the lunar day of [name], I shall perform the *dṛśrāddha* preceded by the Viśvedevas for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, belonging to the [name] lineage and named [names], beginning with the Viśvedevas.
Oṃ, svāhā to all the Viśvedevas! Oṃ, I shall invoke the Viśvedevas!

When it is said, "Invoke [the Viśvedevas]," [he recites]: *oṃ viśvedevāḥ sa āgata śṛṇutām imaṃ havam / edaṃ barhirniṣīdata //* *oṃ viśvedevāḥ śṛṇutemaṃ havaṃ me ye antarikṣe ya upadyaviṣṭha / ye agnijihvā uta vā yajatrā āsadyāsminbarhiṣi mādayadhvam //* "O Viśvedevas, come hither; hear this invocation. Sit down upon this sacred grass (*barhis*). O Viśvedevas, hear this my invocation—you who are in the intermediate space and you who are in heaven, you whose tongue is Agni, and you who are worthy of sacrifice—having sat down upon this *barhis*, rejoice!"
Oṃ! The plants hold consultation together with Soma, the king.
O King, we cause him whom the Brāhmaṇa serves to cross over to safety.
Oṃ! May the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great power come hither.
"May those who are invited here to this Śrāddha be attentive.
"Oṃ, may the Asuras and Rakṣasas who sit upon the altar be struck down!"—thus, three times each, he scatters barley grains.
"Oṃ, I shall prepare the vessel.
Being authorized with "Oṃ, do so," he prepared the purification within the vessel.
"Oṃ, may the divine waters be auspicious for our aid; may they be for our drinking;
may they flow around us for our well-being"—with these words, water is poured into the vessel.
"Oṃ, you are barley; barter away our hatred, barter away our enemies"—with these words, barley is offered.
"I invoke here Śrī, who has fragrance as her gate, who is invincible, eternally nourished, rich in manure,
and the sovereign of all beings"— with these words, one offers the fragrance.
"Oṃ! Those divine waters which have come together with milk—those that are in the atmosphere and those on earth;

golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice, may those auspicious waters be propitious, pleasant, and favorable to us. This is the *argha*; obeisance. Having thus given water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, and having taken up the *pavitra* strainers with this very vessel, he should place the residual drops (*saṃsrava*) and the *pavitra* beside the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having placed the water from the remnants (saṃsrava) into the first vessel, one should set it down facing upwards upon kuśa grass;
over that, one should offer kuśa grass.

"To all the gods, these perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, pairs of garments, and sacrificial threads—salutation! May the offering of the perfumes and other items be flawless! "So be it," is the response of the Brāhmaṇas. (GarP 1.218.10)

Then, the request for permission is: "I shall perform the Śrāddha for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, along with their wives, and for my maternal grandfather, his father, and his father, along with their wives. When the Brāhmaṇas have said, "Do so," one should mutter three times: "Oṃ, to the deities and to the ancestors... (RV 10.14.4).

"Oṃ, for our fathers and grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so Śarman, together with their wives, this seat; Svadhā!"—thus is the offering of the seat on the left side of the Brāhmaṇa.
"Oṃ, I shall invoke the ancestors. When [the Brāhmaṇa] says, "Oṃ, invoke them," [he recites]: "Oṃ, desiring you, we lay you down; desiring you, we kindle you."
"Desiring [us], O Śata, bring the ancestors here to consume the oblation.
Om! May the Soma-loving ancestors, those who have been consumed by the fire, come to us by the paths traveled by the gods;
rejoicing with the *svadhā* offering at this sacrifice, may they speak in our favor and protect us. Thus is the invocation (*āvāhana*).
"Oṃ, struck away are the Suras, the Rākṣasas, and those who sit upon the altar"—with this, there is the scattering of sesame seeds.
Then, water is poured into the vessels placed according to the sequence of the eastern face.

To our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, of such-and-such lineage, together with their wives: these perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, scents, upper garments, and sacred threads are for you; Svadhā! [Offered] by the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.

Then [recite]: *idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame tredhā nidadhe padam*.
"O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation which is placed within this dust"— with these words, one should place the thumb of a twice-born person face down into the midst of the food.
"Apahata" (Strike away)—with this, he scatters barley three times.
"Oṃ, I destroy everything that is impure; all the asuras and dānavas have been slain by me;

"Oṃ apahatā," with which one scatters sesame seeds. Thus, one should scatter food mixed with ghee and drenched in water upon *kuśa* grass on the ground.

Then, having offered a mouthful of water according to the Brahminic sequence, and having recited the *Sāvitrī* with the *Vyāhṛtis* as before, along with the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," he asks the Brahmins representing the gods, "Oṃ, is it pleasing to you? When he has replied, "Oṃ, we are satisfied," there is the sprinkling of the ground and the scattering of rice grains (*tila*) upon a four-cornered mandala.

our father,

Having thus prepared a *piṇḍa* of food mixed with clarified butter in the middle of the line for the grandfather, while reciting the *Gāyatrī* with the *Vyāhṛtis* and the verse "madhu vātā," he places it upon the *kuśa* grass, saying: "O our father, of such-and-such *gotra*..."
"O Śramaṇa Amukadeva, together with your wife, this rice-ball is for you; svadhā!"—

Then, reciting the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis and the verse "madhu vātā" three times, he should scatter rice-balls near the other rice-balls.

With the words "oṃ lepabhujaḥ prīyantām," he should wipe his hands on the remaining Kuśa grass of the layering. Then, using the water from washing the rice-balls, [he should offer it] with "oṃ amukagotra asmatpitaḥ."

"O [Name] Śarman, together with your wife, look upon this water for you; and those who follow you here, and those who follow after you—for them, Svadhā!"—with these words, one pours water over the ancestral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).
Having turned the vessel for the balls upside down and joined his palms in reverence, he should mutter: "O ancestors, rejoice; be refreshed according to your respective portions.
Having touched water, having turned back to the left and facing north, and having restrained his breath three times, he should mutter: "Salutation to the six seasons. (GarP 1.218.24)
Turning back with the left hand alone, he offers flowers, [saying]:
"May there be for me unbrokenness and freedom from misfortune; may my merit lead to peace and nourishment.
Facing south, he mutters: "These rejoicing ancestors have partaken according to their respective portions."
Having loosened his garment and joined his palms, he performs the recitation: *oṃ namo vaḥ pitaro namo vaḥ*.
He gazes at the house, saying: *gṛhān naḥ pitaro datta*.
Then, having looked [at them] while saying: *sadā vaḥ pitaro dveṣma*, and having uttered: *etad vaḥ pitaro vāsaḥ*, he gives the thread, saying: *amukagotra etatte vāsaḥ svadhā*.
Holding a water vessel with the left hand, one should pour a stream [of water] over the *piṇḍas* while reciting "ūrjaṃ vahantīramṛtaṃ ghṛtaṃ payaḥ" and so forth.

One should sprinkle each *piṇḍa* with the water remaining in the vessel previously set aside; then, having invoked the *piṇḍa*, one should offer scents and other articles, place a blade of *kuśa* grass upon the *piṇḍa*, and recite three times: "Oṃ, they have eaten, they have rejoiced, and they have been satisfied; the beloved ones have shouted aloud; the wise ones, possessing their own splendor, have praised you with their newest hymn—O Indra, those who know your two bay steeds. (RV 1.82.2–3). GarP_1,218.26 //

"May the auspicious waters placed in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa be auspicious for us.

"Lakṣmī dwells in flowers; Lakṣmī dwells in the lotus."
"May Lakṣmī dwell in the cow-pens; may there always be well-being for you. Thus is the offering of flowers.

"May this food, drink, and so forth be inexhaustible for our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, of such-and-such lineage, together with their wives"—with these words, one offers sesame seeds and water into the hands of the Brahmins representing the ancestors.

Oṃ! May the ancestors be non-terrible; may our lineage increase; may our donors prosper, as well as the Vedas and our progeny.
May faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. May food be abundant for us, and may we receive guests.

Taking a *kuśa* blade as a *pavitra*, one touches the Brahmin representing the father and other ancestors with that *kuśa* and says, "I shall cause [you] to pronounce *svadhā*. Having turned the alms-bowls face down and performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*dakṣiṇopavītī*), and facing east, he should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with the words: "Oṃ, this silver, for the purpose of establishing the *śrāddha*, I duly bestow upon you, O Brāhmaṇa named Devaśarman of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), together with your wife.
Thus he should give the fee.

Then, regarding the father’s Brahmin, the question is asked: "Are the rice-balls (piṇḍas) well-prepared?

Having offered a stream of milk upon the rice-ball, one moves the rice-ball; then, having turned the rice-ball vessel face-up toward the guest Brahmin, [one recites]: "Oṃ, O Vājins, come to us for food and wealth; you wise ones, immortal, knowers of the Truth (ṛta)."

"The attainment of heaven by the ancestors shall likewise be inexhaustible and certain.

Brahmā said:
I shall now describe the daily *śrāddha*, which is like the previous [rites] yet possesses its own specific characteristics.
"Oṃ! For our ancestors and grandfathers of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such Śarman, together with their wives, I shall perform the *śrāddha* with prepared food upon you.
Here, the rites beginning with the offering of seats should be performed, excluding the Viśvedevas.

I shall now describe the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, which is performed as before with its specific distinctions. On occasions such as seeing the face of a newborn son, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* must be performed facing east, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), using barley, jujube fruits, and *kuśa* grass; it is to be offered through the *daivatīrtha* (the part of the hand between the thumb and forefinger) with salutations at the end and with offerings made from the right side. Grasping the right knee, one should say: "On this occasion of our prosperity [named so-and-so], for our paternal great-grandmother, grandmother, and mother, [named] Amukadevī, belonging to the [so-and-so] lineage; and for [our maternal] great-grandmother, grandmother, and mother, [named] Amukadevī, belonging to the [so-and-so] lineage..."

When the *śrāddha* is to be performed, the invitation to the divine Brahmins is as follows: "The *śrāddha* for the Viśvedevas, known as the Vasus and Satyas, must be performed by me upon you with prepared food.
When he replies, "Oṃ, I shall do so," the invitation to the other divine Brahmins is conducted in exactly the same manner.

Then, having been addressed by him thus: "On the occasion of the increase of [my name], I shall perform for you the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha with prepared food on behalf of my great-grandmother, [name] Devī, of the [name] gotra," the invitation of the Brahmins for the great-grandmother is completed; the invitation of the Brahmins for the paternal great-grandmother and the others is to be done in exactly the same manner.
The request for permission to perform the *śrāddha* for the gods, the ancestors, all the deities, and the Brahmins:
On the seat, [one says], "Oṃ! O Viśvedevas, come hither; hear this our invocation.
Sit down upon this sacred grass (*barhis*)."

Oṃ, O Viśvedevas, hear this call of mine—those who are in the intermediate space and those who are in heaven, those whose tongue is Agni, or whoever else is here—having taken your seats upon this sacred grass (barhis), rejoice!
Oṃ, may they come! Thus is the invocation of the Viśvedevas and the offering of perfumes and other articles.
The recitation of the flawless determination.

Then follows the request for permission for the great-grandmother and the others, the offering of seats, the offering of scents and other articles, and the recitation of the formula for ensuring the rite is flawless (*acchidra*).
In this same manner, the procedure is performed for the paternal grandmother and the mother;
thereafter, the request for permission is made for the paternal great-grandfather and the others.

[The ritual sequence consists of: providing a seat, invocation, offering scents and other items, and performing the request for permission regarding the Great-Grandfather (vṛddhapramātāmaha) and the others.

[Then follows] the formal declaration of the food: "Oṃ, to the gods known as Vasus and Satyas, this food—accompanied by ghee, water, side-dishes, jujube fruits, and curd, and excluding forbidden items—is offered; obeisance. [Then:
"Oṃ, [he of] such-and-such lineage..."
O my paternal grandmother, Mukadevī, Nāndīmukhī!
This food, together with jujube fruits and curd, is offered; obeisance! Likewise for the maternal grandfathers, paternal great-grandmothers, and so forth.
Listen as I describe the specific details of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, which must necessarily be performed first.
First is the invitation, then the washing of the feet, and then the seat.
[The formula is: "Today, for my father, of such-and-such lineage and named Amukadevaśarman, I shall perform his annual *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha with prepared food (*siddhānna*) among you."
The request for permission to perform the *śrāddha*, the offering of a seat, the presentation of perfumes and other items, the preparation of the food,
and the recitation of prayers should be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*nivītin*). Having turned toward the north, one should perform the *atithi-śrāddha*.

Then, knowing that they are satiated, facing south with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (vāmopavītī), one should scatter food near the remains [of the meal] with the mantra "agnidagdhāḥ" (those burned by fire).

One should offer a stream of water upon the lines drawn on the ground with the formula: "O Father, so-and-so Devaśarman of such-and-such lineage, may this water be poured for you to wash; and for those who follow you here and those who precede you, to them be *svadhā*.
The remainder is as before.
Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—220.
Brahmā said:
I shall now describe the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, performed at the completion of one year on the anniversary of the death;
when properly executed at the correct time, it grants the deceased and others a place in the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*).
One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite in the afternoon as before.
[This includes] the invitation of the Brahmins for the grandfather and the others:
"Oṃ, to the gods known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this seat is offered; *namaḥ*."
On the left side, the offering of a seat and the invocation [of the ancestors] are performed. Then,

one seeks permission by saying, "I shall perform the Śrāddha for my grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather, together with their wives," followed by the preparation of three vessels upon which [the offerings] are placed.

Having offered the *kuśa* grass and covered [the vessel] with another bowl, and having completed the rite up to the "sealing without gaps" (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*), he likewise requests permission to perform the *śrāddha* for his father together with his wife, using a name ending in the word "preta," and performs the sealing without gaps for the vessel of the gods.
Having completed that, one should slightly move the vessels in the order of the grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather;

then, having uncovered them, [one recites]: "Oṃ, those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them is this world, svadhā, and obeisance; may the sacrifice be effective among the gods."

*Oṃ ye samānāḥ samanaso jīvā jīveṣu māmakāḥ / teṣāṃ śrīrmayi kalpatāmasmin loke śataṃ samāḥ //* With these two mantras, having poured the water from the vessel for the father into the vessels for the grandfather and great-grandfather— and having set aside the vessel for the great-great-grandfather— one pours the water and the *pavitra* grass from the vessels of the grandfather and great-grandfather back into the vessel for the father.
One should cast [it].
Then, the offering of the *pavitra* (sacred grass ring) contained in the vessel is placed into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors.

With a flower from the vessel, one performs the worship of the head, hands, and feet; then, another water-offering is made into the Brahmin’s hand. Raising the vessel with both hands and reciting "Oṃ yā divyā," [one addresses him as]: "Oṃ, [Name], of such-and-such lineage, my grandfather [Name] Devaśarman, together with your wife."

"This is your *arghya*, *svadhā*! Having taken a small amount of *arghya* water along with the *pavitra* grass from the *pitṛ-pātra* itself into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the grandfather, and having covered that small amount of water with another vessel for the purpose of sprinkling it upon the *piṇḍas*, [he places it] on *kuśa* grass with tips pointing south to the left of the Brāhmaṇa representing the father, for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛbhyaḥ*).
With the words "Thou art the foundation," he places the vessel face down.
The offering of scents and other items, as well as the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, is performed for the grandfather, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather.
One should place the remaining food into the vessel of the great-great-grandfather and the others.
Even after completing the sequence up to the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the grandfather’s vessel, one performs the consecration of the Brahmins’ vessels.

Having performed the placement of the thumb and the scattering of sesame seeds, one should say: "O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, this food—accompanied by ghee, water, and condiments, and excluding forbidden items—is for you; and for those who follow you here, and those whom you follow, to them be *svadhā*."
Then one should offer the *apośāna* water to the deities and others.
Upon the arrival of a guest, one should perform a *atithi-śrāddha*.
At this juncture, the scattering of food (*vikiraṇa*) takes place.
Having asked the question regarding the paternal grandfather and great-grandfather, the question for the paternal Brahmin is: "Oṃ, has it been well-savored by you?

[The response is: "Oṃ, O father of such-and-such gotra, named such-and-such Śarman, together with your wife; this is your *piṇḍa*. And those who follow you here, and those whom you follow—to them, may there be *svadhā*. Then, having completed the declaration of the fulfillment of the *saṅkalpa*, he should divide the *piṇḍa* into two parts, recite the two mantras beginning with "ye samānāḥ sumanasaḥ," and cast them into the vessels of the paternal grandfather and great-grandfather.

Having offered fragrance and other items upon the rice-balls (piṇḍas), the shifting of the rice-balls [to the ground] is performed; then, the question "Was it well-eaten? (svaditam) and so forth is asked of the guest Brahmin, followed by the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for the Brahmins.
The offering of betel-leaf according to the order of consumption;
the pouring of water into the hands of the Brahmins in the order beginning with the great-grandfather, saying, "May it be well-sprinkled; may the waters be auspicious";
and the pouring of water into the hands of the Brahmins representing the ancestors, saying, "May there be inexhaustibility for the lineage; may it attend [upon you]. (GarP 1.220.6)

"May the ancestors be non-terrible (aghorāḥ)," [he says]; when "so be it" is replied, he requests permission from the Brahmins beginning with the grandfather by saying, "Please pronounce the *svadhā*. (GarP 1.220.7)
When it is said, "Oṃ, let it be spoken," [the response is] "Oṃ, let the *svadhā* be spoken for the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the others.
When it is said, "Let there be *svadhā*," [the priest says] "O Brahmin of the ancestors, let the *svadhā* be spoken for the ancestors.
When it is said, "Let there be *svadhā*," [the ritualist performs] the pouring of a stream of water facing south with the mantra, "Oṃ, carrying strength (*ūrja*)."
"Oṃ, may the Viśvedevas be pleased at this sacrifice"—with these words, one offers water with barley into the hand of the Brahmin representing the deity.
Then, "Oṃ, to the deities"—this is recited three times.

Having moved the alms-bowls and sipped water, he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the ancestors beginning with the grandfather; then, he requests a blessing from the Brahmin representing the father, saying, "May blessings be granted to me.

When it is said, "Let it be accepted," the giver says, "May our donors increase," and turning the bowl face upward, he performs the dismissal with the words, "In strength after strength" (*vāje vāje*).
Then, he dismisses the Brahmin representing the father with the words, "Be well-pleased" (*abhiraṇyatām*).
I have related to you the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha as proclaimed by Vyāsa;
Viṣṇu is the Śrāddha, Hari is the performer of the Śrāddha, and Hari is the fruit of the Śrāddha and other rites.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Performance of Śrāddha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The venerable Brahmā said:
O Śaṅkara, listen as I shall speak in brief of the essence of the Dharma—
subtle, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and destroying all sins.
Sorrow indeed robs men of their learning, righteousness, strength, fortitude, happiness, and even enthusiasm; therefore, one should abandon sorrow.
Karma is one's wife, karma is one's world, and karma is one's kinsman;
it is karma that impels a person here toward happiness and suffering.
Giving is the supreme dharma; through giving, everything is obtained.
Through giving, one attains both heaven and sovereignty; therefore, a person should practice giving.
On one side, they say, is a gift accompanied by all excellent sacrificial fees;
on the other side is the protection of the life of a living being who is terrified by fear.
Those who, despite austerity, celibacy, sacrifices, or ritual bathing,
are destroyers of dharma, indeed go to hell.
And those men who are devoted to fire-offerings, recitation, ritual bathing, and the worship of deities,
and who are endowed with truthfulness, forbearance, and compassion, go to heaven.
There is no one who bestows happiness or suffering, nor is there anyone who takes them away;
beings experience only the sufferings and pleasures created by their own actions.
Those for whom life is for the sake of Dharma cross over all difficulties;
who, being contented, would not be able to subsist on fruits and roots?
For everyone indeed plunges into calamities out of a desire for pleasure; this alone would be the most difficult task to accomplish, which is the work of greed.
From greed arises anger; from greed proceeds malice;
and from greed come delusion, deceit, pride, and envy.
He who has abandoned passion, hatred, falsehood, anger, greed, delusion, and pride,
being peaceful and free from evil, goes to the supreme world.
O Hara, the deities, sages, nāgas, gandharvas,
and guhyakas worship here one who is righteous, not one who is wealthy nor one who is lustful.
By means of infinite strength and vigor, or through wisdom or human effort, a mortal obtains that which was unobtainable; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Compassion for all sentient beings, restraint of all the sense faculties,
and the perception of impermanence everywhere— this is remembered as the supreme good.
The birth of that man who does not practice the Dharma while facing death as if it were right before his eyes is as useless as the fleshy protuberance on the neck of a goat.
The killer of a fetus, the killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a cow, the killer of a father, or one who violates the teacher's bed—
by giving land endowed with all excellent qualities, such a person is liberated from these sins.
It is my conviction that there is no gift superior to the gift of a cow;
a cow acquired by righteous means, when given away, delivers the entire lineage.
O Bull-bannered One, there is no gift superior to the gift of food;
by food this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is sustained.
The gift of a maiden, the ritual release of a bull, pilgrimage to sacred fords, as well as sacred learning;
the giving of elephants, horses, and chariots, and of jewels, gems, and the earth.
All other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of food.
From food come the vital breaths, strength, and splendor; from food come vigor, fortitude, and memory.
One should cause wells, step-wells, tanks, and groves to be constructed;
having rescued twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The sight of the virtuous is meritorious; it excels even a sacred pilgrimage site.
A pilgrimage site bears fruit in due time, whereas the company of the virtuous yields fruit immediately.
Truthfulness, self-control, austerity, purity, contentment, forgiveness, straightforwardness,
knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and generosity— this is the eternal Dharma.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of Dharma," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. [Chapter 222] Brahmā said:
I shall now declare the rites of expiation and other practices that crush the flood of hells:
flies, droplets of saliva, women, water on the ground, fire,
cats, and mongooses— these are always pure.
If a twice-born man should, through negligence, consume food touched by the leavings of a Śūdra,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Brahmin is ever touched by another Brahmin who is impure from eating,
he must perform a bath, recite prayers, and take his meal at the end of the day.
Food containing flies or hair becomes pure instantly by being vomited;
so too is the food of one who eats from the palm of the hand, or with the fingers, or with the arm.
If he does not drink water, he shall be purified in a day and night;
however, the water remaining after being drunk that was taken with the left hand is like liquor.
Water contained within a leather bag would be impure; one should not drink it.
Likewise, if a person of the lowest caste (antyajati) should dwell in one's house without being recognized, [the water is likewise unfit].

For the twice-born, the Cāndrāyaṇa or Parāka penance is the means of purification; for a Śūdra, it is the Prājāpatya. Others maintain that this applies once the offense has been subsequently discovered.
Whoever eats cooked food there, one should cause him to perform half a *kṛcchra* penance;
and for whoever eats the food of those [who have already eaten], a quarter *kṛcchra* is prescribed.
And a twice-born man who eats the food of washermen, actors, or those who subsist on bamboo and leather, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a Brahmin should drink water from the wells or vessels of a Cāṇḍāla out of ignorance, he should perform the Sāntapana penance; for a Vaiśya, half of that is prescribed.
If one unknowingly eats at the house of an outcaste Śūdra, a quarter of the penance must be given;
however, if one goes to the home of an outcaste (antyaja), the penance shall be three *kṛcchras* or a *parāka*.
A twice-born man who eats the remnants of food left by an outcaste is purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
when he eats the food of a Caṇḍāla through negligence, he should perform the Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa) penance.
For one born of the Kṣatriya caste, the Sāntapana penance lasts for six nights; others likewise [prescribe] two nights.
If a Brāhmaṇa, through negligence, eats fruit from a single tree where a Caṇḍāla [is present], he becomes pure after a day and a night.
If one who has eaten and is seated, but has not yet sipped water for purification, should touch a Caṇḍāla,
he should mutter the Gāyatrī eight thousand times or the Drupadā verse a hundred times.

O twice-born ones, if excrement or urine has been deposited by Cāṇḍālas or Śvapacas, the penance shall be three nights; however, if it occurs in the presence of those of the lowest birth (antyaja), it is a Parāka.
Having approached women unintentionally, the practitioner there must perform the *parāka* penance;
however, for one born of the lowest castes (*antyajāti*), no expiation is prescribed.
If a twice-born man drinks water from vessels defiled by liquor and the like,
he shall indeed be purified by one-quarter of the Kṛcchra penance and by the rite of re-consecration.
Those Brahmins who have retired from worldly life and dwell among the thunderbolts, fire, wind, and other elements,
collect food, drink, and such, desiring to enter another state of existence.
One should indeed perform three *kṛcchra* penances and three *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts;
the sage Vasiṣṭha has declared that the sacraments, beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), must be performed.
A woman becomes pure by performing the Prājāpatya and other penances after eating twice;
likewise, a twice-born man who has been touched by the leavings of food or by a dog or a Śūdra becomes pure in the same manner.
Having fasted for one night, he is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
however, if he has been touched by one outside the [four] castes, he is purified after five nights.
Continuous streams that are not defiled, dust raised by the wind,
women, children, and the elderly— these are never considered impure.
The mouth of women is always pure; fruit fallen by birds is pure; a calf is pure when discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
Water that stands in water is pure, and that which grows on dry land is pure on dry land;
one should place one's feet right there, and having sipped water (ācamana), one attains purity.
Bell-metal that has not been defiled by liquor is purified by ashes;
however, that which is smeared with urine or mixed with liquor is indeed purified by repeated heating.
Bell-metal vessels that have been smelled by a cow, those that contain the remnants of food from a Śūdra,
and those struck by crows or dogs, are purified by ten applications of ash.

A Brahmin who eats from the vessel of a Śūdra, or who touches the leavings of one who has fasted for three days while consuming the five products of the cow, as well as a dog or a Śūdra who commits such an offense, [must perform penance].
Having touched a woman in her menses, one who has fasted shall be purified by consuming the five products of the cow;
likewise when on a path in waterless regions or infested with thieves and tigers.
If one has urine or feces while holding an object in the hand, one is not defiled;
having placed that object on the ground and performed purification with a concentrated mind, one is pure.
Fermented gruel, curd, milk, buttermilk, and rice-and-pulse porridge—even these may be accepted from a Śūdra; likewise, meat and honey may be taken even from an outcaste.
If a Brahmin or others of the twice-born castes drink liquor made from molasses, flour, or honey,
that twice-born person drinking liquor shall attain purification by drinking liquor that is red-hot like fire.

A Brahmin should recite the Gāyatrī five hundred times, and a Kṣatriya one hundred times; and a Brahmin who has eaten food from a drinking vessel during a period of birth-impurity [must likewise recite it].
A pure Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.
In the case of kings, immediate purification is prescribed during battles, at sacrifices and the like, when they have gone to another country, upon the death of a child, and for the monthly rites.
Likewise, an unmarried girl, a twice-born man who has not yet received the girdle of muñja grass,
a child whose teeth have not yet emerged, and a three-year-old girl [are exempt from impurity].
Their purification occurs after three nights; in the case of a miscarriage, it is after three nights;
for a woman who has given birth, it is equal to the number of months [of pregnancy]; and for a menstruating woman, it is on the fourth day.
During a famine, the ruin of a kingdom, or at the birth or death of a child,
religious observances are not defiled for those who are devoted to the duty of giving.
At the time of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), at a wedding and similar occasions, when gods or twice-born brahmins have been invited,
or even when [the rite] has been previously resolved upon, there is no impurity (*āśauca*) due to death or birth.
Likewise, a twice-born man becomes impure by touching a woman who has recently given birth;
however, he remains pure where the sacred fires are offered oblations or where the Veda is being recited.
For those who constantly perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, no birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall occur;
yet if one eats in an impure house, a twice-born man becomes pure after three nights.
If a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, or a Śūdrā woman is in her menses and they touch one another, the Brāhmaṇī becomes pure after three nights.
A Kṣatriya woman becomes pure after two nights, a Vaiśya woman by fasting, and a Śūdra woman by bathing; however, one should not dismiss the Droṇa-measure of water.
Food brought by a crow or a dog is considered external; one should discard it, but having sprinkled it with water mixed with gold and ashes, one should heat it over a fire.
Having seen a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well,
and having drunk the water of that well, a Brahmin becomes pure in three days;
a Kṣatriya in two days alone, and a Vaiśya after one day at most.
If bone, skin, filth, or even a rat is pulled out from a well,
the water becomes pure once it has been filtered and purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Likewise, one should throw ashes and other such substances into a pond, lotus pool, or similar body of water;
having drawn out six jars of water, it becomes pure through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If menstrual blood has fallen into the midst [of the water], one should remove thirty jars;
likewise for having had sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, or for consuming liquor and beef.
A Brahmin is purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, a Kṣatriya by the Prājāpatya,
a Vaiśya by the Sāntapana, and a Śūdra becomes pure in five days.
When the penance has been performed, one should give cows and feed the Brāhmaṇas;
in cases of play, on beds and such, the wearing of indigo-dyed cloth does not cause defilement.
One should not touch indigo-dyed cloth, for by wearing indigo one goes to hell;
even the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed [are purified].
Upon seeing a bear, they are purified, as is the fifth person associated with them;
thereafter, one should give a hundred cows and provide a feast for Brahmins.
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having constructed a hut;
or the drinker of intoxicants shall cast himself into a well-kindled fire.
A thief of gold should bestow everything upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas;
and one who has violated the Guru’s bed should give a thousand cows and a single bull.
One who has committed a sin should perform a fast while tethering two legs of a beast;
for one who causes a house fire in a wilderness, there should be a *sarvakṛcchra* penance at a watering place.
If a cow dies due to the fault of a neck-ornament, one must perform a penance for a quarter of a *kṛcchra*;
likewise, having caused a fracture of the bones or even a break of the horns of cows, one must do the same.

In the event of a wound to the skin or the loss of the tail, one should drink barley-gruel for half a month; however, for all injuries caused by elephants, horses, weapons, and the like, one must certainly perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor,
the three twice-born castes undergo a rite of re-consecration.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are discontinued for the twice-born upon the performance of the purificatory rite again.
Raw meat, ghee, honey, and oils produced in their proper seasons—
all these are considered pure once they have been removed from the vessels in which they were kept by those of the lowest caste.
Oil and the like, clarified butter, honey-wine, merchandise, and liquids;

likewise, eating once a day (*ekabhakta*), eating at night (*nakta*), eating only what is unasked for (*ayācita*) for one day each, and fasting (*upavāsa*); this constitutes the *pādakṛcchra*, while twice that amount is indeed the *kṛcchrārdha*. GarP_1,222.60 //
That shall be a Prājāpatya penance, which destroys all sins;
a Kṛcchra consisting of seven fasts is known as the Mahāsāntapana.
For three days one should drink hot water, for three days one should drink hot milk, and for three days one should drink hot ghee; this "heated kṛcchra" rite removes all sins.
Fasting for twelve days constitutes the Parāka penance, which destroys all sins. One should increase the food by one morsel during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight.
The milk of a golden-colored cow, white-colored cow dung, cow urine from a copper-colored cow, and ghee produced from a blue-colored cow; GarP_1,222.64.
There should be curd from a black cow mixed with darbha-water;
eight māṣas of cow urine and four of cow dung.
Twelve māṣakas of milk are prescribed, ten of curd are said [to be prescribed], and five māṣakas of clarified butter;
this *pañcagavya* removes impurities.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Expiations," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O Vyāsa, I have now declared with devotion those duties practiced by the sages.
And by those who please Viṣṇu through the service of the Sun and other deities.
Through libations, burnt offerings, and the worship of the twilight,
the Blessed Viṣṇu— the bestower of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation— is attained.
For Dharma is indeed the Blessed Viṣṇu; the worship of Viṣṇu, the libation, the fire-oblation, as well as the twilight prayers, meditation, and concentration—all this is Hari.
Sūta said: O Śaunaka, listen to all that regarding the dissolution of the world;
a thousand cycles of four yugas is known as one day of the single lotus-born Kalpa.
Learn from me the conditions of the ages beginning with Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara:
in the Kṛta age, Dharma has four feet—truth, generosity, austerity, and compassion.
At that time, men who are wise and contented will uphold the Dharma;
indeed, those men shall live for four thousand years.
At the end of the age, the Kṣatriyas were conquered by the Brahmins, as were the Vaiśyas and Śūdras by the twice-born;
and Viṣṇu, the heroic and exceedingly powerful one, indeed slew the Rākṣasas.
In the Tretā Yuga, Dharma stands on three feet, consisting of truth, charity, and compassion;
in that age, men are devoted to sacrifice, and likewise the world arises from the Kṣatriya class.
The red-complexioned Hari was worshipped by men, and men lived for a thousand years;
there Viṣṇu was Bhaumaratha, and the Kṣatriyas slew the Rākṣasas.
When the yellow-complexioned Acyuta has departed, the Dharma will be divided into two parts;
the lifespan of people will be four hundred years, and the progeny will consist of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Having seen there those of small intellect, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Vyāsa,
again divided that single Yajurveda into four parts.
He taught his disciples; hear from me about them all:
Paila for the Ṛgveda and Jaimini for the Sāmaveda.
Atharvaṇa, Sumantu, the great sage Yajurveda,
Vaiśampāyana,
Aṅga, and Sūta himself— the eighteen Purāṇas by whom Hari alone is indeed known.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
The Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, as well as the Bhaviṣya, Nāradīya, Skānda, Liṅga, and Varāha [Purāṇas].
The Mārkaṇḍeya, the Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta,
the Kaurma, the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and immediately after that the Vāyavīya;
these eighteen are specified, and the one known as the Brahmāṇḍa completes them.
Other Upapurāṇas have indeed been narrated by sages;
the first is that spoken by Sanatkumāra, and another is the Nārasiṃha.
The third is designated as the Skānda, spoken by Kumāra;
the fourth is called the Śivadharma, spoken by Nandīśvara.
The wonderful account spoken by Durvāsas, that which was spoken by Nārada thereafter, as well as the Kāpila and Vāmana, and likewise that narrated by Uśanas.
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, and that which is called the Kālikā; likewise the Māheśvara, the Sāmba, and the compendium of all subjects (Sarvārthasañcaya);
furthermore, the Parāśarokta, the Mārīca, and that called the Bhārgava.
The Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), O Sage,
as well as Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Āyurveda, Arthaśāstra, Gāndharva, and Dhanurveda— these, O Śaunaka, are remembered as the eighteen sciences (vidyās).
And at the end of the Dvāpara age, Hari removed the heavy burden [of the earth] when Dharma stood on only one foot and Acyuta had departed into the state of Kṛṣṇa.
At that time, people will become ill-behaved and merciless.
The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are seen in a person;
impelled by time, these too revolve within the self.
When beings, the mind, the intellect, and the senses are abundant,
then one should know it to be the Kṛta Yuga, in which there is delight in knowledge and austerity.
O Śaunaka, know that when embodied beings possess the capacity for rites performed for specific desires and for fame, then it is the Tretā age, born of the quality of rajas.
When greed, discontent, pride, hypocrisy, and envy,
as well as the performance of rites for desired rewards, prevail— that is the Dvāpara age, characterized by rajas and tamas.
When falsehood is constant, when sleep is the means for violence and other evils,
and when sorrow, delusion, fear, and wretchedness prevail— that is remembered as Kali in the mode of ignorance (tamas).
In that [age], people will be lustful and constantly speaking harsh words;
the regions will be overrun by bandits, and the Vedas will be corrupted by heretics.
Kings will subsist on alms from their subjects, overcome by their heads and bellies;
they will be devoid of vows, like mere students, impure, and householders while claiming to be mendicants.
Those who practice austerities while living in villages, who have renounced their vows yet are greedy for wealth,
who are short of stature yet consume vast amounts of food— they are known as thieves in the guise of holy men.
Servants will abandon their master, ascetics will abandon their vows,
Śūdras will accept gifts, and Vaiśyas will be devoted to religious observances.
The people are anxious, and the subjects are like *piśāca* demons;
through unrighteous consumption, the worship of the fire-god and the honoring of guests [are neglected].
When the Kali age has arrived, O Śaunaka, people will no longer perform the ancestral water-rites;
all people will be devoted to women and will be mostly like Śūdras.
In the Kali age, women will have many offspring yet little fortune;
intent on scratching their heads, they will disobey commands when rebuked.
O Brahmins, people afflicted by heresy will not worship Viṣṇu; yet there is indeed one great virtue in Kali, that storehouse of faults. (GarP 1.223.35)
By the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa's names, one shall abandon great bondage;
the fruit obtained by meditating on Viṣṇu in the Kṛta age is attained by chanting in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, [liberation comes] through service, and in the Kali age, by the chanting of Hari's names.
Therefore, O Śaunaka, Hari should always be meditated upon, sung of, and worshipped.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Ages," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 224 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Sūta said:
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, there occurs the occasional dissolution of Brahmā;
and at the end of the kalpa, a hundred-year drought arises.
Then seven fierce suns arise in the sky;
having drunk all the water, they dry up the three worlds.
Having become Viṣṇu and Rudra, he burns the worlds of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Maharloka, along with the mobile and immobile beings of Jana, as well as the nether regions below.
Viṣṇu may burn the three worlds, yet he creates clouds from his mouth;
indeed, great clouds of various colors rain down for a hundred years.
The powerful wind, in the form of Viṣṇu, blows for a hundred years;
when the world has become a single ocean, Viṣṇu, assuming the nature of Brahmā,
lies upon the seat of Ananta during that year in which all things mobile and immobile have perished.
Having slept for a thousand years, that Hari created the world once again.
Now, O Śaunaka, listen as I describe the elemental dissolution (prākṛtika-pralaya).
When a full hundred years had passed, having withdrawn the entire universe and having placed Brahmā within his own body, Hari was liberated through the powers of yoga.
Those who have gone to the abode of Brahmā also go to the supreme state. O twice-born one, there were clouds endowed with the brilliance of the sun during a drought;
then, as those clouds rained for a hundred years, the cosmic egg was filled.
With its inner waters contained within it, the shell of the Lord of the World is broken;
when the full lifespan of Brahmā has passed, it dissolves and merges into the waters.
Thus that support of the world dissolves into water and the earth;
the waters dissolve into fire, and fire dissolves into wind.
Then the wind enters space, and space enters the origin of the elements (bhūtādi); the Great One (mahat) enters the Unmanifest (avyakta), and Nature (prakṛti) enters the Supreme Puruṣa.
For a hundred years Hari sleeps; then, at the end of the day, he emits the manifest world of moving and non-moving beings through the sequence beginning with the unmanifest.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Occasional Dissolution," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 225] Sūta said:
Having understood the three types of internal and other torments and knowing the wheel of transmigration,
one who has attained wisdom and dispassion reaches ultimate dissolution.
I shall first describe the wheel of saṃsāra, from the time of the departure of the breath [at death],
without which the human goal would not become absorbed in the Supreme Self.
A man who dwells above, having abandoned his body, attains another;
he is led by the servants of Yama to the abode of Yama within twelve days.
In that regard, whatever water the kinsmen offer along with sesame seeds,
and whatever funeral cake (piṇḍa) they present, he partakes of that in the world of Yama.
One goes to hell because of sin, and one goes to heaven because of one's own merit;
the doer of evil goes to hell, while the doer of merit indeed goes to the celestial realm.
Released from both heaven and hell, he enters even into the womb of women;
yet that dual seed of his does not become overwhelmed by that [other seed].
From that, there is the *kalala*, consisting of a bubble, and then blood;
from the *peśī* comes the *aṇḍa* (ovum), which is equal to a *pala* in weight, and from that, it is called the sprout (*aṅkura*).
The secondary limbs— the fingers, eyes, nose, mouth, and ears—
depart from the major limbs, and after that, the nails and so forth follow.
From that, the skin arises, and after that, the body hairs and the hair of the head;
then, staying with face downward, the man is born in the tenth month.
Then the deluding power of Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇavī māyā), which causes extreme infatuation,
envelops him in childhood, youth, adolescence, and even old age.
And then, at death, a human being undergoes those respective states;
thus he wanders in this wheel of saṃsāra like a waterwheel.
Even one who has been released from hell is born among sinful wombs;
moreover, a wise man who accepts gifts from the fallen shall go to a lower womb.
Once released from hell, O twice-born one, he becomes a beggar worm;
but having committed an offense against his preceptor, he becomes a dog.
Desiring her [the friend's] wife in one's mind, or even coveting that person's wealth without hesitation,
a living being who treats a friend with contempt is reborn as a donkey.
Having caused suffering to one's parents, one is born as a tortoise;
likewise, he who, having relied upon his husband's sustenance, deceives that very man [is born as such].
He too, having fallen into delusion, is born as a monkey after death;
one who misappropriates a deposit, being released from hell, is born as a worm.
One who is envious becomes a *rākṣasa* even after being released from hell;
and a man who betrays trust is born in the womb of a fish.
Having accumulated grains, one is born as a mouse after death;
but from violating another's wife, one is born as a terrible wolf.
Through attachment to the wife of a brother, a man is born as a cuckoo;
by approaching the wife of a teacher or others, a man is born as a pig.
One who creates obstacles for sacrifices, gifts, and marriages becomes a worm;
so too does he who eats food without having first offered it to the deities, the ancestors, and the Brahmins.
Even if released from hell, one is born as a crow;
and due to insulting an elder brother, one is born in the womb of a crane.
But a Śūdra who has approached a Brāhmaṇī woman is born in the womb of a worm;
having produced offspring in her, he becomes a wood-worm within a log.
An ungrateful person is born as a worm, an insect, a moth, or a scorpion;
likewise, a man who seizes a weaponless person is reborn as a donkey.
One who kills a woman becomes a worm, and one who kills a child is born as such;
moreover, a man who steals food is born as a fly.
By stealing clarified butter one becomes a cat; by stealing sesame seeds, a mouse;
by stealing ghee, a mongoose; and by stealing meat, a crow.
Having stolen honey, a man is born as a gadfly; having stolen a cake, he becomes an ant; but a sinful soul who has stolen water is born as a crow.
If one steals wood, one is born as a Hārīta bird or a pigeon;
but having stolen a golden vessel, one is born in the womb of a worm.
Upon stealing cotton, one is born as a curlew; likewise, a fire-thief becomes a crane.
