Having stolen cosmetic pigments or vegetable leaves, one is born as a peacock.
A man who steals red cloth becomes a *jīvañjīvaka* bird;
one who steals auspicious perfumes becomes a muskrat (*chuchundarī*), and one who steals a rabbit becomes a rabbit.
By stealing a bundle [of goods], one becomes a eunuch; by stealing wood, a carrier of wood; by stealing grass, a worm;
by stealing flowers, a pauper; and by stealing from a beggar, a man becomes lame.
The stealer of vegetables becomes a green parrot (hārīta), and the stealer of water becomes a cātaka bird;
having gone to the most dreadful hells such as Raurava, the stealer of houses enters them as well.
One who steals grass, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, or bark shall become a tree;
this same sequence is observed for those who steal cows, gold, and other such things.
One who steals knowledge shall become mute after having gone through many hells;
indeed, one who offers oblations into a fire that lacks fuel becomes weak in digestion.
Censuring others, ingratitude, violating another's boundaries, cruelty, mercilessness, and consorting with the wives of others; (GarP 1,225.34)

One should recognize from these signs that those who steal the property of others, revile the deities, practice deceit, bind men, exhibit miserliness, and commit the slaughter of humans have not yet been liberated from hell. (GarP 1.225.35)

Compassion toward living beings, discourse regarding the next world, ritual action, truthfulness, speech for the sake of welfare, and the recognition of the authority of the Vedas. // GarP_1,225.36 //
Service to gurus, gods, and ṛṣis, as well as perfected beings (siddhas); self-restraint toward the virtuous;
performing rites with sincerity; and friendliness—these they know to be the characteristics of heaven.
Through the realization of the eightfold yoga, one attains the ultimate fruit.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ripening of Karma and Other Matters," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: I shall now describe the supreme Great Yoga (Mahāyoga) together with its ancillaries, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Listen to this pacification of all evils, which, when recited with devotion, brings about its result.
"‘It is mine’ is the root of suffering; ‘it is not mine’ is its cessation.
Indeed, the great-minded Dattātreya spoke this to Alarka."
The sprout "I" has arisen; the great trunk consists of the aggregates of "mine";
houses and fields are its branches, and whereon the wife is the tender shoot.
With wealth and grain as its great branches, rooted in evil and exceedingly difficult to traverse,
the great tree of ignorance has grown according to the rules for the sake of pleasure and peace.
Severed by the axe of knowledge, they have gone to dissolution in the Lord;
having attained it, they have drunk the essence of Brahman, which is free from passion and devoid of thorns.
The supreme wise ones attain both happiness and liberation;
indeed, O King, neither you nor I have yet achieved the dissolution of the body and the senses.
Neither speech nor the internal organ consists of those subtle elements (tanmātras) and so forth; what, O Indra among kings, do you perceive as this primary principle of ours?
"O King, though he was dead yesterday, this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) has been born today as one composed of the qualities (guṇa);
even in a state of oneness, there is thus a state of separation between the field and the self."

This separation preceded by knowledge occurs when the yogin’s [limited] cognition has perished; that is liberation: oneness with Brahman and non-oneness with the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti).
That is his home where he dwells; that is his food by which he lives;
and that alone is said to be for liberation—whether it be knowledge or ignorance—and not otherwise.
O King, merit and demerit are exhausted through their enjoyment;
likewise, obligatory duties are exhausted by their non-performance.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five *yamas*; then there are the *niyamas*, of which purity (*śauca*) is said to be of two kinds.
Contentment, austerity, tranquility, worship of Vāsudeva, self-restraint,
the lotus posture and others, and breath control which is the mastery over the vital winds.
Each of these is also threefold by way of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
That which lasts ten mātrās is the light; that which is double that is the middling.

That which is joined with three qualities and the measures (mātrās) is declared to be the "excellent" (uttama); when it is joined with recitation and meditation, it is the "embryo" (garbha), while the opposite is the "infant" (arbha).
In the first stage, one should conquer sleep; in the middle, trembling;
and in the third, the digestion [of food]; for the arisen defects are overcome in this successive order.
Having placed the *praṇava* in his heart, he should practice while seated,
touching his genitals and testicles with his two heels, with a one-pointed mind.
Having restrained the activity of *rajas* by means of *tamas*, and likewise that of *rajas* by means of *sattva*,
the knower of yoga, becoming motionless, should remain established in practice.
Having restrained the senses from their objects, as well as the vital breaths and so forth, one should undertake the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) through focused concentration.
Eighteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are prescribed as one concentration (dhāraṇā);
two concentrations are known as yoga by the yogis who perceive reality.
In the eastern channel, in the heart, and here a third in the chest;
in the throat, the mouth, the tip of the nose, the eyes, between the eyebrows, and on the crown of the head.
Furthermore, concentration upon that and upon what is beyond it is taught to be tenfold;
having attained these ten concentrations, one attains the state of the imperishable.
Just as fire cast into fire [is extinguished], so too is the self merged into the Supreme Self;
one should mutter the single syllable "Om," which is the form of Brahman and of great merit.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m* are the three syllables;
these three morae (*mātrā*) are then [the qualities] of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
The first half-mora, which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā), accessible to yogis, and established as the supreme (parā),
is to be known as Gāndhārī, resting upon the Gāndhāra note. This is the imperishable Brahman, designated by the name of the supreme Oṃkāra.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of the gross body;
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of old age and death.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, free from the impurity of the earth;
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of wind and space.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of the subtle body;
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of place and non-place.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of even the subtlest scent;
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of hearing and touch.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of tongue and nose;
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of prāṇa and apāna.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of vyāna and udāna breaths;
I am Brahman, the supreme light, entirely free from ignorance.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, the fourth state, the highest goal,
devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego.
I am Brahman— the supreme light, whose nature is knowledge, eternally pure, awakened, liberated, great bliss, and non-dual— for the sake of liberation.
Sūta said:
Thus, O Śaunaka, I have described to you the eight-limbed yoga that bestows liberation;
by performing the obligatory and occasional rites, those bound by material nature attain dissolution [into the source].
For in saṃsāra, beings do not arise as one; having gone through various states, one who was deluded by ignorance becomes liberated through knowledge once he is freed.
Then that yogi dies neither in suffering, nor as a sick man, nor without kinsmen;
he is not joined with sins, nor does he undergo maturation in hell.
May he not suffer while dwelling in the womb; may he be the imperishable Nārāyaṇa.
The Blessed One, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, is attainable through exclusive devotion.
Through meditation, worship, recitations, proper hymns of praise, observance of vows, sacrifices, and gifts, the purification of the mind is attained; by that, knowledge is obtained.
By means of mantras beginning with the *praṇava* and through recitations, the twice-born attained liberation;
even Indra reached the supreme station, as did the excellent Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The gods attained godhood, the sages reached the state of sages,
the gandharvas attained the state of gandharvas, and kings and others attained the status of royalty.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eight-Limbed Yoga," in the section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa), within the first part of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Chapter 227 of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*].
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim devotion to Viṣṇu, by which everything is attained;
for Hari is pleased by devotion in a way that He is not by anything else.
The remembrance of Hari is surely the root of great welfare, the source of a continuous stream of merit, and the sweet fruit of life.

Therefore, service has been declared by the wise to be the most abundant means for accomplishing devotion; those who chant the names, deeds, and other qualities of the Lord of the World are truly devoted.
Shedding tears out of great joy, with their hair standing on end, they said:
"We are the executors of the divine command of Maheśa, the Sustainer of the World."
Those Vaiṣṇavas who perform their daily rites here while remaining affectionate [toward the Lord],
yet do not hear the imperishable Brahman uttered by the Blessed One through that [Veda], [are as follows].
He who speaks with devotion preceded by prostration is indeed a Vaiṣṇava;
likewise, affection for his devotees, honoring them, and rejoicing in their merits [constitute the marks of a Vaiṣṇava].
Upon hearing his stories, there is joy, tears in the eyes, and transformations of the body;
by him who has, with his whole being and through devotion, fixed his state of mind upon Viṣṇu.
For he is a great devotee of the Lord because his self has been perfected through [service] to the Brahmins;
he constantly provides for the welfare of the world, avoids attachment for that purpose,
personally worships Viṣṇu, and lives in dependence upon Him.
Indeed, this devotion is eightfold; even if a barbarian practices it, he is a lord of Brahmins, a glorious sage, and he attains the supreme goal.
To him gifts should be given and from him they should be received; he is to be honored like Hari.
O best of the twice-born, whether remembered, addressed, or even worshipped, a devotee of the Blessed One purifies—even if he be a Caṇḍāla—by his very presence.
"Show compassion to one who has sought refuge and says, 'I am yours.
Granting fearlessness to all beings—this is the vow of Hari."
One who has reached the further shore of all Vedānta is superior to thousands of mantra-reciters;
one who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is superior to ten million knowers of all Vedānta.
Those who are single-mindedly devoted go to the supreme state by means of their own bodies;
for Viṣṇu is equal [to all] through his singular nature, and therefore he is their ultimate refuge.
Because those whose minds are devoted to Him are declared to be single-minded,
they are most dear to the God of gods, even more so than all other beloved ones.
Even in times of adversity, his devotion is always unwavering;
it is a love for Viṣṇu that is superior and constant, unlike the fleeting affection one feels for sense objects.
For me, who constantly remembers Viṣṇu, she does not depart from my heart;
even though I am a firm devotee who has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas.
One who is not devoted to the Lord of All should be known as the lowest of men;
even if he has not studied the Vedas and Shastras, nor performed sacrifices,
he has accomplished everything by maintaining devotion to Viṣṇu.
Even those who have performed sacrifices, presided over the principal rituals, and mastered the Vedas do not attain that goal which the best of sages, the devotees, attain.
"Whosoever in this world is a Vaiṣṇava, even if they follow false conduct or belong to no stage of life,
purifies all the worlds like the risen thousand-rayed sun."
Even those who are cruel, evil-minded, and devoted to sinful conduct reach the supreme abode if they are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
When firm and unwavering devotion to Janārdana arises, then what need is there for the happiness of heaven? That devotion alone is the cause of liberation.

For men wandering there in this cycle of existence, which is as difficult to traverse as a sea of mud, there is indeed but one hand to hold: that by which Janārdana may be pleased. Yet he does not hear the divine qualities of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods.
That Māra should be known as deaf, excluded from all dharmas.
If, when the name of Viṣṇu is proclaimed, the body of a man does not break out in horripilation, that body shall be like a corpse.
O best of the twice-born, in whomsoever there is devotion, even liberation shall soon occur;
for those men whose minds are absorbed therein, there is in every way the destruction of all evil.
Beholding his own servant with noose in hand, Yama indeed whispers into his ear:
"Avoid him who has taken refuge in Madhusūdana; I am the lord over other men, but certainly not over the devotees of Viṣṇu."
Moreover, even if one of very wicked conduct worships me with undivided devotion,
he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.
He quickly becomes righteous in nature and attains eternal peace;
O best of Brahmins, know this for certain: a devotee of Viṣṇu never perishes.
What need has he for dharma, artha, or kāma? Liberation stands in his very hand, he whose devotion to Hari is firm—the root of all the worlds.
For this divine illusion (māyā) of Hari, consisting of the [three] qualities (guṇa), is difficult to overcome;
those who take refuge in Him alone cross over this illusion.
What remains for men to accomplish through the performance of sacrifice for the sake of propitiating those whose intellect is fixed on Hari?
Viṣṇu is propitiated by devotion alone; nothing else is of assistance therein.
That Great-Souled One, Janārdana, does not attain such satisfaction through various gifts given, nor through flowers, nor even through ointments, as he does through devotion.
Of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, there are indeed two fruits comparable to nectar:
devotion to Keśava at some time, or association with his devotees.
While leaves, flowers, fruits, and water— easily obtained— are always available,
one should instead exert effort toward the ancient Puruṣa, who is attainable only through devotion and whose attainment alone is liberation.
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers dance, saying:
"A Vaiṣṇava has been born in our family; he will deliver us."
Since even sinful men such as Śiśupāla and Suyodhana— who were ignorant and full of insults—
attained liberation, their sins being shaken off by mere remembrance, what doubt can there be regarding those people who possess supreme devotion?
Those who have taken refuge in that Śaraṇa, even though they are devoid of the yoga of meditation,
transcend death and go to that very station of Viṣṇu.

O Mādhava, may this horse of my mind, which has been struck down by hundreds of afflictions arising from worldly existence and wanders about unrestrained through the apertures of the senses like wild horses, be brought under control and bound with the firm tether of devotion to the hitching-post of Your feet.
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme Brahman, yet he is described here as having three divisions;
those who are deluded do not understand this within the paths of the Vedantic doctrines.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "An Exposition on Devotion to the Blessed Lord," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—228.
Sūta said:
The man who bows to that which is the cause of liberation— without beginning or end, unborn, undecaying, and imperishable— becomes worthy of homage by the entire world.
I always bow with devotion, with my mind, to Viṣṇu, who is bliss, non-duality, pure consciousness, the all-pervading Lord, whose abode is the heart.
I bow to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, the witness of all, who, dwelling within, beholds the auspicious and inauspicious of the entire universe.
Even by one who is capable, a prostration performed to the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi) indeed causes trembling among the masses of straws that are worldly existence.
In Kṛṣṇa— whose beautiful dark body resembles the interior of a shimmering rain-cloud, who is the Supreme Person presiding over the worlds, and the ultimate object of knowledge—
a single firm prostration made with the sole intent of devotion is indeed capable of instantly purifying even an outcaste dog-cooker.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one who worships with a salutation attains a destination that cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Even for those rushing across the shoreless ocean of the difficult wilderness of saṃsāra,
a single prostration to Kṛṣṇa will deliver them to liberation.
Whether sitting, lying down, or standing, or wherever one may be, one should take sole refuge in the mantra: "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa."
The word "Nārāyaṇa" exists, and speech is under one's control;
nevertheless, that fools fall into hell—what is so surprising about that?

Even if some man of pure mind were to have four faces, or even ten million faces, he might indeed speak of but a single ten-thousandth part of the qualities of Viṣṇu, the best of gods— or perhaps not at all.
All the sages, beginning with Vyāsa, though praising Madhusūdana,
turn back due to the exhaustion of their intellects, not because of any exhaustion of Govinda’s qualities.
Even when his name is uttered involuntarily, a person is instantly liberated from all sins, just as deer terrified by a lion;
he has thus girded his loins for the journey toward liberation.
Even in a dream, the mere touch of this name destroys an inexhaustible heap of sins for a person; how much more so, then, when the name of Janārdana is proclaimed by a man before his very eyes?
O Brahmin, those who have uttered the names "Kṛṣṇa," "Acyuta," "Ananta," and "Vāsudeva" with their hearts imbued with true devotion,
have not gone to the city of Yama.
Just as the destruction of fire occurs upon the rising of the sun,
even so the destruction of the flood of impurities occurs through the chanting of the names of Hari.
Where is the ascent to the vault of heaven that never returns to decay for those whose minds are darkened by delusion as they travel the long journey?
The proclamation of the names of Hari, the lotus-eyed one, is the provision for the journey;
it is the sole remedy for the effects of the poison when bitten by the serpent of saṃsāra.
By chanting the Vaiṣṇava name "Kṛṣṇa" with patience, a person becomes liberated.
What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by reciting mantras in the Tretā, and by performing worship in the Dvāpara, that one attains in the Kali age simply by remembering Keśava.
He on whose tip of the tongue the two syllables "Ha-ri" reside,
having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra, shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu.
Even if surrounded by thousands of known misdeeds, a person who desires supreme welfare and seeks complete purification,
being devoted solely to the narrative of the praise of Nārāyaṇa, shall certainly not see rebirth again, even in a dream.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Devotion to Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 229 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa].
Sūta said:
May he who offers flowers and even water with the Puruṣasūkta perform the essential worship of Hari, the Lord of all the worlds without exception.
By him who does not worship Viṣṇu, this entire world of mobile and immobile beings would remain unhonored; one should know such a person to be a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who does not meditate upon that Viṣṇu, from whom the activity of all beings proceeds and by whom all this is pervaded, shall become a worm in excrement.
While being cooked in hell, he was addressed by Yama:
"Why did you not worship the god Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions?"
The Lord, who honors all things even with the absence of water and gives his own world,
has he not been honored by you?
Neither that mother, nor the father, nor even a kinsman performs what Hṛṣīkeśa does when he is satisfied and worshipped with faith.
By a person who observes the conduct prescribed for their social class and stage of life, the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is propitiated; there is no other path that causes him satisfaction.
That Great-Souled One, Janārdana, does not attain such satisfaction through various gifts given, nor through flowers, nor through ointments, as he does through devotion.
Neither through wealth, sovereignty, or greatness, nor through progeny or ritual action, nor even through those who are liberated can oneness with Hari be attained; worship of Hari is the root.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—230.
Sūta said:
Having examined all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this one thing is well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times.
What need has he for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices—
he who constantly meditates upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa with undivided mind?
Sixty thousand and sixty hundred sacred fords are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single prostration made to Nārāyaṇa.
Know that among all the various penances and ritual acts that constitute expiations without exception,
the supreme one is the constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇa.
For that man in whom attachment arises even toward committed sin,
the one supreme expiation is the constant remembrance of Hari.
Even he who meditates on Nārāyaṇa for a single moment without sloth attains the state of heaven; how much more so one who is devoted to him as his supreme goal!
For a yogi established in yoga, whatever mental fluctuation occurs during waking, dreaming, or deep sleep,
it becomes one that rests upon Acyuta.
Whether rising or falling, speaking or entering, eating or waking—whoever should remember Govinda, Mādhava; GarP_1,230.8 //
Devoted to one's own respective duty, one should fix the mind upon Janārdana;
this is the teaching according to the scriptures—what is the use of many other words?
Meditation alone is the supreme dharma; meditation alone is the supreme austerity;
meditation alone is the supreme purity; therefore, one should be devoted to meditation.
There is no higher object of meditation than Viṣṇu, and no austerity superior to fasting;
therefore, the contemplation of Vāsudeva is said here to be the most important.
Even that which is difficult to obtain, supreme, attainable, and beyond the range of the mind—
Madhusūdana grants that very thing when meditated upon, even if it is not requested.
Whatever ritual act may fall away from those performing sacrifices through negligence, that becomes complete simply by the remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation.
There is no purifier of evil deeds equal to meditative absorption;
the fire of yoga is the burner of the causes for future bodies.
But the yogin whose meditative concentration is fully perfected, and whose karma has been burnt away by the fire of yoga, attains liberation in this very life without delay.
Just as a fire with rising flames or the wind burns dry grass,
so too does all impurity [burn away] for the yogi when Viṣṇu is established in the mind.
Just as gold becomes pure through contact with fire,
so too is the constant impurity of human beings consumed by Vāsudeva.
Whatever sin remains after a thousand baths in the Gaṅgā or ten million baths at Puṣkara, that perishes when Hari is remembered.
Whatever sin is certainly destroyed by thousands of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
that same sin is destroyed in a mere moment through meditation on Hari.
Neither the wicked speech arising from the influence of the Kali age nor the doctrines of heretics shall affect the mind of that person in whose heart Keśava resides.
That lunar day, that day and night, that conjunction, and that moon,
as well as that very astrological sign, are renowned as sacred whenever Hari is remembered therein.
That is a loss, that is a great defect, and that is the mute dullness of one ignorant of the goal:
if for even a moment, or even for an instant, Vāsudeva is not meditated upon.
For him in whom Govinda is not in the heart, and Acyuta is not in the mind, the Kṛta Age is a Kali Age; for him in whom he dwells, even the Kali Age is the Kṛta Age.
He whose mind is constantly fixed on Govinda, whether he is walking before Him or behind Him, or even while standing still— he is always one who has accomplished his purpose.
O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth,
even the fruit of the status of Indra and the like is an obstacle.
Without abandoning the life of a householder, and having performed great austerity, he—
whose mind is offered to Keśava— cuts through the illusion of human existence.
When Govinda dwells within the heart, people practice forgiveness toward the angry, compassion toward the foolish, and joy toward those of virtuous character.
One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa during acts such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts,
and especially during all rites of expiation for misdeeds.
They have gained their reward, they have achieved victory; how could there be defeat for those in whose hearts Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus, resides?
Even for swarms of insects and birds whose minds are surrendered to Hari, there is indeed an upward course;
how much more so for wise men?
Why is the shade of the Vāsudeva-tree not resorted to— a shade that is neither too cold nor too hot, and which pacifies the gates of hell?
Moreover, O friend, neither the curse of Durvāsas nor even the kingdom of the Lord of Śacī was capable of destroying him, for Madhusūdana had taken up residence in his heart.
Whether one is speaking, standing, or performing other actions according to one's will,
when the thought does not depart, one should consider that the dhāraṇā has been accomplished.

Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, a crown, and a necklace, possessing a golden body and holding the conch and the discus, should always be meditated upon.
Indeed, there is no purifier found here equal to meditative absorption;
even one who eats the food of an outcaste, though sinful, is not defiled by it.
If the mind of a living being is always thus attached to the realm of sense objects,
even toward Nārāyaṇa, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Sūta said:
Whosever mind possesses devotion to Viṣṇu, whom else would that living being ever bow down to?
He at once delivers himself from the ocean of evil.
That is true knowledge where Govinda is; that is true discourse where Kāśyapa is; that is true action which is for his sake—what is the use of much other talk?
That is a true tongue which praises Hari; that is a true mind which is offered to him;
those alone are praiseworthy hands which perform his worship.
The gods know that prostration to the Lord is the fruit for the head; worshiping him is the fruit for the hands;
reflecting upon his qualities and deeds is the fruit for the mind; and praising the virtues of Govinda is the fruit for speech.
Even a heap of sinful karma as large as Mount Meru or Mandara is entirely destroyed by the mere remembrance of Keśava.
Whatever action a person performs, whether good or evil,
by consigning it all to Nārāyaṇa, he is not tainted even while acting.
The fourfold collection of beings, from blades of grass up to the four-faced Brahmā—
the entire world of moving and unmoving things— is fast asleep through your māyā.

When the mind is fixed upon Him, one does not go to hell; even heaven is an obstacle when He is being meditated upon; and even the world of Brahmā becomes insignificant in His presence. If liberation resides within the heart, the Imperishable One grants it even to men of dull intellect—what wonder is there that this [world] goes to its dissolution when Acyuta is glorified?
Those who perform fire-rituals, recitation, bathing, meditation on Viṣṇu, and worship there,
will cross over the ocean of suffering.
The king is the refuge of the kingdom, and parents are the refuge of the child;
Dharma is the refuge of all mortals, and Hari is the refuge of everything.
O best of sages, for those who bow to Vāsudeva, the eternal source of the world,
there exists no sacred ford superior to them.
One should perform worship with priceless jewels and likewise engage in the private recitation of scripture,
constantly and without sloth, meditating upon that very Govinda while keeping him in mind.
A man who regards even a Śūdra, a devotee of the Blessed One, a Niṣāda,
or a Śvapaca as equal to those of the twice-born castes does not go to hell.
Just as one always praises a wealthy person with devotion out of a desire for wealth,
who would not be liberated from bondage by praising the Creator of the universe?
Just as fire that has reached its source burns even moist fuel,
so does Viṣṇu, abiding in such a manner, burn away all the impurities of yogins.
Just as deer and other wild animals do not resort to a mountain on fire,
so too do all evils avoid the man who is devoted to the practice of yoga.
To whatever extent one has faith, to that same extent is one's accomplishment;
by this alone is the power of Kṛṣṇa measured.
Even out of enmity, Śiśupāla, the son of Damaghoṣa, attained the ultimate reality by remembering Govinda; how much more so one who is devoted to Him?
Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Viṣṇu," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 231] Sūta said:
O Śaunaka, I shall now proclaim the hymn to Nārasiṃha as spoken by Śiva;
formerly, all the hosts of Mothers spoke these words to Śaṅkara.
"O Blessed One, we shall devour the entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans; it behoves you to grant us permission for this through your grace."
Śaṅkara said:
"All subjects must be protected by you without a doubt;
therefore, let your minds, which are for the most part inclined toward violence, be quickly turned away."
Disregarding these words spoken by Śaṅkara,
they undisturbedly devoured the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
While the three worlds were indeed being devoured by the host of Mothers,
the Blessed Śiva meditated upon the Lord in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
The god who is without beginning or end, the source of the existence of all beings,
with lightning-like tongue, great fangs, and a garland of quivering manes.
Adorned with jeweled armlets and a crown, decorated with golden filaments,
and resplendent with a great golden waistband.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, adorned with jeweled anklets,
his splendor pervaded the entire pavilion within the belly of the universe.
His body hairs were joined together in shapes resembling whirlpools,
and he wore a great garland composed of all kinds of flowers.
As soon as he was meditated upon, the Blessed One granted him a vision in whatever form Rudra had been meditated upon with devotion.
In that very form, which was difficult even for the gods to behold,
Śaṅkara prostrated before the Lord of Gods and then offered praise.
Śaṅkara said:
Homage be to you, O Lord of the World, who assume the form of Narasiṃha,
resplendent with the shells of your claws that destroy the lords of the Daityas.
O you whose tawny body is adorned with a circle of nails,
homage be to Padmanābha, the beautiful teacher of the world!
O you whose roar is like the clouds at the end of an aeon, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns!
O you who possess the fearlessness of a thousand Yamas, the prowess of a thousand Indras,
the abundance of a thousand Dhanadas, and whose nature consists of a thousand feet!
O you who resemble a thousand moons,
whose stride is like that of a thousand suns and Hari,
possessing the splendor of a thousand Rudras, and praised by a thousand Brahmās!
Chanted over by a thousand Rudras, beheld by the Thousand-eyed One,
the crusher of a thousand births, the liberator from a thousand bonds.
"O you whose eyes possess the speed of a thousand winds, O you who show compassion through a thousand commands!
Having thus praised Hari, the Lord of the gods of gods, who has the form of Narasimha, Śiva, bowing low with humility, addressed him once more."
"The Mothers who were created by me for the destruction of Andhaka,
disregarding my word, shall instead devour these wondrous creatures."
"Having created them, I, the unconquered, am not able to withdraw them;
having first brought them into being, how could I take pleasure in their destruction? (GarP 1.231.19)
Thus addressed by Rudra, Hari, who possesses the form of Narasiṃha, then [spoke]; from the tips of his thousand tongues, Hari, the Lord of Speech, [uttered]: GarP_1,231.20.
Likewise, the omnipresent Hari, having withdrawn all the hosts of gods and the fierce groups of Mothers,
and having brought peace to the world, vanished from sight.
Whoever, with senses restrained, recites this Nārasiṃha hymn, for him it grants all desires, just as Rudra does; of this there is no doubt.
One should meditate upon Nṛsiṃha, whose eyes are like the rising sun, who arises from the white lotus, and who blazes like a flaming fire;
he is without beginning, middle, or end, unborn, ancient, the lord of both the transcendent and the immanent, and the repository of all worlds.
One should recite this; it abandons the continuous web of suffering just as the sun discards the mist.
When one assumes the form of the assembly of mothers, then one remains in their presence.

In order to perform the worship of the Lord of Gods who has assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha, the destroyer of Tripura propitiated that best of deities; having obtained [his favor], may he protect [us] as well as the hosts of Mothers of the world.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Hymn to Nṛsiṃha," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 232] Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the *kulāmṛta*, that hymn which Hara spoke when questioned by Śrī Nārada; likewise, listen as it was told to Nārada.
Nārada said:

He who is always bound by the pairs of opposites— desire and anger, auspicious and inauspicious— and is tormented by the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, is a person of wicked intellect.
In an instant, a living being is liberated from the ocean of death and saṃsāra.
O Blessed One, O Destroyer of Tripura, I truly desire to hear this from you.
Having heard those words of Nārada, the three-eyed Śambhu, Hara, with a gracious countenance, spoke to that ṛṣi.
Maheśvara said:
O best of sages, listen; I shall speak of the supreme nectar of knowledge, the ultimate secret and mystery, which destroys suffering and removes the fear of the bonds of worldly existence.
By whose illusory power the entire world— the fourfold collection of beings from blades of grass up to the four-faced Brahmā, including all that is moving and unmoving— is plunged into deep sleep.
If anyone awakens through the grace of that Viṣṇu,
he crosses over saṃsāra, which is difficult even for the gods to cross.
Intoxicated by the pride of wealth and power, and turning their backs on the knowledge of reality,
living beings, maddened by their children, wives, and families, sink into ruin.
All are submerged in a single ocean like aged wild elephants;
whoever binds you, that fool is like a silkworm.
I do not see liberation for him even in hundreds of millions of births;
therefore, O Nārada, one should always properly worship Viṣṇu, the imperishable God of all gods, and meditate upon him with joy.
But he who always meditates upon Viṣṇu— the omniscient, immovable one, unborn, and without beginning or end, who is established within the self— is completely liberated.
By constantly meditating upon the divine Viṣṇu, who is suited for the womb, one is liberated;
by constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu, who is bodiless, the creator, whose delight is in all knowledge, who is immovable yet omnipresent, one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Vāsudeva— the Guru, Viṣṇu— who is free from conceptual construction, devoid of appearance, beyond proliferation, and untainted, one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— the auspicious, single-syllabled one who is the soul of all things and whose form is the consciousness of the Self— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who transcends speech, who knows the three periods of time, who is the Lord of the universe, the witness of the world, and the highest of all— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu, who is served by Brahmā and the other gods, Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and yogis, one is liberated.
For the entire world, desiring liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra,
is indeed liberated by thus praising Viṣṇu, the giver of boons, while constantly meditating upon him.
Anyone who, desiring liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra,
remains concentrated and constantly meditates upon the infinite and imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, who is established in the universe, the unborn Lord of the universe— Viṣṇu— is liberated.
Sūta said:
In ancient times, when he was thus questioned by Nārada, that bull-bannered Lord explained it to him;
that which was explained by him has been related by me to you.
Constantly meditating upon that very Brahman— imperishable, partless, and undecaying—
you shall surely attain, my dear, the eternal and immutable state.
Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of one whose mind is focused for a single moment.
Having heard from the Lord this preeminence of Viṣṇu, that celestial sage,
having properly propitiated Viṣṇu, attained perfection and reached the supreme state.
Whoever should read or even hear this supreme hymn constantly,
even the sin committed by them throughout ten million lifetimes shall be destroyed.
Whoever recites with diligence this divine hymn to Viṣṇu, proclaimed by Mahādeva, daily attains immortality.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Hymn to Kulāmṛta," in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 233 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
I shall now fully proclaim that hymn spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"I have taken refuge in Dāmodara; what can death do to me?"
I have taken refuge in the Lord who bears the conch and the discus, whose form is manifest, who is imperishable, and who is born from below; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in Varāha, Vāmana, Viṣṇu, Nārasiṃha, Janārdana, and Mādhava; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Puruṣa, the seed of the Puṣkara field, the merit of the world, the Lord of the world, and the Protector of the world; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the thousand-headed God, the eternal, who is both manifest and unmanifest, the Great Yoga; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Great Self, the soul of all beings, the source of sacrifice, not born from a womb, whose form is the universe; what can death do to me?
Having heard this hymn uttered by that high-souled one,
Death, tormented by the messengers of Viṣṇu, departed from that place.
Thus was Death conquered by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya;
when the lotus-eyed Nṛsiṃha is propitiated, nothing is difficult to attain.
This meritorious "Eightfold Hymn to Death," auspicious and a pacifier of death,
was spoken by Viṣṇu himself for the benefit of Mārkaṇḍeya.
For that man who, being pure and with a mind fixed on Acyuta, recites this with devotion three times a day regularly,
there shall be no untimely death.
Having meditated upon the ancient Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa— the eternal and immeasurable— who shines more brilliantly than the sun within the center of the heart-lotus, that yogin likewise conquered death.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Eight-Verse Hymn to Death" composed by Mārkaṇḍeya, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 234 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the hymn to Acyuta; listen, O Śaunaka, for it bestows all things.
Just as Brahmā, when questioned by Nārada, spoke that supreme [teaching], so shall I speak.
Nārada said: "You should tell me how Viṣṇu— the imperishable, the undecaying, the bestower of boons—
is to be praised by me every day at the time of worship."
They are blessed, they are of noble birth, for they bestow all happiness;
their lives are fruitful, those who always praise the Imperishable One.
Brahmā said:
O Sage, I shall proclaim a hymn of praise to Vāsudeva that grants liberation;
listen to it, by which he, when properly praised at the time of worship, becomes gracious.
Oṃ, homage! Homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva; homage to the remover of all [sins];
homage to the one of pure body; homage to the one whose very nature is knowledge.
Homage to the Lord of all gods; homage to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa;
homage to him who holds a shield and sword in his hands; homage to him who wears a garland of lotuses.
Salutations to the foundation of the universe, and salutations to the one clad in yellow garments;
salutations to the one in the form of Nṛsiṃha, and repeated salutations to Vaikuṇṭha.
Homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to the one who reclines upon the ocean of milk;
homage to the one with a thousand heads; homage to the one who lies upon the body of the serpent.
Homage to the one who holds an axe in his hand; homage to the one who brings an end to the kṣatriyas;
homage to the one whose vow is true; homage again and again to the unconquered.
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds, and homage to the wielder of the discus;
homage to Śiva, the subtle, the ancient—homage again and again!
Homage to the one in the form of Vāmana, who took away King Bali’s kingdom;
homage to Yajñavarāha, to Govinda—homage again and again!
Homage to you, supreme bliss; homage to you, supreme syllable.
Homage to you, the true essence of gnosis; homage to you, the bestower of gnosis.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Non-duality; salutations to you, O Supreme Person. Salutations to you, O God who creates the universe; salutations to you, O Originator of the universe.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Universe; salutations to you, O Cause of the Universe.
Salutations to you, O slayer of the Daitya Madhu; salutations to you, O destroyer of Rāvaṇa.
Salutations to you, O slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin; salutations to you, O destroyer of Kaiṭabha.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Salutations to you, O slayer of Kālanemi; salutations to you, whose seat is Garuḍa.
Salutations to you, son of Devakī; salutations to you, joy of the Vṛṣṇis.
Salutations to you, O beloved of Rukmiṇī; salutations to you, O son of Aditi;
salutations to you, whose abode is Gokula; salutations to you, who are dear to Gokula.
Victory to you, Kṛṣṇa, who assumed the form of a cowherd; victory to you, beloved of the cowherd women!
Victory to you, the upholder of Govardhana; victory to you, the increaser of Gokula!
Victory to you, O slayer of the hero Rāvaṇa! Victory to you, O destroyer of Cāṇūra!
Victory to you, O light of the Vṛṣṇi clan! Victory to you, O subduer of Kālīya!
Victory to you, the Truth, the witness of the world! Victory to you, the accomplisher of all aims!
Victory to you, known through the Vedānta! Victory to you, O Mādhava, the giver of all!
Victory to you, the unmanifest refuge of all; victory to you, O omnipresent Mādhava!
Victory to you, the subtle essence of consciousness; victory to you, the stainless mind!
Victory be unto you, O Supportless One; victory, O Peaceful and Eternal One!
Victory, O Lord, nourisher of the world;
victory, O Viṣṇu—homage be to you!

O Hari, you are the guru; you are the disciple; you are the initiation, the mantras, and the maṇḍala; you are the ritual placements (nyāsa), the mudrās, and the commitments (samaya); and you are the means of accomplishment, such as the flowers and other offerings.
You are the support; you indeed are the infinite; you are the tortoise; you are the earth-lotus.
You indeed are dharma, knowledge, and the rest—the powers of the altar and the maṇḍala.
O Lord, you are Rāma, the bearer of the deceptive disguise; you are again that slayer of Khara;
you are the divine Brahmarṣi, and you are Viṣṇu of true prowess.
You are Nṛsiṃha, the supreme bliss; you are Varāha, the upholder of the earth;
you are Suparṇa, as well as the discus, the mace, and the conch shell.
O Lord, you are Śrī; you are the Fist-Being; O God, you are the eternal garland. You are indeed the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, the Śārṅga bow, and likewise the quiver.
You are with the sword and the shield; you are likewise the guardians of the quarters, O Lord;
you are the Piercer (Brahmā), you are the Ordainer, you are Yama, and you are the Consumer of Oblations (Agni).
You are the Lord of Wealth, you are Īśāna, you are Indra, and you are the Lord of the Waters;
you are the sovereign of the Rākṣasas, you are the Sādhyas, you are Vāyu, and you are the Maker of Night.
You are the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins; you are the hosts of Maruts.
You are the Daityas, the Dānavas, and the Nāgas; you are the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, and the birds.
You are the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, the Siddhas, the Pitṛs, and the great gods;
you are indeed the elements, the objects of the senses, and the unmanifest senses as well.
You are the mind, the intellect, and the ego; you are the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Lord within the heart.
You are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation vaṣaṭ, you are the syllable oṃ, and you are the sacrificial fuel and the kuśa grass.
You are the altar, O Hari; you are the initiation, you are the sacrificial post, and you are the fire.
You are the wife, you are the sacrificial cake, you are the hall, and you are both the offering-spoon and the ladle.
You are indeed the pressing-stones and the entire assembly; you are the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) always present.
You are the winnowing-basket and other implements, and you are certainly Brahmā, the pestle, and the mortar.
You are the Hotṛ priest, you are the sacrificer; you are the grain and the animal-sacrificer;
you are the Adhvaryu, you are the Udgātṛ, and you are the sacrifice, O Supreme Person.

You are the quarters, the netherworld, the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens; you are the creator of the stars, and among gods, animals, and humans, you are this entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
O God, whatever is seen— the entire universe and the whole world—
all this is your form, manifested for the purpose of being perceived.
They take refuge in the Supreme Brahman, which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
who knows that stainless one, accessible through yoga and beyond the reach of the senses? (GarP 1.234.38)
The imperishable, eternal Person, unmanifest, unborn, and undecaying;
devoid of dissolution or origination, all-pervading, and the Lord.
The omniscient, devoid of qualities, pure, blissful, undecaying, supreme,
consisting of consciousness, eternal, peaceful, full, non-dual, and imperishable.
O God, those inhabitants of heaven who do not know your supreme state worship you through that form which is seen at a distance during your incarnations.
O Supreme Person, O Lord, how am I able to propitiate you who are so subtle, who are accessible only to the mind, and who are beyond the range of the senses?
O Lord, wherever in this maṇḍala worship is performed according to the prescribed rites with flowers, incense, and other offerings, there all prosperities reside.
Whatever has been worshipped by me through the distinctions of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others,
you should forgive all of that— both what was done and what was left undone by me.
"O Lord, I am unable to perform the worship correctly as it has been described;
whatever recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth have been performed, O Puruṣottama, they are ineffective."
Therefore, out of devotion, I seek your forgiveness for my actions during the day,
at night, at the twilights, and in all circumstances.
O Hari, may my devotion to Your pair of feet be unshakable;
not [in] my body.
Likewise, there is no joy in the [pursuit of] dharma and the other [aims].
O Lord of the World, since my love for you is absolute,
what deed has not been performed by me that serves as a means to attain heaven, liberation, and the like?
O Acyuta, who is able to perform worship or offer praise to you, in whom firm devotion is placed, for you are the bestower of the fruits of all desires? (GarP 1.234.49)
"Today my praise has been honored; forgive me for that. Homage be to you!
Thus has the hymn to Cakradhāra been correctly recited by me.
O Sage, if you desire the supreme state, praise Viṣṇu with devotion."
Whoever praises the Teacher of the World with this hymn at the time of worship, [attains the highest state].
Having severed the bonds of saṃsāra, he will soon attain liberation;
so too shall any other who, being self-restrained and pure, recites [this] with devotion at the three junctions of the day.
O Sage, by this hymn of praise, even he shall obtain all his desires;
one seeking a son obtains sons, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
One who is passionate is freed from disease; one who is destitute obtains wealth;
one seeking knowledge acquires knowledge; and one finds fortune and fame.
Possessing the memory of past births and endowed with intelligence, whatever he desires with his mind,
he is blessed, all-knowing, wise, virtuous, and the performer of all deeds.
He who praises the Supreme Person is truthful in speech, pure, and a giver;
for all those [others] are unfit to be spoken with, as they are excluded from all righteous dharma.
For those who do not perform virtuous deeds dedicated to Hari when they engage in activity,
the mind of that evil-souled person is not pure, and his speech is likewise impure.
He whose devotion to Viṣṇu, the bestower of all goals, is unwavering,
having worshipped according to the rules the god Hari, who grants all happiness— ||| GarP_1,234.58 |||
A person who is full of faith, O best of gods, attains exactly whatever fruit they rightly desire— whether it be action, desire, or anything else—
for there is no distinction made by the Siddhas regarding whom they grant a body, whether that of an Asura or another.

I bow to that Vāsudeva—the unborn, immortal Lord, free from fear and death, whose nature is eternal bliss—who is contemplated as the primordial, pure one by all sages; who is seated within the hearts of all; who knows all as the witness of everything.

I worship with the flowers of my own being the Lord of all worlds—the eternal, well-pleased, exceedingly pure and stainless, devoid of qualities, and in whom all things rejoice in happiness; may that All-Witness, the conscious Self, enter the lotus of my heart.
Thus have I described the supreme power of the highest Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end;
therefore, that Supreme Lord should be properly meditated upon by a man desiring liberation.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu— the ancient Puruṣa whose nature is consciousness, who is the color of the sun, stainless, and pure, the supreme non-dual— what yogi would not attain liberation therein?
That person who, being likewise disciplined and tranquil, constantly recites this hymn,
becomes cleansed of evil and, with his power expanded, goes to the vast realm of Murāri.
He who desires wealth, complete happiness, as well as virtue, pleasure, and likewise liberation—
he, having renounced everything, goes for refuge to Viṣṇu, the supreme, ancient, and most excellent one.

He who has taken refuge in Vāsudeva— the all-pervading Lord, the sustainer of the universe, the pure one, and the cause of the destruction of the entire cycle of existence— who is stainless and free from attachment, attains liberation.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Acyuta," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: I shall now declare the knowledge of Brahman, which is the established conclusion of Vedānta and Sāṅkhya.
Contemplating thus: "I am Brahman, the supreme light, Viṣṇu."
The single light is situated in three ways: in the sun, in the sky of the heart, and in fire;
just as the ghee residing within the milk of cows does not provide strength [to them].
The great power that had emerged, joined with their karma, was bestowed upon them;
likewise, Viṣṇu, though residing within their bodies, did not bring about their welfare.
Without the propitiation of the Vīṇā, the omnipresent Supreme Lord [is not attained];
however, for those whose minds desire to ascend, the knowledge of ritual action has been proclaimed.
For those who have ascended the tree of yoga, knowledge is considered the supreme renunciation;
yet when one desires to know sounds and other objects, passion and aversion arise.
A person joined with greed, delusion, and anger would commit evil;
the two hands, the genitals, the stomach, and speech as the fourth—this is the quartet.
He whose [mind] is thus well-restrained is called a Brahmin by the wise;
he does not take the wealth of others, nor does he commit violence.
The hands of one who does not delight in gambling with dice are well-restrained;
the genitals of one who delights in avoiding the wives of others are well-restrained.
He eats this food without greed, for his stomach is restrained;
he speaks what is true, beneficial, and measured, because his speech is restrained.

For one whose senses, intellect, mind, and [other faculties] are always restrained in this way, what need is there for asceticism or sacrificial rites? For him, there is perpetual unity among the intellect, the mind, and the senses.
This meditation is proclaimed to be either "with seed" (sabīja) or "seedless" (nirbīja).
It is that which joins the intellect, situated between the eyebrows, with the objects of the senses.
When the senses have ceased their activity, yet the mind remains unsettled.
This living being sees dreams that are both external and internal;
thus do the wise say regarding the state of waking.
When he, situated in the heart, deluded by darkness, does not even remember what he knows from whence it came, that state is called deep sleep (suṣupti).
For him who is awake, neither drowsiness, nor delusion, nor confusion arises; thus, the self-controlled one does not perceive objects consisting of words and their meanings.
Having withdrawn the senses from their objects, as well as the mind, and having likewise [withdrawn] the intellect, the ego, primordial nature, and even the intellect itself; ||| GarP_1,235.16 |||
Having restrained even his own nature and abiding in the absolute through the power of consciousness,
he beholds within himself the Self by means of the self as the illuminator of the self.
Consisting of consciousness, immortal, pure, actionless, all-pervading, and auspicious—he is established in the fourth state; of this there is no doubt.
The five qualities beginning with sound and the three qualities beginning with *sattva*—
these indeed constitute the eight petals of the lotus of the *puryaṣṭaka*.
The state of equilibrium produced by the *guṇas* is *prakṛti*, and therein lies the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
The embodied deity, who is indeed of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), resides within that pericarp.
When the individual soul departs, having abandoned the city of eight constituents and primordial nature consisting of the qualities, then it attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Breath control, recitation, withdrawal of the senses,
concentration, meditation, and absorption— these six are the means for accomplishing yoga.
The destruction of evil brings delight to the deities and the restraint of the senses;
that which is joined with recitation and meditation is "with embryo" (sagarbha), while the opposite is "without embryo" (agarbhaka).
The best consists of thirty-six measures, the middling of twenty-four measures, and the lowest of twelve measures; one should constantly recite the syllable Oṃ.
When the *praṇava*, the designator, is known, Brahman, the designated, becomes gracious.
The six-syllabled mantra (*oṃ namo viṣṇave*) should be recited, as well as the twelve-syllabled *gāyatrī*.
The engagement of all the sense organs with their respective objects and the withdrawal of the mind from that [engagement] is proclaimed as *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
Having withdrawn the senses from the objects of the senses, he is indeed well-established;
together with his intellect, he remains steadfast in the practices of withdrawal.
For as long as the time taken by twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) may last,
for that duration one should fix the mind upon Brahman.
For that very [state], meditation has been proclaimed by Brahmā as twelve *dhāraṇās*;
when one is restrained and disciplined, one becomes satisfied—that is called *samādhi*.
The mind of one who meditates intensely does not waver while he is thus contemplating.
Having reached the prescribed duration of time, that is known as *dhāraṇā*;
it is when the mind, attached to the object of meditation, perceives only the object of meditation.
One knows no other object; this is proclaimed as meditation (dhyāna).
While contemplating the object of meditation, the mind attains immobility within that which is to be meditated upon.
That meditation which has been declared as supreme by the sages who contemplate meditation— indeed,
in all cases, the object of meditation alone remains, for the meditator has become absorbed in that very essence.
When one perceives that which is free from duality, that is called samādhi;
the mind, devoid of conceptual construction, should not think of the objects of the senses.

When the mind of that yogin is fully absorbed in Brahman and established in meditative concentration (samādhi), as he meditates upon the Supreme Self abiding within his own self, then it is said: [he has attained yoga].
When one established in samādhi attains identification with that [object], he is proclaimed as such. The mind's lack of stability, delusion, dejection, and negligence [are obstacles].
The faults described for yogins are those that give rise to obstacles to yoga;
for the sake of stabilizing the mind, one should contemplate everything in its gross form.
That vow, having become motionless, shall attain stability while situated in the sun;
for nothing exists in the world apart from the Supreme Self.
Having realized that very one who possesses all forms as the single reality, one is liberated;
one should meditate upon the Omkara, the supreme Brahman, the all-pervading Lord seated upon a lotus.
One should recite [the mantra] devoid of field and knower of the field, accompanied by three measures;
first, one should contemplate Pradhāna within the heart, and above that—
Tamas, rajas, and likewise sattva are the three circles in sequence;
they are black, red, and white, and within them is the Puruṣa known as the individual soul (jīva).
Above that is an eight-petaled lotus of qualities and sovereignty;
knowledge is its pericarp, and higher cognition (vijñāna) is remembered as its filaments.
Dispassion is its stalk, and the supreme Vaiṣṇava dharma is its root;
there, in the pericarp, resides the all-pervading Lord, motionless like the individual soul.
One should meditate upon the syllable Om, the means to liberation, joined within the heart;
if one should give up the vital breaths while thus meditating, one goes to Brahman, who is present in one's own proximity.
Having established Hari within the lotus of the body, one who meditates with devotion and sings praises—
some, through the eye of meditation, perceive the Self by means of the self.
Likewise, others [attain it] through Sāṃkhya wisdom, while other yogins do so through Yoga;
it is the knowledge that illuminates Brahman and severs the bonds of worldly existence.
In this regard, the yoga of one-pointedness of mind bestows liberation; of this there is no doubt.
For he who has conquered his senses and faculties and is truly proud of his knowledge [attains it].
That yogi who is established in the Supreme Self is said to be liberated;
the rules regarding postures and locations do not bring about the perfection of yoga.
All elaborations are proclaimed to cause delay;
Śiśupāla attained perfection through the weight of his practice in recollection.
Practicing yoga, they perceive the Self by means of the self;
they cultivate compassion toward all beings and aversion toward sense objects.
When a yogin keeps his ears, belly, and other organs concealed, he is liberated;
for when a man no longer perceives the objects of the senses through the senses themselves, he is freed.
Like a piece of wood, the yogi who is fully absorbed in Brahman becomes liberated at that time;
having reduced all castes and all fortunes to ashes by means of his sins.
And by the fire of meditation, the wise one attains the supreme goal;
for just as fire is seen through friction, so indeed is Hari perceived through meditation.
The oneness of Brahman and the Self is the yoga that is the highest of the high; liberation does not come through external forms, but rather through internal practices such as *yama* and the rest.
Indeed, that which is the direct realization of the Self through Sāṅkhya knowledge, yoga, and the hearing of the Vedānta is called liberation;
it is the perception of the Self in what is not the Self, and the nature of reality in what is unreal.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Knowledge of Brahman," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 236 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] The Blessed Lord said:
I shall proclaim the knowledge of the Self; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth.
They call non-duality Sāṅkhya, and Yoga is one-pointedness of mind therein. (GarP 1.236.1)
Those endowed with the yoga of non-duality are liberated from the strongest bondage;
through awakening, past, present, and future karma are destroyed.
With the axe of right reflection, having cut down the tree of saṃsāra,
one attains the state of Viṣṇu by means of the sacred ford of knowledge and dispassion.
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—this is called the triple city of Māyā;
everything is contained within this very eternal, non-dual state.
That supreme state is entirely devoid of the activity of name-and-form;
having created the infinite world, the Lord himself entered into it.
"I know this Person, whose nature is consciousness, beyond darkness;
'I am He'—this is for liberation, for there is no other path to freedom."
Hearing, reflection, and meditation are the means for attaining true knowledge;
liberation is not obtained through sacrifice, charity, austerity, pilgrimage, or the Vedas.
Through renunciation, or through certain acts such as meditation and worship, the Vedic injunction is twofold: "Perform action" and "Renounce action. (GarP 1.236.8)
Some have indeed stated here that sacrifices and other rites are for the sake of liberation for those who are already liberated and free from desire, in order to purify the internal organ.
Liberation through knowledge in a single lifetime does not belong to those who perceive duality;
such are the Brahmins born into families of yogis who have fallen from yoga or practiced it wrongly.
A living being is bound by action; through knowledge, one becomes liberated from worldly existence.
One should indeed take refuge in self-knowledge, for ignorance is that which is otherwise.
When all desires that reside in one's heart are liberated, then one attains immortality even while living; of this there is no doubt.
Since it is all-pervading, how does it go? Who goes, and where does it go?
Because it is infinite, no location exists; because it is formless, whence can there be movement?
Because it is non-dual, no one exists; because it is pure awareness, how could there be insentience?
Whatever is designated as "other" is merely the state of the movement of thought and speech within the mind.
How can there be coming, going, or abiding for one who is like space?
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are merely imagined through illusion.
O wise one, that which is the luminous reality is the merit that is indivisible;
just as you are dear to yourself, so are we all dear to you.
O Great Sage, just as the mind is on the path to awakening for all, so it is held to be at all times for all beings and for everything.
I do not perceive here any self-consciousness; therefore, it is full and uninterrupted—the waking state, the dream state as it occurs, and likewise the bliss of deep sleep.
If there is no recollection of a forgotten object, for whom would it arise?
Let this be true; likewise, O Bāṇa, the Supreme is bodiless.
If there were no experience of all pleasures and pains, how could the Omniscient One always and everywhere not be present in the heart of everyone? (GarP 1.236.20)
Relying upon that which is the witness, who could know its activity?
That which is distinct from truth, knowledge, and infinity would not be separate from truth and knowledge.
Bliss is not separate from infinity, nor is infinity separate from bliss;
you alone are the supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and the rest.
Having realized that "I am Brahman," the supreme reality, one becomes all-knowing;
just as when a single object made of clay is known, all this world of moving and non-moving things is understood.
Just as everything becomes golden by means of a single golden gem,
so too does the entire world become [golden] through the knowledge of the Lord who possesses such knowledge.
Just as a rope is not clearly seen due to the defect of darkness,
so too the self is not clearly seen due to the defect of delusion.

The reality is conceptualized otherwise through distinctions such as the "serpent" or the "rope," and the Self is likewise conceptualized otherwise as being like space or possessing form and so forth.
Even that substance which is directly perceived is said to be difficult to see,
just as space and so forth are [described] through qualities such as form, which are otherwise imagined.
For just as a snake is [imagined] in a rope, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, or water in a mirage, O Viṣṇu, so too is the world [perceived]. GarP_1,236.28.
Just as a certain twice-born man, crying out "Alas! Alas! I am a Brahmin! upon the destruction of a planet, might again consider himself a Brahmin through meditation; so it is here.
Similarly, the individual soul (jīva), possessed by māyā, thinks "I am the body";
through the destruction of māyā, it again realizes its own true nature, thinking "I am Brahman."

Just as one whose eclipse has been dispelled is no longer gazed upon with hostility by respected people, so too this [world] is a mere illusion; its destruction does not occur without the vision of one's true nature.
Both are equal in being beginningless; their essential natures are distinct from that [beginninglessness].
Through investigation, one is seen to be truly so, while the other is false.
For even though I am unborn, I manifest all at once after passing away through my own *māyā*; by the will of *māyā*, I become twofold as the Lord and the Consort, the blissful world.
The three qualities (traiguṇya) exist separately in twenty-eight distinct divisions;
eighty-four thousand forms of men and women are observed.
Through these, the entire universe arises by means of illusion (māyā), just as [forms] arise from a fragment;
in the beginning and at the end, these—name, form, action, and so forth—do not exist.
The conceptualization of existence at any time does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality,
just as chariots and such things in a dream do not exist in truth.
Likewise, in the waking state, beings do not exist in their actual presence;
through Māyā, they assume a dual form in the two states of waking and dreaming, which are known as the stages of experience.
Thus, this supreme Brahman is said to be the non-dual, immovable state of deep sleep within the two states of dreaming and waking.
Established only through the investigation of illusion, it dissolves by means of that very investigation;
even that conceptualization, though existing in time, is devoid of any ultimate reality.
Thus, for her,
the sun is established as one; from the existence of that which is born of truth,
there follows the non-truth of existence because of its state of being beyond existence.
Even beyond that knowledge is our infinite Self, which is full within like Śuka;
I am not born because of being eternal, and I am immortal because I have done nothing.
Like a lamp, I am the light in the heart; I am Brahman for the sake of liberation.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Self-Knowledge," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
The Lord said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—237. The Blessed One said:
I shall proclaim the essence of the Gītā as it was spoken of old to Arjuna by him whose self was disciplined through the eightfold yoga and who had reached the further shore of all the Vedāntas.

The attainment of the Self is supreme and nothing else; it is devoid of the self, the body, and so forth, yet it is characterized by the internal organ, the eyes, and the rest, which range from inferior forms up to the body.
For in deep sleep, the vital breath (prāṇa) is perceived as devoid of consciousness;
nor is the "I" the self, because it is associated with suffering and the like, as well as with the cycle of saṃsāra.
Like a smokeless fire with blazing flames,
like the radiant sun,
or like the fire of lightning in the sky, [he dwells] within the heart-center, in the self by means of the self.
The ear and the other senses do not perceive their own respective selves by themselves;
it is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is all-knowing and all-seeing, that perceives them.
For when the Self shines forth like a lamp burning within a cloth,
knowledge arises for men through the exhaustion of sinful karma.
Just as one sees one's own self within oneself in that which resembles the surface of a mirror, so too does one see the sense faculties,
the objects of the senses, and the five great elements.
Having thoroughly discerned the mind, the intellect, the ego, the unmanifest, and likewise the Puruṣa,
one who is pervaded by the Supreme becomes liberated from all bonds.
Having withdrawn the entire collection of the senses into the mind,
and having established the mind within the ego-sense, O Pāṇḍava.
Having established the ego-sense in the intellect, the intellect in primordial nature (prakṛti),
primordial nature in the person (puruṣa), and the person in Brahman, one should place [the self] in Brahman.
Having realized that "I am Brahman, the supreme light," one is liberated.
This house has nine doors, three pillars,
and five witnesses.
The wise one who knows that [the body] is presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the best of sages.
All thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña).

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 238] The Blessed Lord said:
Yama and niyama, O Pārtha, as well as āsana, prāṇasaṃyama, pratyāhāra, and likewise dhyāna; dhāraṇā is the seventh, O Arjuna. (GarP 1.238.1)
And what is called "concentration" is said to be the eightfold yoga for the sake of liberation:
[acting] toward all beings at all times through deed, mind, and speech.
The dharma that consists in the cessation of violence is indeed non-violence; non-violence is the supreme happiness.
That which is performed as violence according to the prescribed rule is proclaimed as non-violence.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma.
The theft that consists of the seizing of property, whether by means of stealth or by force— refraining from that is non-stealing (*asteya*), a means for achieving dharma.
The renunciation of sexual intercourse in all places, at all times, and in all circumstances— whether by deed, mind, or speech— is what they declare to be *brahmacarya*.
The non-acceptance of material things even in times of distress, according to one's will, is called "non-possession" (aparigraha); one should avoid it with great effort.
Purity is twofold: external through clay and water, and internal through one's state of being;
contentment is satisfaction with whatever is obtained by chance, which is characterized by happiness.
One-pointed concentration of the mind and the senses is the supreme austerity;
so too is the emaciation of the body through such practices as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.

The wise declare that the recitation of the Vedānta, the Śatarudrīya, the Praṇava, and so forth, constitutes self-study (svādhyāya) for men, which brings about the purification of the inner being (sattva). GarP_1,238.10.
Unwavering devotion to Hari through the actions of speech, mind, and body— such as praise, remembrance, and worship— is this contemplation of the Lord.
The postures known as Svastika, Padma, and likewise Ardha-asana are prescribed.
Prāṇa is the wind born from one's own body; āyāma is its restraint. It is the withdrawal of the wandering senses from objects as if they were non-existent. (GarP 1.238.12)
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 239.
Brahmā said:
I shall proclaim the Brahmagītā, knowing which one is liberated from worldly existence.
Liberation occurs for people through the knowledge arising from the statement "I am Brahman."
From the knowledge of the meanings of the two words "I" and "Brahman," the knowledge of the sentence arises.
The wise consider the meanings of these two words to be twofold: the expressed (vācya) and the indicated (lakṣya).

The variegated (śabala) is proclaimed as that which is expressed by words and denoted by sentences, while the pure (śuddha) is that which consists of the vital breath, the body, and the self; it is incomparable to the mind and the senses. // GarP_1,239.3 //
Likewise, the form that is not the supreme (avāgra) is served by the word "I" through the Vedas; however, the immediate (pratyak) form, which is non-dual, is realized by the word "I."
The supreme, imperishable bliss-consciousness, accompanied by the transcendental (parokṣa),
which consists of the vital breath and the physical body— that is the second division.
For here, the aspect that perceives what is beyond the senses would be characterized as the "I-maker" (ahaṃkāra);
likewise, by the word *brahman* alone, [the cause] consisting of the vital breath and the physical body [is indicated].
By abandoning both "finality" and "imperceptibility," it will be described as non-dual bliss-consciousness by means of the term *pratyag-brahman*.
And for one who remains having characterized non-dual bliss-consciousness as "I am Brahman" and "Brahman is I," regarding the two referents of the word Brahman; ||| GarP_1,239.8 |||
Furthermore, from the statement "I am Brahman," which aims at the fruit of one's own direct experience,
the knowledge of oneness certainly arises far more swiftly than from the Vedānta.
Liberation arises from unity through the cessation of the effects of ignorance by means of knowledge.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Essence of the Brahmagītā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. The Blessed Lord said:
From that, the existent Brahmā arose; from him, space; from space, the wind; and from that, fire.
From fire comes water, and from that, the earth, which gives birth to the form of the phenomenal world;
from that arises the seventeenth principle, the subtle body (liṅga), as well as the five organs of action.
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ; then the organs of cognition:
the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and the nose; and there are five vital airs.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna;
the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) consists of the mind (manas) and the intellect (dhī); the mind is characterized by doubt.
But the intellect (buddhi), which is of the nature of determination, has this subtle form;
it is the thread of Hiraṇyagarbha himself, characterized by its own effects as its mark.
The elements were indeed quintuplicated from their non-quintuplicated state;
from those quintuplicated elements, the cosmic egg was born.
The body known as the gross (sthūla), which is well-known in the world and possesses feet and other limbs,
consists of the fivefold elements (pañcīkṛta-bhūta) and their effects, and is situated therein.
All that is produced from the body of living beings is said by the wise to be gross; however, the body situated within the Supreme Self is declared to be threefold.
Furthermore, you are the individual soul (jīva) who enters the two bodies;
according to the scriptural statement of its own differentiation, Brahman alone has entered into the two bodies.
Like water and the sun, or like a jujube fruit, the individual soul (jīva) sustains the vital breaths and other functions;
it is remembered as that jīva which is the witness of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
He is distinct from those states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
he is devoid of qualities, without parts, unattached, and of an eternally pure nature.
The Supreme Self alone is that which is conceived as threefold through the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth;
it is situated within the aggregate of the internal organs and is itself the internal organ.
For one who perceives waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there is always a transformation;
I shall now describe waking and the other states in terms of their fruits, actions, and agents.
Furthermore, consciousness through the sense faculties is declared to be the waking state;
