it is the cognition arising from the impressions of the waking state for one who seeks objects.
Dream and deep sleep are the states of the intellect when the collection of instruments [is withdrawn];
its abiding in the causal state of Brahman is by way of the nature of time.
The living being perceives the states of waking and so forth, both sequentially and non-sequentially;
however, at the time of commencing meditative absorption (samādhi), one should first establish [the mind] in its proper state.
Then, when the desire for liberation has arisen and the internal organ has become solitary,
one should dissolve the collection of fields and leave only that field remaining.
Just as a pot is not distinct from the clay because it is its effect, so too there is no vessel or the like that is separate from the fivefold elements.
The learned declare that the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) is distinct from the fivefold-composed elements (pañcīkṛta-bhūta) and the non-fivefold-composed elements (apañcīkṛta-bhūta).
The subtle body (liṅga) is not distinct from the unquintuplicated elements;
it does not exist without the support of earth, nor does that [earth] exist without it.
Fire does not exist without wind, and wind indeed does not exist without space;
space does not exist without Brahman, and pure Brahman does not exist without space.
Then, being of pure nature, there is the non-occurrence of waking, dreaming, and so forth;
it is devoid of the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), having attained conformity with its own self-consciousness.
Eternal, pure, awakened, liberated, true, and non-dual Brahman—these are the meanings of the two words *tat* and *tvam*; and the suffix *-tā* expresses that which is Brahman.
The letter *u*, the letter *a*, and the letter *m*—this is the pair of Ṛks.
"I am Brahman; I am Brahman, the knowledge that increases ignorance. (GarP 1.239.24)
This Self is the supreme light, whose nature is consciousness and bliss;
it is indeed Truth, Knowledge, and Infinity, as proclaimed by the Śruti in the words "Thou art That. (GarP 1.239.25)
"I am Brahman, untainted; I am Brahman, all-pervading. That Person who is in the sun, that am I, the beginningless one.
This essence of the Gītā was spoken to Arjuna, by means of which there is indeed dissolution into Brahman.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Essence of the Brahmagītā," in the Ācārakāṇḍa of the first part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 240— Hari said:
O Rudra, this essence of the Gāruḍa Purāṇa has been proclaimed by me to you, while Brahmā and the others were listening; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Rudra, he who reads or hears this, which brings about knowledge, fame, splendor, fortune, victory, health, and so forth, shall become all-knowing and go to heaven.
Brahmā said:
"O Vyāsa, thus have I heard this Purāṇa of Viṣṇu, which bestows liberation.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this meritorious *Garuḍa* [Purāṇa], Brahmā spoke thus to us.
Having attained Hari through meditation on Brahmā, who was the foremost among Dakṣa, Nārada, and others,
I, Sūta, have likewise narrated this supreme Purāṇa to you.
Having heard which, one who has attained all desires shall obtain the fruit of Brahman;
therefore, Viṣṇu spoke this most essential Gāruḍa [treatise] to Garuḍa.
"It bestows the great essence, the wealth of the desire for Dharma, and liberation and so forth.
Sūta said:
"O Śaunaka, the preeminent Gāruḍa Purāṇa has been proclaimed to you."
That which Vyāsa formerly spoke to me as the essence proclaimed by Garuḍa—
having heard that auspicious Gāruḍa Purāṇa from Brahmā,
Hari, while meditating on the Lord, divided the single Veda into four parts.
Śuka indeed told me those eighteen Purāṇas;
however, this most excellent Gāruḍa Purāṇa has been narrated by me to you, O Śaunaka.
In the midst of the sages who were listening, he asked about the expounder of all things;
whoever should read it, or even listen to it, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind—
Whether one writes it oneself, causes it to be written, or indeed preserves it in a book, one will surely attain the purpose of the Dharma;
and one who seeks the purpose of the Dharma shall attain that purpose.
One who desires objects of pleasure shall obtain those pleasures; one whose aim is liberation shall attain liberation.
Whatever one desires, all that shall be obtained by listening to the *Garuḍa*.
A Brāhmaṇa shall become one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas; of this there is no doubt.
And a Kṣatriya here on earth becomes a protector of the Kṣatriyas as well.
Indeed, no one else shall hear this Purāṇa which is equal to the Vedas;
if that foolish-souled man should speak it, he would incur the loss of his fame.
Furthermore, if a learned Brāhmaṇa who has been consecrated should speak it to anyone else,
this Gāruḍa [Tantra] must be heard by all those who have been consecrated by Brāhmaṇas.
Just as Viṣṇu is, so is Tārkṣya; by means of the hymn to Tārkṣya, Hari is praised.
Having heard the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa] and Vasurāja, he indeed obtained everything.
Varuṇa said:
I pay homage to the mighty-armed Lord who has Garuda as his vehicle,
who dwells above Viṣṇu, and who has terrified the great asuras.
Salutations to you, O destroyer of the pride of the Nāgas, who increases the joy of Vinatā; O you who show partiality toward the virtuous, O blameless one, who are gazed upon by the wretched Daityas.
By their mutual curse, Supratīka and Vibhāvasu became an elephant and a tortoise, the two brothers remaining joined together.
When it is raised up, it is one *yojana* in height; it is twice that length in extent;
the tortoise is three *yojanas* in thickness and has a circumference of one hundred *yojanas*.
O bird, those two low-born ones with four arms must not be eaten by you;
they have been liberated from the fault of the mutual curse.
"O King, why do you speak thus out of a taste for the land of the Niṣādas?
Therefore, the Lord of the Niṣādas has been released by you, and even there, a Brahmin has been [spared] by you."
There, you split the branch of the banyan tree that had grown to a height of tens of millions of yojanas, where the Vālakhilyas were stationed.
Having made an effort, you placed an elephant and a tortoise upon your nails,
and they were completely surrounded on all sides by waterless, supportless space.
All the gods, led by Śakra, were conquered by you in battle;
long ago, O son of Kaśyapa, you brought back that Soma after extinguishing the fire.
Having rendered the two Nāgas sightless with dust by means of their gaze-poison,
did he not strike them with his sharp-pointed [weapon], while they were paralyzed and their minds destroyed?
"Even though you brought the Soma, it was not taken by you out of devotion;
therefore, you have indeed become the mount for Viṣṇu, occupying the place of his banner."
Having cast Soma onto the darbha grass by you, the Nāgas were deceived;
and you swiftly seized the vessel of nectar, O slayer of Brahmā!
O best of the twice-born, it was there that Vinatā, whose tongue had been split in two by the serpents,
was released from slavery after Kadrū had previously defeated her in battle.
"Uccaiḥśravas—what is his color? "He is white," he said; but he replied, "I consider him to be black, as I have seen him before. (GarP 1.240.29)
Did you yourself previously cast off your wing by means of a vajra-strike?
It was for the sake of Dadhīca’s vajra and Śakra, and not otherwise.
When the Lord of the Gods saw that which had been brought for his side,
then your name "Suparṇa" became established throughout the three worlds.
By mere meditation, both stationary and mobile poisons are destroyed;
and whoever recites or hears this shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Sūta said:
Having heard the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa], Vasurāja indeed attained everything;
the blessed Garuḍa, meditating upon Viṣṇu, attained everything.
It is said that the man who recites this meritorious Gāruḍa Purāṇa shall attain all his desires and then reach the supreme goal.
By reciting even a single quarter-verse, there shall be the destruction of all evil;
for whomever this exists in their home, everything shall be theirs here in this world.
The wisdom that resides in the hand of one who holds the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa] is within his grasp;
whoever reads or hears this shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Through hearing [this] and so forth, one shall attain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
one seeking sons obtains sons, and one seeking desires attains desire.
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking victory obtains victory;
even a sinner through such acts as the killing of a Brahmin shall attain purification from that sin.
Even a barren woman obtains a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband;
one seeking security attains security, and one seeking enjoyment shall obtain enjoyment.
One who seeks auspiciousness shall obtain auspiciousness; one who seeks virtues shall attain virtues;
one who seeks the meaning of poetry shall attain poetic skill; and one who seeks the essence shall attain the essence.
One who seeks knowledge attains that wisdom which crushes all saṃsāra;
this is the auspicious and blessed Gāruḍa [tantra], proclaimed by Garuḍa.
There shall be no untimely death for him who recites even a single verse;
by reciting even half a verse of this, the destruction of wicked enemies is certain.
Having heard this from Sūta at the sacrifice of Śaunaka, Tuṇḍin, meditating upon "I am Brahman" along with the sages, was liberated by the one whose banner is Garuḍa. Om.
Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Garuḍa Purāṇa," in the Ācāra-kāṇḍa of the first part of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the first part, the section on conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*), in the glorious *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.
